In those earlier years, buildings changed one by one or a couple at a time, not in one fell swoop. “If they all go vacant at once, how long would it take for a new use to come about for all of them?” questioned Paul Steinke, president of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 A few of the buildings are afforded some protection through historic designation. Dorrance Hamilton Hall was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1956, the National Register of Historic Places in 1971, and has been included in the National Park Service's Historic American Buildings Survey.
 Furness Hall at 15th and Pine Streets was built in 1875 and designed by Frank Furness. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Three others were added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places: Furness Hall in 1956, the Philadelphia Art Alliance in 1970, and Gershman Hall in 2017. The two off-Broad residence halls, Juniper Halll and Spruce Hall, have been included in the proposed Washington Square West Historic District . Although not yet reviewed by the Philadelphia Historical Commission, its rules and regulations stipulate that, once nominated, properties are deemed to be under the agency's legal protection from demolition.
 The University of the Arts is a private entity, but the magnitude of this event will have a widespread effect far beyond that individual institution, and will likely require involvement by many sectors to find a solution. “If they’re all vacant, we’re going to need people to imagine and plan new uses for them,” said Steinke. “If conversions are considered, the Alliance could be an advisor regarding the properties, such as ideas for funding sources for historic properties.” Rallying cries have been raised at the state and municipal levels, as well as by other Philadelphia institutions like Temple University, which is currently involved in talks about a possible Temple and Uarts merger.
 Tags: Frank Furness John Haviland South Broad Street University of the Arts 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Along Kingsessing Waterfront, Visions for a Brighter Future Come Into Focus
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
On a long enough timeline–years, decades, centuries–nothing in a city’s landscape remains the same. Buildings rise and fall, as do neighborhoods. From prosperous, to diminished, and then back again. The hope in Kingsessing is that renewal is in the cards and soon.
 Any Philadelphian can rattle off a list of troubled neighborhoods in the city. Statistically speaking, this southwest neighborhood qualifies. Poverty rates in many Census tracts there run higher than the already-troubling citywide average of 23 percent, some exceeding 40 and 50 percent. Vacancy rates are as high as one-in-five homes. Parts of the neighborhood are no stranger to gun violence. 
 Compounding the problem is Kingsessing’s disconnectedness from Center City. That is both literal–a lack of convenient walking, biking, and transit options double or triple commute times to Center City compared to West and North Philadelphia communities the same distance away–and figuratively, as residents of the area routinely decry a lack of political attention from within the confines of City Hall.
 But is this whole mode of operation set to change? In May, the Environmental Protection Agency held a news conference along the banks of the Schuylkill River to announce $2 million in funding to cleanup an old contaminated oil transfer site in Kingsessing, which would clear the way for a proposed extension of the Schuylkill River Trail, construction of an adjacent rest station, and completion of a planned biotech campus nearby.
 WRT rendering showing green space and housing at Bartram Village. | Image: Philadelphia Housing Authority, 2020 Bartram Choice Neighborhood Plan
 Peer a little closer at the picture and more promising developments pop out: the now-underway $250 million renovation of the nearby Bartram Village public housing development, a proposed effort by SEPTA to upgrade the area’s trolley service, and a bevy of new recreational programs at the nearby Bartram’s Garden. And of course, the granddaddy of them all: a $4 billion overhaul of the former Philadelphia Energy Solutions refinery just across the river from the neighborhood by developer Hilco Redevelopment Partners.
 Squint, and it sure looks like the kind of transformations envisioned in a Lower Schuylkill Master Plan , developed by the City along with public and private partners a decade ago: more jobs in modern industries, better transit, greener environs. In short, a major elevation of the quality of life for many residents of Kingsessing.
 In fact, for Councilmember Jame Gauthier, who was raised in Kingsessing and represents the 3rd District, a significant transformation of the area at this point looks like a given. “The culmination of all of the public and private development is absolutely transformative. There’s no doubt about that,” Gauthier said. “It will ensure that the Southwest will go from this area that really has been ignored over time to a major economic center, a major area for recreation, a major area for transit, and a nicer place to live.” The challenge is in implementation, she added, and perhaps most pressingly, is determining who will benefit. “The question now is, how can we complete all these major projects, and who are we centering?” said Gauthier.
 One of Philadelphia’s Oldest Communities 
 “Firsts” can be relative, but no matter how you slice it, Kingsessing has some pretty good historical claims.
 Prior to the arrival of Europeans, the earliest known date of Indigenous inhabitation of the greater region can be traced to 8500 B.C., near Harrisburg. At some point in the millenia after, humankind reached what is now the Philadelphia area. Evidence has shown that the area of Bartram’s Garden was used as a hunting ground or gathering place sometime between 3000 B.C. and 1500 A.D.
 By the time of European arrival, the area was part of Lenapehoking, the territory of the Lenape. It was they who named the area of what is now Southwest Philadelphia Kingsessing, or more accurately Chincessing , which translated to "bog meadow" or "place of the big shells." 
 An illustration showing colonists of New Sweden encountering the Lenape, first with violence and later with a trade agreement. Swedes gave one of their settlements the Lenape name Chinssessing, which is now known as the Kingsessing section of Southwest Philadelphia. | Image courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 Then came the Swedes, who served as the first European settlers of the area in the 17th century. They indeed made the first permanent colonial settlement in what is now Pennsylvania, when in 1643, Swedish Lieutenant-Colonel Johan Printz constructed a fort and buildings on Tinicum Island, which is now part of Delaware County. Two years later, in 1645, a settlement was established in Philadelphia proper, in Kingsessing, where the Swedes also built the area’s first grist mill on Cobbs Creek.
 According to a history of the neighborhood posted on Bartram's Garden's website, “Many of the colony’s freedmen lived in Kingsessing, which today has maintained its name and a similar location along the southwest bank of the Schuylkill River." William Penn wouldn’t make his landing in that other part of modern day Philadelphia until 1682.
 Of course, much of Kingsessing wouldn’t see heavy urbanization until much later. According to a history compiled by Center City-based design firm WRT , the Kingsessing area remained largely rural during the British colonial era through to the late 1800s. In 1728, John Bartram purchased a tract along the river’s west banks and established the nation’s first botanical gardens, drawing visitors such as Benjamin Franklin, George Washington, and Thomas Jefferson. Much of the surrounding area became devoted to similar country estates or farmland, including Andrew Hamilton’s Woodlands estate.
 Rowhouses built in the late 19th and early 20th centuries surround an 18th century survivor in Kingsessing, a 1764 farmhouse on Vogdes Street just off of Woodland Avenue. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 In the late 19th century, the area finally began to industrialize along with many U.S. cities, particularly along waterways. Estates in Kingsessing were subdivided for industrial and residential uses, especially as the electric streetcar arrived in 1894 and improved commute times to other areas of the city.
 “[The area] soon became home to heavy industry including oil refining, manufacturing, distribution, and waste management,” the WRT report states. “As the riverfront slowly changed from green to industrial, waves of Irish, German, Lithuanian, Polish, Italian, and Jewish immigrants settled nearby, forming a thriving working-class neighborhood.”
 Of course, that would all give way to a downturn that plagued cities across the country: a post-World War II hollowing out of urban industries, white flight, and all around disinvestment. Perhaps nowhere was more symbolic of the change than at Bartram Village, a collection of residences purpose-built to house workers in the defense industry as World War II raged, which were then sold to the Philadelphia Housing Authority in 1958 for use as public housing in a Census tract where the poverty rate is now 52 percent.
 Fresh Prince, Fresh Hope 
 On July 23, 2006, the front page of the Philadelphia Inquirer offered that “for a brief moment” the day before, “the violence that grips residents in the Kingsessing section of Southwest Philadelphia became a backdrop." On that day, native son Will Smith had returned to lead a march against violence down Chester Avenue, drawing a crowd of several hundred people, many of whom wore white for peace. "Will the parade help?" one 72-year-old resident, Josephine Blow, mused to a reporter. "I don't really know."
 Indeed, in 2002, then-mayor John Street had certified a 40-acre area of Kingsessing blighted in order to open the door for redevelopment, an action which appeared to have little impact in the years after. Then, in 2019, a massive explosion and fire at the 1,300-acre Philadelphia Energy Solutions oil refinery across the Schuylkill shuttered the facility, which first became operational in the mid-1800s. It looked like things couldn’t get much worse for this stretch of Schuylkill River.
 Yet, like a forest that requires a wildfire in order to start anew, the winds of change are now blowing. Following the closure of PES, Hilco stepped in to propose a massive redevelopment of the land, which it is now calling the Bellwether District. According to Amelia Chassé Alcivar, executive vice president of corporate affairs for Hilco, the vision is to attract modern industries, providing an estimated 19,000 permanent jobs in the area, ten-fold what PES had provided prior to its closure. “Divided into a 750-acre logistics campus and 250-acre innovation campus, the project is poised to strengthen Philadelphia's position as a life science and innovation hub, while also bringing supply chain logistics, manufacturing, cold storage, port, and rail uses,” Chassé Alcivar said.
 Philadelphia Energy Solutions oil refinery in March 2021 and after Girard Point was cleared in July 2022. | Photos: Hilco Redevelopment Partners
 After clearing the land of the former refinery’s massive footprint, Chassé Alcivar said Hilco began vertical construction of the logistics campus this spring, with construction completed on the first buildings expected by the end of the year.
 Across the river in Kingsessing proper, promises of newer, better jobs are also being made. The Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation (PIDC) is developing a Lower Schuylkill Biotech Campus , which it envisions as an “opportunity for development partners to cultivate a world-class urban campus for modern cell and gene therapy bioproduction,” in line with Philadelphia’s booming life sciences sector. Renderings show sleek modern office buildings on a pair of 20-acre campuses immediately north and south of Bartram’s Garden.
 Kevin Lessard, senior vice president for communications and government affairs for PIDC, did not offer an anticipated timeline for development. However, in an email he confirmed PIDC has acquired the necessary parcels and is working “diligently” to prepare the now-vacant land for development, including remediation of environmental issues in the soil and groundwater and “enhancing existing infrastructure” in the area. “This project provides long-overdue investments in a predominantly African-American community that has not received adequate investment or resources and where heavy industrial uses in the area have contributed to substantial environmental justice issues,” Lessard said.
 Trails and Trolleys 
 Better places to work are always great, but what about play? One of the most exciting developments for riverfront recreationists in the city is the planned opening of a new swing bridge across the Schuylkill River, connecting Gray’s Ferry and the Bartram area, just south of the Grays Ferry Avenue Bridge. Although the project was delayed as the new bridge truss was being fabricated, the Schuylkill River Development Corporation states it is now slated to open in mid-2025.
 Patrick Monahan, regional organizer with the Bicycle Coalition of Greater Philadelphia, said the bridge will provide a crucial link in extending the Schuylkill River Trail to a final stretch in Southwest Philadelphia before ultimately terminating at Fort Mifflin. However, the bridge should also prove a useful link for more mundane uses, connecting residents of Kingsessing not only with all of the recreational opportunities along the Schuylkill Banks, but enabling biking as a feasible option to commute to Center City. “I live in West Philly and to reach [the SRT in Center City], I would have to go down 47th Street and hit Grays Ferry Bridge. That does have a separated bike lane, but once you get spit out onto Grays Ferry heading east, it’s quite a nightmare,” said Monahan. “To have this off-road connection would be really critical for residents in West Philadelphia area. Once it opens I know it’ll be highly utilized.”
 The Ecosystems education center and mussel hatchery planned for Bartram's Garden. | Rendering: Bartram's Garden
 Bartram’s Garden has plans to further leverage the new connection, with a planned welcome center along the trail just south of the new bridge. Plans are early and full funding not yet secured, but executive director Maitreyi Roy envisions a place for riders to both relax and learn more about what the community has to offer. “We felt that once people crossed over to the west side toward the garden, it made sense for us to welcome people. As a trail user for the first time, you might not know where you are,” Roy explained. “It’ll be a place for a rest stop, to fill up your bottle with water, maybe get a cup of coffee, but also get maps and some orientation to the west side of the trail, the garden, and further down on the trail.”
 Elsewhere in the park, Bartram’s Garden continues its push to get more Philadelphians from surrounding neighborhoods fishing, kayaking, and gardening along the river. To further support that mission are other major capital projects, including a new education center and mussel hatchery and a FloatLab classroom that enables visitors to step out onto the water at eye level and learn about the area’s ecosystem and history. Nearby, the Southwest Philly Concrete Cowboys are also planning the development of a new stable. 
 Plans for FloatLab on the Schuylkill River include history and science education. | Rendering: Bartram's Garden
 For those not down with getting around via bike or horseback, SEPTA is also planning a major renovation of Kingsessing’s trolley lines with the Route 36 line, which runs from Island Avenue in Southwest Philadelphia up Lindbergh Avenue and into Center City, getting particular love. SEPTA communication officials did not respond to requests for comment on proposed enhancements, but the PIDC’s Lessard filled in some of the details. “PIDC played a critical role in helping SEPTA secure $25 million in federal RAISE grant funding for Route 36 trolley modernization and Complete Streets investments that will improve safety and the travel experience for all road users, including transit riders, pedestrians, and cyclists,” Lessard said. “Placemaking elements like murals, artistic lighting, seating, and other streetscape improvements will also be part of the project. Route 36 will be the first in SEPTA’s system to have new, ADA-compliant trolleys and trolley stops.”
 The Big Picture 
 Together, all of the planned improvements along Kingsessing’s waterfront look a lot like the fruition of the Lower Schuylkill Master Plan, which was finalized in 2013. The ongoing $250 million redevelopment of Bartram Village will provide better housing and retail options for some of the area’s most vulnerable residents, while also working to offer job training. Then, quality jobs in modern industries will open up in the new life sciences and logistics hubs at the Biotech Campus and across the river in the Bellwether District.
 A vision of the Bellwether District upon completion. | Rendering: Hilco Redevelopment Partners
 Connecting it all will be better public transit via the trolley and a new bike-to-work opportunity via the swing bridge. That corridor will double as a recreational wonderland, enabling residents of Southwest Philadelphia with seamless access to Center City’s Schuylkill River waterfront, and residents of Center City to new recreational opportunities at Bartram’s Garden and beyond.
 On paper, it’s an exciting transformation that appears poised to provide the most significant uplift in Kingsessing in generations, but, as always, the devil is in the details. Both Hilco and the PIDC say jobs generated in the areas will be occupied by current community residents, enabling them to stay and enjoy the newly established amenities of their neighborhood.
 A new biotech campus near Bartram's Garden has been proposed. The long-awaited completion of the pedestrian swing bridge will connect the east and west banks of the Schuylkill River Trail. | Rendering: Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation
 Gauthier said she’ll be watching. “My office has been pretty focused on making sure public sector agencies–SEPTA, PIDC, Streets, the Housing Authority–making sure all of these stakeholders are working together and working with the community, centering the community, asking them what they need,” Gauthier explained. “We know the risks. It’s what we’ve seen in other places, that neighborhoods become places that are not for the people living there and stewarding those neighborhoods through good times and bad times. People get displaced when [we make] investments only with an eye to who is coming, rather than who is here.”
 Tags: Bartram's Garden Kingsessing Oil Refineries redevelopment 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: Marine Barracks
author: Alan Jaffe and Natalie Hope McDonald
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Marine Barracks 
 Location: 4801 South Broad Street
 Architect: Henry Ives Cobb
 Built: 1901
 The Philadelphia Navy Yard’s older, distinguished cluster of buildings was designated as a National Register Historic District in 1999. The district includes Building 1, a storehouse/office erected in 1875 in the Italianate style, the Beaux Arts Commandant’s Office, and the Victorian officers’ homes on the riverfront designed by civil engineer/North Pole explorer Robert Peary.
 None have been listed on the Philadelphia Register yet. A good place to start would be the virile Marine Barracks, designed in 1901 by Chicago-based architect Henry Ives Cobb, whose commissions included the Newberry Library and the University of Chicago’s main quad. The Marine Barracks shows Cobb’s flair for the Romanesque style, with its arched stone arcade along the first floor, terra cotta capitals, and carved stone eagles perched atop globes in honor of those who first used the quarters.
 Like much of the reimagined Navy Yard, the building has been repurposed by technology, innovation, and investment firms, and on weekends, community groups use the former military parade grounds out front as a setting for festivals and fundraisers. The City should also appreciate and designate the resources of the historic enclave at the Navy Yard.
 Tags: Philadelphia Navy Yard Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Unlisted Philadelphia

title: Cristo Rey Sees the Light in Solar Technology
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
Cristo Rey Philadelphia High School at 1717 W. Allegheny Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Cristo Rey, a interfaith-based Catholic high school in Nicetown-Tioga, is an environmental role model for all schools in Philadelphia, but it had humble beginnings.
 "We started in an old, empty elementary school, Our Lady of Hope, near Broad and Olney," said Tom Shoemaker, president & CEO of Cristo Rey Philadelphia High School. "When we moved to 1717 Allegheny Avenue in 2019 it had been a 150 year-old tricycle factory on a seven-acre industrial wasteland. We knocked down everything except the five-story warehouse and added a 50,000-square-foot contemporary building. You can still see the tricycle factory, the exposed beams, and big factory windows." In fact, you can see one of the factory's vintage trikes in the school's foyer.
 August Mecky, a German immigrant, bought the property at 1705 W. Allegheny Avenue in 1897 and started a tricycle company. The factory was built in 1910 by his son-in-law, Richard G. Ledig, who was an inventor. A. Mecky Company expanded its original line of tricycles with baby buggies, pedal cars, scooters, automobiles, and toasters. Its biggest sensation was the 1938 Velo-King Velocipede Tricycles which are now coveted by collectors.
 A. Mecky Company letterhead from 1912. | Image: Worthpoint.com
 However, it is the school's roof that makes Cristo Rey truly exceptional. In January, Solar States completed a large-scale installation of solar panels. "We worked personally with Micha Gold-Markel, the founder of Solar States," said Shoemaker. "We also have three green roofs that produce oxygen, which lowers the temperature generated by all the asphalt in this part of the city."
 "Now that we have solar panels, we want to build it into our science curriculum," explained Shoemaker. "We can take students to the roof and track in real time how much solar energy we are creating."
 "Cristo Rey will receive at least 30 percent of the cost of the installation back from the federal government as a result of the Inflation Reduction Act," said Gold-Markel. "We anticipate a minimum of $20,000 of savings per year as a result of installing this solar array and it could reach as high as $35,000 per year depending on the final incentives for which they qualify."
 An aerial view of Cristo Rey High School's 457 solar panel array. | Photo courtesy of Cristo Rey High School
 "We used all of the good solar space, so the roof was maximized. It is a 219 kilowatt solar array with 457 solar panels, which is anticipated to absorb 25 percent of their overall energy usage," Gold-Markel explained.
 Other schools in Philadelphia with solar panels include Albert M. Greenfield Elementary School, Phillip Randolph High School, and Frankford High School. "Most of these have small solar arrays nowhere near the size of Cristo Rey," said Gold-Markel.
 In addition to a small financial contribution by their parents, all Cristo Rey students earn their tuition by participating in a work-study program one day a week at leading law firms, corporations, medical centers, and businesses. This financial model has enabled the school to partner with CHOP, Wawa, Comcast, Jefferson University, Campell Soup Company, Blue Cross Blue Shield, and others. By the time they graduate, students not only have gained confidence, but often have a strong sense of direction regarding their future. This includes students who worked for Solar States. "Students contributed to our sales, ops, and marketing teams," said Gold-Markel. "They showed up with energy and excitement. It was a great experience."
 The former A. Mecky Company warehouse as renovations began. | Photo courtesy of Cristo Rey High School
 Architect Jennifer Crawford of Blackney Hayes was the lead designer of repurposing the abandoned factory into a modern school. "John McConnell, the founder of the school, was very insistent on saving the building, and it turned out to be the correct decision. We won a historic preservation award," Crawford said.
 "I was trying to create a sense of presence that would feel cohesive with the existing building. When we took out the existing beams and wood flooring in the factory we reused them in creating the reception desk, the sanctuary floor, and the surround entryway in classrooms," explained Crawford. "I wanted to tie the new with old. We located an old window in disrepair on the ground floor of the factory and all the new windows use the same profile." The new school also includes a gymnasium/health center, a new turf soccer field, parking, and outdoor instructional and gathering spaces.
 Prior to construction, Crawford attended meetings open to the surrounding community where residents expressed their concerns about the long-derelict industrial site. "Listening to them, my goal was to create a space of pride and safety," she said. Crawford is especially proud of the floor-to-ceiling picture window in the sanctuary above the main entrance. "Students can look out the window and see their own neighborhood below, then look above and see the skyline of Philadelphia where their future lies," she said.
 Top: The school's foyer showcases a tricycle manufactured by the former factory. Bottom: Elements of the original warehouse can be seen in Cristo Rey's classrooms. | Photos courtesy of Cristo Rey High School
 A Cristo Rey student who worked at Blackney Hayes one day a week for three years while in high school recently went on to major in architecture at Jefferson University. "He is now a paid summer intern at our firm," said Crawford, adding, "Architecture in not well represented by the African American community, and the student is seeing an example for others."
 This success story is not unique for Cristo Rey. "We are one of 40 Jesuit schools across the country bound by a mission to provide a college prep education to exclusively low income children. Our students come from families all over the city with an average yearly income of $40,000," said Pugh. "100 percent of our 2024 graduates are going on to college, including Harvard, Notre Dame, Fordham and Georgetown."
 This is the kind of springboard that is taken for granted in suburban high schools with students from affluent families who can afford tutors and SAT prep, but it breaks the mold for urban students from low income families. Students who graduate from Cristo Rey schools go on to earn bachelor's degrees within six years at rates that are twice as high than their demographic peers. "We offer a challenging curriculum," Shoemaker said. "More importantly, we expect our students to succeed. For many of them, that is a new experience."
 Tags: adaptive resuse Catholic Schools industrial history North Philadelphia Solar Energy 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: History is Alive at Ivy Hill Cemetery
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
Ivy Hill Cemetery is known as the final resting place of professional athletes, Grammy-nominated soul singers, and a Kennedy Center honoree. It also holds the remains of Philadelphia natives whose stories inform current events, including the controversy over Confederate memorial statues, corporate malfeasance, recognition of Negro League players, urban sprawl, and the role of art in documenting and preserving history.
 Notable occupants include boxers Joe Frazier and Matthew Saad Muhammad, Major League third baseman Bill Gray and pitcher Ed Lafitte, Negro League pitcher Bill Byrd and infielder Mahlon Duckett, Philadelphia-born soul singers Harold Melvin, Fayette Pinkney, and Joni Sledge, Kennedy Center Honoree Marion Williams, and James R. Ludlow Wray, the Philadelphia Eagles’ first head coach and co-owner.
 Under the leadership of Ivy Hill’s secretary-treasurer David Drysdale, Jr., notoriety doesn’t necessarily merit special treatment. “My father always said, ‘Everybody buried here is a dignitary to their own family,’” Drysdale explained. “Everybody gets treated the same.”
 The gatehouse of Ivy Hill Cemetery. | Photo: David Bell
 Drysdale has been working at Ivy Hill Cemetery and Crematory since 1973, starting part-time as a teenager, then full-time after college. He followed his father, David Drysdale, Sr., the previous secretary-treasurer, with 42 years of service, and maternal grandfather, Watson Moody, who attended to Ivy Hill families for 56 years. His son David Drysdale III is a groundskeeper, and his 16-year old grandson, Brayden, joins the team this summer as a weed cutter.
 Opened as the Germantown and Chestnut Hill Cemetery in 1867, the 87-acre facility located on Easton Road in Cedarbrook was renamed Ivy Hill Cemetery in 1871. The non-sectarian cemetery and crematory was chartered as a nonprofit organization. It provides in-ground, crypt, and niche burial, cremation, and a chapel for funerals and memorial services.
 Lesser-known occupants of Ivy Hill include the union-busting railroad executive who died in a hotel room under mysterious circumstances, the Civil War veteran who was captured at Gettysburg, a family of artists that lived in a stone mansion built on the site of a Revolutionary War battleground, and the last living member of the Philadelphia Stars baseball team. However their lives ended, their stories have relevance today.
 The Civil War Veteran 
 At the outbreak of the Civil War, Germantown native Melville Freas (1841-1920) enlisted in the Union Army, Company A, 150th Pennsylvania Volunteers, known as the Bucktails. Taken prisoner at the battle of Battle of Gettysburg on July 1, 1863, along with four friends from Germantown, he was held at the Confederate prisoner of war camp at Belle Isle near Richmond, Virginia.
 The statue and headstone of Melville Freas. | Photo: David Bell
 Freas was paroled on March 23, 1864—the only one of the five neighborhood friends to survive Belle Isle—and eventually returned to Germantown to work as a letter carrier and auctioneer. In 1909, Freas publicly opposed plans to erect a monument to Henry Wirz, who had been convicted and hanged in 1865 for crimes he committed as the commandant of the Confederacy’s infamous Andersonville Prison.
 As the number of statues dedicated to Confederate Army figures around the country peaked, in 1914 Freas commissioned John M. Gessler & Sons of West Philadelphia to make a granite statue of himself in uniform for placement on his lot at Ivy Hill. His headstone honors the four comrades who were among the almost 1,000 Union prisoners who died at Belle Isle: Louis Vogle, Philip Hammer, Charles Grant, and George Shingle.
 The Union Buster 
 By the afternoon of December 14, 1889, James Wormley, the owner and manager of the Wormley Hotel on H Street NW in Washington, D.C., was worried enough about one of his guests to call the police. The man in room 57 hadn’t been seen since the night before and wasn’t answering his locked door. Accompanied by a police officer and hotel staff, Wormley used a stepladder to reach the transom and peer into the room.
 He saw the body of the man who was checked-in to room 57 lying on his back, arms at his side, and a pistol on the floor near his right hand, apparently the result of a self-inflicted gunshot wound to the head. The coroner didn’t examine the body at the scene, but, relying on statements by Wormley and a Pinkerton detective, ruled the death a suicide. The deputy coroner, a senior Washington Police Department official, and a doctor who resided in the hotel publicly disagreed. They suspected murder.
 Franklin Benjamin Gowen was born in the Mt. Airy section of Philadelphia on February 9, 1836 to a Pennsylvania German mother and an Irish Protestant father. By the age of 30 he was doing legal work for the Philadelphia and Reading Rail Road (P&R). “In January 1870 [he] was elected president of that company at a crucial moment in the history of the coal region,” wrote historian Jake Wynn on his website.
 An undated portrait of Franklin B. Gowen. | Image courtesy of Winninghistory.com
 Established in the 1830s to carry anthracite coal from Schuylkill County to Philadelphia, under Gowen the P&R continued its expansion by acquiring smaller rail lines and building new facilities. As miners were organizing to protest low wages and dangerous working conditions, Gowen embarked on a plan to control the supply of coal, even though his company’s charter prohibited it. “Throughout the 1870s, Gowen used legal and extra legal maneuvering that led the P&R into the anthracite coal business,” noted Wynn. “The railroad became the largest owner of coal lands in Schuylkill County.”
 This put Gowen at odds with the Workingman’s Benevolent Association (WBA), which represented the miners. In 1875, an unsuccessful strike to protest wage cuts made the WBA all but irrelevant and led to the rise of the more clandestine and radical Molly Maguires. “The Mollies were a secret society based among the Irish coal miners in the anthracite fields of northern Pennsylvania in the 1860s and 1870s,” according to historian John Kearns.
 On the night of July 23, 1877, unrest by striking railroad engineers led to mob violence and vandalism in Reading, Pennsylvania. Railroad officials called in a unit of the Pennsylvania Militia, ostensibly to protect P&R property. Caught in the 7th Street Cut—a narrow ravine with high walls—and ambushed from above with rocks and bricks, the soldiers fired on the crowd, killing at least 10 and wounding many more in what was to become known as the Reading Railroad Massacre.
 Meanwhile, Gowen hired Pinkerton detectives to infiltrate the Molly Maguires and sought to bar them from the coal mines, while publicly disparaging them as communists linked to radicals in Europe. “It was probably inevitable that Gowen, being who he was and the miners, being who they were, would clash,” reported Frank Whelan for Allentown television station WFMZ. “Northern Irish Protestants and Irish Catholics had a historical record of conflict at least as far back as the 1690s.”
 The Wormley Hotel in 1888. | Photo courtesy of Winninghistory.com
 That clash culminated in a series of arrests and trials that resulted in the conviction and execution of 20 Mollies between 1877 and 1879. In some cases Gowen acted as special prosecutor. “The Molly Maguire trials were a surrender of state sovereignty,” Kearns concluded. “A private corporation initiated the investigation through a private detective agency. A private police force arrested the alleged defenders, and private attorneys for the coal companies prosecuted them. The state provided only the courtroom and the gallows. 20 men were convicted and hanged on the basis of very dubious evidence.”
 Gowen was eventually ousted as president of the P&R and went back into private practice, which brought him to Washington, D.C. in December 1889. A 2002 book by Patrick Campbell, descendant of one of the Mollies, reignited unanswered questions about evidence connected with Gowen’s death. These include the position of the body, angle of the wound, blood on the handle of the gun, an overturned light and chair, removal of potential evidence by Wormley, and failure to conduct an autopsy.
 “Since I had a very personal interest in the Gowen story because he was involved in the execution of my grand uncle, I wondered if my relatives in Pennsylvania had anything to do with Gowen’s death,” Campbell wrote in Who Killed Franklin Gowen ? “Was he murdered by some of my Molly Maguire relatives from Pennsylvania, or did he really commit suicide?"
 The Last Philadelphia Star 
 Mahlon Duckett (1922–2015) joined the Philadelphia Stars of the Negro National League at the age of 17. The Overbrook High School graduate was voted the League’s Rookie of the Year in 1940 and went on to play nine seasons with the Stars, covering third base, second base, or shortstop. His final season was with Homestead Grays in 1950. Founded in 1933, the Stars played in the Negro National League from 1934 to 1948 and the Negro American League from 1949 to 1952.
 Described by the Negro Leagues Baseball Museum as a “light-hitting, smooth-fielding, versatile infielder,” Duckett played with or against Satchel Paige, Josh Gibson, and Jackie Robinson, to name a few Negro League luminaries. His fondest baseball memory was the time he went up against Paige in an exhibition game in Yankee Stadium. “When you faced him you were just trying to get a base hit,” he told radio station WBUR at an event honoring Negro League players in 2010.
 “You know, Satchel didn’t give up too many hits, and he threw me a pitch and I just swung and hit it. And I hit it to right field and it went into the stands and I was just as shocked, I guess, as Satchel and the other people because there wasn’t too many home runs hit off of Satchel.”
 Mahlon Duckett played for the Philadelphia Stars from 1940-49. | Photo: Ebay.com
 Duckett and Stars catcher Stanley ‘Doc’ Glenn told WBUR’s Jeremy Bernfeld what it was like playing in the Negro Leagues in the 1940s. “In just about all of the southern towns and cities we was (sic) unwelcome,” Duckett said. “A lot of the whites came out because they wanted to see what Negro League baseball was like, but, as far as the conditions, it was horrible, terrible. They called us names and we had no place to eat, as a rule. A lot of times we didn’t have any place to sleep.” Glenn added, “All of the hotels in every city, North or South, were prejudiced and we weren’t allowed. They simply wouldn’t rent you rooms, but that’s the way it was all over.”
 After his year with the Grays, Duckett worked as a letter carrier for the United States Postal Service, retiring in 1988. “Duckett spent his years after baseball working as an ambassador for the game,” noted Patrick Gordon, in his Philadelphia Baseball Review obituary for Duckett. “He spoke to audiences, including children, about life in the Negro Leagues and the legends he shared the field with. As the last surviving member of any Philadelphia-based Negro team, the Phillies honored Duckett several times over the past few years at Citizens Bank Park. Philadelphia lost a significant connection to its storied baseball past with the passing of Negro Leaguer Mahlon Duckett.”
 The Family of Artists 
 For much of the 19th century, Philadelphia nurtured a family of commercially and critically successful artists who celebrated the area’s natural landscapes and flora in their paintings and drawings. Russell and Mary Smith, along with their children Xanthus and Mary, routinely exhibited at the annual shows of the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts (PAFA) and sold their works through local galleries.
 Russell Smith (1812-1896) was a native of Glasgow, Scotland. His parents moved the family to Western Pennsylvania in 1819. “The Smith children were educated at home, and Russell showed an early interest in art,” according to the Smithsonian Institution’s Archives of American Art. “Around 1827, Smith began painting backdrops for theaters and within six years had achieved a national reputation for his theatrical painting.”
 After Smith moved to Philadelphia in 1835 to paint large canvas drop curtains for the Walnut Street Theater, he began earning commissions to paint for theaters along the East Coast. “Even while engaged in theatrical work, Smith continued to paint landscapes which were exhibited at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts and the Artists’ Fund Society of Philadelphia,” most years between 1834 and 1889.
 Russell Smith and his granddaughter Polly in 1885. | Photo: Public Domain
 In 1838, Smith married Mary Priscilla Wilson (1819-1874), a native of Milestown, Philadelphia County, painter of flowers, and teacher of French, Latin, and drawing. She had works on display in the 1838 and 1940 Artists’ Fund Society shows and the 1860 and 1869 PAFA shows. “Mary Priscilla, although not a well-known painter, did beautiful flower studies and was an unusually educated woman for her day, educating both of her children at home,” wrote Charlottle Ridpath in the 1943 edition of the Old York Road Historical Society Bulletin .
 Xanthus Smith (1839-1929) was born in the family home on Locust Street. A year later, seeking undeveloped open space outside of the city, elder Smith moved the family to Philadelphia County. The house, known as Rock Hill, was located between Branchtown and Milestown near Mary’s family and the current intersection of Old York Road and Chelten Avenue. “From a painting of the home, we see a cozy white house nestled among beautiful large trees with a brook running through the meadow,” Ridpath wrote in 1943. 
 Born at Rock Hill, Mary Russell Smith (1842-1878) showed early interests in nature and painting, both of which her parents encouraged. Starting in 1859, she exhibited at PAFA 15 times, the last two posthumously. “In contrast to her father and brother, who had learned the rudiments of art by copying drawings or engravings from books, she sketched directly from nature,” Robert Torchia wrote in the catalog produced for a series of exhibitions staged by the Old York Road Historical Society in 1998. Frequent subjects were chickens that she raised, along with wild squirrels, rabbits, and birds. “Her paintings of chickens were popular with Philadelphia art collectors and sought after in England,” according to the Archives of American Art. Ridpath noted that “her pictures were admired and purchased as fast as she could produce them.”
 Russell Smith painted Chew House, Germantown in 1843. | Image courtesy of Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts
 Returning from a family tour of Europe in 1852, the Smiths found a growing city creeping north toward their tranquil homestead. Desiring a place in the countryside that offered privacy and expansive natural views, they settled on a tract of land sitting atop Edge Hill, west of Jenkintown, Montgomery County, the site of a series of Revolutionary War skirmishes, sometimes generously known as The Battle of Edge Hill.
 “On the summit of Edge Hill overlooking [the village of] Weldon stands the residence of Russell Smith; being of tower-like design, it has formed a conspicuous feature from the time of its erection in 1854,” wrote Samuel Fitch Hotchkin in The York Road, Old and New . “Square, of stone, and upward of fifty feet in height, with stone cornice, flat roof, and no projecting woodwork, it resembles many towers in different parts of Europe, and for years after its construction it formed a feature of interest the country over, being visible for from five to ten miles in every direction.” As children, the property provided Xanthus and Mary with a natural playground complete with Revolutionary War artifacts. As adults, along with their parents, it provided inspiration and subject matter for their paintings and drawings.
 Xanthus started painting seriously after the family trip to Europe and move to Edge Hill, first exhibiting at PAFA in 1856 while still a teenager. He joined the United States Navy at the start of the Civil War, and, as clerk to the captain of the flagship of the South Atlantic Squadron, made detailed drawings of the ships he saw. These were to serve as the factual basis for paintings he would create after the war. He did not witness any battles, but undertook extensive research to ensure accuracy. “He referred freely to his former acquaintances for details of action [and] position of ships, and many of his preliminary paintings were checked and corrected by the officers in charge of the ships involved,” noted Ridpath.
 The Smith family's headstone at Ivy Hill Cemetery. | Photo: David Bell
 “In the absence of extended photography, it is probable that his paintings represent some of the most authentic records of the [naval] actions of the Civil War.” His skill, along with great interest in Civil War subjects leading up to the 1876 Centennial earned him lucrative commissions and recognition as one of the most important maritime artists of his time.
 Paintings and sketches by Russell and Xanthus still serve as permanent records of bygone natural landscapes and historic residences as they existed in the second half of the 19th century. These include, to name a few, A Scene on the Wissahickon, Schuylkill Above Manayunk, Edge Hill Road, The Great Elm on the Lime Kiln Road, Chartiar’s Creek , and Lt. Ingersoll’s House, were all created by Russell. Xanthus' works include View of Weldon, Residence of Wm. C. Kent- Jenkintown Station, Morton Hedge-Branchtown, On the Tacony, Pennypack Scene, and Mather’s Cottage-Cheltenham .
 Russell, Mary P., Mary, and Xanthus, along with his wife Mary B. and their daughter Pollie, lived out the remainder of their lives on Edge Hill. Locally known as “The Castle,” the Smith family home was sold in the 1950s. Still standing and privately owned, the property currently houses the studio of sculptor Christopher Collins.
 A Nice Life 
 Easy-going and affable, Drysdale spoke warmly about the public response since authorities publicly identified Joseph Augustus Zarelli as the so-called “boy in the box” last year for the first time since his body was discovered in 1957. A new headstone marks his gravesite, alongside older ones dedicated to “America’s Unknown Child” and the “Unknown Boy.” “People from around the country visit the site. People from all over the world send cards and toys,” Drysdale said.
 The original chapel at Ivy Hill Cemetery. | Photo: David Bell
 Like the 1918 influenza pandemic before it, in 2020, COVID-19 pushed Ivy Hill’s human and physical resources to its limits. “The worst thing I saw in all the years I’ve been here was COVID,” said Drysdale. “It was terrible.” Normally, Ivy Hill performs 600 cremations per month, referred by funeral homes in the greater Philadelphia area. “We had 175 bodies over a two day stretch.” It got to the point where Drysdale had to cap the number of daily cremations. To protect family members and workers, he closed the chapel and limited attendance at graveside burials to 10 people. “Some family members had to watch from parked cars. It was sad.”
 Reflecting on his more than 50 years at Ivy Hill, Drysdale focused on the family members who had loved ones buried there. “It’s a nice life, it’s interesting. Some days it’s tough. Everyday you watch people cry. You never get hardened to it unless you’re a hard person. Every funeral is different. Every family is different. We think about the family. If we can give them a little bit of peace, then that’s the best thing we can do.”
 Tags: African-American history Civil War history historic cemeteries Philadelphia artists 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: Op-Ed: Preserve Cultural Legacy, Too, Through Rebuild
author: Ashley Hahn
bodyText:
Editor’s Note : A version of this story was published in the Spring 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Kingsessing Recreation Center at 4901 Kingsessing Avenue was built in 1916. It is currently undergoing major renovations through the Rebuilt program. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Rebuild was billed as a generational chance to reinvest in and rehabilitate our parks, recreation centers, and libraries–many historic but few designated–and the program may be former Mayor Jim Kenney’s most positive preservation legacy. While preservation is not an explicit Rebuild objective, it is one of its outcomes. Rebuild represents a renewal of our collective commitment to stewarding the city’s legacy public assets, honoring their civic promise, their enduring programs, the deep and generational community relationships they support, their historic architecture, and quality public design. That’s just the kind of layered preservation our current moment demands. To date, however, Rebuild’s focus has been largely physical. The task ahead is to foreground forms of cultural preservation as part of Rebuild’s projects.
 Our historic Carnegie libraries and recreation centers like Kingsessing or Athletic are public places that were built to express clear civic pride. But their impressive architecture is not their primary heritage value. They are even more important because of their continued use as public places where residents gather, bond, learn, remember, and grow. Their social and cultural legacies demand serious preservation attention.
 Consider Francis J. Myers Recreation Center in Southwest Philadelphia, a historic (undesignated) former Presbyterian orphanage transformed into a recreation center in the 1960s thanks to a deeply invested community. Despite lean and difficult years, its community and a dedicated staff kept Myers Rec running. Its overdue renovation and redesign through Rebuild retains the original orphanage-turned-recreation building and replaces a 1960s addition with new spaces that provide better natural light, circulation, and recreation spaces. Physically, it’s a preservation victory, not because the building was designated or because preservationists were particularly vocal, but because the original building was sturdy enough to be reused. There is reason to hope, too, that Myers Rec’s tight community will ground its future in its strong social ties and a common past. Projects like this should be celebrated as preservation victories, but they should not be accidental.
 For its larger projects, Rebuild’s process includes community engagement, largely to keep neighbors informed and give them a voice in shaping design interventions. Typically, this type of engagement does not emphasize the kinds of memory work that would prize the shared histories and generational stories that give these places meaning. But Rebuild’s engagement activities, particularly those taking place over long planning periods, are potent opportunities to connect with the lived experiences and memories of thousands of Philadelphians. Preservationists are uniquely positioned to help broaden the program’s scope to be more inclusive of the cultural and social values of these places, as recognized by their communities. That way, as a recreation center or library changes, their futures may truly reflect their significance.
 George A. Vare Recreation Center at 2600 Morris Street was demolished in 2022. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Vare Rec Center in Gray’s Ferry was one of the city’s largest and most impressive. But after more than 100 years of continued use and inadequate reinvestment, the building was evidently too far gone to be rehabilitated and has been razed. Rather than rely on the building as a vessel of memory, a team led by Make the World Better Foundation worked with the Vare community to build a collective archive, including oral histories, family photographs, and contemporary community portraits. This kind of deep memory work has been all but missing in Rebuild projects, partly as a function of budget and capacity.
 As our historic civic assets see much-needed reinvestment, physical changes should be accompanied by efforts similar to those at Vare, ensuring the rich community pasts woven through these places are appreciated and sustained. Achieving this requires values-centered preservation methods that are all but missing from Rebuild conversations. But there are points of convenient alignment. The City’s Department of Planning and Development is piloting a cultural resource survey process, and it would be wise to expand this effort to City-controlled Rebuild sites. For preservation advocates, this is a chance to find common cause with other communities of interest and actively democratize Philadelphia preservation by meeting people where they are and helping to surface the attributes they value about the places they share.
 Mayor Cherelle Parker has signaled support for Rebuild to continue, and helpfully, the revenue from the soda tax is still earmarked for this purpose. Preservation advocates need to stand with public space advocates and residents to demand that Mayor Parker deliver on the promise of Rebuild and set up maintenance funding to prevent us from needing another Rebuild anytime soon. The way to make that case isn’t through arguments about irreplaceable historic architecture, but the ties that bind communities together through these places.
 Tags: Department of Parks and Recreation historic renovation op-ed Rebuild 
 About the Author
 Ashley Hahn is a writer and researcher focused on public space, public life, and preservation. She is a lecturer in the Department of Historic Preservation at the University of Pennsylvania, where she led a 2023 studio on Rebuild sites in Southwest Philadelphia.

title: Rebuilding More Than Places
author: Starr Herr-Cardillo
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Terrence Finley didn’t set out to get into construction. Up until about a year ago, the 32-year-old was working in an entirely different field when his cousin sent him a link to sign up for a carpentry academy, part of the city’s Rebuild initiative, which trains cohorts in partnership with Eastern State Penitentiary Historic Site. Intrigued, Finley applied and, before he knew it, was one of the program’s top participants, building skylight covers to protect and weatherproof roofs at the National Historic Landmark.
 Terrence Finley, an apprentice with Local 164 of the Carpenters Union, works outside the Kingsessing Recreation Center. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Less than a year later, Finley landed a full-time apprenticeship with Local 164 of the Carpenters Union. Smith Construction, his sponsor, is the general contractor on the rehabilitation of Kingsessing Library, a historically designated Carnegie library undergoing a $7 million upgrade by Rebuild, the Kenney administration initiative launched in 2016 to tackle deferred maintenance in Philadelphia’s public parks, libraries, and recreation centers.
 Rebuilding Community Infrastructure–Rebuild, as it’s usually called–wasn’t conceived as a preservation initiative, but in many ways, it is one. Rebuild takes a multifaceted approach, working primarily with existing buildings and sites, some of which are historically designated, addressing deferred maintenance and making much-needed updates.
 Perhaps too ambitious in scope for its own good, when the Kenney administration launched Rebuild in 2016, the goal was to address 72 sites. But several years later, only 17 projects have been completed. That said, they have only spent about $120 million of the $500 million initially envisioned.
 Union carpenter Phil Mascio builds a door trim surround at Kingsessing Library. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Rebuild, at its core, is an effort to infuse hundreds of millions of dollars into neglected community resources across the city. This type of public infrastructure is critical to any city’s health, but especially a large, poor city like Philadelphia where many of its hundreds of playgrounds, parks, and recreation centers provide services to historically underserved neighborhoods.
 Rebuild bills itself as a public-private partnership, with a funding structure supported largely by philanthropic groups like the William Penn Foundation, which has pledged up to $100 million toward the cause, the John S. and James L. Knight Foundation, and others. Another key funding source is the Sweetened Beverage Tax passed in 2016, although it remained tied up in litigation until 2018. Then, the COVID-19 pandemic struck another blow to Rebuild’s ambitious timeline, wreaking havoc on the global supply chain and causing massive delays, price surges, and uncertainty across the construction industry. Rebuild’s slower-than-planned progress has not come without its share of challenges and scrutiny. But it’s worth noting that despite the setbacks, the initiative has made a good faith effort to stay true to its lofty values.
 Holistic Repairs 
 Rebuild’s approach to projects is meant to extend beyond the physical rehabilitation of buildings and infrastructure. It’s a holistic approach that centers people in the process. “[Rebuild] is as much about the people as it is about the place,” said Kira Strong, executive director of Rebuild, when asked how the initiative connects to preservation. “I think preservation has really moved [toward] the people part of things.”
 For many large-scale projects, community engagement can too often feel perfunctory, but it can be transformative–for residents and the project–when given adequate time and effort. Rebuild also promised to cultivate training opportunities, particularly among women and people of color, for Philadelphia residents looking to break into the building trades. That’s an ambitious goal in and of itself and has gained traction thanks to a partnership with Eastern State Penitentiary’s Preservation Trades Center. In addition, the initiative is intentionally cultivating a portfolio of contractors that includes a high percentage of women-and minority-owned businesses, another commitment that has a big impact, but can slow down progress, as onboarding new vendors and working with smaller firms can take more time.
 Participants in the carpentry training program at Eastern State Penitentiary, co sponsored by the city’s Rebuild initiative. | Photo courtesy of Rebuild
 It’s been a learning curve, but Finley’s trajectory is exactly what the team behind Rebuild wants to see. “The transition from Eastern State [Academy] to actually getting full-on apprenticeship with the carpenters union, that was basically set up by Rebuild,” said Finley. He’s being modest. He was still required to complete the interview, skills assessment, and math assessment as any applicant would. But trades academy participants are evaluated during the six-week program, and companies like Smith Construction make note of attendees who show promise.
 It’s probably more likely that workforce training grads who move into union apprenticeships like Finley will find themselves working on new construction more than historic buildings, which is why the early exposure to the specific challenges and process of working at historic sites through the trades academy is so valuable. Finley says what he learned about preservation at Eastern State is coming into play at Kingsessing Library. Part of the process involved painstakingly removing and reinstalling historic millwork in the reading room. “It’s a slower, more meticulous process,” Finley said. “You learn a lot more because when you’re removing things and putting it back, you need to record and label everything.” Finley is specializing in general carpentry, and he expects to work on a range of projects. He finds all of the work interesting, including the precision required for older buildings. “I would say you get a real sense of pride putting something like that together … knowing that this building was standing a hundred years ago and the work that I do here could help keep it standing for another hundred years.”
 Dedicating Resources for the Public Good 
 The provision of public amenities like recreation centers, playgrounds, and libraries came about in the mid-19th century, along with the rise in indoor plumbing. Reform movements aimed to supply public baths, particularly to poorer families who could not afford private bath houses. According to the Philadelphia Department of Recreation, nine free public bath houses were built in Philadelphia between 1884 and 1898. In 1906, a group called the Playground Association of America was formed, followed the next year by the Playgrounds Association of Philadelphia. These organizations advocated for the creation of public playgrounds, highlighting them as places where children could learn to be good citizens. Soon, the initiative was formalized through Philadelphia’s city government when a Playgrounds Committee was formed to assess the need for additional recreation areas across the city, which ultimately led to a bill launching the Philadelphia Department of Recreation. The first city-funded facility–Starr Garden Playground and Recreation Center–opened in 1911, and by 1928, the City boasted 48 distinct recreation sites, 14 of which had buildings with gymnasia and 37 of which had public pools.
 Top: Starr Garden, the first recreation center built by the City of Philadelphia, shown here in a 1913 Board of Recreation report. Bottom: Kingsessing Library front elevation. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Around the same time, industrialist and steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie donated more than $40 million to fund 1,679 libraries across the United States. The Kingsessing Library, on 51st Street between Kingsessing and Chester Avenues, was the 22nd Carnegie library in Philadelphia. It is listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in the Carnegie Library Thematic Historic District , along with four other Rebuild sites. Kingsessing Library is a classic Carnegie design. Light streams into the reading room through the large windows, and the high ceilings and open floor plan make the space feel ample and inviting. It shares a block-sized parcel with Kingsessing Recreation Center, built in 1916 and one of the city’s earliest recreation centers. Both are undergoing major upgrades and renovations through Rebuild, while preserving the building envelopes and historic detailing.
 “Our goal is to be rebuilding and renovating existing buildings,” said Angela Dixon, Rebuild’s deputy director of design and construction, although she noted that many need serious retrofitting to be brought up to code. “ADA accessibility is a big factor,” she added. While the majority of Rebuild’s projects involve some form of reuse, when they are not working with historically designated buildings, there are times when they opt for new construction. “One of our new buildings in construction now is Vare Recreation Center. It had a lot of structural issues, and it was determined that a new building would better suit the site and community.” Following a cost-analysis, structural assessments, and rounds of community engagement, Rebuild made the call that the block-sized site in south Philadelphia could better serve the desired needs with the freedom to totally reorient the building.
 Community Heirlooms 
 Kingsessing is one of Rebuild’s largest sites. It includes two historic buildings located on a block-sized parcel and needed a significant amount of design work to bring buildings up to code. The combined $32 million investment will cover top-to-bottom work on both buildings, including ADA upgrades–like an elevator for the library–a new HVAC, an outdoor story circle, and a new turf field. Throughout the project, Rebuild leaders say they’ve remained committed to community engagement and wanted to be responsive to the feedback they’ve received, which has stretched the project timeline. The Kingsessing projects have a committed core stakeholder group, said Strong, and they’ve remained engaged throughout the process, although some have expressed frustration with the timeline.
 The Kingsessing Recreation Center entrance hall. | Photo courtesy of Rebuild
 Still, Rebuild’s commitment to the community engagement process is impressive. For the Kingsessing site alone, the program held six public meetings and numerous smaller “touchstone” meetings with key stakeholders. It circulated four public surveys that generated more than 800 responses, 87 percent of which came from within a 10-block radius and 50 percent within a three-block radius of the site.
 “I think it’s interesting to not just talk about historic preservation, but preservation of a neighborhood,” said Cassie O’Connel, a senior project manager overseeing the Kingsessing Library and Recreation Center projects. “There’s a long history of people in the neighborhood being involved with programming, a lot of cultural memory and events that have happened at these sites.” That cultural memory and associated values and concerns came through in the process. Rebuild reviewed survey data and looked for common themes and issues across responses.
 Amanda Colon-Smith, Rebuild’s community engagement director, likens these sites to community heirlooms. “People want to pass this down to the next generation,” she said. “We always work very closely with folks who are history keepers and culture keepers.”
 Soliciting community input for the rehabilitation of the Kingsessing Recreation Center and Library. | Photo courtesy of Rebuild
 Moving forward, it’s important to the Rebuild crew that sites are maintained well and often so that such massive overhauls won’t be necessary in the future. Dixon said they are working very closely with Parks and Recreation so that they understand future maintenance needs. “We really do have maintenance in mind when doing the design work,” she said.
 Despite the bumpy start, Rebuild’s completed projects have been successful. There’s no guarantee that the initiative itself will be maintained. Mayor Cherelle Parker has said she intends to continue the program, although she’s suggested her administration will conduct a review to identify areas of inefficiency. Most good preservation work takes time. Now that Rebuild has made it past the initial hurdles and has ironed out the process, maybe it’s worth recalibrating expectations. After all, good things are worth waiting for.
 Tags: Department of Parks and Recreation historic renovation public spaces Rebuild 
 About the Author
 Starr Herr-Cardillo is a freelance writer and historic preservation professional working in the nonprofit sector. She holds a master’s degree in historic preservation from the University of Pennsylvania.

title: Black Labor Leader Ben Fletcher Honored with New Mural
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
The new Ben Fletcher mural at 301 S. Columbus Boulevard will be dedicated on Saturday, May 18. | Rendering courtesy of Mural Arts
 On Saturday, May 18, a dedication and celebration of a new mural honoring Black labor leader Ben Fletcher will take place on the Delaware River waterfront. The public artwork is the culmination of a collaborative effort between Mural Arts, the Philadelphia branch of the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW), and the Racial Justice Committee of Philadelphia Democratic Socialists of America (PDSA). The mural will draw attention to a period of local history that often gets lost among communism, the Red Summer, the Negro Renaissance, the Great Migration, and World War I. It will also highlight the 111-year anniversary of a strike that resulted in a better work environment for Philadelphia’s dock workers.
 Working Man 
 Fletcher, former head of Local 8, will be immortalized with the same smug look that has come to define his story. Local artist Jonathan Pinkett drew inspiration from a negative of Fletcher’s infamous mugshot he found on eBay. “It was the period of time when he decided to organize unions. He had to work his ass off,” Pinkett said.
 Fletcher's little-known history is about a relatable character. He was a Black child born in 1890 to parents who arrived in Philadelphia as part of the First Great Migration. Not much is known about his upbringing and his family. The 1910 census recorded him as a 20-year-old living in shared accommodations in the Point Breeze section of South Philadelphia. His profession is listed as a laborer most likely working on one of the piers along the Schuylkill or Delaware Rivers. Historian's believe that his affiliation with unions began around this time. During this period, African Americans and other racial and ethnic groups were relegated to certain jobs from which they could not move upwards. Low pay and long hours were two of the realities Fletcher endured with his co-workers. These conditions prepared them for finding solutions to improve their situations through unionization.
 This mugshot of Philadelphia union activist Ben Fletcher was taken in 1917. | Photo: Public Domain
 Philadelphia’s Local 8 was founded in 1913. It is part of the Marine Transport Workers Industrial Union of the IWW, alternatively known as the Wobblies. Fletcher and his fellow founding union members had no other alternatives but to use radical tactics and sabotage as ways of slowing down productivity or striking to have their voices heard.
 On May 14, 1913, Fletcher, along with 4,000 other dock workers, staged a 14-day strike that halted domestic and international trade. The act positioned the police and the owners of shipping and stevedoring companies against an organized working-class force composed of 52 percent Black, 39 percent Polish and Lithuanian, and 9 percent Irish and Italian workers. Until the 1920s, this strike was remembered with a day-long festival where dock workers gathered to celebrate their victory with a day off and a parade along the waterfront.
 Soapbox 
 A report by FBI Agent Henry M. Bowen made on July 4, 1917 described Fletcher as a southern agitator with no real education and a "bad gunfighter” despite him never brandishing a weapon. Despite his lack of education, Fletcher was still able to lead the union around his belief that workers’ power could usher in a new society and that would require obliterating the color line, building a durable solidarity, and attending to working people’s immediate needs. His voice, sense of humor, and refusal to compromise drew people to him as he bellowed out from his soapbox to fellow dockworkers.
 Fletcher's efforts changed after the entry of the United States into World War I in April 1917. Despite asking fellow union members to work diligently as a show of support to the Allies, the Wobblies were labeled as criminals due to their critical views of the United States, specifically their views on war. The Espionage Act of 1917 turned members of the IWW and various chapters into “anti-patriots” who could face jail time, loss of employment, and possibly death by the police due to the unionists’ communist sympathies. Increased fears based on xenophobia and the dreaded Red Scare fed off the hysteria during a time when workers were needed to ramp up production.
 Benjamin Harrison Fletcher poses with a young Benjamin Fletcher Homer in the 1940s. A friend named his son in honor of the labor leader. | Image courtesy of the Industrial Workers of the World
 By September of 1917, Local 8 and IWW halls in Philadelphia were raided by the FBI and local police. Similar raids were also happening in other IWW offices throughout the country, leading to a slow dissolution of the unions by the U.S. government as it punished leaders with extended jail times and high fines.
 Fletcher served 10 years in Leavenworth Federal Penitentiary and was fined up to $30,000, effectively breaking the Local 8, but not Fletcher. He continued to organize and give speeches until suffering a stroke in 1933. He lived the remainder of his life in Brooklyn, New York. Fletcher passed away in 1949, and his remains were interred in an unmarked grave.
 Path to a Mural 
 In 2022, I was lucky to be connected with Peter Cole, professor of history at Western Illinois University and author of the book, Ben Fletcher: The Life and Times of a Black Wobbly . During that time, work on creating a public artwork with Mural Arts was already underway. The IWW, Philly DSA: Racial Justice Committee, and Cole received funding and approval, but progress was delayed due to COVID-19.
 Why should such an obscure character be immortalized? According to Cole, “Fletcher was one of the country’s greatest Black radicals ever, and today a great many people are increasingly interested and hungry for inspirational, educational histories of such folks.”
 Painter Jonathan Pinkett, at center, and attendees of the Ben Fletcher Community Paint Day at Cherry Street Pier in March. | Photo: Keshler Thibert
 Matthew Atwell, a member of PDSA, shared his elation at the completion of the mural during a Ben Fletcher Community Paint Day in March 2024. Atwell has been a part of this project since 2021 when he learned about Fletcher and Cole's book via a class on racial capitalism.
 Along with the mural, the installation of a Pennsylvania state historical marker at the same site is in the works.
 The Ben Fletcher mural will be officially dedicated on Saturday, May, 18 from 2:00 pm – 4:00 pm at 301 S. Columbus Boulevard. The celebration will include classic Wobbly songs, food, and stories about Fletcher and Local 8 history. The event is free and open to the public. RSVP here: https://www.phillydsa.org/ben_fletcher_mural 
 Tags: African-American history Delaware River waterfront labor unions 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Partial Collapse of Graffiti Pier Leaves Future Park Plans in Limbo
author: Adam Litchkofski
bodyText:
A 10-20 foot section of Graffiti Pier's easterly point, pictured here in 2017, collapsed into the Delaware River on the morning of July 31. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 It was nothing short of a miracle that no one was found in the watery rubble of Graffiti Pier on in the early morning hours of July 31 after a 15-foot chunk of the pier collapsed and plummeted into the Delaware River. Not so miraculous now, however, may be the future of the beloved industrial ruin as we know it.
 The future of colorful trestle walls cemented into Pier 18, a former coal-loading pier in Port Richmond once used by the Reading Company, has been hanging in the balance for decades. The partial collapse last Wednesday will either be another nudge towards its sale or could see to its destruction.
 Since 2018, the Delaware River Waterfront Corporation (DRWC) has had plans to purchase the land from Conrail, the current owners of the property, to formally make it a public green space. Encapsulating much more than just Graffiti Pier, the riverfront property spans over 150 acres—from Cumberland Street to Allegheny Avenue—and includes seven other abandoned piers.
 DRWC’s plans include making trails wider and the area ADA-accessible, cultivating marshes, building new concrete walls to prevent erosion, erecting fences along the edges of the pier, and planting native plants and trees on the pier and in the surrounding area. However, due to the collapse, the nonprofit organization's expansive proposal may be affected.
 “It is too soon for us to determine how this will impact DRWC’s acquisition and future development of the pier,” said Joe Forkin, president of DRWC, in a public statement. “But it is our strong hope that we can continue working with Conrail, who are the current owners of the property, to finalize the long anticipated purchase agreement that will ultimately allow DRWC to provide meaningful public space for the community in and around the Graffiti Pier property.”
 Men take a tour of coal-loading Pier 18 in 1948. | Image from Reading Company Annual Report, 1948
 Conrail has owned the former coal-loading pier for nearly half a century and, while it hasn’t been in use since 1993, the company still has legal control over the land.
 “Making [Graffiti Pier] a public space and allowing public access, or even leaving it alone is not something Conrail is interested in,” said Karen Thompson, DRWC’s director of planning, policy, and engagement, in April. “They’re a railroad company, so let us formalize it as a public space and protect that resource, because again, that's not what Conrail does.”
 In 2021, Conrail was found to be in violation for failing to submit a required pier report, a standard structural assessment inspection of the piers on the property. According to the violation notice issued by the City , piers in Philadelphia are required to be inspected every three years. The property has had 10 violations since 2010. Conrail officials did not respond to a request for comment.
 Beyond potentially losing an important piece of Pennsylvania railroad history, the possible loss of Graffiti Pier as a street art haven is daunting. Unlike any other place in Philadelphia, the pier harbors endless space for artistic expression. It also serves as a shaded escape from the city grid, especially in sweltering summer months where temperatures linger near 100 degrees.
 “First and foremost, shame on Conrail for holding future parks and public space in Philly for ransom, as they have here with Graffiti Pier as well as large parts of the future Rail Park,” said Conrad Benner, local public art advocate and founder of the art blog Streets Dept . “Having left these spaces abandoned for decades, Conrail's delay and inaction seems to suggest that they do not care about the people of Philadelphia, particularly the communities surrounding their neglected properties. It's time they finally end the neglect and sell these properties to local organizations who can seed what's already been growing there.”
 A family of five sets off to explore Graffiti Pier on a Saturday morning in 2017 despite gusty winds and 40 degree temperatures. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 City Councilmember Mark Squilla, who represents the district that the Graffiti Pier property is a part of, will meet with Conrail this week to discuss possible options for the pier. “Councilmember Squilla supports the plan to create an open space for the public, but nothing can move forward unless they decide to sell the property,” said Anne Kelly, Squilla’s chief of staff.
 An investigation into what caused the collapse, and whether or not it will happen again, is just getting underway. Until more information is made public, supporters of Graffiti Pier will have to continue playing the waiting game.
 “My hope is that the damage Conrail's neglect has created at Graffiti Pier will not stop it from becoming an official park. That is, a park that is safe from collapse, made more accessible, and that maintains the essence of this well-used and beloved space,” Benner said. “The desired path is clear and leads to the maintenance of Graffiti Pier and preservation of it as a public green space and non-curated, creative outlet for Philadelphians.
