As far as I see it, this is the mandate from the people of our city who've cultivated and cared for the pier since it was abandoned.”
 Tags: Delaware River Waterfront Corporation Graffiti Pier Port Richmond public art railroad history 
 About the Author
 Adam Litchkofski is a writer and photographer based in Philadelphia. He is a student at Temple University where he is pursuing a degree in journalism with a minor in environmental studies. He cares deeply about the outdoors and loves covering topics involving environmental justice, land preservation and conservation, and people’s relationship with nature and the world as a whole.

title: Revival of North Philly Landmark Slams to a Halt
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The Beury Building at Broad Street and Erie Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 When the National Bank of North Philadelphia building went up at 3701 N. Broad Street in 1926, the impressive 14-story, Art Deco structure made a clear statement: North Philly had arrived. “Now Open! North Philadelphia’s First Skyscraper!” declared an ad placed by builder Wark Co. in the Philadelphia Inquirer in June of that year. “A commanding structure, a beautiful structure, and need we add, a well-built one.”
 Nearly 100 years later, the building has become greatly diminished, decades of dereliction and decay having left it a literal shell of what it once was. Today, the building is best known to many–especially the millennial crowd–as the “BONER 4EVER” building on account of eponymous graffiti tags spanning half its height. Those dialed in to local history and architecture call it the Beury Building. Whatever its name, the building’s strong bones indeed still stand, and the surrounding blocks, also diminished since a Roaring Twenties heyday, hope a potential revitalization can once again elevate the neighborhood.
 News broke this month that those dreams are presently deferred, with a bevy of local outlets reporting that financing for a complete transformation of the building had fallen through for owner Shift Capital, leaving a decade-old promise adrift as the developer searches for another lender. Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, says those in his circle have known for months that the project had hit serious turbulence.
 “It's obviously disappointing, as many of us were eagerly anticipating the rehabilitation of this prominent landmark,” Steinke said. “It harkens back to the Divine Lorraine , which also sat vacant and decaying for many years before its celebrated rehabilitation in 2018.”
 Shift Capital did not respond to requests for comment, but in interviews with other media outlets, representatives for the firm said that $23 million in financing for an overall $70 million price tag to convert the building into a Marriott Hotel had been rescinded by unnamed parties at the 11th hour. In an interview with the Inquirer , Shift Capital principal Nancy Gephart said investors had grown queasy about “providing a loan in an area untested for hospitality,” while real estate trade publication Bisnow , which broke the news earlier this month, tied the issue to problematic national economic trends related to high interest rates and construction costs.
 Renderings of Shift Capital's plan to convert the Beury Building into a Marriott hotel. | Images: Shift Capital
 Whatever the exact causes, the news is unwelcome in North Philadelphia, where a community-led push to revitalize the Broad, Germantown, and Erie Avenues area is on. In 2017, Mayor Jim Kenney launched a task force for the busy North Philadelphia hub, identifying many areas for improvement. The corridor was among the 12 percent of city streets where 50 percent of traffic deaths and injuries happen. The City determined there was also a need for more public spaces and business revitalization.
 Over the past seven years, according to a City-provided timeline , municipal government has worked with local community groups like Called to Serve CDC to improve the corridor, from actions as small as helping businesses install new awnings and more attractive signage to obtaining millions of dollars in funding for new plazas and streetscapes. Jobs have also become a priority: Called to Serve launched a workforce development program, while WHYY reported that Shift Capital “signed a community benefits agreement that would have employed local residents and ensured contracting with minority-owned businesses.”
 Community leaders are also working to provide spiritual revitalization in the neighborhood. The Philadelphia Historical Commission has worked with residents and community organizations to pilot Treasure Philly! , a program exploring ways to capture the cultural value of a neighborhood beyond the usual paradigm of building designation and historical placards.
 In a 2023 interview, Amelia Price, corridor manager for Called to Serve and longtime resident, said many neighbors have living memories of a very different North Philadelphia in the mid-20th century, recalling a shopping district and family-oriented community, not the one where many live in fear of gun violence today.
 She and other advocates likened their efforts to the sankofa bird, a Ghanian symbol conveying the importance of remembering the past in order to progress. “His head is pointed toward his tail, which means you can’t look forward unless you reach back and grab your roots,” Price explained.
 Party on North Broad 
 An photograph of Broad Street and Erie Avenue following the completion of the National Bank of North Philadelphia in 1926. Exact date unknown. | Photo: Public Domain
 In 1985, the Beury Building was successfully added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. 60 years earlier, architects and decorative artists of all types gathered in Paris for the 1925 Exposition internationale des arts décoratifs et industriels modernes (International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts) in Paris. Americans in attendance took home a new architectural vision and a shorthand to match: Art Deco.
 While use of the architectural style exploded in cities like New York, “relatively few examples of pure Art Deco” exist in Philadelphia, the Beury Building’s nomination notes. “Rather, the city’s Deco style is generally identified by its marriage of ‘modernism’ with classically derived details,” it adds, referencing the Liberty Title & Trust Building at Broad and Arch Streets and Market Street National Bank building just east of City Hall.
 In this context, the construction of the National Bank of North Philadelphia at 3701 N. Broad Street in 1926 was game changing: “In an area characterized by elegant rowhouses, the Beury Building stands as an important North Philadelphia landmark unusual in its scale and character,” the nomination concludes.
 In the century preceding the building’s arrival, North Philadelphia transformed from a primarily rural area to modern urban enclave. While similar growth in some sections of the city overtime had led to modestly-designed rowhouses for the working class, the housing stock in North Philadelphia was instead “elegant,” the nomination notes, as the corridor “developed as a hub for Philadelphia’s nouveau riche entrepreneurial class.”
 Dr. Charles Ezra Beury, the first president of the National Bank of North Philadelphia and the second president of Temple University. | Photo: Public Domain
 Indeed, current residents such as Price still hold deep appreciation for streets like the 3700 block of North 15th Street, where two and three-story rows with ornate cornices and bay windows led to regular nominations for Most Beautiful Block awards as recently as the 1980s. Elsewhere in the neighborhood, the nomination notes, wealthy North Philadelphians employed famous Philadelphia architects such as Willis Hale, James Windrim, and Frank Furness to design their abodes.
 However, the crowning achievement was the bank. By the 1920s, residential buildout of the area was nearly complete, as was the Broad Street subway line, finished in 1924. At the beginning of that decade came the founding of the National Bank of Philadelphia. Its first officers and board of directors were selected amongst their industrious peers. Serving as the bank’s first president was Charles Ezra Beury, whose lifelong accolades include officerships for several prominent banks and companies, diplomatic assignments, philanthropic endeavors, and a role as Temple University's second-ever president, a post he held from 1926 until 1941.
 According to the historic nomination, a bank building originally constructed at the current address stood for only five years, before the bank’s leadership enlisted architect William H. Lee the architect of Temple University’s Conwell and Sullivan Halls, to design the 14-story Art Deco structure that stands today. A May 29, 1927 edition of the Inquirer heralded its scheduled opening the next day, stating the building’s basement, street-level, mezzanine, and second floor would house the banking institution with 10 stories of leasable office space above, crowned by “a recreation room for bank employees” on the top floor, beneath a domed roof. “Uptown’s first skyscraper,” the paper splashed in all caps above an adjacent photo of the building.
 Crash and Slow Burn 
 The Beury Building in 1978. | Photo courtesy of Image courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 While the National Bank of Philadelphia “gained immediate popular support” and expanded after its opening, the good times were short lived. With 1929 came the crash of the stock market on Black Tuesday, and the Great Depression that followed claimed the bank as one of its victims. By September 1930, an ad placed by the Bankers Trust Company officially renamed 3701 N. Broad the Beury Building in honor of Dr. Charles E. Beury. Just three months later, Bankers Trust would itself go belly up .
 In the ensuing decades, publicly available records suggest the Beury building continued to be used for office space with advertisements for leasing appearing into the late 1970s. Yet, by the following decade it had clearly fallen into disrepair. In 1985, City officials applied for grant money to pay for a planned $5.8 million rehabilitation. By 1992, a North Jersey developer named Mohammad Mizani was illegally employing inexperienced, unhoused people suffering from addiction to remove asbestos from the building, a crime for which he later received an 18-month prison term.
 A decade later, the graffiti arrived in vertical lettering: “FOREVER BONER” spanning seven stories from the south approach, and “BONER 4EVER” spanning five stories on the north. While some accounts date the graffiti to 2008, Google Street View images show the tags present by 2007. According to a background post provided by Streets Dept , the prominent graffiti is actually the work of two artists, either feuding or collaborating, whose complimentary tags inspire giggles or sighs depending on the eye of the beholder.
 The Beury Building's amusingly iconic BONER 4EVER graffiti was painted in the early aughts. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 What isn’t amusing is the disinvestment and deep fraying of the social fabric that has also befallen the neighborhoods surrounding the diminished Beury Building. In 2012, the promise of a better day appeared to arrive when Shift Capital acquired the building and set out on initial plans to perform environmental remediation and redevelop the building into apartments and commercial space at a price tag of $33 million. Those plans later shifted to a deal with Marriott to turn the building into a 172-room hotel, with Shift Capital principal Gephart noting to WHYY that the building has 11 hospitals and universities within three miles and nary a hotel in sight.
 Gephart added that the firm had assembled an extensive array of support to make the project happen, including historic preservation tax breaks, a $2 million state grant, and another $2.5 million donation from Marriott itself. Gephart told WHYY that Shift Capital remains committed to the plans, as long as it can find a new lender to plunk down $23 million.
 Steinke, with the Preservation Alliance, said underlying trends appear to put it all up in the air. “We are seeing a general slowdown in construction due to higher interest rates and the increased cost of borrowing for construction projects. The real estate business is famously cyclical, and, after a long lasting boom period over the past decade, we are finally witnessing a slowdown,” explained Steinke. “There are signs that it will be moving in the other direction soon, but there is usually a lag before the beneficial effects of lower interest rates are seen. Let's hope Shift Capital remains committed.”
 Tags: adaptive resuse Development Historic Banks North Broad Street North Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Public Art Examines Freedom and Slavery at Declaration House
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
Sonya Clark's Declaration House exhibition at 7th and Market Streets. | Photo: Steve Weinik for Monument Lab
 When Thomas Jefferson penned the words “We hold these truths to be self-evident, that all men are created equal,” he was the enslaver of scores of Black people back home in Virginia. This fact may be familiar to Hidden City readers. It is less well-known, however, that when Jefferson came to Philadelphia as a delegate to the Second Continental Congress, he was accompanied by a 14-year-old enslaved boy. The boy served as his valet, on call 24 hours a day to take care of Jefferson’s clothing, grooming, and other personal needs. He may well have been in the room, or at least not far from it, when Jefferson inked his most famous lines. This boy, Robert Hemmings, was also the half-brother of Jefferson’s wife and the future uncle of Jefferson’s children by Hemmings' enslaved sister Sally. Hemmings’ presence during that long, hot summer of 1776 adds a layer of complexity to the hypocrisy inherent in the Declaration of Independence, our quintessential founding document.
 This complexity is at the heart of Declaration House , an art and history exhibition on the southwest corner of 7th and Market Streets curated by Monument Lab. Enormous blinking eyes fill the windows of Declaration House, a 1976 reproduction of the home Hemmings and Jefferson stayed in as the Declaration of Independence was being drafted. The installation is the brainchild of renowned artist Sonya Clark who was challenged by Monument Lab to bring Hemmings to the center of the question, “What does the Declaration of Independence mean to us today?”
 Given that no known images of Hemmings exist, Clark sought to represent his presence by showcasing the eyes of descendants of his extended family, people who share Hemmings’ genetic material. A fortuitous and unplanned collaboration with Thomas Jefferson's Monticello and the Getting Word African American Oral History Project expanded the project to include the eyes of descendants of all the families enslaved at Monticello. Clark led a team that took video portraits of people ranging in age from seven to over 70. Images from Monticello’s archives were animated to include the eyes of deceased family members from as long ago as the Civil War.
 On the surface, Clark’s work, "The Descendants of Monticello," is simply a rotating set of blinking eyes projected onto screens that are housed in the windows of an ersatz Colonial-era building. If you happen to spot it as you wait for the bus on Market Street or catch a glimpse as you walk by, it will strike you perhaps as odd, or melancholy, or strangely haunting. But if you linger a bit and ponder all that this installation conveys, it may just shift how you see the city of Philadelphia, the United States of America, and the Declaration of Independence.
 An Essential Crossroads 
 A postcard depicting what the Graff House, where Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independance, would have looked like in 1776. | Image courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 The southwest corner of 7th and Market Streets, if shown in time-lapse photography from Jefferson’s time to ours, would reveal a microcosm of Philadelphia history. The house was erected in 1775 for German American brick maker Jacob Graff and his wife Maria, on land purchased from Edmund Physick, the British-born agent of William Penn who was one of the founders of the American Philosophical Society. When Jefferson rented the furnished second floor of the newly-built home, 7th and High (Market) Streets was in the outskirts of the city, surrounded by open fields and across the street from a stable. The location was desirable to Jefferson, as he sought the quiet needed for a serious writing project. Hemmings likely slept in the attic or in the hallway outside of Jefferson’s bedroom.
 After two years, the Graff family sold the house to neighbor Jabob Hiltzheimer, a German immigrant who perished, like so many other late 18th-century Philadelphians, during the yellow fever epidemic. The house was then sold to brothers Simon and Hyman Gratz, members of a prominent Jewish merchant family. Also known as loyal patriots and generous philanthropists, they were founders of the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, and their estate established Gratz College.
 As Market Street became increasingly commercial, the building, to which the Gratz family had added a fourth floor, housed a printing company. In 1883, the structure was torn down. At one point, a bank designed by Frank Furness stood on the site. From the late 1940s through at least the late 1960s, the Tom Thumb dining counter and take-out stand occupied the corner.
 Tom Thumb diner was built in the site of the Graff House, which was demolished in 1883. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 A Lit Brothers advertisement from the July 4, 1960 issue of The Philadelphia Inquirer reads, “Two good American institutions, the hot dog and the hamburger, stand as testimonials to our nation’s neglect of ‘one of the notable sites in the world.’” Lit Brothers invited potential customers to view a replica of the historic house displayed in a store window. In 1963, a state historical marker signifying the site as the place where Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence was installed on 7th Street next to the popular lunch spot.
 Eventually, the property was incorporated into Independence National Historical Park. In 1975, the impending Bicentennial inspired the National Park Service to build a reconstructed version of the Graff House along with a Brutalist visitor’s center adjacent to the site. Although Declaration House has been closed to visitors since 2013, there are plans to refurbish and improve the structure in time for the Semiquincentennial in 2026.
 All Roads Lead to 7th Street? 
 The rebuilt Declaration House upon completion in 1975. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 If the corner of 7th and Market Streets is a microcosm of Philadelphia, Monument Lab director Paul Farber is convinced that 7th Street from Walnut to Race Streets is Philadelphia’s archetypal street. Consider the wealth of cultural sites (PhillyCam, WHYY, the African American Museum of Philadelphia), retail establishments ( Jewelers' Row , Lit Brothers), city buildings (the Independence Branch of Free Library, Constitution High School), and federal sites (the Federal Reserve Bank, the James A. Byrne United States Courthouse, and a federal detention center unfortunately sited across from the African American Museum).
 7th Street also contains two of our most controversial, yet promising empty buildings: the former Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) and the now-vacant Philadelphia History Museum at the Atwater Kent. This stretch from Washington Square to Franklin Square touches on Washington Square West, Market East, Old City, Chinatown, and Center City, but it is not fully part of any of these neighborhoods. Should the proposed Philadelphia 76ers arena ever be built, the 7th Street corridor promises to transform in ways yet to be seen.
 African Americans in Old Philadelphia 
 John Trumbull's 1819 painting, The Declaration of Independence, July 4, 1776 . | Image courtesy of Yale University Art Gallery
 The Declaration House project is about so much more than its historic location. The colossal eyes gazing out are sending a message about reversing centuries of intentional erasure. Our collective view of the signing of the Declaration of Independence looks something like the image above. What we don’t see is that the hallways and outdoor areas just beyond this room would have been populated with enslaved people ready to attend to the needs of the delegates who had brought them to this city. 41 of the 56 men who signed the Declaration of Independence were enslavers.
 Black people had been on the shores of the Delaware River since before the arrival of William Penn. By 1776, Philadelphia had many Black residents. The area we now call Washington Square was a potter’s field and a community gathering place for both the enslaved majority and the less numerous free Black people. The Forten family, for example, had been in Philadelphia for four generations and was able to garner a bit of wealth by working at the busy Delaware River port. Nine-year-old James Forten , who had been educated at the Friends’ African School, was present when the Declaration of Independence was read aloud in public for the first time. Forten went on to serve in the Continental Army, run a highly successful sailmaking business, and become a financial and moral leader of the Black community.
 By the time Jefferson returned to Philadelphia in the 1790s to serve as Secretary of State in George Washington’s cabinet, the city was not only the national capital, but was also emerging as the national center of free Black life. Hemmings’ brother James was accompanying Jefferson at this time, and he would certainly have seen and interacted with members of the city’s vibrant, ambitious, and growing Black community.
 Making the Invisible, Visible 
 A 1955 advertisement for Dromedary pound cake mix perpetuates a whitewashed version of Monticello, the home of Thomas and Martha Jefferson. | Image: Etsy
 Jefferson’s image is widespread and well-known. It graces our nickel, the $2 bill, and many public buildings including the Market Street side of the Declaration House annex. Of Hemmings, there is no likeness. Disparity exists in the written record as well. Historians have access to over 50,000 letters written by Jefferson. There are only four known letters written by people he enslaved. (During the time the Declaration House project was underway, the marriage certificate of Hemmings' daughter was discovered, revealing his signature. That is why I am spelling his last name as Hemmings, while using the more common Hemings for the rest of his family.) Black people outnumbered whites in and around Monticello by a factor of about 11 to one, but mainstream historical narratives long strained to portray Jefferson’s home, the only private home on U.S. currency, as a white space. There is a stark asymmetry between Black and white images, words, and presence in popular history surrounding Jefferson. These multiple and extreme imbalances in Jeffersonian history are emblematic of the challenges we face in trying to get a more inclusive view of our nation’s history.
 By using the eyes of the descendants of Monticello in her work, Clark admonishes us to remember that Black people have been a part of the American story since long before the creation of the United States. The work also reminds us that Jefferson’s mountaintop home, like so much of the country’s wealth, was built by enslaved labor. The oversized, watchful eyes in the Declaration House windows bid us to broaden and to complicate our understanding of the founding generation. Like Hamilton: The Musical, the Declaration House exhibition provokes us to picture groups of people well beyond a bunch of white men in wigs and britches as being integral to the story of American independence.
 The Hemingses of Monticello 
 A photograph from the early 1900s of Monticello. | Photo courtesy of Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 While Declaration House asks us to think about the absence of Black people in the standard American historical narrative in general, it also speaks specifically to the families enslaved by Jefferson.
 Jefferson, who had been attended to by enslaved people since childhood, claimed to despise the institution, but he never hated it enough to rise above his own self-interest as a large landholder. One way he assuaged his conscience was by the favorable, albeit complicated, treatment he showed the Hemings family.
 The matriarch, Elizabeth Hemings, came to Monticello following the death of Jefferson’s father-in-law, John Wayles. Accompanying her were her children, six of whom were fathered by Wayles. Members of the Hemings family were simultaneously Jefferson’s in-laws and his property. As such, they were set apart from the scores of other enslaved people that Jefferson owned and inherited from his father-in-law.
 As they became young men, Elizabeth’s sons Robert and James Hemings were trained in skilled trades, a barber and a chef, respectively, permitted to work for wages they could keep, and allowed to come and go as they pleased. These privileges were conditional: the brothers had to be willing to serve Jefferson when he asked. Robert and James were the only two people Jefferson freed during his lifetime, although Jefferson was deeply hurt by Robert’s request for freedom. It was with great reluctance that he allowed his erstwhile manservant to live permanently with his wife in Richmond rather than to remain tied to Jefferson at Monticello.
 A Family Secret 
 Artist Sonya Clark in front of her installation "The Descendants of Monticello" at Independence National Historical Park. | Photo: Steve Weinik for Monument Lab
 The best known of Elizabeth’s children, of course, was Sally Hemings. Years after the death of his wife, Jefferson had six children with Sally, his wife’s half-sister who was 30 years his junior. Four of their children lived to adulthood. Where this relationship sits on the continuum between rape and a loving connection will never be fully understood. Their two oldest children left Monticello as young adults and lived the rest of their lives as white people. The two younger children were freed in Jefferson’s will, fulfilling a pledge he had made to Sally Hemings decades earlier when their intimate liaison began.
 Jefferson, a profligate spender with a taste for luxury, was perpetually in debt. At the time of his death, 90 percent of his wealth was in his human property. Thus, unlike Jefferson’s offspring, the other people enslaved at Monticello were sold and scattered as his executors settled his estate.
 Not surprisingly, Jefferson’s white descendants did not acknowledge that they shared an ancestor with members of the Hemings family. Repudiation of the Jefferson-Hemings bond by family members, scholars, and the public hardened through the decades as Founding Fathers mythology proliferated.
 "The Descendants of Monticello" is on view at Declaration House until September 8. | Photo: Steve Weinik for Monument Lab
 In 1998, however, science got in the way of these denials when DNA evidence showed a link between Jefferson and the Hemings family. In the 2008 Pulitzer Prize and National Book Award winning The Hemingses of Monticello, Annette Gordon-Reed put her degrees in both law and history to work to prove beyond a doubt that Sally Hemings bore Jefferson’s children.
 Although the Thomas Jefferson Historical Society was founded in 2000 to continue the fight to deny Jefferson’s paternity, the 21st century has mostly seen widespread acknowledgement of the Hemingses’ blood ties to the Jefferson family. Monument Lab’s partners at Monticello and Getting Word are leaders in bringing these formerly concealed stories to light. Their work leads us to wrestle with the enormous complexity, the deep connections, and the profound contradictions that are embodied in the gigantic eyes currently in the windows of Declaration House.
 The official closing date for "The Descendants of Monticello" installation has been extended to December 1. The interactive Declaration House exhibition ends September 6. If you go between noon and 5 p.m. Friday through Sunday, step into the courtyard where you can get more information and can also express what the Declaration of Independence means to you. Responses will be shared with the National Park Service. View the eyes projection any evening after dark for the next three months when the display reaches its full power. At the very least, make sure you pass by this remarkable Philadelphia crossroads and get a glance of a powerful, memorable work.
 Tags: African-American history art exhibition Declaration House Monument Lab public art slavery Thomas Jefferson 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Wish You Were Here: 30 Years Later, the Sears Tower Lives on in Our Memories
author: Edward W. Duffy
bodyText:
The massive Sears complex on Roosevelt Boulevard was imploded in 1994. | Photo courtesy of Langan
 On October 31, 1994 the Sears Eastern Regional Catalogue Headquarters on Roosevelt Boulevard was imploded. This ended the 74-year reign of the complex and its 14-story clock tower as the gateway to Northeast Philadelphia.
 Yet, its memory lives on in the minds of the thousands of Philadelphians who worked or shopped there. Some vestiges remain as well. Its power plant's chimney serving as a billboard for Home Depot, one of the stores in the shopping center that replaced it, and its fire station, a miniature of the old Sears headquarters that serves and protects the surrounding Oxford Circle community.
 Memories remain especially strong among former employees because Sears cultivated its morale with its own house newspaper, the Sears News – Graphic , an "all employees picture newspaper." Employees were encouraged by the company to feel like they belonged to an extended family. Sears prided itself on promoting from within, and its officers and Sears owners, the Rosenwald family, were on a first name basis with many of the workers.
 An aerial view of the Northeast Philadelphia Sears Tower complex in 1939. | Photo: Public Domain
 Sears, originally Sears, Roebuck and Company, focused on catalogue marketing to farm households. When the economic Panic of 1893 set in, Roebuck sold his interest in the firm to Julius Rosenwald, a Chicago clothing manufacturer who was one of their larger creditors. By 1908, Rosenwald had become the company's president and Sears prospered under his leadership. In 1919, Julius decided to expand the company's catalogue business to Philadelphia and sent his son Lessing Rosenwald to scout out a suitable location. Lessing identified a 120-acre farm located ideally at the junction of two railroads, the Pennsylvania and the Reading, which would compete for Sears' business with their best possible services and freight rates. Philadelphia was the site of Sears' fourth mail order facility. The company would eventually have 14 of them with Philadelphia being its second largest in facility with over 5,000,000 square feet of space, second in sales volume, and employing 7,000.
 Lessing stayed on in Philadelphia as the mail order facility's general manager from its opening in 1920 until 1929. He eventually became the chairman of Sears from 1932 until 1939. After 1939, Lessing devoted his life to collecting rare books and art and managing the family charity. In 1941, he donated 2,600 rare books to the Library of Congress and prints and drawings to the National Gallery of Art. These came from his collection housed in the gallery wing of his home, Alverthorpe Manor, that he had built in Jenkintown in 1939. Lessing's family charity was a major benefactor making fellowship grants to African American artists, writers, researchers, and intellectuals and to various Jewish charities. 
 A rendering of a new Sears, Roebuck & Co. retail store planned for Roosevelt Boulevard next to the Sears Tower complex. The building was designed by Ballinger Co. and opened for business on August 10, 1955. | Image courtesy of Image courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 Sears branched out into department store retail sales and added a location the Philadelphia mail order plant in October 1925. This was the company's fifth outlet. 30 years later, Sears built a stand-alone three story department store within the Roosevelt Boulevard complex.
 The grand opening of this new store on August 10, 1955 occurred near the peak of Sears' success as America's largest retailer, with 400,000 employees and $19 billion in annual sales. The opening was the occasion for a grand celebration with the company's chairman cutting the ribbon. Lessing returned as the event's honored guest and renewed acquaintances with many who knew him as their former boss while chatting with many long-service employees. That day the new store's 1,100 employees served 30,000 customers.
 Left: The smokestack of Sears' former power station is now a billboard for Home Depot. Right: Engine 70 at 4800 Langdon Street was designed to resemble the old Sears Tower. | Photos: Ed Duffy
 The company's catalogue sales gradually declined as big box discount stores like Walmart and Kmart spread across the United States. Sears issued its final general catalogue in 1993. After the Philadelphia mail order plant's 1994 implosion, 48 acres of the property were redeveloped as a shopping center and the remaining 72 acres were sold to Cardone Industries, a successful aftermarket auto parts manufacturer. Improvements to Cardone's new site consisted in part of shifting the demolition debris of the Sears tower into the abandoned Pennsylvania Railroad cut that separated its warehouses from Whitaker Avenue, providing the company with direct access there. T he bricks used in constructing the Sears tower were manufactured less than a mile away at the Keystone Brick Company. The 132-acre brickyard was sold to the United States government for a naval aviation supply facility during World War II. In the end, the bricks were returned to the earth from which they came.
 Tags: demolition Northeast Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Edward W. Duffy is the author of "Philadelphia: A Railroad History" (Camino Books, 2013) and "Philadelphia Celebrates: Three Great Anniversaries - 1876-1926-1976" (Camino Books, 2017).

title: A Victory in Villanova: Oakwell Will be Saved
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
The grounds of the Oakwell estate were designed over a 50-year period by landscape architects the Olmsted Brothers The legendary firm designed New York City’s Central Park, the grounds of Biltmore Estate in Asheville, North Carolina, the U.S. Capitol grounds in Washington, D.C, and F.D.R. Park in Philadelphia. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Philadelphia's Main Line gave a communal sigh of relief this week. The six-year debacle between the Lower Merion School District (LMSD) and preservationists over the fate of Oakwell, an historic estate, was finally resolved. Seemingly, everyone involved won.
 LMSD made the decision to not turn Oakwell's heirloom forest into a middle school playing field. Instead, it has agreed to sell Oakwell to Natural Lands, a non-profit that connects people with the environment. “We are thrilled to have the opportunity to expand Stoneleigh and are immensely grateful to the leadership of the Lower Merion School District,” said Natural Lands president Oliver Bass.
 This historic reunification refers back to 1877 when a Pennsylvania Railroad executive purchased 65 acres in Lower Merion, named it Stoneleigh, and hired the most famous landscape architects of the day, the Olmstead Brothers. In 1919, when the owner gifted a portion of the estate to his son, it became known as Oakwell. Now, both Oakwell and Stoneleigh will be reunited and protected by Natural Lands.
 The Oakwell estate’s mansion was built was built in 1922. It was designed by architect William Wayne, Jr. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Samantha Chapman can see the trees of the Oakwell estate from her office window at Villanova University. "I'm just ecstatic. You can't estimate the biodiversity benefit to our community," she said. As a biology professor and co-director of Villanova's Center for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Stewardship (CBEST), Chapman and her students have been deeply invested in the preservation of Oakwell since LMSD first seized the historic 13.4 acre estate by eminent domain in 2018. When you are the wealthiest school district in the state and one of the richest in the nation, you can do things like that with impunity. However, LMSD did not count on the push back from the community–not just from the faculty and students of Villanova, but from area residents, parents, teachers, students, lawyers, conservationists, preservationists, ornithologists, architects, and, yes, journalists.
 For years, Deb Robbins stood in front of LMSD's administration building for "Fire Drill Friday Protests" with a group of concerned neighbors holding signs that read, "Honk if you want to save trees!" A founding member of Save Oakwell , Robbins can finally put down her sign. "It has been terrific to see the most recent school board and superintendent respond thoughtfully to the concerns of the students and community. Decisions made a few climates ago, as it were, may no longer be in the best interests of the kids or their planet," said Robbins. She was referring to the leadership of Dr. Steven Yanni, who became superintendent of LMSD in August 2023. After listening to both sides, he steered the Oakwell dispute to an environmental victory.
 From November 2022 until LMSD fenced off Oakwell at the end of May 2023, Jamie Singer, a communications consultant and board member of the Ardmore Historic Society, led free Sunday tours of Oakwell. "I am thankful that Oakwell will not only be saved, but will thrive under Natural Lands’ guidance. This is the resolution we’d hoped for—that Stoneleigh and Oakwell are reunited and will provide the history, environment, and biodiversity that will benefit generations to come," said Singer.
 Oakwell’s historic greenhouse complex was once used as an educational site for a horticultural training program for women. During WWII it was used to cultivate victory gardens. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Erin Betley, a conservation biologist, Lower Merion resident, and mother of LMSD students, views the outcome through a historic lens. "Before it was subdivided from the Stoneleigh estate, Oakwell was the home of an early horticultural school for young women. How fitting that over a century later, this biodiverse landscape will once again be a place of learning about sustainability and resilience for our community and in the capable hands of Natural Lands."
 Kathleen M. Abplanalp, director of historic preservation at Lower Merion Conservancy, is enthusiastic about her organization's collaboration with Natural Lands to establish a conservation easement on the Oakwell property. "This effort will help preserve a significant historic landscape and reconnect it with Stoneleigh. The partnership reflects a shared commitment to protecting and enhancing local natural and historic resources for future generations."
 James D. McLaughlin, an international corporate attorney and Lower Merion resident, laid the blame with LMSD's Board of Directors. "The upcoming sale by LMSD to Natural Lands represents a victory for community action against an entrenched Board that had refused to listen to its taxpayers opposed to the Board's ridiculous desire to misappropriate taxpayer funds by wasting them on needless sports facilities and environmental destruction. The Board has a long way to go in terms of its own re-education.
 The Stoneleigh mansion and grounds were gifted to Natural Lands by former owner Otto Haas’ family in 2016. The public garden is open and free to visitors. The sale of Oakwell to Natural Lands will reunify the two estates. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Another attorney, Philip Rosenzweig of Silverang, Rosenzweig & Haltzman, LLC, believes the outcome was due not so much to the school board or the honking of horns on Montgomery Avenue, but to one woman. "I want to express gratitude that LMSD did the right thing and everyone wins," said Rosenzweig. "However, I believe that everyone in Lower Merion owes a debt of gratitude to Kelly Biesecker. Her property is adjacent to Oakwell, and she single-handedly funded the legal the fight against the school district for three years. She was passionate about preserving the ecology of Oakwell and was willing to spend thousands to do so. Had she not created the zoning appeal there is no way LMSD would've been willing to sell. I am in awe of her!" he said.
 If you are planning to visit Oakwell, be patient. It is not open to the public yet. "Oakwell is currently still owned by LMSD," said Kit Werner, senior director of communications of Natural Lands. "We have several hurdles to clear before Natural Lands takes ownership, which would likely be at the end of 2025." In the meantime, visit Stoneleigh, a Natural Garden next door at 828 County Line Road in Villanova. Admission is free and it is open Tuesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.
 Tags: Lower Merion Oakwell Olmsted Brothers suburbs Villanova 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: Disston Mansion, Time Capsule of North Philly’s Gilded Age, Heads to Auction
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The former mansion of Albert H. Disston at 1530 N. 16th Street in North Philadelphia. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At 4:30 a.m. on October 21, 1883, Albert H. Disston took his last breath somewhere in the confines of his dizzying mansion in North Philadelphia. A scion of the world-renowned Disston Saw Works family, Disston was just 34. He left behind a wife, three children, and the four-story, late-Victorian behemoth Disston had completed and moved into just months prior.
 Some 140 years later, the Disston empire is all but gone and the rest of the industrialist-fed opulence of North Philadelphia much faded. However, a well-preserved time capsule in the form of Disston’s 1530 N. 16th Street mansion is still available and freshly back on the market for the right price.
 The property will go up for auction on Wednesday, August 28, its first sale since 1946 when the home entered the real estate portfolio of Father Divine’s International Peace Mission Movement . A week prior to its sale, auctioneer Barry S. Slosberg Inc. opened the residence’s doors for inspection, giving members of the public and media an opportunity to take in the estate’s splendiferous interior. “It’s an incredible property,” said Alan Le Coff, an associate for Slosberg overseeing the auction. “It’s about 95 percent intact.”
 The radiant foyer of the Disston Mansion. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Spanning more than 40 rooms, much of the mansion’s original grandeur is indeed still apparent. According to Slosberg, the home was built for a cost exceeding $150,000, which amounts to around $4.7 million today. It shows. Every nook and cranny of the home’s main floor–dominated by a living room, dining room, foyer, and parlor–drips with gold leaf, marble flooring, hand-carved oak trim, and soaring doors, mural ceilings, and crystal chandeliers. Along the southern side of the home runs an old carriageway with an elevated marble platform emanating from the house to greet disembarking passengers. Across an interior foyer is a centrally-located staircase leading to labyrinth-like upper floors where rich woodwork continues to abound, wowing lay and expert visitors alike.
 “The Disston House remains a singular testament to one of Philadelphia's premier manufacturing fortunes,” noted historian Donna Rilling in her extensive survey of the home for the Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS) filed in 2000. “It is one of the few surviving mansions built for the city's industrial and professional elite in this vicinity and is a contributing property to the North Broad Street Mansion Historic District .”
 However, the home bears some signs of its age. A two-story rear addition built in the 1920s shows wear and evidence of water damage, particularly on the second level where its floor has begun to buckle. Plaster and paint have given way to exposed substructure in places throughout the residence. Yet, all together, the stewardship of the Peace Mission has left the Disston Mansion an intact and awe-inspiring structure awaiting what comes next.
 He Came. He Sawed. He Conquered. 
 An undated portrait of American saw maker extraordinaire Henry Disston. | Image courtesy of The Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 Henry Disston, father of Albert, was born in 1819 England to a machinist father and died in Philadelphia in 1878 as the progenitor of what would become the largest saw manufacturing operation in the world, the Disston Saw Works once located in Tacony .
 According to a history of the man and his company compiled by “historic handsaw aficionado” Erik von Sneidern, Disston’s arrival at age 14 was fraught with hardship from the get go. He was orphaned when his father died three days after their arrival, according to a family history and then suffered decades of unfortuitous apprenticeships, business ventures, and further personal tragedies.
 However, Disston's fortunes changed by the middle of the century. In 1855, he became the first saw manufacturer to also make his own steel. The real boon arrived with the Civil War. The Morrill Tariff Act of 1861 placed high tariffs on foreign imports including steel, helping Disston to corner the domestic market. Profits further rolled in when he sold steel tools to the Union during the Civil War. In the postwar years, Disston and his five sons continued to grow the business. In the 1870s, they began purchasing tracts in Northeast Philadelphia to build a massive saw works and empire that would see the company reportedly gain a 75 percent market share of American hand saw sales by the 20th century.
 An 1884 engraving showing Disston & Sons Saw Works in Tacony. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 Albert Disston, Henry’s second son born in 1849, did not get to enjoy the family fortune for long. Historical narratives and records offer comparatively little information on Albert. A Central High School graduate with an apparent talent for finance, he worked for several years in the company’s accounting department before officially joining as partner in 1871, precipitating a company name change to Henry Disston & Sons. Other historical records of the 1870s list him as among the directors of the Philadelphia Fire Insurance Company, suggesting financial activity outside of the family business, and also name him as a regular racer of yachts along the Delaware River.
 Other records suggest he was a “financial whiz” capable of quickly adding up sums over multiple columns of a spreadsheet, and his 1883 obituary noted Albert was indeed "Chiefly remarkable for his ability as a financier. A large portion of the responsibility for the monetary affairs of the great saw works was his… and of late years his control has been undivided,” it added. Whatever his exact role in the company, it is obvious from the opulence of the 16th Street mansion that Albert shared in its fortunes.
 “A Handsome Marble Residence” 
 An architectural drawing of the east elevation of 1530 North 16th Street. | Image courtesy of Historic American Buildings Survey
 Like contemporary Philadelphia, Albert Disston’s efforts to build arrived at a time of some distress in the marketplace. To design and build his mansion, Disston tapped notable architect Edwin F. Durang, most known for his Catholic churches and schools, including both St. Joseph’s Prep and Roman Catholic. In a May 1882 edition of The Philadelphia Inquirer , the newspaper reported that the city’s “hesitating builders” were delaying construction of properties due to high prices of supplies and labor. Among those interviewed was Durang, who mentioned that, in addition to work for churches and hospitals, he was working on “building a handsome marble residence for Albert Disston at Sixteenth and Oxford.”
 A Philadelphia Register of Historic Places nomination from 1982, which included the Disston Mansion and 14 other properties on its block, noted their significance in the “architectural and social heritage” of North Philadelphia. According to the document, a collection of independently designed homes on the block in the late 1800s proclaimed “to the world that the residents within belonged to a new managerial class created by the industrial revolution and resulting commercial boom.”
 The Disston mausoleum at Laurel Hill Cemetery was built in 1879 with blue Westerly granite by Smith Granite Company. The freestanding French Renaissance monument on Millionaires Row cost $60,000 and took over 12 stonecutters to construct. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The interior design of the Disston Mansion fell to George Herzog, a Munich-born emigree best known for his interior work at the Philadelphia Masonic Temple and within the homes of other well-to-do Philadelphians of the time, including Peter A. B. Widener and William Lukens Elkins. “The relative restraint of [the building’s] Italianate facade and exterior detailing gives no hint to the deeply complex and sumptuous interior appointments, some of only a handful still surviving that are attributed to George Herzog,” notes the HABS survey .
 Disston’s October 1883 obituary suggested the home was completed and occupied only a month prior to his demise. The listed cause of death was bizarre: a “slight sprain of the ankle” suffered in Atlantic City three weeks prior led to a localized case of gout, which then “spread rapidly” until it reached his stomach, after which Disston quickly succumbed. His funeral was held days later in the parlor of the 16th Street mansion, which The Inquirer reported was attended by “many prominent gentlemen” including “ex-mayors, councilmen, and a number of members of the bar.” A procession was led to Laurel Hill Cemetery, where Disston was interred in the family’s mausoleum, one of the largest monuments within the cemetery.
 Divine Life After Death 
 1530 N. 16th Street in 1926 after The Progress Club purchased it to use as a clubhouse. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 Historical records indicate that after Disston’s demise, the possession of his mansion fell to his wife, Kate Ellen Disston. In 1896, 13 years after Albert’s death, the widow remarried with ceremonies held within the mansion. Four years later, their daughter, Florence Disston, was also married in the home, according to The Philadelphia Times . “The ceremony was performed in the drawing room, which was entirely in white, a small impromptu altar having been erected at the side of the room amidst a profusion of flowers,” while a string orchestra played nearby, the newspaper reported.
 While the family still possessed the home, renovations were made. Most notably, in 1906, the firm of Hale & Kilburn was retained to construct a third story room. Although the firm specialized in “decorations and railway car seats,” and seemed “an odd choice,” the HABS survey notes that the company’s president Henry S. Hale was a neighbor to members of the Disston family and that his firm also manufactured “fancy walnut trim” such as that used in the renovation.
 The home would leave the family in May 1920, when Jacob S. Disston dispensed with a pair of properties. The 16th Street mansion went to the Progress Club, which The Philadelphia Times described as a “well-known up-town social organization.” The club immediately made its mark on the property, contracting for the construction of a two-story “palm room” to the rear of the property. The following February, The Inquirer reported a lavish house-warming for the organization with 2,000 attendees filling the mansion’s confines.
 1530 N. 16th Street on October 10, 1932 when police seized two kegs and four half-barrels of beer at The Progress Club during Prohibition. | Photo courtesy of Image courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 According to the 1982 Philadelphia Register nomination, the arrival of the Progress Club came during an era of transition for the neighborhood, when white protestant families left the area and a Jewish community took root, “led by members of the Blumenthal, Ginsberg, Schwartz, and Wolf families.” Indeed, a March 1923 article in The Inquirer noted that several hundred prominent members of the Jewish community were to gather at the Progress Club over dinner and plan the reception of Chaim Weizmann, a biochemist and political leader who assisted with the creation of the 1917 Balfour Declaration and later became the first president of a newly-established Israel.
 The club’s run at the Disston Mansion was relatively short-lived. In 1931, the building passed from the club to the Blumenthal family. An August 1935 notice in The Inquirer reported the Blumenthals then sold the property to the Bible Institute of Pennsylvania, a Christian educational institution now known as Cairn University and located in Bucks County, for $40,000. Additional newspaper records indicate the Disston Mansion served as the institution’s primary headquarters, with commencement day exercises held in its auditorium.
 Father Divine arrives in Philadelphia in 1939. | Photo courtesy of Image courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 However, the mansion would find true stability a decade later when, in 1946, the Unity Mission Church Home and Training School, a church within the International Peace Mission movement of Father Divine, purchased the property. The Peace Mission, whose heyday peaked in the 1930s, used its robust resources to purchase numerous real estate holdings during the mid-20th century. The organization’s website suggests the property was used for numerous purposes. “Here Bible classes are held for all desiring to attend. A large auditorium classroom and a beautiful spacious Holy Communion Dining Room are maintained, as well as a Rectory for the Dean.” Le Coff added that he understands the mansion was used as a sort of bible study and training facility, with the former palm room used as a banquet space, and, at one point, was also zoned for 15 boarding rooms.
 Yet, as the Peace Mission’s membership diminished over the decades, the organization has divested various real estate holdings, the most recognizable among them the Divine Lorraine at Broad Street and Fairmount Avenue. Le Coff said his company has more recently auctioned other holdings for the organization, including the Lippincott Mansion at 507 S. Broad Street and the Ellis Mansion at 1430 N. Broad Street . Members of the Peace Mission continued to occupy the Disston mansion until just several years ago Le Coff has been told.
 After the likely sale of the Disston home, the organization’s properties in the region appear to have shrunk to just two: the crown jewel Woodmont Estate in Gladwyne , and the Circle Mission Church Home and Training School at Broad and Catherine Streets .
 1530 N. 16th Street under the ownership of Unity Mission Church in 1963. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 Despite the dwindling assets, those in the historical preservation community say the organization has remained a superb steward of its properties. The HABS survey notes the organization repaired the Disston Mansion’s stained glass windows in 1984. Le Coff said that 17 of 19 current such windows are certified. Two were stolen about five years ago, but later tracked down by the FBI. The Peace Mission also repaired and restored a dining room fireplace in 1991.
 “It’s an incredibly well preserved, over the top Victorian residential confection,” said Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 As for its future, Le Coff expects about a dozen potential buyers, although the Peace Mission has a right to reject even the highest bidder. His firm has largely cleaned out from the building about 30 boxes of memorabilia from the Peace Mission era, including the removal of a portrait of Father Divine from the home’s main foyer and restoration of an original mirror and woodwork in its place. He has some guesses about what could come next. “There’s a variety of possible uses, from a bed and breakfast, to apartments, to condos, to some type of entity, educational or social,” said Le Coff.
 A look inside Disston Mansion on North 16th Street. Photographs by Michael Bixler.
 Tags: Father Divine mansions North Philadelphia Victorian architecture 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Two Philly Institutions Celebrate Anniversaries with an Exhibit on Puerto Rican History
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Philadelphia has seen numerous waves of immigration from different countries and cultures over the course of its history, including a large number from Puerto Rico after World War II. “We have to start before that, back to the Spanish American War," to fully consider the city’s relationship with Puerto Rico, noted Selena Bemak, programs and communications coordinator at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP).
 That is where a new exhibit, HSP 200 + Taller 50: Uncovering and Preserving Puerto Rican Stories begins, with the 1898 conflict that yielded Cuba’s independence and the United States' acquisition of Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines.
 A 1915 bulletin published by the Capilla Católica Hispana de la Medalla Milagrosa (Spanish Chapel of Our Lady of the Miraculous Medal). | Image courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 During that war, Major General John Rutter Brooke served as military governor of Puerto Rico. “He was beloved by the islanders,” said Bemak. “After the war, he was offered the governorship, but had to decline it because he was reassigned to the military governorship of Cuba.” He was a Pottstown native who led troops in the Civil War, including the battles of Gettysburg and Antietem, as well as the 1890 massacre at Wounded Knee. After his retirement, Brooke lived in Philadelphia and donated his papers to HSP, which contain a wealth of documentation of the city’s relationship with the island at that time.
 The Brooke papers were just one of the sources the curators mined for the exhibit. “A lot of items came from the Balch Institute,” Bemak said, referring to the Philadelphia organization that had collected materials on several ethnic groups in the United States and merged into HSP in 2002. “I was pleasantly surprised to find so much material in so many places.” Another fruitful source was the Jane Campbell Collection, an exhaustive set of over 100 scrapbooks of Philadelphia newspaper clippings, postcards, and photographs compiled between 1890 and 1921.
 Domingo Negron’s mother, sisters, nieces, and nephew pose on Mother's Day with a picture of President John F. Kennedy in the background. Circa 1960s. | Image courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 Puerto Rican migration to the mainland increased with the Jones–Shafroth Act of 1917, which conveyed citizenship to Puerto Ricans. “The main driving factor of Puerto Rican migration was employment,” explained Bemak. At the time, Philadelphia was home to industries that were familiar to Puerto Ricans, including cigar manufacturing, sugar refining, and the garment industry. “Until the 1950s, Philadelphia had a prominent cigar business presence,” said Bemak. “It made for an easy transition from the island.”
 “One of my favorite items in the exhibit is our Eisenlohr cigar box,” noted Masada Devine Melendez, the archivist for Taller Puertorriqueno. The Otto Eisenlohr & Brothers, Inc. was founded in Philadelphia in 1850, with the “Cinco” cigar being their most popular product. A rival, the Bayuk Cigar Company, came along in 1896, whose best-known product, the "Philadelphia Hand Made" is still made, as the "Phillies” brand.
 As Puerto Ricans arrived and gained employment in these industries, they settled near the work in Kensington, Northern Liberties, and Spring Garden. This knowledge of the kind of work Puerto Ricans did and the neighborhoods they gravitated to helped Bemak hone her search for items.
 This ceremony in 1977 led by the Spanish Merchants Association celebrates the revitalization of North 5th Street, known as El Bloque de Oro (Golden Block). The man on the far left is Nelson Diaz, the first Puerto Rican to graduate from Temple University's Law School (1972). Diaz went on to have a distinguished legal career, serving as a Philadelphia Common Pleas judge, city solicitor, and general counsel at the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development during the Clinton administration. | Image courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 The exhibit also highlights the post-war migration surge of the 1950s. At that time, much of the Puerto Rican community moved north, creating the 5th Street corridor known as El Bloque de Oro (the Golden Block) from about York Street to Allegheny Avenue. That coincided with the founding of civic and cultural organizations, including Concilio, the Council of Spanish Speaking Organizations in 1964 and Taller Puertorriqueno in 1974. In its inaugural year, Concilio sponsored a Puerto Rican Week Festival, which was the precursor to the annual Puerto Rican Day Parade, which it still hosts.
 For this exhibit, the collections of the two collaborating organizations complemented each other. While HSP owns an exhaustive archive of documents, “We have an artifact collection and an art collection,” said Devine Melendez. Examples from Taller’s Eugenio Maria de Hostos Archives include Vejigante masks and maracas made from coconuts, Taino carved clay objects, and carvings of Puerto Rico’s distinctive coqui frogs. “It’s a natural match,” said Justina Barrett, HSP’s chief learning and engagement officer. “They’re not an archive, but they understand what we’re doing.”
 Of particular note is a display about a 1979 Taller oral history project, called Batiendo la Olla, or Stirring the Pot. The 65 interviews resulted in a book documenting the variety of Puerto Rican experience in Philadelphia, with some participants who were born on the island and came to Philadelphia, others were Philadelphia born, and still others returned to the island after being here. The original tapes reside in Taller’s archive, and some appear in the HSP online exhibit Neighbors/Vecinos . “As part of our anniversary celebration, we’re going to create a new edit of the book and also have some new interviews,” said Devine Melendez.
 Millito u su Nuevo Sonido plays a show at Mario’s Continental Lounge, 268 N. Ontario Street, in 1984. Musicians include [back left] Freddy Banchs (bass), left to right – Jose Figeroa (campana), Willie Aponte (bata) seated, Millito Velasques (cantante singer, director, guiro), and Nasario de Jesus (guitar). | Image courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
This collaboration is the fourth in HSP’s year-long celebration of its 200th anniversary. “We centered it around five themes from our strategic plan,” explained Justina Barrett, director of education and programs at HSP, with this exhibit representing the theme “America’s Promise and Its Many Voices.”
 A workshop entitled “Peopling Pennsylvania: Puerto Rican Ancestors” will be held on September 24. On September 26, HSP will present a lecture by journalist Juan Gonzalez, co-host of the news program Democracy Now! entitled “From Puerto Rico to Pennsylvania: History, Challenges, and Amor Boricua.”
 HSP 200 + Taller 50: Uncovering and Preserving Puerto Rican Stories is on display at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, 1300 Locust Street, through October 11. The free exhibit is open Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Fridays from 10:00 a.m. until 4:00 p.m. and Wednesdays from 1:00 until 7:00 p.m.
 Tags: Hispanic heritage Historical Society of Pennsylvania Immigrants 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: 50 Years of Social Justice Through the Lens of Harvey Finkle
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
Steve Robertson Advocating for More Health Care Funding for the Disabled, Harrisburg, 1992. | Photo: Harvey Finkle via Woodmere Art Museum
 Visitors to Woodmere Art Museum's new photography exhibition, In the Moment: The Art & Photography of Harvey Finkle , will not be able to trust their eyes. An image of a mother tossing her toddler in the air appears to be a beach scene. It's not. A man shouldering a huge American flag seems to be sitting on a bench. He isn't. Photographs that look as if they were taken in Kensington yesterday are actually from the 1990s. In all, these stunning black and white images showcase a 50-year career of social documentary photography that almost didn't occur.
 "I grew up at the end of the world," said Finkle , referring to Oxford Circle in Northeast Philadelphia when it was bordered by farmland. Born in 1934 into a working class Jewish family, Finkle never had the luxury of considering photography as a profession. After serving two years in the Army and graduating from Temple University, he got a job as a case worker for the City's Welfare Department.
 AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power (ACT UP) Demonstration for AIDS Funding , 1990s. | Photo: Harvey Finkle via Woodmere Art Museum
 Finkle first picked up a camera in his mid-30s in 1968 to record the birth of his first child. Yet, as a social worker and an activist deeply concerned by the poverty and injustice he witnessed every day, he began carrying a small Leica CL camera everywhere he went. It’s a quiet camera that could focus quickly. Finkle could walk into crowds of people or enter their homes and take pictures largely unnoticed.
 Another social worker may have been denied access, but Finkle's warm personality opened every door. "He's the sweetest guy in the world, exceedingly patient and thoughtful," said Antongiulio Sorgini, guest curator of the exhibition. "Harvey earned the trust of the people he photographed, going to their tent cities with blessings from the group. His images have a slow fuse to them, revealing more information the longer you look at them," explained Sorgini "For instance, it takes a while to actually see a homeless person sleeping under a cardboard box."
 Homeless, 1991. | Photo: Harvey Finkle via Woodmere Art Museum
 Mastering the art of photography didn't happen overnight. "I don't think I took a print I liked for three years," Finkle said. To hone his craft, Finkle joined a photography critique group in West Philadelphia. However, it was seeing a photo exhibition of Harry Callahan at the Museum of Modern Art in 1962 that ignited Finkle's passion for black and white photography at a time when colorful Kodachrome film reigned supreme.
 Callahan, like Finkle, was self-taught. Also like Finkle, he had a day job. Callahan worked as an engineer for Chrysler before devoting himself exclusively to photography. However, in Finkle's case, his career as a social worker, along with his lifelong advocacy for social justice, became the subject of his photography.
 Mariluz and Demitre Gonzalez, Kensington Welfare Rights Union Tent City II , Philadelphia, 1996. | Photo: Harvey Finkle via Woodmere Art Museum
 Aside from taking photos, Finkle was fascinated by the process of developing film and seeing an image come to life, a phenomenon mostly unknown in today's digital world. "I rarely cropped," he said, referring to manipulating the original image. I don't think there is one photo in the Woodmere exhibition that is cropped."
 Finkle was personally involved in almost every social justice movement that evolved in Philly, from the AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power (ACT-UP) and American Disabled for Attendant Programs Today (ADAPT) to Kensington Welfare Rights Union (KWRU) and Project HOME. If there was a protest, Finkle was there. And so was his camera.
 Indonesian Service in a Row House Mosque , Philadelphia, 2002. | Photo: Harvey Finkle via Woodmere Art Museum
 In 1958, Finkle moved his family to Bella Vista. “I liked to walk the streets and shoot in the streets," he said. Meanwhile, Finkle became involved with a grassroots association called the People’s Fund, which was founded in 1971 by a group of activists seeking to spur liberal social change by funding organizations like the National Lawyers Guild and Women United for Abortion Rights.
 Finkle went on to earn his masters degree in social work from the University of Pennsylvania, where he later established a curriculum around the aging and the elderly. He also became an activist for the deaf community following the birth of his two children, who are both deaf.
 Pete Seeger outside the Nixon Campaign Headquarters , Philadelphia, 1972. | Photo: Harvey Finkle via Woodmere Art Museum
 In 1972, he transitioned to photography full time. "I shot for organizations I knew. Labor unions, social agencies, nonprofits, hospital publications, and the occasional wedding," he said. "When digital came out, everything became immediate. Even the social change groups wanted the photos fast. So, I would take two cameras with me, one for film and one digital."
 Finkle has published numerous books of his photographs, including Urban Nomads , Still Home: Jews of South Philadelphia , Reading , Independent Living: The People Behind the Movement, Mothers , Under One Sky , and Readers . His work in the late 1980s focused on the new wave of immigrant and refugee families who have settled here and as well as the transgender movement.
 Dreamer Activists Rally at US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Headquarters , Philadelphia, 2014. | Photo: Harvey Finkle via Woodmere Art Museum
 Finkle put down his camera in 2019 when he began to lose his vision. However, at 90, he is still involved actively in exhibitions that document his involvement with social justice. He is known for his generosity, donating his photographs to the organizations he documented and, now, donating this entire exhibition to Woodmere Art Museum.
 Interestingly, the one photo in the exhibition unrelated to social concerns is Finkle's' Homage to Thomas Eakins . It shows a lone rower on the Schuylkill River enshrouded by fog. It has a quality of romanticism not found in any of his other images.. "I was driving by Strawberry Mansion Bridge. I started taking photos of the bridge and the boat appeared," he said. "It's not always planned."
 In the Moment: The Art & Photography of Harvey Finkle is on view now at the Woodmere Art Museum until January 5.
 The museum is also featuring another exhibition, The Photo Review: Best of Show 2024 . An opening reception to celebrate both exhibitions will be held Saturday, September 14 from 1-4 p.m. The event is free and open to the public.
 On Saturday, October 19, from 2-3:30 p.m., there will be a discussion of Harvey Finkle's photography. The panel will be moderated by curator Antongiulio Sorgini with commentary by Andrew Mendelson, former chair of Klein College of Communication and Media at Temple University and a professor at Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at CUNY, Cheri Honkala, co-founder of Kensington Welfare Rights Group, and Philly street photographer Zoe Strauss. Registration for the event is required. 
 Tags: documentary photography Harvey Finkle 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: A New Book Illuminates the Life and Work of a Forgotten Architect
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
For several years, a team of historians, archivists, and photographers have been working to return a forgotten architect to the historical record. Not just any architect: Minerva Parker Nichols (1862-1949) was the first woman to establish an independent architectural practice and she did that in Philadelphia.
 An exhibition at the Architectural Archives of the Weitzman School of Design at the University of Pennsylvania was presented last year, and now, a book, Minerva Parker Nichols: The Search for a Forgotten Architect, has been published. “We wanted to build an archive in the absence of one, and the book is part of that archive,” explained Molly Lester, associate director of the Urban Heritage Project at Penn Design and co-curator of the exhibit. “There are no texts out there about Minerva.” Her collaborators on the book are William Whitaker, curator and collections manager of the Architectural Archives, Heather Isbell Schumacher, archivist at the Architectural Archives, and architectural photographer Elizabeth Felicella.
 Born during the Civil War, which took her father’s life when she was an infant, Nichols' early years were spent in Peoria and Chicago, Illinois before moving to Philadelphia with her remarried mother, sister, and stepfather in 1876.
 Portrait of little-known architect Minerva Parker Nichols. Photographer unknown. | Photo courtesy of Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 In the late 19th century, college-based architectural studies were not yet well established. Apprenticeships were more the norm for entry into the profession, although unlikely to be available to many women. There were, however, institutions that offered programs in drafting, and Nichols opted to enroll in one, the Drawing School of the Franklin Institute.
 She orchestrated an extremely quick transition into her career, submitting her first entry in a design competition, acquiring an apprenticeship, and securing her first commission all within a few months of her graduation in 1886. Within three years, Nichols had established her solo practice.
 For information about her personal life, Lester turned to a memoir of sorts, called The Baddest Day . “It’s a photocopy of stories she told her grandchildren around 1944,” Lester explained. “One of them wrote them down, and another family member illustrated them. It’s the most complete record of her early life, although somewhat unofficial.”
 The Wallace Munn House at 1012-1014 Oak Lane Road is one of Minerva Parker Nichols' many residential commissions in Philadelphia. | Photo: Elizabeth Felicella
 In 1891, at the age of 29, Nichols married Unitarian clergyman William Nichols. A few years later they left Philadelphia for Brooklyn, New York and Connecticut after that. She continued to practice architecture while raising their four children, rejecting the common trend of the time for women to retire from their careers upon marrying.
 Despite practicing for only eight years in Philadelphia, she left behind a substantial body of completed work, much of which still exists today. These include buildings in Mount Airy, East Oak Lane, Germantown, Powelton Village, Overbrook, Darby, Rutledge, Wyncote, Narberth, Berwyn, and Bala Cynwyd.
 Beyond the team’s extensive research, mounting of the exhibit, and now authoring this new book, Lester says they hope others will join them in further discovery. “As I was writing, we tried to make ‘breadcrumbs’ for anyone who comes after us to see where more research might lead,” she said. “We were upfront on what we didn’t know.”
 New Century Club of Philadelphia at 124 S. 12th Street was completed in 1892 and designed by Minerva Parker Nichols. It was demolished in 1973. | Photo courtesy of Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS), Library of Congress
 One of the things that seems to remain unknown is the question of why history has overlooked Minvera Parker Nichols. It wasn’t because of her gender—she clearly was well-known and well-regarded during her career. A contributing factor may have been her emphasis on residential architecture, with only a handful of other types to her credit.
 During her lifetime she received much press coverage for her work and not merely owing to the novelty of her position. For example, in March of 1890, The Philadelphia Real Estate Record and Builders’ Guide published a front-page profile of her, the first profile of an architect it ever ran, after 220 issues. She was well-known nationally. For instance, Nichols' wedding in Philadelphia was reported in a newspaper in Lincoln, Nebraska. In addition, she herself authored many articles and columns, often in women’s magazines, but always dealing seriously with architecture.
 The new volume is several books in one: a detailed biography, an architectural catalog, and selections of Minerva’s writings. Beyond her personal biography and her architectural record, they all contribute to an interesting look at a wide swath of American cultural and social history, from the Civil War through World War II.
 “My hope is that this book would take Minerva seriously,” said Lester. “And we wanted the book to be taken seriously, not just a coffee table book.”
 Minerva Parker Nichols: The Search for a Forgotten Architect by Heather Isbell Schumacher, Molly Lester, Franca Trubiano, and William Whitaker is published by the Weitzman School of Design of the University of Pennsylvania and distributed by the Yale University Press.
 Tags: book review Minerva Parker Nichols Women's history 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: In Germantown's Food Desert a New Co-op Blooms
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
The new Weavers Way Co-op food market at 328 W. Chelten Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Weavers Way Co-op opened the doors to its fourth location on May 15. The new food market in Germantown will undoubtedly take the pressure off its smallest location in Mt. Airy, where squeezing through an aisle requires the agility of a contortionist. The 6,000 square foot space at 328 W. Chelten Avenue is large enough for customers to do wheelies with their shopping carts. It also break the barrier in one of Philadelphia's many food deserts where a 2023 study found that 29.8 percent of residents experience food insecurity.
