 Until now, there has been nowhere in Germantown to purchase organic, locally grown produce, organic meats, and vegan and vegetarian products. True, there is a Save-A-Lot, a Dollar Store, and the Chelten IGA supermarket just down the street. However, judging by Yelp reviews of all three, they leave much to be desired for consumers. And while A&N House of Produce a mile away offers rock bottom prices, none if its produce is organic and far from locally grown.
 "Market studies have shown that the Germantown community has a tremendous amount of ‘food dollar leakage'," said Weavers Way general manager, Jon Roesser. "80 percent of food consumed at home, regardless of the family's income, is being purchased outside of the neighborhood."
 The grocery shopping habits of Harry Saffren, a Germantown resident since 1978, are common. "I shop at Costco in Plymouth Meeting, Trader Joe's in Fairmount, and ShopRite in Hunting Park," he said. "With Weavers Way a half block from my house, I'll be able to walk there every day and decide what I want for dinner."
 Throughout the 1950s, Chelten Avenue was a grocery mecca with a thriving Food Fair, Penn Fruit, and Acme. In a stroke of poetic justice, the new Germantown Weavers Way will be located at the site of the old Acme, which closed in 1972. Until 2015, the property served as JEVS Human Services. The building has sat vacant since.
 An Acme Markets grocery store, seen here in 1964, occupied 328 W. Chelten Avenue until 1972. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 While the residential real estate market has picked up in Germantown, and there are a number of examples of revitalization, the arrival of Weavers Way is something of an outlier. To succeed, it has to cut across all of the neighborhood's diverse demographics, from residents of Alden Park to college students and middle class families to the retired elderly and the working poor.
 Camille Poinvil, Weavers Way's Germantown planning and outreach coordinator, isn't leaving this up to chance. For two years, along with manager James Mitchell, she has been laying the groundwork. "I've been hosting community events and workshops on mushroom cultivation and how to buy a house," said Poinvil. "I also have a table at various community events and canvasing door to door." The feedback has been enthusiastic. "People love the idea of the community ‘owning' their own grocery store," said Poinvil. "We're not Whole Foods. When you become a co-op member you are an owner. You have more power with Weavers Way than you would have with any privately-owned market."
 The Germantown store carries many of the same products found in our other Weavers Way locations, but it will also feature products made in Germantown, including Ethiopian bread and lentils from Salam Cafe, Merzbacher's bread, Ultimo coffee, and meat products from Ed Hipp in Olney.
 Like all other Weavers Way locations, it accepts EBT cards and offer a variety of discounts to low-income shoppers and seniors. If new customers take advantage of a co-op membership, they will also see costs reduced by the many different discounts available to cardholders. Just like chain supermarkets, the co-op also offers weekly deals. The new Germantown store has also applied for WIC certification, a federal program that provides free nutritional food for pregnant women and mothers of infants.
 While most Philly co-ops get their produce local farmers, Weaver's Way has its own farms– one at Awbury Arboretum and the other at Saul Agricultural High School. However, right next to its organic produce, the co-op also offer natural produce at lower prices to appeal to customers on a budget. 
 Re:Vision Architecture exposed beams and brick and retained the original terrazzo floor in its redesign of the former Acme grocery store. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Re:Vision Architecture in Manayunk, a firm that focuses on sustainability, took the lead in repurposing the former Acme. "It's such a perfect building for Weavers Way," said Scott Kelly, founding principle of Re:Vision Architecture. "After the Acme closed, the next occupant carved up the inside into offices so you couldn't see the original structure. Everything in the middle came out. We brought it back to its original 1950s glory, including the exposed brick masonry."
 "We understand issues society faces on climate change," Kelly said. "We don't waste. We repurpose. Rather than tear down, we renovate." This includes preserving the Acme's original terrazzo floor and freight elevator. Tipping their hat to the past, the font chosen for the sign on the front of the Germantown store is intended to mimic the building's old Acme signage.
 "We added "Food Market" to the outside of our stores to make it clearer to passersby who we are. Over the years, many people have been confused by our name, thinking we are some sort of weavers guild," said Roesser. "Our goal is to create a clean, welcoming grocery. We want everyone to feel like it is their co-op."
 Tags: adaptive resuse food cooperatives food deserts Germantown 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: Young People’s Continental Congress to Put Fresh Eyes on the Nation's Founding
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
Carpenters' Hall will host the Young People’s Continental Congress this week. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence is on July 4, 2026. The many scheduled events leading up to the sequential include the Young People’s Continental Congress (YPCC) presented by Carpenters' Company and National History Day. YPCC kicks off this week and is set to recreate the events of the First Continental Congress.
 The First Continental Congress took place within Carpenter’s Hall as a reaction to the various acts and taxes imposed by the British government. In session from September 5 to October 26, 1774, it was succeeded by the Second Continental Congress which went on to declare independence from the British Crown in 1776 after the Battles of Lexington and Concord in 1775.
 Students and educators will meet in Philadelphia this week to discuss and learn about the events leading up to the original Congress. YPCC will bring together children from high schools based in the original 13 colonies to conduct both independent and group research on the 56 original representatives, their roles, and politics. The program will be followed in July 2025 with a second YPCC, where a crop of students will be chosen through open enrollment and an application process that will attract participants from across the United States.
 The central goal of the program is to “connect history to issues of contemporary relevance and engage young people in understanding and addressing them,” according to a YPCC press release. “In the 2018 National Assessment of Education Progress (NAEP) Civics Assessment, over 75 percent of American students scored below proficient. According to the 2022 results, the nation’s score has declined since the 2018 evaluation," according to the press release.
 I have concerns about the long-term effectiveness of a program predicated around a singular event. I also wonder how it will impact children in Philadelphia who may not receive a well-rounded education in social studies and civics due to overcrowding and underfunding in certain city schools, which can lead to the lack of effective teaching.
 I reached out to Ismael Jimenez, director of social studies curriculum for the School District of Philadelphia, who shared his thoughts and plans to bring these lessons to students beyond YPCC. “Teachers are taught and expected to engage students with thought-provoking conversations and critical thinking.” One of Jiminez’s programs, Invisible Architects of Freedom, is part of the School District’s initiative to unravel the myth around the country’s founding by poking holes in the narrative of America and highlighting the different voices and perspectives present during that time. He said students have latched on to this new approach with enthusiasm.
 According to Jimenez, many Philly students feel disconnected from national history. In response, the School District plans to increase school trips and history-based events that have been otherwise underfunded and lacking.
 Michael Norris, executive director of Carpenters’ Hall, said that there are ongoing goals to establish a local version of the program that will continue past 2026. It may include an after school program or history club to connect students with local history.
 I spoke to a few educators in both primary and high school about their expectations of teaching social studies and the YPCC. Their comments ranged from not having the time to actually teach, poor parent participation, and the pressure to do well in the Pennsylvania System of School Assessment. When asked how students are responding to learning history, they stressed that extracurricular programs were quite beneficial, especially children belonging to marginalized groups. Programs such as Young Heroes Outreach Program hosted by The National Liberty Museum, History Hunters, Youth Reporter Program hosted by Stenton House Museum, and the PECO Family Membership program through the Museum of the American Revolution assist in bringing history into schools and to parents who are typically unable to meet teachers’ requirements.
 I spoke with Liz Taylor, the Philly YPCC teacher representative from Julia R. Masterman School. She paraphrased a quote by historian Ira Berlin. “History is an argument about the past. It is important that students are able to tap into different arguments and find the sources of them so they can come up with their own conclusions and defend them.” Hopefully the YPCC program and the events leading up to the 2026 sequential, together with existing local programs, will be widely accessible for all Philadelphia students in the years to come.
 Tags: Carpenters' Hall education School District of Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Florida County to Acquire and Sink SS United States
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
Okaloosa County, Florida intends to purchase the SS United States to create an artificial reef along the coast of Destin-Fort Walton Beach. | Photo: Chandra Lampreich
 The SS United States is destined to make history again—this time as the world’s largest underwater artificial reef. Under the pending agreement between Okaloosa County, Florida and the SS United States Conservancy, Philly's "ghost ship" docked on the Delaware River would be relocated to the Florida Gulf Coast and sunk off Destin-Fort Walton Beach to create habitat for marine life. In conjunction with an on-shore museum, the project is designed to honor and preserve the vessel’s legacy. The deal could mark the beginning of the end to the legal wrangling between the Conservancy and its landlord, Penn Warehousing & Distribution, Inc. (PWD), while providing Okaloosa County with substantial economic benefits associated with recreational fishing and scuba diving.
 Although Okaloosa County and the Conservancy signed off on a contract late last month, County commissioners have yet to approve the agreement and the $9 million budget allocation. A vote scheduled for September 3 was postponed until the 17th at the request of County administrator John Hofstad, who told commissioners, “There’s been a wrinkle with the pier operators,” and asked that the vote “be pushed two weeks to the next meeting to allow us time to work out the issues.”
 “If the SS United States is successfully deployed, it would take over the title of the largest artificial reef in the world,” according to Jennifer Adams, director of Okaloosa County’s tourism development department. “The economic impact of large vessel artificial reefs is substantial and multifaceted, benefiting tourism, the fishing industry, and marine conservation," she explained. "These reefs generate significant economic activity and provide both direct and indirect benefits to coastal communities.”
 While the agreement provides the final missing piece to the county’s five-year artificial reef plan, it also ends the Conservancy’s search for a future for the ship that is both practical and respectful of its historical significance. Designed by William Francis Gibbs and launched in 1951, the SS United States was touted as the most powerful, technologically advanced ship of its kind. On its maiden voyage, the 990-foot long ship crossed the Atlantic Ocean in three days, 12 hours, and 12 minutes at an average speed of more than 34 knots (39 mph), breaking the record for the fastest eastbound crossing by an ocean liner. The ship then turned around and broke the westbound record on the trip home. Both records still stand.
 The SS United States was launched in 1951. | Photo courtesy of the SS United States Conservancy
 Competition from airlines and other factors led to the SS United States being withdrawn from service in 1969. A succession of owners failed to bring it back to life, and by 2009, then-owner Norwegian Cruise Lines put the vessel up for sale. With the SS United States in danger of being scrapped, the Conservancy stepped in and purchased the ship in 2011. Under the leadership of Gibbs’ granddaughter, Susan Gibbs, the Conservancy envisioned “a future where the SS United States is a sustainable waterfront attraction, providing jobs and important public amenities, while educating and inspiring future generations,” but restoration and redevelopment plans have yet to be funded and implemented.
 Meanwhile, the operator of Pier 82, where the SS United States is berthed, has sought to have the ship removed. PWD doubled the docking fee to $1,700 per day, and when the Conservancy did not increase its payments, claimed that the organization was in violation of its 2011 berthing agreement. On March 11, 2022, PWD terminated the vessel’s tenancy and subsequently filed a civil suit in federal court for back pay and removal of the ship from its berth on the Delaware River.
 In June of this year, U.S. District Court Judge Anita Brody denied the claim for back pay, but ruled that either party had the right to terminate the berthing agreement, given sufficient notice, and ordered the Conservancy to remove the SS United States from Pier 82 by September 12. “PWD’s claim for monetary damages for breach of contract is without merit,” the judge wrote in her memorandum opinion. “The Conservancy’s failure to pay at the daily rate of $1,700 does not amount to a breach of the berthing agreement or entitle PWD to any damages.” She continued, “I will recognize PWD’s notice of intent to terminate given on March 11, 2022, but will not give effect to the termination on the date set by PWD, as it did not incorporate reasonable notice.”
 The Conservancy sought a three-month delay of the September 12 deadline, but last month, Brody denied the request while leaving the door open for an extension if, before the deadline, the organization secures a contract to remove the ship. The contract with Okaloosa County would meet that requirement if certain contingencies are met. These include reaching an agreement with PWD by October 4 to extend the September 12 deadline until the County can move the ship, and the County completing the due diligence it began in August. This consists of securing contracts for fuel tank surveys, fuel disposal, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) surveys, towing logistics, hull inspection, insurance, and any necessary environmental remediation. “However, if it is determined after the due diligence is complete that our costs for remediation are prohibitive, the project will not move forward,” Adams advised the commissioners.
 The SS United States has been docked at Pier 82 in South Philadelphia since 1996. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The $9 million deal includes the $1 million sale price, $1 million toward the land-based museum, and the remainder for remediation, transport, and deployment as a reef. It allows the Conservancy to remove certain items of historic interest, such as the builder’s plate, one five-bladed propeller, bridge table, whistle control box, and radar mast.
 The Conservancy declined to provide a comment for this article, but posted the following on social media. “We completely understand that the prospect of reefing the SS United States may be challenging to contemplate, [and] reefing is not the Conservancy’s preferred scenario. In an intense and all-hands-on-deck effort to keep the ship safely afloat, we have conducted a massive nationwide search for a new temporary location—a search that has thus far yielded no viable alternatives. With our hand being forced by Penn Warehousing, and scrapping being the only other viable option, we believe reefing is the more dignified outcome.”
 Tags: Delaware River South Philadelphia SS United States 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: Spruce Hill Historic District Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
4200 Spruce Street was built circa 1890 and designed by Andrews, Jacques, and Rantouyl. It is the former home of financier Clarence Howard Clark, Jr. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At its meeting on July 12 the Philadelphia Historical Commission voted in favor of adding the Spruce Hill Historic District to the local register and approved two new construction projects that will each lead to the demolition of historic industrial buildings.
 The Spruce Hill Historic District, Southeast Quadrant , is comprised of the area between Spruce Street on the north, Baltimore Avenue and Woodland Avenue to the south, and between 39th and 43rd Streets. Of the 572 properties contained there, 94 percent were deemed to be either significant or contributing to the historic district.
 St. Andrew’s Chapel at 4205 Spruce Street was built in 1919 and designed by Zantzinger, Borie, and Medary. It is part of the campus of the former Philadelphia Divinity School of the Protestant Episcopal Church. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 An attorney for two large property owners in the proposed district, Campus Apartments and University City Housing, first questioned whether the nomination was complete and correct, claiming that the proposal indicated it was a part of a larger historic district of which an inventory of contributing properties had not been done. At the same time, he called for a continuance in case the Historical Commission found the nomination to be complete and correct.
 The nomination was submitted in October 2023. It was reviewed by Historical Commission staff in February and by the Historical Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation in June, both of which found the nomination was complete and satisfied several criteria for designation.
 The Leonard Apartments at 4101 Baltimore Avenue. Built in 1928, designed by Israel Demchick. The Italianate twin next door at 4105 Baltimore Avenue was built in 1869 by developers Henry Townsend and Charles Este. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Historical Commission first voted to affirm the completeness and correctness of the nomination, then voted to deny the request for continuance, pointing out that notices to property owners had been given five months ago. Finally, it voted unanimously to add the historic district to the Philadelphia register, modifying the name to the Spruce Hill Southeast Historic District, citing its significance in the economic and cultural development of West Philadelphia as a streetcar suburb and its body of buildings with distinctive mid-to-late 19th and early 20th century architectural styles including Italianate, Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Second Empire, and Georgian Revival. Many of the buildings are the work of significant architects such as Theophilus P. Chandler, Willis G. Hale, G.W. and W.D. Hewitt, and Samuel Sloan. 
 The Washington Square West Historic District was also up for a vote at this month's meeting, but the Historical Commission issued a two-month continuance at the request of several property owners and a homeowners’ association who are opposing the nomination.
 John Stortz & Son at 208-12 Vine Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 208-12 Vine Street, a complex of buildings of the John Stortz and Son Store , the oldest of which dates to 1780, was individually designated in 1984 and was listed as contributing to the Old City Historic District in December 2003. The owner, the current John Stortz, was given permission to demolish the buildings in October 2023 , owing to financial hardship and pending approval of building plans, zoning, and financing. Based on the recommendation of the Historical Commission’s Architectural Committee, the full Historical Commission approved the plans without review or comment.
 4045-61 Main Street in 2023 and a rendering of the proposed residential redevelopment of the historic industrial site. | Images: Google Street View and CBP Architects
 4045-61 Main Street, the Littlewood & Company Dyers and Bleachers complex, was built in 1869 and was listed as a significant property within the Main Street Manayunk Historic District in 1983. In 2023 the current Littlewood family was granted permission to demolish the historic industrial complex based on financial hardship. While the proposed plans retain some of the facades of the original buildings that face Main Street, public commenters and some Historical Commission members objected to the seven-story height and mass of the new construction, which will include 162 residential units. Approval was ultimately granted with a 6-5 vote.
 Tags: Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission Spruce Hill 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Pennsylvania's Historic Tax Credit Increased to $20 Million
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
On July 11, the Pennsylvania General Assembly passed its 2024-2025 budget. It was 11 days past the deadline, but offered some good news for historic preservationists and adaptive reuse developers. The new budget included tax code changes that raised the historic tax credit program to $20 million from its previous cap of $5 million.
 Most states offer a tax credit on projects that rehabilitate historic properties. Pennsylvania’s program was established in 2012, allocating $3 million a year with a per-project cap of $500,000 or 25 percent of qualifying expenses. Seven years later, it was increased to $5 million, where it has stood until now.
 On average, the credit supports roughly 15 projects per year, about half of the applications submitted, with many receiving less than the maximum $500,000. In Philadelphia, one only needs to look around to see the large stock of historic buildings and the amount of development in the city to see that the potential use could be much greater.
 “Developers have told us they stopped applying because it was such a small amount of money relative to the overall cost of a project, and with the process being so uncertain,” said Mindy Crawford, executive director of Preservation Pennsylvania, a nonprofit organization that champions the preservation of historic buildings and structures throughout the Commonwealth.
 Last October, the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia and Preservation Pennsylvania hosted a symposium in West Chester to launch a drive to increase the historic tax credit. Representatives from Pennsylvania’s surrounding states explained their programs, all of which were more generous, ranging from tiny Delaware with $8 million to New York and West Virginia with no cap at all.
 “We identified it as a priority to increase the number of properties repurposed or rehabilitated,” explained Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance, which, along with Preservation Pennsylvania, mobilized to build a broad coalition of preservationists, architects, developers, business associations, and historians to lobby for the increase. “We argued that adaptive reuse of historic buildings returns more jobs than any other investment in the state, and Pennsylvania has been missing out.”
 They found a supporter in State Senator Nikil Saval (D-Philadelphia), who joined with his co-chair on the Urban Affairs & Housing Committee, State Senator Frank Farry (R-Bucks) to co-sponsor the bill. The PA Historic Tax Credit Coalition formed by Steinke’s and Crawford’s organizations successfully lobbied their representatives in both chambers, and the issue made it into this year’s budgetary process.
 With demands always exceeding available funding in the state budget, the program’s structure as a credit rather than an appropriation helped it gain support. “We’re not allocating money, just knocking a little off the revenue side,” Farry pointed out. “Then, on the business side of the ledger, there’s the opportunity to get that revenue back, and more, with tax-paying construction jobs and tax-paying tenants.”
 “It’s significant progress,” noted Saval. “We’ll start to resemble other states in what they allocate.” He went on to note that, despite the bill's origination in the Urban Affairs Committee, the tax credits are distributed throughout the state. “In rural areas, where there is less development pressure, tax credits can be an incentive to make projects feasible.”
 The former Metropolitan Opera House at 558 N. Broad Street was restored and reactivated in December 2018 after decades of deterioration. The developers, Eric Blumenfeld and Holy Ghost Headquarters in partnership with Live Nation, used historic tax credits to help fund the $56 million project. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Advocates are now turning their attention to a few more issues they say need to be resolved to really improve the program. They’re calling for an increase in the per-project cap from the current $500,000 to $2.5 million. According to Crawford, that larger amount is fairly typical of other states’ programs. Also, they’re seeking to change a current restriction from the Department of Revenue that bars projects with a nonprofit partner.
 “We’re going back to the legislative leadership and explain why they’re needed,” said Crawford. “We’d like to get a bill passed now rather than waiting until next year.”
 Also on the coalition’s to-do list is to keep legislators apprised of the increase’s effect, and to continue to press for something closer to their original goal of $50 million. “While I want to show the impact of going from $5 to $20 million, I still want to extrapolate what we could do if we were funded like other states,” said Crawford.
 Saval hopes the increased funding will make reuse projects more prominent in their communities and demonstrate their value to other societal concerns, like housing availability and sustainability. “A lot of times we do things that a small percentage of the population care about, but in fact have far-reaching effects,” said Farry. “The preservation part is important, but it also helps the housing crisis.”
 “Historic preservation at its heart has a social mission,” said Saval. “It’s deeply felt by Pennsylvanians when an unused or underused building is brought into new use. It can be an economic driver in a community.”
 “Even if you’re not interested in the preservation field, anyone can see the value of getting a building back into productive use and on the tax rolls,” agreed Steinke. “It’s about the health of our communities.”
 Tags: adaptive resuse historic tax credit Renovation 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Historical Commission Approves Long-awaited Washington Square West Historic District
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on September 13, the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved one new historic district and offered favorable comments on the nominations of four properties to the National Register of Historic Places . It also approved a one-month continuance for the proposed designation of the Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) at 700-34 Race Street.
 The proposed boundary of the Washington Square West Historic District. | Image: Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia
 The bulk of the meeting was taken up by the nomination of the Washington Square West Historic District . It began with several requests for a continuance, with some property owners claiming the Historical Commission’s required notification was not done or not done properly.
 After lengthy comments by property owners, the nominators, the public, and the staff’s explanation of their notification process, Historical Commission members voted unanimously to deny the continuance request, with one abstention, one recusal, and one absence. The Historical Commission then proceeded to review the nomination, again hearing from the nominators, property owners, and the public.
 William Way Community Center on Spruce Street contributes to architectural and LGBTQ+ history within the newly designated Washington Square West Historic District. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The proposed historic district comprises roughly 26 city blocks, with 1,441 resources, of which 767–more than half—are already individually designated. The period of significance begins in the 1740s with the creation of Mikvah Israel cemetery and continues up through the 1980s for its important role in the history of the city’s LGBTQ community .
 The Historical Commission again voted unanimously to approve the designation, with one abstention, one recusal, and one absence, after omitting several vacant lots and parking lots from the list of contributing properties. They agreed with the nomination that the district satisfied six criteria for designation, owing to the area’s significant social history among Philadelphia’s Black, LGBTQ, and immigrant communities, the presence of several distinctive architectural styles with many the work of noteworthy architects, and the likely presence of archaeological information.
 The Continental Building at 4th and Market Streets. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The first of the nominations reviewed for the National Register was the Continental Building at 400 Market Street . Built in 1970 and designed by architects Berger and Caltabiano, it is an example of the use of precast concrete in corporate and institutional buildings that was prevalent in the 1960s and 1970s. It is not listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 The bell tower of St. Elisabeth’s Episcopal Church in Point Breeze. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 St. Elisabeth’s Episcopal Church at 1900 S. 16th Street was built in 1889 as a mission to the Church of the Evangelists. Its rector, Henry Percival, was a prominent priest in the Anglo-Catholic movement, which sought to return certain Roman Catholic practices to Episcopal services. The church was designed by the architectural firm of Baily and Truscott in a pre-Romanesque style. Until recently, it was the longtime home of True Gospel Tabernacle Church. The Historical Commission added it to the local register in 1967 and more recently approved an adaptive reuse plan for it .
 The loading facility and the boiler house of Weisbrod & Hess Brewery in Kensington in 2016. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Weisbrod & Hess Brewery complex at 2421 Martha Street and 2423-39 Amber Street was built in 1885 and is one of the best examples of the work of Adam C. Wagner, who designed numerous breweries in Philadelphia in the German Rundbogenstil style. The brewery was one of the most prominent in the city during the late 19th century and up until prohibition. It originally included 10 buildings, seven of which survive and are proposed for designation in this nomination. The boiler house and storage house buildings were listed on the Philadelphia register in 2017.
 Willow Steam Generating Plant in Callowhill. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The final nomination was for the Willow Steam Generation Plant at 411-419 N. 9th Street , which is not listed on the local register. It was built in 1927 and designed by architect John T. Windrim, who also designed several Philadelphia Electric Company plants , including the former Delaware River Generating Station (now called The Battery), as well as the Franklin Institute. Willow Steam is an example of energy plants in the 1920s that provided steam heating for commercial buildings.
 The Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) in 2015. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The nomination of the Roundhouse to the Philadelphia Register was submitted by Docomomo US-Greater Philadelphia and the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia in December 2022, reviewed by the Historical Commission staff seven months later, and reviewed and recommended by the Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation in September, 2023. Two lengthy continuances followed: the first, for five months, was approved in October 2023 and the second, for six months, in March 2024. This third continuance places the nomination on the Historical Commission’s October 2024 agenda.
 September's meeting, along with the meeting in August, included several recently appointed Commissioners, which brings the Historical Commission to its full complement of members. New members include Franz Rabauer, a realtor, filling an open general appointed position, Zachary Frankel, filling the long-open appointed position slated for a real estate developer, Thomas Holloman, designee for City Council President Kenyatta Johnson, Kyle O’Connor, representing the Department of Public Property, and Kareema Abu Saab, representing the Department of Commerce.
 Tags: historic district Historical Commission Meeting Report National Register of Historic Places Philadelphia Historical Commission Police Administration Building Washington Square West Willow Street Steam Generation Plant 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Survival and Revival Along Philadelphia's Portico Row
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
Portico Row on the 900 block of Spruce Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Ever wonder who lived in your house or on your block 100 years ago? That is what motivated Judith Benedict, a retired urban planner, to pour through countless Census records, newspapers, and Philadelphia Historical Commission files. She tracked down every resident of her block on historic Portico Row, which is on the south side of the 900 block of Spruce Street.
 "I did it all online during Covid," said Benedict, whose efforts resulted in a written social history of everyone who ever lived on Portico Row since it was built in the early 1830s. Benedict documented them all, from wealthy 19th century merchants to 20th century demi-monde. Now, she wants to introduce them to you.
 Benedict and two other Portico Row resident history buffs, Bob Tunick and Peg Fitzpatrick, are hosting a terrace party on Sunday, September 29, from 3-5 p.m. to celebrate the block's 193-year survival and revival. "There will be music and refreshments, plus an opportunity to learn about the people who lived on the block," said Benedict.
 Thomas Ustick Walter and his family circa 1850. | Photo: Public Domain
 That history began in 1831 when Philadelphia merchant John Savage commissioned architect Thomas Ustick Walter to design 16 Greek Revival-style homes, each with distinctive Pennsylvania blue marble porticos and wrought iron fences. Each of the eight mirror-image pairs shares a common entrance, or portico, supported by Ionic columns. Portico Row is the last surviving example of its type of housing in Philadelphia.
 For an architect who had worked in the studio of William Strickland at the age of 15, Walter would become known for his Neoclassical style. Portico Row was one of the architect's more modest achievements. The previous year, he had designed the nearby Spruce Street Baptist Church (now Society Hill Synagogue) and the following year he drew up the plans for Moyamensing Prison , an immense Gothic structure with battlements at Reed Street and Passyunk Avenue. The prison was demolished in 1968 and is now an Acme supermarket. Not long after, Walter designed Girard College's Founder's Hall, considered one of the finest examples of American Neoclassical architecture in the United States. However, his legacy achievement was his work on the United States Capital, and he also takes credit for co-designing Philadelphia City Hall 40 years after his work on Portico Row.
 "This strip of homes has gone through good and bad periods over the years," said Tunick, who has lived on Portico Row since 1988. The block's early residents included Sarah Josepha Hale, editor of the first successful women's magazine, Godey's Lady Book, and gained immortality when she wrote "Mary Had a Little Lamb." Another neighbor was Isaac Hull, commander of the USS Constitution in the War of 1812. The Philadelphia High School for Young Ladies also called the block home.
 A lithograph of Portico Row by Martin Rosienkiewicz from 1837. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 By the early 20th century, much of Philadelphia's elite had moved west of Broad Street, opening Portico Row to immigrants and working class tenants. Owners of single family houses took in tenants, dividing their spacious rooms to accommodate more people. These were employees in the nearby grand department stores on Market Street, as well as craftsmen, lawyers, and medical students. There were exceptions. "One early owner kept a house in his family for almost 100 years, from 1840 to 1938," said Benedict. Another home, owned by Pennsylvania Hospital at 10th and Spruce Streets, was filled with nurses.
 The Great Depression eventually transformed Portico Row's elegant townhouses into cramped rentals, chopping up apartments into boarding units. Tenants included musicians, machine operators, sailors, and women who worked in Locust Street nightclubs. In 1958, Portico Row was placed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places and it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1977. If not for those historic designations, Portico Row may have gone the way of the bulldozer. Fortunately, in the 1970s, the City stepped in with an eye on the newly created Society Hill Historic District, along with former Mayor Richardson Dilworth's renovation of Washington Square.
 All of the attention came just in time. One of the historically designated houses had been decimated by a fire that destroyed its roof. "By then, eight of the 16 houses were owned by the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority (PRA)," said Benedict. "The City changed the zoning from commercial to residential and owners had to convert rooming houses into apartments of no more than eight units each." The owner could also sell the property to the PRA. According to Benedict, some sold their properties to the City and others sold to individuals who said they would abide by the City's guidelines. However, several houses sat vacant for up to seven years.
 Structural damage after a fire in 1970 threatened the continuity of Portico Row. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 "According to the Census, in 1960 there were 327 residents," said Benedict. "A mere 10 years later, in 1970, there were only 42 people living on the block. The 2020 Census lists 170."
 Today, seven of Portico Rows buildings are rental apartments, seven are condominiums, and two are single-family homes. Many of the original architectural details have survived, including the 14-foot ceilings, fireplaces, and original moldings over the doors. "Some of the fireplaces are black marble with Ionic columns," said Tunick.
 "I believe it is the only full-block strip of matching 19th century homes in the city," said Tunick, who did his share of photographic research. "I visited The Athenaeum of Philadelphia , The Library Company, the Free Library, the Philadelphia City Archives, the Philadelphia Historical Commission, and the Pennsylvania Historical Society and came up with some beautiful old images of our block, which I had printed and framed. They now form a little gallery in the first floor hallways of two buildings."
 Ornate entryway lettering on Spruce Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 "This is our first effort at a block party," said Tunick. "There will be posters attached to each wrought iron fence with historical details of the particular buildings, including the stories of the people who lived there. We are looking forward to an exciting day discussing our block's history."
 Speaking of the September 29th celebration of Portico Row, Fitzpatrick added, "This get-together is not just about history. It is about community and getting to know your neighbors, not just on our block but also from other areas of the city."
 The Portico Row Terrace Party will take place on the 900 block of Spruce Street on Sunday, September 29 from 3-5 p.m. Email Peg Fitzpatrick at p.fitzpatrick@pmginc.net for more information or to volunteer. 
 Tags: Events Neo-Classical architecture rowhouse Washington Square West 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: In Memoriam: Celebrating Aaron Wunsch, Champion of Historic Preservation
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
Aaron Wunsch, historic preservation advocate and professor of architectural and landscape history at the University of Pennsylvania. | Photo courtesy of Emily Orr for Dumbarton Oaks, 2021
 To those who knew him, Aaron Wunsch was both an intellectual and an adventurer. He was a man equally within his element inside the confines of his classroom–conversing with a generation of students on the ins and outs of historic preservation–as he was outside, traipsing around Philadelphia to hammer tarps and tin onto the roofs of historic buildings he simply could not stand to see decay.
 Now, friends, colleagues, and the city’s historic buildings will somehow have to do without him. Wunsch passed away at his home in Germantown on Friday, September 20, at age 53 after a years-long fight with cancer. The details of his illness, death, and indeed much of his life are most eloquently rendered in a journal Wunsch’s wife, Jillian Galle, thoughtfully maintained for friends and family throughout his journey. More meaningful words cannot be written than those found there.
 However, Hidden City would be remiss without honoring the legacy of a giant of Philadelphia’s preservation community, who indeed supported and believed in the importance of this publication since its infancy. “The thing that stood out to me about Aaron,” said Peter Woodall, project director of Hidden City, “is that he was an academic who was also a fighter: against developers and, at various times, the Historical Commission, the Preservation Alliance, and the University of Pennsylvania itself, even though he taught there and, later, was in the process of seeking tenure. He was involved with the life of the city in so many different ways. Aaron was about as far from being a resident of the ivory tower as can be imagined,” Woodall said.
 We asked some of his students, friends, and colleagues to help us further remember Wunsch.
 Students Recall a Brilliant, Passionate Professor 
 The First Baptist Church of Germantown at 40 E. Price Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 When Molly Lester arrived on the campus of the University of Pennsylvania in 2010 to pursue a masters degree in historic preservation, she drew Wunsch as a professor. It was the start of a relationship that would extend to thesis advisor, friend, and colleague. Lester now serves as associate director of Penn’s Urban Heritage Project.
 One of the things she discovered early on was just what kind of a mind Wunsch possessed– and how forcefully he could apply it. “I’m sure you’ll hear this from a lot of people. The man had the most encyclopedic knowledge about architecture, but then also about sources related to architecture,” Lester said, laughing as she recalled an 11th hour suggestion for her thesis. “My deadline was the next day, and he still had brainstorms for sources I should be checking.”
 This obstinacy is something others in Wunsch’s sphere also recall, but Lester said any friction from his intellectual convictions were mollified by his heart. She called him a ceaseless “cheerleader” of her work and career, starting with her selection of Minerva Parker Nichols , the first American woman to operate her own independent architectural practice, as her thesis topic. Lester said Wunsch actually didn’t know much about Nichols at first, which is why he insisted on pursuing sourcing as rigorously as possible. “He at one point, later in the process, said there’s probably an article in this or a book,” she said. “That was the first time that it occurred to me and really planted a seed.” Lester has since published several articles and co-authored a book on Nichols, as well as organized exhibits, all with Wunsch’s continued support and advice.
 Anthony Hita enrolled in Penn's preservation program in 2016 and, despite his role as a student, quickly struck up a collegial relationship with Wunsch, who he recalled for his passion and respectful demeanor. Hita came to preservation as a second career after serving as a pastor in the United Methodist Church. He was among the oldest students in his cohort, but Hita's friendship with Wunsch helped put him at ease. “He and I would just talk. He worked a lot with churches and would often bounce ideas off of me,” Hita said. “In some ways I almost felt like I was his pastor. He was teaching me, but I was giving him an ear to express frustrations.”
 Wunsch’s mentorship led to success for Hita in more ways than one. While enrolled in Wunsch’s class on historic documentation, Hita was assigned the First Baptist Church of Germantown, now referred to as Polite Temple Baptist Church, an 1852 church designed by Philadelphia architect Samuel Sloan. As Hita was wrapping up his degree, he said Wunsch also nominated him to serve as an ambassador for the annual Vernacular Architecture Forum. After graduation, Hita took such an interest in the Germantown church that he worked with Wunsch on its successful inclusion to the National Register of Historic Places. Hita added that he will “forever be grateful” for the influence Wunsch had on his life.
 A Close Colleague Reflects on Friendship, Legacy 
 Aaron Wunsch, center, with Frank Matero and Deacon Lloyd Butler at 19th Street Baptist Church in 2014. | Photo courtesy of Weitzman School of Design, University of Pennsylvania
 Frank Matero, Gonick Family Professor and chair of the Historic Preservation Department at Penn, remembers first seeing Wunsch when the latter gave “one of the great talks” at a conference on the history of the American cemetery hosted by Penn. A few years later, Matero created his first faculty position as chair in architectural history and filled it with his first hire: Wunsch. Matero said on a personal level he felt a kinship with Wunsch because of their shared academic eccentricities. “As you can imagine, there also aren’t too many people around that can have conversations about gravestones and cemeteries,” Matero said, noting Wunsch authored two books on the subject.
 In addition to their love of architecture and history, the two would travel to attend rare book fairs and also had a habit of investigating the diviest bars they could find, often at Wunsch’s insistence on exploring the local fare.
 His passion for busting out of the ivory tower also manifested professionally, as Wunsch revolutionized the department into one focused on public history, which, as Matero explains, calls for valuing the input of the greater public in determining which buildings and landscapes are worthy of preservation, as opposed to defaulting to the professional architects and historians who dominated the early movement. In practice, that meant Wunsch professed, both literally and figuratively, applying scholarly principles outside of the classroom. “He was a public intellectual. He really believed that what you do as a scholar needs to find its way into advocacy for whatever cause it was you believed in,” explained Matero. “He really brought a whole new dimension to the program.”
 In practice, that also meant bumping up against counter forces. “It put him into conflict with a lot of people. I’ve always said, he’s a friend, a colleague, and a pain in the ass,” Matero said, laughing. “He just had very high principles, and he didn’t like to compromise.” Indeed, in another journal entry Galle recorded that Wunsch had summoned the energy to joke that a regular nemesis to his preservation efforts, historian George Thomas, had not “killed me yet!”
 Like others, Matero said that Wunsch’s at-times demanding exterior rested on a foundation of selflessness. He estimated Wunsch taught as many as 600 students during his tenure at Penn, perhaps 150 as thesis advisor, and invested “enormous amounts of time” in getting his charges to enjoy and excel in preservation.
 A 19th Century Man 
 Germantown Boys and Girls Club at 23-25 W. Penn Street in 2017. | Photo: Bradley Maule
 Jeffrey A. Cohen, the Term Professor in Growth and Structure of Cities at Bryn Mawr College and a member of the Philadelphia Historic Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation, noted that Wunsch’s scholarship focused on “mid-19th century designed landscapes” such as cemeteries, parks, and planned suburbs. “[He delved] deep into the documentation and intentions that shaped these very intentional new places and situated them richly within the larger scope of American cultural history,” Cohen explained.
 Cohen also witnessed Wunsch’s spirit of can-do-ism in protecting spaces firsthand. After initially getting to know each other when Wunsch worked for the National Park Service's Historic American Buildings Survey, the two would meet up at VAF meetings and helped plan the Philadelphia conference in 2019. Yet, it was impromptu projects and forays that Cohen particularly valued, often with “our erstwhile co-conspirator” archivist Sandra Markham. “With her we embarked on seat-of-pants jaunts, whose climax could have been captured in an action-shot depicting an extended staring-contest with a building, venturing readings of its form, design conversants, setting, and authorship–sometimes until the owner came out to invite us in or to shoo us away,” Cohen recalled.
 Appreciation for Wunsch’s escapades also extended beyond academia. Yvonne Haskins, an attorney and community activist in Northwest Philadelphia, recalled working closely with Wunsch to preserve the Germantown Boys and Girls Club, built in 1898, after a highly-controversial demolition plan surfaced about a decade ago. Eventually, the efforts, also championed by architectural historian Oscar Beisert and Penn archivist J.M. Duffin, resulted in a successful compromise that led to an award-winning adaptive restoration of the building.
 Haskins said Wunsch appeared with her publicly at Historical Commission meetings to advocate for the building and also met privately to strategize, even as powerful forces arrayed against the building, including David L. Cohen, a former Comcast executive, Mayor Ed Rendell Chief of Staff, and Penn trustee. “Cohen, who was with Comcast at the time, wanted to put a hockey rink on the site, on this tiny little street,” Haskins said. “But we won that battle.”
 What stuck out most to Haskins was Wunsch’s intelligence, eloquence, and passion. Elsewhere in Germantown, Haskins recalled Wunsch and another gentleman taking it upon themselves to climb atop dilapidated Germantown Settlement buildings to nail tarps onto their roofs and protect them from negligent ownership. Many have since been obtained by the city and are heading for redevelopment.
 Haskins said there was more that she and Wunsch wanted to accomplish, but during their last meeting in 2022 it became clear there just wouldn't be time. “The last time we were together, I went over and visited him,” said Haskins. “We had tea for about three hours. I remember he said to me he felt great, and that he didn’t know how it had happened, but he was getting prepared to die.”
 Spiritual Preservation 
 Church of the Atonement, looking southwest from 47th Street. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 While Wunsch’s spirit has now departed its earthly confines, Matero believes his greatest professional legacy will endure within the brick-and-mortar of Philadelphia’s religious institutions: the historic churches and synagogues for which he endeavored to “move the needle for their public awareness and preservation,” he said.
 Along with Polite Baptist, churches including Germantown’s Mount Vernon Baptist Church, Trinity Lutheran Church, the Church of the Atonement in Kingsessing, and 19th Street Baptist Church in Point Breeze all benefited from his advocacy.
 Matero noted that Wunsch’s familial background was “half-Quaker, half-Jewish,” but that Wunsch himself was not particularly religious. Why then, did so much of his work focus on historic religious buildings in Philadelphia? Matero again pegs it to Wunsch’s love for 19th century architecture. “Aaron was all about the 19th century and churches and other religious institutions in this country that really had their heyday in the 1800s,” Matero explained. “So, for him, they were the quintessential architecture of the period.”
 Thaddeus Squire, a philanthropic management professional and chief commons steward for preservation nonprofit CERT , said Wunsch’s work was instrumental to that organization’s efforts to preserve buildings such as 19th Street Baptist Church, Mount Vernon Cemetery, and two 18th century houses in West Philadelphia. “CERT is really a collection of Aaron Wunsch projects,” he said.
 Often, Squire explained, Wunsch would identify a building or place in need of saving and approach him to help identify philanthropic opportunities or other means of doing so. Yet, Wunsch would also advocate publicly, becoming a key figure in pushing back against city political and power structures, Squire said, that dismiss preservation as frivolous. “It’s a loss for the community. He was kind of the rabblerouser and good trouble raiser in historic preservation in Philly,” said Squire.
 19th Street Baptist Church in Point Breeze. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 All else failing, Squire also witnessed Wunsch as a man ready to roll up his sleeves and do the work himself. Perhaps nowhere was that more evident than at 19th Street Baptist Church, where Wunsch helped organize a “massive student initiative” about 15 years ago to help analyze and stabilize the 19th century church, Squire recalled. Photos from a contemporaneous WHYY article depict Wunsch donning a hardhat atop a ladder in the church’s sanctuary, where he was part of a hodgepodge team making emergency roof repairs. “He was constantly fixing holes and doing things that were quite dangerous, actually,” Matero said. “He really put himself at risk.”
 In a cosmic coincidence that would make even the most skeptical stop and wonder, several of Wunsch’s contacts noted that as word spread he had entered hospice in recent weeks, so too did news emerge that 19th Street Baptist Church, a building Wunsch had long fought for, would likely be heading for demolition after a protracted battle. "Sometimes things may not be intended, but they rhyme,” said Hita, the former pastor. “It felt like the end of a season that was going with the end of his seasons as well.”
 The loss of such buildings that Wunsch and his colleagues, despite their best efforts, failed to save appears to have stayed with him until the end. In another journal entry, Galle wrote that he became distressed upon counting on his fingers a number of recently demolished churches. It was only after reminding him of his preservation successes, fortified by the well wishes of all those who knew him, that he was soothed.
 Now it is for the rest of us to try and find solace in Wunsch’s successes, soothed by the continued existence of the places he fought for, and motivated by his memory to save the next ones.
 Editor’s Note: Hidden City recognizes that Aaron Wunsch’s circle of admirers is vast. While we were only able to contact and include a few of those confidants in this piece, we were amazed by and encouraged those who have not done so to take in the scores of incredible memories and photographs posted lovingly by Aaron’s friends and family on KudoBoard .
 Tags: Aaron Wunsch Historic Preservation obituary 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Queen Anne Abode and Arts and Crafts Interior Listed on the Local Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
3343 W. School House Lane was built in 1896 and designed by Horace Trumbauer. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Philadelphia Historical Commission approved two distinctly different nominations to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places and reviewed two requests for construction on previously designated sites at its meeting on June 14.
 The home at 3343 W. School House Lane in East Falls was built in 1896 and designed by Horace Trumbauer for Samuel Tobias Wagner, a civil engineer who designed bridges, water filtering systems, and methods of testing construction materials. His great-uncle was William Wagner, the founder of the Wagner Free Institute of Science. The Historical Commission approved the designation owing to its association with Trumbauer and its embodiment of characteristics of the Queen Anne and Shingle styles. While not participating in the nomination process, the current property owner, Thomas Jefferson University, did not oppose it.
 The former main sales floor of the Jacob Reed’s Sons’ Store at 1424-26 Chestnut Street in 2014. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 By contrast, the second designation was the subject of opposition. The former main sales floor of the Jacob Reed’s Sons’ Store at 1424-26 Chestnut Street, a rare nomination of an interior space, was originally designated in May 2022. The exterior of the building was placed on the local register in 1966.
 The property owner appealed the designation of the ground floor interior in the Court of Common Pleas, which remanded the designation back to the Historical Commission for reconsider. The Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation again recommended designation at its November 2022 meeting. A number of continuances followed. At its June 2024 meeting, the Commission once again approved the designation.
 Moravian tiles above the Jacob Reed store's entrance. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Built in 1904 architect William L. Price, the interior's reinforced concrete construction, the first for a commercial building in the city, created a distinctive interior with a series of arches and a vaulted ceiling. The main sales floor also represents a major commercial interior in the Arts and Crafts style, with stained glass lunette windows, tile work from Henry Chapman Mercer’s Moravian Pottery studio, and murals by local artist Gertrude Monaghan.
 The owner’s attorney again contested the nomination, claiming the property did not meet the criteria for designating an interior. They claimed that historic designation would hinder the adaptive reuse of the building. In a roll call vote, the Historical Commission unanimously approved the designation of the interior features listed as contributing in the nomination. Non-contributing features such as retail display fixtures, light fixture, and carpeting were excluded.
 The former St. Martin’s Coal Company Office at 7600 Germantown Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Two requests for new construction on the sites of previously designated properties were also a study in contrasts. The first proposal featured an unusual parcel of land in Northwest Philadelphia. The former St. Martin’s Coal Company Office at 7600 Germantown Avenue occupied a long narrow plot of about 1.2 acres, wedged between the 37-acre New Covenant Church campus and a former railroad line that now constitutes a portion of the Cresheim Trail.
 The full parcel was designated in August 2021, focusing on the 1916 Colonial Revival style building fronting Germantown Avenue. The construction request noted there would be no changes to the existing office building, but would add eight single-family attached homes behind it. Because the parcel is currently zoned RSD-3, Residential Single Family Detached, the developer, Cresheim Green Associates, is seeking a zoning variance. The property lies within the Wissahickon Watershed Overlay District, which limits the amount of impervious surface to no more than 45 percent, but received Philadelphia Water Department approval because the plans indicate 95 percent of the lot will be pervious.
 John Stortz & Son at 208-12 Vine Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In another construction request, the Historical Commission moved a step closer to permitting the demolition of one of the oldest industrial buildings in the city, the John Stortz & Sons workshops at 208-212 Vine Street. The oldest structure in the collection dates back to 1780. The site had been individually designated in December 1984 and listed as contributing to the Old City Historic District in December 2003. The Historical Commission approved the buildings' demolition in October 2023 after the owner claimed financial hardship.
 The Historical Commission reviewed an in-concept design for a six-story, 65-foot-high building with a roof deck, containing 35 units and a 7-car garage, offering comments and suggestions regarding the building’s cladding and other materials. The applicant will present revisions to the Architectural Committee for review and recommendation, and then return to the Historical Commission for final approval. After that, when financing and a zoning application have been approved, demolition will be permitted to go forward.
 Tags: Center City demolition East Falls historic interiors Historical Commission Meeting Report Horace Trumbauer Philadelphia Historical Commission 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Mt. Airy at a Crossroads
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
In the 1920s, Mt. Airy left behind a sleepy, bucolic past and burst forth with 20th century offerings. Developers poured money into its main commercial strip along Germantown Avenue, constructing new Art Deco buildings and businesses to cater to an influx of new residents. Suddenly, there was a bustling new game in town along Northwest Philadelphia’s main thoroughfare.
 A century later, in many ways, Mt. Airy once again has the feel of a quieter community tucked between the more heavily-trafficked neighborhoods of Chestnut Hill and Germantown. But is history set to repeat itself?
 In July, Quintessence Theatre Group closed on a $2.3 million purchase of the front portion of the Sedgwick Theater, a 1928 Art Deco playhouse in the heart of Mt. Airy’s commercial district and the crown jewel of its Roaring Twenties renaissance. With major renovations planned for the building’s former lobby, which now serves as a 150-seat performance space, and dreams of one day restoring the full theater to its former spellbinding glory, Quintessence producing artistic director Alex Burns thinks big things could once again be in store for his native Mt. Airy.
 Quintessence Theatre Group plans to renovate the Sedgwick Theater at 7137 Germantown Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler | Rendering: Voith & Mactavish Architects
 “This is a new era for the theater and will just bring literal light to the avenue,” Burns said, referencing plans to install a new, well-lit marquee that will protrude from the Sedgwick’s facade. “Our hope is that it won’t only benefit Quintessence, but will expand the sense of a nightlife district in Northwest Philadelphia. Bring in new restaurants, bring in new retail, bring in an exciting new energy.”
 The rumblings of redevelopment extend far beyond the footprint of the Sedgwick. Buoyed by a 2019 zoning overlay that allowed for higher rooflines, greater density, and less parking along Germantown Avenue, real estate developers are making fresh incursions into Mt. Airy. Just down the block, TierView Development is transforming the former National Bank of Mt. Airy . Built in the heyday of the 1920s, the three-and-a-half-story bank is now undergoing the most significant change in its history, as Tierview will maintain and restore the building’s Wissahickon schist facade while constructing 19 new residential units via an overbuild and connected new construction to the rear.
 Next door, developer Stuart Udis in May completed a $1.73 million purchase of the ornate Tourison Building , named for a family of developers who built both the Sedgwick Theater and much of East Mt. Airy’s housing stock in the early 20th century. Udis pulled permits this summer to rehab the building’s limestone facade and renovate nine existing upstairs apartments. He’s also seeking a new restaurant tenant for a ground floor corner retail space that has sat empty for years.
 Main Street Development and Blake Development Corporation's plans for the former site of Trolly Car Diner at 7619 Germantown Avenue include 114 apartments and 6,654 square feet of commercial space. | Photo: Michael Bixler | Rendering: M Architects
 A few blocks removed, on Mt. Airy Avenue, Udis is also pushing ahead with the construction of 12 new townhomes and an 18-unit apartment building at the site of a former auto shop. Udis said he now has a total of $35 million in investments in the neighborhood and is obviously high on its redevelopment potential. “It’s a neighborhood where people want to live,” he said.
 Nearby, the beep-beep-beeps and bang-bang-bangs of more new construction ring out. At the former site of the Trolley Car Diner along the neighborhood’s border with Chestnut Hill, Main Street Development has started vertical construction on a five-story, 114-unit apartment building, which will also include some 6,000 feet of commercial space, a project of unprecedented scale for the strip.
 At the far other end of Mt. Airy’s commercial corridor near the border with Germantown, yet more development awaits. Along this stretch, well-known Northwest Philadelphia developer Ken Weinstein has already converted part of the historic St. Michael’s Evangelical Lutheran Church into a pediatrics office and is still seeking a new use and tenant for the main chapel. He is also plowing ahead with more projects nearby, having recently redeveloped a Colonial-era home into a green housewares business and last year plunking down $950,000 to buy the Pelham Trust Company Bank, a locally-beloved 1907 structure he aims to turn into a destination restaurant. “It’s a really exciting time for Mt. Airy right now,” said Weinstein.
 The former Pelham Trust Company bank at 6740 Germantown Avenue and the Walder-Essig House (aka Beggarstown School) at 6669 Germantown Avenue have both been renovated for adaptive reuse recently. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Yet, not all are sold that it is for the best. Linda Bell, president of the community organization East Mt. Airy Neighbors, has lived in the neighborhood for all of her 70-plus years. She notes Mt. Airy is a diverse community with a history of debate about which way to steer it, so it can be difficult to pigeonhole community sentiment. Still, she quipped that “even Stevie Wonder can see” the neighborhood and its demographics are changing.
 For Bell, what has always tied together local residents of all backgrounds is a desire for a middle class, quiet way of living. She believes Mt. Airy has already lost some of that character. Not just from deep-pocketed transplants paying record rates to move into the area, but also large apartment buildings that propose to include affordable housing units. “We do not like to be sitting on top of each other. We like to spread out. We like our grass, we like our trees. If you want to live up here, you need to live up here,” Bell said. “Our families came here for a better way of life. We’re not against development, but the designs of the developments are breaking up the culture that we know as Mt. Airy.”
 Agrarian to Art Deco 
 Glen Fern, pictured here in 1884, tucked into the woods at the end of a path at Allens Lane. The stone house, farmstead, and mill was purchased by Thomas Livezey in 1747. | Photo courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 The most significant period of transition in Mt. Airy's history– from farmland to early Philadelphia suburb– was cemented a century ago, according to a history of the neighborhood compiled for the successful nomination of its historical district in 2019. Originally, the landscape served as a hunting ground for the indigenous Lenape, who traversed the area through an established trail that later became Germantown Avenue. In the 17th century, William Penn purchased tracts of land in the area from the Lenape and sold them to European settlers, with about 175 residents settling in Germantown by the end of the century. The purchase of their Germantown plots also came with rural “side land” lots located in the area of modern day Mt. Airy.
 The following centuries saw the significant growth of Germantown and Chestnut Hill, but Mt. Airy largely remained farmland. That began to change as the City took control of the neighborhoods in 1832, converted Germantown Avenue from a toll-based turnpike to public road in 1874, and various interests created a wealth of public transportation options in the last decades of that century.
 “The rail lines and the trolley made it practical to live in Mt. Airy and commute daily to work in other parts of Philadelphia, such as the business district in Center City,” the Planning Commission noted in its historic district nomination.
 French Village in West Mt. Airy was built by real estate developer George S. Woodward in the late 1920s. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Dating to Colonial times, the uber-wealthy had also built large country estates in the area, including William Allen, Chief Justice of colonial Pennsylvania and financier of Independence Hall, whose former Mt. Airy estate now lends its name to the neighborhood. However, with the arrival of the rail lines, a diversity followed. “Between 1880 and 1920, property developers such as Henry Houston , Ashton Tourison, Frank Mauran, and George S. Woodward built and sold developments in Mt. Airy of more modest year-round houses, ranging from large houses for the upper middle class to twins and rowhouses for those with lower incomes,” the nomination explained.
 By the 1920s, Mt. Airy had caught up to the times. Redevelopment along its Germantown Avenue corridor brought in three-story mixed use buildings: ground floor shops serving the neighborhood’s 25,000 residents with apartments above. A White Swan Hotel– a stopover inn for travelers on the way to points further west, which also found itself the target of prohibition raids– was torn down to make way for the mixed-use, Art Deco Tourison Building. Next door, civic leaders built the National Bank of Mt. Airy and deposited hundreds of thousands of dollars. Yet, it was Tourison’s 1928 opening of the Sedgwick Theater, designed by architect William Harold Lee, that “confirmed Mt. Airy’s change from rural to residential neighborhood,” the nomination concluded.
 More Change in the Air-y 
 St. Michael’s Evangelical Lutheran Church at 6671 Germantown Avenue in Mt. Airy. Developer Ken Weinstein converted part of the church complex into pediatric offices. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Those with living memories of Mt. Airy’s more recent history agree that the neighborhood’s commercial strip has continued to change in the century since it came into its own. Yet, they offer different perspectives on whether that is a good thing.
 Alex Bartlett, a native of West Mt. Airy and historian currently working as archivist for the Chestnut Hill Conservancy, said during the 1970s, “There just weren’t a lot of reasons to shop” on Mt. Airy’s Germantown Avenue. Sure, there were a few grocery stores and places to buy trading cards and grab a coke, he explained, but there were also a number of darkened store fronts and an abundance of businesses offering services like vacuum repair and furniture reupholstery that didn’t draw much foot traffic. More often than not, his family ended up in Germantown or Chestnut Hill for retail outings. On the whole, Bartlett said he’s OK with the direction Mt. Airy is currently heading, seeing it is a continuation of momentum that took a hit from COVID-19. “I think Mt. Airy was doing fairly well and is picking up where it left off before the pandemic,” said Bartlett.
 Michael Boyle, also a native son who is preparing to close up shop on an Owen’s Antiques store he has owned for two decades that is catty-corner from the theater, shares a similar perspective. He also recalled an undesirable corridor in the 1970s and credits a revitalization of McMenamin’s, a long-running tavern and neighborhood institution, for helping to seed change. He said the neighborhood already now has high quality restaurants like Jansen and La Trattoria and thinks the strip would benefit from more vibrant, boutique shops like the kind that draw regular foot traffic to Chestnut Hill.
 Bell isn’t sure that is what Mt. Airy needs. She laments the loss of service-oriented businesses like laundromats, hardware stores, and grocery stores that served practical purposes for middle class families living nearby. She also feels priced out of many of the neighborhood’s newer eateries. “Back in the day, we had more diversity in business owners and types of businesses, and that, to me, felt more doable, and more walkable,” said Bell. “How many coffeeshops, how many little pubs can you have? Talking about drawing people from other neighborhoods into your neighborhood. For what?”
 Bell also fears for Mt. Airy’s coveted greenspace. On this point, Bartlett agreed. Both say one of the things they most enjoyed growing up in Mt. Airy were the natural breaks in the strip, where rows of homes and businesses would give way to large pockets of greenspace, particularly visible today in campuses like the New Covenant Church and Lutheran Theological Seminary. “I would also argue development is hurting Mt. Airy because we had [open space] gaps, but they’re going away,” Bartlett said. “Sometimes you can have too much of a good thing. It depends on which side of the fence you’re sitting on.”
 Unarrestable Development? 
 National Bank of Mt. Airy at 7208 Germantown Avenue was built in 1926 and designed by Norman Hulme. An overbuild construction project will bring 19 new residential units to the property. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 To what extent further change can even be curtailed in Mt. Airy is uncertain. At the same time as it was nominating Mt. Airy’s historic district in 2019, the Planning Commission was also working with City Council to upzone the area. Among other changes, the rezoning allowed buildings with frontage on the Germantown Avenue corridor to reach heights of 55 feet by-right, as opposed to 38 feet. Developers quickly pounced, leading to the redevelopment of the National Bank of Mt. Airy and the large Main Street Development apartment building.
 Weinstein said a lot of what’s now happening in Mt. Airy has to do with the overlay opening the door for development trends already being felt in other areas of the city. However, he believes much of the change is locally organic, with the Mt. Airy Community Development Corporation and a handful of local real estate developers pushing to improve Germantown Avenue for the better part of two decades. In 2007, that led to the creation of a Business Improvement District, which levies an assessment for all business owners to pay for programs like street cleaning and beautification measures along the neighborhood’s commercial corridor. A latest initiative has raised $2.8 million to install nine pedestrian crosswalks and curb bump outs along the avenue in the years ahead.
 Weinstein also feels the creation of the historic district, which requires developers to keep existing facades intact and otherwise adhere to aesthetics, helped to strike a balance. He said both the CDC and the BID backed it, a “rare” event for development-focused organizations. “We want the commercial corridor to remain historic in nature,” Weinstein said. His biggest concern for the neighborhood is thus not new redevelopment, but the possibility of diminished service along SEPTA’s two regional rail lines serving East and West Mt. Airy, a major amenity of the greater neighborhood.
 Philip Dawson, executive director of the Mt. Airy CDC, is also a proponent of continuing new development in the neighborhood. He particularly calls attention to the east end of Germantown Avenue outside the historic district, where in the last five years a new apartment building and grocery store opened, while businesses like a boutique ice cream parlor and bicycle repair shop also moved in. “People are seeing an opportunity in Mt. Airy, and that’s a good thing,” Dawson said. “Because it’s an area that has a historic building stock, [which takes a] significant investment, some of which has kind of languished for some time. Now we’re seeing that flip beginning to happen.”
 Juston Lee Locklear, the owner of Avenues Cafe, a coffeeshop he opened in the heart of Mt. Airy’s historic business district in 2021, said he hears all perspectives from his patrons, some of whom are indeed transplants from Center City or Brooklyn. On one hand, he gets the concerns over development. As a resident of Passyunk in South Philadelphia, he dislikes walking by new construction there that is completely incongruous with the older housing stock.
