As a Black, Indigenous, and LGBTQ+ business owner, he is also sensitive to concerns around gentrification and the differences of people’s lived experiences. “The locals see that change. More cars on the street, increased property values, and some of these new developments the locals cannot even afford,” Locklear explained.
 At the same time, he can’t help but look out the large front window of his shop on a slow Tuesday, a gleam in his eye for the 160-plus new units of housing going up within walking distance. “As a business owner, the more the merrier,” Locklear said. “I want to have a very eclectic group of individuals, from locals, to new people looking to find their favorite coffeeshop, or someone who just moved here and are like, ‘Wow.’ Because Mt. Airy is very creative. It’s a melting pot. It’s beautiful.”
 Tags: adaptive resuse Development Mt. Airy Northwest Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Searching for the Song of Philadelphia: Introducing Hidden City's New Podcast
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Song of Philadelphia creator and host Julien Suaudeau started his career in Paris, in documentary film. | Photo: Anne Duchene
 Next week, Hidden City launches its first podcast, "Song of Philadelphia," a creation of author and filmmaker Julien Suaudeau (listen to the trailer HERE ). The concept is straightforward enough: Frenchman moves to Philly and sees and hears what we can not. But telling Philly stories is never straightforward, as Julien discovers, microphone in hand, in search of the intimate, personal Philadelphia. How much remembering and forgetting happens in our city every day? Can you hear the past humming through the present on the streets of Philadelphia?
 Each episode centers on Julien's encounter with a single Philadelphian. As, little by little, he builds a sound mosaic of the city. This fall, Hidden City will produce three episodes of Song of Philadelphia; three more will follow in the spring, with bonus episodes in the summer. We expect this rhythm to continue for years to come. And you will find it on your favorite listening platform ( Apple and Spotify ) and HERE on a special podcast page.
 Please join Hidden City for a Song of Philadelphia launch party at Vox Populi October 16 at 7PM . You can meet Julien and hear from the subjects of the fall's three episodes.
 To introduce the show, which I'm helping to produce, I asked Julien to give us some insight. How did this Parisian become so fascinated by Philadelphia?
 Nathaniel Popkin : A Parisian walks down the Ben Franklin Parkway toward City Hall….this is beginning to sound like a bad joke. But really, what did you see when you arrived in Philadelphia in 2006 (the year of Franklin's 300th birthday)?
 Julien Suaudeau : French people are so used to bullying our Belgian neighbors with stereotypical jokes—we couldn’t possibly complain when the joke is on us. The truth is, I had no idea who Ben Franklin was back in 2006. He was hardly more than just a name to me then—and a quote, the liberty vs safety dilemma that came back into style in the aftermath of 9/11. The history of his stay in Paris may be important to Philadelphians and in the US, but it is not something that we learn in French schools. So, when I first arrived here in August 2006, I knew of the “historic” element of Philadelphia, but I didn’t pay much attention to it. What struck me right away in Philly, as someone who had just spent a year in Vancouver, was how real it felt. To me, it was a real city—busy, messy, dirty, smelly, noisy—not a sanitized work/living arrangement.
 I sometimes think of that also in terms of place vs space. The surroundings of Vancouver are beautiful—the Rockies in the distance, the Pacific Ocean, the clean air. But I didn’t feel at home there. When I arrived in Philly, something familiar came through right away. Maybe it was that infamous grit, that “Philly thing” that gets overbranded these days. I am generally skeptical when the rough side of citiness or the sadness of the land is romanticized, but I do love a city that misbehaves. Oh, and going back to that summer of 2006, I remember the mugginess, the smell and the thickness of humidity as I drove down Washington Avenue to go get furniture at Ikea. I also remember the first time I spotted the giant silhouette of the SS United States, across the parking lot off Delaware (Columbus) Avenue. I had never seen a ship that big. It was like an uber-metaphor of industrial blight, greatness rusting into oblivion, and a very concrete materialization of the passage of time.
 Song of Philadelphia launches on all podcast platforms October 17.
 Nathaniel : How has your sense of Philadelphia evolved in 18 years?
 Julien : I think you always see and hear more as a newcomer or as an outsider. When you live anywhere long enough, unless your urban awareness is out of the ordinary, you always end up unseeing and unhearing, especially realities and aspects of life that may disrupt the storytelling that fits your interests and needs. That happens in Philly as much as in any city: unseeing unhoused people, overdoses, police brutalities, poverty, gun violence, underfunded public schools. The case of Kensington is extreme, both because of the scope of the crisis and the local policies that were implemented in response to it: how can you convince yourself, as an elected official or a voter, that cordoning off an entire neighborhood with police and/or a military presence is good governance? We can’t just decide that broken doesn’t exist, convince ourselves that we can just snap what bothers us out of existence and make it invisible. A better stance, I think, is to accept that broken is a part of us, and that it doesn’t make us ugly or less special to the rest of the world. This is one of the main lessons I have learned in and from Philadelphia. And, today, I feel like a Philadelphian as much as I am a Parisian. I don’t have to choose between one or the other, I’m fine with being a weird hybrid, and with the fact that I will keep changing, bouncing back and forth between these two poles of my world, sometimes feeling more from here, sometimes more from over there.
 Nathaniel : You've written four novels in French since coming to Philly— Dawa (2014), Le Français (2015), Ni le feu ni la foudre (2016), and Le sang noir des hommes (2019). Did you think, finally! I've arrived in the place where I can write the great French novel? In other words, did you need to get some distance to write?
 Julien : No doubt, but only because my first three novels were about contemporary France—the big mess (that’s what dawa means as a slang word, borrowed to Arabic) that we are still in as a postcolonial country that won’t accept itself as such. I had to take a few steps back to see the big picture. It was like looking at a painting: you always need to move to a certain distance and to a certain angle to make sense of it. To find a certain moment, too. It’s all a matter of perspective: I had the idea for Song of Philadelphia as I was walking in Paris one summer, surrounded by very Parisian sounds, and I found myself wondering which aspects of the Philadelphia soundscape I missed the most, or which Philadelphian sounds I would pick to explain my other home to people who have never been here. Home, back home. Which is which, now? Where am I really from? And does it mean anything? That’s when I realized that there is no signature sound of Philadelphia, except for the Philly Sound, of course! There is an infinite supply of city sounds, in Philly as anywhere, because there are so many of us, and we all experience the city in a singular way and build/store our memories according to our individual experiences in the city. This is the polyphony, the stream of consciousness that I am trying to capture in the podcast.
 Not the Seine down there. Julien Suaudeau on Lincoln Drive. | Photo: Anne Duchene
 Nathaniel : In what ways does going back to Paris every summer infect your experience of Philadelphia? Or vice versa…What about the City of Brotherly Love do you carry with you to the City of Light? (A more straightforward way to ask: what about Philadelphia do you miss when you're in Paris….and vice versa)
 Julien : I know what I don’t miss: the heat, the humidity, and the need to turn on the AC to make it through the day or to get some sleep. Because of climate change, we do have more and more heat waves in Paris, but it is mostly dry heat, and the absence of AC kind of removes the agency to make things worse for the planet. You just feel miserable and wait it out. The other thing I don’t miss when I am away is the loudness. Jean-Luc Godard used to joke that Americans talk loud because their country is too big and they can’t hear themselves unless they scream. What I do miss is the chorus of voices, the rhythm of them all. Because English is not my native language, when I hear it spoken it always sounds as if it’s coming out of a movie or a music album. I grew up listening to British and American indie bands and watching American cinema. One of my greatest satisfactions as an adult is that I don’t need a translation anymore to read something that was written in English. I guess that’s why, almost twenty years in, I still marvel at the voices of Philadelphia. The personalities, the stories and the memories they carry. I miss that warmth and that energy when I’m somewhere else. French people, especially in Paris, have a much more hushed way of talking to each other. They are also less guarded, I think, when it comes to talking about themselves or what’s on their mind, whatever they’re going through. I love the idea that the podcast is about sitting down with someone and having them open up to share something that is part of themselves—not the most American thing to do, in my experience. The other thing that requires a major adjustment when I go back to Paris in the summer is my perception of time: everything moves more slowly. I don’t think I miss the American rush, the no-nonsense efficiency, the Wawa cup in one hand and the cellphone in the other, but there’s something about the Philadelphian pulse that I carry with me when I go away. It’s like time zones: I always know what time it is in Philly, no matter how far away I am.
 Nathaniel : Is it possible to experience two cities at once? How does this work for you?
 Julien : And three, four, even! On any given day in Philly, I always find myself in a moment that overlaps with another moment experienced in Paris, or in London, or in Brussels, the other cities where I lived long enough to have this built-in storage device, this archive of experiences that only rise to the conscious level when something happening elsewhere reminds me of the trace they left. The ghosts that live with us are not just people we’ve lost or that we don’t see anymore: they are moments, feelings, emotions. It is very tempting for me to slide down the rabbit hole of those reminiscences, which can take the form of what Baudelaire, who knew a thing or two about walking around the city, called correspondances : I smell this on Italian Market, which triggers the taste of something I ate long ago in the fifth arrondissement, across from a movie theater that was showing a movie I first saw in the West End. I could spend days just contemplating the ways those memories signal to each other. I guess, in a way, Song of Philadelphia is an attempt to find a sound translation to that process and to experience it collectively, with a community of listeners, not by myself. You just have to walk around and find the gateways, the portals.
 Nathaniel : I recently read Ni le feu ni la foudre (Not Fire Nor Lightening), told in multiple first person voices as the narrator-characters navigate the present and the past (through personal/place memory). Does this approach inform what you're hoping to do with Song of Philadelphia?
 Julien : Definitely. One can never get enough stream of consciousness in their life. Virginia Woolf’s Mrs. Dalloway is one of the rare books I go back to: it’s as if the flow keeps going when you close the book, and yet you are never disoriented (or it’s a pleasant disorientation) when you open it again. Like radio stations in the night: they keep broadcasting airwaves even when almost no one is listening in. I want to record as much of Philadelphia as I can, not to put it in a museum, like an artifact, but to highlight some of the deep-seated rhymes, overlays, matching notes in the infinite tap of experiences and memories that make up the city. Our collective stream of consciousness is woven into the fabric of the city.
 Nathaniel : The log line for Song of Philadelphia is: How much remembering and forgetting happens in our city every day? Can you hear the past humming through the present on the streets of Philadelphia? Julien Suaudeau came over from Paris in 2006 and started to hunt for sounds and stories. Now you can listen to his audio archive, Song of Philadelphia, an exclusive podcast from Hidden City. Is part of the premise to elicit from Philadelphians their hidden stories? As if to dig through the individual minds and memories to create a collective experience?
 Julien : It depends on the meaning that you assign to eliciting something that’s hidden. If it’s about extracting, probing, investigating even, this is not what I’m doing. I don’t see myself as a journalist reporting a story, or trying to get to the bottom of it. I am more of a listener, an archivist, and a storyteller. I listen to the stories people entrust me with, I record them, and I edit them with sounds that I grab as I go. Those stories are hidden in the sense that they are personal experiences or memories, and that the medium is audio, not visual. On the same token, focussing on sound makes us aware of so many layers of the city and of our lives that we are no longer paying attention to. At the end of the day, Song of Philadelphia will be something like a sound mosaic of the city, a time capsule of what it was like to live here in the 2020s. Just kidding: I have no idea where this will take me. The city and the infinitive number of ways we experience it will show me the path. I also like the idea of a constellation of stories. If one object defines Philly for me, it’s the star bolts that keep so many of our walls straight (sort of). Something about them touches me: they indicate a weakness, but they are also evidence of support, resilience. We’re still here, and we should be proud to be a vulnerable city. A good story, one you can empathize with, is when the storyteller opens their heart to you. Philly is that open book to me.
 Nathaniel : How do we hear the past humming through the present?
 Julien : There’s this French pastry called mille-feuilles —one thousand layers/sheets. I don’t have the physics skills to go into Einstein’s theory of eternalism—you should read Alan Moore’s Jerusalem if you want to see how it unfolds as a literary experience – but the idea that everything that happens doesn’t stop happening just because our narrow subjectivity can only process a linear timeline is very appealing to me. A city is a juxtaposition of thin places: sites where you can see the past leaking through the present. I guess the official, touristy version of that here is Independence Hall-style horse carriage tours of Society Hill. That’s what the majority of outsiders are drawn to in Philly: the alpha of the nation. We assume that colonial-era buildings and cobblestone streets are the baseline. That was my perception when I first got here, but as time went by I have realized that this is a very narrow, Eurocentric way of looking at history. What did this place look like before it was called Philadelphia, or Pennsylvania? Who was here? Can we explore the past without the sense of ownership that comes with naming things? Memory can be deceitful and self-serving, in that we can warp it to shield ourselves from what was there before what we’ve been taught to remember, or even from the complexity of what really happened. But it’s really the one tool we have to expand our conception of time. The sound of someone trying to remember, to piece out a chain of events or to recall a specific moment—I don’t know of many things that move me more. When that person is sharing their story with you, you are literally listening to a time-travel experience, and they are inviting you on that journey.
 Nathaniel : What do you see (hear, experience) in Philadelphia as an immigrant that some of us crusty natives can't or don't?
 Julien : I’m not sure. The sound that the crust makes when it crumbles?
 Nathaniel : What sort of past sounds (or what specific sounds) do you wish you could still hear?
 Julien : The song of Philadelphia before the internal combustion engine. The voices of my children when they were three-years old. They didn’t speak much English, but they had such a badass Philly accent.
 Nathaniel : There are quite a lot of podcasts where people tell their personal stories. What's going to make this one stand out?
 Julien : The accent, again. No one can speak English like I do.
 Nathaniel : This is not the only podcast you're working on. With the Citizen, you're producing People Left Behind, which tells stories of survivors and co-victims of gun violence in Philly. How do these two shows relate?
 Julien : Both are 100 percent Philly-made and Philly-centered. This is me trying to contribute to my community, to make it a better place, and also trying to fit in. I do so by telling stories, because this is my trade. So much in the world is broken, damaged, or a source of pain and suffering. Stories don’t fix anything, but they provide a structure – they help us make sense of stuff that can often feel meaningless. And they give agency to the people telling them. It brings me great joy to be the go-between, the one to share what they have to say or what’s on their mind with the world.
 Nathaniel : You also head up the film dept at Bryn Mawr. I've heard that French people know something about the cinema…what role did movies play in your understanding of Philly?
 Julien : I was obsessed (this is not a figure of speech) with Trading Places when I was a child. I knew the dialogues by heart and can still deliver them—in the French dubbed version. Later, it was Blow Out , Mikey and Nicky . I went back in time as I got older. And now, I teach at a college where Katherine Hepburn is an alum—she was admitted in 1924, one hundred years ago. Because The Philadelphia Story is really The Main Line Story (on a Hollywood soundstage), I feel compelled to set the record straight and tell the Philly Philly story—show the world the dark side of the moon, if you will. But there’s more to my lifetime attraction to Philadelphia than the movies. The Philly Sound, The Roots. Charles Barkley… You should have seen me as a six-foot, fourteen-year-old power forward on the basketball courts in Paris.
 Nathaniel : Let's say I'd like to tell my story on Song of Philadelphia. How do I get in touch?
 Julien : Just holler. Eventually, I will hear you. Here’s an email address to reach out if you don’t have the patience to wait: songofphiladelphia@hiddencityphila.org. And tell your friends and neighbors that I’m looking forward to hearing from them, too.
 Tags: Immigrants literature podcast soundscape West Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Nathaniel Popkin Hidden City Daily co-founder Nathaniel Popkin’s latest book is To Reach the Spring: From Complicity to Consciousness in the Age of Eco-Crisis.

title: Admirers of North Philly’s Diamond Theater Race Against the Clock
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
It’s a bit hidden, but it's there. Heading up Germantown Avenue in North Philadelphia, on the right just after the intersection with Diamond Street, something suddenly breaks up the flow of flat facades of brown-and-beige rowhouses. An old marquee juts out over the sidewalk of a triple-wide building and catches the eye, which then drifts to beautiful ornamentation elsewhere: colorful little pendants and terra cotta flourishes tucked into corners and a crowning, decorative pediment containing a grotesque face, its mouth agape.
 What is this thing? Peer closer and the faded outlines and empty lightbulb sockets of a sign above the marquee spell it out for you. It’s the Diamond, a century-old theater whose further existence remains in question, according to those who have come to love it.
 Call Andy Molholt the leader of that crowd. By day, the Kensington resident is a successful musician, known for his work as guitarist for indie-rock outfit Speedy Ortiz and previously Laser Background. Yet, in his spare time, Molholt has gained an interest in historic preservation, particularly of Philadelphia’s diverse and endangered old-time movie theaters, whose extant numbers have been in decline since their heyday in the first half of the 20th century.
 The Diamond Theater at 2119-2123 Germantown Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 According to a 2011 article by architect Shawn Evans on PhillyHistory.org's blog , as of 1932 the city had at least 275 movie theaters of various sizes–from grand Center City venues offering thousands of seats to tiny neighborhood nickelodeons. However, by 2013, as Rachel Hildebrandt wrote previously for Hidden City , only half that number remained and only a handful still in use as theaters.
 Since then, Molholt has watched as more were razed, most notably Chestnut Street’s Boyd Theater , which, until its demolition in 2015, was Center City’s last great movie palace. “It was an absolute crime that the place was destroyed,” Molholt said.
 The downward trend line has made Molholt nervous, particularly for the theater in his neck of the woods, the Diamond. Built circa 1922, the building made it about 50 years as a theater. At one point its name was changed to Teatro Puerto Rico to cater to new arrivals to the city from the Caribbean island, before converting more recently into a house of worship. Last year a for sale sign went up above the old theater’s marquee. Word came down that it was being eyed as a potential demo-and-redevelop job by a prospective buyer.
 The threat transformed Molholt from admirer to activist. Teaming up with experienced preservationists, namely The Keeping Society of Philadelphia ’s Oscar Beisert, the building has now been nominated for listing on Philadelphia’s Register of Historic Places , which would offer legal protection against the demolition or alteration of the building's facade. With hearings due this fall, the race to protect the Diamond Theater is on.
 A Theater for Every Neighborhood 
 The Bijou Theater at 8th and Arch Streets circa 1890s. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 If you grew up like Molholt, a native of suburban Hatfield in Montgomery County, your memories of going to the movies probably involved driving to the one or two area multiplexes: big theaters with multiple screens showing most of the latest major movie releases. If, like Molholt, you relocated to the city, you may have also learned to love arthouse theaters like the Ritz. Yet, if you dig just a little deeper, you come to learn just how truly rich the city’s theater landscape once was. 
 The craze began in December 1895 when the Lumière brothers of France, whose name appropriately translates to “light," are typically credited with orchestrating the first public screening of a motion picture using their invention, the Cinematograph, in Paris. In his 2011 piece for PhillyHistory.org, Evans noted that moving pictures debuted in Philadelphia around the same time, first appearing at the Bijou Theatre (1889-1967) near 8th and Race Streets. Indeed, an August 1896 advertisement in The Philadelphia Times touted the Cinematographe at the Bijou and offered up an already robust daily schedule of viewings, including the somewhat quizzically titled films Arrival of the Mail Train , The Gardener and the Bad Boy , and The Instantaneous Sausage Machine . "The most marvelous life-motion picture projector ever seen,” the ad nevertheless insisted. “Showing the most interesting, most life-like, and the funniest pictures ever exhibited in this country.”
 The former Bijou Theater, now named New Garden Theater, in 1938. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 In his research Evans noted that the Bijou sat in the heart of what was then a theater district and showcased “brief, silent experiments of the moving image.” While the theater had seating for 1,200 people, smaller, nickelodeon theaters came to dominate over the next two decades, taking their name from the common five-cent cost of admission. More than 130 were built by 1917, but gave way to more robust theaters as the release of full-length films ramped up that decade, requiring comfortable theaters for larger audiences. With “screen time” during that era of course limited to movie houses, hundreds more were constructed in all parts of Philadelphia into the early 1930s to cater to public demand. “The finest of the movie palaces were located in Center City, although many were built in the outlying neighborhoods,” Evans observed.
 In a recent email, Hildebrandt said the theaters quickly began playing an important role in American life and had deep and lasting cultural impacts. “The theater was a type of third space, and it thrived as a place for folks to gather and be,” Hildebrandt noted. “It also had a lot of influence on society. I'm reading a book now that traces fashion trends to their origins. Film was key in introducing Americans to the ‘French girl’ aesthetic, for example.”
 Birth of the Diamond 
 The Diamond Theater in 1945. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 In the early 1920s, moving pictures would reach a little corner of North Philadelphia. There in 1922, a few blocks northeast of what is now SEPTA's Temple University train station, the Cohocksink Amusement Company purchased a series of dwellings at 2117 to 2123 Germantown Avenue to clear the way for what would become the Diamond Theater, according to research assembled by Beisert for the building’s historic nomination.
 Shortly thereafter, the project flipped from Cohocksink to The Diamond Amusement Company, which oversaw construction between July 1922 and January 1923. The name attached was Michael “Mike” Lessy, a Russian-Jewish immigrant who also operated the Collingswood Theater in New Jersey and the Standard Theater in Camden, as well as a Aurora Theater just opposite of the Diamond, which was known to have associations with Universal Pictures. Architecture firm Neubauer & Supowitz was hired to design the building. In the nomination Beisert concluded that it was likely that David Supowitz, a “prolific Jewish architect and designer of theater buildings in the Philadelphia region” who primarily designed the Diamond.
 The auditorium of the Diamond Theater. Date unknown. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 Beisert added that the building’s design was very much in line with the times. Constructed of brick, terra cotta, and steel, its Classical Revival facade matched the Georgian, Greek Revival, and Palladian styles of theaters like the Chestnut Street, Walnut Street, and Fox theaters. Beisert particularly noted a pair of arched, second-story windows that originally flanked the Diamond’s marquee before later being mostly infilled. “With the projecting iron balustrades, these balconies gave the building a sense of importance, as though one of the actors might come out and wave to a crowd on Germantown Avenue,” Beisert waxed.
 The theater’s roughly 960 seats was on par with most further-flung theaters of that time, representative of “a neighborhood or small-town theater building type,” Beisert wrote. However, its interior space was well-appointed, with Lessy ordering renovations as early as 1926 and adding central air in 1935. “The early interior included a central screen that looked very much like an elaborate stage that was flanked by speakers set in frames that mimicked Palladian windows,” Beisert explained.
 Changing Times 
 The Mastbaum Theater at 20th and Market Streets. Date unknown. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 The end of this heyday of grand theaters snuck up quickly, particularly as the introduction of “the talkies” killed off silent films and the need for more robust spaces such as orchestra pits. “For the most part, the era of these elaborate buildings was over even before the Great Depression began,” Evans wrote, adding the economic cataclysm only steepened the trend.
 Perhaps most emblematic was the Mastbaum Theater , a large, 4,700-seat theater at 20th and Market Streets that was built in 1929 and torn down just 29 years later. Many theaters of all sizes would follow, particularly as technological and sociological trends converged in the mid-20th century. “Theaters were ubiquitous from roughly 1890 until the 1960s, when television became accessible to middle class families,” Hildebrandt explained. “In addition to TV, urban neighborhoods changed as a result of deindustrialization and white flight to the suburbs. Considering this, many held on longer than one might expect.”
 By the time her 2013 article was published, after Hildebrandt performed a full accounting of the city’s past and present movie houses, she concluded that of an original list of nearly 400 theaters just 135 remained. Very few of these were on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, and, in the decade since, several more have met their end, including the Bluebird , Columbia , Girard , Poplar , Royal , and Strand theaters to name a few. Even still, some hold on, particularly in historic corridors outside of Center City where they are often “masked by modernization and hidden in plain sight,” Hildebrandt said.
 Enter the Diamond. According to Beisert, the theater existed in its original form until about 1950, when it began to transform along with the greater neighborhood, as Puerto Rican immigrants moved in following World War II. Lessy, the original proprietor, died in 1948. Two years later, Josephine Trilla applied for permits to put up signage advertising the Diamante (Spanish for diamond) Theater. A change in ownership became official in 1960 when Felix Rodriguez purchased the property from Lessy’s estate and shortly thereafter renamed it the Teatro Puerto Rico. It appears the venue may have served as somewhat of a neighborhood institution: a June 1964 article published by the Philadelphia Inquirer laid out the trials and tribulations of the surrounding community and featured a photograph of the theater. “Spanish language films are featured at Teatro Puerto Rico on Germantown Avenue near 6th and Diamond Streets in the heart of the Puerto Rican settlement,” the caption noted. Beisert also discovered in his research its significance to Puerto Rican residents as a place of “community and social engagement” and as one of the "few Spanish language" theaters in the city.
 Its history since then is a bit hazier. Beisert found that its run as Teatro Puerto Rico appeared to cease in 1975. 36 years then passed until a church, The Iglesia Ministerio Maranatha Pentecostal, purchased the property in 2011, apparently worshipping there until a few years ago. Newspaper records suggest a record shop and nuisance bar may have operated at the address prior to the church's ownership, although it is unclear whether such functions utilized the actual theater space. The property historically included two smaller shops and storefronts flanking the main entrance.
 The former Diamond Theater, since renamed Teatro Puerto Rico, circa 1960s. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 By the early 2000s, Google Street View images show a shuttered and nameless facade that persisted until at least 2012, followed by some restoration work and signage denoting the church’s occupancy by 2014. Evidence of upkeep continued until the for sale sign went up sometime in 2023. That is when Molholt sprang into action.
 The musician’s interest in theaters grew out of his appreciation for interesting, creative spaces. In his 20s, Molholt lived in a DIY warehouse in Philadelphia that put on music shows. Once he stumbled upon the historical theaters dotting the city’s landscape, he dreamed of perhaps one day converting one into a proper venue. Then he witnessed the destruction of several favorites, including the 2021 demolition of the Richmond Theater in Port Richmond and The Strand at 12th Street and Girard Avenue the same year. This prompted Molholt to leave a message several years ago with the owner of the Diamond Theater, which City records currently still list as the church, expressing his appreciation for the building and asking for them to call him before any potential sale was made public. When the theater was placed on the market, Molholt toured the building and found it in decent condition. Both the interior and exterior have undergone significant renovations over time that have removed or at least hidden many of the original architectural details, but overall the building remains structurally sound, he said. Molholt also got in touch with the selling agent and came to understand that a New York investment firm was eyeing the property “to destroy it and turn it into condos.”
 Unable to swing financing for the building himself, Molholt turned to Beisert, whom he’d met during an earlier protest of the demolition of another historic building. Molholt established a crowd-funding a campaign to allow Beisert to research and write the historic nomination for the Diamond, aiming to spare it from a fate of demolition regardless of who takes ownership.
 On one hand, Molholt is cognizant of not wanting to bigfoot long-time residents. However, he also believes in the value of such buildings, both for their original history and continued importance as the city evolved. “The current owner has had it for a decade and probably lived in that area when it was at its worst,” he said. “But a bunch of beautiful old buildings getting destroyed and turned into soulless condos that no one can afford isn’t exactly good for the neighborhood either.”
 The building’s fate potentially hangs in the balance as the Philadelphia Historical Commission considers the historic designation application this fall. On Wednesday, October 16, the Historical Commission's Committee on Historic Designation voted to recommend that the building satisfies criteria for listing. However, the final decision will fall to the full Historical Commission, which is currently scheduled to consider the application at a Nov. 8 meeting. As someone who’s toured the country and played to audiences in spaces not unlike that of the Diamond, Molholt remains hopeful. “On a recent tour I had the pleasure of playing six or seven old, beautiful theaters that were movie palaces that have been converted into live music spots,” Molholt said. “The fate of all these doesn’t have to be condos."
 Tags: adaptive resuse Hispanic heritage Historic theaters Norris Square North Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: When Hot Dogs Threatened the Wissahickon Valley
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The Wissahickon Valley has just about everything one could want in a park. There’s the beautiful sight of light filtering through the leaves of a towering oak, then reflecting off of the gently flowing creek below. In summer comes the sweet songs of the wood thrush and scarlet tanager. Year round, dozens of miles of rugged trails, coated with the sparkling dust of Wissahickon schist crushed underfoot, invite visitors to take it all in. But where, they may ask, are all of the hot dogs?
 If you’ve ever found yourself pining for a pig in a blanket during a visit to this natural gem of Northwest Philadelphia, know that you almost had it your way. As recently retold by Philadelphia-based architectural conservator Kate Cowing during a talk at the park’s Valley Green Inn in mid-May, the humble frankfurter was once at the center of a controversy that echoed through the Wissahickon Valley in Depression-era Philadelphia.
 A political cartoon published in the Philadelphia Bulletin satirizing the "Hot Dog Crisis" of 1937. | Image courtesy of Chestnut Hill Conservancy
 On one side was a movement to modernize the city’s park system by adding robust, active recreation. In the Wissahickon this took the form of a plan championed by the Fairmount Park Commission and federal Works Progress Administration (WPA) to vastly transform the park with playing fields, picnic areas, and, yes, numerous confectioners selling sweets, meats, and other assorted treats from stands along the trails.
 Opposing this vision was, who else, but the Chestnut Hill crowd. In today’s times, it’s the racket of pickleballs going "pop-pop-pop" that stirs the ire of the inhabitants of this well-to-do neighborhood. Yet, in November 1937, as Cowing retold, it was an article in The Philadelphia Inquirer entitled, “Hot Dog Stand Menace Looms in Wissahickon,” that publicly laid bare the transformational plans. The locals in opposition had a powerful ally in Francis Reeves Strawbridge, director of Strawbridge and Clothier department store, who at the time was president of the Friends of the Wissahickon (FOW), which came out against the plans. Pennsylvania State Senator George Woodward was also a member of the FOW. Woodward was a resident of Chestnut Hill who took no effort to hide his disdain for the proposal. “I think the plans are rotten,” Woodward said, according to Cowing’s research.
 The Fairmount Park Guard station at Forbidden Drive and Allen Lane was built in 1938 by President Franklin D. Roosevelt's Works Progress Administration. The wood and stone structure was restored to its original condition in 2005 after years of neglect. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 If you’ve walked the Wissahickon, you obviously know who won. Ultimately, the plans were scaled back to a much more modest WPA effort to build more utilitarian, rustic, low-slung buildings that still dot the park’s trails today. Cowing detailed the history of both these structures and their ties to the 1937 controversy decades ago in her master’s thesis for the University of Pennsylvania. The document, and Cowing’s expertise, remain essential to understanding and preserving the buildings’ legacies.
 “That graduate thesis is a foundational document that's used by the Friends, by the Parks department, and by many others as we circle back to these buildings,” said Ruffian Tittmann, current executive director of the FOW. “Both for a great deal of interest in the built history of the Wissahickon and a great deal of need in stewarding those buildings.”
 Efforts to Save a Landscape 
 A woman stands in front of the ruins of an old water wheel and the crumbling stone walls of an old mill on the banks of the Wissahickon Creek in 1906. | Photo courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 Visiting the Wissahickon today, it is easy to imagine the park as some virgin woodland, untouched for centuries as development grew around it, hot dog proposals be damned, but Cowing noted it is anything but. Well before the Depression-era controversy, the Wissahickon was indeed a site of both industry and recreation and of the seediest kind. Before the 1,800-acre valley was acquired by Fairmount Park in 1868, more than 60 mills lined the course of the creek, with a turnpike (now Forbidden Drive) used to transport goods into the city. During the same era when Edgar Allen Poe and other famous writers hailed the natural beauty of the Wissahickon, its banks were also rife with the busyness of industry. “Over the years there have been log mills, dye mills, nail-cutting mills, oil mills, and textile mills,” Cowing explained.
 Also present were seven inns catering to tourists. Some were nice places to visit, and others were infamous for different reasons. “Valley Green always had a great reputation,” Cowing said. “But some of them were real dives. At the Old Log Cabin Inn there were gangs that came and fought each other. It actually kept wild animals in the inn, including two bears that were tied to chains and apparently knew how to unpick locks.”
 The Old Log Cabin Inn. Date unknown. | Photo courtesy of Chestnut Hill Conservancy
 Then, things changed. Liquor laws killed most of the inns, Cowing said. Fairmount Park took over, and a 19th-century, nationwide Park Movement to beautify landscapes in their natural splendor took root. “[The movement advocated] picturesque parks and that they would be an antidote to urban life and add to the quality of family and community,” Cowing explained.
 After the Fairmount Park Commission took over, many of the park’s buildings were rapidly removed in line with the Park Movement ethos. Then, in the early 20th century, an effort to close the Wissahickon’s turnpike to vehicular traffic was made. Local groups formed to support the cause, including the FOW, which celebrates its centennial this year. They were ultimately successful in leading to the naming of Forbidden Drive. That set the table for the largely natural and motor-free landscape Philadelphians still see today.
 Parks and Pork 
 This watercolor from 1914 shows League Island Park, later renamed Franklin Delano Roosevelt Park, before the Park Reform Movement of the 1930s. | Image courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 The Wissahickon’s freshly-minted sylvan character would be tested before long. Twin events conspired against it. First, the onset of the Great Depression and its waves of unemployment hit the area, including Chestnut Hill, where many Italian immigrants had moved to mine and mason stone to build nearby homes, giving the neighborhood much of its character today. Local make-work projects funded by prosperous citizens aimed to ease the pain of newly unemployed men, but such efforts would soon be subsumed by President Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s WPA.
 Also afoot was a new park philosophy, called the Park Reform Movement, in which active recreation was now being championed across the nation. Fairmount’s system was deemed too old fashioned, Cowing said, helping lead, for example, to the development of playing fields and a golf course at Philadelphia’s aptly-named FDR Park. “City parks were supposed to give city people places to go to expel their energy," Cowing noted. "Ball fields, golf courses, slides, picnic areas, tennis courts, et cetera, et cetera.”
 A national study by Lebert Weir, then-director of the National Recreation Association, called out Philadelphia’s park system as one of the nation’s worst laggards, but not for long. The desire to upgrade the city’s parks dovetailed with WPA efforts and resulted in a city-wide, $16 million overhaul between 1935 and 1942.
 NIMP: Not In My Park 
 A Philadelphia Inquirer artist's conception circa 1930s of what Wissahickon Valley Park would look like with hot dog stands dotting the banks of the creek. | Image courtesy of Chestnut Hill Conservancy
 Within this effort to overhaul, the Wissahickon Valley was a bit of an odd duck. The Inquirer expose of November 11, 1937 launched controversy over proposed changes to the park before they were even publicly announced, and the newspaper led, of course, with the hot dog.
 “The ‘hot dog menace,’ repulsed at Valley Forge…” the story began, citing an earlier effort to offer concessions at that Montgomery County-based historical landmark. “… threatened yesterday to invade the winding valley of the Wissahickon.”
 A bit further down, the paper added some mustard. “Blueprints are ready; the money has been appropriated, workers are available,” the piece continued. “And ere next summer arrives the blossoming trees may vie for honors with Coney Island stands, and the scent of new-born violets and arbutus may be lost in the blanketing odor of fresh fried hot dogs.”
 However, included within the article were early hints of weakness among the reformers pushing for a massive repurposing of the park. Quoted was Alan Corson, chief engineer for the Fairmount Park Commission, who told the newspaper that public blowback could halt the plans. “The whole scheme is subject to change,” Corson said. As Cowing's research shows, it did indeed, and dramatically so.
 An architectural drawing of the north elevation of Lincoln Drive Guard House, 1939. | Image courtesy of Chestnut Hill Conservancy
 Initial plans for the park were robust: 10 picnic areas with lawns, 12 toilets, 12 shelters, four larger shelters, 600 picnic benches, 16,000 feet of paths with 12 rustic bridges, six tennis course, three baseball fields, the planting of 1,168 trees and 10,000 plants, and the installation or repair of more than 20,000 feet of fencing. Plus quarrying, repairing dams, building stone retaining walls, and on. Enough work for 1,031 men for 10-months at a cost of $833,869.
 However, following public blowback, the initial work was reduced to three guard shelters, three toilet buildings, three picnic shelters, two trailhead structures, and the adaptive reuse of two remaining mill buildings. By the end of the WPA’s work in the valley in 1943, its output had grown modestly to the construction of a total of 13 new buildings and the renovation of three existing buildings, but nothing nearly approaching the original proposal.
 “There were so many letters to the editor that it really took the city by surprise,” Cowing said of the public outcry that led to the vast reduction in plans. “The idea that the WPA would actually ruin this natural wonderland that the park only created 60 years before just was horrific.”
 Preservation, Not Preservatives 
 Bell's Mill Guardbox circa 1930s. | Photo courtesy of Chestnut Hill Conservancy
 When Cowing began the work for her 1997 thesis on the WPA-era buildings of the Wissahickon, she said she found several in serious disrepair, some even beyond saving. “Nobody had looked at these buildings in a comprehensive manner before. The collective memory of their construction had disappeared,” Cowing explained during her presentation at Valley Green Inn. “They were just sort of missing in action.”
 Her work also came at a pivotal moment. There was a debate within local Wissahickon Valley supporters whether or not to try and save the aging buildings or let them disappear fully into the past. Yet, members of the FOW saw fit to fund Cowing's thesis, and after it was published the organization, along with the City’s Department of Parks & Recreation, endeavored to repair and preserve the buildings into the future using historically-appropriate materials. Tittmann specifically recalled the repair of a WPA-era building near Mt. Airy Avenue after a damaging fire in 2006. “They used the thesis as a document that guided that restoration effort,” he explained.
 Cowing said that of the 16 WPA-era buildings, 12 remain. Most of them, she added, are textbook examples of the National Park Service guidelines of the time, which called for buildings to blend into their surroundings. In the Wissahickon, that meant they were largely constructed of Wissahickon schist stone from a local quarry and topped with log roofs and wooden shingles made from felled trees in the valley. The buildings are also low-slung and one-story, with “super low” pitch. “They emphasized horizontality and essentially had an obtrusive nature,” Cowing said.
 Thomas Mill Comfort Station circa 1930s. | Photo courtesy of Chestnut Hill Conservancy
 The bathrooms were especially concealed, tucked away amongst shrubbery and utilizing honeycomb-like terracotta pipes to allow for light and ventilation while concealing their function.
 Of the remaining structures, perhaps the most recognizable is Ten Box, a curiously-shaped structure at the intersection of Forbidden and Lincoln Drives, which is bisected by a large covered passageway that allows for recreationalists to follow the Wissahickon Bike Trail along the Monoshone Creek. According to the FOW’s website , the structure originally served as a guardhouse, replete with a wood stove and working telephone. It’s the latter device from which the building gets its name: numerous call boxes along the Wissahickon were identified by their number, and this one was the 10th along the trail and the only that remains. However, the phone line no longer functions today, and another past use for a bicycle vending operation has also come and gone.
 The bicycle concessions at the Ten Box in 1940. | Photo courtesy of Print and Picture Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 Moving up the creek, additional WPA-era buildings include several guard boxes and picnic and comfort shelters, capped at the other end by an entry building at Bells Mills.
 Today, the structures primarily serve the public as places to simply get out of the elements. Tittmann said some WPA-era bathrooms were considered as a part of an ongoing effort by FOW to explore the addition of more restrooms within the park, but she adds that several are located in flood prone areas unfit to house an active vault toilet.
 Still, many admire their historic value. Bruce Bohri, a spokesman for the Department of Planning and Development said that the buildings are not listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, but are owned by the City and “maintained to historic preservation standards.”
 When asked for his views on the WPA structures, Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, said he thinks they could potentially “merit designation as a thematic historic district, much like the historic subway entrances, Carnegie libraries, and historic street paving, which are all designated as thematic historic districts,” Steinke noted. “It wouldn’t be a simple undertaking, but it would be great if someone would do it.”
 Tags: Fairmount Park food history Wissahickon Valley Park WPA 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: New Name for College Avenue Honors Civil Rights Activists in North Philly
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
Earlier this month a cut of College Avenue flanking the campus of Girard College was given the honorary name "Freedom Fighters Way." | Photo: Scott Foley
 On Friday, October 4, North College Avenue was officially given the honorary name of Freedom Fighters Way. The renamed street runs along the side of Girard College, the 43-acre boarding school surrounded by a 10-foot high, 14-inch-thick stone wall.
 Nearly 60 years ago, these walls saw round-the-clock protest marches that were part of an effort to force the school to admit Black students. Following the lead of attorney Cecil B. Moore, the firebrand leader of the Philadelphia NAACP, activists sang and held signs as they circled the segregated fortress in the middle of their neighborhood.
 Girard College: Philadelphia’s Signature Civil Rights Struggle 
 Civil rights protesters march along the wall of Girard College on College Avenue in 1965. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 Girard College was created by the City of Philadelphia in 1848 using funds provided by the estate of wealthy financier Stephen Girard. In his 1831 will, Girard stipulated that the money should be used to support a boarding school for “poor white male orphans.” After the 1954 Brown v. Board decision banned segregation in public schools, City Councilmember Raymond Pace Alexander filed suit to desegregate Girard College. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled that as a City-run institution, Girard College had to admit African American students. School leaders turned control over to a group of private trustees to maintain the whites-only policy.
 The segregated school in the midst of what had become a Black neighborhood was a daily affront to many North Philadelphia residents. Moore thought direct action would be the most effective means of putting pressure on the Girard College board of trustees to end their exclusionary practices. Beginning on May 1, 1965 and continuing for seven months and 17 days, Moore and his followers marched around the walls of Girard College day and night. Many of the protestors were young people in their teens and 20s who came to call themselves the Young Militants.
 Cecil B. Moore addresses a crowd during demonstrations in 1965 pushing to desegregate Girard College. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 The marchers faced harassment from police officers that sometimes escalated into physical confrontations and arrests, but they continued to show up. When Martin Luther King Jr. visited Philadelphia in the summer of 1965, he and Moore held a joint rally in front of the school. Local and national attention put increasing pressure on city and state officials to find a resolution to the Girard College conflict.
 The board of trustees refused to budge. In September 1965, Governor William Scranton asked two well-known attorneys, William Biddle and William T. Coleman Jr., to bring a suit in federal court. Once the lawsuit was filed on December 16, 1965, the daily Girard College protests, the longest sustained protest in Philadelphia history, were called off. Sporadic demonstrations continued until May 1968 when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that the trustees were required to break Girard’s will and desegregate the school. On September 11, 1968, the first four Black students were enrolled at Girard College.
 Celebrating the Freedom Fighters 
 A new mural by Artists Felix St. Fort and Gabe Tiberino honoring the Cecil B. Moore Philadelphia Freedom Fighters at 2201 College Avenue was completed in 2021. | Photo: Scott Foley
 Today, the freshly renamed street is graced with a mural commemorating the civil rights activism of attorney Cecil B. Moore, deejay Georgie Woods, and the many young people, including the Young Militants, who followed their lead. Although Moore and Woods are both deceased, the October 4 street renaming ceremony featured many key figures from the protests of 1965. The Young Militants, now in their 70s, are officially known today as the Cecil B. Moore Philadelphia Freedom Fighters.
 The ceremony was organized by Girard College, a school that is now over 90 percent Black with slightly more female than male students. As in the years before desegregation, the school is a tuition-free, weekday boarding school for students in grades 1 to 12 from single-parent households. Legislation for the honorary street name was sponsored by first-term City Councilmember Jefferey Young, Jr., a proud Girard College alumnus. Young served as emcee and also made speech in which he fondly recalled his time as a Girard College student: “The camaraderie, the love that you get when you’re a student at Girard College. This is family. No matter what year you graduated, you are family.”
 Other speakers included Girard College President David P. Hardy and three of the first four African American students to attend Girard College and then graduate in the late 1970s. The most touching speeches were given by members of the Freedom Fighters, the septuagenarians who were once justice-minded teens.
 Freedom Fighter Karen Asper Jordan participated in the protests in 1965. | Photo: Scott Foley
 Alexis Moore, Moore’s eldest daughter and an honorary Freedom Fighter, recalled how her father, a strict disciplinarian, did not allow his own daughters to participate in the Girard College marches. Bernyce Mills DeVaughn read a list of fellow Freedom Fighters who have passed away, starting with her sister Deborah Louise Mills Bachelor, who at 14-years-old was injured by police and horses used by police at the protests. Her list included Lieutenant George Fencl, leader of the Philadelphia Police Department's plainclothes civil disobedience squad, who often protected the Young Militants from the heavy-handed tactics of uniformed police officers.
 Richard Watson, a 19-year-old freshman at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts when the protests began, described how his experiences drawing and participating in the Girard College protests shaped his life as an activist artist. Vivian Crawford, who worked as an attorney for Philadelphia public schools, shared that many retired police officers, then working as school police, thanked her for the beach homes and other luxuries they could afford due to the massive overtime payments they received during the many months of the protest. Like several other speakers, Jibril Abdul Jalil told the Girard College students, “We loved you before we knew you,” a common Freedom Fighter refrain.
 Kevin Kelly honored his late brother Mel Dorn, the founder of the Freedom Fighters. Karen Asper Jordan, current president of the group, emphasized that the area around Girard College was and continues to be a cohesive neighborhood despite how North Philadelphia is portrayed in the media. A shout out was given to Eugene “Freedom Tree” Watkins, a Freedom Fighter in a wheelchair due to injuries sustained during his days as a Young Militant. Kenneth Salaam, aka Freedom Smitty, used his baritone voice to evoke the struggles of the past as an inspiration to the leaders of tomorrow.
 Connecting Communities 
 Freedom Fighters and students of Germantown Friends School hold new signs for College Avenue. | Photo: Scott Foley
 Andrea L’Tainen, a teacher at Germantown Friends School, also spoke at the event. In February of 2023, Freedom Smitty led a series of assemblies with lower school students. L’ Tainen’s third graders were so moved by his recollections that they wanted to find a way to honor him. Sensing an opportunity to give her young charges a real-world experience in the art of writing persuasive essays, L’Tainen tasked the students with crafting letters to convince Councilmember Young to support legislation for an honorary street name. Young was receptive to their carefully worded messages.
 Girard College staff, the Freedom Fighters, and teachers and parents from Germantown Friends collaborated to bring neighborhood groups on board and to garner the requisite signatures for a petition asking for the name change. Like most honorary street renaming resolutions brought before City Council, the proposal passed easily.
 Germantown Friends School and Girard College students hold their own march along College Avenue. | Photo: Scott Foley
 The Germantown Friends students, now fourth graders, were among the many enthusiastic attendees at the street renaming ceremony. Students from Girard College were there, and the school's high school choir performed “We Shall Overcome,” albeit with a spicy hip-hop flavor. Following the ceremony, the young people participated in a march, complete with homemade signs with civil rights messages, to the imposing Founders Hall at the entrance to Girard College.
 It was an uplifting day that brought together Philadelphians of different ages, races, religions, and socioeconomic statuses. Many tears were shed by the Freedom Fighters who were able to speak directly to the beneficiaries of the risks taken and sacrifices made six decades ago during their teen years: today’s Girard College students. The proud smiles of the Germantown Friends students conveyed their collective understanding that even children can make a difference in how we honor the heroes among us.
 To learn more about the Freedom Fighters and the desegregations of Girard College, watch Making History Productions' Emmy Award winning 23 minute film: Cecil's People: The Freedom Fighters .
 Watch the Freedom Fighters Street Renaming Ceremony here.
 Tags: African-American history Cecil B. Moore civil rights Girard College Girard College protests North Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Places to Save: Fall 2024
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Monumental Baptist Church 
 Location : 4101 Ludlow Street
 Built : 1884
 Threat : Stalled development
 On the northwest corner of 41st and Ludlow streets is the former Monumental Baptist Church , a modest, but important African American house of worship. While the building was successfully nominated by the Keeping Society of Philadelphia to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2017, its future is uncertain as approved development plans have stalled.
 The second-oldest African American Baptist congregation in Philadelphia and Pennsylvania and the first in West Philadelphia (then Blockley Township) occupied the site at 4101 Ludlow Street from 1829 to 1967.
 During that period, the congregation was an anchor of West Philadelphia’s African American community.
 The current building was constructed in two phases in 1884 and 1914. Its brick masonry has been painted a vibrant red and white on the street-facing elevations. As Monumental’s membership increased in the mid-1900s, congregants needed a larger space. In 1967, they moved to 50th and Locust, where they still reside, and sold the 41st property to St. James Pentecostal Church. They occupied the property until 2019, when it was sold to a real estate developer. Prior to this, it was likely the oldest site in West Philadelphia that was continually occupied by Black Philadelphians.
 In 2020, a development scheme emerged to adaptively reuse the church as a rock-climbing gym. The Philadelphia Historical Commission approved the plan to repurpose the first floor and mezzanine and construct a four-story addition for climbing. Unfortunately, the property’s commercial building and zoning permits have expired, as construction did not begin within three years. The building is currently vacant and in deteriorating condition.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Big Brothers Big Sisters Headquarters 
 Location : 230 N. 13th Street
 Built : 1945
 Threat : Stalled development
 William Harold Lee designed the brick, two-story building at the corner of N. 13th and Florist Streets in 1945. The building is a distinctive example of the Art Moderne style, with an asymmetrical façade and horizontal emphasis. The design feature curves at the southeast corner and southern elevation in the projecting bay, canopy, and windows. Warner Bros. used the building for a decade to convey movies from production companies to movie houses. It was constructed during the final years of the golden age of film and is a testament to Philadelphia’s role in the film industry’s distribution sector. Subsequent uses included offices for a law firm, an insurance company and, notably, NFL Films from 1967 to 1982.
 In 1983, it was purchased by the Big Brothers Big Sisters Association (BBBSA) and the building served as their national headquarters until 2014. Freestanding Modernistic letters atop the cornice, in a similar style to the original, marked BBBSA’s tenure in the building. In 2008, the Preservation Alliance successfully nominated the building to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 In 2014, a plan emerged to utilize the historic structure as a base for a hotel tower. The Historical Commission approved the 12-story–later revised to 15-story–overbuild. The requisite permits were filed between 2018 and 2021, but limited physical work has occurred except for the addition of signage advertising the development. Earlier this year, the building was listed for sale. As the it languishes, some of the iconic lettering has disappeared due to either theft or deterioration.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Chestnut Street Arcade 
 Location : 1812 Chestnut Street
 Built : 1925
 Threat : Demolition
 In April, a zoning demolition permit was filed for 1812-14 Chestnut Street . The building was designed by Gravel & Hall in 1925 as the Chestnut Street Arcade. The two-story Beaux Arts building was a covered shopping arcade featuring an arched public walkway that extended from Chestnut to Sansom Streets. It afforded retailers lower rents while being adjacent to the bustling shopping corridor of Chestnut Street.
 The ground floor was modified in the late 1960s to house Theater 1812, which featured live performances. In 1983, Budco, later acquired by AMC, took over the theater, and converted it to a movie house. It closed in 1992 and the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers (PFT) occupied the space. Today, Boyds rents the ground-floor windows for displays at both 1812 and 1816, which PFT also owns.
 PFT acquired zoning permits for the demolition of both properties shortly before listing them for sale. A zoning permit alone is not enough to bring the buildings down–a building permit for demolition is also required. At the time of publication, PFT is under an agreement of sale with the owner of 1810 Chestnut Street, formerly Freeman’s Auction House, who has plans and permits to construct a 20-story overbuild there. The developer is considering incorporating 1812-16 Chestnut Street into the proposed project. The Preservation Alliance advocates for reusing 1812 Chestnut Street in the scheme rather than demolishing it.
 The property contributes to the National Register Center City West Commercial Historic District, but is not on the Philadelphia Register, which regulates demolitions. The original arcade archway is still visible from Sansom Street.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Overseas Motor Works 
 Location : 1501 Fairmount Avenue
 Built : 1930
 Threat : Stalled development
 The Art Deco commercial building at Fairmount Avenue and 15th Street was designed by architect Samuel Brian Baylinson in 1930 as an automobile showroom. The one-story, cast stone structure, with large display windows and a prominent corner two-story tower, was one block away from the established “ automobile row ” of North Broad Street, which became a 29-property thematic historic district in 2021 on the strength of a Preservation Alliance nomination.
 Baylinson’s design is an architecturally distinctive example of the Art Deco style, with its refined ornament of fluted columns, decorative swags, medallions, floral friezes, and urn finials. It utilized monochromism, with the ornamentation rendered in the same cast stone as the rest of the building, creating sculptural, but uniform elevations. The structure remained connected to the auto industry, containing a foreign auto sale and repair shop from 1981 to 2016.
 The Preservation Alliance successfully nominated the building to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2015. The property was proposed for residential conversion with a four-story addition for 20 residential units. The new addition would occupy the rear portion of the site and be set back 30 feet from Fairmount Avenue. The Historical Commission approved the design, and permits were issued in 2021.
 Interior demolition began in early 2023, leaving a stripped skeleton of steel framing behind the stone elevations. Since then, the shell has been left open to the elements, with no signs of the new construction proceeding. There are currently no active permits for the site, leaving the preserved facade supported by wooden bracing.
 Tags: Automobile Row historic churches modernism Places to Save 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Beaux Arts Firehouse and Other Landmarks Added to the Local Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
On August 9, the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved the designation of a firehouse in Francisville, a church in Germantown, an early filmmaking studio in North Philadelphia, and the residence of a prominent African-American community leader in Mt. Airy.
 Beginning in the late 1800s, Sharpnack Street was once the center of the African American community in East Mt. Airy. The house at 106 E. Sharpnack Street , constructed in the 1850s, is one of the oldest buildings still standing on the street and represents the early development of the immediate area. As the one-time home of Hattie Hill Huckabee, and its later use by the Douglas Political Club, the home represents the political, social, and historical heritage of African Americans in the neighborhood.
 The former home of African American educator and leader Hattie Hill Huckabee in Mt. Airy. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 After a career in education in Alabama, Huckabee moved to Philadelphia with her husband in around 1921, subsequently founding community organizations in East Mt. Airy, including the Douglas Political Club and the Women’s Civic and Welfare Club of the 22nd Ward in Germantown.
 A second designation was reviewed for St. Stephen's Methodist Episcopal Church of Germantown and Burial Ground at 5209-13 Germantown Avenue , reflecting the cultural, economic, and social history of the community owing to its legacy as a place of public and religious gatherings as well as its distinctive architectural style. The Historical Commission also found the the church's former burial ground and its large area of undeveloped land have the potential to yield archaeological resources. The three-story parsonage on the property was individually designated in 1957. When the second nomination was reviewed by the Historical Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation, the property owner opposed it, citing financial concerns. They have since put the entire parcel up for sale.
 Engine Company 13 at 1517 Parrish Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Engine 13 Firehouse at 1517-19 Parrish Street was placed on the local register for legal protections amid Francisville's ongoing construction boom. The ornate, Beaux Arts landmark was built in 1901 as part of the Philadelphia Fire Department's effort to modernize its citywide stations. t was designed by Philip H. Johnson , who served as the architect for the Philadelphia City Department of Public Health. In that position he also designed a number of hospitals, libraries, recreation centers, and municipal buildings.
 The Siegmund Lubin House, second building from the right, in North Philadelphia. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The final nomination reviewed was the Siegmund Lubin House at 1608 N. 15th Street. The three-story brick rowhouse with its prominent Italianate cornice served as Lubin’s primary workplace and studio from 1897 until 1899. Lubin was an important early motion picture pioneer and became an international figure in filmmaking, equipment manufacturing, and exhibition. His work contributed to the role that Philadelphia, and in particular, North Philadelphia, played in the early history of filmmaking.
 1108 S. Front Street in Pennsport. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Historical Commission also declined to legalize an addition and roof deck on an early 19th century rowhouse at 1108 S. Front Street that had been designated historic in 1965. The addition was constructed without the Historical Commission’s review or a building permit. Despite receiving a Stop Work Order from the Department of Licenses and Inspection in February, the construction project continued. An earlier application for legalization was denied by the Historical Commission's Architectural Committee. At this month's meeting the applicant proposed removing the home's new roof deck and pilot house. The Historical Commission denied approval again, owing to the massing of the addition and its vinyl cladding, which are visible from the street.
 Tags: African-American history fire stations Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Places Saved: Fall 2024
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Weisbrod & Hess Brewing 
 Location : 2421 Martha Street
 Built : 1899
 This summer, the former Weisbrod & Hess Brewery’s boiler and washhouse building opened as Picnic, a casual dining space. Defined Hospitality, owners of Kalaya, Suraya, Pizzeria Beddia, and Condesa, purchased the hulking industrial space with a prominent smokestack in 2021 and it underwent a complete rehabilitation by Stokes Architecture and Katherine Lundberg of Briquette Studio. A large dining area occupies the south side of the building, a kitchen area and wine shop sit on the north side, and a private dining area is on the second level.
 With 35-foot ceilings, intricate brickwork, curved windows, and keystones, the building represents the eminence of Weisbrod & Hess at the turn of the 20th century. German-born George Weisbrod and Christian Hess founded their brewery in the 1880s at the height of Philadelphia beer making. In 1899, Germantown-born architect Adam C. Wagner was commissioned to design the boiler and washhouse for the sprawling brewery. Like much of the complex, it features the Rundbogenstil, or round-arch style, a German variation of Romanesque.
 When Prohibition began in 1920, Weisbrod & Hess turned to producing soda and resumed beer making after the law's repeal in 1933. Only five years later, the company went bankrupt and closed. A majority of the complex was demolished over the years, with the structures that remained decaying. They were successfully nominated to the city’s historic register in 2017 by the Keeping Society of Philadelphia. In recent years, other buildings built for Weisbrod & Hess across Martha Street have become home to additional restaurants, turning the former brewing complex into a hub for Philadelphia foodies.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Darna Lofts 
 Location : 1705 N. 7th Street
 Built : 1888
 The Moorish Revival building at 7th Street and Cecil B. Moore Avenue is extraordinary and symbolic of the movement of religious and ethnic groups in and out of North Philadelphia over the past 200 years. It was built in 1888 as Adath Jeshurun Synagogue for German Jewish immigrants. Designed by J. Franklin Stuckert, the building’s eclecticism reflects Islamic and Russian Orthodox styles through its onion dome (now lost) and Moorish-style keyhole windows.
 In 1911, it was sold to an Orthodox Jewish congregation, Ohel Jacob, then in 1967 to the Shalom Baptist Church, later to a German Lutheran church, and in 1982 to New Greater Straightway Baptist Church.
 In 2019, New Greater Straightway sold the property. Since the building was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1986, the new owners were able to take advantage of a new preservation incentive that allows CMX-3 zoning uses and forgoes other requirements, such as minimum parking ratios when renovating a locally designated property.
 Surmounting severe structural deficiencies, Finch Development recently transformed the building into 22 affordable family apartments. The project team efficiently used the sanctuary’s height to create bi-level units. Perhaps the most impressive improvement is the removal of shutters covering the circular and keyhole windows and replacement with aluminum thermal break and insulating glass.
 Thanks to the multidenominational powers that be, this project again contributes significantly to the upward trajectory of the neighborhood.
 Tags: adaptive resuse historic breweries historic synagogues Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Places Saved
