title: Restoration Role Model: Birch Knoll
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Birch Knoll: The 1949 International Style house designed by Philadelphia architect George Daub and restored in 2023 by k YODER design carefully obscures its six levels. | Photo: Jeffery Totaro
 Designed in the International Style by Philadelphia architect George Daub in collaboration with Albert Clauss, Birch Knoll was built for the president of Newtown Square’s Aronimink Golf Club in 1949. The glass, steel, stone, and wood structure fell into disrepair after a 2011 renovation, and new owners sought to restore the midcentury modern aesthetic. Kevin Yoder of k YODER design spoke with Extant magazine about the firm’s work with Baroni Building Company on the restoration, which earned a Grand Jury Award at the 2024 Preservation Achievement Awards.
 Extant Magazine (EM) : What attracted you to this particular project?
 Kevin Yoder (KY) : The pedigree and International Style design of the home attracted us, along with the clients’ strong desire to save the house from foreclosure and willingness to “do the right thing” with preservation. The client reached out to k YODER design because of our experience restoring midcentury modern homes.
 The restoration architects paid particular attention to Daub's original entry, emphasizing the connection to interior and exterior spaces. | Photo: Jeffery Totaro
 EM : What was most important to preserve?
 KY : The character-defining design elements were most important to preserve–particularly the original entry stair, with its triangular plan shape, whose form created a dynamic relationship to the original stone wall and central circulation. Despite its horizontal and low-slung appearance, the house’s form is actually quite complex when you realize it’s a split-level design with six levels. It was important to preserve the architectural integrity of the house in general and the rigor and complexity of the precise vertical window alignments because they provide visual unity.
 EM : What was the client’s original vision? Did it change over time?
 KY : The clients were inspired by houses of Frank Lloyd Wright and interested in creating better indoor-outdoor connections. This motivated us to add sliding walls and doors where previously single- hinged doors or no access existed and to create larger windows where possible. The clients also wanted to reestablish cohesion of finishes and restore original elements. This evolved early in the design process to continue the stone on the interior anywhere it appears on the exterior, such as at fireplaces and chimneys.
 The entry stair was among the character-defining elements of the house that k YODER design preserved in the renovation. | Photo: Jeffery Totaro
 EM : What was the biggest preservation challenge?
 KY : Overall, returning the home to its original residential feel, with a natural wood siding finish, was a big challenge because the exterior envelope was so deteriorated. It had been painted over, so it looked like a school or commercial building, and the bulky replacement windows lacked the refinement or slim profiles of the originals. We had to balance the need to adjust and increase the thickness of the exterior skin for the Ipe rainscreen (hardwood cladding) and proper window installation detailing, while maintaining all the complete vertical window alignments and details. We reconciled the fenestration types and maintained the size and pattern of the original window divisions, which originally were double-hung operable window divisions. We considered adding horizontal divisions to match the original look, but chose to be more honest in using single-plane casements where double-hung ones originally existed.
 EM : Did you look to any role model for inspiration or example?
 KY : Because we did not have the original drawings as a reference, and we only had a few original photos at the project onset, we looked to other residential projects by George Daub and other modernists such as Neutra and Gropius. K YODER design has been fortunate to work on many mid-century modern houses, so we’re familiar with design detailing, material choices, and local resources.
 Tags: Midcentury Modern Renovation Restoration Role Model suburbs 
 About the Author

title: "On Buried Ground" Honors Lives of the Forgotten at Christ Church
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
On Buried Ground will be featured at Christ Church Neighborhood House in September during the 2024 Fringe Festival . The dance-theatre performance and exhibition is an interpretation of research initiated by Michelle Belden, archivist of Christ Church Preservation Trust, on the lives of Alice of Dunk’s Ferry and four enslaved children named Violet Plumsteed, Charles Merchant, William Richards, and one identified only as “Unnamed.” Each have burial records at CHrist Church, but, to date, their actual grave sites have not been found.
 The performance, funded with a Pew Charitable Trust grant and additional support from the National Endowment for the Arts, began as a solo work of art in 2021 by choreographer Shayla Vie-Jenkins. The performance inspired former interim director Hannah Opendaker and Christ Church staff and it has now been expanded with the help of playwright Rayne (Angela Bey) and director Nia Benjamin.
 Rayne (Angela Bey), Nia Benjamin, and Shayla Vie-Jenkins. | Photo: Grayce Carson via Christ Church
 Benjamin said the newest iteration of the performance is not a historical re-enactment. "We wanted to focus on the humanity of these figures. To find our way in, we started with a series of open-ended improvisations using movement, poetry, and texts from Black writers and from our playwright, along with sound and music," they explained. "It was a very intuitive, collaborative process. We wanted to feel first, and organize the information second. The historical facts became a skeleton for us to dress a larger, more personal, more expressive world on top of it.”
 Questions surround the lives of the enslaved children whose burial records were found. Since the documents pertain to the early-to-mid 18th century, one can only speculate about their brief lives beginning with their owners and how the deaths of the children. The burial records list them as Violet Plumsteed, “a nogroe girle slave of the Widow Plumsteed,” Charles Merchant, “a negro boy beloning to Mr. Taylor Merchant,” William Richards, “a negro boy beloning to Jos. Richards,” and Unnamed, “a negroe child of Sharpers.”
 Choreographer Shayla Vie-Jenkins during her solo performance of On Buried Ground at Christ Church in 2021. | Photo: Christ Church
 “These children have no gravestones. They have no family we can find who grieved for them," said Benjamin. "Their spirits became the inspiration for the second half of our performance. We wanted to create a work of art that would care for their memory and remember them as full of life, of joy, as bodies who play and dream, not work and struggle.”
 Did their parents mourn them at Congo Square ? "We wish we knew more about the interments of this time period, but, so far, it has eluded us,” said researcher Carol Smith at Christ Church. She said a combination of Belden’s work on the family trees of 14 African American families, and the adaption of modern databases and searches into baptisms, marriages, and burials, are how staff uncovered the history of African American life at Christ Church. Smith explained that only the widow Plumstead had a burial record, which is dated 1790.
 Performers rehearse On Buried Ground inside Christ Church in 2024. | Photo: Grayce Carson via Christ Church
 Yet, one of the biggest mysteries is the location of burial plots belonging to slave owners within the church yard. To date, the only identified owner is Pierce Butler who now has a plaque stationed next to the family vault explaining the Butlers' connection to the slave trade. Smith said the staff feels indebted to Alice of Dunk’s Ferry whose story and memory are important in the recounting of the history of African Americans and Christ Church and the indispensable source of inspiration for On Buried Ground .
 "The performance is part ritual, part church service, and part homecoming celebration. It is joyous and confrontational and poetic and big," Benjamin said. "It is a performance that wraps around you from all sides and asks you to investigate your understanding of Philadelphia’s history and who has been hiding in the shadows.”
 On Buried Ground will take place from September 4 to 14 at Christ Church Neighborhood House, 40 N. American Street. For more information see the event's website: www.neighborhood-house.com/projects/on-buried-ground/ 
 Tags: African-American history Christ Church performance art slavery 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Penn Design Conference Considers the Past and Future of Concrete
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
This year marks the 200th anniversary of a monumental development in building materials: the invention of artificial Portland cement. “Today, cement is the second most consumed substance on earth, after water,” noted Frank Matero, professor and chair of the Department of Historic Preservation at the Weitzman School of Design of the University of Pennsylvania.
 Portland cement, a basic ingredient in concrete, is made by heating limestone, or calcium carbonate, in a kiln with other materials. Its name was coined by its inventor, Joseph Aspdin, who found its color resembled that of Portland stone, which had been quarried in England beginning in the Roman era.
 Concrete, the most widely used building material in the world, is a composite comprised of a binder such as Portland cement mixed with filler materials like stones and sand.
 An old advertisement for a concrete house kit. | Image courtesy of Frank Matero
 Penn Design is marking the anniversary this weekend with a conference called Cement Age / Concrete Nation. The event devotes a day each to two different focuses. “We wanted to touch upon different topics and different disciplines,” explained Irene Matteini, architect and lecturer in the Department of Historic Preservation. “No other building material has evolved so quickly and extensively.”
 The first day will present the history of various forms of concrete in architecture and the building trades, both domestically and in other countries. The second day will look to the future by discussing both preservation issues and how to improve concrete’s sustainability. On Sunday, a field trip to the Lehigh Valley, considered the birthplace of American artificial cement, will visit cement plants.
 Matteini said the program takes a broad look at the topic. “With concrete heritage, you have to keep an open mind and involve a lot of different participants, like engineers, scientists, conservationists, and architects. It’s a complicated subject.”
 An old Portland Cement Association print advertisement from the 1960s showcases the Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) and its precast concrete panels. | Image courtesy of Michael Bixler
 The conference includes a companion exhibit entitled Concrete on Paper. “It looks at the rise of concrete in building through the development of cement and how it was sold to architects and the public,” said Matero. “It changed the face of the modern world.”
 As the home of several iconic buildings that utilized the material, “Philadelphia is a remarkable place to study concrete,” Matero added. “You have an array of buildings that used different concrete methods. It was a great period,” Matteini agreed, referring to the so-called Philadelphia School of the 1950s and 60s, whose best-known architects included Louis Kahn and Robert Venturi. 
 The exhibit features a section called “Icons of Philadelphia,” highlighting several important local concrete buildings, such as the Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse), International House , Beth Shalom Synagogue, and the Municipal Services Building .
 An advertisement from the 1960s for Lehigh Cements featuring the Municipal Services Building. | Image courtesy of Michael Bixler
 While citing the 200th anniversary as a rationale for hosting a conference on concrete, Matero noted another reason on the minds of the Penn Design school faculty. “We want to encourage an appreciation of an under-appreciated material and collection of buildings,” he explained, noting their similar intent two years ago when the school hosted a symposium about rowhouses . “Concrete is more than Brutalism. With time and education of the merits of concrete’s structure and uses, people’s appreciation will grow.”
 However, those merits exist along with downsides. “Cement is the third largest carbon dioxide emitter on the planet,” Matero pointed out. Talks will include ideas and developments in reducing its carbon footprint during manufacturing, use, and end-of-life.
 With many major concrete buildings passing the century mark, conservation is also an important topic. Matteini and others will describe efforts to enhance education in the subject. “Here at Penn, we launched a seminar on concrete conservation this past spring,” she said. “And a consortium of European countries started CONCRETO Academy in January of this year. The idea was to start a training school in concrete conservation.”
 Other presenters of concrete conservation topics include the Getty Conservation Institute and the International Masonry Institute of the International Union of Bricklayers and Allied Craftworkers.
 Cement Age / Concrete Nation will take place on October 4-6 at the Kleinman Energy Forum, Fisher Fine Arts Library, 220 South 34th Street. The exhibit Concrete on Paper is on view now through May 1, 2025 on the first floor of the Fisher Fine Arts Library at the University of Pennsylvania. Gallery hours are from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays.
 Tags: building materials modernism 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Exploring Puebladelphia and the Future of the Italian Market
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
The gateway of the Italian Market's northern half on 9th Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Bella Vista (Italian for beautiful vista) belongs to the area originally known as Moyamensing (Lenape Indian word for place of judgment). The Italian Market along 9th Street lies within. Over the past 25 years, the rapidly changing historic commercial corridor has experienced decline, blight, and renewal that has coincided with the arrival of Mexican nationals, which have given new life to the stretch between Wharton Street and Washington Avenue.
 Some may argue that the most recent arrivals are simply part of an immigration cycle which has brought many groups into this area, ranging from Lithuanians, Irish after the Great Famine, Black Americans during Reconstruction and The Great Migration, and, of course, Italians after Unification. Today's the most recent group are Mexicans.
 Welcome to Puebladelphia 
 El Pueblo Meat Market is one of the oldest Mexican businesses on 9th Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 During my conversations with the Head Consul of Mexico, Carlos Obrador, and Consul Valeria Ramirez-Siller, Obrador recounted that many transplants to Philadelphia are originally from the Mexican state of Puebla, causing Philly to be referred to as Puebladelphia. Many other people came from the central states of San Luis Potosi, Guanajuato, Tlaxcala, and the southern states of Oaxaca and Chiapas. When I asked how and when Mexican nationals started their mass migration into the region, Obrador replied, “mushrooms.”
 In the 1970s, the Philadelphia region became an attractive economic destination for the massive influx of Mexican migrants due to the demand for labor at the many mushroom farms throughout Kennett Square, Oxford, Avondale, and Toughkenamon, Pennsylvania. Many of these migrants stayed and became nationalized under the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986.
 By the 1990s, a large wave of Mexican nationals arrived in Philadelphia because of its low cost of living and labor opportunities. These new groups settled in Norristown, North Philadelphia, and South Jersey. Yet, after the installation of NAFTA (North American Free Trade Agreement) in 1994, they found themselves pushed out of the many temporary migrant laborer positions.
 El Mercado de la Calle Nieve 
 Casa Mexico transformed Connie's Ric Rac dive bar and music venue into a colorful eatery. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 From the late 1990s to the 2000s, South Philadelphia, specifically the 9th Street market area, was hit by hard times. According to a Philadelphia Planning Commission report in 2000, the area was labeled as blighted due to the many vacant buildings, tax delinquencies, and open spaces.
 In 2006, the late Frankie Tartaglia, former owner of music venue Connie’s Ric Rac (now Casa Mexico), told PhilaPlace.org , “If you go past Washington Avenue, that’s where all the business is. People on the other side of 9th Street say this is where people go to die.”
 To get a clear idea of what transpired during this period, I contacted Michele Gambino, a life-long resident, acting business manager of the South Ninth Street Business Association, and producer of the annual Italian Market Festival, who has worked in many roles around the market for over 20 years. Gambino explained that “Every neighborhood has its high and low points. Unfortunately, a number of elder residents decided to move on, leaving many store fronts vacant.”
 Children assemble at Sacks Playground off of Washington Avenue for the Cinco de Mayo parade. | Image courtesy of Consulado de México en Filadelfia
 A new period of migration began around 2006 when the market began redevelopment projects to revitalize the area. It was also during this time a high number of Mexican workers seeking employment opportunities also appeared.
 For background context, Obrador was quick to point out that Philadelphia has always had close ties to Mexico. This relationship is primarily due to the long-standing reputation of Philly being a city proud of its history and support of immigrants. The connection became heightened when anti-migrant sentiments flared in the early 2000s causing migration from primary destinations such as New York to more community-based areas. This is reflected in census data, which highlights that up to 15,500 people of Mexican heritage claimed Philadelphia as their home between 2000-2010.
 Always a Migrant Community 
 Immigrant-owned businesses like Christina Martinez’s South Philly Barbacoa have reinvigorated the Italian Market. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Gambino recounted the 2006 incident at Genos cheese steak stand owner Joey Vento posted an offensive, now long gone sign that read “This is AMERICA. When ordering, speak English.” She explained that only a small minority of people along 9th Street felt that way. “The market has always been a place for immigrants. A place where they live and where they work and where their children attend the local schools. Gambino said that the neighborhood still has that feel. “Now there are different types of immigrants. That’s the fabric of South Philadelphia. It may see different types of immigrants, but it is still a great place. Same idea. Same takeaway.” 
 A traditional dance and ritual is performed on 9th Street during Día de los Muertos (Day of the Dead) in 2023. | Photo: Mickey Herr
 As Gambino and I discussed the shops along the market, I imagine a walk along 9th Street from Washington Avenue to and Christian Street where you will still see the many long-standing Italian shops, such as DiBrunos, Isgros, and Villa di Roma. As you progress south, the Mexican shops, which include the Blue Corn Restaurant, Tortilleria San Roman, and Alma del Mar, appear before giving you one little bit of nostalgia upon arriving at Fante’s Kitchen Shop, Espositos, and Giordano’s Fruit and Produce. At the intersection of 9th Street and Washington Avenue you begin to notice the South East Asian influence in the area as well.
 The space parallel to the original site of Anastasi Seafood, which was demolished in 2022 for the dormant Icebox condominium construction project of Midwood Investment & Development, has come alive with new shops and restaurants like San Miguel Archangel with Quincerea dresses in the window, Arepa Grub Spot, and Discolandia. The Michelin-star-winning South Philly Barbacoa and Casa Mexico lead visitors down to South Philadelphia's dueling cheesesteak triangle, Pat’s and Genos.
 Is It Still the Italian Market? 
 The stretch of storefronts on 9th Street bounded by Wharton Street and Washington Avenue was largely underutilized and blighted in the early aughts. The area has come alive with Mexican-owned restaurants and businesses in the last 15 years. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 A review of property records throughout the market highlights a different 9th Street. Along with the long-term Italian-owned properties are a high number of Asian-owned buildings in the formerly blighted areas purchased during the 2000s, with very few properties belonging to persons with Hispanic names.
 Although both Gambino and Obrador professed excitement over future neighbors and changes, while I tend to be more pessimistic. Someone once summed up gentrification as taking what’s interesting or ethnic about a community and gutting it in preference to what the new community prefers with only the shell remaining from what was there before.
 A 2016 article, “ South Philly via Palermo, Puebla, and Saigon ,” by Thomas Fox Parry tells the stories of various business owners and how they earn just enough to support families and keep going, but their profits are slim. As property values increase, what will the 9th Street Market become as older generations retire and new generations find that working long hours for decent, but not substantial pay is not attractive How will this be impacted by the addition of newer neighbors who may be less interested in placing roots and more interested in being in a trendy, developing neighborhood?
 Detail of a mural on the facade of Ometeotl Tattoo at 9th and Annin Streets. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Icebox condominium project appears be stalled and, ironically, the empty, fenced-in lot is currently a blight itself along 9th Street. However, eventually something residential and expensive will be built in that space. Whether it will improve or change the neighborhood has yet to be seen.
 A few years ago articles appeared pondering whether the Italian Market should be renamed. I believe that the point is moot. Names of neighborhoods simply tell us how a community began. Today, the Mexican American community in the market is now part of the rich historical narrative of 9th Street and the surrounding neighborhood.
 Tags: Bella Vista Hispanic heritage Immigrants Italian Market neighborhood history 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: A New Book Elevates the Work of Black Philadelphia Writers
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
“If we needed a capital of Blackness, we’d make it Philadelphia.” So says Charles D. Ellison in his 2019 prose poem, “Philadelphia, Where Blackness Transcends.”
 Ellison’s piece is the final entry in a new anthology, A Black Philadelphia Reader: African American Writings About the City of Brotherly Love, published by Penn State University Press . The editor of this collection, Louis J. Parascandola, is neither Black nor a Philadelphian. He is a professor of English at Long Island University in Brooklyn, New York with a deep interest in the Harlem Renaissance and experience editing anthologies.
 Parascandola noticed that several prominent Harlem Renaissance writers– Alain Locke , Alice Dunbar Nelson–had Philadelphia ties. This led him to search for other works by African Americans from Philadelphia. Parascandola was surprised by how many there were and further surprised that there was no anthology of Black Philadelphia writers. Such a collection is certainly needed, given that Black people have had a continuous presence in the city since the mid-1600s, and Philadelphia is over 40 percent Black, the highest percentage of any major American city.
 In the introduction, Parascandola explains that “the focus here is not just on writers with a Philadelphia connection, but on the authors’ views of the city itself.” The cumulative effect of reading the essays, letters, poems, memoirs, short stories, and novel excerpts is a multi-faceted, multi-generational, multi-voiced portrait of the city over time.
 The writings are organized chronologically and divided into four sections: Early Black Settlement Until the Pre–Civil War Years (Beginnings – 1849), The Pre–Civil War Years Through World War II (1850 – 1949), Decline, Racial Turmoil, and the Development of the Post–Industrial City (1950-1999), and Philadelphia in the Twenty-first Century and Beyond (2000 to the present).
 Before each section, Parascandola includes a brief description of relevant Philadelphia history during the period to be covered. As a person who has taught, studied, developed curriculum, produced films, and written about local African American history for 20 years, I realize that this was no small feat. It was researching this history, rather than choosing the writings, that took the bulk of his efforts during the six years it took him to complete the book.
 Parascandola reached out to me when he heard about my book Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy that was published by Temple University Press in February 2024. His book was published the next month. We both recognized that my research would have benefitted enormously from his book and vice versa.
 City of Neighborhoods 
 The corner of 23rd and South Streets in 1975. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 Like most anthologies, one can choose readings selectively based on one’s purpose or interest. I looked at the book through a Hidden City lens and focused on aspects of the built environment as I read. A Black Philadelphia Reader reveals a great deal about changes to the spatial dimensions of the city’s African American population.
 In the earliest portion of the book, nearly all the writers– James Forten , Absalom Jones, Robert Purvis , and William Whipper –lived in the neighborhoods we now call Society Hill. Richard Allen, founder of the African Methodist Episcopal church, described purchasing a lot on the corner of 6th and Lombard Streets, a parcel of land that has remained in Black hands for longer than any other in the nation and is still home to Mother Bethel AME Church.
 As the 19th century progressed, Blacks moved to other parts of the city, a process described in an excerpted portion of W.E.B. Du Bois ’ The Philadelphia Negro: A Social Study. In this 1899 publication, Du Bois explains, “There was time in the memory of living men when a small district near Sixth and Lombard streets comprehended the great mass of the Negro population of the city. This is no longer so. Very early the stream of the black population started northward, but the increased foreign immigration of 1830 later turned it back. It started south also but was checked by poor houses and worse police protection. Finally with gathered momentum the emigration from the slums started west, rolling on slowly and surely, taking Lombard street as its main thoroughfare, gaining early foothold in West Philadelphia, and turning at the Schuylkill River north and south to newer portions of the city.”
 During the decades following World War II, African Americans lived in many parts of the city, but the corridors of Lombard Street and South Street remained cultural hubs. For example, in an excerpt of William Gardner Smith’s 1954 novel South Street, a character named Claude who has married a white woman and moved away, finds himself drawn back. “One evening, while out alone, walking, Claude felt again the pull of South Street—the need, if only for one evening, to go back to the old loved neighborhood and see the old, familiar faces, and old, familiar bars. He walked along South Street, peered into a few of the bars and in the Postal Card , and then turned into Broad and walked to Lombard Street, and down the stairs to the Showboat .”
 David Bradley’s 1975 novel, also titled South Street, describes a similar scene: “There was no one on the corner where Gray’s Ferry met Twenty-second and Twenty-second met South: the police, spying any of the local citizens, assumed they were there to rob the liquor store or the food market, and ran the duly convicted offender away. But a little way downtown, near the junction of a nameless alley and South Street, was a dim entranceway, a hole in the wall with a thick wooden door hanging open, and out of it came belches of heavy-beating jukebox music and stale tobacco smoke.”
 Children playing in an entryway of James Weldon Johnson Housing Project at 25th and Norris Streets in 1949. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 During the post-war era, North Philadelphia became an increasingly Black neighborhood. Former Black Panther Party chairperson Elaine Brown was born in North Philly in 1943. Her 1992 memoir, A Taste of Power: A Black Woman’s Story, describes her 13th birthday party which took place shortly after she and her mother had moved from York Street to the James Weldon Johnson Housing Project at 25th and Norris Streets. “All the ‘youngbloods’ from the ‘Avenue’ arrived in a pack. The Avenue was the street gang that controlled the territory that included 21st and York Streets. They had named the gang after Susquehanna Avenue, the main street running through the territory. Even though I now lived in Norris Street gang territory, I was, in spirit, part of life on York Street, part of the Avenue.”
 In his 1994 novel Losing Absalom , Alexs Pate describes a fictional North Philadelphia street. “The 2500 block of West Whither Street, as in most of North Philadelphia, the surface of summer sunlight that reflected hope was deceiving. The internal hemorrhage of unemployment, the open flow of drugs, and governmental indifference all added to the gradual deterioration that was affecting the neighborhood.”
 Not surprisingly, several works deal with the MOVE bombing on Osage Avenue in West Philadelphia. Parascandola includes an excerpt from John Edgar Wideman’s 1990 novel Philadelphia Fire . In her 1987 poem “elegy (for MOVE and Philadelphia)”, Sonia Sanchez writes:
 c’mon girl hurry on down to osage st
 they’re roasting in the fire
 smell the dreadlocks and blk/skins
 roasting in the fire.
 West Philadelphia is also the setting for other pieces of writing such as “4951 Walnut Street” by poet Yvonne Chism-Peace. Asali Solomon’s short story “Secret Pool” is about the University City Swim Club. Yolanda Wisher’s poem “5 South 43rd Street, Floor 2” evokes the multicultural spirit of the 21st century neighborhood:
 Once we went into a store sunk into the street,
 owned by a Cambodian woman. She sold everything,
 from evening gowns to soup. Over to Walnut and 45 th ,
 where the Muslim cat sells this chicken wrapped in pita,
 draped in cucumber sauce. The pregnant woman
 behind the counter writes our order out in Arabic.
 We grab a juice from the freezer, some chips,
 eye the bean and sweet potato pies.
 Pretty much every neighborhood with a sizable Black population, from Germantown to Wynnefield, makes some appearance in the pages of this anthology.
 The Right to Ride 
 The route 23 trolley passes Vernon Park in 1976. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 Another leitmotif of the book is public transportation. William Still ’s 1867 A Brief Narrative of the Struggle for the Rights of the Colored People of Philadelphia in the City Railway Cars is an impassioned argument against the status quo in which Black people paid a fare, but had to stand outside of the streetcars, exposed to the elements. Still recounts, “Riding on the platform of a bitter cold day like this I need not say is almost intolerable, but to compel persons to pay the same as those who enjoy comfortable seats inside by a good fire, seems quite atrocious.”
 Similarly, Harriet Jacobs, author of Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, goes from elation at her newfound freedom to deep disappointment when she boards a train from Philadelphia to New York after fleeing enslavement in North Carolina. Upon learning that Black people were prohibited from riding in first-class rail cars, she writes, “This was the first chill to my enthusiasm about the Free States. Colored people were allowed to ride in a filthy box behind white people, at the south, but there they were not required to pay for the privilege.”
 The Route 23 trolley/bus, known as the longest, busiest route in the city, makes four separate appearances in the book, including in a heartbreaking short story by Becky Birtha entitled “Route 23: 10th and Bigler to Bethlehem Pike.” The narrator has aroused her children from sleep to ride the trolley through the night because there is no heat in their North Philadelphia apartment. “Cherise, sugar, we at the end of the line again. Go up there and put these quarters in the man box. No, Junie. This trolley gonna keep running all night long. Time just come for the man to turn the thing around. We ain’t getting off. This trip ain’t over yet.”
 City of Brotherly Love? 
 Children swim in the fountains along the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art in 1979. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 As a lifelong Philadelphian reading this collection, I gained a deeper insight into the struggles and righteous anger experienced by the city’s Black residents over centuries. The book also increased my admiration for the creativity, resilience, energy, and craft of Black people who have written in every genre about the place that we call home. Although many landmarks and institutions in the book are particular to Black residents, plenty of others, from Wanamaker’s to 30th Street Station, from Girls’ High to Reading Terminal, are universal Philadelphia touchstones. Pulitzer Prize winner Gregory Pardlo’s “Philadelphia Negro,” exemplifies aspects of living here that override race and unite us as residents of the city:
 …as a youngster, I thought every American a Philadelphian
 Negro, blue-eyed soulsters and southpaws alike getting
 strong now, mounting the art museum steps together
 like children swept up in Elton’s freedom from Fern Rock
 to Veteran’s Stadium, endorphins clinging like liberty
 themed tourist trolleys unloading outside the Penn Relays…”
 Author Louis Parascandola will discuss his book at the Parkway Central Branch of the Free Library on Saturday, February 1, 2025 at 1 p.m.
 Tags: African-American history book review Philadelphia writers 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Untold Stories of Brave and Brilliant Women Revealed at Idenlea
author: Erin Betley
bodyText:
On a crisp fall morning in 2021 I hugged my young daughters as they boarded a school bus and waved as it disappeared down the steep incline of our neighborhood in the Philadelphia suburb of Bala Cynwyd. Inexplicably, a long-simmering curiosity pushed aside my worries about a looming work deadline. I felt compelled to finally investigate the history of our home of six years, a Dutch Colonial built in 1926. A neighbor directed me to the website of the Lower Merion Historical Society. I was soon scrutinizing 1908 and 1913 atlases showing the area that later became my neighborhood: two parcels intriguingly labeled with the names of Jane Viola Myers, M.D., Dr. Hannah E. Longshore, and Lucretia L. Blankenburg. 
 Fast forward three years, and I am now pushing aside the bikes and tools in our garage to make room for a massive crate, the culmination of a journey of discovery and connection, of dusty archives and late nights, of tears and jubilation. Inside the crate is a luminous blue and gold Pennsylvania historical marker, awaiting its moment in the sun to reveal the long-hidden story of a family of remarkable women who also called my corner of the world home, a place they named Idenlea.
 1908 Atlas of Lower Merion Township showing the Idenlea estate in Bala Cynwyd. | Image courtesy of Lower Merion Historical Society
 Although my training as a scientist prepared me to ask questions, then collect and analyze data to answer them, nothing prepared me for the thrill of the historical research that I began that fall day, because evidence is everywhere! In atlases and archives, in old newspapers and death certificates, in place names and living memory, just waiting to be pieced together into a historical marker nomination to honor Dr. Longshore (1819-1901), her sister Dr. Myers (1831-1918), and her daughter, Lucretia Mott Longshore Blankenburg (1845-1937). All three were determined leaders in the causes of abolition of slavery, women’s rights, suffrage, and women in medicine. They championed civic and municipal reform, especially during Lucretia’s years as the First Lady of Philadelphia alongside her husband Mayor Rudolph Blankenburg.
 Here I share moments of discovery about compelling aspects of this family’s story–moments that connected with my awakening about the role of local history in helping us understand our own place and time.
 Hannah 
 An undated photograph of Hannah Longshore. | Photo courtesy of Drexel Legacy Center
 When I discovered that the connection between Idenlea and the names on the atlas was not yet something Google could reveal, I made my first research visit to a historical archive, the Longshore Family Papers documenting the some of the origins of women in medicine at the Legacy Center Archives and Special Collections at Drexel University College of Medicine.
 Buried in this collection is the Autobiography of Thomas Longshore . As I skimmed the looping cursive it became apparent that this was not the life story of the writer and prominent abolitionist. but was in fact a detailed account of his wife, Dr. Hannah E. Longshore. I learned that Hannah and her sister Jane’s curiosity about the natural world and commitment to social justice was nurtured by their father, educator and abolitionist Samuel Myers. While both girls had big dreams about higher education, the family couldn't afford tuition at Oberlin College, one of the few educational institutions open to women in the 1840s. With the support of their father, Hannah and Jane self-educated on topics ranging from botany to literature while they helped maintain the family farm in Ohio.
 When Elizabeth Blackwell and her peers began to challenge the system of educating physicians in the United States, Hannah seized an opportunity to enter the profession of medicine. Along with her supportive husband and their infant daughter Lucretia, the family traveled by wagon to Philadelphia where she apprenticed with her brother-in-law, Dr. Joseph S. Longshore, a founder of the city’s new Female Medical College of Pennsylvania (later Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania), the world’s first school established to train women in medicine.
 1852 Public Lecture Course given by Dr. Hannah E. Longshore, co-organized with her friend, fierce abolitionist, and women’s rights activist Lucretia Mott. | Image courtesy of Drexel Legacy Center
 Hannah graduated in the first class of the college in 1851 in a ceremony that required police protection due to threats to the students. She became the first woman physician to open a medical practice in Pennsylvania and the first woman faculty member of an American medical school. The collection at Drexel contains a powerful memory in an autobiographical speech given at her alma mater when she was nearly 80 years old. “ The first women physicians in Philadelphia did not find their paths strewn with flowers, nor their advent welcomed by the general public or by the profession. I went to one of the leading pharmacists to purchase some ounces of drugs. The proprietor said, ‘I will not sell the drugs to you! You are out of your sphere! Go home and darn your husband's stockings! Housekeeping is the business for women!' I informed him that my house was probably as well kept as his and that the stockings were darned. As a graduate of the Female Medical College, chartered by the Legislature of Pennsylvania, I proposed to practice medicine as long as the women of Philadelphia saw fit to employ me and I had the strength to work. ” 
 As Dr. Hannah created a career path that simply hadn’t existed for women, her sister Jane joined her in Philadelphia to enroll in the college. Within a few years, they were practicing medicine alongside each other, treating the women and children of Philadelphia, regardless of their race, class, or ability to pay, for a combined 70 years. During their long careers, these daughters of a struggling farmer earned enough to purchase a hilltop property in Cynwyd and commission architect Isaac Pursell to design a three-story stone house featuring distinctive arches and a clear view of Philadelphia from its windows. The home was the family’s country retreat from busy careers and activism in the city. They named it Idenlea to honor the matriarch of their Quaker family, Paulina Iden Myers.
 Lucretia 
 An undated portrait of Lucretia Blankenburg. | Photo courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 In 1928, Hannah’s daughter Lucretia Blankenburg published an autobiography along with her biography of her husband. Copies of this book are scarce. When I finally tracked one down, I was delighted to see Lucretia had signed it herself in blue ink.
 Lucretia was raised in a dynamic household at the center of the biggest issues of pre-and post-Civil War America, recalling that “the success of my mother as a doctor brought many advanced thinkers and reformers to our home.” Like her mother, Lucretia became an exemplary woman, her long life dedicated to service and progressive ideals. She was known as the “Grand Old Lady of Philadelphia,” a renowned leader who worked to make things better for people from all walks of life, whether that be through protections and playgrounds for children, representation and rights of women, education reform, or labor laws.
 An inspiring inscription and signature by 83-year-old Lucretia Mott Longshore Blankenburg in “The Blankenburgs of Philadelphia”, her biography of her husband Rudolph and memoir of her own life. | Photo: Erin Betley
 My visits to the archives of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania provided insights into the lives of the Blankenburgs. One item in particular encapsulated what this woman meant to the city and beyond. For Lucretia’s 80th birthday, notable figures in Pennsylvania organized a luncheon attended by over 100 civic and women’s organizations and assembled a commemorative volume testifying to the impact of her work. When I submitted a call slip for the volume, I had little idea what to expect, and was surprised to flip through hundreds of gilded pages with entries by political leaders and extraordinary friends like artist Violet Oakley and suffragist Jane Campbell. I could not understand how a woman of Lucretia’s stature had no public recognition in the city that she worked to transform, strengthening my resolve to bring her story out of the shadows.
 Jane 
 An undated photograph of Jane Myers. | Photo courtesy of Drexel Legacy Center
 Dr. Jane V. Myers is the most elusive of the three women of the Idenlea estate. Lucretia described “Aunt Jane” as a private person who did not seek the public attention enjoyed by the rest of their family, but let her successful medical career speak for itself.
 The most evocative trace of Jane comes from a 1950 oral history by a Bala Cynwyd resident, hidden in the files of the Lower Merion Historical Society. “We also had characters in our neighborhood. Of these I must mention Dr. Jane V. Myers who brought me into this world. She was a strictly modern woman of her day, and felt that female attire of her time was ill-suited to the needs of a professional woman. And so instead of shirtwaists and feminine headgear, she wore men’s suits–coats, vests, trousers, and derby hats–that is until she was arrested for wearing clothing unbecoming a woman. This happened more than once. She fought it out and ultimately compromised to the extent of wearing a skirt instead of trousers, but kept the rest.” I found this profile to be utterly endearing, a small indication of the fierce self-determination that distinguished Jane’s life. 
 Loved Ones Lost 
 Of all the ways that learning about these women has influenced my own life since I first read their names, one memory stands out. A visit to a cemetery turned into an enduring mystery.
 First, some context. Philadelphia’s great reform power couple had a simple beginning. As the country emerged from the Civil War, Lucretia met a kind German immigrant named Rudolph Blankenburg. The city’s 1876 Centennial Exposition launched their political consciousness, and each found their own path in public affairs. They were blessed with three healthy daughters, birthed by the skilled hands of their grandmother and great aunt. And yet, over a period of 20 years, the family suffered crushing loss as all three girls succumbed, one by one, to infectious diseases and were buried in the family plot at historic Fair Hill Burial Ground in Germantown. Reflecting on these compounded tragedies that stole the next generation of this remarkable family, Lucretia wrote “We resolved to do all we could to help others and improve civic affairs.” 
 A young Rudolph and his daughter Julia hand in hand at their farm in New Jersey. | Photo courtesy of Drexel Legacy Center
 Reading Lucretia’s words about the loss of her three daughters made my heart ache. I decided to visit their graves and stopped to buy a bouquet of white roses on the way, knowing it had probably been close to 100 years since someone had paid respects. I started at Chelten Hills Cemetery in North Philadelphia, the final resting place of Dr. Myers. I asked a staff member to direct me to the gravesite. She disappeared into the office before returning to tell me there was no record of her burial. Mystified, I then drove to Fair Hill Burial Ground to find the rest of the family. A groundskeeper pointed me to a section of dense headstones. I was stunned to find grass-covered gaps where the family’s markers had once been.
 I took my white roses back home and pulled up the cemetery's records. My heartache turned to bewilderment as it became evident that on the same day in 1921, the remains of 11 family members were disinterred and cremated at Chelten Hills Crematory. I reached out to Chelten Hills for more information. The answer arrived as scanned pink notecards that constituted the cemetery’s filing system a century ago. The cremains of the remarkable women of Idenlea and their family members were retrieved by Quaker undertaker Ellwood Heacock, the first president of the Philadelphia NAACP. But then what? And why? The historical record contains no clues other than the timing of the disinterment, a date that has everything to do with Idenlea. 
 What has Become of the Mayor? 
 An undated photograph of former Philadelphia Mayor Rudolph Blankenburg. | Photo courtesy of Drexel Legacy Center
 The mystery about the final resting place of this family hinges on how Lucretia came to live in her Aunt Jane’s Idenlea estate, which, in turn, links to the story of her husband, the only independent mayor in the history of Philadelphia.
 Rudolph Blankenburg married into a family of powerhouse women and was determined to leave a worthy legacy. After the loss of his last surviving child, he shifted his focus from humanitarian causes to launch a 20-year battle against the entrenched political machine of Philadelphia and its corrupt business associates. His pursuit of good government earned him the nickname "Old Warhorse of Reform.”
 In 1911, he ran for mayor on a platform that foreshadowed modern campaigns: a focus on education, reducing wasteful use of City funds, transparency and accountability, and an administration “not for the profit and gain of the few, but for the benefit of all.” During his years of service at City Hall, he delivered on his promises, despite the efforts of the machine to oppose his reforms.
 Mayor Rudolph Blankenburg with his cabinet in the Reception Room at City Hall on May 4, 1914. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 After leaving office in early 1916, Rudolph’s health faltered. He was interred alongside his beloved daughter, Julia, just a month after a stroke took Dr. Myers. Bereaved Lucretia relocated to the family estate of Idenlea to grieve their losses. A few years later, Congress passed the 19th amendment granting women the right to vote, and Lucretia resolved to move back to Philadelphia to resume her social activism. She sold Idenlea to a developer, moved into the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel, and inexplicably chose to disinter the remains of her entire family and relocate them to a place that is now unknown and lost to time.
 Of the 31 male mayors of Philadelphia from the Civil War-era to the election of Cherelle Parker, six are still living and all others remain in their final resting places. For many, that is Laurel Hill West, which is less than a mile away from Idenlea. However, there can be no visit to the final resting place of Mayor Blankenburg who battled the political machine of his day and fought for women’s rights alongside his family. I hope that a final piece completing this puzzle will emerge one day so that those of us inspired by this family’s stories can pay our respects.
 A Profound Legacy 
 Neighborhood friends playing in the snow in front of Idenlea in Bala Cynwyd. | Photo: Erin Betley
 The house that Jane and Hannah built in 1890 is perched at the highest point of our neighborhood. Since I did most of my research while my daughters slept, I often found myself gazing at it from the windows of my home office, musing about how my findings might connect with conversations that happened behind its stone walls long ago. While I was often moved by the persistence of these brave and brilliant women, there was only one discovery that brought me to tears because of its profound significance. A few months into my research, I was scrolling through late night search results when something unexpected caught my eye: in 1921, as Lucretia was busy relocating to Philadelphia from Idenlea, she gave a stunning gift. Lucretia used the proceeds of Idenlea’s sale to establish two memorial scholarships at Bryn Mawr College, in honor of her mother and her aunt, for women who also had big dreams of pursuing medicine. These two scholarships have supported the careers of women in medicine to this very day, over 170 years after the first women physicians received their medical degrees. Together, Hannah, Jane, and Lucretia created a legacy of generations of changemakers who continue to shape our lives today and carry on the purpose of those who came before them.
 A dedication ceremony for the Pennsylvania historical marker honoring the women of Idenlea is scheduled for Sunday, September 15 at 2 p.m. See Lower Merion Historical Society's website for more information: https://lowermerionhistory.org/events/women-of-idenlea-estate-state-historical-marker-dedication/ 
 For a comprehensive exploration of Erin Betley's research on Idenlea, watch her 2022 public presentation for Lower Merion Library System: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Wu47lDIk55o 
 Tags: Lower Merion medical history suburbs Women's history 
 About the Author
 Erin Betley is a conservation scientist and educator at the American Museum of Natural History and Vice President of the Lower Merion Historical Society.

title: From Pigskins to Dead Heads: Remembering Legendary JFK Stadium
author: Edward W. Duffy
bodyText:
John F. Kennedy Stadium anchored the southern end of Broad Street for 66 years. Originally named Sesquicentennial Stadium, it opened to much fanfare on April 15, 1926. It was demolished in 1992 to make way for what was first called Spectrum II, then the Wachovia Center, and more recently the Wells Fargo Center. The origins of the stadium were a culmination of the public’s growing fascination with spectator sporting events in the late 1800s, its specific location in an isolated swamp known as The Neck (or Varesville), and the controversies surrounding planning for the 150th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.
 The Rise of Philly Stadiums 
 An aerial view of Baker Bowl in 1928. | Photo: Public Domain
 Philadelphia’s population nearly doubled between 1870 and 1900, and this period coincided with growing enthusiasm for professional and collegiate sports. At the turn of the century the city hosted two professional baseball teams: the Philadelphia Phillies of the National League and the Philadelphia Athletics of the American League. There were also semi-pro and amateur baseball and football teams including those supported by Philadelphia companies such as the Pennsylvania Railroad. The Phillies were the first team to build its own stadium, located at Broad and Huntington Streets, known as the Philadelphia Ball Park. It was constructed of brick and steel and opened in April 1887. After a fire in 1894, the stadium was rebuilt with attendance capacity of 18,000 and named the National League Park. After a 1923 renovation it became known as the Baker Bowl .
 The Grand Stand entrance to Shibe Park in 1913. | Photo: Prints and Photographs, Library of Congress
 Philadelphia’s second professional league baseball park opened in 1901 at 29th and Oxford Streets in Brewerytown with a capacity of 13,600 spectators, but its unexpected popularity, causing thousands of fans being turned away, led the Athletics to built a new stadium only eight years later. Shibe Park on Lehigh Avenue opened in April, 1909 with seating capacity of 23,000. Later known as Connie Mack Stadium, it was baseball’s first steel reinforced concrete ballpark.
 Pennsylvania Railroad's Penmar Park circa 1920s. | Photo: Public Domain
 Pennsylvania Railroad (PRR) constructed its 6,000-seat Penmar Park in 1903 at Belmont and Parkside Avenues for its employees through the company's sponsorship of its PRR YMCA. It relocated its field here from PRR's previous site at 41st Street and Westminster Avenue adjacent to its 40th Street passenger station . The Parkside site previously held the railroad’s Centennial Depot when the Centennial Exhibition of 1876 was staged nearby. PRR’s employee football team had existed since 1886, playing against local college and athletic club teams. PRR made its multi-sport field available to the community, hosting games played by local high schools, colleges, and the Philadelphia Stars of the Negro National Baseball League. In that era it was common for large companies such as Midvale Steel and U.S. Gauge to field their own semi-pro teams, and the Philadelphia Stars played against several of them. My stepfather, a former member of the U.S. Gauge company team, recalled playing against them.
 A postcard photograph of Franklin Field in 1936. | Photo: Prints and Photographs, Library of Congress
 The University of Pennsylvania (Penn) opened its football, baseball, and track stadium, first known as the Penn Bowl and later Franklin Field, in 1905 with a seating capacity of 30,000. It was designed by architecture firm Frank Miles Day & Brother. By 1916, the stadium was already at maximum capacity. Penn officials began discussions with the City to build a 100,000-seat stadium on the nearby Woodlands estate at a cost of $1 million and to designate it as a combined collegiate and municipal facility. At the same time, department store extraordinaire John Wanamaker suggested that Philadelphia host the Sesquicentennial International Exposition of 1926 (Sesqui). The two ideas became linked.
 Staging the Sesquicentennial 
 A 80-foot illuminated Liberty Bell was placed over Broad Street near Marconi Plaza in South Philadelphia during the Sesquicentennial International Exposition of 1926. | Photo: Public Domain
 Serious planning for the Sesqui began in 1920 with Mayor J. Hampton Moore’s appointment of a planning body led by Edward W. Bok, head of Curtis Publishing Company. A point of disagreement immediately arose. The majority of decision makers wanted to host an Old Home Week event focused on Philadelphia’s historic role as the site of the Declaration of Independence. The event was to occur in and around Independence Hall. They wanted the surrounding neighborhood, by then a rundown warren of single room occupancy boarding houses and taller building obscuring the view of Independence Hall, to be restored to its original appearance. A minority of realtors and building contractors wanted an international exhibition housed in temporary structures built for its one year duration in order to generate economic activity. A compromise was struck. The neighborhood surrounding Independence Hall would be restored and the exhibition buildings would be built on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, which had been recently cleared of the old buildings occupying its route. Architect Paul Phillippe Cret produced a concept plan for restoring the neighborhood including an Independence Mall stretching north from Chestnut Street to the new Delaware River Bridge (now called Benjamin Franklin Bridge).
 Plans changed radically after the election of a new mayor, W. Freeland Kendrick, who assumed office in January 1924. Beholden to the Vare family of contractor brothers who funded his election campaign, Kendrick took charge of the Sesqui planning committee and declared that Philadelphia’s celebration would focus on an international exhibition to be constructed on the swampland in The Neck. Today such a site would be described as freshwater intertidal wetlands. Much of the proposed site was owned by the Vare family and the City would lease it from them, improving their land by filling in the wetlands with material dredged during construction of the North Broad Street Subway. Vare Brothers Contracting was hired to truck in the material down there, of course.
 An aerial view of Municipal Stadium under construction in 1925 and during its opening event on May 1, 1926. | Photos courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 Declaring that the negotiations with Penn were pointless, Kendrick claimed that the City needed a municipal stadium with a capacity of 250,000 and rejected the university's offer in March 1925. Penn had constructed its stadium’s lower tier in 1922 and then proceeded to add a second tier after negotiations with the City were terminated. Designed by Day & Klauder, this 65,000 seat multi-sport facility is the largest two-tiered stadium in the United States.
 Kendrick hired architects Simon & Simon to design the stadium, a horseshoe shaped structure modeled after Harvard Stadium in Boston. When Kendrick’s grandiose structure was costed out, its capacity was pared back to 125,000 at twice the cost of the original Franklin Field alternative and finally to a permanent seating capacity of 86,000. His transparent bait-and-switch alternative selection process left many apprehensive about how Kendrick would stage the Sesqui. In April 1925, the first of several thousand 30-to-40 foot long white pine piles was driven for the stadium's foundation at Broad Street and Pattison Avenue.
 Municipal Stadium in 1937. | Photo courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 The Sesqui seemed to be plagued with bad luck from start to finish. Weather during the lead up to the event was unusually rainy, hot, and humid. Its exhibits were late in being constructed on the difficult, unstable site and some were even finishing or installed after the celebration had ended. Visitors complained about the lack of hotel rooms, and word spread that the Sesqui was not worth the trip. The event closed having attracted only a quarter of anticipated attendance. Its soaring deficit was met by the mayor with funds originally borrowed to extend the subway to Roxborough.
 Two notable Sesqui events were held in the new stadium: a Catholic mass service and a boxing match. The mass, celebrated by Philadelphia’s Cardinal Archbishop Dennis Joseph Dougherty on a rare cloudless day, attracted 108,000 worshipers on October 3. The boxing match featuring the heavyweight champion Jack Dempsey, the "Manassa Mauler," against Gene Tunney, who had been the U.S. Marine Corps champion boxer of the American Expeditionary Corps in France, occurred during an all-day rainstorm attended by 120,000 fans on September 23.
 A "Touch of Grey" at JFK 
 20,000 fans of The Beatles gathered at JFK Stadium to see the Fab Four play on August 16, 1966. It was their last concert in Philadelphia. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 Following the Sesqui, Municipal Stadium, renamed John F. Kennedy Stadium in 1964, soldiered on, a white elephant remembered as the site of many Army-Navy games, Philadelphia Police Department Thrill Shows, dwarf car races, and various collegiate sporting events. The Philadelphia Eagles used the athletic field for practice and the northern end of the stadium horseshoe as the site for an inflated structure or "bubble" providing them with an enclosed space.
 As mega rock concerts grew in popularity, the stadium became a go-to Philly venue for scores of music legends like The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, Led Zeppelin, Sly and the Family Stone, and many others . It was also host to the Live Aid concert in 1985 along with Wembley Stadium in London. At one of these events an attendee who was a civil engineer noticed cracks and gaps in the walls, which he attributed to differential settlement. He alerted the City’s building inspectors who commissioned an engineering study. It concluded that the structure was imminently dangerous and its estimated repair would cost a prohibitive $25 million. The stadium was closed on July 7, 1989 moments after a Grateful Dead concert ended.
 The Philadelphia Police Department's Thrill Show circa late 1960s. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 JFK Stadium’s ultimate demise was precipitated that year through attempts by Philadelphia 76ers owner Harold Katz to escape leasing space at the Spectrum nearby and entering into negotiations with the State of New Jersey for a new arena in Camden. When word of this reached Philadelphia Mayor W. Wilson Goode, he directed his staff to negotiate a solution which would keep the team in the city.
 The Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation reached out to the Spectrum's owner, Ed Snider, and entered into discussions for the construction of a new arena in the city. The site Snider chose for it was JFK Stadium. He neither expected nor requested public subsidy for its construction, but he did assume that the City would deliver him a cleared and environmentally clean site with utilities and adequate highway access. Responsibility for preparation work fell to PIDC using grant funds provided by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.
 A streaker makes a victory run around JFK Stadium at the Philadelphia Flyers Championship Parade on May 28, 1975. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 The Eagles practice bubble was relocated to Packer Avenue. In March 1992, a demolition contract was awarded to Alcon Demolition Company of Fort Lee, New Jersey. Fortunately, "as built" construction drawings still existed to assist planning the demolition. Original blueprints on linen had been nibbled away by mice. They were still mostly legible, but they were not always accurate. There was no indication in the old architectural and engineering plans that the stadium had been constructed with wind braces, but they were there, hidden behind the sandstone parapets. The first swing of the three-ton wrecking ball bounced harmlessly off of the building.
 Later, another comparison of the drawings with the actual building revealed an additional feature undisclosed on the plan: a locked storage room. Breaking down the door, the astonished workers discovered a human skeleton sprawled among a pile of empty beer cans. Hadn’t Edgar Allen Poe foretold this scene in his Cask of Amontillado ? Could this poor soul have been a lost Dead Head? Suspecting a crime scene, police were summoned, but quickly determined that the skeleton had been a display model perhaps from a biology class.
 The crowd at the Live Aid concert at JFK Stadium on July 13, 1985. | Photo courtesy of Kathy Borchers Photojournalism Collection, Robert S. Cox Special Collections and University Archives Research Center, University of Massachusetts Amherst
 After a two year hiatus, while Snider assembled his construction financing, his Spectrum II project was finally under way in the summer of 1994 and was completed in August 1996. Snider hosted a grand party at the new arena for everyone associated with its construction, an event that is fondly remembered by those who attended it.
 Tags: Philadelphia music history Sesquicentennial South Philadelphia sports Stadiums 
 About the Author
 Edward W. Duffy is the author of "Philadelphia: A Railroad History" (Camino Books, 2013) and "Philadelphia Celebrates: Three Great Anniversaries - 1876-1926-1976" (Camino Books, 2017).

title: For Whom the Trolley Bell Tolls: Resurrection of Rail Travel on Route 23 Unlikely
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The Philadelphia Transportation Company’s Route 23 trolley loop at Germantown Avenue and Bethlehem Pike in Chestnut Hill in 1959. | Photo: A. W. Maginnis Collection, PhillyTrolley.org
 Like many Philadelphians, Don Mason has lovely memories of the old Route 23 trolley. Born in 1952 near the boundary of Mt. Airy and Germantown, his father for a time was an operator for the vintage green and cream trolley cars that would regularly run up and down Germantown Avenue. The trolley tracks by day were the fixation of childhood mischief for Mason and his friends– many a penny were flattened, as were a few other not-to-be-mentioned foreign objects. By high school, its significance became utilitarian, as Mason rode the 23 back-and-forth each day as part of his journey to Cardinal Dougherty High School. Yet, more than anything, it was a certain mystique of the trolley that Mason remembers: the rumbling and clattering cars going by day and night, sparking the imagination, sometimes quite literally.
 “One of my very favorite things was, when I was in high school and would come out, it would still be kind of twilight outside,” Mason said. “In the winter when we’d have freezing rain, the wires would have ice on them. The trolley would come by and you’d get a free light show. These beautiful blue sparks would shoot off the wires. It was incredible how big the sparks were.”
 It has now been more than three decades since SEPTA, in 1992, ended regular trolley service on the route 23 line and swapped in buses instead. Initial promises to eventually return the trolley cars have given way to silence and deep public skepticism that it will ever happen. In fact, in many places along the trolley line’s original 13.8-mile run from the top of Chestnut Hill to South Philadelphia, the rails have been removed or paved over , seemingly burying any chance of return.
 The old Route 23 trolley track passes by the Walder-Essig House on Germantown Avenue in Mt. Airy. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Yet, for some hope still springs eternal, particularly in Northwest Philadelphia where the trolley’s rails and overhead wires have largely been maintained at taxpayer expense. A few times a year, Mason or another local will post on social media with a favorable reminiscence. Others will join in and wonder if it would ever be possible to see the 23 trolley run again. The notion also has support from potentially influential individuals like developer Ken Weinstein, previous owner of the Trolley Car Diner at the intersection of Germantown Avenue and Cresheim Valley Drive. “Trolleys bring a nostalgia to our community. Trolleys attract tourists and people that otherwise might not take public transportation. There is a big upside to putting the trolley back on the tracks,” said Weinstein.
 Others think it might be time to give up the ghost. Nicole Brunet, policy director of the Bicycle Coalition of Philadelphia (BCP), says trolley rails can present a hazard to cyclists and even motorists. Most notably, a former employee of the coalition fell off her bike while crossing the tracks at 11th and Reed Streets in South Philadelphia in 2013, shattering her teeth, breaking her jaw, and requiring months of recovery on a liquid diet. The incident sparked some argument between the often allied communities of bicyclists and public transit enthusiasts. The City eventually paved over or removed trolley tracks from at least a dozen problematic intersections along the former 23 route.
 However, along the northwest stretch of the line on Germantown Avenue–roughly 5.5 miles from Chestnut Hill to Broad Street–much of the trolley infrastructure remains in place. In fact, in the late 2000s, some 15 years after the last regular Route 23 trolley ran, infrastructure was even restored on one segment of the stretch during a PennDOT repaving project.
 The disused trolley track of Route 23 slices through the intersection of Germantown and Lehigh Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 There are still no new indications SEPTA plans to ever restore trolley service to the route. In fact, available evidence is to the contrary. Brunet said the trolley lines still present a hazard: not only to bicyclists, but also pedestrians and motorists who would benefit from traffic calming measures. After a pair of pedestrian hit-and-run deaths on Germantown Avenue in the Germantown neighborhood in 2022, the BCP worked with SEPTA and nearby community groups to develop a safety plan. Yet, many traffic calming measures along the avenue were a no go due to the continued presence of the trolley tracks, Brunet said.
 “The community was like, ‘Why can’t we get traffic calming? People are going way too fast,'” explained Brunet. “[SEPTA said] the only way it can add traffic calming is if it basically paves over the trolley tracks. Because you can’t add speed bumps where there are trolley tracks. You can’t do the corners. There’s a lot of things that are just impacted by trolley tracks.”
 A Rolling Start, a Sudden Stop 
 A horse-drawn trolley run by Peoples Passenger Railway Company, which established one of the city's earliest trolley transit systems. | Photo: PhillyTrolley.org
 Philadelphia saw the arrival of its first trolley in 1858, according to a history compiled by trolley enthusiast and former Hidden City contributor Mike Szilagyi . Running from Kensington to Southwark via 5th and 6th Streets, it was a very different beast than today’s trolley, relying on literal horsepower to run back and forth.
 Over the next 40 years, the mode of transportation would explode, with more than 66 trolley companies forming by 1895 to shuttle passengers across much of the city’s grid. Electrification leading to the demise of the horse-drawn trolley by 1897. The exact history of the part of the network that came to be Route 23 is a little fuzzy, but a WHYY article compiled in 2011 traces it to the establishment of a Germantown Avenue Line that by 1877 ran between what is now East Mt. Airy and 8th and Dauphin Streets.
 A more definitive history compiled by SEPTA in 1974 completes the picture. By 1890, the Germantown Avenue line had been combined with 4th and 8th Street lines and renamed the “Pelham line.” It extended southward to 4th Street and Snyder Avenue. Further mergers in 1913, 1920, and 1926 saw the route reach its full length, from Chestnut Hill to 11th Street and Pattison Avenue, a 25.5-mile roundtrip length that SEPTA declared the “longest known trolley route in the world.”
 A Route 23 trolley rolls down Germantown Avenue in the 1940s. | Photo: PhillyTrolley.org
 Without an independent reference or further detail about how that superlative was determined, its authenticity is difficult to confirm. What is certain is that the Route 23 trolley, as SEPTA came to call it, for a time was both a commercial and cultural success. In 1983, trolleys citywide were generally on the ropes, according to a Philadelphia Inquirer article titled “Streetcars rolling toward a shaky future.” By that time, just seven surface streetcar lines were still operational, primarily in North Philadelphia. Much of their infrastructure was on its last legs.
 “The physical plant is totally exhausted,” said John Tucker, then-SEPTA’s chief operations planner, in the 1983 article. “The track, the overhead wires, the substations, cables, cars, all must be renewed. It’s limping along on rubber bands and bubble gum.”
 However, the same piece quoted officials as saying that of all the lines, Route 23 was “most likely to survive,” referencing its history, world-recording-holding length, and revenue generation. “It’s a rolling cash register,” the Inquirer quoted SEPTA’s transportation director.
 Route 23 was also the stuff of romance. A feature that year in the Daily News entitled “Going all the Way on Rt. 23,” likened riding the line to a first date, where a passenger new to the city could learn all about its people and neighborhoods, starting in Chestnut Hill and then winding through the Northwest, into Nicetown, North Philadelphia, Center City, and onto South Philadelphia. “The 25-mile long No. 23, in a couple of years, may be endangered,” contributor Emma Edmunds wrote. “But for now you get a panorama. A rider can sample Philadelphia the way one tastes wine at a testing party–taking little sips that make you want more.”
 A Route 23 trolley at 11th and Morris in 1968. | Photo: David Wilson
 Yet, before a decade was out, the line had indeed become endangered. Or quite possibly, extinct. “SEPTA pulls plug on trackless trolleys, to use buses,” blared a headline in the February 14, 1992 edition of the Daily News . Although that piece primarily focused on SEPTA’s decision to remove three trackless trolley routes from service in North and Northeast Philadelphia, it also quoted union officials saying that the agency planned to swap in buses for trolleys on Route 23 before the end of that month. Seven months later, another article in the Daily News noted SEPTA had indeed pulled the trolleys off the line, as well as Routes 15 and 56, for much of the year, citing “frequent breakdowns and high maintenance costs.” The agency stated it planned to restore service upon purchasing a new fleet of 80 light rail cars several years later.
 Weinstein, a then-chief of staff for Happy Fernandez, a former city council member and transportation committee chair, said his recollection was that he and others were skeptical even then that the trolleys would return as SEPTA had claimed the operating deficits for running buses were lower than for trolleys.
 Still, signs of hope flickered. In 1994, SEPTA offered a Center City antique trolley loop from Callowhill to Bainbridge Streets using old Route 23 lines on 11th and 12th Street to try and lure tourists. Similarly, SEPTA for a time maintained irregular, chartered trolley service on the 23 line in 1997. Advocates rode one to a City Hall meeting where they blasted the agency for failing to restore full service. Agency officials admitted no long-term capital funding had been set aside for the project, but said the line was included in the “long range capital program.” Years stretched into decades, and the ups and downs continued.
 A Route 23 trolley passes by Vernon Park in Germantown in 1976. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 In 2003, the last chartered trolley rolled down Route 23, but, three years later, SEPTA restored the Route 15 trolley on Girard Avenue, a line it has since remained committed to. In 2008, PennDOT performed a $17 million reconstruction of Germantown Avenue in Mt. Airy and elected to include the reinstallation of new Route 23 trolley tracks and overhead lines. A spokesperson recently told Hidden City that the decision was primarily at the behest of local residents and that the trolley portion of the project cost about $170,000. The agency has not made a decision either way whether it will repeat the favor in the future. A Philadelphia City Planning Commission document from 2008 claimed that SEPTA remained “committed to restoring the Route 23 trolley” and had set aside $390 million for Route 23 and 56 trolleys in the 2013-2020 capital program. A Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission study the following year similarly said SEPTA was committed to restoring some form of fixed-rail transport on Route 23 by 2022.
 However, hope dimmed in the years after. In 2015, SEPTA told The Chestnut Hill Local it planned to further study the issue and make a determination sometime around 2026. By 2022, Jen Dougherty, agency manager of long-range planning, noted during a virtual meeting that SEPTA had shifted its focus to modernizing the trolley lines servicing West Philadelphia and had no formal plans for Route 23. In more recent court testimony, SEPTA track department director Philip Metzger reiterated that the agency has “no plans to reinstate trolley service” on the line.
 SEPTA’s communications team did not respond to a list of questions for this article. Matthew Cassidy, communications manager for the Philadelphia Office of Transportation and Infrastructure Systems (OTIS) signaled the unlikely return of the 23, pointing to the city’s current CONNECT transportation plan . “[The] transit plan calls for improvements in trolleys and for investments in regional rail. It does not recommend bringing back the Route 23 trolley,” Cassidy stated. “The transit plan focuses on improving frequency on regional rail, which our research concludes would provide better service to Northwest Philadelphia than restoration of the Route 23 trolley.”
 One Road, Two Paths 
 A Route 23 trolley passes through the intersection of Germantown Avenue at Venango Street in 1980. | Photo: Drew Jacksich via Wikimedia Commons
 Like other trolley aficionados, Weinstein thinks the mode of transit still has merit, even on Germantown Avenue.
