There’s the touristy allure of an old-timey trolley rolling down the historic corridor, drawing people to visit and shop in the Northwest neighborhoods. There are also environmental benefits to be had by the electrified ride of the trolley. Weinstein thinks that one of the most common criticisms of the trolley–its inability to navigate around obstructions like double-parked cars, causing delays and bunch ups–could actually be viewed as an antidote to present concerns over road safety. “We’re trying to slow traffic down now because we see the benefit of that,” Weinstein said. “You could do what we’re about to do in Mt. Airy and do pedestrian crossings and traffic bumpouts. But you could also run trolleys, which would slow down traffic.”
 For all these reasons, Weinstein is on board with one day returning the Route 23 to full, daily service of some form of light rail transportation. He is also a realist and said his understanding is that while much of the street-level infrastructure remains in Northwest Philadelphia, the restoration of equipment to power the line would require a major, expensive capital investment that is exceedingly unlikely with SEPTA facing a potentially existential fiscal cliff next year. “We’re not going to see trolley cars anytime soon,” Weinstein says.
 A 1Route 23 trolley travels down 12th Street while crossing Passyunk Avenue in the late 1990s. | Photo: Mike Szilagyi via PhillyTrolley.org
 Brunet noted that her recollection is that SEPTA also said during the 2022 Germantown meeting that it would have to replace rails in that neighborhood for the 23 trolley to run there again, another unlikely capital investment for the cash-strapped agency. SEPTA previously told Hidden City that restoring Route 23 trolley service would also require creating new wheel-chair accessible stations at considerable expense, estimating total needed investment to restore the line at $100 million as of 2015 .
 Paving also costs money. In recent court testimony, the agency said it costs about $1 million to pave over a mile of trolley tracks. As a policy matter, Brunet would like to see bike lane infrastructure separating from in-use trolley routes wherever possible–an improvement slated for an upcoming project on Woodland Avenue–and for the City to make hard decisions to pave over those that haven’t seen a trolley car in decades.
 “We like public transit. It’s part of a historical makeup of Germantown Avenue,” Brunet explained. “[But] this is just another example of our aging infrastructure. We should be paving over them consistently if they’re not in use.”
 Tags: public transit railroad history SEPTA trolleys 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Demolition of Historic 19th Street Baptist Church Imminent
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
Work to raze 19th Street Baptist Church in Point Breeze could begin on Monday, September 16. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 150 years ago, the Memorial Church of the Holy Comforter was built in Point Breeze. Yet, the now-historic church almost certainly won’t be around to see even one more year. In fact, its continued existence might be down to days.
 Its current owners, 19th Street Baptist Church, as well as the Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I) and others familiar with the church at 1249 S. 19th Street all say that absent a truly divine intervention, it will be demolished by the end of the year, and potentially as soon as Monday, September 16. That would mark a sudden end to an otherwise long and winding story, in which numerous individuals have attempted to save the building for several decades.
 The leaders of 19th Street Baptist Church, which has owned the building since 1944 and by whose name it is commonly referred to today, said that their attention has turned toward salvaging materials, including stained glass windows and an old church bell, and attempting to see if a connected school-slash-parish house can be saved. The latter is in better condition than the main sanctuary, said church pastor Reverend Wilbur D. Winborne, Sr., adding that he and other staff are currently working with an engineer to file a report with L&I to potentially make a case for saving it. The congregation vacated both spaces several years ago and currently worships at the Navy Yard.
 However, members of the preservation community say there are factors beyond the oft-maligned machinery of the City’s agencies that have led to the likely demolition of the 19th Street church, including the stewardship of the building by church leadership. Thaddeus Squire, a philanthropic management professional, has for years worked alongside other preservation experts, such as University of Pennsylvania professor and architectural historian Aaron Wunsch, to try and secure either philanthropic support or private financing to restore the building. Now, on the precipice of demolition, Squire said no small amount of responsibility for the failure to save the structure falls on the church itself.
 In turn, the church’s current leadership points to racial and economic transgressions, dating all the way back to a disputed endowment transfer in the 1940s, which, they claim, deprived their congregation of many millions of dollars that could have been used for proper upkeep of the church.
 It is a complex, contested tale. It is also undeniably a sad one.
 The Birth of a Blue Collar Congregation 
 An undated drawing of Memorial Church of the Holy Comforter, which latr became 19th Street Baptist Church. | Image courtesy of The Friends of 19th Street-CultureTrust of Philadelphia
 The church’s start as Memorial Church of the Holy Comforter was a decidedly more joyous occasion. According to a history contained in the building’s successful nomination to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1984, credited to Jefferson M. Moak, former executive secretary of the Philadelphia Historical Commission, the church was a Furness & Hewitt-designed structure created to support a kind of working-man extension of Old City’s prestigious St. Peter’s Church congregation.
 In 1868, the nomination notes, the Lewis family of Philadelphia, members of St. Peter’s, founded and funded a mission in the southwest of the city connected to the church. Originally occupying different, temporary grounds near 19th and Federal Streets, daughter Margaretta S. Lewis donated several tens of thousands of dollars to construct The Memorial Church of the Holy Comforter, named in honor of her deceased mother.
 The 1984 nomination places the creation of the church in further historical context. Following the Civil War, the “tremendous growth” of the city saw the transformation of Point Breeze and Gray’s Ferry from farmland to residential neighborhoods, especially as industries sprung up “along the railroad line on Washington Avenue.” But there was a dearth of churches: while the “spiritual needs of the Episcopalians” were served by the Church of the Holy Apostles at 21st and Christian Streets, the nomination states, an 1876 atlas showed Holy Comforter as the only large church south of Washington Avenue.
 “Several other churches owned property and/or buildings in the area, but did not possess the extensive facilities as [sic] Holy Comforter,” the nomination notes. “Of the church buildings located in the neighborhood in 1876, none save [Holy Comforter] have survived.”
 In a 2012 article for Hidden City , Wunsch further explored the history. In the mid-19th century, the newcomers to this section of Philadelphia were primarily working-class Irish and Scottish immigrants and their native-born families, Wunsch noted, to an extent that a roadway to the area from Old City was at the time designated “Irish Tract Lane.” Some of these families had converted to Episcopalianism and “Old St. Peter’s wished to see more of them,” Wunsch wrote, and so founded Holy Comforter as a mission church. “Holy Comforter was meant to engender both devotion and socio-economic uplift,” he concluded.
 The church’s cornerstone was laid at the corner of 19th and Titan Streets during an official ceremony on June 15, 1874, according to an article in the next day’s Philadelphia Inquirer . Placed within it was a box that reportedly contained, and presumably still does, the following: a "Holy Bible, Book of Common Prayer, copy of the Churchman of June 13, 1874, copy of the Episcopal Register , the Philadelphia Inquirer and other daily papers, gold and silver coins, and a parchment” marking the occasion. “The Memorial Church of the Holy Comforter will, when completed, be quite an acquisition to this growing neighborhood, and will supply a want which has long been felt,” the Inquirer concluded.
 Godly Shrine, Serpentine Design 
 The church's unique, serpentine stone facade has been decaying for decades. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 One may think it odd to design a Christian church with a serpent-like facade. Yet, there one presently sits in South Philadelphia, the quirky product of the vision of architects George W. Hewitt and Frank Furness.
 The selection by the congregation of the venerable Furness & Hewitt architecture firm to design its new church was “not surprising,” notes the 1984 historic nomination. Hewitt had trained in the offices of Joseph Hoxie, John Notman, and John Frasher, it observed, meaning he likely previously worked on several other Episcopalian churches constructed during that era. That work carried over into the firm Fraser, Furness & Hewitt as the architects of several additional Episcopalian churches in Center City, Germantown, and Roxborough.
 Hewitt is credited as the primary architect of Holy Comforter, but also shared a “common language” with Furness, Wunsch noted, evidenced by “the building’s wayward massing, playful asymmetries, and delightful (perhaps winking) palette.”
 The 1984 nomination further details the original construction design as a “simple A-frame church,” with a corner tower that was once crowned by an octogonal, 120-foot-high spire. Attached was a two-story Sunday school building, which shared with the sanctuary architectural features including stonework and archways, while also topped by its own smaller corner tower and church bell.
 Perhaps the church’s most notable design feature is its exterior “serpentine” stone facade, green in color, which Wunsch wrote gives the church the air of “an alien green projectile launched by old-line Protestants into a burgeoning red-brick neighborhood,” and its color and scale-like appearance mimics that of a snakeskin.
 Wunsch also mused that the choice of the green serpentine stone could have been an homage to the homelands of the church’s original congregants. However, in time the feature would also prove a complicating factor in the building's demise.
 Rebirth as a Baptist church 
 An undated photograph of the congregation of 19th Street Baptist Church during services in the sanctuary. | Image courtesy of The Friends of 19th Street-CultureTrust of Philadelphia
 By 1944, St. Peter’s congregation had declined to “roughly 250 souls,” notes the 1984 historic nomination, and, with financial resources dwindling, determined to close its mission work at the Holy Comforter in Point Breeze. It found a ready buyer in 19th Street Baptist Church.
 “In [St. Peter’s] wake came different stewards, voyagers in the Great Migration who brought new life to so many of the city's aging religious structures,” Wunsch noted. “Along with a baptismal pool and other physical changes came passionate sermons, a legendary choir, and visiting dignitaries.”
 Reverend Winborne said the church, like many Black congregations, has served an outsized role in the surrounding community. In its early days at 19th Street, the church was a vibrant place with full morning and evening services. At different points, it was visited by the Reverend Jesse Jackson, Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr., and other religious leaders. It was also valued as a true sanctuary against the hardships of a once-segregated and still-unequal America.
 “When you think about the African American church, and when you think about the climate and culture of the day, if you’re in a Black Baptist church on Sunday–you’re a preacher, deacon, trustee, choir member–you are somebody,” Winborne said in an interview. “Because when you’re going back out into the community, when you look at the elements of racism and segregation, the church is your oasis.”
 Winborne also connects that era of oppression to the church’s modern day struggles. When exactly the church building began to encounter serious maintenance issues is unclear, but the historical record suggests it has been a slow, mostly unabated slide toward deterioration. By the 1984 nomination, the Historical Commission described the church’s condition as poor, with “deteriorating stonework and several of the original doors replaced.” At an unspecified earlier date, the congregation had also removed the church’s spire due to its “unsafe condition,” the Historical Commission noted in its nomination, leaving just a two-story stump in its place.
 In the late 1990s and early 2000s, 19th Street Baptist Church filed a pair of lawsuits against St. Peter’s, alleging that the will of original benefactor, Margaretta Lewis, had left a financial endowment to pay for the church’s upkeep in perpetuity, but that St. Peter’s had concealed its existence and kept the money at the time of sale.
 The claim, chronicled most authoritatively in a 2000 Daily News piece entitled “Holy War,” was ultimately unsuccessful, first dismissed by a Philadelphia Common Pleas judge and later in federal court. The article noted 19th Street Baptist Church’s former, charismatic pastor Reverend Charles Walker and attorney Robert Sugarman claimed an original trust of $80,000 could have been worth upward of $100 million by 2000, which would have been far more than enough to pay for several hundred thousand dollars in repairs Reverend Walker said the church needed at that time. However, lawyers for St. Peter’s denied the merits of the case and also claimed that remaining trust monies were nowhere near the amount the church was seeking. “Documentation about the trust’s value is scarce, but [a court order] of Sept. 9, 1945 listed a balance of principal at $22,763.84,” the Daily News reported at the time.
 More than two decades later, the wound remains open. The Daily News article recalled how an aide to Walker had searched City records and found the will of Lewis, which set off the legal action. Winborne said that aide was him. “Look at her will. You will see the language in the will where the trust that she had for the church was to be connected to the building,” said Winborne.
 Salvation Efforts Fall Short 
 Deacon Lloyd Butler leads a tour of the church's sanctuary in 2018. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The deterioration of the church appeared to accelerate following the failed lawsuits. By the end of the 2000s, 19th Street Baptist Church had moved its services from the sanctuary to the Sunday school building, which the congregation now refers to as a fellowship hall. In 2011, L&I deemed the church officially unsafe and put fencing around the exterior of the premises after an earthquake shook loose stucco from its facade, according to an article by Ashley Hahn for Plan Philly . Preservation experts add that serpentine stone is notoriously difficult to maintain, due to a chemical makeup that leaves it vulnerable to erosion, particularly from acid rain.
 Hahn also chronicled subsequent efforts to then “save” the building, in which preservationists such as Wunsch and the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia worked to secure a few thousands dollars in emergency funding. With the money for supplies in hand and a capable carpenter in the church’s deacon Lloyd Butler, Wunsch wrote in his 2012 Hidden City piece that emergency repairs were performed including the replacement of wooden beams in the sanctuary and installation of corrugated metal roofs to keep out the elements.
 The efforts to stabilize the church’s condition led to a hopeful reprieve, but were set back by subsequent developments. Squire said he understands that 19th Street Baptist Church took out a sizable loan, which current debt holder PNL Companies dates to 2012, to help make repairs to the church. A 2015 WHYY article chronicling ongoing efforts to repair the church noted that congregants had raised $50,000 for further repairs, but made no mention of such a loan.
 Phil Cook, current trustee of 19th Street Baptist Church, said there was some “discrepancy” around the repair loan, including a dispute between the church and a contractor hired to perform work, and a dispute over “the distribution of funds from the bank to the contractor,” and litigation ensued.
 Inside 19th Street Baptist Church's sanctuary in 2018. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 At some point, the church fell behind on the debt and it was sold to PNL, a Dallas-based firm specializing in purchasing distressed commercial mortgages. In a written statement, PNL partner Dan Levitan confirmed PNL currently holds the debt, but said he worked closely with the church’s leadership, as well as benefactor and former Philadelphia Mayor Reverend Dr. W. Wilson Goode Sr., to try and preserve the church’s existence.
 “[Goode] told me that on the death bed of his friend, the long-time [Pastor Walker], that he would look after the church's welfare. I assured Dr. Goode that our company's intentions were to work with the church,” Levitan said.
 As Levitan tells it, this led PNL to make several concessions, including an extension of the loan’s maturity date and modification of its terms “to give the church sufficient time to raise the funds to save this historically significant Point Breeze building.”
 Specifically, Levitan said PNL agreed to forgive half of an existing balance of $564,000 if the church agreed to use the freed up resources to repair the church. Yet, an agreement for the arrangement also included a clause that stipulated the church could not sell the building to a for-profit developer for a 1o-year period or would have to pay back the full balance.
 Inside 19th Street Baptist Church's sanctuary in 2018. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Levitan said nine months after the deal was inked, articles appeared in the Philadelphia press stating the church was looking to sell the building to a preservation-minded buyer, with Winborne remarking to The Inquirer that other South Philadelphia churches had sold for upwards of $2 million.
 “Clearly, PNL would never have consented to write off $281,774.05 of the loan balance had we known the church intended to sell the property for a large profit and relocate from Point Breeze,” Levitan said. “We notified the church leaders in writing of our concerns, but never received a response.”
 Winborne, who left 19th Street Baptist Church to lead a different congregation in New Jersey for 17 years before returning as lead pastor in 2014, admits the church could have better handled its past finances. He says former Reverend Walker wore many hats, including missionary, and thus dispensed of some resources elsewhere. He said he was personally taken aback by the deterioration of the building upon his return to the congregation.
 “There were times when he took the resources that should have gone for, in my opinion, some maintenance,” Winborne said. “It went to somebody else who was in a worse off situation than we were.”
 Inside 19th Street Baptist Church's sanctuary in 2018. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Winborne also pointed to societal-level issues. There is the church’s insistence that it was shorn of its rightful financial endowment in a pre-Civil Rights America. There is also the modern continuation of inequality in which Black communities hold less resources and struggle to access financing he said. “We’re not in the circles. We don’t have the skill set. We don’t have anybody who’s a multimillionaire. We don’t know the lawyers. We don’t know the people to put a deal together,” said Winborne.
 He also showed no penchant for hiding his disdain for PNL, writing in a recent newsletter to church members that 19th Street Baptist Church still had “the claws of the vulture capitalist on our side.” “In a sea of gentrification and an ocean of buildings we have come up empty,” he added.
 Squire, who said he has been involved in years-long efforts to find a new source of capital large enough to save the church, attests that numerous applications to find philanthropic support were declined, which, he explained, is a common challenge for churches of all denominations. However, Squire said he did identify a potential lender in a “faith-based,” Black-owned firm called Crossing Capital, and also approached Ian Smith, a Black, Philadelphia-based architect to mock up some adaptive reuse options. Essentially, Squire said he had been trying for one last push to spare the church from demolition, including potentially selling the building to an adaptive reuse developer and paying off the full PNL debt with the proceeds.
 Yet, he claims 19th Street Baptist Church took an “astonishingly long time” to do their part of the paperwork and seemed intent on minimizing PNL’s financial take. "There’s a lot of animus between the church and the lender, or the debt-holder, that seems to be deeply personal,” Squire said. “They just were not interested in any scenario where [PNL] got paid back. And, at the end of the day, that was the kind of fundamental sticking point on all deals.”
 Demolition Pending, Perhaps Imminently 
 19th Street Baptist Church's fellowship hall in 2018. The congregation hopes to save its Sunday school building from demolition. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Exactly when the wrecking ball might arrive at 19th Street Baptist Church is somewhat unclear and potentially malleable. Squire said a date of Monday, September 16th had been privately conveyed by the City. Asked to confirm, Shemeka Moore, a spokesperson for L&I, suggested via email it could very well be the case.
 “Yes, this property is on the imminently dangerous list and could be demolished in the interest of public safety,” Moore wrote. “However, the owner still has time to get permits and start repairs. This would stop the property from being demolished.”
 A focus appears to be on the adjacent fellowship hall, which both Winborne and Squire said is in better condition than the sanctuary and may be able to be salvaged. However, the two are structurally connected and thus the City has requested engineering work to investigate.
 “We’re waiting for the engineer’s report to give it to the City, so they know exactly what to shore up,” Winborne said, adding he expects the City could potentially wait as long as the end of fall before performing demolition. “[The engineer] understands the urgency and the hope is very, very soon.”
 Cook, the church’s trustee, also pushed back on the notion that the church has let its buildings reach the brink of demolition out of spite for PNL. “The hope is we get a partner,” to save at least the fellowship hall, Cook said. “Hopefully it’s a nonprofit partner, but if it’s a for-profit partner, then, you know, the church is obligated to pay its debt. We’re not trying to shy away from any of that.”
 At the same time, Winborne hinted a new chapter may be in store for the parcel, noting he’d spoken with politicians who expressed a general need for land in South Philadelphia for new developments like senior centers.
 “When you look at the size of the footprint when the main sanctuary comes down, my question is, where is there another parcel of land that large in Center City South?” Winborne posited. “Paul says in Romans, ‘All things work together for the good, for those that love God.’ So I’m an eternal optimist. There is opportunities for good.”
 Editor’s note : Thaddeus Squire is a founder of Hidden City Philadelphia, but retains no professional position with this publication.
 Tags: 19th Street Baptist Church Church demolition demolition Frank Furness Point Breeze South Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Georgian Revival Tower in Center City Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At a brief meeting on October 11, the Philadelphia Historical Commission added one new property to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, approved new construction in a historic district, and gave an additional continuance to a nominated property.
 The former The Provident Trust Company at 17th and Chestnut Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Provident Trust Company building at 1628-36 Chestnut Street was constructed as a 12-story tower in 1928, with two two-story additions following in 1946 and 1987. The Historical Commission designated it based on its Georgian Revival style which was designed by the architectural firm of Rankin and Kellogg. The prominent Philadelphia firm designed commercial and institutional buildings such as the former Philadelphia Inquirer building on North Broad Street, the East Falls Public Library, and the U.S. Post Office at 30th and Market Streets.
 4124-28 Parkside Avenue and the proposed addition. | Rendering: Living City Architecture
 A proposal for a new three-story building of multi-unit housing was approved following several modifications at the recommendation of the Historical Commission’s Architectural Committee. The site is the side yard of the 1894 building at 4124-28 Parkside Avenue , a significant property in the Parkside Historic District .
 The former Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) at 750 Race Street was completed in 1962 and designed by Geddes, Brecher, Qualls and Cunningham. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The nomination of 708-34 Race Street , the former Police Administration Building, also known as the Roundhouse, received a fourth continuance and will now be reviewed at the Historical Commission's November meeting. It was submitted in December 2022 by Docomomo US/Greater Philadelphia and the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia and reviewed and recommended for designation by the Historical Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation in September 2023.
 Also at this meeting, architectural historian Robert Thomas noted his completion of two four-year terms as Chair of the Historical Commission and solicited nominations for a new chair. New member Zachary Frankel was nominated and approved. A principal at Frankel Enterprises, he described himself as a developer “primarily of affordable housing.”
 Tags: Center City Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission Police Administration Building 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Grave of Georgia Enslaver Discovered at Old Pine Church
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
Old Pine Street Presbyterian Church at 412 Pine Street was founded in 1768. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 A weathered headstone has stood for more than two centuries in the northwest corner of the Old Pine Street Presbyterian Church's cemetery. Upon it’s re-discovery in 2021, Kevin Williams, president of Old Pine Conservancy, remarked at how the headstone sparked his curiosity, especially due to its size, which suggests that it was made to remember “someone of high status.”
 What he and the Conservancy soon discovered is that this headstone belongs to James Hamilton, a former Georgia plantation owner who once owned over 600 enslaved people and spent his last years in Philadelphia.
 What makes this discovery even more interesting is that near Hamilton are the final resting places of members of the Second African Presbyterian Church, which include Pastor Stephen Gloucester, a former enslaved person who became a minister and an abolitionist, his wife, and fellow Pastor Benjamin Templeton
 Their stories have become part of an ongoing work-study research project by both the Conservancy and Temple University students Mary Greenberg and Adrian Nuñez into Hamilton’s life, how his story led him to Philadelphia, and, most importantly, how this project will change the narrative of this old church.
 Hamilton’s Circle of Friends 
 Slave quarters at Hamilton Plantation at Saint Simons Island, Georgia. | Photo courtesy of Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress
 Born in Strathaven, Lanarkshire, Scotland in 1767, Hamilton arrived in the Southern Colonies most likely in 1784 because this period coincides with the slow rebuilding of the South after the American Revolution and the emergence of many opportunities, especially in trade.
 According to Duke University’s archives and manuscripts collections, on his arrival to Charleston, South Carolina, Hamilton established working relationships with Henry Bethune & Co. of London, a business that most likely dealt in the slave trade. At this time, he purchased a townhome at No. 13 Broad Street in Charleston.
 When Hamilton met his wife, Nancy Isabella Steedman, is unknown, but records from the collections state that she was born in London. They had two children: Agnes Rebecca and George.
 We also do not know when and how he met his business partner, John Couper, but they later formed Hamilton & Couper. By 1800, they had purchased land at Gascoigne Bluff on St. Simon’s Island in Georgia. The many properties that they purchased included three other coastal Georgia plantations.
 A drawing by artist Donovan Nelson depicting the Igbo Landing Mass Suicide. | Image courtesy of the National Museum of African American History and Culture
 At the Hamilton Plantation, the main product was cotton as well as ships for the transportation of both enslaved people and products. During this period, Hamilton eventually owned over 650 enslaved, ranging in ages from 1 to 67 years old, establishing him as one of the biggest enslavers in the region. The majority of his slaves are listed in his records.
 Letters from friends, business associates, and slave owners Zephaniah Kingsley Jr. and George Gibbs provide some insight into Hamilton. In a letter dated August 1801, Gibbs reports that he is having difficulty procuring a ship captain to deliver "your negroes to St. Simons.” Another interaction, which involves Couper, implies that Hamilton had requested Igbo enslaved people captured in Nigeria, but they ultimately rebelled, massacred, and committed mass suicide by drowning after their arrival to Georgia in 1803. This incident was referred to as the Igbo Landing Mass Suicide and is believed to be the first Black slave resistance. What is especially noteworthy is that this incident occurred during a period when the capture and smuggling of enslaved Africans was largely illegal.
 The University of Georgia’s collection of Hamilton’s papers gives us a peek at the goings on within his plantations and his business dealings with both Couper and another business named McCredie & Hamilton. These papers highlight the scope of his interactions with individuals from Liverpool, Stockholm, Paris, Rotterdam, the Mediterranean, India, the West Indies, as well as throughout the American South. The collection also has a complete list of enslaved, promissory notes, and bills of sale from his estate.
 Although it is not clear why he came to Philadelphia and lived at 260 Walnut Street, it is well documented that many Southerners found respite from the region's humid weather and found social circles to their liking in the North.
 Detail of James Hamilton's list of enslaved people. | Image courtesy of Old Pine Conservancy
 As noted in An American Aristocracy by Daniel Kilbride, “The city also had a southern orientation. Sympathetic observers and critics alike detected a strong affinity between its fashionable society and the southern gentry.” Hamilton most probably enjoyed what Scotsman Thomas Hamilton (not related) noticed while traveling through Philadelphia in 1830, “There is no American city in which the system of exclusion is so rigidly observed as in Philadelphia.”
 Hamilton passed away at the age of 66 in 1829. As a member of the First Presbyterian Church, his plot and an additional 899 plots were moved to Old Pine’s cemetery in the 1840s. After his passing, his estate was trusted to his sole living grandchild, Isabella Hamilton Corbin, and two legatees, Richard Washington and Elizabeth T. Corbin.
 By 1848, his estate was valued at $1 million, which included 764 enslaved. The executors of his estate invested in U.S. Treasury bonds of the State of Pennsylvania during and after the Civil War.
 John and Stephen Gloucester 
 An undated portrait of John Gloucester. | Image courtesy of the Presbyterian Historical Society
 In 1810, John Gloucester paid $1,500 to manumission his wife and four sons. One son was the future preacher Stephen Gloucester, who was born in the territory south of the Ohio River (later to become Tennessee) in 1776.
 Gloucester found his purpose in life through preaching Christianity to his fellow slaves. He was freed by Reverend Gideon Blackburn who purchased him in 1806.
 Gloucester joined the First African Presbyterian Church and served as its minister until his passing in 1822. His son Stephen became a minister, an abolitionist, the publisher of the Colored American, a supporter of the Underground Railroad, and founder and pastor of the Second African Presbyterian Church.
 An etching showing First African Presbyterian Church, which was built at 7th Street below Shipppen (Bainbridge) Street and dedicated in 1811. | Image courtesy of the Presbyterian Historical Society
 Unfortunately, Stephen’s fortunes turned in 1842 when an Irish mob attacked a parade in honor of the abolition of slavery in Jamaica. This was later referred to as the Lombard Street Riot. Second African and Smith’s Hall, both on Lombard and 4th Street, where both burned down during the three-day riot.
 After building Lombard Street Central Presbyterian in 1844, he passed away in 1850 due to pneumonia and was placed in a grave with wife Ann that was forgotten until rediscovered in 2008. The couple was moved to Old Pine that same year. Also discovered within the vault was Benjamin F. Templeton who served as a pastor at Lombard Street Central Presbyterian for two years before his the untimely passing in 1858 at the age of 40.
 Mistaken Identity 
 James Hamilton's headstone at Old Pine Street Presbyterian Church. | Photo: Keshler Thibert
 Williams recounted how he originally thought Hamilton's headstone belonged to Colonel Ralph Isaacs, the secretary to George Mathews who was working as a special agent for the federal government to try and take Florida from the Spanish. Williams said when he learned that Hamilton owned enslaved people, he was conflicted, “I think Old Pine is a great mosaic of Antebellum America, a story that can’t be told without slavery, but it is also a terrible disappointment that such a prolific slave owner was in our graveyard.”
 When asked how the discovery Hamilton, along with Gloucester and Templeton, will change the narrative of the church, Williams remarked, “I view it as an opportunity to memorialize the enslaved.” He said Old Pine’s plans are to link the names of the enslaved to their signage and include this information during tours of the burial grounds. He hopes that the work will not only uncover more about Hamilton through research and put the stories of the enslaved at the forefront, but also that something good can come from having had such a large enslaver buried at Old Pine.
 Although Hamilton was hidden in plain sight, there are still plenty of stories regarding Antebellum Philadelphia that have not been told—yet. Northern slavery and relations with the South are still taboo topics at many organizations. Not long ago, Philadelphia institution that found any mention of their connection to the “peculiar institution” would quickly distance themselves from real evidence no matter how verifiable it is. Fortunately, the city, and the country, is moving onward toward more discoveries like the Gloucesters, Templetons, and others. Researchers will eventually dig up new leads wherever they are found and eagerly follow them wherever they may go.
 Tags: African-American history historic cemeteries historic churches Old Pine Street Church slavery 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: A Ghostly Endeavor at the University of Pennsylvania
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
In 1883, the University of Pennsylvania received a bequest from Henry Seybert (1801-1883). He was a wealthy Philadelphian who had commissioned the casting of the Centennial Bell for the city’s 1876 celebration, which contains metal smelted from British and American cannons from the Revolutionary War and from Union and Confederate cannons from the Civil War. It now hangs in the belfry of Independence Hall.
 The first part of the gift established the Adam Seybert Professor in Moral and Intellectual Philosophy, named for Seybert’s father, who earned a medical degree from Penn in 1793, served on the faculty, and later was a member of Congress. It was one of the earliest endowed chairs at the university and still exists today.
 However, there were strings attached to the gift. The duties of the professor who held the chair included taking part in an investigation to find grounds for belief in a spirit world. Thus, the Seybert Commission for Investigating Modern Spiritualism was created in 1883 at Penn.
 A playbill from 1864 advertising the performance of a magician that claimed to be able to contact the dead. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 In the 19th century, spiritualism was a popular subject whose adherents believed it was possible to communicate with the dead, particularly with the assistance of a medium. Increased interest in the subject occurred in the aftermath of the Civil War, prompted by the massive number of casualties. Numerous self-proclaimed mediums flourished, especially in New England and the mid-Atlantic, often operating in suspect ways.
 The “proof” of the mediums’ communications with the spirit world included slate writing, moving objects, and rapping sounds, all seemingly generated by ghosts, and purported photographs of spirits as shadowy figures alongside the actual human subject.
 The officials at Penn took the requirement seriously and appointed a commission of distinguished faculty. In addition to the first Adam Seybert Professor George Fullerton, it included the University’s Provost, physician William Pepper (who went on to found the Free Library of Philadelphia, the Penn Museum, and the Wistar Institute), biologist Joseph Leidy, neurologist Silas Weir Mitchell, chemist George Augustus Koenig, and Horace Howard Furness, a Shakespearean scholar who provided quotes from the Bard of Avon for the stained glass windows of the Penn library designed by his brother Frank Furness, now the Fisher Fine Arts Library.
 Members of the First Association of Spiritualists in front of their temple at 12th and Thompson Streets in 1917. | Photo courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 “This was a big deal. It was an important civic project,” said John Pollak, curator of research services at the Kislak Center, which houses special collections and rare books at Penn. “These were the major minds of the nation in a way and certainly of this university. They took on the responsibility of doing a formal study of what they called modern spiritualism.”
 Furness served for a time as the acting chair of the commission and as such read newspaper accounts of mediums’ activities throughout the Northeast, visited many of them, and often paid them to demonstrate their abilities. He kept meticulous notes of his investigations, as well as newspaper advertisements and business cards advertising mediums’ services, expense ledgers, and correspondence from people interested in the commission’s findings. “This was news at the time,” said Justin McDaniel, professor of religious studies at Penn, whose focus on southeast Asian religious practice often looks at supernatural beliefs. “You would have the front page of the Inquirer say ‘Group at Penn to prove the existence of ghosts.’”
 A playbill from 1865 advertising an evening with illusionists and spirit world summoners Professor and Madame Wiseman. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 The Seybert Commission met from 1883 to 1887. Despite their best efforts, and their charge in Seybert’s will to investigate "all systems of Morals, Religion, or Philosophy which assume to represent the Truth, and particularly of Modern Spiritualism," they were unable to verify the existence of a spirit world. Although their report in 1887, published by the J. B. Lippincott Company, was titled “Preliminary Report of the Commission Appointed by the University of Pennsylvania to Investigate Modern Spiritualism in Accordance with the Request of the Late Henry Seybert ,” it was never followed by a final report and the commission was disbanded.
 Furness’s papers are held today by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, and Penn’s Kislak Center houses the records of the Seybert Commission, as well as the Henry Seybert Library of Modern Spiritualism , a collection of printed materials on the subject.
 Tags: Occult University of Pennsylvania 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Behind the Scenes: Navigating Philadelphia's Complicated Park Upgrade Process
author: Amanda Price
bodyText:
Outside of Philadelphia’s Rebuild initiative , which aims to invest in more than 70 parks and recreation centers in the city, the path to upgrading city-owned parks and playgrounds is not entirely straightforward.
 Philly has more than 500 public parks. Over 400 of those are overseen by the Department of Parks and Recreation. Notably, Parks and Recreation does not have its own budget to directly fund park improvements. Almost all upgrades are funded through the City's capital budget in partnership with City Council members. According to Philadelphia's 2024 capital budget, 60 percent of funding is allocated toward “building thriving neighborhoods,” which includes upgrades to Park and Recreation facilities.
 Philadelphia residents wanting a change in their neighborhood can contact Parks and Recreation to request an upgrade, but the best first step would likely be a call to the local Council member. Funding for park projects needs approval by a Council member, unless funded by an outside private source, such as a nonprofit organization. 
 Council members weigh the needs of their entire district within their pool of City funding. Therefore, it can take some time to get park projects started, as evidenced by a playground improvement request in Mt. Airy.
 Christopher Moore is president of Friends of Cliveden Park. Group members volunteer their time to maintain park grounds and the Cliveden House. It also hosts events for the community. The group recently played an important role in the city-wide Love Your Park weekend in early November. Cliveden Park was chosen as a "Signature Site" and hosted more than 100 clean-up volunteers.
 Moore, a long-time resident of the neighborhood, became president of the group in 2016. The following year he petitioned Parks and Recreation to renovate the park’s key feature: the playground.
 Friends of Cliveden Park president Christopher Moore (middle) surrounded by community members at Love Your Park weekend 2024 . | Photo: Steve Weinik for Friends of Cliveden Park
 Cliveden Park playground consists of one main structure situated on artificial turf with a separate swing set. Today, the turf has holes in it, the monkey bars are loose, and the slide heats up to extreme temperatures in the summer. According to Moore and his wife, Sam, it’s been that way for a while.
 “We moved to Britton Street in 2005 and our kids were playing [on the playground]…back then. And they’re adults now. It still looks the same,” Sam, also a Friends of Cliveden Park member, recalled.
 At the time of the initial renovation request in 2017, Parks and Recreation came out and surveyed the playground. “Because the process is that… even if you get somebody to fund it, they (Parks and Recreation) have to come out, and then it has to go up for bid to do the project and they have to do blueprints,” Moore explained. At the time of the survey, Parks and Recreation informed the group it did not have funding in place to make the changes. It was suggested that the group try and make the upgrades themselves.
 Moore and the Friends group proceeded to request sponsorship from Home Depot, but never received a reply. They also attempted fundraising, but with a price tag of several thousand dollars, were not able to raise sufficient funds.
 Each following year, Moore attempted to get the playground renovation realized. He and his wife viewed it as a safety issue. “Every year something happens to a kid on that playground. Every year,” Sam said. “The monkey bars need to be fixed. That’s how the kid broke his arm. He slipped and fell,” Moore added.
 In 2023, Moore was volunteering as a voting machine operator at Cliveden House and met a resident who happened to be friends with local Council Member Cindy Bass. They helped arranged a meeting, and Bass and representatives from Parks and Recreation performed a playground site visit in late 2023.
 The Friends group explained the site’s health hazards, and Bass agreed to fund a new playground. Her office submitted the official project request to Parks and Recreation, who now owns the project.
 “The improvements to Cliveden Park Playground have long been in the works,” Bass stated. “We’ve visited several times with Parks & Recreation staff requesting substantial changes to the very old and antiquated playground equipment. I’m pleased and proud to be able to say that we’ve been able to get some designs and begin to move forward with this process," Bass continued. "We expect that in spring 2025 this project will be fully underway, and a new playground should spring from that site, which the community desperately needs. It’s been a long time since there’s been any major improvements, and the community really deserves a better play space.”
 A rendering of Cliveden Park Playground's upgrades. | Image: Department of Parks and Recreation
 The plan includes a new playground structure, new safety surfacing, and new amenities such as benches, security cameras, and trash cans. As is typical to the City process, Parks and Recreation hosted a community meeting in January 2023 to present project blueprints and gather local feedback. Community members voted for the color scheme of the new playground and shared suggestions.
 Jane Anderson, the architectural projects coordinator overseeing this project at Parks and Recreation, said, “We are impressed with the dedication and advocacy the Friends of Cliveden Park have demonstrated towards improving the playground at Cliveden. In January, we held a productive community meeting where a large group of residents came together to provide the City with critical insight into the park's needs and to share their vision of a new playground. We are excited about transforming the park into a place children and families can enjoy, and thankful to Council Member Cindy Bass and her staff for not only being partners on the design proposal, but for playing an instrumental role in securing funding for the project.”
 The next step is putting the project up for bid, so the department can select one of its contracted vendors to perform the work. Construction is set to begin in the spring of 2025 and take around four months to complete. The estimated budget for the playground renovation is $232,000.
 Moore and his wife look forward to witnessing a new playground for the children to play on. “This has been a thorn for the longest for me and it’s finally getting done. I said like three years ago. ‘This is it. I’m not being the president [of Friends of Cliveden Park] anymore.' My wife said, ‘Well, you need to stick with it ‘til you get the playground done.'”
 Despite issues with the current playground, “the kids still come out here and play faithfully,” he added. “With so much going on in the city right now, you want to have a safe place for the kids to come. The kids are our future and we have to treat them right, give them something good."
 Tags: Department of Parks and Recreation public parks 
 About the Author
 Amanda Price is a journalist, writer, and elementary school teacher living in Mt. Airy. She is passionate about Philadelphia green space & social justice.

title: "The Big Story" Dives Deep Into Philly TV News History
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
For anyone who has lived in Philadelphia for more than 30 years, there will be a lot of familiarity with the events and stories covered in The Big Story: The Oral History of Philadelphia TV News by former WPHL 17 television news reporter David Grzybowski.
 The book, published this fall by Temple University Press, delivers an unexpected analysis of all Philadelphians, especially our idiosyncrasies into how we treat local news heroes as well as newcomers. A line that successfully gets these messages across comes from the chapter titled, “Philadelphia’s Relationship with Its TV Broadcasters.” Matt O’Donnell, an anchor and reporter from 6ABC, is quoted in the book. “I don’t know if we are celebrities or not, but the one thing about Philadelphia—there’s a trial period, and they watch you. They want to see what kind of person you are, and they want to see if you are one of those people who slack off or give maximum effort each time. Once they see you are one of those people who give maximum effort, you are good.”
 Keshler Thibert sat down with Grzybowski to learn both the process on compiling an oral history of local newscasters and his personal takeaways from this project.
 Keshler Thibert: Let’s go back to 2019, when you and the editor at Temple University Press, Ryan Mulligan, were discussing book ideas. You mention in the acknowledgments that a light went off in your mind when the idea was tossed around.
 David Grzybowski: I think everyone and their mother in the city just loves local television and primarily Philly TV personalities. I think nostalgia plays a huge role in people’s household watching habits. We treat our TV news reporters, and anchors like they are movie stars. In my opinion, no other city in this country is like this to the extent that we are.
 KT: What was it about this topic that attracted your interest?
 DG: I caught the itch to write another book, and, obviously, you want to write about something that is near and dear to your heart. So, I put my head down, got it together, and did my research.
 KT: Being a former reporter with Channel 17 WPHL, you are already familiar with a number of behind-the-scenes stories covered in The Big Story. Which one of these stories and behind-the-scene comments made you change your perception of the event itself?
 DG: All of them. I was born in 1991. Anything predating that was definitely interesting to learn about, especially the MOVE bombing (1985), Three Mile Island (1979), and Pope John Paul II’s visit (1979).
 What opened my eyes is how the industry adapted in the late 1970s to today with technology and how people did their jobs as journalists. When people read this book, they will see how the industry has been changed by the stories, learn intricate details that they probably did not know about before, and see names that they may not have seen in a while, but may make them remember.
 KT: You know how personal Philadelphians think about their news anchors. Was there any point in the writing process when you began to reconsider the topic or felt that it may not come together the way you wanted it to?
 DG: There are a lot more chapters to the book. We had to cut them out for spacing. It could have easily been a 550-page book. If there is anything I would like to reinsert, I kind of ask about it in the chapter titled “Building Trust with Viewers,” which is about this new age over the last four to eight years of misinformation on social media and how that plays a big part in delivering the news.
 KT: You cover some very dark and sad periods in local history. The Budd Dwyer suicide in 1987 in front of the press and Gary Papa’s death of prostate cancer in 2009. Were you worried about bringing up such sensitive events?
 DG: Not really. That is the beauty of this book. It covers everything from a sports championship parade to tragic events, such as losing anchors Jim O’Brien and Gary Papa. There really was not a story that made me think "I should not touch this" and that is the beauty of journalism and celebrating Philadelphia television. I did not want this book to be a cookie cutter. I wanted it to be the good, the bad, and the ugly.
 KT: You were able to reach a wide array of anchors, reporters, camera personal, and staff. Was there any one you were surprised allowed you to interview them? Anyone who you were not able to interview?
 DG: Getting Jim Gardner involved was definitely critical and took a long time. Not only just Jim, it took a long time to get a lot of the current on-air staff at Channel 6, NBC 10, CBS 3, and FOX 29. It probably should have come out a year or two ago, but COVID-19 hindered doing that.
 KT: When did you officially start writing and putting together this book? You started around the onset of the pandemic. Didn’t your life change during this period with the addition to your family?
 DG: I think it was February 2019. Research took a while, but the biggest thing is getting everyone together for an interview. I would say that I have 200–300 hours of interviews that I transcribed and put together.
 KT: There are multiple comments about how Philadelphians feel toward their news anchors and the community they have developed. Is this still valid in regards to anchors Gary Papa, Larry Kane, Vernon Odom, Pat Ciarrocchi, and Dave Roberts? Even Mike Jerrick and the Good Day cast. Those names roll off my tongue. Can the same be said about the newer anchors?
 DG: I honestly think that this book is coming out at an interesting time. There is a new wave of Philadelphia TV news anchors. Jim Gardner is no longer at WPVI, and there are other changes to the city. You see a lot of younger talent. I think the biggest thing is that Channel 6 is most successful when personalities come together, whether they are new or old, as they have a connection to Philadelphia. If they are here for 7 or 17 years, it goes a long way. We are at an interesting point because younger people are coming over and the older anchors are retiring.
 KT: You did not include any of your own comments, especially in the sections referring to the 2015 visit by Pope Francis and the Mummers Parade. You were a reporter for WPHL 17 for both. Why did you make the choice to keep your own voice out?
 DG: I did not want to be involved in the oral history. Not my words, but their words repurposed to tell a story. The only time you hear my opinion is in the acknowledgments. 
 KT: You appear to write about the topics you are intimately familiar with. Thus far, sports and the news. You’ve worked for the Mummers Parade for a number of years now, haven’t you?
 DG: I have been an executive producer for three years and I have been working with the Mummers for eight years, with the string bands and the fancy brigade at the Convention Center.
 KT: I went into The Big Story thinking that it would be mostly a linear narrative of the people, places, and things of the local broadcasters. After the overview of the TV news stations, you get into events such as the MOVE Bombing, Three Mile Island, Blizzard of 96, Pier 34 Collapse, as well as the controversial "Storm of the Century" to even the change of the Channel 6’s theme. As I read, I remembered where I was during those times and watching it live on air. I started to lament a bit. The book started to feel more like a time capsule.
 DG: I think you’re going to read this book and see names you have not heard in a long time, but you remember their faces. Like a George Mallet from FOX 29 who did Good Day Philadelphia or a veteran reporter from Channel 6. Even Charles Barkley is in a few chapters. That is the beauty of this book. You are going to recognize Ed Rendall, Ray Didinger, Michael Barkann, Larry Mendte, Mike Strug, and all the other iconic people.
 Tags: book review interview journalism television 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: Zakian Carpets
author: Alan Jaffe
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Zakian Carpets 
 Location : 4930 Parkside Avenue
 Architects : Unknown
 Built : 1956
 A few blocks west of the Centennial District’s magnificent, restored rowhouses and apartment buildings on Parkside Avenue is a remnant of the neighboring business area. Proclaiming its singular identity on Parkside row is Zakian Carpets, a century-old family enterprise and commercial landmark.
 The Zakian business began in the 1920s as a door-to-door Oriental rug cleaning service. In 1956, the business moved to Parkside and built a midcentury modern showroom of block glass and steel, crowned by an electric sign that spells out the family name in red capital block letters and “Carpets” in green, 1950s-cool cursive script. The 30,000-square-foot rug-cleaning plant also occupies several 19th-century brick buildings that were resurfaced while preserving two stone gargoyles.
 One other eclectic element of the building was added to the showroom facade in 2015–a mural representing the “Armenian Orphan Rug” and commemorating the Armenian genocide.
 This fourth-generation Philadelphia family business, with its distinctive mid-century building and sign, deserve recognition and protection by listing on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places .
 Tags: Parkside Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Unlisted Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Alan Jaffe is the assignment editor and project manager of FactCheck.org at Annenberg Public Policy Center. He is a former editor of the Philadelphia Inquirer and a contributing writer of Extant, Billy Penn, and Plan Philly.

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: USS Olympia
author: Alan Jaffe and Bryan Mckinney
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Name: USS Olympia 
 Location: 211 Columbus Boulevard, Penn’s Landing 
 Builder: Union Iron Works, San Francisco
 Built: 1892
 Generations of Philadelphians recall their grade-school field trip to the floating historical artifact, the USS Olympia . Moored on the Delaware River at Penn’s Landing since 1957, the vessel is under the stewardship of the Independence Seaport Museum. It is a National Historic Landmark and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, but has yet to be included on the Philadelphia Register.
 USS Olympia’s place in history is secured. The cruiser was deployed in 1898 under Commodore George Dewey to the Battle of Manila Bay, where Dewey uttered the command, “You may fire when you are ready, Gridley,” and proceeded to defeat the Spanish fleet. The world’s oldest steel warship served as a symbol of American naval power until it was decommissioned in 1922 and has survived as a waterfront museum since 1957.
 Unsuccessful attempts to preserve USS Olympia’s neighbor downriver, the SS United States , show the need to protect this other maritime icon through designation on the city’s historic register.
 Tags: Delaware River waterfront maritime military Penn's Landing

title: Restoration Role Model: Ohio House
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Restoring the chimneys posed the biggest preservation challenge in terms of materials. The repair involved infusing the inside of the bricks with a strengthening solution, then infusing their surface with a breathable, water-repellent solution. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Before the Fairmount Park Conservancy could move into its new headquarters in the 19th-century Ohio House, the organization sent its conservation team to implement a series of desperately needed repairs at the Gothic Revival-style building. Extant spoke with the Conservancy and Director of Conservation Tom McPoyle about how the team of preservationists balanced modern needs and safety standards with architectural preservation.
 What was the building’s original use? 
 Ohio House is one of only four park buildings that remain from the Centennial International Exhibition, also known as the World’s Fair of 1876. At the time, the U.S. had 37 states, and 26 of them constructed exhibition buildings. Ohio House showcased the Buckeye State’s natural resources, made from sandstone mined from 21 Ohio quarries. The building was open intermittently after the fair and had been shuttered for decades before briefly reopening in 1976 for the bicentennial celebration. It became the Centennial Cafe in 2007, then the Hungry Bear Cafe before closing in 2016.
 What was most important to preserve? 
 The objective of the Conservancy’s building conservation services team is always to preserve the historic building materials and respect the integrity of the building. The function of inside rooms needed to change. But instead of moving walls, we moved doors to create better access points. The Conservancy took a preservation-minded approach and found the function of each room by looking at the spaces “as they are” and envisioned the best ways to use each space, rather than assuming there would be a need for big alterations.
 The Conservancy found the function of each room by looking at the spaces “as they are” and envisioned the best ways to use each space, rather than assuming there would be a need for big alterations. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 What was the original vision for the restoration? 
 The original vision was to create useful, functional office spaces without doing major surgery. Some new dividing walls needed to be added, but this was done without cutting through the original flooring or plaster walls or destroying the baseboard and window trim. We scribed the walls around these features so that in the distant future, if the building has a new use, the new dividing walls could be removed and the original floor plan restored. We measured original features for scale and size, but made the trim and doors minimal and more modern so they are easily distinguished as alterations but blend in visually.
 What was the biggest preservation challenge? 
 The chimney restoration was the biggest preservation challenge. A previous contractor had either aggressively power-washed or maybe sandblasted the brickwork, removing the protective skin created during the brick’s firing process. Without their protective skin, these bricks pull in and hold large amounts of moisture. The repair involved infusing the brickwork with a strengthening solution, patching some cratered areas and infusing the surface with a breathable water-repellent solution.
 Did you look to any role model for inspiration or example? 
 An indispensable resource for the exterior restoration at Ohio House was original photos and documents created for the Centennial Exhibition in 1876. From the photos, we could confirm what was intact and what was missing on the three main elevations of the building. We also confirmed the types of materials, along with the names of suppliers, from 1876 documents. The original glass in the windows was manufactured with a high-silica limestone quarried in Ravenna, Ohio by the Diamond Glass Company.
 Tags: adaptive resuse Centennial Exposition Fairmount Park Conservancy Renovation Restoration Role Model Victorian architecture 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Op-ed: Sustaining the Ecosystem that Gives Life to Chinatown
author: Di Gao
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Photo courtesy of No Arena PHL
 Years ago, when I was a graduate student in the University of Pennsylvania’s historic preservation program, I would bike to Philadelphia’s Chinatown whenever I felt homesick. It was the third Chinatown I would get to know, the first being Seattle’s Chinatown where my father worked and the second being Manhattan’s Chinatown where I lived after moving to New York. These neighborhoods inspired me to pursue historic preservation as a career. Today, I am leading the America’s Chinatowns initiative at the National Trust for Historic Preservation, a project that aims to mobilize preservation action to help protect the cultural identity of these vital neighborhoods. Last May, I returned to Philadelphia’s Chinatown to stand with local advocates to announce the naming of the neighborhood to the 2023 11 Most Endangered Historic Places list , calling attention to the recurring threats of large-scale development that have impacted the neighborhood, most recently in the form of the proposed 76ers basketball arena.
 Chinatowns nationwide have faced similar patterns of displacement from big development efforts that have divided, fenced in, and demolished these neighborhoods. In response, Chinatowns have drawn on traditions of activism, mutual aid, and home-grown innovation to maintain their way of life and protect their neighborhoods. At times, communities have turned to planning and preservation policies, but many of these formal tools fall short of effectively protecting what makes Chinatown, Chinatown.
 To understand why and how we can do better, we must understand what exactly we are trying to protect. From communities doing this work, I hear that the priority is in sustaining the Chinatown ecosystem.
 This means a great deal beyond the physical buildings and includes preserving the ways of life that animate them. Mom-and-pop businesses, residents, cultural traditions, affordable housing and commercial space, the food economy, schools, space to practice lion dance, and places of worship are some examples of this ecosystem. It also means encouraging newer generations of entrepreneurs who respect the history of the neighborhood and sustaining legacy businesses. Beyond what can be seen at street level, legacy institutions, small property owners, and community-based organizations are supporting the ecosystem in myriad visible and invisible ways. These groups also emphasize community organizing, awareness building, advocacy for equitable resources, and representation in public decision-making where Chinatown populations have historically faced barriers to participation. This ecosystem has kept Chinatowns centers of community life for more than 170 years.
 941 Race Street was completed in 1900 and designed by Edwin Gilbert. It has seen many reuses over the last century. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 To preserve this ecosystem, many Chinatowns today are concerned with protecting affordability in the wake of gentrification, often accelerated by large-scale development. Keeping property ownership in the community has helped preserve lasting affordability, preventing outside interests who have different visions for these historic enclaves from taking over. Community ownership has been maintained by family associations, legacy property owners, community development corporations, and newer entities like community land trusts (see examples in Boston and Los Angeles).
 A recent article in Preservation magazine explores how five different Chinatowns are working to preserve their futures. Some are leaning into Chinatowns’ role as places of connection and shared culture by investing in the creation of community hubs that will be physical homes to cultural exhibits, neighborhood resources, and gathering. Others are investing heavily in placekeeping and placemaking efforts to bring 24/7 activity back to Chinatowns, while attracting newer generations and audiences. Others are establishing legacy business support programs like grants and succession planning.
 Some Chinatowns are actively exploring historic designation as a form of protection, although there are concerns that these policies focus too much on physical buildings and offer little benefit when it comes to preserving more vital parts of the ecosystem. These barriers are significant. Only nine Chinatowns out of the dozens we identified are listed on the National Register of Historic Places and more research is needed to understand the potential benefits. Perhaps another option is the cultural districts model. Chicago's Chinatown, which is known as the only growing historic Chinatown in the country, just became a state-designated cultural district and could serve as a model.
 Looking at how other communities of color navigated similar challenges can be insightful for Chinatowns. The Preserving African American Places report offers a compendium of case studies on how communities have inspired neighborhood-based solutions for equitable development to fight displacement and gentrification. One case study highlights the downzoning effort in San Francisco’s Chinatown in the 1970s and 1980s to preserve affordable units in the shadows of the tech boom that was converting affordable housing to office space, highlighting the ways government, private sector, and community advocates work together to manage change.
 Philadelphia’s Chinatown has an incredible history of activism and resilience. There is enormous potential and hunger to mobilize preservation resources and reimagine the tools, tactics, and strategies we can harness collectively to protect dynamic neighborhoods like Chinatowns for future generations.
 Tags: Asian American history Chinatown Immigrants Sixers Arena 
 About the Author
 Di Gao is the senior director of research and development at the National Trust for Historic Preservation. She is responsible for developing new preservation initiatives, and her work is currently focused on the intersection of preservation and equity, inclusion and social justice, and mobilizing preservation action to better support America’s Chinatowns and other ethnic enclaves.

title: Challenges for Chinatown, Again
author: Starr Herr-Cardillo
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 As you pass through the stately, intricately tiled Friendship Gate marking the entrance to Philadelphia’s Chinatown, you’re met with streets crowded with pedestrians maneuvering around market stalls that spill out onto the sidewalk, overflowing with heaps of fruit, stacked sugarcane, neatly piled bags of rice, and other goods. Illuminated signs in combinations of Chinese and English project from stuccoed 19th-century rowhouses, identifying what are now busy restaurants packed with patrons. The neighborhood has an energy–especially on the weekends–and it’s a part of Philly, like the Italian Market or South Street, that makes you feel like you’re in a big city.
 Philly’s Chinatown is more than 150 years old, making it one of the oldest remaining Chinatowns in the United States. Like Chinatowns across America, it grew out of a culture of discrimination and segregation–racism initially sanctioned by Congress via the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882–and the Chinese community’s subsequent adaptation, providing affordable housing, safety, and a sense of community for Chinese and other immigrants. Chinatown today is shaped by a diversity of Southeast Asian cultures including Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese.
 From the outside, it’s a neighborhood that’s been relatively well- preserved. While there’s no Chinatown historic district listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, a number of its buildings are designated individually, although none but the Chinese Cultural Center –opened in 1955 as the Chinatown YMCA–were nominated for their connection to the Chinese history of the area. Part of the neighborhood is also protected to some extent by a zoning overlay restricting the height of new development.
 The Chinese Cultural Center near the corner of 10th and Cherry Streets. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Perhaps driven by necessity or affordability, the majority of Chinatown’s old brick rowhouses have been adapted over the centuries, with ever-changing storefronts and facades modified with decorative flair that honors Chinese architectural style.
 Historic plaques and archival photos are all that remain of Chinatown’s earliest businesses and buildings, such as the city’s first Chinese laundry established in 1870 at 913 Race Street and the Far East Chinese Restaurant that opened in 1908 at 907 Race Street. The neighborhood’s physical identity is characterized by more recent additions, like the magnificent Friendship Gate, designed in the Qing Dynasty style by artist Sabrina Soong and dedicated in 1984, the 10th Street Plaza completed in 2011 and guarded by two giant Foo dogs flanking a statue of the Chinese scholar General Lin Zexu, and powerful murals by Lily Yeh, Arturo Ho and Josh Sarantitis that celebrate the community and its history.
 Yet, Chinatown’s identity is more nuanced and centered around people. Talk to folks in the Chinatown community and they’ll point out that there have been a few constants for the area. Currently on their minds is the fact that Chinatown has been continually threatened or divided by large-scale developments like the Vine Street Expressway. Now, a proposal for a new $1.3 billion arena for the Philadelphia 76ers has united the neighborhood around a cause once again .
 Students for the Preservation of Chinatown protest on June 10, 2023. | Photo: Noel Chacko
 Of greater value than a sports arena to Philadelphia’s Chinese and Asian American community are the essential resources always provided by the neighborhood, like language, housing, and immigration services, particularly critical for older, lower-income residents and those who are not English speakers.
 The arena may be the main focus at the moment, but there are other threats facing Chinatown even if the proposed plan doesn’t come to pass. The National Trust for Historic Preservation recently highlighted America’s Chinatowns as places that are uniquely at risk of physical and
cultural displacement. In 2023, the Chinatowns of Philadelphia and Seattle were added to the list of America’s Most Endangered Historic Places by the National Trust.
 Extant talked to Mary Yee of the Save Chinatown Coalition, Henry Leong, who directs the Chinese Christian Church and Center, and Kaia Chau of Students for the Preservation of Chinatown and the Ginger Arts Center about how they feel the neighborhood has evolved, the threats it faces, and what’s essential to preserve Chinatown and its community into the future.
 Resilience and Resistance 
 Mary Yee is currently the facilitator of the technical planning committee of the Save Chinatown Coalition. In the 1970s, she helped found Yellow Seeds, a radical student group from which grew a bilingual Chinese- English newspaper of the same name, as well as Asian Americans United. Yee has been involved in many facets of the fight to preserve Chinatown, including opposition movements against the Vine Street Expressway, the proposed Phillies stadium, a federal prison, and the Foxwoods Casino.
 What’s your sense of Chinatown as a community? What are the constants, and what has changed over the years? 
 Chinatown has been important historically as a center not just for Chinese Americans but for Asian Americans in the Delaware Valley. Our community is being continually threatened by these infrastructure projects. Historically, it’s been an issue of racial discrimination against our neighborhood, and every time we struggle against a big project, we’re in the news and the people in the City agencies acknowledge us. When the second one comes around, it’s like we’re invisible again. I would say that this is implicit bias–this is basically white supremacy. The fact that we’re still around is a symbol [of] our resilience and our resistance.
 It feels like the Chinatown community is pretty well-organized. Does it feel that way on the inside? 
 Overall, yes. The major organizations–that is PCDC (Philadelphia Chinatown Development Corporation), Asian Americans United, and the Save Chinatown Coalition, which represents a lot of other organizations–are all united in their opposition to the arena and the position that we will not sign a community benefit agreement (CBA). I think in any situation, you never have 100 percent consensus. But overall, given the surveys that have happened and the public meetings, over 93 [percent] to 95 percent of the people have voiced that they are against the arena and against signing the CBA.
 Anti-arena posters are ubiquitous on walls and storefronts throughout Chinatown. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 In your opinion, what are the main threats facing Chinatown, and what are the steps required to preserve it? 
 The most immediate threat is the arena, but the ongoing threat is gentrification. A community land trust, which is one thing that should have happened a long time ago, could have mitigated that. As far as preservation goes, some of us are trying to get a cultural historic designation possible in Philadelphia. Right now, most of the designations are based on architectural significance. Other cities or states have a cultural district designation. At the same time, we need to have more support for our arts and culture organizations and our youth organizations. It would be great if we could have more anchor institutions in the community. For instance, in Little Tokyo in Los Angeles, they have a Japanese American Museum, sports facility, two or three Buddhist temples, [a] historic site [connected to the history of Japanese internment camps], some senior housing. They do have cultural historic designation from the city and the state. They have also instituted a real estate investment trust [Community Impact Fund], which is community-run.
