This allows for a moderate interest rate and using funds to buy land to be held in a community trust, or to subsidize rents for legacy businesses, which are being threatened by gentrification. Those are some strategies that could be used to protect Philadelphia’s Chinatown.
 Maintaining a Spiritual Core 
 Harry Leong is currently the center director at the Chinese Christian Church and Center, which has been an organization in Philly’s Chinatown community since 1941. Leong grew up in Chinatown and also serves as the president of the Philadelphia Suns, a community youth group with about 250 active members that focuses on sports, service, cultural activities, and promoting the community. He also serves on the Board of Directors for the Philadelphia Chinatown Development Corporation.
 What’s your personal connection to the neighborhood? 
 I was born and raised in Philadelphia Chinatown. I continue to live here. My family owns a building right next to the church, so I have a five-second commute to work.
 What role does the Chinese Christian Church and Center play in the community? 
 CCCC (C4) is the spiritual home to close to 600 adults and over 150 children in three-language-speaking congregations (Mandarin, Cantonese and English). What people may not know is that the church developed from the outreach center reaches out to hundreds of metro Philly-area inhabitants each year.
 What’s remained constant, and how has the neighborhood changed since you were a kid? 
 Growing up, we were such a tight-knit community. We were like a village and people knew each other. If you did something wrong, news would get back to your family before you even got home. I just remember being disciplined as a kid by neighbors, and today we don’t even know our neighbors.
 An article published by The Philadelphia Inquirer on April 8, 1966. Image: Newspapers.com
 What do you think is one of the most pressing issues for Chinatown and its preservation? 
 In the 1990s, there was a large number of immigrants that came into the area and [many settled in Chinatown]. Later, a lot of immigrants came with more money and would go straight to the suburbs. The Philadelphia Suns members used to be primarily from Chinatown, but today maybe 90 percent of our 200-plus people do not live in Chinatown, primarily because of the shortage of housing in the community. There is not enough low-to moderate-income housing in the area. We’re in Center City, and we’ve come to a point where high prices have come into our neighborhoods and pushed out a lot of the families. There’s also been a shift in generational priorities, and the next generation is not interested in taking over family businesses. If you walk around the community, you see that there are a lot of new businesses within the last 15 years. Today, if you’re here for 15 years, that’s an old business.
 Reclaiming What Was Almost Stolen 
 Kaia Chau is a second-generation activist and the co-founder and co- leader of Students for the Preservation of Chinatown (SPOC) and the Ginger Arts Center, a new community youth arts center “run by the youth, for the youth” located in a storefront at 447 North 12th Street. The initial setup and opening of the center was supported by a grant from the Leeway Foundation, which funds artists working toward social justice. She’s a recent graduate of Bryn Mawr College, where she majored in international studies with minors in Asian American studies and Chinese.
 What role do you see Ginger Arts playing in Chinatown? 
 As someone who was born and raised in Philly and has spent so much time in Chinatown growing up, I really remember just having a lack of third spaces. In Chinatown, we have a private Catholic school and we have a charter school–FACTS (Folk Arts Cultural Treasures Charter School)–that the community had to fight for and build for ourselves due to the fact that our neighborhood never had a proper public school. There aren’t really parks, there aren’t libraries. I love Chinatown and it’s a really great community, but I feel like it has been neglected in a lot of ways and lacks services that should be a fundamental right for any neighborhood. I think Ginger Arts came about because we were like, “If we had all this money and resources, what would we build for Chinatown?” And when we came across a grant opportunity from the Leeway Foundation, we thought, this is our chance to actually do that. I’ve found that a lot of high schoolers who come here feel just really safe and comfortable. This is a place that they want to come to. We have a lot of high school volunteers who have spent so much of their time helping to build the space because they’re so passionate and excited about the space.
 Menu from 1920 for "The Far East" Chinese Restaurant, at 907 Race Street. The building's facade is substantially intact. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 The multigenerational dimension of this neighborhood feels really significant, and it’s not something you see everywhere. Ginger Arts seems to be really stepping into a role. 
 The mother of Taryn Flaherty (co-founder and co-leader of SPOC) and my mother have been super involved in Chinatown activism our whole lives. I think when we started SPOC, we were led by this responsibility to preserve Chinatown from the very Asian or Chinese value of giving back to your elders [to] thank them for their sacrifices, and we saw that in what our moms did. Even though growing up I didn’t have many third spaces, the spaces I did feel safest were places like FACTS, which my mom and Taryn’s mom founded, along with so many other amazing activists in Chinatown who played a role in raising us. Having gone through college now and thinking back to my childhood, these are the establishments and people now that I feel I owe a lot to, and I want the generation after me to feel the same way, feel as safe as I did growing up. So, I think Ginger Arts is an extension of a generational tradition of organizing in Chinatown.
 How do you think about preservation, and what do you think preservation of Chinatown in the future looks like? 
 I remember when we were looking for spaces to rent out for the center, a lot of us were adamant that we needed to be in Chinatown proper. Usually if you think about Chinatown, you think about whatever is south of Vine. But rent is super expensive and it was really hard to find an open space, so we started looking north of Vine in the Callowhill area where we are now. At first, I was kind of bummed out because it would’ve been really cool to be in Chinatown proper. But then I was thinking a lot about the history of Chinatown and realized that it didn’t really end at Vine Street and there are still so many Chinese and Asian-owned businesses that extend past Vine Street. The expressway is just one of the many developments that stole land from Chinatown. I think us taking up the space here is really like a reclamation of land that was stolen from us. Even thinking about places like FACTS, Asian Arts Initiative, and the Chinese Christian Church Annex, those are places that exist in the footprint of what would’ve been the baseball stadium [proposed] in 2000. These are all examples of ways the community has reclaimed land that was almost taken from us and built things that are really nourishing and serving the community.
 Chinatown Development Projects and Proposals Over the Years
 (green were proposed and haven’t happened) 
 Independence Mall, 1950-1967
 Vine Street Expressway, 1957-1991
 The Gallery at Market East, 1977-1983
 Center City Commuter Connection, 1978-1984
 Federal prison, 1992
 Pennsylvania Convention Center, 1993-2011
 Phillies stadium, 2000
 Foxwoods Casino, 2008
 76ers arena, 2023
 Tags: Asian American history Chinatown displacement gentrification Immigrants Sixers Arena 
 About the Author
 Starr Herr-Cardillo is a freelance writer and historic preservation professional working in the nonprofit sector. She holds a master’s degree in historic preservation from the University of Pennsylvania.

title: Center City's Fashion Era: Where Did it Go?
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
If you are of a certain age, and have an eye for fashion, you might recall when the shops on Walnut Street were as exciting as the Avenue Montaigne in Paris. No, really.
 Flash forward to the present. Nan Duskin, Philly's first purveyor of couture fashion, is gone. So are all the dazzling shops that followed in her wake: Toby Lerner, Knit Wit, Plage Tahiti, Max Mara, Burberry, Coach, and others, along with the city's last elegant department store, Bonwit Teller. Of the multitude of shops that carried designer fashions during that era, only two are still thriving: Sophy Curson at 221 S. 19th Street and Joan Shepp 1811 Chestnut Street. I wanted to know why.
 Sophy Curson's still flaunts its midcentury flair at 221 S. 19th Street. | Photo: Howard Silverman
 "We are a family business and we had this store built in 1951," said David Schwartz, a third generation owner of Sophy Curson which first opened by Schwartz's great aunt in 1929. The store was designed by architect Beryl Price and, according to a 2019 nomination for the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places , it "personified mid-20th century Modernism and stood out among more traditional architecture of the Rittenhouse Square neighborhood… and exhibits sleek new materials and glassy open asymmetrical storefront with a pedestrian entrance framed by beige Roman brick." Unique for both its time and present day is the store's name, presented as a signature in cursive gold font. If you are a fan of mid-century modern architecture, this building is a classic.
 Schwartz credits the store's longevity to owning the property. "Many of the other boutiques in the neighborhood rented and, at a certain point, they had to leave when rents increased," he said. According to Schwartz, that was also the fate of Nan Duskin. Born Anna Dushkin (anglicized to Duskin), a Jewish Lithuanian immigrant with a 6th grade education, Duskin got her start as a stock girl for Bonwit Teller. "She was very intelligent and connected with her customers as a buyer at the Blum Store in the 1920s," said Clare Sauro, director & chief curator of the Robert & Penny Fox Historical Costume Collection at Drexel University. "This allowed her to partner with a young woman of means in 1926 to open the Nan Duskin shop in early 1927. Fashion/retail was one of the only career paths for women at the time, and you didn't need a lot of money to set up a small shop."
 An advertisement for Nan Duskin from 1957. | Image: Ebay
 By then, Duskin, who now went by "Nan," had married August A. Lincoln, a banker, and lived with him at the Warwick, a stone's throw from her shop at 18th and Sansom Streets. "Mrs. Lincoln weathered the storm of the Great Depression and flourished when others failed–a testament to her unerring eye, understanding of Philadelphia's social elite, and confidence in her own abilities," Sauro explained.
 Ultimately, Duskin purchased three houses on what had been prime real estate before the Depression, 1723-29 Walnut Street, and converted them into Philly's premiere luxury department store. Women traveled from across the country and around the world to shop at Nan Duskin, including Princess Grace Kelly, who left her castle in Monoco to shop on Walnut Street.
 A Bonnie and Clyde inspired fashion shoot from 1968 showcasing Nan Duskin and John Wanamaker clothing. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 A brilliant businesswomen, Duskin didn't just go to Paris couture shows as a buyer. She also copied their designs for her own label. She knew her customers personally–wealthy matrons who never looked at price tags. Duskin believed that fashion history should be taught at universities and gave lectures at Drexel University's School of Fashion Design. "After she retired, Duskin partnered with the curator of the Drexel's Historic Costume Collection to build our collection, personally soliciting current and former clients to donate to us," said Sauro. "There is a Nan Duskin label, or connection due to her efforts, on many of our very best pieces dating from the 1950s-1990s."
 In 1956, the Nan Duskin storefront was renovated with a marble and limestone facade and a three-story bronze entrance that created the illusion of entering a museum or cathedral. Three years later, Duskin sold her store at the zenith of its success. Under new ownership, the business continued to thrive through the 1970s and opened two branches on the Main Line. However, in 1989 a new set of owners made a fatal move. They relocated Nan Duskin from Walnut Street to a 30,000 square foot space inside the newly-opened Rittenhouse Hotel.
 The three buildings at 1723-29 Walnut Street was once owned and occupied by Nan Duskin. | Photo: Howard Silverman
 Unable to pay the exorbitant rent, the business went belly up the following year. Fortunately, Duskin died before her bespoke fashion emporium became a Borders book store, then Ann Taylor, and finally H&M, as if descending an elevator to the bargain basement of fast fashion. Today, the three properties that comprised Nan Duskin are once again divided. They are currently rented by Madewell, a pricey jean company, and a large retail space that is, for now, boarded up.
 Ann Gitter, another equally industrious female entrepreneur, started Knit Wit in the late 1960s in the former Packard Building at 317 N. Broad Street. Shoppers found her despite the unlikely location. Business eventually grew enough to claim a prime spot at 1729 Chestnut Street with Gitter's other shop, Plage Tahiti, around the corner at 128 S. 17th Street. In 2014, she moved Plage Tahiti's inventory into her Chestnut Street location. After 50 years in business, Gitter closed up all of her shops in Pennsylvania, including one in Bryn Mawr. A Knit Wit store in Margate, New Jersey is still in operation today.
 Meanwhile, since its opening in 1963, Main Liners and other suburbanites have been drawn to the King of Prussia Mall, where Neiman Marcus, Balenciaga, Boss, Burberry, Cartier, and other luxury stores are lined up like slot machines in Las Vegas. While thousands of shopping malls have closed across the nation, it is still impossible to find a parking space at the King of Prussia Mall on a Saturday.
 Aside from the high rents, the advent of malls, and online shopping, nothing hurt the upscale shops of Walnut and Chestnut Streets as much as the May 2020 looting and fires in Center City, which reduced two historic buildings to rubble and resulted in the permeant closure of multiple stores. 
 Joan Shepp at 1811 Chestnut Street. | Photo: Howard Silverman
 Meanwhile, Sophy Curson has managed to remain in one location for 73 years and has been in business for 95. Schwartz believes this is due, in large part, not just to owning the property, but also to being trained as a buyer by his mother. "We have customers who have been coming to us for generations and, sometimes all three generations come at the same time for a family event," he said. "Lately, I have been stocking Tom & Linda Platt dresses. They are very colorful and have beautiful prints."
 Besides Sophy Curson, the only other high end shops to remain in the city are Joan Shepp and Boyd's. Shepp opened her first store in Lafayette Hill in 1971 and relocated to the 1600 block of Walnut Street in 1999 with an eye-popping list of designers, from Stella McCartney to Comme de Garcons. If anyone is the reincarnation of Nan Duskin, it is Joan Shepp. Her shop is the last bastion of unpredictable and unapologetic couture in Philly.
 Following Joan Shepp's locations is like reading the tea leaves of Center City real estate. She started on Walnut Street, briefly hopped over to Liberty Place, and is now at 1811 Chestnut Street, which she runs with her daughter Ellen. According to rumors, Shepp may someday come back to Walnut Street. Will that spark a resurgence of upscale, independent stores owned by women? One can only hope.
 Tags: Center City retail history 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: Parker Administration Orders Historical Commission Appointees to Reject Roundhouse Designation
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on November 8, the Philadelphia Historical Commission added six new properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, but denied the long-awaited designation of the former Police Administration Building , also known as the Roundhouse, at 700-734 Race Street.
 The Police Administration Building after it was vacated in 2022. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 The meeting began routinely, with the Historical Commission reviewing three requests for continuance. What was not routine was its denial of one of those requests to delay considering the nomination of the Roundhouse for three more months to allow the several new Commission members to review the large amount of material associated with it. Those materials included the City’s own reports on its 10-month public engagement project, “ Framing the Future of the Roundhouse ,” which recently won a Core Values award from the International Association for Public Participation USA. The three-month continuance, requested by the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, was denied in a surprise move by members of the Historical Commission.
 The nomination of the Roundhouse, submitted in December 2022 by Docomomo US/Greater Philadelphia and the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, proposed including it on the Philadelphia Register based on six qualifying criteria. Designed and built between 1959 and 1962 by Philadelphia architectural firm Geddes Brecher Qualls & Cunningham and engineer August Komendant, whose work made significant contributions to Philadelphia and beyond, it is a distinctive example of Expressionist (né Brutalist ) architecture and precast concrete use in buildings that represents major innovations at the time.
 An old Portland Cement print advertisement from the 1960s acquired from Ebay showcases the Police Administration Building and its precast concrete panels. | Image courtesy of Michael Bixler
 The building exemplifies the progressive era of the late 1950s and 1960s in Philadelphia under Mayors Joseph Clark and Richardson Dilworth, which strove to make City government in general and the Philadelphia Police Department specifically more open to and supportive of the community. Today, it remains an established and familiar visual feature of its neighborhood and the city. The nomination specifically excluded the adjoining 1.3-acre parking lot, leaving it free for development.
 Ian Litwin of the Department of Planning and Development, gave an overview of the public engagement effort , for which he served as project manager. It summarized the participants’ recommendations in four areas: removal of the surrounding concrete wall (not a part of the original building), acknowledge its past, incorporate youth programs on site, and continue to include public engagement in its redevelopment. Many respondents noted they had been unaware of the original intent of the building, and it reinforced their desire to use it for community benefit.
 An aerial view of the Police Administration Building in 1962. Despite urban legend, the building was not designed to look like handcuffs. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 In addition to over 90 previously submitted supportive comments, more were heard at the meeting, from numerous public attendees as well as the architects and historians on the Historical Commission. New Commission Chair Zachary Frankel, a real estate developer, claimed the building is “largely unusable” with a deteriorated and outdated interior. Others objected to Frankel's cursory conclusion that did not include any sort of research or studies. Moreover, supporters pointed out that this designation would only apply to the exterior, which, by all accounts, is in very good condition.
 The Roundhouse's sculptural wave. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The tie vote was largely along representational lines, with developer Frankel joining the City department designees in voting “no.” When Historical Commission voting falls along representational lines, there is usually an obvious, but unspoken reason. Historian David Brownlee, a former, long-time Commission member, once pointed out to Hidden City , “It was the case that City appointees were not uncommonly asked to support the interests of the mayor. If the mayor wants something, they are not placed there to express their own opinions.”
 At this meeting, that was confirmed by Donna Carney, designee of the Philadelphia City Planning Commission, who prefaced her vote by stating, “It’s the position of this administration to not support this nomination, so, as a designee of the Planning Commission, I vote no.”
 According to City’s intention as indicated in “Framing the Future of the Roundhouse,” the next step presumably would be an RFP from the City for redevelopment of the site. Under Mayor Cherelle Parker's administration, demolition of the internationally recognized Modernist landmark will likely be included in future plans.
 The Diamond Theater in North Philadelphia. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The six approved designations represented a range of property types. The former Diamond Theatre at 2117-23 Germantown Avenue in North Philadelphia, currently known as the Iglesia Ministerio Maranatha Pentecostal, was approved owing to its Classical Revival style and terracotta ornamentation. Built in 1922, its tenure as a Spanish-language theatre was significant in the social history of Philadelphia’s Puerto Rican community.
 The Convent of St. Therese of the Child Jesus at 6633 Ardleigh Street in East Mt. Airy was also designated. The architectural firm of Gleeson & Mulrooney designed it for the Sisters of St. Joseph in 1941 in the Jacobean Revival style along with many other Archdiocese buildings in the mid-20th century in Philadelphia's outer neighborhoods and suburbs. It represents the heritage of its community, the Little Flower Parish.
 Another religious building, at 34-36 East Sharpnack Street , currently the Sanctuary Church of God in Christ, was added to the local register. Built around 1896, it is the historic site of Grace Baptist Church and is associated with three significant figures: Rev. Dr. Jeremiah Alvesta Wright, Sr. (1909-2001), his wife, Dr. Mary Elizabeth Henderson Wright (1916-2005), and their son, Rev. Dr. Jeremiah Alvesta Wright, Jr. (1941-present). The building also represents an important period of African American community history in Germantown and Mt. Airy, when Grace Baptist Church expanded from a local congregation to having regional and national influence.
 The G. Harry and Mary E. Davis House in East Mt. Airy. | Photo: Philadelphia Historical Commission
 A private residence was approved for designation. The house at 40 W. Tulpehocken Street in Germantown, known as the G. Harry and Mary E. Davis House, was designed by architect Charles F. Collom in the Queen Anne style in 1887.
 The property at 8527-29 Germantown Avenue , built for the Chestnut Hill office of the Germantown Trust Company, was designated owing to its Colonial Revival features. Constructed in 1927 by Arthur H. Brockie, a prominent local architect of the first half of the 20th century, it reflects the environment of Chestnut Hill and Germantown during that time.
 The former headquarters of the Union Republican Club in Center City. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 While those designations were unanimously approved, the final successful designation at 1039 Chestnut Street met with some opposition. It had served as the headquarters of the Union Republican Club from 1878 to 1901 and for the Republican City Committee until 1934, a time of notorious corruption in Philadelphia. Designed and built by the firm Yarnall & Cooper in 1878, its brickwork facade represents a 19th century eclecticism and makes it a prominent feature of the neighborhood. On the National Register of Historic Places it is listed as contributing to the historic district.
 The owner for the past 40 years and a consultant argued that the building is in poor condition, has been altered, and, as an emblem of an infamous period in Philadelphia political history, should not be celebrated. The majority of the Historical Commission, however, voted to designate the building based on its architecture and history.
 The Historical Commission approved the demolition of a structure within the Main Street Manayunk Historic District . The building at 11 Shurs Lane is a remnant of the C.O. Struse and Sons Coal Company, which was the site of a major fire in 1959, resulting in a condemnation and subsequent demolition of parts of the complex over the years.
 Owners of 11 Shurs Lane plan to demolish remains of the C.O. Struse and Sons Coal Company and redevelop the parcel with residential construction. | Photos: Google Street VIew and designblendz
 The historic district, the City’s first, was created in 1983 by Philadelphia City Council, rather than the Historical Commission. It was designated without an inventory of properties and was subject to a different set of codes, which can make decisions concerning demolitions and new construction problematic. The Historical Commission relies on the Main Street Manayunk National Register Historic District inventory, but that often includes buildings that no longer exist.
 The owner proposes to erect a mixed-use building four stories tall with 42 residential units, 37 parking spaces, and first-floor commercial space with entrance on Shurs Lane. The designs incorporate materials from the original structure’s remaining wall into the new construction’s facade.
 Tags: Brutalism Historic theaters Historical Commission Meeting Report Mayor Cherelle Parker modernism Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Police Administration Building 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Northwest Apartments Historic District Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on January 10, the Philadelphia Historical Commission spent much of the time reviewing the designation of a new thematic historic district. It also considered requests for alterations to historic properties and commented on nominations to the National Register of Historic Places.
 The Northwest Philadelphia Apartments Thematic Historic District comprises 30 properties near the Chestnut Hill West SEPTA Regional Rail Tulpehocken, Upsal, Carpenter, and Richard Allen Lane stations in Germantown and Mount Airy. The Philadelphia Register of Historic Places includes individual designations for four of the properties, while three are on the National Register.
 Cresheim Valley Apartments at 7200-04 Cresheim Road were built in 1914 and designed by Henry DeHoff. The featured postcard shows the apartment complex shortly after its completion in 1914. | Photos: Michael Bixler and West Mt. Airy Neighbors
 Embodying characteristics of several architectural styles, including Tudor Revival, Colonial Revival, Neoclassical, Italian Renaissance, Beaux Arts, and Art Deco/Moderne, many of these buildings differ from more urban apartment complexes. Their inclusion of suburban-like features such as lawns and landscaped courtyards are blended together with the tree-lined streets of the neighborhood. Built between 1910 and 1940, they transformed the area into a suburban-like, middle-class enclave.
 The Historical Commission approved the designation in a roll call vote of 10 to one after hearing public comments in favor of the nomination and objections from owners of two buildings within the proposed district.
 1927 Diamond Street, designed by Willis G. Hale, and adjoining empty lots. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 A revised proposal for three new buildings within another historic district was also reviewed. The Diamond Street Historic District was created in 1986 and features a collection of large post-Civil War Victorian houses along Diamond Street between Broad and Van Pelt Streets. The proposed sites are currently all vacant lots along the 1900 block. One was demolished before designation, while the other two were taken down after designation, despite one, attributed to Willis G. Hale, being listed as significant and the other as contributing to the historic district. After weighing in on various design elements, the Historical Commission approved the proposal .
 Yet another historic district was on the agenda with the nomination of the Hahnemann Medical College and Hospital Complex Historic District to the National Register of Historic Places. These nominations are overseen by the appropriate state agency, in this case, the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission (PHMC). In the process, PHMC is required to solicit comments from the appropriate local government, which in turn must also provide a forum for public comment. The Historical Commission speaks on behalf of the City of Philadelphia in historic preservation matters including the review of National Register nominations. Within its meetings the Commission provides an opportunity for the public to weigh in.
 The Gothic entrance to Hahnemann Hospital on Broad Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Historical Commission offered comments on the collection of Hahnemann buildings, which occupy the block located at 225-31 North 15th Street and 216-48 North Broad Street. Contributing buildings include the Hospital Building (1928 South Tower/1979 North Tower addition), the New College Building (1938/1970), the Nurses’ Residence (1963), the Myer Feinstein Polyclinic Building (1908/1967), and the Bobst Building (1967). Much of the complex was included in the local register in 2021 and 2022 , which focused primarily on the 1928 original hospital building and the 1938 Klahr Auditorium.
 The Historical Commission cited the significance of the complex in Philadelphia’s medical history, playing a prominent role in the city for nearly a century, as well as the mid-rise and high-rise towers that represent popular architectural styles for hospital and educational buildings in the mid- to late-20th century.
 Interstate Storage Warehouse at 3935-61 Germantown Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 A second National Register nomination was for the Interstate Storage Warehouse at 3935-61 Germantown Avenue. The seven-story, reinforced concrete building with a brick facade was designed in 1924 by Moores & Dunford. The architecture firm of became nationally known for its distinctive styles of warehouses, which created an important visual feature of the urban landscape in the United States and Canada in the early 20th century. The building is currently not listed on the local register therefore it is not legally protected. Historical Commission members offered comments in support of the nomination.
 Tags: historic district Historical Commission Meeting Report Northwest Philadelphia Philadelphia Historical Commission Willis G Hale 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: A Song of Survival and Loss
author: Starr Herr-Cardillo
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Sun Ra, the visionary jazz artist and Afrofuturist movement founder, famously said, “In order to save the Earth, I had to go to the worst spot on the planet, and that was Philadelphia, which was death’s headquarters.” Jazz fans who know and love the city have embraced the sentiment, which inspires the same brand of defiant underdog pride as the famous billboard that proclaimed, “ Philadelphia isn’t as bad as Philadelphians say it is. ”
 “Death’s headquarters” or not, Philadelphia has historically been an indisputably important epicenter for music, particularly jazz, and Sun Ra’s legacy is a distinctive part, along with artists like Bessie Smith, The Roots, and Boyz II Men. Part of Philadelphia’s musical distinction, said Jack McCarthy, the consulting archivist for The Philly Jazz Legacy , is that it has contributed truly “transformative figures” in so many different genres over centuries. He also noted that the sheer diversity of its musical contribution is so wide-ranging, from classical to jazz, rock and roll, gospel, and R&B.
 A uncredited publicity photo of Sun Ra for the 1973 Magic City reissue.
 Like virtually all of American music history, Philadelphia’s story is inextricably linked to Black artists and Black history. Groundbreaking African American artists from Philadelphia, like Francis “Frank” Johnson, an exceptionally talented composer and instrumentalist in the 19th century, were major figures in early American music. Johnson and his band of free Black musicians were the first American musicians to tour Europe. Marian Anderson, whose former home is now a National Historic Landmark and museum, faced racial discrimination in her hometown, but was invited to sing at the White House by Eleanor and President Franklin D. Roosevelt.
 Unfortunately, Sun Ra’s classification of Philadelphia as “death’s headquarters” may have been somewhat prophetic, at least when it comes to the survival of the venues that once brought in and fostered all of this musical talent and collaboration. Today, Philadelphia’s surviving musical landmarks aren’t particularly centralized. There’s no defined entertainment strip like you’d find in other major American music cities like Nashville, Memphis, or New Orleans. And, unfortunately, scores of the incredible venues that used to be clustered around thoroughfares like South Street, Ridge Avenue, and 52nd Street, which saw the likes of Billie Holiday, Duke Ellington, Clifford Brown, and Dizzy Gillespie, have already been lost.
 “If you go to New Orleans, or Memphis, or Nashville, the celebration and promotion of musical heritage as a key part of their tourism and hospitality industries is striking,” said McCarthy. “I just think that Philadelphia, whose musical legacy is incredibly rich and as important as those other cities, doesn’t do a good job of promoting that in a coordinated, efficient or effective way.”
 Watercolor portrait of Francis Johnson, date and artist unknown. | Image courtesy of The New York Public Library
 The preservation of music doesn’t solely rely on the tangible survival of buildings, though. It lives on in recordings and through influences picked up and carried forth by current and future artists and, in that sense, the legacy of Philadelphia-based musicians has been wide-reaching. Many physical structures connected to parts of the story in Philadelphia do remain, from long-standing institutions like the Metropolitan Opera House or the Academy of Music, to the former residences of famous musicians who were born in or made Philadelphia their home, like John Coltrane and Billie Holiday.
 While we may not have a Music Row or Beale Street, there are plenty of stories to be told through the remaining built environment. Three relatively recent additions to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places attest to the rich and varied music history through a variety of building types: the home of Sister Rosetta Tharpe, Sigma Sound Studios, and the former residence and current studio space of Sun Ra and the Sun Ra Arkestra. All have been listed in the past four years for their connection to music history.
 Sister Rosetta Tharpe House, Designated May 11, 2022 
 From 1962 to 1973, the modest brick rowhouse at 1102 Master Street was home to Sister Rosetta Tharpe, the “godmother of rock ’n roll.” Tharpe, who was born in Cotton Plant, Arkansas in 1915, rose to fame after years of singing gospel music in churches with her mother throughout the 1920s and 1930s. The musical prodigy began singing at the age of four and became known for her singing and distinctive style on the electric guitar. She is credited with inspiring several rock and roll megastars throughout her career, including Elvis Presley, Little Richard, Eric Clapton, Keith Richards, and Johnny Cash.
 Sister Rosetta Tharpe playing “Didn’t It Rain?” at the Charlton Train Station, Manchester, England, 1964. Photographer unknown. Inset: 1102 Master Street in Yorktown, where Tharpe lived from 1962 to 1973.
 Tharpe’s career took off in the late 1930s when her performances at the Cotton Club in Harlem were met with critical acclaim. Shortly after at age 23, she recorded her first songs for Decca Records. Her distinctive style had a growing audience outside of the church-going crowd, and she became one of the first commercially successful gospel artists. In 1938, Tharpe was invited to perform at Carnegie Hall in a concert dedicated to Bessie Smith intended to showcase the history of African American music to a predominantly white audience as a means to bring about social change. The show, “From Spirituals to Swing,” was presented by producer and talent scout John Hammond.
 In 1959, Tharpe and her husband, Russell Morrison, moved to Philadelphia, settling in their Yorktown home in 1962 where they lived until her death in 1973. During this time, Tharpe continued to perform and record, touring in Europe with Muddy Waters. She also regularly sang at the Bright Hope Baptist Church down the street from her home. Her former residence is marked with a historical marker, erected in 2011, and was added to the Philadelphia Register in 2022.
 Sigma Studios, Designated November 13, 2020 
 Sound engineer Joe Tarsia’s Sigma Sound Studios, the birthplace of Philadelphia’s eponymous music style, churned out dozens of hits that defined “Philly Soul” since its opening in 1968. The unassuming yellow brick building at 210-212 N. 12th Street was the headquarters for Philadelphia International Records, founded by Kenny Gamble and Leon Huff, who, along with Thom Bell, produced hits like “If You Don’t Know Me by Now” by Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes and “Me and Mrs. Jones” by Billy Paul. The studio’s in-house band, MFSB (Mother Father Sister Brother), contributed to the distinctive sound and style. The Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia sponsored the successful nomination of Sigma Sound’s headquarters to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2020. The nomination elaborates on the studio’s significance: “Just as soul music in the 1960s was synonymous with Motown Records in Detroit, Stax Records in Memphis and the Muscle Shoals sound of Fame Studios, Philadelphia in the 1970s became the undisputed center of the soul music pantheon, with Sigma Studios its primary center of production.”
 MFSB, or Mother Father Sister Brother, the studio musicians for Sigma Sound Studios, where dozens of Top 10 hits were recorded | Photo by Don Hunstein ca early 1970s. Inset: 210-212 S. 12th Street in Center City
 Although the exact future use of the former studio remains in limbo, the audio archives of Sigma Sound Studios live on in the archives of Drexel University. When Sigma closed, thousands of tapes ended up in a storage unit in New Jersey and, fortunately, eventually made their way to the university’s archive. “Any archive is full of stories, waiting to be had,” Toby Seay, the director of Drexel’s University Audio Archives, told a PBS reporter on a tour of the collection. The tapes reveal parts of the recording process, including isolated instrumental tracks, early versions of well-known songs, the progression of musicians learning songs, and even music that never made it out of the studio. Seay and students working in the archives have digitized thousands of tracks and have resurrected the music of a band called the Nat Turner Rebellion, who recorded at Sigma, but never released an album. A Drexel class was able to find the publishers and strike a deal to produce the never-before-heard record on their label Mad Dragon Records using the master tapes from their recording sessions at the studio. The album, Laugh to Keep from Crying , was released in 2019.
 Sun Ra House, Designated March 12, 2022 
 The designation of the Sun Ra House at 5626 Morton Street in Germantown was a strategic move, in part prompted by a partial collapse a year earlier. Members of the band have been living and rehearsing in the space since the 1960s, and the current Sun Ra bandleader, 100-year-old Marshall Allen, took over the house after Sun Ra’s death in 1993 and still lives there today. The three-story Second Empire rowhouse, bought in 1964 by Nathan and Henrietta Allen (parents of Marshall Allen), is clad in Wissahickon schist, a typical row for the neighborhood. Shortly after the collapse, a jazz philanthropist stepped in to fund the necessary repairs. The designation of the house to the Philadelphia Register was supported by the band and celebrated widely by news outlets and music blogs.
 Sun Ra and His Arkestra at Balloon Theatre, Cairo, 1971. | Photo: Hartmut Geerken. Inset: 5626 Morton Street in Germantown, which is still home to members of the Sun Ra Arkestra.
 Sun Ra (born Herman Poole Blount) displayed musical talent as a young child and spent his youth composing and performing music. He began studying music education in college but dropped out after having a vision that would change the trajectory of his life. He believed he had traveled to Saturn and spoken with aliens and that his new life’s mission was to speak through music. Blount spent several years playing and performing in Chicago, where he connected with radical African American political organizers and became a fixture of the avant-garde jazz scene. He and his band would wear over-the-top science fiction-inspired costumes while performing, incorporating electronic instruments into their arrangements.
 In 1952, Blount changed his name to Le Sony’r Ra, and by 1961 he and his Arkestra had moved to New York City, where they lived communally. The living arrangement allowed the flexibility for spontaneous rehearsals, something that continued at the house on Morton Street, where several band members lived from 1968 to 1993. Sun Ra became a defining Philadelphia band, performing locally, often for free in a park near their home, on WXPN radio, and in clubs across the city. Sun Ra’s legacy has become clearer with distance, and the influence of his music and philosophy still resound from Morton Street to the rings of Saturn.
 Deciphering Philadelphia’s musical heritage may take some effort and intention, but McCarthy and others who are passionate about music history, like Faye Anderson of the place-based nonprofit All That Philly Jazz, The Philadelphia Sound Preservation Project, and Ars Nova Workshop, do their best to bring those stories to life through preservation, shows, tours, written histories, and other creative projects that bring these sites to life.
 1. Billie Holiday, 1409 Lombard Street 
 Known as “Lady Day,” she was called the greatest jazz vocalist of her time. Starting in 1933, she recorded with Benny Goodman, Teddy Wilson, and others. Notable songs include “Lover Man” and “Strange Fruit.” In this city, she often lived here.
 2. The Dixie Hummingbirds, 2435 N. College Avenue 
 A renowned African American gospel vocal group originally formed in 1928, members received a National Endowment for the Arts Heritage Fellowship in 2000. They influenced popular musicians, including James Brown, Stevie Wonder, and The Temptations. Their version of Paul Simon’s “Loves Me Like a Rock” won a Grammy award in 1974. Founder James B. Davis (1916-2001) lived in this home, which served as the group’s headquarters.
 3. Elizabeth Taylor Greenfield, 1013 Rodman Street 
 Greenfield, who lived here, was one of the 19th century’s leading singers, known as the “Black Swan” because of her great vocal range. Her performances were hailed in the United States and in England where she sang before the queen.
 4. Francis Johnson, 536 Pine Street 
 “America’s first native-born master of music” lived here. Johnson was a prolific African American composer, trumpeter for the 1st Troop, City Cavalry, and bandmaster for the 128th Regiment, Pennsylvania, Volunteer Infantry. He was a major force in early American music and traveled widely.
 5. John Coltrane, 1511 N. 33rd Street 
 A pioneering African American jazz musician, composer and saxophonist Coltrane used African and Indian elements to create a distinctive style, which at first shocked audiences, but ultimately gained wide acceptance. He lived here from 1952 to 1958.
 6. Lee Morgan, 52nd and Chancellor Streets 
 Jazz trumpeter, composer, and key performer of hard bop, Morgan joined the Dizzy Gillespie band and played with Art Blakey and John Coltrane. As a bandleader, he cut more than 30 albums and is known for “The Sidewinder,” a crossover pop hit and jazz standard. He performed here at the Aqua Lounge.
 7. Marian Anderson, 1910 Fitzwater Street 
 World-renowned contralto, Anderson sang in this church as a child. She toured Europe and the U.S. starting in the 1930s. Her concert at the Lincoln Memorial in 1939 drew 75,000 people. She was the first African American in the Metropolitan Opera in 1955. She was a delegate to the United Nations in 1958. She died in 1993.
 8. Paul Robeson, 4951 Walnut Street 
 A Rutgers athlete and Columbia law graduate, Robeson won renown as a singer and actor. He was a noted interpreter of Negro spirituals. His career suffered because of his political activism, and he lived his last years here in retirement.
 9. Pearl Bailey, 1946 N. 23rd Street 
 Bailey, who lived here in her youth, became one of America’s most prominent entertainers. She sang with the big bands during the 1940s and gained her greatest fame in the 1967 Broadway production of “Hello, Dolly!”
 10. Sigma Sound Studios, 212 N. 12th Street 
 Established in 1968 by Joseph Tarsia, Sigma was known worldwide for its distinctive sound and recording innovations. Hits by The O’Jays, Stylistics, and others produced at 212 N. 12th Street by Gamble, Huff, and Bell drew top recording artists such as David Bowie and Stevie Wonder.
 11. Sister Rosetta Tharpe, 1102 Master Street 
 One of gospel music’s first crossover superstars, Tharpe popularized the genre by including secular music elements. A guitar virtuoso and charismatic performer throughout America and Europe, she toured with Count Basie, Cab Calloway, and Benny Goodman. Her home was here.
 Tags: African-American history Philadelphia music history 
 About the Author
 Starr Herr-Cardillo is a freelance writer and historic preservation professional working in the nonprofit sector. She holds a master’s degree in historic preservation from the University of Pennsylvania.

title: Documenting Building Ghosts and the Stories They Contain
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
There exist all kinds of visual evidence of Philadelphia’s deep history: preserved and reconstructed colonial buildings, adaptively reused commercial properties, and abandoned sites. And then, there is evidence seen through the lens of an absence. Referred to as “building ghosts,” they occur when a building that is conjoined to another is demolished, leaving outlines of its structure on the remaining building.
 “That’s part of the dynamic here,” noted historian Molly Lester, associate director of the Urban Heritage Project at the University of Pennsylvania Weitzman School of Design. “Rowhouses are built adjacent to each other, so they leave a ghost when one is removed.”
 Lester partnered with Michael Bixler, editorial director and chief photographer of Hidden City, in documenting some of Philadelphia's building ghosts in a new book, Building Ghosts: Past Lives and Lost Places in a Changing City, published by Temple University Press.
 In late 2020, Lester and Bixler searched the city, discovering scores of building ghosts. It was an ideal pandemic project, documentation done while solitary and outdoors. “We’d go out separately, scouring different sections of the city,” said Bixler. “With the pause on construction, it gave us more time to document them in our survey. Once building projects restarted, it was a race against time.”
 The resumption of construction activity could yield a never-ending supply of building ghosts, so the authors gave themselves two limitations. “We decided to keep from going back to revisit ghosts,” recalled Bixler. And, they set a four-month limit to their work collecting the visual documentation. “I acknowledge there is an arbitrariness to this four-month period,” said Lester. “We had to invent a time frame to bracket it.”
 “I would begin photo documentation in the morning. Because our survey was so vast and spanned the entire city, I had to hustle quite a bit," explained Bixler. “But I took plenty of time to consider how the sun hit each address, ideal framing, and how to capture not just the ghost, but often the entire building and a bit of the neighborhood for nuanced urban context.”
 1025 Buttonwood Street, 2020 | Photo: Michael Bixler
 While Lester and Bixler didn’t coin the term “building ghost,” they did create “legacy ghost” to describe one that has been on view for a long time, and will likely remain so, as opposed to one that only appears briefly before new construction starts. They also came up with the classification “double ghost,” where a missing rowhouse leaves a ghost on the side of both of its neighbors.
 The duo found the most ghosts in North Philadelphia. Many there are legacy ghosts, whereas in Center City and Fishtown they tend to get built over rapidly, owing to the difference between neighborhoods that have experienced disinvestment versus those where there is more real estate development and gentrification. Bixler spent roughly a month photographing building ghosts in North Philly.
 Another geographic difference appeared as an underrepresentation in the Northeast and Northwest sections of the city. “Northeast Philly's building stock is too young to be considered replaceable,” explained Lester. “And Northwest Philadelphia has so few ghosts because density is a factor in leaving a building ghost, and there, buildings were constructed with more space around them.”
 2323 N. 10th Street, 2020 | Photo: Michael Bixler
 As Bixler focused his lenses on their subjects, his thoughts went beyond just capturing the perfect photograph. “I was trying to dignify each ghost and their adjoining buildings. In a way, I wanted to treat them with emotional care,” he said. “We wanted to separate ourselves from ruin porn.”
 “A larger theme is our attitude about the disposability of these places, but there was a tension and a risk of voyeurism,” agreed Lester, who had her own methods of creating that separation. As a historian, she wanted to document the stories of some of the lives those buildings had contained.
 “I used the same resources as for higher profile buildings: newspaper articles, aerial photographs, city directories, deed abstracts,” she said. “You could find these threads that would tell stories. Sometimes I’d find a lot, or nearly the whole history of the house, and sometimes just one person.”
 1801-03 Fairmount Avenue, 2020 | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The stories range from the amusing, like the tall undertaker who wrote a letter to the editor of the Philadelphia Inquirer railing against the War Production Board’s mandate on how long coffins could be during World War II, to the poignant, learning about a family that experienced the deaths of their children, with each buried in different cemeteries. “It carries an additional responsibility because they didn’t ask for these internal aspects of their lives to be exposed,” Lester noted. “There is a risk of over exposure. I hope I did it justice.”
 Of the nearly 200 building ghosts that Bixler photographed, a final 120 are represented in the book with 40 of them receiving Lester’s historical essays.
 A planned book launch event at the headquarters of architectural firm KieranTimberlake led to the creation of a companion Building Ghosts exhibit. Curators Sarah Kaizar and Huwayda Fakhry interpret some of the photography and essays from the book through an installation that incorporates video, printed scrims, and 400 pounds of reclaimed material from Revolution Recovery, a construction and demolition waste recycling company in Northeast Philadelphia. The exhibition is currently on view at the Bottling House, named for the former Ortlieb’s Brewery building the firm occupies at 841 North American Street, through April 4.
 1935 Diamond Street, 2020 | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The authors feel their book is a timely project and will appeal to both a narrow and a broad audience. “At first, we were going to have a website,” recalled Bixler. “The idea of a book was always there, but we weren’t sure if an editor would get it.”
 “I intentionally avoided jargon that an academic audience might use,” noted Lester. “There is a growing cross section of people who care about cities and think about cities.”
 “The preservation of old buildings, uncovering the histories of everyday people who don’t usually get covered–the audience for this subject matter is getting larger and more diverse,” added Bixler.
 Molly Lester and Michael Bixler will discuss Building Ghosts: Past Lives and Lost Places in a Changing City at the Athenaeum of Philadelphia, 219 S. 6th Street, on January 6, 2025 at 6 p.m. See event details and register here: https://philaathenaeum.org/event-detail/?event_id=25288 
 Tags: book review building ghosts demolition photography rowhouse 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: From Enslaved to Empowered: The True Story Behind One Woman’s Remarkable Legacy
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
Cremona Satterthwaite was a former slave, a landowner, and mother of the five bi-racial grandchildren of the first mayor of Philadelphia. Her family tree grew to include some of the city’s most prominent African American families, including the Montiers and Bustills, as well as the legendary singer, athlete, actor, and activist, Paul Robeson. A new book by Donald Scott Sr., The Montiers: From Enslavement to Paul Robeson and Beyond , takes a deep and wide look into their place in Philadelphia history from Colonial times to the present.
 “Cremona’s story is significant because she had the strength, vision, fortitude, and intellect to navigate a controversial inter-racial relationship, intense racism, and entrenched sexism, leading to generations of trendsetting and illustrious African American families who survive into the 21st century,” Scott explained. 
 Although sources differ on the subject of Cremona’s ancestry, they generally agree that she was born in 1710 and was enslaved in the household of Humphrey Morrey. Maps, documents, and histories of the time variously spelled his last name as Murrey, Morry, and even Merry. He was a successful merchant, appointed by William Penn as the first mayor of Philadelphia, and one of the founders of Cheltenham Township, then part of Philadelphia County. Like many fellow Quakers of the time, Morrey was a slaveholder before The Society of Friends embraced abolition. After his death, his son Richard freed the family’s enslaved, but kept young Cremona on as a maid.
 While Richard was married to his first wife, he and Cremona had a relationship that produced five children between 1735 and 1745. “Despite enduring questions about the exceptionally complicated dynamics of Cremona and Richard’s bond that may have been arguably or partially predicated on a slave–master and/or employee–employer relationship, (one of her descendants) the late Dr. William Pickens III postulated that they likely had a deeply loving and reciprocal relationship,” Scott wrote in his book. On the other hand, he acknowledges, “we likely will never know the exact nature or depth of Cremona’s relationship with Richard,” and wonders if it was consensual and whether Morrey simply felt morally obligated to provide for Cremona and their children.
 Either way, in 1745, Richard ended the relationship and moved to Philadelphia. The next year, at a time when it was unheard-of for a Black woman to own land, he transferred 198 acres in northwest Cheltenham Township to Cremona. Around the time of Richard’s death, Cremona married John Fry, a former slave. “When Richard died, there were very few liberated Black Northern women who were able to gaze across their own land,” wrote Scott. Named after the African homeland of many of its residents, the community of Guineatown grew on part of Cremona’s property that was centered near Limekiln Pike and Waverly Road, currently known as the neighborhood of Edge Hill, in Glenside, Montgomery County.
 Cremona’s older daughter, Elizabeth, married Cyrus Bustill, “a prosperous black businessman.” Her younger daughter, known as Cremona Jr., married John Montier, also formerly enslaved. Two years after Cremona’s death in 1770, the Montiers built a house adjacent to Limekiln Pike that still stands.
 Rich in detail, Scott’s book paints a vivid picture of the African American experience in Philadelphia over the past 350 years. He goes into great detail about the past and lingering dynamics of slavery, sexism, and racism in the City of Brotherly Love, while celebrating Cremona’s legacy through the lives of her descendants and their spouses. These include the original member of the Free African Society and baker who made bread for the Continental Army, successful business owners, educators, artists, activists, a co-founder of the NAACP, and the great Paul Robeson.
 “One thing appears to be certain,” Scott concluded. “Despite questions about the degree to which Richard was in love with or dedicated to Cremona and their children, the couple gave birth to an exceptionally important African American family legacy.”
 Scott is no stranger to researching and writing about African American history. His previous works include Camp William Penn 1863-1865, a detailed history of the first and largest federal training facility for Northern-based Black soldiers , located in Cheltenham, Remembering Cheltenham, and scores of articles for newspapers, magazines, and websites. He has taught writing, history, and literature at Community College of Philadelphia, Cheyney University, Peirce College, and Temple University.
 Scott recently completed the first draft of a book about people of color and others on the RMS Titanic and is currently working on a project focused on his own maternal and paternal family histories dating back to his mother's Gullah Geechee ancestors on 18th century coastal plantations in South Carolina and Georgia.
 “African American history is particularly relevant today considering the adverse political movements attempting to cover up our mighty accomplishments and the often very painful past,” said Scott. “That makes it all the more imperative to keep the illuminating flames of truth glowing so that we as a nation—and frankly the world—can heal by not repeating the horrors and gross mistakes of the past.”
 Tags: African-American history book review Montgomery County Quakers slavery 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: The Sounds of Philly Reverberate Around the World
author: Jack McCarthy
bodyText:
The Met at 858 N. Broad Street. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 In 2026, all eyes will be on Philadelphia as we celebrate the 250th anniversary of the nation’s founding and our city’s pivotal role as the birthplace of American democracy. However, for millions of people around the world who know little to nothing about American history, Philadelphia is known more as an incubator of great music than as the place where the Declaration of Independence was written.
 The city has produced some of the world’s greatest music and musicians: the sublime sonority of the Philadelphia Orchestra, widely considered one of the greatest symphonic ensembles, the timeless appeal of Philly Soul, the sophisticated rhythm and blues style created by songwriter/producers Kenny Gamble, Leon Huff, Thom Bell, and others, the groundbreaking jazz innovations of Dizzy Gillespie, John Coltrane, Lee Morgan and a host of local greats, and the infectious pop rock sounds of Charlie Gracie, Chubby Checker, Bobby Rydell, and other teen idols who came out of Philadelphia in the late 1950s and early 1960s, when the city was one of the nation’s most influential popular music centers. It is no exaggeration to say that Philadelphia music has changed the world.
 The Philadelphia Opera House (now called The Met Philadelphia) received national attention when it opened in 1908. The neoclassical facade and white brick exterior contrasted mightily with the red brick and brownstone houses that neighbored it on North Broad and Poplar Streets. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Philadelphia’s musical prominence began in the late 18th century, when the city was the political and cultural capital of the young United States, attracting the greatest musicians from both America and Europe. These artists created a vibrant musical scene and established traditions that continue to shape American music. At the same time, Philadelphia had the nation’s largest population of free Black people in the 18th century. In the early 20th century it drew hundreds of thousands of African Americans escaping the South as part of the Great Migration. These new arrivals brought their own distinct Southern musical traditions with them. The merging of the various African-and European-derived musical traditions gave rise to an especially rich musical environment, one that produced some of the world’s most beloved, influential music.
 Philadelphia’s record of preserving the sites and structures of this rich musical history is a mixed one, however. There have been notable success stories, to be sure: the Philadelphia Orchestra’s stewardship of its original home, the ornate Academy of Music, which opened in 1857 and is the oldest opera house in America still used as such, concert promoter Live Nation’s 2018 restoration of The Met, the massive Metropolitan Opera House that opened on North Broad Street in 1908 and is now an active concert venue once again, and the adaptive reuse in 1997 by business incubator the Enterprise Center of the former studios of WFIL radio and TV at 46th and Market streets, built in 1948 and home of the enormously popular teen music and dance TV program American Bandstand, which broadcasted nationally from the site from 1957 to 1964.
 The auditorium of the Royal Theater on South Street in 2017. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Yet, for every success story there have been many losses. Dozens of 19th-and early 20th-century concert halls, opera houses, and theaters have been demolished–structures that were a direct link to a time before the advent of recordings and radio, when live performance was the only way to experience music and audiences flocked to such venues for entertainment. In two cases–Musical Fund Hall on Locust Street and the Royal Theater on South Street –we are left with only the facades of buildings that have important stories to tell.
 Musical Fund Hall opened in 1824 and served as the city’s main concert hall until superseded by the Academy of Music in 1857, while the Royal opened in 1920 and was one of the premier venues for Black entertainment in the city into the mid-20th century. Both buildings were on the National Register of Historic Places, but were delisted after their auditoriums–their chief historic features–were replaced by condominiums.
 Uptown Theater at 2240 N. Broad Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Two important sites in Philadelphia Black music currently face uncertain fates: the Uptown Theater on North Broad Street, where legendary DJ Georgie Woods, “the Guy with the Goods,” produced shows from the late 1950s to early 1970s that featured the biggest names in Black music, and the Sigma Sound Studios building on N. 12th Street in Center City, the recording studio where most Philly Soul hits were created.
 The nonprofit Uptown Entertainment & Development Corporation, which owns the long-shuttered Uptown, has ambitious plans for a combined entertainment venue/museum/commercial leasing space. However, some initial fundraising success notwithstanding, it has been unable to raise the millions of dollars necessary. Local music buffs are hoping to do something creative with the Sigma Sound building, but its private owner wants to develop the property. There is better news with the John Coltrane House on N. 33rd Street in Strawberry Mansion, where the legendary saxophonist lived from 1952 to 1958 and where he had a spiritual and musical awakening in 1957 that changed the course of jazz forever. After years of decline and tangled legal issues, there is finally a credible plan to preserve the house and create a museum and cultural arts center around it.
 The Paul Robeson House at 4951 Walnut Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Other area house museums are preserving important Philadelphia musical legacies as well: the Marian Anderson Museum & Historical Society, Paul Robeson House & Museum, and Mario Lanza Institute & Museum. Sadly, despite strong objections from the community, Lanza’s birthplace and childhood home on Christian Street in South Philadelphia was demolished in 2018 for residential development.
 Music is one of Philadelphia’s greatest contributions to the world, a unique part of the city’s heritage that makes it an important cultural center and a special place to live and visit. As we gear up for celebrating the nation’s semiquincentennial, in addition to focusing on places like Independence Hall, let’s also focus on preserving and highlighting the sites and structures of this key part of Philadelphia and American history.
 Tags: African-American history Historic theaters Metropolitan Opera House Philadelphia music history Royal Theater Uptown Theater 
 About the Author
 Jack McCarthy is a longtime Philadelphia archivist and historian who has held leadership positions at several area historical institutions and directed a number of major archives and public history projects. His chief areas of expertise are Philadelphia music history and Northeast Philadelphia history. McCarthy has served as consulting archivist and historian for the Philadelphia Orchestra, Mann Center for the Performing Arts, and Philadelphia Jazz Legacy Project. He regularly writes, lectures and gives tours on Philadelphia music. McCarthy's book "A Century of Music Under the Stars: A History of the Mann Center for the Performing Arts and Robin Hood Dell" will be published by Temple University Press in 2025. McCarthy was president of the Friends of Northeast Philadelphia History for many years and currently directs the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia’s Poquessing Creek Trail of History project, which focuses on the Byberry section of Far Northeast Philadelphia.

title: In Powelton Village, Historic Mansions Keep Up With the Times
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
When we think of wealthy, high society enclaves in Philadelphia the usual suspects come to mind: Rittenhouse Square, Chestnut Hill, and the Main Line. Yet, in the early to mid-19th century, affluent Quakers turned farmland into an enclave of lavish estates in another area. They called it Powelton.
 Shaped like a pie wedge, Powelton is bordered on the north by Spring Garden Street, on the east by the Schuylkill River and along the southwest by Lancaster Avenue. Powelton remains unique with its large collection of authentic Victorian architecture, including early Italianate, Second Empire, Queen Anne, and Colonial Revival. There are even a few buildings that defy classification.
 Mark Brack, who served as the resident architectural historian at Drexel University until his retirement in 2022, has an insider's perspective of how Powelton managed to preserve its architectural heritage. "I have lived in Powelton for 17 years, and I was chair of Powelton Village Civic Association's preservation committee when we campaigned to make our neighborhood part of the Philadelphia Historic Register in 1972," said Brack.
 A block of well-maintained Victorian twins in Powelton Village. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Brack chalks up the success of that campaign to the number of long-term activist community members. "But we all feel endangered," he said. "Powelton is only 14 percent owner-occupied. The rest is owned by landlords who rent to students."
 "Powelton had been a National Register Historic District for decades, but that affords no protection whatsoever," said Brack. "We raised money to hire a professional to create a report and submit it to the Philadelphia Historical Commission . They approved it in 2022 ," he explained. It was the City's largest historic district in almost 20 years, containing 817 buildings. If you want to make changes to a building now or demolish it, you have to go through the City and they will turn you down. I have never lived anywhere with such a sense of civic responsibility."
 While almost every house in Powelton is historic, this article looks into five built in the late 19th century that have been repurposed and well preserved.
 The former home of George Burnham at 3401 Powelton Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 One of the oldest houses, 3401 Powelton Avenue, was built in 1886 for George Burnham, one of the founders of Baldwin Locomotives, the largest manufacturer of steam locomotives in the world. Burnham hired architect Theophilus Parsons Chandler Jr., the founder of the Department of Architecture at the University of Pennsylvania, to design a house that matched his ambition.
 The result was a two-and-one-half story building and a gate house with a cupola of massive stone that combined Romanesque and Gothic with heavy rusticated stone, limestone trim, and a porch arch. The most interesting feature of the building is the use of curved elements.
 Burnham was an early member of the Union League of Philadelphia and the prestigious Powelton Club, a place where power and politics were traded over a game of wisk. His daughter, Mary A. Burnham, a member of the New Century Club, used her family's wealth and influence to become a major contributor to the Pennsylvania suffrage movement, leading a string of 150 women-filled automobiles up Broad Street during the 1916 presidential election.
 The mansion stayed in the Burnham family until the 1930s when, like many Powelton private homes, it became a rental property. According to the 1950 Census, the Burhnam estate became a nursing home that primarily served elderly Jewish immigrants. Even in the early 1960s, when property values tanked and the once-popular shopping areas along Lancaster Avenue were abandoned, Powelton remained a desirable area for students and faculty.
 When Drexel's Lambda Chi Alpha Fraternity moved into the historic Burnham mansion in 1966, no one blinked. By that time Powelton was the center of Philadelphia's counter culture and anti-war movement. By comparison, a frat house was a sign of financial stability. Over the years, the fraternity spent millions of dollars to preserve the mansion's original grandeur.
 The mansion at 216 N. 33rd Street was built for famed beer brewer Frederick A. Poth. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The next industrialist to build an estate in Powelton was Frederick A. Poth, a German-born brewer . By 1875, his brewery was the largest in the United States. In 1887, he commissioned Albert W. Dilks to build a red brick and brownstone German Gothic home with a sweeping bay porch and turrets echoing High Victorian style at 216 N. 33rd Street. Dubbed "the castle on the corner," this four-story mansion containing 16 bedrooms was well-suited to the large extended families of the day which, in Poth's case, included rooms for four servants.
 After Poth's death in 1905, his mansion stayed in the family when one of his daughter's married another German-born industrialist. By 1920, it became a rental property. One of its tenants, Drexel's Dean of Women, made for an easy transition to the property becoming the home of Drexel's Alpha Pi Lamda fraternity in 1939.
 After closing in 2003 due to structural problems, the fraternity launched a large-scale fundraising campaign. The Poth mansion reopened in 2008, functioning as a residence to more than 20 undergrads. 
 Mary Bancroft, a 19th century women's health advocate and the grandmother of painter Maxfield Parrish, lived at 300 Baring Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The same year Poth built his dream house, a two-and-one-half story Victorian twin with elaborately milled porch latticework, turned posts, and balustrades was built for Mary Bancroft at 3300 Baring Street. Bancroft was the widow of Edward Stephen Parrish and the grandmother of artist Maxfield Parrish. The painter visited the home as a child and returned there when he studied at Drexel University. In 1889, Bancroft was a founding member of the West Philadelphia Hospital for Woman, specializing in maternity and obstetrics, which later was absorbed by the University of Pennsylvania.
 The stately home passed through various affluent owners until 1930 when it was bought by a Russian Jewish immigrant. After his death, the deed was passed to the remaining women in the family until 1956. As was the case for many grand Powelton mansion at the time, the massive stone house became a rental property in the 1960s.
 A 1996 ad in the Philadelphia Inquirer described the 100 year-old property as a "Glorious triple-sized, 14 room, stone single family home on corner lot w/ double garage, wrap porch, 4.5 bath, magnificent stained glass windows."
 In 2009, this late 19th century mansion became the Cornerstone Bed and Breakfast. While the massive size, upkeep, and age of the property may have deterred others, it was exactly what Jill Moody had in mind. A Philly native, Moody grew up admiring her grandmother's inn in New Hope, Pennsylvania. Moody doesn't run the B&B by herself. Her parents are working partners and there is an innkeeper. All of the rooms are much the same as when Maxfield Parrish was a student, with high ceilings, large windows, and period furnishings. It's most striking feature is the brightly painted porch latticework that now welcomes guests from across the nation and around the world.
 Max Riebenack, son of Bavarian immigrants and former controller of the Pennsylvania Railroad, built his Gothic mansion at 34th Street and Powelton Avenue in 1888. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 On the southeast corner of 34th Street and Powelton Avenue is yet another beautifully preserved and repurposed Victorian mansion. It was designed in 1888 by architect T. P. Lonsdale for Pennsylvania Railroad magnate Max Riebenack. While we may wince at the solid gold toilets of Mar-a-Lago, there was nothing subtle in the scale or style of this limestone castle with its medieval towers and sheathed turrets with conical red slate-shingled roof and wrap-around porch.
 Riebenack was one of the founders of the Powelton Club, treasurer of the Union League, and a member of Merion Cricket Club, Engineers Club, and the Philadelphia Yacht Club. He occupied the majestic mansion from 1900 with 11 family members, an English butler, a cook, two maids, and a servant.
 Following Riebenack's death, the building was acquired by Drexel University in 1928 and was used for its Domestic Science program with a nursery school on the first floor. In 2001, Drexel converted the mansion into Ross Commons, a student center containing dining areas, the office of the student union, lounges, and meeting rooms and, since 2011, the popular Sabrina's brunch spot. While this conversion updated the interior, much of the exterior appears today as in 1888 with the exception of the enclosure of its former wrap-around porch.
 3709 Baring Street was built for affluent Quakers in 1879. It is now home to the neighborhood's first Black-owned bed and breakfast. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Powelton has always been racially diverse, but it never had a Black-owned B&B until 2018. That is when Brooklyn residents, Glenn Pogue and his wife Monique Greenwood, opened Akwaaba Philadelphia at 3709 Baring Street in a Powelton property that dates back to 1879.
 The couple's goal was to create a space where African American guests could feel comfortable without excluding other cultures. Akwaaba means “welcome” in a dialect spoken in Ghana and is the name of all of the couple's inns, starting with their first one in the Bed Sty section of Brooklyn that they opened in 1995. With Akwaaba B&Bs in Cape May, Washington, D.C., New Orleans, and the Poconos, opening one in Philly completed their collection of luxury inns.
 The original owners of the Baring Street mansion were Quakers. By 1910, the property was owned by a widow who took in boarders. In 1950, it became the Friendship Coop House, a Quaker housing cooperative that still exists today offering affordable housing to low-income community members. In 1999, the home became the Spruce Hill Manor Inn.
 When Greenwood, former editor-in-chief of Essence magazine, first saw the 5,000-square-foot, three-story mansion with a cupola, she recognized its potential. The couple renovated and redecorated its six suites to pay tribute to Philadelphia's Black musical legacy. Meanwhile, original, ornate woodwork, stained glass, and marble fireplaces convey the property's history throughout the inn. In June 2024, Greenwood opened Akwaaba Tea Salon around the corner at 3811 Lancaster Avenue which offers high tea on weekends.
 The author would like to thank the Powelton Village Civic Association for its online historical map and detailed history of every house. 
 Tags: adaptive resuse Powelton Village West Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: Philadelphia's Little-known Black Literary Societies of the 19th Century
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
This illustration featured in a 1839 edition of the American Anti-Slavery Almanac shows a schoolmaster preventing a free Black woman and her two children from entering his institution. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
