 Philadelphia was generally considered a relatively safe place for Black Americans in the decades leading up to the Civil War, yet they were barred from most of the city’s educational and cultural institutions. As a result, many organizations were established by Black residents during this time to address those needs and interests.
 One of the earliest was the Reading Room Society, founded in 1828 by a group of men led by prominent businessman William Whipper, who also co-founded the abolitionist group the American Moral Reform Society. It functioned primarily as a lending library and book discussion club.
 The Philadelphia Library Company of Colored Persons, founded in 1833, fostered literacy and public speaking for its members with lectures, debates, and readings. When the organization formally incorporated three years later, its Christ Church’s Right Reverend Bishop William White, the first Presiding Bishop of the Episcopal Church of the United States following its split from the Anglican Church of England, was an early benefactor who donated books. The library held its meetings in the basement of the African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas at 5th and Adelphi (now St. James Place) Streets. By 1841, its membership had grown from the founding nine men to about 100. Its library contained nearly 600 volumes. A similar organization was the Rush Library Company and Debating Society of Pennsylvania, established just three years later.
 African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas, founded in 1792, was the first Black Episcopal Church in the United States. The Philadelphia Library Company of Colored Persons held meetings in the church's basement in the mid-1800s. | Image: Public Domain
 These early groups were formed by and open to adult men, so alongside them sprang up organizations for women and younger men. In 1831, about 20 women, including Sarah Mapps Douglass, organized the Female and Literary Society of Philadelphia. At their weekly meetings, the group would critique each other's literary writings which were submitted anonymously for review. It was followed a few years later by the creation of the Minerva Literary Association, which focused on recitations of both original and selected works.
 The Young Men’s Union Literary Association was created in 1839, restricting its membership to men between the ages of 18 and 40 “of strict moral character.” One of its founders was John Pierre Burr , a son of Aaron Burr and Mary Emmons, of Haitian background. The organization soon changed its name to the Demosthenian Institute after the ancient Greek orator Demosthenes, signaling their commitment to practicing public speaking through lectures and debates. They also produced a weekly journal, the Demosthenian Shield.
 By 1841, several prominent Black men and women created the Gilbert Lyceum to explore both literary and scientific studies, including Sarah Mapps Douglass and her parents Grace and Robert as well as notable abolitionists Robert and Harriet Purvis .
 1854 saw the establishment of the Alexandrian Institute, which soon changed its name to the Benjamin Banneker Institute of the City of Philadelphia, in honor of the 18th century African American astronomer and scientist Benjamin Banneker. While several of its founding members were men in their late teens and early 20s, women don’t seem to appear in the minutes of the Institute. It was noted, however, that Sarah Mapps Douglass taught evening classes on physiology and hygiene to women at the organization's meetings. William T. Catto was a founding member and his son Octavius V. Catto later served as member and recording secretary. The caterer Henry Minton was a member, donating two books in 1858.
 A Pennsylvania State Historical Marker at at 409 S. 11th Street honors the founding and former location of the Benjamin Banneker Institute. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Membership was open to “any male person of good moral character, and of ordinary literary attainment.” Active members were expected to deliver “an original lecture, essay, poem, or oration before the Institute.” Meetings were held on the second Wednesday of each month at various locations, including Benezet Hall on South 7th Street between Lombard and South Streets. Examples of their discussions included “That the secret practices of vice have a greater influence on a community for evil than the open practices of vice” in June 1858 and “In embracing religion, are men influenced by love to God or fear of punishment?” on July 28, 1858.
 In the group's meeting minutes in May 1858, it was noted that delegates representing the Banneker Institute presented the group’s credentials to the Literary Congress in their hall on the southeast corner of 9th and Spring Garden Streets, but when a vote was taken at a subsequent meeting, they were turned down, learning that three associations had “instructed their delegates to ‘vote against any motion made to admit a colored society.’” Those voting in favor expressed regret to the Banneker delegates and urged them to reapply at a later date. The report noted, “We, however, are of opinion that it would be a compromise of dignity to make an application after having been refused.”
 Members of the Institute also operated the Banneker House, a resort for Black Americans near the beach at Cape May, New Jersey due to the policy of segregation at the shore.
 The Banneker Institute was active until 1872 and is considered the predecessor to the Afro-American Historical Society which Banneker member Robert M. Adger founded in 1879. Today, a historical marker commemorating the organization is at 409 S. 11th Street.
 Tags: abolitionist history African-American history Octavius Catto Robert Purvis 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: What a Long, Strange Trip It's Been: "Getting There" on Philly's Public Transit Roller Coaster
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The year is 1914. Philadelphia's already robust public transportation system is set to grow. The city has 600 miles of electrified streetcar lines running on nearly every major thoroughfare, but that isn't enough for then-Mayor Rudolph Blankenburg, a reformist who took office promising to improve city services like mass transit.
 Upon his inauguration, less than 15 miles of the city's rail services were high-speed, a number dwarfed by New York and Chicago. Yet, Blankenburg's pick for transit director, an experienced railroad executive named A. Merritt Taylor, came up with a plan. It called for an increase to nearly 60 miles of high-speed service, at a cost of more than $1.5 billion in today's dollars, starting with the creation of the Broad Street Subway.
 In a speech at the subway's groundbreaking, Blankenburg promised Philadelphians they would soon be able to travel from one part of the city to any other in less than 30 minutes, all for the cost of a nickel (about $1.50 today). For his part, Taylor likened the city's public transportation network to a human circulatory system and warned that without improvements, the “body as a whole must suffer.”
 New SEPTA trolleys, designed by French firm Alstom, are expected to be delivered by 2027 and will replace all trolleys running on city and suburban lines. | Rendering courtesy of Alstom.
 Here we are a century later and officials with the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority (SEPTA) are warning of an impending “death spiral” for the region's public transportation system. Stricken by the expiration of federal emergency COVID-relief funding and ridership levels that remain below pre-pandemic norms, SEPTA raised fares on December 1 and warned that far harsher increases, along with drastic service cuts, will come. Originally targeting the first half of 2025 for dramatic changes, SEPTA scrapped those plans after Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro in late November flexed $153 million in federal transportation funding to aid the beleaguered agency. However, SEPTA warns that is a fix with a lifespan measured in months, not years. Unless state lawmakers in Harrisburg develop a longer-term solution, the ax continues to hover.
 Why is it so hard to make public transit work in Philadelphia, a dense city where hundreds of thousands of people each day shuttle to and fro on buses and trains? What happened after Blankenburg's speech that led to such decline a century later? Can history tell us anything useful about where we are now and where we're headed?
 After all, as Erick Guerra, professor of city and regional planning at the University of Pennsylvania's Weitzman School of Design pointed out, we have been here before. It was little more than a decade ago that SEPTA was also speaking in apocalyptic terms, releasing “ doomsday maps ” showing dramatic cuts to commuter rail and bus services if more funding wasn't received. “SEPTA has financial crises that come up time and time again, every five to 10 years,” Guerra said. “This is probably the biggest one since 2013.”
 Trains, Pains, and Automobiles 
 Conductors stand by a horsecar at 6th and Jackson Streets in 1894. | Photo courtesy of the Library Company of Philadelphia
 Anyone with a lick of knowledge about transportation modes has likely already surmised, correctly, that the advent of the automobile played a large role in the decline of public transportation over the past 100 years. Yet, the full picture is more complex.
 John Hepp, a retired professor of history at Wilkes University, is a scholar of the history of Philadelphia's public transportation systems . Its lineage can technically be traced all the way to 1688, when a ferry between Philadelphia and what is now Camden established the first fixed-route passenger service accessible to the public. Something resembling our modern system didn't begin to take shape until the mid-19th century.
 In 1832, commuter trains on the Philadelphia, Germantown & Norristown Rail Road began to shuttle passengers along that corridor with stops also in East Falls, Chestnut Hill, and other Montgomery County destinations. In the inner city, what started as private vendors pulling horse-drawn carriages along thoroughfares like Broad, Market, and Chestnut Streets began to modernize not too long after with the rise of the horse-drawn trolley car, explained James Wolfinger, a historian, Dean of St. John's University's School of Education, and author of Running the Rails , a history of labor relations in Philadelphia’s mass transit systems. Laying rails for such trolleys required professionalization. By the late 1850s, horse-drawn streetcars belonging to the Frankford and Southwark Philadelphia City Passenger Railway Company began operating.
 Such streetcar services quickly expanded to other areas of the city. By the time Philadelphia hosted the nation's Centennial Exhibition in 1876, it could boast “one of the finest transportation systems in the country,” Hepp explained. Further modernization occurred in the 1890s, when in just five years, electric trolleys replaced every horse-drawn counterpart (as well as some short-lived cable car lines) in the city and became the ubiquitous mode of transportation for Philadelphia's growing middle class.
 Mayor Samuel Davis Wilson, at left inside the front car, leads a tour with businessmen of the South Broad Street subway extension in 1938. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 Early in the creation of these trolley lines, most owners were small-time outfits operating perhaps just a single line and often named after the street on which it traveled. With money rolling in, larger companies saw an opportunity. By buying up these smaller interests and combining services, they could both make the rider's experience more seamless and, of course, gain market share. By 1902, virtually all of the streetcar lines consolidated under ownership of the Philadelphia Rapid Transit (PRT), a holding company formed by Peter A.B. Widener and William Elkins, and the commuter trains by the Pennsylvania and Philadelphia & Reading systems. However, this era of consolidation was built on a shaky foundation.
 All of those acquisitions left PRT with a lot of sunk costs that it would need to recoup in the decades ahead. By the 1910s, the first motorized buses began to appear in the region and within a decade were replacing trolleys on some routes. While the private passenger car was at first much more a luxurious novelty than a utilitarian vehicle, that of course would change with the advent of mass production.
 For a time, Philadelphia's mass transit kept chugging along and further modernizing. Between 1905 and 1908, the PRT opened the elevated Market Street Subway line, giving the city its first rapid transit line. Yet, by the 1920s signs of financial a nd organizational weakness start to emerge. Public funds began to buttress the system, particularly evident in Philadelphia when City Hall paid to extend the Market Street line to Frankford in 1922 and for the construction of the Broad Street Subway shortly after.
 The major turning point, as for so many other things in American life, came in 1929 with the onset of the Great Depression. In the ensuing years, commuter rail service was curtailed and commuter trolley lines abandoned, either taken over by buses or nothing at all. In 1934, the PRT declared bankruptcy and reemerged as the Philadelphia Transportation Company (PTC) in 1940. World War II brought a short reprieve as ridership rose, but suburbanization and the creation of the highway system in the post-war years further hollowed out public transit's historic revenue base and siphoned off federal transit dollars. Successive companies would take on the city’s transit infrastructure, but none successfully.
 “It's cultural. People want cars. People don't want to be riding around in old fashioned trolleys,” Wolfinger noted, adding that it is a problem compounded by a further transition to buses as the primary form of public transportation. “You can imagine who ends up riding on the bus. Somebody who doesn't have any other options,” he said.
 Three women uses roller skates for transportation in West Philadelphia during a Philadelphia Transportation Company strike in 1953. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 As early as the 1930s, cities across the country began to step in to take control of public transportation systems. Yet, it took until 1964 for Philadelphia to follow suit with the establishment of SEPTA, an intergovernmental agency overseen by a 15-member board composed of appointees from the surrounding counties and the state government.
 At first, there was hope that such efforts might actually be able to make the math work, said Hepp. Earlier in the 20th century, cities such as San Francisco and London had successfully taken over public transit services. If Philadelphia could eliminate the profit motive of private industry and reinvest in services to make transit more attractive, the thinking went, perhaps it could at least break even on regular operations. “That was the dream of SEPTA,” Hepp said.
 However, it never came to pass. Today, public transit systems in the United States remain heavily subsidized. Nationwide, even the most economically-viable transit systems like those found in New York City and San Francisco rely on public subsidies to cover at least 25 percent of their costs and often far more. SEPTA ranks among some of the most dependent of major agencies, according to a 2022 study from the Eno Center for Transportation , with total fares adding up to just about 35 percent of revenues, a number that fluctuates somewhat year-to-year, and the rest of the balance dependent on subsidies. Experts point out that building and maintaining highways also requires public subsidization. It turns out, there is no free ride for anyone in our modern era of transportation.
 A Bumpy Ride for SEPTA 
 Public transportation in Philadelphia, as in many other big cities around the country, hasn't been a profitable enterprise for about a century now. So why, as Philadelphia Inquirer reporter Thomas Fitzgerald pointed out last June , has SEPTA had a demonstrably more tumultuous time than most, including the most transit worker strikes for any operator in the nation over the past six decades?
 "Welcome to Pennsylvania politics," Guerra said. Regional counterparts such as Boston and New York City, along with their suburbs, tend to have outsized influence within state politics, for economic and demographic reasons, he noted. “Three-quarters of residents of Massachusetts are in metropolitan Boston. There are a lot more positive views about public transit,” he explained.
 In Pennsylvania, Philadelphia and Pittsburgh are both geographically, and often culturally, isolated from Harrisburg. “At the end of the day, urban transit is not a priority for most of the Pennsylvania legislature,” said Hepp. “So, how you get urban transit paid for is you come up with a deal.”
 At various times in its history, SEPTA has found a relief valve somewhere, whether that be through federal or state coffers. With federal money drying up and unlikely to turn back on soon under the Trump administration, Hepp suspects Democrats in Harrisburg will have to give ground on something significant in the next legislative session to unlock any lasting fix for SEPTA. “Are they finally going to let Republicans sell off the state stores?” Hepp pondered.
 Final agreements signed in sale of PTC to SEPTA in 1968. Pictured are Albert G. Lyons, president of Philadelphia Transit Company, Mayor James Tate, and James J. McConnon, chairman of SEPTA. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 Regardless of the difficulties of keeping public transit afloat, Wolfinger pointed out that generations of leadership have seen fit to keep the trains running, however meagerly. In the early 1960s, President John F. Kennedy, a transit supporter, found allies in politicians like Philadelphia Mayor Richardson Dilworth, who, in March 1961, testified to Congress in support of a federal mass transit funding bill. Key to Dilworth's lobbying was his assessment that automobile traffic was strangling metropolitan areas like Philadelphia. “Philadelphia has gone about as far as it can on its own to preserve the high-speed transit and commuter railroads,” Dilworth testified. Meanwhile, New Jersey Senator Harrison A. Williams, Jr. told the committee that an over reliance on highways had led cities to conclude that congestion was striking “at the jugular vein of their economic capability, choking central city commerce and business.”
 While pleas to Washington for a time sufficed, with every president from Kennedy to Carter supporting some form of robust financial assistance for public transportation, it was never enough to fully rebuild the nation's aging mass transit systems before rollbacks began in the Reagan era and continued through successive presidencies. That has left many systems, including Philadelphia, predominantly dependent on state funding and has led to the many clashes between City Hall and Harrisburg over the past half century.
 Hepp added that he believes SEPTA at times hasn't done itself any favors and has made some “moronic” decisions. He points in particular to the leadership of David Gunn, general manager of the system from 1979 to 1984, who he faults for failure to smoothly navigate the transition of commuter rail lines from private to public control.
 “To me that was SEPTA's greatest crisis because SEPTA proved it couldn't handle a basic transition that every other transit authority in the northeast corridor had handled one way or the other,” remarked Hepp. “SEPTA actually had to be ordered by a court: ‘Do you job.'”
 A pedestrian in 1981 passes by graffiti at 11th and Market Streets protesting SEPTA. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 Despite all of the trials and tribulations, experts say they believe most politicians in Harrisburg generally have still understood the importance of mass transit, to keep the economic engine of the Southeast Pennsylvania humming along, even if they extract their pound of flesh to pay for it. “There are reasons to be hopeful about compromise, despite the kind of dire political situation,” Guerra said. “Despite lower ridership, the SEPTA system is still extremely important to the regional economy and local economy, and Philadelphia is extremely important to the tax base of Harrisburg.”
 Guerra thinks SEPTA will indeed survive this most recent fiscal crisis. However, he does not downplay the challenging spot the agency finds itself in. In addition to regular funding obstacles, SEPTA also has to deal with recalcitrant social issues like the opioid epidemic as well as lingering effects of the pandemic including decreased ridership. In a worst case scenario where funding doesn't arrive, the agency could protect some core services by maintaining service levels, but that would likely require entirely eliminating lesser traveled routes. “I think SEPTA will survive. I don't think at the end of the day the agency is at risk of collapsing,” Guerra maintained. “That said, if you don't get any new sources of funding, it will be a radically different system.”
 Tags: public transit SEPTA 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Behind the Facade: the AJ Holman Building and a Man of the City
author: Zachary Matusheski
bodyText:
The controversial Philadelphia 76ers arena plan brought renewed attention to both Market East and Chinatown after the proposal was unveiled in 2022. The historic significance of this area became a hot topic with community groups highlighting the damage the plan posed to Philadelphia’s cultural landscape and architectural history. It is easy to see how the arena would have ruined one of the most vibrant Chinatowns in the northeast. Less easy to capture, but no less significant, is how the plan threatened the buildings wedged between the proposed arena and the Convention Center. The AJ Holman and Company building at 1222-26 Arch Street is one such building. A nativist turned Democrat turned Republican in the tumultuous mid-19th century, Andrew Holman’s biography and his company’s history speaks to Philadelphia's complicated history related to racial justice and equality. Appreciating the historical significance of the Holman Building adds further evidence as to why Center City developers should prioritize protecting the city’s historic buildings as they consider alternative plans to revitalize Market East, especially as the 76ers plan has been shelved and the neighborhood faces significant store closures like that of Macy’s in the Wanamaker building .
 Holman Building at 1222-26 Arch Street was built in 1881 by Wilson Brothers & Company. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Philadelphia’s unique position in the 19th century as the “Athens of America” brought young bookbinder Andrew J. Holman to the city from Salem, Massachusetts in 1837. Philadelphia had a large, influential community of publishers throughout the 19th century. Historian Paul Kahan, author of the newly released book, Philadelphia: A History , noted that the region’s resources, especially its forests and anthracite deposits, made Philadelphia, “the place to be” for publishing in the 1800s. Kahan wrote, “Philadelphia in this period is Los Angeles and New York combined. It’s the place where magazines and newspapers and the things people read around the United States were being produced.” Luckily for Holman, he made early connections with the Harding family, especially Jesper Harding, then the publisher of the Philadelphia Inquirer and one of the largest Bible publishers in the city.
 A little more than a decade after arriving in the city, Holman, then in his early 30s, joined in the rough and tumble politics of the Philadelphia region. By 1848, he became commissioner of Kensington, then not a part of the city, but on its outskirts until the consolidation of 1854. He was soon embroiled in a controversy over how he handled the contract for the Kensington Water Works, successfully defending the local company he hired to do work on the system that supplied water to Philadelphia in the 1850s and 1860s.
 Photograph of the AJ Holman and Company building as it looked in the 1880s. | Photo courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 Defending his reputation in the press over this contract did not make Holman gun shy about participating in Philly’s bruising politics . Over the late 1840s to mid-1860s, Holman served in a variety of political roles across three major parties. In August 1849, about five years after the violent anti-immigration and anti-Catholic riots in Kensington, Holman served on the credential committee of the Native American Party, an anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic party. The brewing controversy over slavery caused Holman to change parties not long after his work for the Native American platform. In November 1850, Holman and his friend, publisher William W. Harding, attended a major rally in support of the Fugitive Slave Law at the Chinese Museum at 9th Street between Chestnut and Walnut Streets. This law, part of the Compromise of 1850, required citizens of northern states to return escaped enslaved people to their enslavers. Speakers at the event, including party vice president and then-mayor George M. Dallas, denounced abolitionists and claimed the enforcement of the fugitive slave law would “vindicate the supremacy and sovereignty of the law.” Holman and Harding both included their names in a pamphlet of support of this event. By 1855, Holman had risen to be president of the Democratic Citizens of the 19th Ward, a new organization established following the 1854 consolidation of Philadelphia that drew Kensington into the city. A few years later, Holman successfully ran as a Democrat for Common Council.
 While it was unusual for Native American Party members to become Democrats, frequent changes to political identity were common in the 1800s. Parties then, “were not at all stable. We’re living through a period now where the parties are as homogenous as they’ve ever been. But that was not the case in the 19th century,” explained Kahan. It was common for people to change parties many times over their life as parties rose and fell.
 A March 1864 poster announcing rally to raise money for a bounty for Civil War service led by Andrew J. Holman. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia.
 To wit, Holman’s identity as a Democrat would not last long. At the onset of the Civil War, he broke with many in his party to side with the federal cause. In July 1861, Holman praised Pennsylvanians who had rallied to defend the Union, specifically highlighting those from Philadelphia who had marched to Baltimore to quell secessionist activities there, an action Holman said, “reflect credit upon the great city” and testified to Philadelphia's troop's “proficiency and excellent behavior.” Holman’s family put their money where their mouth was as two of his sons, Ebenezer and Jesper, joined the military. Ebenezer served in the 19th Pennsylvania Volunteer Infantry. Over the course of the war, Jesper rose to the rank of major in the 2nd Pennsylvania Artillery. He was wounded twice while leading charges against the Petersburg defenses, injuries that led to his premature death in 1881. Holman also became involved in raising bounties to induce city residents to serve, leading a rally the 19th Ward in March 1864 to raise support for the cause and avoid the imposition of a draft. In case his sentiments were not already clear, Holman made his separation from the Democrats permanent when he endorsed Abraham Lincoln and the Union Party ticket in the 1864 election.
 Second and Third Street Railway as it looked in the early 1890s. AJ Holman was re-elected to the company’s board of directors multiple times in the 1870s and 1880s. | Photo courtesy of Print and Picture Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 With this last change, Holman’s involvement in formal ward politics fell, but he remained active in civic life. In the years after the war, Holman became involved with the Second and Third Street Railway (STSR), rising to its board of directors. Incorporated in 1858, the STSR ran routes from Bridesburg to Southwark via Kensington and Center City. By 1874, a railway guide in the collection of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania highlighted STSR as the “only direct line to Frankford without change of cars.” Kahan highlighted the importance of this work as railways “knit the city and the outlining communities together” while also forming “a really important part of the city’s identity” as a manufacturer and operator of rail transportation. This work on the railway not only benefited Holman financially, but also satisfied his desire to be involved in public life.
 AJ Holman and Company's exhibit at the Centennial Exposition of 1876.| Photo courtesy of the Print and Picture Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 Building a bigger publishing business also matched these goals. In 1872, Holman founded AJ Holman and Company, a publishing house focused mostly on Bible production. Four years later, Holman participated in the Centennial Exposition of 1876. This massive undertaking celebrated not only the 100 year-anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, but also Philadelphia's position as a nationwide leader in the country’s cultural, scientific, and commercial life. A guide to the event praised Holman and other publishers for the “artistic effect” of their exhibit with cases built with “enameled iron locks, hinges, and door handles.” As further testimony, the Centennial Photographic Company took a picture of the Holman exhibit for its collection, a photograph currently preserved by the Print and Picture Collection of the Free Library of Philadelphia.
 Holman followed the success of his company’s show at the Centennial with rapid expansion. In 1878, Harding sold his Bible and album publishing company to Holman. Then, in October 1880, Holman purchased the building on Arch Street from the estate of John B. Myers, an auctioneer and former vice president of the Union League. Holman hired the Wilson Brothers, the engineering firm that had worked on the Philadelphia Times Building, the Reading Terminal train shed, and other large projects.
 A Bible published by the AJ Holman Company in 1872. This copy was owned by the Shearer family of Massachusetts. It is now in the collections of the National Museum of African American History and Culture. | Photo courtesy of the Smithsonian Institution
 Unfortunately, tragedy colored these triumphs and Holman’s efforts to leave a legacy for his children. His wife, Ellen, died in 1877. Four of his sons died over the 1880s, with two, Ebenezer and J. Nathaniel, dying months apart in 1887. In 1891, Holman began suffering from heart trouble. He died on October 14, 1891 while reading a newspaper at his home at 1424 Arch Street, less than two blocks from the AJ Holman and Company building. The Philadelphia Inquirer , no longer owned by the Hardings, commented that given his illness, “no serious tears were felt for him either by his physician or family.” Holman is buried with his wife and children in a plot in Laurel Hill Cemetery East, none too far from other prominent Philadelphia families of the 19th century.
 For its part, the Holman publishing house continued on well past its founder's death. The company stayed family-owned until the early 1960s when it was sold to the J.B. Lippincott Company, another prominent Philadelphia firm. By 1979, the Holman company was sold again and moved to Tennessee where it was merged with other publishers and continues to produce Bibles.
 Tags: Centennial Exposition Chinatown industrial history Market East 
 About the Author
 Zachary Matusheski is a historian born and raised in the Philadelphia region. He earned his PhD in American history from Brandeis University. Matusheski's writing on the intersections of U.S. political and military history has been published by Marine Corps History, Ohio Valley History, and other venues.

title: Remembering Philly’s Original NFL Champs
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Frankford Yellow Jackets won the NFL championship in 1926. | Photo courtesy of Print and Picture Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 Long before the Philadelphia Eagles won the 2018 Super Bowl, and even before their pre-Super Bowl championships in 1948, 1949, and 1960, the city laid claim to another NFL title with the Frankford Yellow Jackets.
 The team was founded in 1899 as the Frankford Athletic Association. They first played at a new athletic field at Oxford Avenue and Leiper Street called Wister’s Park, which was near the newly-built Frankford High School. The team later moved on to Brown’s Field on Oxford Avenue between Oakland and Pratt Streets. In 1923, their home was Frankford Stadium at Frankford Avenue and Devereaux Street, also known as Yellow Jacket Field, until its demolition in 1931 following a fire. They played sandlot games or against college teams before joining the nascent National Football League (NFL) in 1924,
 Over 15,000 men bought $50 bonds to fund the franchise. Once expenses were covered, any excess income was given to Frankford-area charities at the end of each season.
 When the NFL began, it allowed only 18 players on a team, so most played both offense and defense. Today’s teams are allowed up to 53 players, filling positions on offense, defense, and special teams which include punters, punt receivers, and field goal kickers, as well as having a large and equally specialized coaching staff. In the early days, it was common for the coach to be a current player as well, as in the case of Guy Chamberlin, who played end and coached the Yellow Jackets in its second and third seasons between 1925 and 1926.
 Frankford Yellow Jackets football program from 1926. | Image: Public Domain
 A number of other things were different in those early NFL days. The teams did not all play the same number of games in a season, and, rather than play a championship game at its end, the title was awarded to the team with the highest winning percentage by dividing its number of wins by the sum of its wins and losses, excluding ties. Also, it wasn’t until the league’s 10 season in 1929 that football regulations regarding length, circumference, and inflation pressure were established.
 The Yellow Jackets were the only NFL team that had to play its home games on Saturdays because of Philadelphia’s Blue Laws that prohibited sports events on Sunday. This created a grueling schedule of playing a home game on Saturday, then boarding a train to travel to another city to play a scheduled game on Sunday.
 The Yellow Jackets were an instigator in a controversy surrounding the 1925 championship, which has been debated off and on for decades. The Pottsville Maroons appeared to clinch the title over the Chicago Cardinals (now Arizona) in a late season matchup. A few days later, the Maroons went on to beat the Notre Dame Fighting Irish in an exhibition game at Shibe Park in Philadelphia. The Schuylkill County team was sanctioned for infringing upon the Yellow Jackets’ territory, suspended from the league, and stripped of their title, which passed on to the Cardinals. Oddly, the Chicago team generated their own scandal by recruiting four high school students to play for one of their opponents, the Milwaukee Badgers, ensuring an easy win to take the title away from the Maroons. The 58-0 game was supposed to be removed from the Cardinals’ record, but it stands to this day.
 The Yellow Jackets played in the NFL for eight seasons, from 1924 to 1931. They won the championship in 1926 , with coach Chamberlin at the head, in a tied shutout game against the Maroons in front of 7,000 fans on a chilly December day at Frankford Stadium.
 Frankford Yellow Jackets player Henry "Two Bits" Homan in 1926 during the team's championship season. | Photo courtesy of the Frankford Historical Society
 That season, the league had grown to 22 teams, including several from cities we no longer associate with professional football, like Providence, Rhode Island (the Steamrollers), Duluth, Minnesota (the Eskimos), or Hammond, Louisiana (the Pros). Professional football at that time was not the money-making juggernaut it is today. Of those 22 teams in the 1926 NFL season, it proved to be the last for 12 of the teams. In fact, for four teams–the Brooklyn Lions, the Hartford Blues, the Los Angeles Buccaneers, and the Louisville Colonels–it was their first and last season.
 Even as the NFL expanded, league teams, including the Yellow Jackets, continued to compete against college teams, which were more popular at the time. In October, 1929, The New York Times reported “Charley Rogers, star halfback for Pennsylvania in 1925 and 1926, and now playing with the Frankford Yellow Jackets, ran 50 yards for a touchdown against the Red and Blue varsity today on Franklin Field.”
 At this time, some teams were growing stronger and more lucrative, but others still struggled. The year after the Yellow Jackets’ championship, the NFL decided to purge itself of weaker teams. Its membership dropped to just a dozen franchises. Over the next few years, new franchises joined the NFL, while others went out of business.
 In Frankford, the Great Depression caused a decline in gate receipts, and the team went into receivership. For the 1931 season, the Yellow Jackets rented the Philadelphia Ball Park at Broad Street and Lehigh Avenue for home games, hoping the city would back the team. It wasn’t enough, and they folded mid-season with a 1-6-1 record.
 The Philadelphia Fire Department's trucks in Frankford sport Yellow Jackets' inspired logos. | Photo courtesy of the Philadelphia Fire Department
 Philadelphia’s lack of a pro football team did not last long. In 1933, a new NFL franchise was awarded to a syndicate headed by Bert Bell and former Yellow Jackets player Lud Wray. Both men had played at the University of Pennsylvania–Bell as quarterback and Wray as center–and they subsequently coached there as well. The new team was christened the Philadelphia Eagles. Wray became its first head coach.
 Today, the Yellow Jackets are remembered in the Pro Football Hall of Fame by the inclusion of two of its players, Guy Chamberlin and tackle William “Link” Lyman, who played in the 1925 season. As part of their 75th anniversary celebration, the Eagles paid tribute to the Yellow Jackets by wearing a uniform in Frankford’s powder blue and yellow colors.
 A small tribute to the Yellow Jackets remains in the neighborhood. Engine 14 and Ladder 15 at the Philadelphia Fire Department's station at 1652 Foulkrod Street each bear the team's logo.
 Tags: Football Frankford sports 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Op-ed: Philadelphia Deserves More Thoughtful Approaches to Historic Preservation
author: Randy Mason
bodyText:
Chinatown's 40-foot Friendship Gate was designed by artist Sabrina Soong and installed in 1984. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Recent decisions made by Mayor Cherelle Parker’s administration involving historic preservation reflect a deep misunderstanding of the value of culture to thriving cities. The choices to threaten Chinatown with the Sixers arena project and refuse legal protection for the Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) are short-sighted, damage the diversity of Philadelphia's cultural heritage, and reflect a narrow vision of both preservation and urban redevelopment.
 Both decisions have been long in the making, informed by detailed studies and public conversations . There is every reason to expect that wise decisions would result. Yet, we are getting the opposite.
 It is well understood that contemporary preservation doesn’t mean putting the past under glass. In every quarter of the city one finds examples of historic buildings, blocks, and landscapes from the last three centuries being used, loved, activated, and developed. This is central to Philly’s vibe and its identity–how we Philadelphians think about ourselves as a city. Keeping and using a collection of the city’s most distinctive places, reflecting its culture and history in both its brightest and darkest moments, is what makes Philly Philly.
 Much has been said and written about Chinatown. The arena proposal is questionable in fiscal terms. It is devastating to anyone who values culture as a reason to love, live, and invest in cities, whether you are from Chinatown or not. As an outsider to that process, I can only note the complete lack of surprise that billionaire sports-team owners are getting their way. The Sixers and its enablers are convincing the City, against all evidence, that this vanity project will create shared prosperity and that sacrificing the integrity of Chinatown is worth the short-term financial benefits and political boost that the deal brings Mayor Parker. If a city can’t support the diversity and vibrancy of neighborhoods like Chinatown, it won’t thrive in the long term. The Parker Administration must take a longer view.
 The former Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) at 750 Race Street was completed in 1962 and designed by Geddes, Brecher, Qualls and Cunningham. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The question of preserving the Roundhouse is complex . The history, design, and economic potentials clash dramatically. Dreadful histories of police brutality coexist with masterful architectural design and great economic value. How do we preserve and redevelop the building in light of this? The question should not be whether to preserve the place or not, and rather how to adapt it.
 It is typical in historic preservation work to think about these decisions from distinct angles, according to the multiple kinds of value such projects can create. Cultural value comes from our shared understanding of a place as a work of art or design, or its association with important stories. Whether proud or shameful, the significance of these stories to the city’s history is what matters. I would argue that all of the stories connected to the Roundhouse need to be remembered and reckoned with, not ignored and forgotten. Social value comes from citizens gathering, protesting, celebrating, or otherwise using the place to symbolize civic life. Environmental value resides in the building’s embodied energy and avoidance of the environmental damage required to demolish, landfill, and rebuild. Last, but never least, economic values realized by redeveloping, or demolishing, the place depend on markets and government policies—the costs and benefits are purposefully distributed among private owners and the public sector. Adaptation for new uses, running tourism attractions, and creating cultural institutions are all time-tested strategies for creating economic value while sustaining other values, too.
 There are many precedents, in Philadelphia and elsewhere, for protecting the complicated values of difficult buildings or buildings with difficult histories. They can be given new lives that create cultural, social, environmental, and economic value for the city. Look no further than Eastern State Penitentiary : a place of dark history and deep injustice converted, through artistically inspired and development-minded preservation, to an engine of social value, creativity, and tourism marketing. Other examples include Cherry Street Pier and the Bok Building. Each project found a creative and effective path to create continuing flows of cultural, social, and economic values. Other cities have their examples, too. Consider New York’s thriving Tenement Museum or Hong Kong’s Central Police Station complex. In fact, you won’t find a successful city anywhere in the world without its examples of this general urban preservation principle: cities have to be culturally complicated AND economically creative in order to thrive. You can’t create these conditions without a strong historic preservation vibe.
 Eastern State Penitentiary was an active prison from 1825 to 1971. It officially opened to the public as a historic site in 1994. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Philly should be a national model for using preservation to stimulate development by building on our social and cultural assets and reckoning honestly with social justice past and present. Yet, if decisions made by the Parker administration hold–bargaining away Chinatown and demolishing the Roundhouse–these opportunities will be squandered. To ignore the values and preservation-led opportunities of Chinatown and the Roundhouse is a careless urban redevelopment strategy.
 As next decisions about Chinatown and the Roundhouse come down to the wire, Mayor Parker should listen to a range of Philadelphians’ voices and consider long-term costs and benefits, not only the short-term economic interests. As history has shown, shiny new megaprojects in Philly often deliver few lasting economic benefits and are a distraction from meaningfully reflecting on the past. And, well, if we don’t know much about our past….
 Tags: Chinatown Immigrants Mayor Cherelle Parker op-ed Police Administration Building redevelopment Sixers Arena 
 About the Author
 Randy Mason is a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Weitzman School of Design and directs the Urban Heritage Project.

title: Center City Woolworth's and Calvary United Added to the Local Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Calvary United Methodist Church in West Philadelphia. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Philadelphia Historical Commission added four properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places and reviewed other matters relating to historic properties at its meeting on December 13.
 A nomination was approved for Calvary United Methodist Church at 4740 Baltimore Avenue in West Philadelphia. Constructed between 1905 and 1907, the church building is an example of late 19th century ecclesiastical English Gothic style architecture, with large stained-glass windows and tracery by Tiffany Studios, crenellation, limestone trim and detailing, and Tudor arches. The church is an established, familiar visual feature of the Cedar Park neighborhood, situated prominently the five-points intersection of Baltimore Avenue and 48th Street. In 2022, Calvary United was one of nine recipients to receive the National Trust for Historic Preservation's Trustees Emeritus Award for Historic Site Stewardship.
 The former Woolworth's in Center City. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Historical Commission voted in favor to designate the old Woolworth's store at 1330-36 Chestnut Street. The International Style building was constructed in 1949 and was part of the company’s attempt to develop large flagship stores in several downtowns in the United States and Canada. With its horizontality, minimalist aesthetic with Art Deco/Streamline Moderne references, and white facade, the building stands out from others in the area, making it a distinctive feature of Center City and this block in particular.
 Oak Lane Trust Company Bank in Oak Lane. | Photo: Julia Hayman, Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia
 The former Oak Lane Trust Company Bank at 6701-19 N. Broad Street was also placed on the local register. Architect Ralph B. Bencker designed it in 1923 in the “Chaste Deco” version of the Zig-Zag subtype of the Art Deco style, which was popular in the Philadelphia region. On Chaste Deco buildings, exterior decorative ornaments were in the same materials as the rest of the building surface, typically limestone, granite, or concrete, giving each facade a uniform appearance. Bencker went on to design many other Art Deco buildings in the city, including the Rittenhouse Plaza and the Wellington Apartments on Rittenhouse Square, the Ayer building on Washington Square, and many Horn & Hardart automats.
 The Edwin T. Chase House in Germantown. | Photo: Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia
 The house at 449 Locust Avenue in Germantown was built for prominent Philadelphia lawyer Edwin T. Chase in 1861 by John Riddell, one of the most prolific residential architects in mid-19th century Philadelphia. The three-story stone Italianate-style house is typical of Riddell’s own type of domestic pattern book architecture that defined that era. The designation was modified to remove a rear section of the long lot to allow the recent owner to develop it.
 St. Peter's Church in Society Hill. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 St. Peter’s Church at 301-15 Lombard Street was given approval to construct a new one-and two-story building on a surface parking lot for a classroom, office, and a combination gymnasium-assembly facility. Historically, a public school and several rowhouses had stood on the site, but were demolished several decades ago. In 1999, the lot was listed as contributing to the Society Hill Historic District , owing to its potential for having archaeological potential. The Historical Commission had approved an earlier construction proposal contingent upon an archaeological survey, which had been scrapped, although the investigation was conducted and yielded no significant resources.
 St. Elizabeth’s Episcopal Church in Point Breeze. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 A former church property at 1900 S. 16th Street received final approval for a conversion to multi-family residential and event space use. The complex, originally St. Elizabeth’s Episcopal Church, was built during the late 19th and early 20th century. It was designed by Baily & Truscott and was designated historic in 1986. The Point Breeze landmark was home to the congregation of True Gospel Tabernacle Church since the 1990s.
 An amendment to the Victorian Roxborough Historic District was requested. The district was designated for its architecture and community heritage with a period of significance of 1830 to 1930. The applicant requested the removal of the properties at 360-66 and 369 Lyceum Avenue. The former is classified as contributing to the historic district and contains a 1855 Italianate-style villa and three rowhouses facing Conarroe Street that were built in 2000 and not listed in the district inventory. The property at 368 Lyceum Avenue contains three non-contributing buildings constructed around 2013.
 The Historical Commission voted to revise the district boundaries to exclude the three rowhouses, 353-55 and 368 ½ Conarroe Street, that are located within the 360-66 Lyceum Avenue site.
 A continuance to the Historical Commission’s January 2025 meeting was granted for a proposal to create the Northwest Philadelphia Apartments Thematic Historic District .
 Tags: historic churches Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Metropolitan Hospital and a City That Would Not Let it Rest
author: Lee O Neill
bodyText:
The Philadelphia Historical Commission recently voted against placing the Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) on the local register of historic places to protect it from demolition. That decision opens the door for redevelopment of the site. Will the Historical Commission’s decision be repealed? Will there be a redevelopment of the site and will that project seed a positive transformation of the area? Or will it be a typically insensitive Philadelphia cash-grab high rise? 
 While the Roundhouse has become the center of a preservation battle, its golden twin across the street to the north remains quietly ignored. That building is a condominium complex known as the Metro Club. It was obviously designed to resemble the style of the Roundhouse, but what isn’t transparent to motorists exiting or entering the Vine Street Expressway is that the building was the fifth and final home of Metropolitan Hospital, an osteopathic institution that was a not-always-silent witness to the transformation of Center City
 The former Metropolitan Hospital at 201 N. 8th Street was converted into condominiums in the early 2000s. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The history of Metropolitan Hospital is a tangled mess. City directories from the 1920s show a Metropolitan Hospital at 1433 Poplar Street and a Stomach Hospital at 1903 Green Street. By 1930, the Stomach Hospital on Green Street became the Metropolitan Hospital, and the Metropolitan Hospital on Poplar Street became the Metropolitan Apartments. Got that? Both buildings were relatively small and were typical of the kind of facilities that served as hospitals in those days–one or two lots, three or four stories, and scattered in neighborhoods throughout the city. The hospital’s neighbors included the Dolan College of Embalming, the Highway Mission Tabernacle, a Dominican convent, Spring Garden AME Church, and lots of three-story row houses.
 In 1944, the hospital came under the direction of a group of 50 osteopathic physicians. According to the Philadelphia College of Osteopathic Medicine, currently located on City Line Avenue, “Osteopathic medicine is a ‘whole person’ approach to medicine–treating the entire person rather than just the symptoms. With a focus on preventive health care, Doctors of Osteopathic Medicine (DOs) help patients develop attitudes and lifestyles that don’t just fight illness, but help prevent it, too.” Then, as now, osteopathic medicine is considered an alternative therapy. In addition to the college, there were hospitals in West Philadelphia and North Philadelphia at the time Metropolitan Hospital reinvented itself.
 The former YWCA building at 1800-1812 Arch Street, date unknown. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 Metropolitan Hospital immediately began expanding with a new lab and an x-ray department. It soon needed more space and started looking for new home. In 1949, it purchased the YWCA building at 1800-1812 Arch Street. The facility would have a large, closed-circuit television screen broadcasting from the operating theater, 200 beds, a floor for psychiatric patients, and an outpatient clinic. There was also room for 150 doctors plus residents and nurses as the hospital would continue to serve “any person, regardless of race, creed, color, or economic background.”
 The Women’s Auxiliary got busy raising money, but this may have been a bigger project than anticipated. The Hospital Planning Agency felt that “the old YWCA building is not a desirable location for a hospital. The building is too old to modernize and, in the minds of many people, it is a ‘firetrap.’” The hospital's administration changed direction and, in the summer of 1950, sold the YWCA building and purchased the Joseph Price Memorial Hospital at 241 N. 18th Street for $70,000. Price was a noted physician from the turn of the century, and the hospital was another of those small, local hospitals, this one serving the Fairmount area. The old YWCA found its way into the hands of the Philadelphia Bible Society, but it was eventually condemned to make way for the Comcast Technology Center.
 Meanwhile, Metropolitan Hospital's new location allowed it to expand services, but its tenure in the new building was not long. The Schuylkill Expressway had been under construction since 1951, the same year that Vine Street was expanded to 10 surface lanes. Not long after, plans were developed for the Expressway to connect to a depressed section of Vine Street between 17th and 21st Streets. The new Metropolitan Hospital was sitting right where the eastbound surface lane of a new Vine Street would became an onramp for the Schuylkill Expressway, so it was taken by eminent domain. The hospital needed a new home. Again.
 300 Spruce Street before and after being converter into Metropolitan Hospital. | Photos courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 In 1954, hospital officials closed a deal on an eight-story building at 300 Spruce Street in Society Hill that was previously served as a cigar factory, a textile factory, and a Coast Guard quartermaster depot. It had the construction, air-handling, and parking that would be important to a hospital. At that time, a factory converted into a hospital in Society Hill was not out of place.
 Metropolitan Hospital moved into its new quarters in 1955 and began expanding as intended. It was the center of osteopathic care for Center City and South Philadelphia as well as a neighborhood hospital. In 1963, it received a federal Department of Health, Education, and Welfare (HEW) grant for $2 million ($20 million today) to build a three-story service building and convert an existing storage floor into space for hospital beds. By this time time, however, there was a constituency that considered a hospital definitely out of place in the neighborhood. Society Hill had been in decline for several decades, becoming one of Philadelphia’s most blighted neighborhoods. That began to change in the 1950s, when, under the leadership of city planner Edmund Bacon, the Greater Philadelphia Movement, the Redevelopment Authority, and the Old Philadelphia Development Corporation (among others), began a revitalization project that would transform the entire area. This meant that when Metropolitan Hospital applied for Zoning Board of Adjustment (ZBA) approval for the project, it was met with strong local opposition in the first act of what would become a dramatic, contentious, and disruptive eight-year drama.
 Initially, neighbors were concerned over the loss of open space and parking as well as increased traffic. The hospital began to scale back the project to eliminate the need for a variance, but, without a ZBA decision, HEW pulled the grant. The hospital revised its plans and satisfied the need for a variance, announcing plans to resubmit its application to HEW.
 300 Spruce Street in 1987. | Photo courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 At the same time, Cuthbert Latta, attorney and a resident of Society Hill, filed a petition with HEW urging it not to renew the grant on the grounds that using federal funds for the hospital expansion was at cross-purposes with federal funds being used for the revitalization of Society Hill as a residential neighborhood. Later in the fall, Governor William Scranton, Mayor James Tate, and Senators Joseph Clark and Hugh Scott wrote their own letters to HEW echoing Latta, but adding that they would support expansion for the hospital anywhere, but its current location.
 With the backing of state and local government in place, HEW rejected Metropolitan Hospital’s application. Recognizing the needs of the hospital for expansion, the City provided it with a list of possible sites. By the summer of 1964, Metropolitan Hospital decided on a 350 bed, $6-8 million site at 8th Street between Race and Vine Streets, just north of the new Philadelphia Police Department headquarters and part of the Independence Mall Urban Renewal Area project.
 The Independence Mall project, also known as Independence Mall IV, was another slum clearance initiative, this time tied to transportation improvements chiefly connecting the Vine Street Expressway to the Benjamin Franklin Bridge. All of the buildings bounded by 7th, Vine, 9th, and Arch Streets would be demolished except for the Roundhouse and three buildings associated with St. Michael’s Zion Evangelical Church. The concept of transforming the area around Independence Hall and the other historic Colonial-era buildings of Old City and Society Hill, in conjunction with transportation improvements, had long been a part of the agenda for renewing mid-century Philadelphia. Independence Mall IV would eliminate Skid Row's mixture of cheap hotels, disreputable saloons, and underutilized industrial buildings in favor or new light commercial and industrial users, such as Metropolitan Hospital.
 A rendering of Metropolitan Hospital published in The Philadelphia Inquirer in 1967.
 The Redevelopment Authority announced in July that the new 350 bed (later scaled back to 250 beds) hospital would be located at 201 N. 8th Street . Funding for purchasing the land and constructing the facility in the image of the Roundhouse would be cobbled together from federal and state government, the City of Philadelphia, and the hospital itself.
 The relocation of the hospital would then allow the Redevelopment Authority to acquire and demolish the old Metropolitan Hospital on Spruce Street to advance the renewal of Society Hill. Cypress Square, a cooperative effort of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, the Redevelopment Authority, and the Old Philadelphia Development Corporation, was dedicated in 1980. Today, Cypress Square is legally protected within the Society Hill Historic District and the properties are all valued at well over $1 million each.
 Once an agreement was reached on relocating the hospital, demolition of 144 buildings and 27 acres of land commenced, obliterating the entire Skid Row district , including the much beloved Bijou Theater, a former home of burlesque. When the bulldozers left the area, the only remaining building was St. Michael’s Zion Evangelical Lutheran Church (also known as Old Zion Church). The church had played a large role in Philadelphia’s German speaking Christian community since 1742 and was initially spared destruction. Eventually, finances and a dwindling congregation caught up with it. In 1971, the decision was made to relocate to a new building on North Broad Street. The church was demolished, making way for Metropolitan Hospital's parking lot.
 Bijou Theater, pictured here in 1966, was demolished for construction of Metropolitan Hospital. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 The decision to relocate the hospital took some time to be realized. Plans for a Roundhouse lookalike on the site of the old Bijou Theater for the hospital were announced in 1967, but increasing construction costs and labor difficulties slowed down the project. The new $11 million hospital with six operating rooms, 250 beds, 11,000 feet of emergency space, and the latest in pediatric and cardiovascular care opened in April 1971.
 The Daily News described the new Metropolitan Hospital as “the most modern structure on the Philadelphia skyline.” However, despite the good vibes created by moving into a new building, the next few years for the hospital were difficult.
 Initially, the problem was labor. Most hospitals were experiencing staffing difficulties in the 1960s and 1970s. Metropolitan Hospital’s shortage was exacerbated when a security guard shot and killed a picketer in a scuffle in 1972. The labor issues were resolved following the shooting, but resurfaced throughout the medical industry between 1988 and 1992.
 The hospital also had serial accounting problems. In 1984, a leading physician was convicted on charges of defrauding Medicare and two insurance companies. In 1987, a former accounting supervisor was charged with forgery and theft amounting to nearly $500,000.
 A photograph from 1972 taken from roof of the PSFS building shows Metropolitan Hospital, at left, and the Police Administration Building in the center of the frame. | Photo courtesy of Temple University Libraries, Special Collections Research Center
 More important were economic pressures in the hospital industry as a whole and a decision to expand Metropolitan Hospital by buying two other medical enterprises in 1979. Today, the University of Pennsylvania, Jefferson University, and Temple University operate large clinical, teaching, and research medical facilities, but this was not how it worked 50 years ago. Small neighborhood hospitals, like Metropolitan Hospital, provided services to their communities, however that economic model was becoming precarious.
 Throughout the 1980s, The Philadelphia Inquirer and Daily News featured stories on the sketchy finances of hospitals, labor problems, hospitals going into receivership or closing, and a decline in care and increase in mortality rates. Metropolitan Hospital was invariably included with the medical facilities in trouble. The list of hospitals that have disappeared, either through closing or being absorbed by one of the survivors, is long and includes Mount Sinai , St. Agnes, Methodist, Giuffre, Philadelphia General, St. Mary’s, St. Joseph’s, Hahnemann, John F. Kennedy Memorial, and many, many others.
 While dealing with these problems, Metropolitan Hospital also had the burden of financing its decision to buy two area osteopathic hospitals in 1979. Humana sold the Tri-County Hospital in Springfield, Pennsylvania and the Park View Hospital in Kensington to Metropolitan Hospital for $37 million. Administrators stated at the time that “the two hospitals are profitable, but not to the extent that we would like.” The sale was contingent on Metropolitan Hospital obtaining financing (they issued $59 million in tax-exempt bonds), regulatory approval, with plans to convert Humana’s two for-profit hospitals to Metropolitan’s non-profit status. All hurdles were cleared in 1981. Former CEO Wayne Byerly said at the time, “The decade of the 80s will be a decade of consolidation of health care facilities and in order to provide better health services and contain patient costs, competition between hospitals must be eliminated.”
 The purchase did not work out as intended. In November 1988, Metropolitan Hospital agreed to new management in response to a request from the Philadelphia Hospitals Authority. The Authority was concerned about the hospital's future $65 million in debt obligations related to the purchase as it was down to $1 million in cash reserves. Moody’s and Standard and Poor’s had downgraded Metropolitan Hospital’s status to “non-investment grade.”
 This photograph published by The Philadelphia Inquirer in 1986 shows hospital workers on the picket line at Metropolitan Hospital.
 Six months later, after failing to find a buyer or merger partner, the hospital declared Chapter 11 bankruptcy following another reduction in its credit rating. It didn’t take long for this chapter of the story to end.
 In January 1990, Metropolitan Hospital sold the Tri-Valley Hospital and the Park View Hospital for $19.5 million, while continuing to operate the 8th and Race Streets facility. The hospital also changed its name to the Benjamin Franklin Medical Center to show that this was “a fresh start… a new identity to go with the new thrust” according to a spokesperson at the time. Three weeks later, it rescinded the name change as there already was a Benjamin Franklin clinic near Washington Square.
 In May, Metropolitan Hospital affiliated with Cooper HealthCare of Camden, with Cooper making clear that this was not a sale or a merger. As the hospital in Philadelphia continued to operate under bankruptcy protection, former Mayor Wilson Goode announced that his preferred site for a new courthouse was the location of the hospital if it didn’t emerge from bankruptcy. While that drama was playing out, a judge approved the sale of Metropolitan Hospital to a new group, the Franklin Square Hospital and Hampton Hospital Group, the only bidder for the debt-plagued medical center. Franklin Square Hospital would continue to operate there until the bankruptcy judge could evaluate the division of the remaining assets.
 MetroClub continues to operate as apartments, while the fate of the empty Roundhouse across the street hangs in the balance. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 And yet, the problems continued to pile on. In August 1991, Great Western Funding sued the Franklin Square Hospital for fraud, alleging that it provided capital to Hampton Hospital Group, but weren’t properly repaid. In June 1992, the State of Pennsylvania sued the hospital for failure to make payments to its unemployment fund. By November, Cooper HealthCare reemerged to take over operations of the Franklin Square Hospital. Three months later, the FBI announced a probe into the hospital’s finances. On August 6, 1993, Cooper mercifully closed the hospital.
 There were a few attempts to revive the building, including an assisted living facility, a “supermarket of ministries,” a long-term care facility, and, finally, residences. After several years of neglect, MetroClub condos was announced in 2005 and has occupied the building ever since, putting a final CLOSED stamp on the epic saga of Metropolitan Hospital. However, depending on what happens to the Roundhouse, the story of the building at 8th and Race Streets may enter yet a new chapter.
 Tags: adaptive resuse Hospitals 
 About the Author
 Lee O'Neill is a Bella Vista resident who recently retired after more than 20 years in nonprofit management. He now spends a good deal of time in pursuit of one of his major obsessions: the history of ordinary Philadelphia people and Philadelphia institutions. His other obsessions include music. O'Neill's work has appeared in several Boston and national publications and a food blog called "Kilt in the Kitchen."

title: In Northwest Philadelphia, Five Historic Train Stations Will Be Revived With Reuse
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Gravers station at 300 E. Gravers Lane. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The neighborhoods in Northwest Philadelphia are some of the city’s most stable, where change doesn’t happen very fast. Recent developments, however, are about to transform well-known landmarks that have been sitting dormant for years.
 Five shuttered train stations along the two SEPTA Chestnut Hill Regional Rail lines will be receiving new lives thanks to the long-term leases the transit agency has just given to developer Ken Weinstein, founder of Philly Office Retail. “It’s the first time Septa has given a 99-year lease,” Weinstein noted. “Turning them over to us will actually save them money, relieving them of upkeep and maintenance.” SEPTA estimates it will save approximately $150,000 in annual maintenance costs. Renovation of the five stations will cost roughly $1.34 million.
 Two of the stations, Mount Airy and Gravers, are on the Chestnut Hill East line. Sources place the construction of Gravers station at either 1879 or 1883, while Mount Airy’s origin is confirmed at 1875, with improvements added in 1883. Both are the work of architect Frank Furness in the Queen Anne Stick Style with gables, hipped roofs, and a port cochere on the street side. Gravers is the larger and more elaborate of the two, mostly brick with timber sections, a shed porch, and a semicircular tower rising from the ticket office and topped with gables, dormers, and a conical roof.
 Both stations are individually listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Additionally, Gravers contributes to the Chestnut Hill Historic District on the National Register and is on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 Mt. Airy Station at 119 E. Gowen Avenue. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 The other three stations–Tulpehocken, Upsal and Carpenter–are along the Chestnut Hill West line. All three were added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1981. Tulpehocken is both individually designated and part of the Tulpehocken Station Historic District listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
 The three stations are of similar design: two-story brick with multiple gable dormers, a second story wood porch supported by a canopy below, and station agent’s bay on the track side, which allowed the agent, who was also the telegraph operator, to watch for trains in both directions down the tracks and activities on the platform, while seated in the office.
 The stations have sometimes been attributed to Furness, but that is incorrect. They are the work of Washington Bleddyn Powell and William H. Brown, who were contracted by the Pennsylvania Railroad for many of its stations. Herbert Harwood, Jr., in his book Philadelphia’s Victorian Suburban Stations , doubts the Furness attribution, citing their more conventional design than other Furness station buildings and noting that the founder of the West line, the Pennsylvania Railroad “always was a more conservative company” than the Reading Railroad, which ran the East line.
 Weinstein is well-known for his adaptive reuse of buildings in Germantown and other parts of Northwest Philadelphia and has had his eye on these stations for a decade. “Back then, we surveyed the community around the Carpenter station about removing the ticket office and reusing the building and the response was positive,” he recalled. "But at the time we couldn’t get SEPTA to move on it. This year after they closed the ticket offices, SEPTA put the buildings out to bid.”
 Carpenter station at 201 Carpenter Lane. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The development of the Chestnut Hill West and East train lines were each instigated by a wealthy and influential landowner in their respective areas. In 1832, the predecessor of the Chestnut Hill East line, the Philadelphia, Germantown, & Norristown Railroad opened, running from 9th and Green Streets to a station at Germantown Avenue and Price Street. It was extended four miles to Chestnut Hill in 1855 and renamed the Chestnut Hill Railroad. 15 years later, it became an appendage of the Reading Railroad line. The station at Mount Airy was added even though the area was sparsely populated at the time. It was, however, close to the home of Reading’s president Franklin Gowen.
 The president of the Pennsylvania Railroad, George Roberts, responded to the competition by establishing their own line on the west side of Germantown Avenue. One of the railroad’s directors, Henry Howard Houston, had been buying and developing parcels around his home near Tulpehocken. Inspired by fellow board members who had developed housing tracts along the railroad’s Philadelphia Main Line, he began buying up land in Mount Airy and Chestnut Hill, ultimately acquiring more than 3,000 acres from Allens Lane to the Montgomery County line and on both sides of Wissahickon Creek. He convinced the Pennsylvania Railroad directors to extend the train line beyond Germantown and into Chestnut Hill and donated hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth of land for the right-of-way.
 Beginning in the 1880s and continuing to the 1930s, Houston and his son-in-law George Woodward built around 300 houses in the section of Chestnut Hill now referred to as St. Martin’s, which is named after the neighborhood church. The development included the 250-room Wissahickon Inn, designed by George W. Hewitt and his brother William D. Hewitt with stained glass by Ann Willet. Located at 500 W. Willow Grove Avenue, it is now part of the Springside Chestnut Hill Academy campus.
 Woodward went on to create several developments with distinctive architectural styles, including French Village at Emlen Street and West Allens Lane , and Cotswold Village along Navajo Street, W. Willow Grove Avenue, and Lincoln Drive.
 Upsal station at 6460 Greene Street. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 When considering possible uses for the train stations, Weinstein has a significant success story that precedes this new project: the station building at Richard Allen Lane station on the West line, which houses a popular cafe with an apartment on the second floor. “We saw the benefit over 23 years at the Richard Allen Lane station for restoring and reusing,” he noted. Unlike the large-scale factory and warehouse conversions he’s done, these are small buildings without a large return on investment to look forward to. “These are not money makers. They’re important to us as community gathering spots.”
 The five stations differ in their zoning, lot sizes, and parking facilities. Carpenters, Mount Airy, and Gravers are zoned for Residential Single Family Attached, Upsal for Residential Single Family Detached, and Tulpehocken, while not listed in the Office of Property Assessment database, appears to be within an RM3-Residential Multi-Family zone. Available parking ranges from none at Mount Airy to 93 spaces at Carpenter.
 At the Tulpehocken station, West Central Germantown Neighbors (WCGN) maintains a garden of fruit trees and native plants and shrubs, established over 10 years ago with help from the Philadelphia Orchard Project. “It’s always evolving,” said Marjorie Russell, WCGN former board member, president, and current garden volunteer. “We lose a few trees and gain a few trees. We currently have two pawpaw trees, an Asian plum tree, a row of serviceberries, a hornbeam, a sugar maple, and native pines and holly, among others.”
 For a retail tenant to be successful, Weinstein feels it needs to be used not just by commuters and the neighborhood, but as a destination as well that some customers would drive to. “Upsal is most likely to succeed as a coffee shop because it sits on Greene Street and is accessible to neighborhood.” Upsal housed a cafe in the 2010s.
 Tulpehocken station at 333 W. Tulpehocken Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 He is intrigued by the potential of the Gravers station, as it is tucked away in a residential area. “For the other three, we’re likely envisioning offices or studios on the first floors and residential on the second.” Weinstein believes this mix of commercial and residential is successful, because it provides 24/7 use and therefore security that other transit sites don’t have.
 Some of the stations have been vacant for years, so regardless of their future use, they’ll need a lot of rehabilitation. “The conditions are similar to Richard Allen Lane when we took that on—fair to poor,” Weinstein noted. “They’re all likely to be a gut job on the interior.”
 Another development along the Chestnut Hill West line is the recently designated Northwest Philadelphia Apartments Thematic Historic District . It consists of 30 apartment buildings, in close vicinity of the Chelten, Tulpehocken, Upsal, Carpenter, and Richard Allen Lane stations.
 Constructed between 1910-1940, the apartments transformed the area into a middle class suburban-like neighborhood, with landscaping and lawns that harmonized with the surrounding leafy streets. The collection of buildings feature elements of numerous architectural styles, including Tudor Revival, Colonial Revival, Neoclassical, Italian Renaissance, Beaux Arts, and Art Deco/Moderne.
 The district features different types of apartment complexes that were common in the early-to mid-20th century. The garden apartments are generally three or four stories, usually one building consisting of several wings in a U-shape that encloses a courtyard. If the complex was sited on a corner property, the building wings would often follow each street. Low-rise flats are characterized by a rectangular shape, either a single building or several identical ones, four to six stories high, while mid-rise flats are five to 14 stories, often topped with an ornamental cornice or parapet.
 Cresheim Valley Apartments at 7200 Cresheim Road. | Photo: Michael Bixler
