 Four of the properties already have individual designation: Alden Park Manor at 2961 W. Schoolhouse Lane, Cresheim Valley Apartments at 7200 Cresheim Road, Malvern Hall at 6655 McCallum Street, and Wood Norton Residences at 370 West Johnson Street.
 Alongside those positive developments, many in the neighborhood remain concerned about the future of the Chestnut Hill West line.
 SEPTA has long had structural budget deficits , which have been exacerbated by inflation and decreased ridership dating back to the pandemic.The deficit for 2025 is projected to be $213 million. Last November, Governor Josh Shapiro provided a one-time $153 million funding supplement that enabled the transit agency to reduce a planned fare increase from 21.5 percent to 7.5 percent. However, without a permanent increase, SEPTA officials anticipate having to enact service cuts and fare increases of about 20 percent by the fall. Governor Shapiro recently released his budget proposal for the fiscal year that begins July 1, 2025, which includes roughly an additional $165 million for SEPTA, as well as funds for other transit systems in the state. SEPTA officials believe this proposed increase would give it financial security for about five years.
 Tags: adaptive resuse Ken Weinstein Northwest Philadelphia Renovation train stations Victorian architecture 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Helping Hand Rescue Mission Imperiled by Revolving Door of Developers
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The townhouse project next to Helping Hand Rescue Mission in East Poplar has been under construction for three years and is currently only 10 percent complete. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 From its base on North 6th Street between Green Street and Fairmount Avenue, the Helping Hand Rescue Mission plays many roles in that support. As its name suggests, it is a place where the homeless can have a meal, get some new clothing and other supplies, or just take a break off the streets for an afternoon. Another important program is their youth group, offering after school tutoring and a social gathering place for kids, especially from the General Philip Kearny public school just around the corner. Helping Hand is also the home of Christ Community Bible Church.
 The building at 610 N. 6th Street was constructed in 1833, originally as a Presbyterian Church and later a Hasidic synagogue, which sold it to Helping Hand in 1961. Although Helping Hand has been at this location for over 60 years, its roots go back to 1905. It describes itself as “serving our Philadelphia community through two World Wars, two pandemics,” but goes on to note that it is “now hoping to survive one new tough construction challenge.”
 For decades, it has been a resource for the East Poplar neighborhood, particularly the townhomes and apartments to the west, some of which have been affordable units either via Section 8 housing vouchers or owned by the Philadelphia Housing Authority.
 One of those apartment complexes, Fairmount Manor, was Helping Hand's immediate neighbor to the west, across a decommissioned block of North Marshall Street. Its owner, Philip Pulley, partnered with PRDC Properties in 2022 to demolish the complex and replace it with townhouses and apartments, the same year another of his properties, Lindley Towers at 1220 Lindley Avenue in the Logan section, experienced a partial collapse.
 That incident is only one in a long line for the developer, with others including another partial apartment building collapse in Francisville, multi-million-dollar defaults on government mortgages, and a conviction on federal voter fraud charges.
 Plans for the new development included 407 residential units, surrounding Helping Hand's building on the north and south sides with two six-story apartment buildings with commercial space, and with a series of townhouses to the west, across a re-opened Marshall Street.
 A posting on PRDC Properties’ blog from March 2021 blog states, “PRDC Properties anticipates breaking ground on 650 Fairmount in the Fall of 2021. This mixed-used project at 6th & Fairmount will continue to reshape one of Philadelphia’s hottest neighborhoods, Northern Liberties.”
 This rendering of 650 Fairmount, now called "Citizen Northern Liberties" by the current developer, shows luxury townhomes and condominiums consuming Helping Hand Rescue Mission in placement and scale. | Rendering: ISA
 Today, the project is no longer listed under its “current properties,” having been sold to Accurate Builders from Lakewood, New Jersey and known as “May Fairmount LLC.” The new owners hired the same contractor, Pelco Builders of Coatesville, Pennsylvania, that PRDC had recommended. What has followed is a series of lawsuits and counter lawsuits between them, leading up to foreclosure and takeover by the bank Amzak Capital Management of Boca Raton, Florida. A new contractor for the townhouses, Camfred Construction of Bala Cynwyd, is now under contract.
 The townhouses are named “Citizen Northern Liberties” according to a banner along one of the fences at the construction site. “This neighborhood used to just be called North Philly,” scoffed one neighbor who requested to remain anonymous. “Then, when urban renewal came in the ‘70s, it was changed to East Poplar. Now, the realtors want to call it Northern Liberties.” The realtor’s website describes them as “The Citizen, Philadelphia's brand-new exclusive community of stately residences, all with access to an on-site in-ground pool.”
 Amid all of this legal wrangling, the neighbors, both Helping Hands and nearby residents, have experienced unannounced street closures, water pressure problems, sidewalk removals, and other issues over the course of the past three years. Helping Hands has had to move its youth program from its dedicated space to sharing with the building’s cafeteria because the rear entrance is blocked by the construction. It used to be a safe way for the kids to exit the building and walk home without encountering traffic. The construction project has also been fined by the Department of Licenses and Inspections for not providing a safe walkway along 6th Street. “Kids are coming here to get their homework done and they have to worry about getting hit by a car,” said one youth leader from the program.
 While Helping Hands had established a Community Benefits Agreement (CBA) with the original developer, in retrospect Adam Bruckner, the mission's director, believes they weren’t tough enough negotiators. “You need to have punishing language in a CBA,” he said. “With lots of ‘what ifs’ and ‘if nots’.”
 On March 2, a community meeting was held for residents to share their stories and discuss ways to remedy the situation. The mix of neighbors attending, some decades-long residents from the west side of 6th Street, as well as more recent arrivals in the new construction on the east side, had similar grievances. Bruckner seemed to know them all by name.
 Although various elected officials were invited, only the leader of the 14th Ward, Arthur Green, was present, and offered to be a conduit to City Council and the Mayor’s Office on their behalf. “Philadelphia–the police, City Council—is overwhelmed,” he said. “We need to be patient, but we need to have our voices heard.”
 Philadelphia residents in other neighborhoods that are busy with construction have had similar conflicts, although perhaps not as drawn out as this one. “It’s been three years,” Bruckner pointed out. “And they’re about 10 percent done.”
 Despite all the negative incidents that have transpired, he is holding out a glimmer of hope. “Helping Hand is contractually owed some money and construction work,” he explained. “This became impossible to collect with PRDC and Accurate, but Amzac seems online to honor the CBAs.”
 Tags: adaptive resuse East Poplar gentrification homelessness new construction Northern Liberties 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: The Mummers’ Signature Tune and the Composer Who Wrote It
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
When the Mummers gather to strut up Broad Street on New Year’s Day, you can be sure that you will hear a particular song multiple times as each string band passes by. “Oh Dem Golden Slippers” is easily recognized by legions of Mummers fans, but not as many would know the origins of the tune, its composer, or its ties to Philadelphia.
 The song was written by James A. Bland in 1879. He was born on October 22, 1854 in Flushing, Long Island and was descended from freemen on both sides of his family. His father, Allen Bland, graduated from Wilberforce University as one of the first college-educated African Americans in the United States. During James’ early childhood, the family lived in Philadelphia, where legend has it, he became infatuated with music upon hearing an elderly Black man playing the banjo.
 African American composer James Bland wrote roughly 600 songs, yet only a small fraction were published under his name. | Image courtesy of Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 When Bland was in his teens, the family relocated to Washington, D.C. where his father worked in the U.S. Patent Office and he enrolled in Howard University. At that time, the school’s strict rules forbade students to attend any sort of entertainment event. Bland would sneak away to see minstrel shows, eventually leaving the school in 1873 without graduating and ultimately joining Callender’s Original Georgia Minstrels as a singer and banjo player.
 Part of that troupe was purchased by J. H. Haverly in 1878 and renamed Haverly’s Colored Minstrels, so Bland may have performed in Philadelphia at the theater at 259 S. Broad Street that Haverly had built two years earlier. He had great success performing in England with that troupe, even appearing before Queen Victoria and the Prince of Wales in 1881.
 In addition to performing, Bland was a prolific composer, penning around 600 songs, yet only a few dozen were published under his name. In 1878 he wrote “Carry me back to old Virginny,” which became widely popular when white minstrel star George Primrose performed it.
 Original sheet music for “Oh Dem Golden Slippers” published in 1879. | Image courtesy of Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 “Oh Dem Golden Slippers” was published by Oliver Ditson and Company, a Boston publisher, with a Philadelphia branch headed by J. Edward Ditson as J. E. D. & Co. at 1712 Chestnut Street. It is thought to be a parody of a spiritual, “Golden Slippers,” popularized by the Fisk Jubilee Singers.
 The tune “became the definitive Walkaround number,” according to authors David Jasen and Gene Jones, in their book Spreadin’ Rhythm Around: Black Popular Songwriters, 1880-1930 . The walkaround began in the 1840s as a solo dance, but evolved into a competitive dance. The troupe would gather in a semi-circle and clap along to a fast tune while individuals or couples would take turns showing off some elaborate dance moves.
 At the height of his popularity, Bland was earning about $10,000 a year, which was an enormous amount at that time. However, Bland was careless with money and soon became destitute. He lived mostly in Philadelphia as he traveled around the East Coast for performances. He died on May 5, 1911 of tuberculosis at age 57 and was buried in an unmarked grave in Merion Memorial Park in Bala Cynwyd.
 Mummers and New Year's Day revelers party on Chestnut Street in 1888. | Image courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 It is possible that Bland may have witnessed the Mummers parade while he was living in Philadelphia. After a long history of individual mummers' groups cavorting in various neighborhoods, often accompanied by rifle shooting into the air to mark the new year, the City of Philadelphia established a coordinated parade in 1901.
 Not long after that, Charles Dumont, the captain of the Dumont String Band, made a suggestion in a rehearsal that would permanently alter the repertoire of the Mummers. “It was sometime prior to 1910 that Charles Dumont said, ‘let’s try this song,’ and everyone started dancing,” explained Mark Montanaro, curator of the Mummers Museum and former Comic Division performer. “So, we’ve been using it ever since.”
 Original sheet music for Bland's "Carry Me Back to Old Virginny." | Image courtesy of Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 After Bland’s death, a few performers kept his music alive, including classical soprano Alma Gluck, who recorded “Carry Me Back to Old Virginny,” and W.C. Handy, who programmed a few of Bland’s songs in a Carnegie Hall concert in 1928. "Carry Me Back to Old Virginny" was the state song of Virginia from 1940 to 1998, and today is designated as the emeritus state song.
 In 1946, the American Society of Composers, Authors, and Publishers (ASCAP) raised funds to erect a memorial tombstone for Bland at Merion Memorial Park with financial support from the state of Virginia. The epitaph doesn’t mention “Oh Dem Golden Slippers,” but refers instead to his more popular “Carry Me Back to Old Virginny.” The Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission installed a historical marker for Bland in 1961 at the cemetery entrance.
 Top: An illustration from December 31, 1900 published by the Philadelphia Inquirer anticipating the newly organized New Year's Day parade. Bottom: An event program for the first official Philadelphia Mummer's Parade in 1901. | Images courtesy of Susquehannavalley.blogspot.com
 In 1948, the Lions Clubs of Virginia established the Bland Music Scholarships Program to assist educational opportunities for Virginia youth, awarding over $25,000 annually. James A. Bland was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1970. 
 In 2025, the Philadelphia Mummers Parade will feature 14 string bands, three comic clubs, 10 wench brigades, and one fancy club. Also on New Year’s Day, 10 fancy brigades will perform two shows at the Pennsylvania Convention Center. The one-and-a-half-mile parade route starts at 9:00 a.m. at 17th and Market Streets, winds around City Hall, and continues down South Broad Street to Washington Avenue, with performance stops at Sansom, Pine, and Carpenter Streets. There will be more than a few renditions of James A. Bland’s “Oh Dem Golden Slippers” heard along the way.
 Tags: African-American history Mummers Mummers Parade Philadelphia music history 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Watershed Restoration Efforts Aim to Manage Stormwater
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
Historic renovation isn’t just for buildings. In response to increased rainfall attributed to climate change, stakeholders are directing resources toward restoring and protecting some of nature’s bygone capacity to absorb, filter, and slow stormwater runoff, which the Philadelphia Water Department (PWD) acknowledges as “the primary cause of pollution in our local rivers and creeks.”
 Fueled in part by PWD, along with significant private foundation and government agency funding, nonprofit organizations, schools, businesses, municipalities, and citizen scientists are taking measures designed to slow the flow of runoff with the goal of reducing flooding and some of the pollution in the city’s waterways. These include rain gardens—shallow pits of native plants designed to capture and store rain water—and riparian buffers along streams that feature native trees and shrubs meant to control erosion and provide shade that lowers water temperature in the summer.
 Wingohocking Creek (left), Tookany Creek (right), and Frankford Creek (foreground). | Photo: David Bell
 Rain lands either directly on bodies of water, on the ground, or on impervious surfaces, such as streets, parking lots, and pavements. In general, when it falls on lawns, gardens, or forests, rainwater either gets soaked into the ground or flows on top of the ground as runoff, picking up fertilizer from lawns and farms and loose soil from construction projects.
 When rain falls on impervious surfaces, the runoff flows downhill, grabbing motor oil, road salt, and other pollutants on its way to nearby creeks and rivers, either directly or via storm drains designed to move water quickly. In Philadelphia, where stormwater and sewage often share a combined sewer system, rain storms frequently overwhelm infrastructure, causing runoff mixed with raw sewage to be discharged into the Delaware River and its tributaries.
 Hands On, Feet Wet 
 Streamkeeper David Bell sampling for chloride. | Photo courtesy of Tookany/Tacony-Frankford Watershed Partnership 
 I became more aware of how runoff impacts local waterways as a volunteer streamkeeper with the Tookany/Tacony-Frankford Watershed Partnership (TTF). The TTF watershed encompasses 29 square miles in Montgomery and Philadelphia counties. Headwater tributaries in Abington and Cheltenham townships join to form Tookany Creek, which becomes Tacony Creek in Philadelphia. Tacony Creek meets the sewer outfall that once was Wingohocking Creek on the grounds of the Juniata Golf Course to enter the Delaware River near Bridesburg as Frankford Creek. Launched by the PWD in 2000, and incorporated as an independent nonprofit organization in 2005, TTF’s work includes implementing restoration projects collectively known as Green Stormwater Infrastructure (GSI) along creeks in the watershed from Abington to Philadelphia.
 “The number one challenge to many of our suburban watersheds is urban runoff. Therefore, many of the restoration efforts that we undertake focus on reducing the volume of stormwater entering our creeks,” said Ryan Neuman, TTF’s upstream conservation leader. “These efforts begin in the headwater creeks of the watershed, taking many forms such as rain gardens, bioswales, and subsurface stormwater storage, all aimed at slowing down stormwater. Especially in a highly urban watershed such as the TTF, the headwaters are often where we have the most space for these projects and where we can have the largest impact. As water flows downstream, pollutants such as sediment aggregate. When we work to improve water in the headwaters we are simultaneously improving water downstream as well.”
 Along with co-stream keeper Rebecca Schultz , I monitor a site on Tookany Creek, making and reporting monthly observations of its health and the presence of wildlife. In addition to its GSI projects, TTF provides citizens with opportunities to engage with their watershed through stewardship, recreation, and education.
 Volunteers plant native trees to control erosion. | Photo courtesy of Tookany/Tacony-Frankford Watershed Partnership 
 In that vein, TTF introduced me to the Penn State Extension (PSE) Master Watershed Steward (MWS) program . After 60-plus hours of training and volunteering, I was a certified MWS, joining colleagues in Philadelphia and surrounding counties to help manage stormwater with rain gardens and other GSI, remove trash and aggressive invasive plant species from waterways, engage with local elected officials on watershed and stormwater issues, and offer watershed outreach and education to adults and children at community events. Annual informational MWS recruiting sessions are held in December, and training begins in the spring.
 TTF also provides regular training for streamkeepers, held in cooperation with our counterparts in the Pennypack and Wissahickon watersheds. Sessions on construction site runoff and road salt proved to be especially relevant to me.
 Not long after training on construction site runoff, while passing a local high school construction site during a rain storm, I noticed brown water running off the hillside directly into a storm drain that emptied into a nearby creek. The main problem with too much soil in a waterway is that it contains nutrients that can cause algae blooms. When the algae die off, bacteria feed on them, consuming oxygen and releasing carbon dioxide in the process. This can cause oxygen dead zones where fish cannot survive. In some instances, the sediment can smother life on the bottom. GSI has limits in its ability to remove runoff soil before its enters waterways, so stopping it at the source is most effective.
 A call to the county soil conservation district secured what turned out to be a false promise to visit the site. An email to a township official resulted in action. The next day, she informed me that the township engineer visited the site, saw that soil containment measures originally put in place had failed, and ordered the contractor to correct the problem. I went back during the next rain and saw that runoff from the site was mostly clear, although I couldn’t determine if the fix reduced the amount of water headed for the storm drain.
 Salting the Water 
 An exposed salt shed. | Photo: David Bell
 The salt issue is more complicated. When it snows, states, municipalities, businesses, and homeowners routinely apply sodium chloride to highways, streets, parking lots, driveways, and sidewalks. Rightly seen as a safety measure, the problem is that people often use much more salt that is necessary. Salt can corrode cars and infrastructure and harm plants. What is left after a snowfall remains on hard surfaces until it gets washed away by rain or melting snow, ending up in our fresh water creeks.
 Historically, salt levels in our creeks have tended to spike after winter snow events—often to levels that are toxic to aquatic life—before dropping in the spring, summer, and fall. Sampling and analysis by TTF and the Stroud Water Research Center over the past three years determined that levels of sodium chloride in Tookany Creek and its tributaries remain high year-round, even after winters of little or no snow. Data from the Izaak Walton League’s Salt Watch program confirm that this is a regional problem. As a consequence, salt has worked its way into our ground water and drinking water.
 Municipalities around the country—places that get more snow than we do—have re-trained their operators, adopted best management practices, and turned to alternative products to reduce their impact, while ensuring public safety. Although local officials are aware of the problem, they have yet to address it in a quantitatively meaningful way. Water suppliers, such as PWD and Aqua, are not equipped to remove salt from drinking water, and GSI measures don’t work on salt, so reducing the amount that is applied, sweeping up the excess, and/or finding alternatives to sodium chloride are necessary to keep the problem from getting worse.
 Outdated Wastewater Infrastructure 
 A diagram of combined sewer overflows. | Image: Philadelphia Water Department
 Around 60 percent of Philadelphia is served by a combined sewer system, where runoff and sewage flow through the same underground pipes. “During wet weather, this older section of our system often overflows,” notes PWD's website. “As a result, billions of gallons of stormwater and diluted sewage flow into local waterways each year.” This is known as combined sewer overflow (CSO).
 Philadelphia has three wastewater treatment plants and 164 outfalls where CSOs routinely discharge runoff and sewage into local creeks and rivers during and after rain events—for some waterways, as often as once a week or more, on average. “On Labor Day in 2019, just a quarter inch of rain caused a 9-fold spike in sewage and stormwater at Frankford Creek in Juniata Park, resulting in an overflow,” noted John Rumpler, clean water director and senior attorney for Environment America.
 Construction site runoff feeding into a storm drain that feeds into Tookany Creek headwaters. | Photo: David Bell
 In response to enforcement actions brought against Philadelphia by the Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) and the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for violations of state and federal laws, respectively, the City signed consent orders committed to reducing the volume of stormwater that enters its combined sewers. Dubbed "Green City, Clean Waters," the 25-year plan details how PWD will implement green infrastructure measures, expand stormwater treatment capacity, and repair and improve existing infrastructure.
 Officially launched in 2011 and scheduled to meet pollution reduction goals by 2036, PWD says that in the program’s first 10 years, system repairs and the installation of more than 2,800 green tools at nearly 800 sites throughout the city kept more than 2.7 billion gallons of polluted water from entering local waterways.
 To encourage community support of its stormwater management efforts, PWD offers a Home Stormwater Guide, incentives and private development services for businesses, mini-grants to organizations, and a guide to transforming schoolyards—available on its Green City, Clean Waters website .
 A Critical View 
 A GSI map showing green infrastructure in Philadelphia. The green dots represent public sites and the blue dots represent private project sites. | Image: Philadelphia Water Department
 “Despite significant efforts over the past decade, Philadelphia’s wastewater system still pours billions of gallons of pollution into local waterways,” said Rumpler. “While eschewing a comprehensive overhaul of the conventional sewage system, the City’s plan made bold commitments to green infrastructure that aim to restore some of nature’s capacity to absorb stormwater before it overwhelms sewers or pollutes rivers with runoff.”
 However, Rumpler noted that the average volume of CSOs has gone down relative to precipitation. “In the 13 years from 2010 to 2022. CSOs per inch of precipitation declined from a rolling 3-year average of roughly 333 million gallons to about 273 million gallons—a decrease of about 18 percent.” He calls on the City to take measures to dramatically reduce the number and volume of CSOs, including rapid deployment of green infrastructure to capture stormwater that causes combined overflows.
 Research on quantifying the effectiveness of GSI to filter nutrients and pollutants is mixed, depending, in part, on modeling assumptions and other variables. Keeping nutrients and pollutants out of the runoff to begin with is more effective than trying to filter them out on the way to a sewer or waterway. A study from Villanova University, published in the August 2024 issue of the Journal of Hydrology , examined the effectiveness of GSI that the PWD installed along Tookany-Tacony/Frankford Creek. The authors concluded, “The results demonstrate the complexity in assessing urban streams and their interactions with urban runoff and GSI, and the stochastic nature of what GSI receives.
 A rain garden next to Jenkintown Creek. | Photo: David Bell
 “While many studies have shown the benefits of GSI to improve runoff retention, water quality, and CSO releases, the influence of GSI on urban hydrographs in larger watersheds in large cities such as Philadelphia has been less clear. GSI is typically designed to target smaller, more frequent storms, and Green City, Clean Waters (GCCW) aims to manage the first inch of stormwater on site. As the first stormwater control plan to rely so heavily on GSI, GCCW has the potential to serve as a guideline for future urban stormwater management.”
 GSI’s ability to capture runoff from all-but-severe storms shows promise. A 20-year study on the benefits of a rain garden installed at Villanova in 2001 determined that it “was found to manage 86.2 percent of all rainfall in its watershed.”
 GSI measures have limits when it comes to mitigating sever storms. “They are designed to capture the average storm, which should account for most of the rain that falls in a year,” said Dr. Laura Toran, professor of hydrology at Temple University's College of Science and Technology. “If designed well, GSI is good at delaying and reducing stormwater runoff. We should focus our efforts on designing and monitoring basins to ensure that they are doing that."
 Tags: climate change Frankford Creek Northeast Philadelphia Philadelphia Water Department pollution Tacony Creek watershed 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: Finney & Son
author: Alan Jaffe and Bryan Mckinney
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Finney & Son 
 Location : 531 North 12th Street
 Builder : Unknown
 Built : c. 1865
 The Finney & Son building, a 19th-century relic in Callowhill, has led many lives. Three generations of Finneys used the one-story structure as a showroom for mausoleums and cemetery monuments from 1865 to the 1960s. The yellow terra-cotta block facade, likely added in the 1920s or 1930s, resembles a burial vault adorned with multicolored garlands and wall niches.
 Today, the Finney building lives on. A sculptor used the offbeat space as a studio in the 1980s. In the mid-2000s, DJ and local music producer Diplo, now a world-famous Grammy-winning superstar, transformed it into headquarters for his Mad Decent record label, hosting Christina Aguilera, Shakira, and M.I.A. The Mad Decent moniker is still embedded in the entry sidewalk.
 In 2010, the building became the Philadelphia Mausoleum of Contemporary Art, home to film festivals honoring the late, great movie director David Lynch, neighborhood celebrations, art exhibitions, and music performances. The reborn Finney building has weathered closures by the Department of Licenses and Inspections for zoning and fire safety issues and possible demolition over concern for the front wall. Surely this storied, stubborn survivor deserves preservation and designation on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 Tags: Callowhill Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Unlisted Philadelphia

title: In Season 2 of Song of Philadelphia Podcast: The Resilient City
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Today, Hidden City releases the trailer of season two of Song of Philadelphia , the podcast hosted by Julien Suaudeau that is creating a citywide sound mosaic. The new season will launch May 1 with an episode dedicated to Chinatown, as Suaudeau catches up with the Save Chinatown activist Kaia Chau. You can listen to Song of Philadelphia on Spotify and Apple and you can play the season two trailer right here.
 http://hiddencityphila.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Season-2-trailer.mp3 
 "Aside from location changes, season two will feel different because it comes with a theme—hanging in there—that unifies the storylines of my three guests," says podcast host Suaudeau. "Kaia Chau, Kevin Dublin, and Larry Robin all have a personal experience with adversity and trauma. And the three of them, in their own distinctive way, came up with a form of resilience that has implications for all of us Philadelphians."
 Suaudeau, a professor of Film Studies and French at Bryn Mawr, came of age in Paris. Song of Philadelphia is where the Paris in his mind and memory meets the Philadelphia of his everyday, and with microphone in hand. In this way the podcast becomes a reservoir of voices. "Aside from bringing structure and meaning to life, which is the purpose of stories for me, the joy of turning personal stuff into something universal, at least at the local level, is what drives me in the Song of Philadelphia adventure," Suaudeau says. "What I want is for listeners to want to get to know my guests, be friends with them. I’m excited and honored to be the messenger of such compelling storytellers."
 Two cities reflected; Julien Suaudeau in Eagles green in Paris | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 "All season one guests were friends who kindly agreed to give me their time and to share their Philly memories to get the podcast started," he says. "I cannot thank them enough for entrusting me with their personal stories. In season two, the setup was very different. I knew Kaia and Larry professionally, and I didn’t know Kevin. It was an amazing experience to establish a proximity with them as they mapped out their city and reflected on all things Philadelphia."
 "They embody the city's endurance in different neighborhoods: Chinatown, North Philly, Center City. I see their ethics of loyalty and not giving up on Philly as a powerful inspiration to face the political moment that we are in," he says.
 Kaia Chau and other No Arena activists | Photo: Peter Woodall
 In season two's first episode, Kaia Chau reflects on the No Arena fight. "Chinatowns across the US are situated very uniquely, in downtown of whatever city you’re in," she says. "They were built there in the late 1800s because downtowns were the least desirable place to live. It was a process of discrimination and segregation. But now downtowns have become prime real estate. This is why they are targeted for large development projects. Developers see Chinatowns as neighborhoods that are easy to take advantage of and to take over because a significant portion of their population doesn’t speak English and may not be documented. Pushback is not expected. With the No Arena coalition, we changed the expected outcome.”
 Joe Frazier's Gym, a monument itself to personal and communal resilience, is the subject of episode two. “Joe Frazier’s Gym was the heartbeat of North Philly," says episode two's guest, Kevin Dublin. "You needed help? You went to Joe. I don’t care if you were a fighter or not. I cannot count the times I saw him change a random guy's tire. Fix an engine. He’d step out with his tools and pop the hood. A world champion!"
 Dublin, who boxed there as a younger man, is leading the effort to save the building, which is empty now, having most recently housed a furniture store, and is in danger of being demolished . Says Dublin in episode two: "The man saved my life. He saw me in a street fight. ‘You fighting for nothing,' he said. ‘Do you know you can get paid for this' When I went back to the streets and ended up inside, he took care of my family. I wouldn’t be here if it wasn't for Joe. That’s why I’m fighting for his legacy. It’s not just about a building. It’s Joe’s spirit. The city owes him more than we know."
 Making season one, Suaudeau says he was able "to to hear the multiple layers—subjective, temporal—that make up the thing we called Philadelphia. How many cities exist within the city? What is the best way to unfold them and make them audible to listeners? It felt less like a new knowledge than a very uplifting confirmation that I was on the right track with the podcast." In season two, Suaudeau has evolved his interviewing technique to reveal more about the each episode's guest, and the city, too. "People will remember more and be more fluent when they’re walking. I experimented with that in the bonus winterlude that I did in Paris during my father’s final months . Because you’re out there, you have to be quicker on your feet. Also, what you say is instantly woven in the fabric of the city, by contrast with the artificial blankness of a studio. Recording interviews on the go is a pretty tall order because of background noise and because the weather is often in the way. But I’m getting used to, and hopefully better at it."
 Larry Robin at Robin's Bookstore, circa 2002 | Photo: Greg James
 This comes to bear with episode three's guest, the legendary bookseller and activist Larry Robin, founder of Moonstone Arts. "People don’t know how to talk to each other anymore," Robin tells Suaudeau on the podcast. "This has nothing to do with political ‘polarization.' I think we’re just losing our ability to articulate things—to have constructive arguments. And if language dies, what do you think happens to humanity, in this country or elsewhere? Polarization is not a problem when you know how to express yourself and how to listen. We can deal with it, as long as we’ve learned how to disagree without hating and killing. I see poetry as an attempt to understand each other. A way to avoid the civil war, really.”
 Tags: Center City Chinatown immigration Joe Frazier's Gym literature North Philadelphia podcast Preservation Song of Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Nathaniel Popkin Hidden City Daily co-founder Nathaniel Popkin’s latest book is To Reach the Spring: From Complicity to Consciousness in the Age of Eco-Crisis.

title: Historic Church of the Assumption Heads to Sheriff’s Sale
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The Catholic doctrine of the Assumption of Mary holds that at the end of her life, Jesus' mother was taken into heaven, both body and soul, sparing her the earthly indignity of interment and decay. Will the historic Philadelphia church christened in her honor also be saved from physical demise? An answer may soon be forthcoming.
 The striking church at 1133 Spring Garden Street, constructed in 1849, will go up for sale by the Philadelphia Sheriff's Office on April 4, according to notices posted earlier this month . The impending sale could mark major movement for the property following more than a decade of limbo after neighbors and preservationists rescued the church from demolition at the 11th hour in 2013, only to watch time slowly chip away at its Gothic-Revival facade and forlorn interior.
 The genesis of the sale is a matter of some mystery. The building appears to still be owned by John Wei, a Chinatown-based developer who purchased it for $1.2 million in 2012 and swiftly attempted to make good on a demolition permit obtained by the prior owner. However, a court threw out the old permit, and Wei never applied for a new one. Since then, the church has sat vacant, unused, and abandoned, save for a brief flirtation by Wei of turning the property into a 45-room hotel.
 The sheriff's notice suggests Wei owes a creditor $3.9 million in unpaid debt, precipitating the sale. Additional public records indicate a time of financial hardship for Wei, including a filing of bankruptcy in 2023 and penalties of more than $5 million in a civil suit that asserted Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act (RICO) violations against Wei and associates. Also in 2023, Wei divested from the nearby Willow Street Steam Generation Plant , another notable neighborhood behemoth he had eyed for redevelopment. Wei and associated representatives could not be reached for this story.
 The Church of the Assumption was added to the local register for legal protections in 2009 . While the sale of any property listed on Philadelphia Register of Historic Places could signal danger, Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, said this one also presents opportunity. “I kind of take the sheriff’s sale notice as potentially a good sign, in that maybe it means a different developer will pick it up and convert it to another use,” he said. 
 The Ascension of Assumption 
 Just five years before the Church of the Assumption opened its doors, Philadelphia was shaken by a number of violent Nativist riots in 1844 , an explosive outgrowth of anti-immigrant sentiment among the city’s Protestant citizens toward newly arriving Italian and Irish Catholic populations.
 The latter were apparently undeterred. Construction of the church was completed 1849. The architect, Patrick Charles Keely, was a prolific designer of churches who drew up plans for more than 600 over the course of his career. The Church of the Assumption stands as the earliest surviving of all his works. According to the building's historic nomination, prepared and submitted by Andrew Palewski, “The Church of the Assumption is a surprisingly intact and unaltered example of Keely’s antebellum churches… virtually indistinguishable in appearance from its 19th century visual records."
 Designed in the Gothic Revival style, the nomination makes note of its dramatic brownstone facade, crowned by a pair of square towers and slender spires that provide a visual landmark to those traveling down Spring Garden Street. “Numerous Gothic-inspired forms and details characterize the facade, including buttresses, the prevalent use of the pointed lancet arch, windows with elaborate tracery, and the overall verticality of the design,” the nomination states. “The two octagonal engaged columns dividing the central block of the facade and the steeply pitched gable roof of the building, currently covered by slate, are other hallmarks of the Gothic Revival style.”
 Three carved wooden doors adorning the facade mark the only entrances into the church. In total, the Church of the Assumption originally contained 42 works of stained glass. As of 2009, some were broken or removed, including a pair that is now on display in the stained glass collection of the Frances M. Maguire Art Museum at Saint Joseph's University.
 An August 1849 notice in the Public Ledger makes note of the church’s “magnificence,” listing Hugh & Stewart as stone-cutters, John Keenan as carpenter, and J.T. Allen as plasterer. “This church, when completely finished, will add another to our many specimens of architectural and mechanical skill and superiority, and reflects great credit among all concerned," the notice reads.
 The church is said to sit at the precise location where Benjamin Franklin conducted his infamous kite-and-key experiment in 1752, and its twin spires may even be in dedication to the event, according to historical records reviewed by Hidden City contributor Harry Kyriakodis . Also documented is the church's connection to two Catholic saints: Bishop John Neumann, who helped consecrate the church, and Saint Katharine Drexel, who was baptized there 1858.
 Seeking Salvation on Spring Garden 
 In 1899, the Church of the Assumption received a major renovation. A century later it was in a state of decline. In 1995, the Archdiocese of Philadelphia closed the church. In 2006, it sold the property to Siloam Wellness Center, a HIV/AIDS nonprofit . Just three years later, neighbors and preservationists moved to successfully add the church to the City’s historic register as a proactive measure against Siloam’s efforts to demolish it.
 A back-and-forth legal battle ensued. In 2010, the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved a demolition application from Siloam on the basis of financial hardship by a 5-5 vote, the tie broken by a subsequent vote by then Historical Commission chair Sam Sherman. In 2011, the Callowhill Neighborhood Association appealed and won a reversal from the Philadelphia Board of Licenses and Inspections Review.
 Siloam in turn successfully appealed to the Court of Common Pleas, whose 2012 decision left the Church of the Assumption on the very precipice of demolition . Ultimately, the nonprofit's sale of the building the same year to Wei was enough for a Commonwealth of Pennsylvania judge to again reverse course, ruling in November 2013 that the original demolition permit was now moot. Wei never filed for a new one, which would have required him to make a fresh case for financial hardship in order to pursue demolition.
 Since then, news about the church’s fate has become scant. Steinke said Wei invited him to his offices several years ago to reveal plans to turn the church into a hotel, requiring modest alterations to the rear of the building in order to create space for vehicles to pick up and drop off guests. “I said, ‘If brought to the Historical Commission, I think we could support you on that in exchange for getting the building restored on the outside and reactivated,’” Steinke explained.
 Indeed, City records show Wei received a permit to convert the church into a 45-room hotel in 2018, pending additional approvals from the Historic Commission and other entities. Yet, there are no signs Wei further pursued such a development, as both Steinke and members of the Callowhill Neighborhood Association said they have seen no activity at the building in recent years.
 Business entities and law firms associated with Wei either did respond to requests for comment on the Church of the Assumption’s pending sheriff’s sale or denied involvement. Steinke, however, remains hopeful that something good may come to pass. “Structurally, [the church] is still sound. It doesn’t look great, but I think it is a building that still could be rehabilitated,” he said. “There are a lot of churches around town that have been turned into apartments. No reason to believe this one couldn’t be as well.”
 Tags: abandoned buildings Callowhill Church of the Assumption Edwin Forrest Durang historic churches Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: A Modern Masterpiece in Rittenhouse Square Makes Market Headlines
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The home and studio of architect Frank Weise at 307 S. Chadwick Street is currently on the market for $3.3 million. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 For 45 years a former stable tucked away on a small side street in Rittenhouse Square was a frequently evolving project of modernist architect Frank Weise. Today, the building is being sold for $3.3 million .
 307 S. Chadwick Street was originally built as a carriage house around 1895. It was purchased by Weise in 1958. The architect began designing the building's renovation in 1960, reworking plans until construction began six years later. Year-by-year drawings, now housed within the Frank Weise Collection of the Architectural Archives at the University of Pennsylvania, show the evolution, with the resulting design moving away from pure Modernist styles to incorporating historic features. “I lived in the area for a long time,” recalled Franz Rabauer, the building's listing agent. “It was always such a treat to walk by and see something unique like that.”
 The front facade has three different treatments: an open first level, stacked brick arches in the middle and topped with a metal clad mansard roof on the top three floors that feature large round and trapezoidal openings. “The residence occupies the fourth, fifth, and sixth floors under the mansard roof,” explained Rabauer. “The studio was on the first, second, and third floors.”
 Frank Weise in his studio on Chadwick Street circa 1960s. | Photo courtesy of the Frank Weise Collection of the Architectural Archives at the University of Pennsylvania
 Weise was born in Brooklyn, New York and moved with his family to Philadelphia, where he attended Simon Gratz High School and subsequently earned a Bachelor of Architecture at the University of Pennsylvania in 1942. He then worked for a short time in the offices of renowned architects Louis I. Kahn and George Howe. Weise went on to complete a masters degree at Harvard in 1945, studying under Bauhaus founder Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer. He later attended Black Mountain College in Western North Carolina. Weise established his own architectural firm in Philadelphia in 1949.
 Weise’s portfolio of work in the Philadelphia region remains remarkably extant. Between 1949 and 1962, he completed around 30 single family residential commissions. In Philadelphia, they range from rowhouses in Washington Square West to single family detached homes in Roxborough and Wynnefield. His work in the suburbs included projects on the Main Line, Delaware and Bucks Counties, and Collingswood, New Jersey.
 In the 1960s, Weise worked on two distinctive developments: Washington Mews around 11th and Lombard Streets, and Camac Village along the 1200 blocks of Lombard and Pine Streets and the 400 block of S. Camac Street. One of his few nonresidential projects is the District Health Center #6 at Girard Avenue and N. 4th Street.
 The studio, living area, and foyer of 307 S. Chadwick Street. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Weise is also remembered for his contributions in the 1970s to the renovation of Society Hill’s Head House Square and the restoration of Eastern State Penitentiary in the 1980s. He was a founding member of the Wilma Theater and the Theater of the Living Arts and designed the 1965 renovations of the latter.
 Today, as the I-95 cap project is proceeding with the aim to reunite Old City and Society Hill with the Delaware River waterfront, it revives an idea Weise had advocated for in the 1960s, when Philadelphia’s span of the highway was being built. As a result of his efforts at that time, a portion, the Vine Street Expressway, was built below street level.
 After Weise’s death in 2003, his house and studio was inherited by his daughter who, for a time, maintained a design firm in the studio portion. Until recently, another firm occupied the space. The property is zoned RSA-5 Residential Single Family Attached. The total square footage is nearly 4,000, although officially it is listed as smaller. “When measuring square footage, areas under the roof don't count towards the total. That’s the residential portion,” said Rabauer.
 In 1983, 307 S. Chadwick Street was listed within the boundary of the Rittenhouse/Fitler Residential Historic District by the National Register of Historic Places, but classified as an “intrusion” or non-contributing building. In 1995, the Philadelphia Historical Commission likewise labeled it as non-contributing to the historic district, although all of the other converted and altered carriage houses on the block were designated as contributing. In 2023, the architect's studio and home at 307 S. Chadwick Street was nominated by the staff of the Historical Commission and added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. 
 Tags: historic houses Midcentury Modern modernism Rittenhouse Square 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Why We Are Making the First-Ever Color Photographic History of Philadelphia
author: Peter Woodall
bodyText:
Italian Market, July 10, 1969. | Photos: Sam Nocella for the Philadelphia Bulletin courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University
 As you may have heard by now, Hidden City is in the middle of a Kickstarter campaign for our next book: PHILADELPHIA IN COLOR, 1950-1990 . Our goal is to create the first-ever color photographic history of Philadelphia, which is a book we believe Philadelphia needs—desperately.
 The origins of this project actually go back to 2009 when I first read about the photographer Vivian Maeir. She was a nanny in Chicago who, unbeknownst to anyone, was also world-class street photographer. Her negatives documenting Chicago in the 1950s and 1960s were discovered in a storage locker. I remember thinking, "Why doesn’t Philly have a Vivien Maier?" For that matter, why do we have only two or three photography books that capture the life of the city during this period?
 How do we understand Philadelphia's past? Through books, films and material culture, which combine with personal experience to create our conception of the city. This is why it is so disappointing that there have been so few serious books of photography showing our city during this period, and none in color.
 Interior page views of Philadelphia Discovered , 1964. | Photos: Joseph Nettis
 The sixties brought several boosterish efforts, the best of which was Philadelphia Discovered , and all were in black and white. In 1988, Temple University Press brought out Philadelphia Stories 1920-1960 , a touchstone of social history, also in black and white.
 So, we are aiming to make up for this visual history deficit it in a major way. How else to capture, for our own imaginations, the special textures of various eras, the cars, the fashions, the gestures, the social life, the signs, the storefronts?
 First Steps 
 In 2013, two years after starting this website, I stumbled upon the photos of David Wilson on Flickr. Wilson was part of a subculture of “rail fans” who would photograph trolleys and trains. He had visited Philadelphia as a teenager in the late 1960s and took a bunch of color photos that showed major commercial intersections and neighborhood life, as well as the trolleys he loved so much. We published a selection of his photos , and they were a huge hit.
 Photo: David Wilson, 1968
 The same thing happened when we published color photos of Center City taken in the 1980s that one of our contributors, Rachel Hildebrandt, had purchased on Etsy.
 Unknown photographer ca. early 1980s | Courtesy Rachel Hildebrandt
 In 2020, we published an amazing series from famed architect Denise Scott Brown. She had photographed South Street in the early and mid-1960s, around the time it was in danger of being torn down to build the Crosstown Expressway.
 Photo: Denise Scott Brown ca. 1964
 To this day, those three photo essays remain among the top 10 most popular stories Hidden City has published. So, the wheels started turning. Philadelphia may never discover its own Vivien Maier, but perhaps we can create a portrait of the city using the work of multiple photographers that is actually richer than the work of a single person. 
 Five years later, and after more than a year of intensive effort, we're ready to bring tell you about our project, which aims to fulfill that vision. We decided on the years 1950 to 1990 because prior to 1950 color photography was very rare, and after 1990 it was common. We chose color, despite its rarity, because it helps people connect to the past in a way that black and white photos do not. We wrestled with how to organize the book and ultimately decided to do so by decade, so that readers will be able to see how the city changed. Captions will only include the date, location and photographer so that the images can take center stage; we will include a detailed appendix to provide the necessary historical context.
 Digging Deeper 
 We expanded our search for photos to include any and every source we can think of, from museums and libraries to newspapers and archives.
 Astonishing material turned up in unexpected places. Pennsylvania Horticultural Society (PHS), for example, photographed almost entirely in color to emphasize its beautification efforts. Even in the 1950s PHS used color slides to document its window box program, which you see below.
 Archivists across the city have been extraordinarily helpful allies in our search. Temple University's Special Collections Research Center (aka Temple Urban Archives) is scouring their boxes for Philadelphia in color. The John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archive at William Way LGBT Community Center scanned several dozen photographs, many of them taken by Bill Way himself. Taller Puertorriqueño welcomed us into their archive of photos of street life and street fairs along the Calle de Oro.
 Photos courtesy of Taller Puertorriqueno
 We recently went to the archives of the Philadlephia Chinatown Development Corporation. Coincidentally, they had just discovered in the back of their storage unit these streetscapes someone put together of Chinatown in the 1970s. There are six of these poster boards covering nearly every Chinatown block.
 We knew that we wanted the book to show places that have been lost, with the area around Independence Hall at the top of our list. Fortunately, the archives of Independence National Historic Park document this period.
 We also tapped into the world of serious amateur photographers, such as Harry Drasin, a med student at Temple in the 1960s, who took photos between classes.
 Carmen Theater, Germantown Avenue. | Photo: Harry Drasin
 Along the way we’ve connected with Philadelphia’s community of professional photographers active in those years, like Harvey Finkle , Jack Carnell, and Stephen Perloff .
 Photos: Harvey Finkle
 Photos: Jack Carnell
 Photos: Stephen Perloff
 eBay has been an ongoing source of slides, especially, including these images of Shibe Park; the first photo was taken the night of the final game , October 1, 1970 and the second during its 1976 demolition.
 We've even gone to some truly unexpected places to track down photos. A guy who hosts a fishing podcast saved the photos on the wall of a bait and tackle shop in Northeast Philly when it closed.
 Photos courtesy of Cut & Retie with Joe Cermele 
 And then, of course, we have recently asked our readers and followers to submit their own family photos . Hundreds of photos have been submitted through phillyincolor.org already, and we are hoping to double that by the end of April.
 Photos submitted to Phillyincolor.org by members of the public
 This project has a serious goal: understanding how Philadelphia responded to an era of decline. Here is a photo taken by Ed Bacon and another by Dick Swanson from the Environmental Protection Agency’s Documerica project in 1973. You can see how photography helps you see things in different ways, particularly when they are intentionally juxtaposed.
 This book is an opportunity to uncover so much previously missing history and paint a portrait of Philadelphia that can appeal to anyone who has ever lived in or loved this city.
 To make it happen we need your help. We published our last book, Philadelphia: Finding the Hidden City , with Temple University Press, but chose to do this one ourselves. A book like PHILADELPHIA IN COLOR, 1950-1990 is too expensive to be supported by an author’s royalty from a local publisher, and foundations rarely support books. This is what Kickstarter is for—projects that wouldn't happen by traditional means.
 PHILADELPHIA IN COLOR is our chance to bring these decades back to life. It will be a true love letter to the city, made for Philadelphia, by Philadelphia.The more money we can raise, the bigger and better the book will be. Won't you help us give Philadelphia the book it deserves ?
 Tags: Archives book review Philadelphia in Color photography 
 About the Author
 Peter Woodall Peter Woodall is the Project Director of Hidden City Philadelphia. He is a graduate of the UC Berkeley School of Journalism, and a former newspaper reporter with the Biloxi Sun Herald and the Sacramento Bee. He worked as a producer for Radio Times with Marty Moss-Coane and wrote a column about neighborhood bars for PhiladelphiaWeekly.com.

title: Places Saved: Winter 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Hawthorne Hall | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Hawthorne Hall 
 Location : 3849 Lancaster Avenue
 Built : 1895
 Hawthorne Hall, located at the intersection of Lancaster Avenue, Saunders Avenue, and Hamilton Street in Powelton Village, was built in 1895 as a striking example of Victorian architecture. Constructed by developers Arthur Wright and Adolphus Prentzel, the building was part of a unified block of mixed-use structures featuring rust-colored brick, terra-cotta sculptures, and arched windows, which served as an impressive gateway to the city. It originally housed a drug store, post office, and various fraternal organizations.
 Over the years, Hawthorne Hall served as a versatile community space due to its stage and balcony seating. It hosted meetings, performances, boxing matches, and church services. In 2012, People’s Emergency Center (PEC) purchased the largely unused and derelict property and mounted a campaign for the building’s stabilization.
 With a vision to preserve its historic charm while introducing modern use, a developer purchased the property in 2021. A renovation project transformed the hall into six two-bedroom, two-bath apartments. The renovated spaces feature 12-foot ceilings, gourmet kitchens, and luxurious bathrooms, combining historic details with contemporary style.
 Hawthorne Hall’s renovation symbolizes the continued revival of Lancaster Avenue, a corridor caught between blight and redevelopment. This project preserved a significant piece of Powelton Village’s history and enhanced the neighborhood’s diverse character and architectural heritage.
 SEPTA Presidents’ Conference Committee (PCC) Trolleys. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 SEPTA Presidents’ Conference Committee (PCC) Trolleys 
 Location : Route 15
 Built : 1947
 SEPTA’s iconic green and cream trolleys, a staple on Route 15 between West Philadelphia and Port Richmond, have been restored and returned to service. Originally built in 1947, these historic PCC trolleys served the community for decades before being removed from service in January 2020 for restoration. Trundling through rain, snow, and road salt had corroded the cars’ frames, requiring extensive repairs. For four years, amid a global pandemic and ensuing supply chain issues, SEPTA ran buses along the trolleys’ path.
 SEPTA’s Trolley Restoration Team undertook the recent restoration effort, meticulously refurbishing eight trolleys, with 10 more in various stages of completion. The team reverse-engineered and fabricated parts that were no longer manufactured at a fraction of the cost of new cars. Their innovative approach included extensive research and reviewing original blueprints from the 1940s to maintain the authenticity of these classic vehicles.
 In addition to restoring the trolleys’ original charm, SEPTA also updated them with modern amenities, such as air conditioning and SEPTA Key readers, to enhance passenger comfort and convenience. While reintroducing the beloved streetcars, a combination of trolleys and buses will continue to serve Route 15 to allow SEPTA to maintain service frequency. As one of the last fleets of its kind in regular service in the United States, these trolleys continue to be an integral part of Philadelphia’s transit heritage.
 Hotel Anna & Bel | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Hotel Anna & Bel 
 Location : 1401 E. Susquehanna Avenue
 Built : Earliest section dates to 1769
 The former Penn Home has a long and storied history dating back to the 18th century. Established in 1852 as the Penn Asylum for Indigent Widows and Single Women, the building provided nonsectarian living accommodations for elderly widowed and single women of limited means. In 1858, the asylum purchased the 18th-century country seat of the Austin family, located at what is now Susquehanna Avenue and Belgrade Street in the Fishtown neighborhood. Over the next century, the institution expanded significantly, acquiring neighboring parcels and constructing numerous additions to the original “Mansion House” building. Throughout its 162 years of operation, the asylum was a community pillar, offering essential social services and evolving into a geriatric facility before closing in 2020. In that same year, the property was successfully nominated to the local register by the Keeping Society of Philadelphia.
 The new hotel, which took nearly two years to develop, has repurposed the 18th-century complex into a 50-room inn that blends historic character with modern amenities. The interior rooms on the second floor have French doors opening onto a balcony overlooking a Mediterranean-inspired courtyard. This leafy courtyard is a highlight of the property, complete with a heated outdoor pool. Hotel Anna & Bel also features two full-service dining concepts open to the public, further integrating the hotel into the Fishtown community. The transformation of the Penn Home into Anna & Bel preserves the site’s rich history while providing a new space for visitors to experience the vibrant cultural scene of Fishtown.
 Tags: adaptive resuse Fishtown Places Saved Powelton Village SEPTA 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: MLK House in Camden to Undergo Major Rehabilitation
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
The MLK House, at left, sustained considerable damaged after a fire tore through the building in March 2023. The exterior has been stabilized, and efforts to rebuild the civil rights landmark will begin this year. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The long-awaited first phase of restoring the fire-ravaged home where Martin Luther King, Jr. once lived in Camden, New Jersey in now underway. The repairs include a new roof and structural improvements funded by $40,000 in donations and an insurance payout of $150,000.
 The MLK House is the temporary residence inhabited by the civil rights leader during his years as a student at Crozer Theological Seminary from 1948 to 1951. During this time King and his close friend Walter McCall encountered Northern-based racism in Maple Shade, New Jersey. They were refused service at Mary’s Cafe and had a .45-caliber gun pointed at them. This incident has been cited as leading King into becoming a civil rights activist. In the 74 years since that incident, the MLK House at 753 Walnut Street has had a run of bad luck that resulted in the house being added to Preservation New Jersey’s 2024 most endangered sites list. 
 Jeanette Lily Hunt, who knew King and whose father-in-law owned the two-story home and rented out the rooms, has long seen the importance of preserving the landmark. She and local activist Patrick Duff shared a dream to secure funds to establish a learning center there for Camden residents and visitors. After multiple setbacks, including damage by squatters, the house continued to deteriorate. Then, in 2016, a deal fell through with Cooper’s Ferry Partnership, and a $229,000 grant was redirected to the Fire Department in 2018.
 A chance meeting between Amir Khan and Hunt changed the trajectory of the house. Khan, a long-time resident of Camden, recounts what convinced him to get involved. “I always knew the history [of the house], but there was no huge burning desire to restore it. Our space, New Beginnings, works with formerly incarcerated people who are dealing with homelessness and the evicted population. We have never dealt with historical landmarks," he explained. Ultimately, it was hearing Hunt’s dream that made the 2021 deal happen.
 At this time, the estimated cost to repair and convert the house into a community center and office for the Camden NAACP is around $450,000 with a prospective completion in 2027. To earn its historical designation, existing elements, including the floors and stairs where King once walked, are being preserved.
 Martin Luther King Jr. lived in Camden, New Jersey from 1948 to 1951 while attending Crozer Theological Seminary in Chester, Pennsylvania. | Photo courtesy of Colgate Rochester Crozer Divinity School
 In 2021, the New Jersey Historic Trust provided a $99,789 grant to the City of Camden to research and identify civil rights-era sites. With these funds, Hunter Research, Inc. was commissioned to interview, document, and develop future content for the MLK House derived from testimonials by King's family and local civil rights activists such as the Monk Brothers (Richard, Winston, and Hooper), Luther Wallace, one of the founders of the Black Peoples Unity Movement, Donald “Ducky” Birts, a community leader and activist, and historian Yocontalie Jackson.
 Khan sees the entire project as a stepping stone to establishing historical markers, not only at the MLK House, but for other notable heroes throughout the city. “The story needs to be told." Khan recounted the incident at Mary’s Café on June 11, 1950 that prompted King and McCall file a report at a police station for the breach of New Jersey’s anti-discrimination law. The case later involved the local chapter of the NAACP as counsel and was used as part of a drive to desegregate spaces. The issue was so important that King asked his soon-to-wed brother Alfred Daniel King to postpone his wedding so he could be at the trial.
 Kelly C. Ruffel, executive director of Preservation New Jersey, sees the future use of the MLK House as a cultural center that is “more than just the history of Dr. King in Camden, but how his legacy still impacts the community at large.” She said that it will be “a place to foster new ideas, create new community initiatives, and bring awareness to social injustices facing our nation.”
 After renovations are completed and the center opens in 2027, the project's second phase is slated to begin with the addition of a 10,000-square-foot property similar to The King Center in Atlanta, Georgia. The property next door at 755 Walnut Street is owned by the City of Camden and will be donated after the completed MLK House project is granted a historical designation. In the end, the fully realized goal is “something that will be passed on for generations to come,” according to Khan.
 Tags: African-American history Camden civil rights historic houses Martin Luther King New Jersey 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Places to Save: Winter 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 Furness Residence Hall at 1451-1499 Pine Street. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 University of the Arts Campus 
 Location : South Broad Street
 Built : Various
 Threat : Closure and vacancy
 The sudden closure of the University of the Arts (UArts) in Philadelphia raised concerns about the future of the numerous historic properties in its real estate portfolio, many of which are located on South Broad Street, also known as the Avenue of the Arts. UArts has long been the steward of these significant landmarks and its closure leaves their fate uncertain.
 Some of these buildings, such as Hamilton Hall, the oldest building on Broad Street dating to 1826, Gershman Hall, and the Art Alliance, are protected by designation on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. However, even this cannot prevent the threats of decay and vandalism without proper oversight.
 Terra Hall at 201 S. Broad Street. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Several other buildings lack such protection, leaving them vulnerable to demolition or inappropriate redevelopment. Among the notable unprotected buildings is Terra Hall, 201 S. Broad Street, originally built in 1912 as a Ritz-Carlton Hotel designed by Horace Trumbauer. Similarly, 329 South Broad Street, an office building from the 1920s, and the Arts Bank, 601 South Broad Street, a circa-1900 South Western National Bank turned arts venue, are not designated.
 Without active institutional use, the buildings could face prolonged vacancy and an uncertain future, leading to significant alterations or loss of historical integrity. Redevelopment could erase important pieces of Philadelphia’s architectural and cultural history on the Avenue of the Arts. With the dissolution of the university still in its early stages, the long-term fate of these structures remains unknown.
 Parke Building at 17-23 S. 52nd Street. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Parke Building 
 Location : 17-23 S. 52nd Street
 Built : 1913
 Threat : Vacancy
 The 52nd Street corridor has long been the heart of West Philadelphia, thriving as the neighborhood’s unofficial main street since the completion of the Market Street Elevated rail line in 1907. At the corner of Ludlow and 52nd streets stands the seven-story Parke Building, a visual anchor since it was built in 1913. Designed by H.H. Markley and built by George F. Pawling & Company, the building boasts a distinctive facade of limestone, granite, and terra-cotta tiles. Built for both commercial and residential uses, the building reflected architectural and technological advancements of its time.
 The building has housed various businesses, including the namesake Parke Bank. However, the area declined during the mid-20th century, leading to numerous vacancies. In the 1960s, the building was donated to the Opportunities Industrialization Center (OIC), which provided job training to local residents until 1983. The West Philadelphia Economic Development Corporation acquired the building in 1991, renaming it the Renaissance Center. Regardless of these efforts to repurpose the building, it continued to face challenges and was eventually sold in 2017.
 Despite its prominence, the building is vacant and decaying. In 2021, a new owner proposed converting it into apartments while preserving its architectural character, but these plans have stalled, leaving the building’s future uncertain. Preserving the Parke Building is crucial to maintaining the character and history of the 52nd Street corridor.
 Garden State Park Gatehouse at 2200 Marlton Pike West. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Garden State Park Gatehouse 
 Location : 2200 Marlton Pike West, Cherry Hill, NJ
 Built : 1942
 Threat : Vacancy
 The Garden State Park Gatehouse in Cherry Hill is a living testament to a pivotal era in the township’s history. Opened in 1942, the Garden State Park Racetrack quickly became a nationally renowned thoroughbred racecourse, transforming Cherry Hill into a regional entertainment hub. The site once drew crowds of 30,000, hosting elite athletes and horses and serving as a cornerstone of community life. A devastating fire in 1977 destroyed many of the original structures, but the racetrack was rebuilt and reopened in 1985. As time passed, the racetrack declined in popularity and in 2001 held its final race. Much of the 200-acre site has been razed and redeveloped. The Gatehouse, a small brick building with wrought iron gates, is the only remaining structure.
 As Cherry Hill continues to evolve, the Gatehouse is threatened by redevelopment plans. Residents, backed by Mayor David Fleisher, have rallied to preserve this crucial piece of history, garnering more than 1,400 signatures on a petition supporting preservation. A 2020 proposal for a betting parlor on the site included a commitment to preserving the Gatehouse. Those plans stalled, and the property is listed for sale, leaving the building’s future uncertain.
 The Gatehouse is a symbol of Cherry Hill’s rich cultural heritage. Its preservation is essential to honor the past and maintain a tangible connection to the community’s identity. While not currently on the New Jersey or National Register of Historic Places, the Gatehouse should be integrated into any future developments, safeguarding its legacy for future generations.
 Tags: New Jersey University of the Arts West Philadelpha 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Philadelphia's Oldest Surviving Bar Parties Like It's 1759
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
A Man Full of Trouble Tavern was spared demolition during urban renewal in the 1960s as part of Philadelphia city planner Edmund Bacon's vision for what would become Society Hill. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 When A Man Full of Trouble Tavern first opened in 1759 along the banks of Dock Creek at the corner of Spruce and Mattis Streets this was not where you'd find Benjamin Franklin discussing electricity over a beer. No, Franklin was lifting a pint at City Tavern, a posh spot several blocks and class distinctions away where members of the First Continental Congress met. Meanwhile, the aptly named A Man Full of Trouble Tavern quenched the thirst of dock workers, stevedores, and others who did not wear ruffled shirts or silk hose.
 In the 1700s, 2nd and Spruce Streets was not Society Hill. It was the Dock Ward where a man could drink away his troubles on the first floor of the tavern and share a bed on the second floor. In the 1830s, Watson's Annals of Philadelphia described it as "A Man Fill of Mischief." Regardless of its name changes, the historic tavern stood its ground for centuries.
 Over the next 200 years, it was known as Naylor's Hotel starting in 1851 and was described as a "ramshackle, two-story, wooden lodging." Around 1900, it was a grocery store and in the 1950s it was a wholesale chicken market. By that time, all of Dock Street was an open-air food market.
 If not for Philadelphia city planner Ed Bacon's reimagining the Dock Ward as "Society Hill" in the 1960s, this historic tavern may have been bulldozed like everything else in the path of urban renewal. "In 1962, the lopsided, decaying property was bought by City Councilmember and historic preservationist Virginia Knauer and her husband, lawyer Wilhelm “Bill” Knauer. They were amateur historians and avid antiques collectors," said Bob Skiba, archivist at Williams Way LGBT Community Center and president of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. "For the next few years, supported by an endowment from the Knauers, the museum flourished and costumed staff welcomed visitors," Skiba explained. "By the early 1990s, interest had waned. The tavern was only open to the public one day a month. Virginia, realizing that this was impractical, gifted the property to the University of Pennsylvania in 1994." The drafty, 3-room 18th century tavern was then used by the school to provide housing for visiting scholars and faculty.
 127 Spruce Street in 1961. | Photo courtesy of Prints and Photographs, Library of Congress
 It was around this time that Old City resident Dan Wheeler, an attorney and real estate investor, set his heart on owning Man Full of Trouble. "It was in bad shape. It was the only pre-Revolutionary War tavern in the city and it was never open," said Wheeler. "When Penn finally put it up for sale, it was marketed as a condo conversion. I bought it because I'm a veteran and I care about our history."
 "I am a serial collector," admitted Wheeler. "I started as a fanatical record collector of 78 rpm blues from the 1920s and 1930s." These days, he goes online to bid at Freeman's or Christie's auctions for Revolutionary War muskets and related memorabilia.
 To restore the tavern, Wheeler hired Justin Detweiler of John Milner Architects, a firm whose reputation for historic preservation has accrued prestigious awards for their work at Christ Church, Stoneleigh Mansion, and Fairmount Waterworks. "Underneath the carpeting, we found the original wooden floors, and we put a new roof on the building," said Detweiler. "In the attic, we discovered a box of historic wall paper that had been reproduced in the 1960s," he said. "We put it up on the second floor. We also designed the interior paint colors based on an original palette of historic Philadelphia paint colors and has them custom made."
 Interior restoration includes an ADA accessible restroom addition. The second and third floors retain the original historic antique wide floorboards. There are new kitchen cabinets, appliances and fixtures, as well as all new bathroom finishes throughout the building. No need to light a candle to see where you are going.
