New historically-inspired light fixtures have been installed throughout the building. "Much of what exists was historic," said Detweiler. "Where needed, we added new hand-forged hardware by Heritage Metalworks."
 The newly-restored tavern features a taproom downstairs and museum of Philadelphia artifacts upstairs. | Photos Michael Bixler
 The tavern is actually two rowhouses joined together. 25 people can fit into the bar on the first floor. Wheeler's museum of American history collectibles is on the second and third floors and includes a Revolutionary War cannon.
 "The third floor of the museum will be for special exhibits. I would like to partner with local artists to display their work," said Wheeler. As for the bar, he rented space to Succession Fermentory, a farmhouse brewery. All of their beers are brewed with locally sourced ingredients.
 In March, the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia announced that A Man Full of Trouble will receive a 2025 Grand Jury Award for excellence in historic preservation.
 Tags: adaptive resuse bars dock street Renovation Society Hill 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: Places Lost: Winter 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 The former Woolworth’s building. | Photo: Google Street View, 2019
 Building: Former Woolworth’s
 Location: 6174-82 Ridge Avenue
 Built: Circa 1920
 The demolition of the former Woolworth’s building in Roxborough marks the end of an era for what was once a community retail hub. Although not originally built for the Woolworth Company, the building became part of the chain in the 1930s, operating until the company’s closure in the 1990s. Since then, it housed various businesses, including a JCPenney, Thrift Drug, and state liquor store before its final use as a dollar store and day care.
 One of the building’s notable features was its Streamline Moderne facade, which included bright red paneling and red and cream striped awning. The exterior stood as a significant remnant of mid-20th for the mural on its southern elevation, which faced the Roxborough Pocket Park.
 Unfortunately, the Ridge Avenue Roxborough Thematic Historic District did not protect the building from demolition, as it was constructed after the 1908 period of significance. Instead, its demolition will make way for a five-story apartment building with 94 units, an underground parking garage, and larger commercial spaces. The new development will significantly change this stretch of Ridge Avenue, historically lined with low-rise, mixed-use buildings that created a pedestrian-friendly main street feel. The loss of the intact row of historic commercial structures alters the character that defined this section of Roxborough’s identity for generations.
 Buildings : 100 Block of South 19th Street
 Location : 113-119 S. 19th Street and 1823-1821 Sansom Street
 Built : 113, mid-20th century; 115-117, circa 1920; 119, circa 1870; 1823, circa 1907; 1821, mid-20th century
 The demolition of 113-119 S. 19th Street and 1823-1821 Sansom Street marks the first step in a project initially proposed four years ago. The three four-story structures along 19th Street and smaller-scale buildings along Sansom Street date to the mid-19th and early 20th centuries, but were not listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, falling just outside the northern boundary of the Rittenhouse- Fitler Historic District . The demolished buildings had housed various businesses over the years, including Cavanaugh’s Rittenhouse sports bar on Sansom Street and Topper’s Spa at 115-117 S. 19th Street.
 The demolition is part of a plan to construct a 54-story apartment tower on the site, known as Harper Square. This tower will be a companion to The Harper, a luxury apartment building completed in 2019 on the opposite side of 19th Street. The buildings were once planned to have their facades preserved as part of the new development. However, this plan was ultimately abandoned, and the buildings were entirely demolished in the fall. The corner property at 121 S. 19th Street is listed on the Philadelphia Register and will be preserved.
 The destruction of 113-119 S. 19th Street and 1823-1821 Sansom Street is a significant loss of historic fabric in the core of Center City, just steps away from Rittenhouse Square. With the current construction financing environment, many fear that in the short term the site will sit vacant until new construction begins.
 Tags: Center City demolition Places Lost Roxborough 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: A New Art Exhibition Ponders the Perpetual Cycle of Urban Transition
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
Contemporary Ruin future visions is currently on view at The Leonard Pearlstein Gallery, 3401 Filbert Street, until May 22. | Photo: The Leonard Pearlstein Gallery
 When I was a child growing up in Philadelphia, I harbored a hope that one day the city would be finished. There would be no more scaffolding, no construction sites, no road work or other infrastructure projects. The finished city would be free of dilapidation and blight. As an adult, I recognize that the nature of cities is to be forever falling down and building up, deteriorating, and renewing. Contemporary Ruin future visions, a new exhibition at Drexel University’s Leonard Pearlstein Gallery, brilliantly put together by multi-disciplinary artist and first-time curator Nancy Agati, returned me to my childish vision. Urban life, although guaranteed to be characterized by a perpetual cycle of construction and demolition, still has the potential to be the most beautiful, inspiring, and sustainable way that people can live. The show is about the past, present, and future of Philadelphia in particular and cities in general. It features artwork of varied media that interpret urban existence using imagination, personal vision, creativity, and, in many cases, a great deal of research as well.
 Depicting Transition 
 Paintings by Sophie White. | Photo: The Leonard Pearlstein Gallery
 Some Philadelphia neighborhoods have been altered significantly in recent decades, often to the dismay of historic preservationists and architecture critics. Most directly affected by these changes are the long-time residents. Painter Sophie White documents rapid transition of her Fishtown/Kensington neighborhood in a series of plein-air gouache paintings that capture rowhouses slated for destruction, backhoes clearing lots, and Tyvek-clad structures in the ubiquitous, boxy style of new construction. Using an appealing palette, White captures moments in time between what was and what will be in her immediate surroundings. “By making paintings of places on the verge of becoming unrecognizable,” White explained, “I am able to spend time with and mourn the neighborhood as I once knew it, while anticipating what is to come.”
 On the Banks of Sandy Creek by Jennifer Johnson. | Photo: The Leonard Pearlstein Gallery
 Sculptor Jennifer Johnson of Powelton Village also considers changes to her neighborhood’s landscape, but over a much longer time span and on a larger scale. On the Banks of Sandy Creek consists of three-dimensional maps depicting the area in which the Pearlstein Gallery sits during four time periods. The first map, made of smooth brown clay, shows the area in 1725 when it was undeveloped and home to Sandy Creek, a spring-fed stream that is now extinct. The 1925 map recreates the period when the area was known as the Black Bottom and was characterized by dense housing and small industrial sites. Only one row of homes remains in the 1975 map. By this time, the Black Bottom had been cleared through eminent domain to make room for institutional buildings including University City High School. The 2025 map indicates that the 1975 buildings are gone, replaced with large residential, research, and university-related structures. Having lived through this most recent transition, Johnson lamented, “Watching the transformation was shocking, and the invisibility of its past is unsettling.”
 Ruins, Relics, and the Fall of the American Empire 
 Richmond Generating Station, Turbine Hall . | Photo courtesy of Joseph E. B. Elliott
 Joseph E. B. Elliott’s haunting photographs of buildings in poignant decay depict past and present ruins in our midst. For example, his 2013 photo of Saint Bonaventure Roman Catholic Church on the 2800 block of North 9th Street shows rows of pews and vaulted ceilings looking directly out on an alley between rowhouses. The walls are no longer standing. This and many of the structures he has captured are now demolished. Some, however, like Richmond Generating Station on North Delaware Avenue, continue to deteriorate. Not surprisingly, as I contemplated the details of Elliot’s photo, I superimposed a restoration along the lines of The Battery within my mind’s eye.
 Although most of Elliot’s subjects are ornate 19th or early 20th century structures, his photograph of an abandoned 1950s Penn Fruit supermarket on Frankford Avenue is particularly discomfiting. The empty shelves under broad, candy-colored arches reverberates with post-apocalyptic eeriness.
 Don't Tread on Me by Emily Erb. | Photo: The Leonard Pearlstein Gallery
 The theme of a coming collapse is also alluded to in Emily Erb’s gorgeous banners made of resist and dye on silk. In Crumbling Empire , figures from Egypt’s Great Temple of Ramesses II remind us that great civilizations decline, and the oil derricks in the background and a large white car in front imply that American reliance on fossil fuels may lead to our downfall. Don’t Tread on Me , an Ouroboros loop of guns and cars provides another illustration of what ails our nation. On a more optimistic note, her most recent work, Muscular System , shows a human body made of National Park Service maps, reflecting Erb’s belief that “by emulating nature’s forms and processes, we can create more sustainable systems.”
 Canyon by Kelsey Skaroff and Dan Van Dyk. | Photo: The Leonard Pearlstein Gallery
 Canyon , by artist team Kelsey Skaroff and Dan Van Dyk, also presents nature as a superior alternative to capitalism. Skaroff, a painter and gardener, and Van Dyk, an artist and architect, have imagined a future world in which a mix of hearty plants has taken over a mega-warehouse that currently sits on a parcel of American Street in North Philadelphia. The property was previously populated by dozens of trinity rowhomes, all of which were gone by the 1990s. During several decades of abandonment, plants similar to the ones in the installation grew and attracted pollinators, crickets, and katydids. Van Dyk, who has been involved in designing industrial developments, states that “the environmental impact of these developments occurs on a grand and irreparable scale and is problematic and unsustainable.”
 Contemplating the Time Ahead 
 A verdant place where plants have reclaimed the land is one “future vision” portrayed in Contemporary Ruin future vision. The final portion of the show, created by Drexel graduate students enrolled in William Mangold and Sarah Lippman’s Speculative Futures class, depicts a range of other ideas about the urban spaces of tomorrow. Gallery director Mark Stockton notes the that the themes of abundance versus scarcity and equality versus hierarchy evident in the students’ work emerges from their reading of Peter
Frase’s Four Futures: Life After Capitalism. 
 The collective student view is a grim one. However, their thoughtfulness, creativity, and technical skill left me feeling hopeful. If we humans, with our proclivities for demolition and profit-seeking, are the cause of the deteriorating climate, degraded public spaces, and uglification of the urban landscape, perhaps this generation of architects and designers will find the solutions.
 Contemporary Ruin future visions is now on view at the Pearlstein Gallery on the campus of Drexel University. Admission is free and open to the public. See the exhibition's website for hours of operation and special event details: https://drexel.edu/pearlsteingallery/exhibitions-events/Exhibitions/ 
 Tags: art exhibition Drexel University Ruins 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Temple University Uncovers Human Remains at Construction Site
author: Adam Litchkofski
bodyText:
The construction site at Temple University where human remains and caskets were found on April 12. | Photo by Adam Litchkofski
 On April 12, human remains and caskets were discovered at the construction site of Temple University’s new Caroline Kimmel Pavilion for Arts and Communication building. It shouldn’t come as a surprise as the project is taking place on the former site of Monument Cemetery .
 Temple released a statement last week that claims the discovery was anticipated and that there is a plan in place to deal with such situations. “That plan includes notification of the Philadelphia Coroner’s Office, medical examiner, an archeologist, and law enforcement. Per the protocol, crews immediately halted work at the site when the remains were first discovered, and Temple’s Project Delivery Group (PDG) notified the university’s archeological consultant and other appropriate agencies, who then visited the site and directed next steps. We followed their guidance to ensure the remains were handled with the utmost care and respect and per the protocol, did not resume work in that area until directed by the appropriate agencies. Moving forward, PDG will remain in frequent communication with our archaeological partners and continue to follow the prescribed protocol to ensure that any remains are respectfully and properly reinterred.”
 Monument Cemetery was a sprawling Victorian-era graveyard on the west side of North Broad Street between Montgomery Avenue and Fontain Street. Opened in 1837, the grounds held the graves of 28,000 individuals until the cemetery was subject to Temple University expansion in the 1950s.
 When the school acquired a large portion of Monument Cemetery in 1956, bodies were exhumed and their headstones were discarded on the banks of the Delaware River to be used as riprap. Of the alleged 28,000 remains unearthed, only 748 relatives were contacted. The bodies that went unclaimed were reinterred in a mass grave at Lawnview Cemetery in Jenkintown, Pennsylvania. Since then, the site has been utilized as athletic recreation space and parking lots for the university.
 Combined photographs circa 1950 show a panoramic view of Monument Cemetery. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Philadelphia universities tend to have an odd relationship with the past, from University of Pennsylvania and Drexel University’s razing of the Black Bottom neighborhood to make way for real estate development to Temple’s botched exhumation of Monument Cemetery as well as demolishing numerous predominantly African American residential blocks and architectural landmarks for campus expansion. This is not to mention Penn Museum's recent acknowledgement that it possessed the human remains of one of the children killed in the 1985 MOVE bombing in its collection. “Many of these absurdities are owed to the sloppy way that these universities sought to expand after World War II. It was during those years, for instance, that Temple participated in a campaign to characterize Monument Cemetery as blighted so that the property could be obtained on terms favorable to the university,” explained Seth Bruggeman, a professor of history at Temple University.
 “Until that point, the cemetery–beyond serving as an important site of community memory–functioned as a much-needed green space for students, who used it in all the ways you might suspect,” Bruggeman said. “The university, however, wanted expanded parking and more control over its main entrance on North Broad. The acquisition and removal of Monument Cemetery was part of a larger campaign by Temple to rebrand itself in anticipation of the significant expansion it expected by way of federally-sponsored urban renewal.”
 Doug Mooney , president of the Philadelphia Archaeological Forum , has done archaeological work in the city for 20 years. More so than just the universities, he believes the City of Philadelphia is also at fault. “It goes far beyond the universities. [The City of] Philadelphia has a problem with cemeteries, and it is an issue that comes up time and time again. Every time it does, they treat it as if it's the first time such a thing ever happened and profess they don’t know about it,” said Mooney. “There are laws that come into effect in these situations, but they just refuse to acknowledge it because they don't want to anger developers.”
 Mooney researched and discovered that, since 1800, there were at least 53 unmarked cemeteries impacted by construction projects in Philadelphia. Including the sites that were impacted more than once, he calculated 87 separate incidents.
 Headstones from Monument Cemetery were dumped at the base of the Betsy Ross Bridge during construction for use as rip rap. Many survive today and can still be seen. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 What will happen to the human remains discovered at Temple has yet to be announced. According to Philadelphia lawyer Mark Zecca, Pennsylvania law dictates that unmarked burials and burial grounds are protected under the jurisdiction of the Orphans’ Court Division of the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas. For Temple to bury the remains found on its property elsewhere, the university must petition the Orphans’ Court to do so.
 “The news said Temple consulted the City [about excavation]. The City should have informed Temple that in order to get an excavation permit to disturb remains, it needed to get approval of next of kin or Court, because an excavation permit can only allow a permit holder to disturb property that the holder has a right to control," Zecca explained. "Human remains are not property of a land owner, like Temple, just because the remains are present on the land owner’s land. The disposal of remains is under the authority of next of kin or Court.”
 Last summer, a similar case involving the remains of the First Baptist Cemetery in Old City was brought to the Orphans’ Court, where a judge reaffirmed that the remains were in the custody of the court. “The City, however, does not do its job on this issue. The City even claims officially that it has no responsibility, which is false,” Zecca said, sharing the sentiment mentioned by Mooney. “The City does this so as not to ruffle the feathers of developers. The City knows it has authority to stop work in these situations and demonstrates this by asking developers when there is publicity to treat remains ‘with respect’ which is tantamount to implicitly claiming the authority to stop work. A City Council ordinance would clarify the duties that already exist and would be a good thing.”
 When asked to share the plans to rebury the bodies and how Temple will rectify the situation beyond doing what is lawfully necessary of them, the university declined to answer.
 “In this situation with Temple, like in all these situations, these are fellow Philadelphians that are buried there. In many cases, they are the ancestors of untold thousands of current Philadelphia residents. They deserve to be treated with the utmost respect,” Mooney said “And it wasn't a mystery. Nobody stumbled across the cemetery unexpectedly. They knew it was there. Temple should be taking all of the steps to make sure that these remains are respectfully removed from this current property and reburied in an appropriate different cemetery.”
 A rendering of the new Caroline Kimmel Pavilion for Arts and Communication building, looking west at the intersection of North Broad Street and Polett Walk. | Image: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill
 To keep situations like this from happening in the future, Bruggeman stressed that Philadelphia’s universities, and the City itself, need to be responsible stewards to the land. “The missed graves, in my view, are a reminder of the rush to growth during those years, and the ways in which it trumped the sort of rigorous accountability you'd want from an institution whose choices impact everyone who lives in North Philadelphia,” said Bruggeman. “It is what happens when universities put profit before people. Alas, reckless expansion begets reckless expansion. It does so at least until someone in power chooses to do better.”
 Construction crews broke ground on Temple’s new building in March. When the human remains and caskets were discovered in early April, construction was paused, but has since resumed. The project, designed by 89-year-old Chicago architecture firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill, is being funded by a $27.5 million dollar donation by Philadelphia businessman and philanthropist Sidney Kimmel. When the project is completed in 2027, it will house the Caroline Kimmel Pavilion for Arts and Communication.
 Tags: archaeology Doug Mooney historic cemeteries Monument Cemetery Temple University 
 About the Author
 Adam Litchkofski is a writer and photographer based in Philadelphia. He is a student at Temple University where he is pursuing a degree in journalism with a minor in environmental studies. He cares deeply about the outdoors and loves covering topics involving environmental justice, land preservation and conservation, and people’s relationship with nature and the world as a whole.

title: Journalism? To Some Extent. Nostalgia? If You Think So. Art? Well, Sure. History? Of a Certain Sort. Astonishing? Absolutely.
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Small Scale Retail and Street Scenes, 1967-71 (Courtesy Architectural Archive, Penn Design) | Photo: John Nicolais
 Maybe you've seen that rather heroic image of Louis Kahn's Salk Institute in La Jolla, California, the great concrete symmetrical massing opening out toward the Pacific Ocean . One of Kahn's students at Penn, John Dorio Nicolais , a Californian whose father, uncle, and brother were all architects, took the legendary photograph.
 John Nicolais died of Hodgkins disease October 29, 1979, at age 39, three years after opening his own firm and already responsible for photographic monographs of I.M. Pei, Charles W. Moore, and Kahn.
 Philadelphia Set, 1967-19 71 (Courtesy Architectural Archives, Penn Design) | Photo: John Nicolais
 Nicolais arrived in Philadelphia around 1965. Between then and 1969, when Penn awarded him a fellowship to travel to India to study water infrastructure, he wandered the streets of Philadelphia with camera in hand, sometimes on class assignment, with an inquisitive mind and an outsider's fresh eye. Nicolais's photographs, along with those of notable Penn Design colleagues like Denise Scott Brown and Laurie Olin, are in part why Philadelphia in Color 1950-1990 is the deepest investigation of the physical and material experience of Philadelphia ever produced.
 At Hidden City, we are hard into the process of making this tantalizing mosaic happen. For a year, we've been searching high and low for photographs from dozens of organizations, archives, and working photographers. More than 130 readers have contributed family slides and snapshots. On March 26, we launched a Kickstarter campaign to raise $30,000 to underwrite production of Philadelphia in Color. Yesterday, we passed that goal, securing $15,000 in matching donations. Now, there are 72 hours until the Kickstarter deadline (11:30AM Saturday April 26), and a chance to invest more in key elements of the project, resulting in a larger and thicker book, with more photographs and higher quality design and printing. We're aiming for the very best—and your support now can be the difference.
 Small Scale Retail and Street Scenes, 1967-71 (Courtesy Architectural Archives, Penn Design) | Photo: John Nicolais
 Philadelphia Set, 1967-71 (Courtesy Architectural Archives, Penn Design) | Photo: John Nicolais
 Each week, our team meets in the conference room at CultureWorks to assess the hundreds of images that have come in. We try to determine the date each one was taken, and the location, sorting it by decade. Then we project each photograph on a large screen and decide if it might make the cut. We ask if the photo is visually arresting. Can you stop looking at it? (We take Alexey Brodovitch's maxim "astonish me" seriously.) If so, maybe it isn't right. Can you feel the sun or the humidity, the mood of the street, time frozen and also passing? We've noticed that the most compelling photographs are reference points and mirrors, documentary in their function yet also triggering of mind and memory. They are how we know what this city, undergoing such enormous upheaval in the four decades after 1950, was really like.
 All the more so, through the perceptive eyes of a man whose own time was cut so short, whose vision was so concentrated. In John Nicolais's images of storefronts and doorways, peddlers and roller skaters, we see the city's streets as he did in that instant in the mid-1960s, saturated with color, vibrating with messages.
 Fox Theater, 1966 (Courtesy Architectural Archive, Penn Design) | Photo: John Nicolais
 Philadelphia Set, 1967-1971 (Courtesy Architectural Archive, Penn Design) | Photo: John Nicolais
 Only a couple years before Nicolais started shooting on the streets of this city, the Princeton professor Nathaniel Burt, in his book The Perennial Philadelphians (1963), had described Philadelphia as "big and flat and drab…massive, craggy, gray." This was a particular take on Philadelphia, one in fact widely held in the early-1960s, and Burt invests in it. In Center City, he writes, there are "blocks of miscellaneous drabness and dreary nondescript streets of nondescript shops, broken here and there by the raw emptiness of asphalt parking lots."
 Burt suggests there is another much more colorful city besides the dingy, suffocating one he describes (the name he gives it is, in fact, the name-origin of this organization—"sooner or later one is bound to find the Hidden City"). But he fails to take his readers there. Perhaps Burt was blinded by his subject, the city's hereditary upper class, but he didn't perceive that all around him were the seeds of the city that would come to be. That was, despite steep population decline, becoming more democratic, more creative, more open than perhaps ever before.
 John Nicolais did, with vigor, and so did the dozens of photographers whose work we've uncovered, of men racing around a Kensington soccer field in the 1950s, of West Philly juice man's pyramid of fresh oranges in the same era, of boys posing on a West Philly basketball court in 1963, of children romping around Chinatown in the 1970s, of late-80s protests against the censorship of Robert Mapplethorpe's photography.
 1960s (Courtesy Architectural Archives, Penn Design) | Photo: John Nicolais
 Yet imagine if we stopped with Burt, as so many observers of this city have done over the years. We would have it wrong, plain and simple. And in getting the past so wrong how could we understand the present? How could we know what to look for or how to assess or compare?
 This, fundamentally, is why we're pushing so hard to bring this project to life . The story is just that rich, varied, dynamic, democratic, propulsive, and yes, melancholic, and yes, painful. This is the sumptuous reality brought to life.
 Small Scale Retail and Street Scenes, 1967-71 (Courtesy Architectural Archive, Penn Design) | Photo: John Nicolais
 When you have this book in hand you're never going to want to put it down. Make it yours today .
 Tags: deindustrialization Hidden City Independence National Historical Park Italian Market Mummers Philadelphia in Color photography South Street Urban Renewal 
 About the Author
 Nathaniel Popkin Hidden City Daily co-founder Nathaniel Popkin’s latest book is To Reach the Spring: From Complicity to Consciousness in the Age of Eco-Crisis.

title: Touring the Neighborhood with "Chinatown Royalty"
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Kaia Chau in front of 1995 mural depicting the history of Chinese people in the U.S. | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 "My parents were undocumented and so they were not wanting us to get involved with things," Debbie Wei tells Julien Suaudeau in the first episode of season two of Song of Philadelphia , released today on Apple and Spotify. "And I grew up in the suburbs so I didn't have any contact with community or other than you know having trips down to Chinatown to grocery shop." As an adult, Wei became an education activist, in 1985 suing the School District of Philadelphia on behalf of underserved Chinese students and, in 2011, co-founding the Folks Arts – Cultural Treasures Charter School (FACTS) . 
 Listen here, or on Apple or Spotify .
 http://hiddencityphila.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Kaia.mp3 
 Now, her daughter, Kaia Chau, 23, has taken up the mantle, founding a youth center, Ginger Arts Center , on N. 12th Street in Chinatown North. In the first episode of season two of Song of Philadelphia, "Bluer than Indigo," Chau leads her former French professor, podcast host Julien Suaudeau, around the Chinatown of her youth, the stores and pools halls and bakeries, some of these special places lost to time. 
 In season two, Suaudeau realizes his ambition for Song of Philadelphia : to create a dynamic soundscape of the city comprised of stories and memories. As the episodes opens, Chau takes Suaudeau to the Italian Market, where she grew up and where she still works and where, she observes, "Italian, Mexican, and Vietnamese, mostly, and so many other cultures…come together." From there, the two venture north to Chinatown, where Suaudeau learns about the colonial origins of Chinese pastries and why the oldest mural in the neighborhood is about to be covered over. All the while Chau reflects on the immigrant's journey. "My grandfather had a PhD in chemistry and he could not get a job anywhere because he was Chinese," she tells Suaudeau, linking that struggle with Chinatown's ongoing effort to gain some control over its future. That story, and Chau's role in the No Arena campaign, is the subject of part two of this first Song of Philadelphia episode of the season. That episode will be released May 15.

title: New Historic Register Designations Shed Light on Little-Known Philadelphia History
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on March 14, the Philadelphia Historical Commission added seven properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, including a 19th century German burial ground, the home of an undertaker for Abraham Lincoln’s funeral procession, and the site of a historic visit by the head of the Baháʼí Faith in 1912.
 The Historical Commission opened its 750th meeting, and the first in-person assembly since the beginning of the pandemic, with a brief recounting of its history by member and former chair Robert Thomas and Executive Director Jon Farnham. Established as an advisory committee by an ordinance in 1955 during the administration of Mayor Richardson Dilworth, it wasn’t until 1985, under Mayor Wilson Goode, that the Historical Commission was given actual power over designated properties.
 The Edward S. Earley, Undertaker, House, and Business at 549-51 N. 10th Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The property at 549-51 N. 10th Street , the Edward S. Earley, Undertaker, House, and Business was designated, owing to its association with the funeral of President Abraham Lincoln. In addition to providing a special hearse, Earley oversaw the logistics of the ceremony. The journey by train of almost two weeks traveled from Washington, D.C. to Springfield, Illinois and was viewed by millions of Americans, marking the historic moment of the first assassination of a United States president.
 The S.S. Kresge Store at 1520-22 Chestnut Street was built in 1934, designed by the influential Philadelphia architectural firm of Silverman and Levy, with the nomination citing that connection and its Art Deco style. Because the two-story building is zoned CMX-5, the owner expressed concern over potential limits on future development. In response, the Historical Commission restricted the designation to the front and back facades, limiting their purview of any other portions, current or future, to review and comment only.
 The Logan Theater at 4732-42 N. Broad Street in 2022. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Logan Theater at 4732-42 N. Broad Street was designated for its role as a fixture in the cultural and social heritage of the Logan neighborhood. A classic example of grand neighborhood movie theaters of the early decades of the 20th century, it was built in 1923 for the Stanley Company of America by the architectural firm the Hoffman-Henon Company, who designed many of Philadelphia’s theaters, including the Boyd Theatre at 1908 Chestnut Street, the Mastbaum Theatre at 20th and Market Streets, and the Stanley Theatre at 19th and Market Streets.
 In West Philadelphia, the Reed-Hubley Residence at 3708-12 Chestnut Street , built around 1845, represents the era when transportation developments led to the creation of suburban-like neighborhoods beyond central Philadelphia. Today, it is one of the few remaining villas along this portion of Chestnut Street. The nominator also noted its role in the University of Pennsylvania’s efforts in fostering a diverse student body as the home of the Greenfield Intercultural Center for the past four decades.
 A little-known event in the city’s religious history occurred at 1429 W. Mayfield Street in North Philadelphia. In the early 20th century, it was occupied by the Revell family, who were influential members of Philadelphia’s early Baha’i community and is significant for a visit there by the faith’s leader, ‘Abdu'l-Bahá, during his travels in North America in 1912. The house was built in the early 1880s as a part of a workers housing development. The Spiritual Assembly of the Bahá’ís of Philadelphia purchased the house in 2003 and have restored the interior to recreate its original appearance.
 Bethany Lutheran Cemetery at 376 Martin Street. | Photo: Google Street View
 Another addition to the local register is the German Evangelical Lutheran Bethanien Burial Ground of Manayunk and Roxborough at 376 Martin Street . Founded in 1845, it contains around 100 grave markers or other structures, as well as nearly 1,000 burials, including Civil War soldiers and German-speaking Lutheran immigrants who were mill workers and mill owners that contributed to the development of Manayunk and Roxborough. There is the potential for archaeological assets, as the site formerly contained a German Lutheran Church that was demolished in 1873.
 The final designation was for the Beneficial Savings Bank Kensington Branch at 820-26 E. Allegheny Avenue . Its original construction in 1924 and an enlargement 10 years later were designed in the Classical Revival Style by the firm of the influential architect Horace Trumbauer, and a second, Modernist style addition in 1952 was the work of Paul Monaghan, who was also known for Roman Catholic-related buildings in Philadelphia.
 Beneficial Savings Bank at 820-26 E.Allegheny Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In addition to the seven designations, the Historical Commission approved the installation of a mural on the historic building at 1631-37 Arch Street . The 1915 building was designed by architect John Windrim for the Bell Telephone Company and placed on the local register in 2008. The one-story mural with a theme of Holocaust remembrance and education will be added to the east facade, overlooking the Horwitz-Wasserman Holocaust Memorial Plaza, the first public Holocaust monument in the United States. The request noted that the wall was originally a party wall, having been exposed in the early 1960s when the adjacent buildings were demolished.
 The Historical Commission approved a request for a continuance for the nomination of Piers 38 and 40 at 775 S. Christopher Columbus Boulevard , originally submitted in October 2021. It will now be reviewed at the July meeting of the Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation.
 Tags: Abraham Lincoln Historic theaters Historical Commission Meeting Report Horace Trumbauer Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: A New Book Celebrates Philadelphia’s Rich Vegetarian History
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
The Quaker City is responsible for the birth and growth of vegetarianism in the United States, according to Vance Lehmkuhl, author of Revolutionary Peace: How Philadelphia Launched the U.S. Vegetarian and Vegan Movement . “Philadelphia is known for its role in the American Revolutionary War, but what this book tries to bring to light is its important role in an ongoing shift－what we might call Revolutionary Peace.”
 Packed with interesting details and complemented with winsome illustrations by the author, Revolutionary Peace profiles more than 20 people who practiced and promoted meatless diets, including the founding father who touted the benefits of “tau-fu,” the vegetarian who co-founded the Pennsylvania SPCA, and the crusader who inspired the Graham cracker.
 “There's no dispute that Philly is the starting point for U.S. animal advocacy , as well as the driving force behind U.S. vegetarianism for almost the whole 19th century,” said Lehmkuhl. “It’s not random: the originating group were religious dissidents, and Philadelphia’s establishment as a community of enlightenment and religious freedom attracted them.”
 Before there was a movement, individual 18th century Philadelphians of note include Ben Franklin, an on-and-off vegetarian. In 1770, while in London, he sent his friend John Bartram rhubarb seeds, dry peas for making soup, and “Chinese garavances” (soybeans) with instructions on how to use them to make a “cheese” called “tau-fu.” Benjamin Lay and Anthony Benezet were influential abolitionists who came to oppose exploitation of animals. “It was his linking humans’ oppression with their oppression of animals that made Lay unique for his time,” wrote Lehmkuhl.
 A Movement is Born 
 Revolutionary Peace traces the start of the vegetarian movement in the United States to the 1817 arrival in Philadelphia of members of a religious sect known as the Bible Christians. Led by Reverend William Metcalfe, with active support from his wife Susannah, the group believed that humans were not meant to eat animals. “At first, Metcalfe and his Philly congregation struggled,” says Lehmkuhl. “Their views on animals, and against eating them, were largely unwelcome. They were hissed at as ‘heretics’ in the street.” The congregation eventually would grow and become able to afford its own church building on North 3rd Street.
 Meanwhile, Sylvester Graham was promoting a diet that banned meat, alcohol, butter, cheese, sugar, tea, coffee, all drugs, and most importantly, white bread because it was stripped of nutrients. He called for people to make their own bread, using coarsely ground, unsifted whole wheat flour. The flour became know as Graham flour, the philosophy Grahamism, and its adherents Grahamites. “Grahamite boarding houses were established in Philadelphia and other cities. Here people could eat meat-free, drink alcohol-free, and socialize with like-minded people.” Lehmkuhl notes that before Graham and before the word ”vegetarianism” was coined in the 1840s, vegetarians were referred to as Pythagoreans.
 A portrait of Reverend William Metcalfe from History of the Philadelphia Bible-Christian Church for the First Century of its Existence, from 1817 to 1917 (1922) | Photo: Public Domain
 In 1850, Metcalfe, Graham, William Alcott, and others established the American Vegetarian Society and held their first convention in Philadelphia. Describing the “vegetarian feast” that closed the proceedings, the September 13, 1850 edition of the Public Ledger noted “upwards of 30 cooked varieties of food, [including] potatoes, bread, and savory dishes of various kinds.” In addition to serving as secretary, Metcalfe edited and published the Society’s magazine, the American Vegetarian and Health Journal .
 With the deaths of Graham in 1851 and Metcalfe in 1862, the movement struggled. “The death blow to early-19th-century vegetarianism came in the form of the Civil War,” said Lehmkuhl. “Many vegetarians were torn between pacifism and abolitionist warfare. Grahamism, the more severe form of vegetarianism, petered out, and Graham began to be remembered only for his flour.”
 Renewal 
 Lehmkuhl credits Henry S. Clubb with reviving the vegetarian movement in the United States. A strict pacifist, Clubb enlisted in the Union Army at the start of the Civil War, but refused to carry a weapon. He eventually moved to Philadelphia, became leader of the Bible Christians in 1877, launched the Vegetarian Society of America and its Philadelphia chapter, and published the vegetarian magazine Food, Home, and Garden .
 The Philadelphia Times profiled Clubb in October 1895. “As an example of what a vegetable diet will do for a man, Mr. Clubb stands a hale and hearty argument. Although fast approaching the allotted age of three score years and ten, he is still bright-eyed and erect. His hair, although gray, is luxuriant, and his cheeks have a rosy glow indicative of health. He is a brilliant conversationalist, and is at his best when advancing some argument in favor of a vegetable regiment.”
 Lehmkuhl notes that Clubb persevered well into the 20th century. “It was only after his death in 1921 at age 94 that the American Bible Christians finally dissolved, meeting occasionally in each other’s homes, and then not at all.”
 Animal welfare advocate Caroline Earle White. Date unknown. | Photo: Public Domain
 Credit for the most enduring contributions to animal welfare goes to Caroline Earle White. A vegetarian, she co-founded the Pennsylvania Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (PSPCA). When the male-dominated leadership limited her role, she created the Women’s Branch of the PSPCA, currently operating in Bensalem as the Women’s Animal Center. In 1883, she established what would become the American Anti-Vivisection Society in Philadelphia. The organization remains active from its headquarters on Old York Road in Jenkintown.
 “Working with activists such as Mary F. Lovell, Annie Lowry, and Dr. Wilson Cary Swann, she led the way for the installation of [water] fountains throughout Philadelphia.” The fountains provided a basin of fresh water for people, horses, and other animals. Lehmkuhl reports that “many of the fountains remain around the city, though most do not now have running water. One that does, outside of wintertime, is at the [south end] of Washington Square.”
 Evolution 
 Mid-19th century vegetarians who mainly viewed their cause as a moral or social reform issue often identified as pacifists and abolitionists as well. In the early 1900s, more adherents were emphasizing personal health, and with the introduction of the concept of “veganism” in the mid-20th century, avoiding all forms of animal exploitation and cruelty became an important motivation. By the turn of the 21st century, awareness of the role of industrial animal agriculture in the climate crisis underscored the environmental benefits of veganism, along with human health and animal welfare concerns.
 Alfonsie Austin, owner of the now-defunct Basic 4 Vegetarian Cafe at Reading Terminal Market. | Photo courtesy of American Vegan Society
 Revolutionary Peace goes on to recount how the vegan movement emerged and continues to thrive in Philadelphia. It relates how H. ‘Jay’ Dinshah’s experience at a slaughterhouse on Front Street inspired him to found the American Vegan Society (AVS) in 1960, how beginning in 1981, Alfonsie Austin’s Basic 4 Vegetarian food stall in Reading Terminal Market made animal-free food accessible and appealing, and how creative vegan entrepreneurs have made Philly a modern hub of plant-based dining.
 In 2021, the AVS opened the American Vegan Center at 17 N. 2nd Street. With Vance Lehmkuhl as director, the center offers vegan-themed books, cooking demonstrations, and snacks. Lehmkuhl oversees programming and conducts Veg History walking tours. His previous books include Eating Vegan in Philly and V for Veg: The Best of Philly’s Vegan Food Column .
 Tags: book review food history 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: A Performance and Podcast Explore the Complexities of the MOVE Bombing
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
For those over the age of 40, the May 13, 1985 bombing of MOVE on Osage Avenue in West Philadelphia may reignite anger, assumptions, confusion, and shock over the events before and during the conflict between the Black liberation group and the Philadelphia Police Department. A reading of journalist Maida Odom’s play, MOVE Mocks Us All , will take place on Saturday, May 17 at Temple University. The performance, hosted by Klein College of Media and Communication, the Logan Center for Urban Investigative Reporting, and The Philadelphia Inquirer, is being presented to memorialize the events and provide a clearer image of MOVE as an organization and the culture of Philadelphia’s police force from the terms of former mayors Frank Rizzo to Wilson Goode, the city’s first Black mayor. The spoken word play is directed by Ontaria Kim Wilson.
 Odom’s reading caps the six-part series, MOVE: Untangling the Tragedy , a new podcast about double standards of justice, a so-called out of control cult, police brutality, and the inequity that underlined it all,” that was launched this spring. The podcast is hosted and produced by Temple journalism professor Linn Washington Jr. who has been following MOVE throughout his 50-year career as a reporter for The Philadelphia Daily News and The P hiladelphia Tribune . Washington, who initially reported on MOVE after joining the Daily News in 1975, and Odom, former reporter for The Philadelphia Inquirer , were both present on the day of the bombing and reconnected years later.
 The project began in 2024 as a conversation about how to approach the 40th anniversary of the bombing. Washington said that “one thing led to another” as he and Yvonne Latty, the director of the Logan Center and a professor of journalism at Temple, decided that they would do something about it. Latty, the executive producer of the podcast, drew upon her team, including graduate student Natalie Reitz who led most of the research and pulled from the findings of the MOVE Commission and material in the MOVE Collection archived in Temple University Libraries’ Special Collections Research Center.
 Odom is also featured in the podcast as she was stationed directly across the street from 6221 Osage Avenue shortly before the bombing. She was evacuated from her location an hour before the shootout began and a C4-laced bomb was dropped on the MOVE house by a police helicopter. Her experience later became a play written only a few years after the event as a way to process the trauma. The play was performed for limited audiences in both Philadelphia and New York before being retired.
 “I remembered her play and some other things that she had collected, but had never released publicly,” Washington said. He informed Odom about the podcast, which prompted her interest in having the play being part of the series.
 Latty said that the point of the project is “to sort of untangle” the complexities of the circumstances and to help people who may be unfamiliar with MOVE learn about what transpired. Another goal of the podcast is to keep the events from fading from our collective memory.
 The title, MOVE: Mocks Us All, is derived from how “this small band made a mockery of our government systems as well as our collective projected humanity," explained Odom. "It exposed every level of society. Neighbors, government, media, and individuals as antithetical for everything we profess to stand for.”
 MOVE was founded by Vincent “Benny” Leaphart who later changed his name to John Africa. All members took on that surname “as a sign of unity and commitment to the teachings” of their founder, according to writer and member Mike Africa Jr. The group's development came about during the late 1970s when the assassination of civil rights leaders was still fresh in memory. MOVE’s competitive grassroots approach to protest often involved the use of megaphones to spread its message. Taking down MOVE became a long-time project of then Mayor Frank Rizzo who confronted the organization at violent events leading up to the 1985 bombing.
 In book Let It Burn by Michael and Randi Boyette, the authors describe the standoff as “a group of revolutionaries barricaded themselves in a tiny rowhouse in working class Philadelphia. Outside the house is the assembled might of a major metropolitan police force, which has literally prepared for war.” By the end of the confrontation, six adults, two teens, and three children were dead leaving only Ramona Africa as the lone survivor.
 Was MOVE unjustly persecuted by a brutal police force and Mayor Goode's administration? Or were they overly aggressive activists that were a threat to public safety and accountable for their own fate? These are questions that each listener to the podcast and attendee at the reading will be asking themselves. Yet, as we grapple with the answers, Philadelphia City Council recently announced a resolution to mark May 13 as a day of remembrance.
 Although it has been over 40 years since MOVE was founded, Africa's own words highlight what is still often overlooked. “Most people don’t know that MOVE members were animal rights activists. Most people don’t know MOVE members were environmentalists. Most people don’t know that MOVE members were prison rights advocates and civil rights activists. Most people don’t know.”
 MOVE Mocks Us All: A Staged Reading will take place on Saturday, May 17, at 6 p.m. in Tomlinson Theater at Temple University. The performance is free and open to the public. Register for the event and see more details here: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/move-mocks-us-all-a-staged-reading-tickets-1328575167089?aff=oddtdtcreator 
 Listen to the podcast, MOVE: Untangling the Traged y, on Apple and Spotify .
 Tags: African-American history Cobbs Creek performance art Philadelphia Police Department W. Wilson Goode Jr. West Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Remembering Joel Spivak, Champion of All Things "Old Philly"
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Many people and organizations, including Hidden City, are dedicated to preserving Philadelphia history through the lens of its built environment. Joel H. Spivak celebrated all the things that went on in those buildings and neighborhoods. “Joel represented the best of Philadelphia culture,” his longtime friend Len Davidson stated. “He was about funky, folksy, blue collar neighborhood people.”
 Spivak was born on October 25, 1939. Except for a stint in the Army at age 19, he was a lifelong resident of Philadelphia, residing in neighborhoods that included West Oak Lane, Parkside, and South Street.
 He attended Philadelphia College of Art and Drexel University’s Architecture Department. Although he didn’t finish his architectural studies, in the early 1970s he went on to engage in the rehabbing of properties along South Street, after the plans for a cross-town expressway , which caused a widespread abandonment of the corridor, were cancelled. “Joel moved to 4th and South into a place with no plumbing or electricity,” recalled Davidson. “He bought it for around $400.”
 As part of the artistic community that revitalized the neighborhood, Spivak lent his woodworking talents to several of the independent shops and restaurants springing up on South Street at that time. Later, he became one of those merchants himself, when he opened Rocketships & Accessories , a shop dedicated to space-themed toys and paraphernalia, ranging from early Flash Gordon to then-current Star Wars.
 He also was part of the Dumpster Divers. Along with Davidson and others, they would create artwork, furniture and other items from salvaged materials. “The initial stuff that Joel used to do involved things he found on the street, like headboards. He’d take this stuff and make things out of it,” said Davidson. “The first one I saw, he had made a totem pole around 20 feet high out of wood objects. He also made decorative pieces of furniture out of pieces he’d found.”
 Spivak continued plying his woodworking and construction skills long after the renaissance of South Street. In the late 1990s, while working for the non-profit Neighborhood Housing Services, he rehabbed 5735 North Park Avenue, which won a "Best in American Living Platinum Award for Outstanding Home Design in Affordable Housing" from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development.
 Spivak was on a mission to increase peoples’ appreciation of hot dogs by creating and promoting National Hot Dog Month. “National Hot Dog Month was a lot of fun,” recalled his wife, Diane Keller. “Joel collected hot dog t-shirts from around the world. For his 75th birthday in 2014, he cooked and gave out hot dogs in front of Hahnemann Hospital where he was born.”
 Another crusade began in September 1997, when Spivak and Davidson organized the Philadelphia Rowhouse Sports Day Olympics as part of the first Fringe Festival. They blocked off the 200 block of New Street in Old City, behind the Painted Bride Art Center, and played street games like chink, wireball, half ball, stepball, wall ball, and dead box with around 150 attendees. “All things that kids did in the 50s and 60s,” explained Davidson. “All you needed was chalk, a half of a ball, and a stick. Basically, those things had died, but Joel and I were trying to bring them back.”
 After that initial event, they continued to organize games in different neighborhoods, like within the City’s Free Streets program. “People who know it, who played it back in the day, have a visceral reaction when they see us,” said Davidson. “They watch us playing it, but people who are five or ten or forty will try playing it.”
 But it wasn’t just whimsical fun and games for Spivak. He had an encyclopedic knowledge of Philadelphia’s trains and trolleys, which resulted in the co-authoring of books on the subject. “He restored the Wanamaker Monorail that’s now at the Please Touch Museum,” noted Keller, combining his fascination with trains with his building and repairing talents.
 “These are the things that make a city,” said Davidson. “We weren’t looking at it as nostalgia. That’s what Joel was about, saving what makes Philadelphia what it is.”
 Joel H. Spivak, 1939-2025. | Photo courtesy of Diane Keller
 His wide-ranging interests also led to civic engagement. “He was involved in so many things,” said Kvn Josef Shapiro, director of community engagement at Congregation Shivtei Yeshuron Ezras Israel , known as the Little Shul. Located at 2015 South 4th Street, it is the last active rowhouse synagogue in South Philadelphia, founded in 1876 at a time when there were more than 100 in the neighborhood.
 “Around the year 2000, the congregation got a notice from the City, ordering it to repair the building or tear it down,” explained Shapiro. “Joel was one of a handful of people who got it together to save it, helping with fundraising and architectural designs.” He continued to serve on the board of directors until his passing.
 Keller said, “He got more involved in his Jewish heritage later in life,” but still combined some playful creativity with his serious interest in his faith. “He had his second bar mitzvah at the age of 73 at the Little Shul,” added Shapiro. “He made yarmulkes for everyone out of biodegradable paper, with seeds embedded in them, so they could be planted.”
 He also served on the board of trustees of the Old Pine Conservancy, the non-profit that supports the preservation of Old Pine Street Church and cemetery , Old Pine Community Center, and the Presbyterian Historical Society.
 Further afield from his Bella Vista neighborhood, Spivak maintained three small memorial parks for military veterans at 31st Street and Girard Avenue, 3rd and Bainbridge Streets, and Cochran Triangle at 37th Street and Lancaster Avenue.
 Throughout his life he enjoyed mentoring youth, going back to the South Street revival days when he’d teach woodworking to neighborhood kids. “In the 90s he sponsored a youth baseball team, the Buccaneers, at Sacks Playground at 4th and Washington,” added Keller. Adults benefited from encounters with him, too. “One of Joel’s favorite things was to go into a party where he didn’t know anyone, and he could strike up a conversation and hold forth,” Keller said. “I was always so impressed when he talked with people. He made it so personal and fun.”
 Over the decades, Spivak engaged in all his interests and lived his life as the ultimate Philadelphia humanist.
 Nearly a year ago, Spivak had a stroke that left him mostly incapacitated until his death at age 85 on April 21. His family and friends are planning a celebration of his life on May 22nd from 4-7 p.m. at the TLA, 334 South Street. Another memorial is being planned for the Little Shul in October.
 Tags: "Old Philadelphia" Historic Preservation Joel Spivak obituary 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: South Broad Street Landmark Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Philadelphia Historical Commission faced contentious discussions while considering several items on its agenda during the course of its meeting on May 9. Nevertheless, seven new properties were added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, a contested designation was upheld, and new construction on the site of a demolished historic building was approved.
 The latter item proposed to construct eight townhouses at 1600-06 Berks Street , the former site of St. Laurentius Roman Catholic Church, built in 1885 and designed by noted ecclesiastical architect Edwin Forrest Durang. The church was placed on the local register in 2015. After the Archdiocese of Philadelphia closed St. Laurentius as a worship site in 2014 and sold it to a developer who proposed repurposing it into townhouses, the plan was met with community objections. The building lay vacant and deteriorating for years thereafter. St. Laurentius was demolished in 2022 , with the Historical Commission’s approval requiring either the retention of the front facade or the salvaging of historic elements to be incorporated into any new building. It appears that the demolition contractor, HC Site Construction, Inc., did not comply with that requirement and demolished the church in its entirety.
 St. Laurentius Roman Catholic Church in Fishtown was demolished in 2022. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The current construction proposal, submitted by a new owner who purchased the empty lot in March of this year, received scant comment during the lengthy discussion period. Rather, most of it was taken up by expressions of regret by Historical Commission members, questions from the public about the fate of the historical elements, the law department and staff maintaining there was nothing that could be done about them, and individuals urging the Commission to learn from the experience.
 A discussion followed of a potential memorial item or event for St. Laurentius. General sentiment was that a state commemorative marker was insufficient, but ideas like an annual event were deemed impractical. Finally, the construction request was approved, and, as part of the approval, the applicant will design a public display to be permanently affixed to the building, with the design reviewed by the Architectural Committee and subsequently the Historical Commission.
 A nomination for designation of the property at 1505-07 Orthodox Street, the home of the Historical Society of Frankford, evoked some unusual feedback. Unlike most contentious comments which object to the designation, these were in favor of the nomination, but had issues with the nominator and some perceived omissions in the research, and that they wished to submit their own nomination. Architect Frank Watson designed it in 1930 in the Georgian Revival style as a purpose-built historical society that reflects the social and historical heritage of Frankford. The Historical Commission’s approval stipulated that the letters it had received regarding the nomination be incorporated into the materials about the designation.
 The Historical Society of Frankford at 1505-07 Orthodox Street. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 The other six nominations, representing a wide range of city neighborhoods, proceeded more smoothly.
 The property at 756 N. 43rd Street , the Laura Wheeler Waring House, was added to the local register for its association with the artist who lived there from 1927-1948 and was known for her portraits of many figures in the Harlem Renaissance.
 The one-room Maple Grove School at 10151 Academy Road was designated owing to its location on the border of the former Moreland and Byberry townships, reflecting the area’s rural past. It was also noted that the site, at more than three-fourths of an acre of undeveloped land, likely holds archaeological artifacts related to its use as a schoolhouse from 1800 to 1918. The current school was built in 1854 and is attributed to architect Samuel Sloan , who designed Philadelphia School District buildings in the 1850s.
 1631, 1633, and 1635 Francis Street in North Philadelphia. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In Francisville, three adjacent properties, 1631, 1633, and 1635 Francis Street , that date to 1886 were designated for the Queen Anne style used by their builder, Charles C. Haines, and his use of pressed ornamental brick matching those by the Peerless Brick Company of Philadelphia.
 The Southwestern National Bank at 601 S. Broad Street was also added to the local register as a prominent fixture in South Philadelphia during a time of significant neighborhood growth. Dating to the late 1920s, it was designed in the Stripped Classicism style by architect Ralph Bencker, who designed banks, other commercial buildings, and numerous Horn & Hardart Automats in Philadelphia. More recently, the building was known as the Arts Bank and owned by the now-closed University of the Arts , which sold it to a developer in February of this year.
 Southwestern National Bank (aka Arts Bank) at 601 S. Broad Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler 
 Another bank building along Broad Street was added to the local register. At 700-02 N. Broad Street , the Northwestern National Bank shares the intersection of North Broad Street, Fairmount Avenue and Ridge Avenue with other preserved and rehabilitated buildings, including the Divine Lorraine and the Central Presbyterian Church. Built in 1917 in the Classical Revival style by architect Philip Merz, it represents a period when the city’s population spread northward and businesses concentrated along North Broad Street.
 The building at 1839-45 Lombard Street , the home of the former Philadelphia School of Occupational Therapy, was also designated historic. Constructed in 1930 with Art Deco characteristics, it is significant as the work of prominent architect Georgina Pope Yeatman, one of Philadelphia’s first practicing female architects. The school was also noteworthy as the first collegiate medicinal program in rehabilitation therapy.
 Philadelphia School of Occupational Therapy at 1839-45 Lombard Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The request to reconsider the designation of 34-36 E. Sharpnack Street was another subject of contentious discussion between the property owner, Sanctuary Church of God in Christ, and the nominator, East Mt. Airy Neighbors. The church was added to the Philadelphia Register in November, 2024, owing to its association with three prominent figures in both the African Baptist church and the Germantown neighborhood: Reverend Dr. Jeremiah Wright, Sr., his wife Mary Henderson Wright, and their son, Reverend Dr. Jeremiah Wright, Jr. It also reflects a significant period in Germantown and Mt. Airy, beginning in 1896, when Sharpnack Street was a center of the African American community, and continuing until 1968 when the congregation moved to a larger facility at 29 W. Johnson Street. The Historical Commission unanimously upheld the designation.
 Tags: banks Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places St. Laurentius 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Advocates Work to Protect a 125-Year Old Home in Bryn Mawr Linked to Women's and LGBTQ+ History
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
125 years ago, a pioneering woman and math teacher enlisted the help of a well-known Main Line architect, William Lightfoot Price, to design an elegant home for her in Bryn Mawr. Eight decades later, another woman ahead of her time did her best to preserve the historic property in perpetuity. Now, the forward-looking vision of both hangs in the balance in Lower Merion. The Township's Board of Commissioners are wrangling with what to do with the potentially imperiled property, and more widely, how aggressively they want to pursue historic preservation as development pressure builds in Philadelphia’s western suburbs.
 The property in question is 17 Elliott Avenue, a two-and-a-half story, Arts and Crafts style home built in 1900. Located on the first block off of Lancaster Avenue in the heart of Bryn Mawr, the residence is something of a time capsule in the midst of modernity. In past decades, neighboring homes were razed to allow the expansion of Bryn Mawr’s commercial corridor, particularly the offices of water utility Aqua Pennsylvania, which now directly abut the property.
 The home was originally commissioned by Helen Sleeper Pearson, then a mathematics teacher at The Baldwin School, according to a historic nomination of the home authored by historic preservation professionals Arielle Harris and the late Aaron Wunsch . Perhaps more notable was Pearson's long-term “roomate” of four decades, Helen Dean King, an influential biologist who is credited with developing the modern lab rat while employed at the Wistar Institute , a Philadelphia-based scientific organization billed as the first independent biomedical research institute in the United States.
 Also of note, according to the home’s historic nomination, is a purpose-built attached car garage on the rear of the property, which appears to be the first such structure commissioned anywhere in the Philadelphia region. Advocates argue that this confluence of these factors–the unique design of a well-known architect, inhabitation by pioneering women likely of LGBTQ+ orientation, and a historical first in the form of the car garage–make 17 Elliott Avenue a prime candidate for inclusion on Lower Merion’s Historic Resource Inventory , which can offer protections against exterior alterations and demolition.
 17 Elliott Avenue was built for Helen Sleeper Pearson and her partner Helen Dean King in 1900. The home was designed by William Lightfoot Price, a groundbreaking architect of the Arts and Craft movement.| Photo: Michael Bixler
 However, whether Lower Merion’s commissioners deem that appropriate remains an open question. Although the township’s Historical Commission voted to confidently recommend approval of the nomination last fall, the township’s codes require both its Building and Planning Committee and Board of Commissioners to sign off. In a committee meeting held March 12, the nomination met resistance, narrowly staving off a trip to indefinite limbo by a 5-4 vote, before commissioners moved to punt the matter to a May 14 meeting, ostensibly to allow time to gather more information.
 Time may be of the essence. Harris and other proponents of listing say the current owner of the property plans to vacate the property soon and retire to Florida and worry he may sell to Aqua to fuel further expansion of its offices. Neither the owner of the home nor Aqua responded to a request for comment by this article's deadline. Some opposed to the nomination acknowledge the home appears to have significantly deferred maintenance, with the apparent financial burden of repair exceeding the current owner’s capacities. According to information shared by Township commissioners, the owner has expressed opposition to the nomination, citing concerns over his financial security and potential impacts to the resale value of the home.
 The owner’s opposition to the nomination lies at the heart of the debate for the commissioners, whose membership also comprises the Building and Planning Committee. Most appear to acknowledge the home’s historic bona fides. All also seem to agree that the Township has never before listed a property on its historic inventory over opposition of the owner. Yet, where they disagree is whether or not it is time to break with that precedent, setting up an acute question to be answered by the board in the months ahead: shall the Township prioritize preserving historic properties for the benefit of the community or private property rights for the benefit of their owners?
 Price, Pearson, and a Primordial Preservationist 
 That March is Women’s History Month strikes Harris as a compelling cosmic coincidence. A professional preservationist who has made 17 Elliott Avenue a personal passion project, Harris gravitates toward the stories of Pearson and King. Both were born to wealthy families in the 1860s. They used their positions of privilege as springboards to trailblazing lives. Pearson obtained both a bachelor’s and master’s degree from Smith College in Massachusetts and was reportedly the first graduate student ever enrolled there. She later enrolled for further study at Bryn Mawr College, at the time the only women’s college in the nation to offer doctoral studies, and began teaching mathematics at The Baldwin School nearby.
 The only known photo of Helen Sleeper Pearson. Date unknown. | Photo courtesy of Smith College
 King, eight years her junior, was educated at Vassar College and received her doctorate from Bryn Mawr, studying under Thomas Hunt Morgan, a “geneticist who established the chromosome theory of heredity through research on the fruit fly,” according to the historic nomination. Later at the Wistar Institute, through inbreeding experiments, King helped develop the “Wistar rat,” a colony of albino rodents with consistent genetic traits that were soon sold to scientists across the country. King’s professional interests occasionally crossed into treacherous territory: she became a voice for the early 20th century human eugenics movement and expressed comfort for inner-familial marriage under certain conditions. “[This] stands as a reminder of the complex and ethically fraught intersections between science and societal ideologies during that era,” Harris and Wunsch wrote in their nomination, adding that, “As the eugenics movement fell into scientific obsolescence, so did King’s musings on the topic.”
 Pearson and King likely met while the latter was enrolled at Bryn Mawr in the 1890s. By 1900, Census data show the pair were living together at a residence on a small side street in town. That same year, Pearson commissioned Price to design what would become their private and lasting home.
 Scientist Helen Dean King with her Wistar rats. Date unknown. | Image courtesy of The Wistar Institute
 Price, a Philadelphia native born 1861, started his career as a carpenter’s apprentice before receiving architectural training under architect Addison Hutton and possibly Frank Furness. He spent the first part of his career in partnership with his brother, Frank L. Price, primarily designing residences, including in developments in Wayne, St. Davids, Pelham, and Overbrook. Several other homes designed by Price are presently listed on Lower Merion’s historic inventory, although they trend much larger, none more notable than the French Gothic Woodmont mansion in Gladwyne. Yet, that property remains the only Price-designed building listed as a “Tier 1” property, which provides restrictions on exterior alteration.
 Price’s commission on 17 Elliott Avenue was a unique addition to his portfolio that came during a period of professional transition, according to Jeffrey Cohen, the Term Professor in Growth and Structure of Cities at Bryn Mawr College, who spoke in favor of the nomination at the March 12 meeting. From 1895 to 1903, Price practiced independently, culminating in his work designing Arts and Craft-style communities such as Rose Valley. Later, he would help establish the firm of Price & McLanahan under which he practiced until his death.
 Elevation drawings by architect William Lightfoot Price of 17 Elliot Avenue. | Images courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 However, his work on Elliott Avenue was “special,” Cohen said, urging Lower Merion’s commissioners to imagine he and Pearson, and possibly also King, sitting down together to merge their visions. “It was a very customized conversation about presenting their identities in a public way, in the very coded language of architectural form,” Cohen said. “It’s a combination of many adventurous parts, a very animated building.”
 Cohen pointed in particular to the home’s main bifurcated facade, where a large semicircular arch reminiscent of ancient Pompeii dominates the left half, while stone and gothic pointed arches similar to the architecture of Bryn Mawr College rise on the right.
 Yet, the real innovation comes at the rear of the property, advocates say, where Pearson specifically requested an attached car garage, or “automobile stable” using the parlance of the time. According to Harris, an exhaustive search of historical records resulted in the determination that it was a prescient addition and the first of its kind in the Philadelphia region, even though car company executives themselves were building homes on the Main Line at the same time. In 1900, there were just 8,000 registered automobiles nationwide, the nomination found, a number that would grow to 450,000 within a decade. “The inclusion of the attached garage foreshadowed the ubiquitousness that cars would come to have within and beyond the Main Line in the years to come,” it concluded.
 An article published in The Philadelphia Inquirer in 1900 announces William Lightfoot Price's being contracted to design 17 Elliot Avenue.
 All of these elements would come to be very much appreciated by a future owner. Following Pearson’s death in 1942, King sold the home. Subsequent transactions left it, by 1949, with Evalyn Vickers, maternal grandmother of Aaron Wunsch. Eventually the home passed to Lydia Vickers, Wunsch’s mother, who sold the home to its present owner in 1983.
 Vickers currently resides in an out-of-state assisted living facility, and Wunsch, a well-known Philadelphia preservationist and University of Pennsylvania professor who co-authored the Elliott Avenue nomination, passed away from cancer last year. However, Wunsch’s wife, Jillian Galle, acting as an executor of the family estate, said that Vickers placed several covenants on the deed of the house at the time of sale to the current owner. Among them are clauses, she said, that require both exterior and interior features of the house to remain as originally designed, that the family be given right of first refusal for any subsequent sales, and that sale to the neighboring water authority be expressly forbidden. As Lower Merion had no historic preservation ordinance at the time, it was the best she could do to try and protect the home, Galle explained. “She really made this thing watertight. She was fully aware at the time that there was a start of rampant development on the Main Line,” she said.
 The design of the home at 17 Elliot Avenue included an attached car garage, the first of its kind in the Philadelphia region. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Galle, who spoke in favor of the nomination at the Lower Merion meeting, believes a listing on the Township’s historic inventory would add a layer of protection to the property. As it stands, Lower Merion's processes do not take any deed covenants into account: any perceived transgression would fall to the courts to enforce.
 Whether or not the home’s current owner, a retired attorney who Galle said knowingly and willingly agreed to the covenants at the time of sale, has properly maintained the home remains an open question. Several current neighbors spoke at the March 12 meeting supporting his objection to the nomination. One claimed that in recent years, a significant number of stones fell from the building’s facade, revealing a “rotting” substructure beneath. Such rot extends to the home’s windows and roof, he claimed.
 A Debate For the Ages 
 In advance of the Building and Planning Committee meeting, Harris and Galle said they received indications that the Township’s commissioners would vote to reject the nomination, citing their concern over the owner’s objections and past practice of not adding buildings to its historic inventory under such circumstances.
 For a time at the meeting, things appeared headed that way. Public comment came first, with Harris, Galle, Cohen, the Lower Merion Conservancy, and several other members of the preservation community speaking in support, while neighbors and friends of the current owner of 17 Elliott Avenue argued against.
 When it came time for commissioners to decide, chair Joshua Grimes made a motion to postpone the matter indefinitely. But in a surprise turn, Commissioner Sean Whalen objected, saying he believed doing so would effectively kill the effort to list the home and leave it in danger of eventual demolition. “Let’s be real here.
