If we postpone indefinitely, we are throwing this out and saying no to this application,” Whelan said. “Indefinitely is just a death knell to this.”
 The interjection kicked off an hours-long debate among the commissioners. At one point, a vote was called on the motion to postpone indefinitely, which failed, 5-4. Ultimately, a later motion by Commissioner Gilda Kramer to postpone until the May 14 meeting passed by a 6-3 vote.
 Throughout the back-and-forth, Whelan appeared the most ardent supporter of approving the nomination. He noted that nothing in the Township’s codes required commissioners to deny a historic nomination if the present owner was opposed and that the township’s own Historical Commission had found it strongly met the guidelines for inclusion. He also referenced long-running discussions that the Township’s current historic ordinance is inadequate to protect historic properties. In this context, 17 Elliott Avenue presented an opportunity to change the paradigm, he argued. “We’re being asked to make a designation which is opposed by the individual owner. That’s a very serious shift and I get that it’s new,” Whelan said. “However, our historic designation system isn’t working. We need to start to put our foot down.”
 Historic homes on Elliot Avenue were previously demolished to make way for the construction of offices owned by Aqua Pennsylvania. Preservation advocates fear that the water utility company will purchase 17 Elliot Avenue from its current owner and demolish it as well. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Most vigorously opposed was Commissioner V. Scott Zelov, whose ward contains 17 Elliott Avenue. Zelov said he is personally familiar with the owner and knows him to be a “passionate man.” He dismissed concerns over impending sale and demolition of the property as hearsay, and added that, in the past, he had personally protested the demolition of other historic properties. However, noting other, “larger” historic properties in Lower Merion were not fully protected, as well the owner’s opposition, Zelov mused whether efforts were best spent elsewhere and said he did not support the nomination. “This just isn’t the property to change how we do things,” Zelov said.
 Several commissioners expressed mixed feelings, admitting an internal struggle to balance protecting historic properties against development pressure with overriding the wishes of a homeowner claiming significant economic hardship. “This is absolutely gut wrenching. Seven years on the board, this is easily one of the most difficult decisions I’ve had to make,” said Commissioner Andrew Garvin. “Our charge is to weigh the historic significance of this house, with what’s happening in our township, with what’s happening with our residents. It is a big burden to put on the owner.”
 Ultimately the commissioners seemed to coalesce around a compromise of reconsidering the matter at the May 14 meeting. Township staff indicated that would likely allow them time to assemble more information about various aspects of the matter. Yet, they also warned that some questions, such as to what extent a historic listing would actually impact the value of the property, would likely be unanswerable.
 Following the meeting, Galle expressed skepticism of the narrative that the current owner of 17 Elliott is under extreme financial duress, noting that he agreed to the deed covenants that require upkeep of the home and that both he and his late wife were working professionals. However, she also agreed with Harris that there was a new sense of hope, noting the commissioners’ nearly unanimous acknowledgement that the home meets the criteria for historic listing. "I look forward to working with commissioners, township planning, and preservation staff, and the property owner to ensure this property, and its critical role in women's and LGBTQ+ history in the township, can remain protected for future generations,” Harris said.
 Tags: historic houses LGBTQIA+ History suburbs William Lightfoot Price Women's history 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Philadelphia's "Cardboard Genius" Takes Center Stage in a New Exhibition
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
If you want to be amazed and astonished, step into the world of an artist who views autism as his magical power. Cardboard Genius: The Architectural Marvels of Kambel Smith is now on view at Historic Germantown through June 29. Smith, a self-taught artist who grew up in Germantown, builds large-scale, intricate replicas of architecturally significant buildings out of cardboard he salvages from the trash. Museum visitors bend over Smith's buildings like Lilliputians, peering into windows, exclaiming at the attention to detail.
 The scene stealers in the show include Smith's rendition of Philadelphia's Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse), which rises above its pedestrian purpose like a Roman Temple, and the majesty of the Georgia State House with its golden cupola. Kambel's sense of humor hits a home run with his creation of the Germantown Historical Society, the very building in which the exhibition is held.
 "Seeing Kambel's work in the round is a transformative experience," said Tuomi Forrest, executive director of Historic Germantown. "He has shown his art around the world, but not here before. We are getting an extremely positive response with folks from around the region and across the country.
 How does he do it? A plaque on the wall of the exhibition written by Smith's father, Lonnie, answers their question. "He doesn't plan things on paper. He just sees the building in his mind and starts working with a few pieces of cardboard, a knife, and some paint. He brings entire cityscapes to life."
 Chinatown Friendship Gate by Kambel Smith. | Photo: Stacia Friedman
 Since 2019, Smith has had solo shows at major galleries in New York City, London, and Atlanta. His work is in the collections of the American Folk Museum in Manhattan, the John Michael Kohler Arts Center in Wisconsin, the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Philadelphia, and the West Collection in Oaks, Pennsylvania. In 2021, he was a Pew Fellowship recipient. Last August, Smith, now 37, was featured in the New York Times Magazine . The article references Smith's nearly 27-foot-tall version of the Burj Khalida in Dubai, the world's tallest skyscraper.
 "He's a wild card. You never know. He always seems to know what to make," said Lonnie Smith, who is more than just a supportive family member. If not for their father's encouragement, Kambel and his brother Kantai may not have discovered their own unique talents.
 "Kambel and Kantai were both diagnosed with autism as children," said Lonnie who raised his two boys and a daughter on his own. "The beginning of Kambel's life was filled with hardship and trauma. His mother left us, and he didn't fit in. I encouraged my sons to think of themselves not as people with limitations, but instead as ‘Autisarians,' a term I invented to describe beings born with super-human abilities. I made up stories that inspired them both to go beyond expectation," he explained.
 The Roundhouse by Kambel Smith. | Photo: Stacia Friedman
 "During the past 10 years, I have engaged Kambel in a daily storytelling session of improvised science fiction in which I would start the narrative and Kambel would respond by finishing it. This unleashed a spate of drawings by Kambel of characters and fictional landscapes in their shared stories. I became a different person because I had to change my life to suit what they needed."
 As a result, Smith experienced a burst of creativity and confidence, resulting in a series of graphic novels. His father learned how to code so that he could teach Kantai, who is gifted in math. Using that skill, Kantai created an award-winning 17-minute animated film about Austisarians.
 When he was 15, Smith developed an interest in oil painting. He was quite talented but, eventually, the family could not afford to buy canvas. However, there was no shortage of cardboard in the trash. How any young man could turn boxes that formerly transported oranges into monumental works of art defines the meaning of Autisarian.
 "One of his first pieces was a large-scale model of the Philadelphia Museum of Art," said Lonnie. "It was so big, we didn't know how to transport it. Eventually, every room of our Germantown home was transformed into Kambel's studio," he explained. "We needed more space so we recently moved to Reading, Pennsylvania." Neighbors there quickly took notice when Kambel recreated Reading's iconic Pagoda built in 1907. "It was so large he had to work on it on the lawn," said his father. "Within minutes a TV crew showed up!"
 Benjamin Franklin Bridge by Kambel Smith. | Photo: Stacia Friedman
 Chris Byrne, founder and director of the Elaine De Kooning House in East Hampton, New York, first discovered Smith on Instagram in 2018. The timing was critical. As soon as Byrne began representing him, he elevated Smith on the national and international stage. "In 2018, I showed his art at the De Kooning House, then at the Outsider Art Fair in New York in 2019 and, later, in Atlanta," said Byrne. "He's relatively young by artist standards."
 At the Marlborough Gallery show in 2019, Smith's showed replicas of buildings by his favorite architects, Robert Venturi and Frank Gehry. While Gehry's designs would be challenging in any medium, Smith reproduced Gehry's Lou Ruvo Center for Brain Health in foam core board, paper, ink, and acrylic paint, achieving Gehry's feat of making solid buildings appear to be melted steel.
 Smith's family created Autisarian.org , a nonprofit organization dedicated to changing the face of autism by changing the attitude of those challenged by the so-called disorder. On his Facebook page, Smith identifies as an "autistic survivor" and states, "Autism is not a disease. Do not try to cure us. Try to understand us."
 Cardboard Genius: The Architectural Marvels of Kambel Smith is free and open to the public at Germantown Historical Society, 5501 Germantown Avenue, from 12-4 p.m. Thursday to Saturday. See additional details here: https://historicgermantownpa.org/exhibits/ 
 Tags: art exhibition Germantown sculpture 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: The Revolution Will Not Be Alphabetized: Saying Goodbye to Philly's Lettered Bus Route System
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
SEPTA recently replaced six of the seven remaining lettered bus routes, G, H, J, L, R, and XH, with numbers 63, 71, 41, 51, 82, and 81. This major adjustment is part of the transit company's initiative, dubbed " Bus Revolution, that comes just over 100 years since the letter system’s inception.
 Lex Powers, SEPTA’s director of information design, said that this replacement “will go a long way to making the [transit] network clearer.” The overall goal is to help passengers easily navigate the various routes throughout the city.
 Many Philadelphians seem reluctant to lose the lettered system that has long been a part of their lives. Yet, without much fuss or confusion, the replacement has happened. Affected buses will display both the old letter and the new route number until enough time passes to allow the number to become the new normal among passengers.
 As we say goodbye, a question remains. How did the city’s mass transit system receive a mix of lettered and numbered bus routes in the first place? 
 SEPTA's Route E bus at 69th Street Terminal in Upper Darby in 1969. | Photo: David Wilson 
 SEPTA’s current initiative has been part of a 60-year process that eliminated (Route F in 1971), merged (Route Q to 25 and 43 in 1985), and clarified (Route C to 16 and 4 in 2012) transit routes as part of an expanded program that encompasses the entire bus system. This current iteration has dealt with starts and stops due to delays coinciding with fare increases, public outcry, and budgetary shortfalls.
 Powers said that his job is “to respond to a need to make [SEPTA] services, information, and communication more consistent.” He explained that phasing out the final seven routes is “an opportunity to rethink things holistically rather than making ad hoc decisions.” The change was not particularly controversial. Most commuters understood why it had to happen. For the passengers, according to Powers, the goal is to immediately signify that “when people see a number, they know it is a bus. When they see a letter, they know it is a subway or a trolley.” The Bus Revolution was intended to “help people navigate [SEPTA] network with designations that are more intuitive and clearer.”
 Philadelphia Transit Company's "R" bus in 1963. | Photo courtesy of the Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 There are similarities between the current changes to the mass transit designation network and past efforts to improve it. In 1920, some service-related issues were presented to Mayor J. Hampton Moore by the Philadelphia Rapid Transit Company (PRT). A transit commission report dated May 25, 1920, stated that “The present transit service in the City of Philadelphia is so grossly inadequate as to threaten the proper development of the city.” Over the next few years, modernization projects and routes were added to assist with overcrowded routes and to service areas outside the central business district.
 In 1922, the Frankford Elevated began operations, and newly rechristened trolley routes were launched. Route 6 was previously the Huntingdon and Cumberland Line, Route 15 was known as the Girard Avenue Line, and the Bridesburg Line became Route 73. Also put into effect were new transfer privileges that coincided with the new routes to ease passengers’ transitions.
 A postcard from 1926 shows one of Philadelphia Rapid Transit's new "Mitten" gas electric motorbus. | Image: Ebay
 By 1923, trial trips of “Mitten” buses, named after Thomas E. Mitten, president of PRT, debuted with routes designated “Special” which drove up and down Roosevelt Boulevard. Due to this success, the first lettered bus, the A (Broad–Erie), was designated the same year. The local press gave it a positive reception and helped sell its virtues to the public. This excerpt from an article published by The Morning Ledger in 1923 captures the moment. “Like other good things, the boulevard buses will advertise themselves. The enthusiasm with which they were greeted by the public on Sunday, the first day of their operation, and the crowds who rode in them all day in spite of the rain, may be taken as an index of the reception awaiting this type of urban transportation facility when it shall come into more general use.”
 Double decker buses, which were either semi-opened or closed on the top level, akin to what London, New York, and Chicago were utilizing, began to go into circulation. This fulfilled a promise by PRT to passengers to make sure there was a seat for everyone.
 New open-top double deckers bus in service along Roosevelt Boulevard between Broad Street and Erie Avenue in 1923. | Photos courtesy of the Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 As the popularity of lettered buses increased, more lettered routes were added. The letter designation was used to distinguish between the numerical trolleys and the lettered bus routes. By late October 1923, motorbuses were flaunted as a transit option in Center City. “Motorbuses of the type now used on Roosevelt Boulevard are satisfying everyone and should be used whenever practical to relieve the ever-increasing congestion,” stated an article in Service Talks PRT Newsletter from October 23, 1923.
 A plan was made to create an elevated road for motorbuses to help decrease congestion along heavy traffic areas such as Chestnut Street. This plan consisted of trolleys on the ground level and motorbuses on elevated platforms.
 By November 1923, motorbuses were considered as options to use up and down Broad Street, which became a reality by the holiday season with new designations of the A (City Hall to Oxford Circle), B (Frankford to Byberry–Somerton), C (Broad-League Island to City Line), and D (Walnut–63rd to Broad).
 Philadelphia Transit Company's Route 73 bus and Route 15 trolley at the Richmond-Westmoreland Station in 1964. | Photo courtesy of the Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Organizations such as the United Business Men’s Association, Logan Improvement League, Lindley Boosters’ Association, and The Evening Bulletin began to urge passengers to petition the PRT to either extend or include motorbuses in future plans. By late 1924, Mayor W. Freeland Kendrick applauded PRT’s decision to extend Broad Street service at the behest of Councilman John Burrwood Daly to include the C-1 (Rising Sun Avenue, 9th and 10th Streets to Summerville Street, and Wagner Avenue).
 To connect the development of communities to public transit, PRT added the K (Fox Chase to Frankford and Chestnut Hill) to its motorbus lines. By mid-1925, South Philadelphia was included in the motorbus routes offering service from City Hall to the Navy Yard. As the routes reached Z, the lines continued as Special X routes like the XA that went to Willow Grove.
 Today, out of reach and locked behind an unused section of Fern Rock Station, the XA bus sign stands as a fragment of local history that reminds us that cross-city service once connected neighborhoods. Due to decreasing ridership over the years, many of the lettered buses had their routes shortened or changed to numbers by SEPTA.
 Tags: Philadelphia Transit Company public transit SEPTA 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: A New Exhibition Reveals the Material Culture of Our Revolutionary City
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
Fifes and drums, tricorn hats and muskets, and lots of red, white, and blue. Perhaps these are the images that come to mind when you think of Revolutionary-era Philadelphia. A new exhibition at American Philosophical Society Museum, Philadelphia, the Revolutionary City, complicates this stale and limited version of life in the “Birthplace of the Nation” during the messy era in which that birth was taking place. A rich variety of material objects, maps, letters, documents, broadsides, and other ephemera depict Philadelphia from 1760 to the early 1780s as a diverse, dynamic city in which loyalties were sometimes murky and changeable.
 A Multicultural City 
 luʾaḥ. shel shenat 541 [1780-1781] including the parallel Christian calendar, Printer unknown, Lancaster, Pennsylvania, 1780 | Image courtesy of Kislak Center for Special Collections, Rare Books and Manuscripts, the University of Pennsylvania Libraries
Colonial Philadelphia was home to about 30,000 inhabitants, making it the most populous city in British North America. Among the city’s residents were indigenous people, recent immigrants from France and Germany, free and enslaved Black people, and indentured servants, both Black and white. The religious diversity of the city is poignantly illustrated with two memorable items. A 1777 map printed in Paris indicates the locations of Presbyterian, Lutheran, Catholic, Calvinist, Anabaptist, Moravian, and Swedish churches, as well as a variety of Quaker institutions. A tiny almanac from 1780 contains Hebrew annotations and the year 5541 meticulously pasted over 1780 to indicate the Jewish year.
 Workshop of the (North American) World 
 An east perspective view of the city of Philadelphia, in the province of Pensylvania, in North America; taken from the Jersey shore by artist George Heap and engraver John Carwitham. Published in 1778 by Carington Bowles. | Image courtesy of the American Philosophical Society
 Philadelphia’s economic vibrancy is as evident as its cultural richness. Trade cards, similar to small advertisements, are displayed for a cabinet maker, a fabric merchant, and a fishing tackle seller. A pewter tankard, a musket, an earthenware punch bowl, and a tall case clock that may have belonged to Benjamin Franklin are examples of Philadelphia-made goods. An East Perspective View of the City of Philadelphia…taken from the Jersey shore” shows a place of almost dizzying action: a harbor full of ships of varied types and sizes, a skyline dotted with spires, and a port running the length of the city. A powder horn with an engraving of the skyline exemplifies the pride that at least one soldier felt for his hometown. The wide array of printed matter, from newspapers and proclamations to Bibles and engravings, underscores Philadelphia’s role as a center of the printing industry.
 The Fog of War 
 A drawing of the home of Israel Pemberton, a wealthy merchant, member of the Pennsylvania Assembly, and a Quaker exile, on 21st Street in South Philadelphia. Pemberton built the house in 1751. It was demolished in 1860. | Image courtesy of Print and Picture Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 The burgeoning city faced its greatest challenge during the months of September 1777 to June 1778, the period of British occupation. Some residents fled to areas controlled by the Continental Army, and some left for England or welcomed the British to Philadelphia. Many, however, were focused on surviving a time of hardship characterized by severe shortages of food and other goods. Curator Caroline O’Connell avoided using the terms “Patriots” and “Loyalists” given that allegiances often shifted for both practical and philosophical reasons. The story of the Quaker Exile recounted in Ned Donoghue’s 2023 book is retold in the exhibit with a variety of documents including diaries of women, such as Elizabeth Drinker, left behind in the occupied city.
 The willingness of some Philadelphians to cozy up to the British is clear in this verse that accompanied a newspaper delivered during the final days of 1777:
 “Truth is, I always lov’d my King and Church,
 And could not bear to leave them in the lurch,
 To see Rebellion, wear the thin Pretence,
 Of Freedom, Virtue, Truth, and Common Sense…”
 An ornate, engraved ticket to the Meschianza in 1778. Over 400 tickets like this one were issued to elite Philadelphians and British citizens. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 As British troops withdrew, following an extravagant party called the Meschianza, Philadelphians who had been made to give oaths to support General Howe and the British army were required to pledge their fidelity and allegiance to the Pennsylvania General Assembly. Reprisals against those perceived as loyal to the British could be harsh, including at least one hanging for treason documented in the exhibition.
 A Well-Timed Exhibit 
 Philadelphia, the Revolutionary City is not replete with bells and whistles. There are few interactive features other than earphones to listen to documents read aloud and a letter writing station. My advice is to give yourself the time to move through slowly and read most, if not all, of the descriptive materials. You may well find that you have a new appreciation for what our city has endured and a fresh sense of optimism about making it through our own challenging era.
 Philadelphia, The Revolutionary City is on view through December 28. In preparation for the semiquincentennial in 2026, a digital archive, therevolutionarycity.org, is being developed as a central hub for educators, students, and the general public. American Philosophical Society, The Library Company of Philadelphia, Historical Society of Pennsylvania, Museum of the American Revolution, McNeil Center for Early American Studies, and University of Pennsylvania’s Kislak Center are collaborating on the project.
 Tags: American Revolution art exhibition 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: New PATCO Station Caps Franklin Square’s Revival. Will It Last This Time?
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
It is a space that is as old as Philadelphia, named after the city’s most renowned inventor, but can Franklin Square successfully reinvent itself for sustained, present-day use? That is the question that looms behind the recent spate of good-vibes headlines for the eight-acre park at 6th and Race Streets. In early April, politicians, dignitaries, and urbanists alike gathered to celebrate the reopening of a PATCO subway station in the southwest corner of the park, the latest development in an ongoing effort to render progress in this historically-challenged space. For nearly two decades, the nonprofit development company Historic Philadelphia, Inc. has stewarded the park. To CEO Amy Needle, the momentum is all headed in the right direction. “We work really hard at Historic Philadelphia to make sure that Franklin Square is always a friendly, fun, safe place to be,” she said. “[The PATCO station] is another wonderful piece of all the development that’s happened around the square since we opened.”
 Yet, a reading of the square’s history reveals that good vibes have come and gone before after butting up against physical realities borne from past city planning practices. The most recent analogue came 50 years ago when the PATCO station, originally constructed 1934, was previously reopened for bicentennial celebrations. By that time Franklin Square had declined from a 19th century heyday into the heart of Philadelphia's notorious Skid Row . However, a May 1976 Philadelphia Inquirer article hailed the reopening of the subway station and other contemporary improvements, such as the construction of bathrooms and rehabilitation of landscaping and a historic fountain. “If William Penn were alive today he would be pleased with what has happened to the five public squares he envisioned,” the article declared. “[And] the greatest amount of work has been done at Franklin Square.”
 PATCO's Franklin Square station reopened in April. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 Following bicentennial celebrations, ridership at the PATCO stop plummeted and it closed again just three years later. The park’s reputation as primarily the domain of people experiencing homelessness returned, as did its status as the most forsaken of Penn’s parks. “Four of the five squares in Penn’s original grid for Philadelphia have distinctive identities and character,” a 2004 Inquirer editorial offered up. “But the fifth, Franklin Square, sits nearly forgotten in the shadows of the bridge that bears the same name.”
 Indeed, the 1920s construction of the Benjamin Franklin Bridge is one of just several major urban development projects that served to “disconnect” Franklin Square from its surrounding neighborhoods, noted Jeffrey Doshna, a planner and economist at Temple University’s Tyler School of Art and Architecture. While the foot of the bridge boxes in Franklin Square to the east, the mid-20th century hollowing out neighborhoods to the south, for Independence Mall and the Police Administration Building (aka the Roundhouse) , to the west, for the former Metropolitan Hospital , and to the north, for the Vine Street Expressway, effectively placed the park in an urban no-man’s land. “These are all happening in a relatively small geography,” Doshna said. “There’s a long history of kind of wondering, what is the best use here?”
 Inescapable is the park's adjacency to Chinatown. While residential areas near Franklin Square perceived as “slums” were paved over in the 20th century to make way for modern highways and tourist districts, recent proposals like the doomed 76ers arena continue to raise the question: just who is this neighborhood, and its park, for?
 A Wild Past 
 In all of Penn’s parks, quaint notions of some bygone peaceful era are the stuff of myth, explained Elizabeth Milroy, Professor Emerita of Art & Art History at Drexel University and author of a seminal book on the history of the city’s parks, The Grid and the River: Philadelphia’s Green Places, 1682–1876 . “The notion persists that by the time Philadelphia achieved political and economic prominence in the mid-18th century, it was a ‘wholesome grid of streets and squares,’” Milroy has written . “City maps perpetuated this myth, when in fact the immediate needs of the new colony had precluded methodical building. From the start Philadelphians struggled to balance the demands of private entrepreneurship and public works.”
 The land Penn set aside for his five parks proved particularly problematic. While they were meant to be public lands, little to no funding was set aside for their maintenance. As development reached the parks' boundaries, so too did challenges of the commons. Burial grounds, livestock, vagrants, and even public hangings graced the city’s squares. “As the city grew the squares became vague marginalized spaces, vulnerable to abuse,” wrote Milroy in The Grid and the River .
 Detail view of A mapp of ye improved part of Pensilvania in America by Thomas Holme, 1687. North East Publick Square (aka Franklin Square) can be seen in the upper right of the map. | Image: Public Domain
 What was commonly referred to as North East Publick Square–now Franklin Square–was no exception. After being laid out in the early 1700s, the park was slow to develop due in part to marshy conditions, according to a history compiled by John Milner Associates . In 1741, the German Reformed Church at 4th and Race Streets successfully obtained a lease from Governor Thomas Penn to bury its dead in the northeast quadrant of the park, a grant that led to the eventual interment of thousands of bodies. However, when Penn tried to give another piece of the park away just 10 years later to Pennsylvania Hospital, the institution’s reasons for declining indicated a burgeoning public attachment to this public space. “Our fellow citizens would tax us with injustice to them if we should accept,” the hospital’s managers wrote.
 The push-and-pull of who controlled the park came to a head in the 1820s when City Hall approved more than $4,000 in improvements. Following a plan by famous sculptor William Rush, the park was to be relandscaped with gravel walkways winding their way through planted trees and centered around a decorative fountain that still exists today. To solidify this new era, the City formally renamed the five public squares in 1825, christening the northeast square after Benjamin Franklin. Yet, when the German Reformed congregation resisted requests to vacate, the City sued. The landmark case of Commonwealth Vs. Alburger reached the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, where the City won and nullified the 1741 Penn agreement. The park was to be for the people, the court ruled, clearing the way for the development plans to become fully realized by 1850, topped by the donation of a resident live peacock by Adam Eckfeldt, chief coiner at the United States Mint.
 This lithograph from 1839 by John T. Bowen shows the fountain at Franklin Square. The park's central water feature was built in 1837 and still operates today. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 This ostensibly created a golden era of the park, when primarily well-to-do Philadelphians occupied the neighborhoods nearby. However, even here the historical record suggests a more sordid reality. In 1877, a Philadelphia Times piece characterized the park as “infested with bad characters” believed drawn to the area by nearby variety shows. “Disreputable characters of both sexes [deprive] respectable residents of the neighborhoods of the use of the beautiful park by their children, who cannot resort there without being subjected to the vilest companionship and the hearing of the most profane and obscene language,” the paper reported, while quoting then-mayor William Stokley as calling Franklin Square “One of the worst and most troublesome neighborhoods in Philadelphia.”
 Reports throughout the late 19th and early 20th centuries tell a story of two parks: by night, a rough and tumble place where “thieves and thugs” roamed, while policemen chatted nearby with “soiled doves of that locality,” according to an 1894 Philadelphia Times piece. And by day, a place of “vagabond whimsy” where short-skirted ladies came and went and children sprinkled themselves in the fountain’s waters and played “hopscotch in the sun” according to a 1918 description in the Evening Public Ledger .
 Whatever such charm graced Franklin Square would soon be lost.
 Urban Renewal 
 By the early 20th, wealthy families were deserting neighborhoods adjacent to Franklin Square in favor of destinations such as Rittenhouse Square and Chestnut Hill. According to a history compiled for a walking tour by Calvin Nguyen, a former student of Milroy’s and now Indianapolis-based preservationist, some former residences were then converted into “taverns, hotels, and bordellos,” further attracting seedier elements. Even though much of the housing stock was still occupied by lower class residents, city planners turned to the concept of urban renewal that brought about the construction of the highways and tourist districts. “Urban planners saw the area as untreatable and opted to destroy the neighborhood altogether, displacing its residential community in favor of light industrial buildings, commercial spaces, and the Vine Street Expressway," wrote Nguyen.
 A resident of Skid Row watches the demolition of a building at 8th and Vine Streets in 1973. | Image courtesy of the Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 The efforts backfired. Cutoff from residential neighborhoods and foot traffic, a vacuum was created that further pulled in those with nowhere else to go. By 1961, famed urban theorist and author Jane Jacobs infamously described Franklin Square as Philadelphia’s Skid Row in her book The Death and Life of Great American Cities .
“Where the homeless, the unemployed, and the people of indigent leisure gather amid the flophouses, cheap hotels, missions,” and similar sights, wrote Jacobs.
 Yet, contemporary descriptions also gave nods to the humanity that called the park home. Jacobs herself called the regulars of Franklin Square “seedy,” but less threatening and criminal than in other sections of the city. Even as others in the press called for wide-scale renewal of Franklin Square at the end of the 20th century, Lawrence Houstoun, Jr., an urban development consultant, wrote in the Inquirer in 1991 that the state of the park was a simple reality borne of poor planning decisions, rather than the product of nefarious intentions by its regulars. “Franklin Square should be recognized for what city and highway planning have made it–an historic Skid Row park serving the only population that finds it useful and attractive,” wrote Houstoun.
 Merry-Go-Round Again 
 Calls for a fresh start for Franklin Square were eventually answered. In 2004, the Inquirer published an editorial headlined, “Fix Philly’s Fifth Wheel,” which stated that “things are stirring near the fifth square of William Penn.” The Center City District had kicked off a conversation by putting forth a conceptual plan with suggestions including a ferris wheel. The Inquirer further mused of building pedestrian bridges over the surrounding roadways and holding historical reenactments in the park.
 Just months later, then-Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell announced a concrete plan to transfer the park from the Fairmount Park Commission to Historic Philadelphia, which he formed while mayor in 1994, and invest millions of dollars in its redevelopment. “Credit goes to Ed Rendell for seeing the vision of Franklin Square for what it could be,” said Philadelphia Councilmember Mark Squilla, whose district contains the park.
 Franklin Square station's glassy new headhouse. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 That vision came together quickly. By the summer of 2006, the park reopened to the public with $6.5 million in new amenities, including a miniature golf course and carousel (both still in use today), updated landscaping and paving, and a fully repaired fountain, which was originally installed 1838 and believed to be the “oldest refurbished and functioning public water fountain in the United States,” according to Historic Philadelphia . Historical signage also called out the interesting uses of the park’s past: cattle pasture, horse market, military drill grounds, and Revolutionary War powder magazine. Noticeably absent, Nguyen noted, is any signage nodding to the park’s less-rosy 20th century. “Franklin Square should take steps to meaningfully contend with its whole history,” Nguyen wrote, “and think about history as more than a theme for consumption, but as an educational tool for learning about the city’s pasts, present, and possible futures.”
 Before long, PATCO also took a renewed interest in the park. Franklin Square Station was originally opened in 1935 by the Delaware River Joint Commission, but closed in 1939 due to poor ridership. It ran again for just seven months in 1952, then three years following the 1976 Bicentennial. “Given the new developments of Independence Mall, the Police Headquarters, and the Metropolitan Hospital being seen as harbingers of good fortune, there was optimism in the air,” Nguyen wrote. “[But] opening for the bicentennial proved no difference in making the Franklin Square station permanent, again failing to get significant ridership.”
 At the ribbon cutting for the latest revival in April, PATCO general manager John Rink said that history didn’t deter the agency from trying again and with renewed optimism. The old Metropolitan Hospital across the street has been converted to condos, he stated. The adjacent, currently unoccupied Roundhouse offers similar “big potential,” he said. The growth of residential development along Spring Garden Street and in Northern Liberties, along with continued activity in Chinatown and Independence Mall, add to potential foot traffic.
 Prior to the station’s latest opening, PATCO operated just four stops in Philadelphia: one at 8th and Market Streets and three more in Center City along Locust Street. That compares to nine in New Jersey, stretching from Camden into its suburbs. As such, planners initially believed most of the ridership to the park would come from New Jersey, Rink said, but now believe a significant number of riders will visit the park from Center City, especially at just $1.40 a ticket. How well it pays off remains to be seen: the station’s rehabilitation required about $30 million. “The park itself has changed, and now we have the potential to connect our riders,” Rink insisted.
 Residents of Chinatown gather in Franklin Square. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 Historic Philadelphia also continues to make improvements to the park. New bathroom facilities should be completed this month. A complete overhaul of an aging playground is also in the works. Needle also pointed to Race Street, where a soon-to-be-completed “road diet” initiative has reduced the amount of car lanes and added a protected bike lane. Together, the projects cost an additional $7.8 million. Combined with a new Indego bicycle-sharing station at the park, she believes there will be more favorable connectivity for pedestrians and cyclists. Ultimately, she thinks Franklin Square can thread the needle as a place for nearby residents and children to come and enjoy the outdoors, while also serving as a worthwhile destination for tourists near and far. “That’s what all of our public spaces are intended to do, right?” she posed.
 Doshna believes that is possible. He likens Franklin Square’s potential to something like the Italian Market, which provides both a real service to neighborhood residents and draws outside visitors. Even with a history of deep-pocketed proposals like the 76ers arena threatening to disrupt nearby residents, Doshna said regular investments in parks are a good sign. He particularly points to investments like the PATCO stop as providing a beneficial new service to those living nearby. “A train stop is actually much, much better than building a big parking lot for people to drive in,” Doshna said. “If somebody takes PATCO to Franklin Square and goes and eats at a restaurant nearby, there’s no extra car, right? There’s no traffic problems and cars idling.”
 For Squilla, who recently caught a tiger by the toe when he threw his weight behind the 76ers arena plan, Franklin Square’s ongoing development is noncontroversial. “To me, it’s a worthwhile partnership that really could be an example of how we can restore and maintain a lot of our open areas in the city."
 Tags: Franklin Square PATCO public transit Skid Row 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Op-Ed: Philly Must Fight the Erasure of Black History
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
As the Liberty Bell Center neared completion in 2001, archeological evidence revealed that the new home to a symbol of freedom was adjacent to a site that exemplified freedom’s opposite: the remnants of slave quarters for those who toiled in the President’s House at 6th and Market Streets during the nearly seven years of George Washington’s presidency spent in Philadelphia.
 When presented with this startling juxtaposition, the response of Independence National Historical Park’s leadership was to do nothing. An alliance of historians, journalists, local Black politicians, and the Avenging the Ancestors Coalition not only convinced the National Park Service to acknowledge the history of slavery next to the Liberty Bell, but also successfully pressed for a memorial to those enslaved by our first president . In 2010, The President’s House: Freedom and Slavery in the Making of a New Nation opened as part of Independence National Historical Park.
 The monument The President’s House: Freedom and Slavery in the Making of a New Nation on Independence Mall was dedicated in 2010 and designed by Kelly/Maiello Architects. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The creation of the President’s House memorial marked a sea change in how citizens were encouraged to contemplate our nation’s past. Rather than telling a simplistic story of heroic founding fathers creating a nation based on liberty and justice for all, people were prompted to wrestle with the complexity of freedom and slavery at the core of American history.
 Alas, today we are going dramatically backwards. Recently, the World War II service of Jackie Robinson and the Tuskegee Airmen were removed from the Arlington Cemetery website, and the word slavery, as well as an image of Harriet Tubman, were deleted from a National Park Service website about the Underground Railroad. Although these deletions were reversed following public outcry , it is clear that there is an effort underway to return to a sanitized, false, and narrow depiction of American history. The struggles and the achievements of African Americans are being expunged as part of the Trump administration’s anti-DEI mania.
 Citizen Activism Shapes the Landscape 
 In Philadelphia, however, we are well-prepared to fight back against this intended erasure. The 21st century has seen a remarkable increase in visible marking of Black history in the local landscape and in bringing hidden histories to light in the digital space. This work has been accomplished by people of diverse racial backgrounds who care about creating an inclusive and complex understanding of our city’s past.
 36 state historical markers about African American history have been erected in Philadelphia since 2000. At least three of these markers were based on nominations compiled by schoolchildren, including one commemorating a 1967 student walkout that was an impetus for Philadelphia to become the first school district in the nation to require a year of African American history beginning in 2005.
 A Pennsylvania state historical marker at Mount Pleasant in Fairmount Park was unveiled in 2023. It includes the names of Nell, Bernard, Castillis, and Cato who were enslaved by Captain John Macpherson, the mansion's original owner. | Photo: Michael Bixler 
 2017 saw the unveiling of A Quest for Parity, the memorial to 19th century educator and activist Octavius Valentine Catto , on the south apron of City Hall. The statue of Catto was the first of an African American individual on public land in Philadelphia, and it quickly became a gathering spot for social justice demonstrations. Although Mayor Jim Kenney was an advocate for the memorial, it was a leadership board of prominent citizens that saw the project to its fruition.
 In April 2024, members of The National Society of the Colonial Dames in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania , staff at Stenton (an 18th century house museum), and residents of the surrounding Nicetown, Logan, and Germantown communities gathered to celebrate a new memorial to Dinah , a woman who had been enslaved by the Logan family and was credited with saving the mansion from would-be British arsonists in 1777. This monument, the first in Philadelphia to honor an enslaved woman, was the result of a multiyear effort that included Stenton’s African American neighbors in conceptualizing the form a Dinah memorial would take.
 Earlier this year, Taney Street, thought to be named for the Supreme Court Justice who ruled in the Dred Scott case that Black people could not be citizens, was officially renamed to honor educator and civil rights activist Caroline Le Count as the result of a grassroots campaign that began in 2020 .
 Digital Resources 
 In addition, several outstanding websites have been developed that vividly depict different periods in Philadelphia Black history. The The 1838 Black Metropolis uses archival resources to imaginatively recreate the city’s ante-bellum African American community. Temple University’s Civil Rights in a Northern City presents oral history, photographs, video, news articles, and other documents to recount the Girard College protests and the Columbia Avenue riots of the 1960s.
 The (In)Visible Architects of Freedom on the Independence National Historical Park's website contains a remarkable collection of primary sources about Black life in Philadelphia from the 17th through the 19th centuries. Designed for educators, this digital archive was developed by a Mellon Humanities Postdoctoral Foundation Fellow. The National Park Service has recently terminated the grant agreement with Mellon. While reprehensible, this comes as no surprise given the current political climate.
 A Call to Action 
 Many of us feel a sense of helplessness when faced with the countless unprecedented actions of the Trump regime. When it comes to the attempted whitewashing of history, however, we Philadelphians have many ways of countering these efforts. The few examples shared above illustrate our collective power to preserve and memorialize Black history. To continue to build on this momentum, we can all take action.
 Philadelphia has a plethora of historic sites, houses and museums that tell parts of the story of Black Philadelphia . Go visit. The Black Journey Walking Tour and other groups can show you the city through a different lens. We are lucky to have many repositories of information that house information about the city’s Black past for you to do your own research.
 In 1858, Minor Street was renamed Taney Street by the City of Philadelphia to honor Justice Roger Brooke Taney, a staunch supporter of white supremacy. In October 2024, the street was renamed to honor Caroline LeCount, a local Black educator, activist, and abolitionist. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Share what you learn on social media and through word of mouth. When you’re ready, take the next step. Apply for a historical marker or honorary street name. Give a talk at a school or historical society. Lead a neighborhood tour. Too much of Philadelphia’s Black history was obscured for too long. It is up to us to keep the recently acknowledged past accessible no matter who is in power in Washington, D.C.
 On April 25-26, the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) is hosting a Using/Doing/Teaching Black History conference that will provide opportunities to learn about and network with practitioners of local Black history. The creators of the 1838 Metropolis website collaborated on Free, As One , an exhibition currently on display at HSP. For more information about the conference, gallery talks, and the exhibit see the exhibit's website: https://www.portal.hsp.org/upcoming-events 
 Tags: African-American history Donald J. Trump op-ed The President’s House 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Historic Bank in Point Breeze Nominated to the National Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Philadelphia Historical Commission did not add any new properties to the local register at its meeting on April 11. However, it did review new construction in historic properties or districts, alterations to historic properties, and a nomination to the National Register of Historic Places.
 A frequent topic that comes before the Historical Commission is the proposal of modifications to previously designated properties. On Friday it approved the construction of a new three-story building on a parking lot that currently occupies 15-17 and 19-25 South 2nd Street . The owner, a relatively new non-profit called the Tun Legacy Foundation, plans to recreate Tun Tavern, the 17th century watering hole that is said to be the birthplace of the United States Marine Corps, the United States Navy, the Pennsylvania Freemasons, and certain Colonial fraternal organizations. The site is about 250 yards away from the actual site of the original Tun Tavern, built in 1686, which now lies under I-95 near Penn's Landing. The group purchased the two parcels in April 2024 and aims to operate the tavern and donate the profits to charitable causes.
 A drawing of the original Tun Tavern and a rendering of the new one. | Images: Tun Legacy Foundation
 Another proposed construction project was granted at 500 North Christopher Columbus Boulevard next to the historically designated Philadelphia Warehousing & Cold Storage Company building , which dates to 1891. The approval will allow the construction of a six-story rooftop addition and the cutting of openings to add windows to the lower levels.
 The Historical Commission also frequently reviews and comments on proposed modifications to historically designated properties which need to satisfy the guidelines set by the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties.
 Two properties with issues regarding window replacements were reviewed. The first was for the 1849 Gothic Revival house at 3819 THE Oak Road in East Falls that is formally known as Ivy Cottage. The proposal outlined plans to replace 52 windows on all sides, but concerns were raised that the window treatments were not in keeping with the original design of the house. The request was denied.
 Another denial was given to the property at 234-35 S. 8th Street. It was built in 1810 by architect Robert Mills, who would go on to design the Washington Monuments in both Baltimore, Maryland and Washington D.C. The current owners replaced windows without Historical Commission review in February and were now asking for retroactive legalization. The Historical Commission denied the request, deeming the replacement windows as not in keeping with Standard 6 of the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties and Guidelines, which requires deteriorated historic features to be repaired rather than replaced or, where the deterioration requires replacement, the new feature will match the old in design, color, texture, and, where possible, materials.
 First Federal Savings & Loan Association of Philadelphia at 1330-32 Point Breeze Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The final item on the meeting's agenda was to comment on a nomination of a Philadelphia property to the National Register of Historic Places. These nominations are overseen by the applicable state agency, in this case, the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, which must solicit comments from the appropriate local government, which in turn must also offer a forum for public comment. The Historical Commission speaks on behalf of the City of Philadelphia in historic preservation matters and provides an opportunity for the public to weigh in. 
 The nomination was for the First Federal Savings & Loan Association of Philadelphia at 1330-32 Point Breeze Avenue . Founded in 1934, it was the first financial institution in Pennsylvania established under the Federal Home Loan Bank System, which freed up credit in the housing market during the Great Depression. It made homeownership more affordable in that financially difficult period and went on to help fuel the post-World War II housing boom, especially in rapidly growing areas like Northeast Philadelphia and nearby suburban communities. The building is not currently listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. The Historical Commission offered favorable comments in support of the nomination.
 Tags: Historic Banks Historical Commission Meeting Report National Register of Historic Places Philadelphia Historical Commission Point Breeze South Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Places Lost: Spring 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 The S.S. United States. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 S.S. United States 
 Location : Pier 82
 Built : 1952
 The S.S. United States , launched in 1952, served as a testament to American innovation and maritime supremacy. Designed by Naval architect William Francis Gibbs, it was the fastest ocean liner ever built, crossing the Atlantic Ocean in just over three days on its maiden voyage. Constructed with U.S. Navy funding, the vessel was a dual-purpose marvel, serving as both a luxury liner and a potential high-speed troop carrier. Gibbs prioritized safety, avoiding flammable materials wherever possible, even commissioning an aluminum piano to ensure fire resistance.
 During its heyday, the ship hosted presidents, celebrities like Marilyn Monroe, and countless travelers, embodying postwar American glamour and industrial prowess. However, the rise of jet travel in the late 1960s rendered transatlantic liners obsolete, and the S.S.United States was retired in 1969.
 Over subsequent decades, the ship changed hands several times with ambitious plans to transform it into a hotel or museum. Unfortunately, financial and logistical challenges thwarted these efforts, leaving the once-proud vessel languishing at a South Philadelphia pier. In 2024, after years of calls for preservation and advocacy efforts, the ship was sold to Okaloosa County, Florida. 
 Plans are underway to sink the vessel in the Gulf of Mexico off the coast of Destin-Fort Walton Beach to create the world’s largest artificial reef. Before this transformation, the ship will undergo extensive preparation to ensure environmental safety. Although controversial, this new role as a marine sanctuary offers the S.S. United States a unique legacy, continuing its service in a new and innovative way.
 John Stortz and Son store. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 John Stortz and Son Store 
 Location : 208-12 Vine Street
 Built : 208 and 212–1780 | 210–1870
 The demolition of 208-12 Vine Street in Old City marks a poignant loss for historic preservation in Philadelphia. Built in 1780 and 1870, these structures were rare surviving examples of 18th century industrial and mercantile architecture in the neighborhood. Since 1853, the complex housed John Stortz and Son, a historic tool manufacturer with roots in ice skate production that evolved into a diverse tool-making enterprise. In the 21st century, the company shifted its focus to e-commerce and distribution of imported tools, leading to a decline in manufacturing at the Vine Street location.
 The building’s inclusion in the Old City Historic District provided some measure of protection, but that protection proved insufficient in the face of developer pressure. The Stortz family, struggling to adapt the buildings to their shifting business model, filed a financial hardship application to demolish them in 2023, arguing that rehabilitation was too costly and ill-suited for the interconnected complex. Despite alternative proposals by the Preservation Alliance of Greater Philadelphia to integrate the historic structures into redevelopment plans, the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved the demolition in October 2023. The decision came with stipulations requiring secure financing and approvals for a redevelopment proposal before the structures could come down.
 In spring 2024, the Historical Commission approved a six-story apartment to be built on the site, erasing a tangible link to Old City’s industrial heritage. This case serves as a cautionary tale, emphasizing that preservation requires not only policies, but also active stewardship to ensure that Philadelphia’s architectural heritage endures for future generations.
 19th Street Baptist Church. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 19th Street Baptist Church 
 Location : 1253 South 19th Street
 Built : 1874
 The Memorial Church of the Holy Comforter, later known as 19th Street Baptist Church, was built in 1874 to serve the working-class residents of Point Breeze in South Philadelphia. The church was designed by the renowned firm Furness & Hewitt and featured a unique serpentine stone faccade. In 1944, the dwindling congregation of St. Peter’s Episcopal Church, which had founded the Holy Comforter as a mission church, sold the building to the 19th Street Baptist Church. The new congregation thrived in the following decades, becoming a vital part of the community and even hosting prominent figures like Martin Luther King Jr.
 However, the church began to face serious maintenance issues due to the deteriorating serpentine stone, which is vulnerable to erosion. Financial struggles were compounded by a failed lawsuit against St. Peter’s Church over a disputed endowment that the 19th Street Baptist Church claimed was intended for the building’s upkeep. Despite emergency repairs and fundraising efforts, the building continued to deteriorate. A loan taken out for repairs led to further financial strain and ultimately fell into the hands of a firm specializing in distressed commercial mortgages.
 Multiyear attempts to secure funding for restoration or find a preservation-minded buyer were unsuccessful. The church was ultimately deemed unsafe by the city’s Department of Licenses and Inspections and slated for demolition in the interest of public safety. The Historical Commission approved the demolition of the imminently dangerous sanctuary in October 2024 , but spared the adjacent fellowship hall, which is in better condition.
 Tags: demolition historic churches industrial history Places Lost SS United States 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Court OKs Plan to Sell Historic Mount Vernon Cemetery to Green Burial Company
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
Mount Vernon Cemetery in Allegheny West will celebrate its 170th birthday, and potentially its rebirth, in 2026. A plan is now in place to transfer the historic burial ground along Lehigh Avenue to the Steelmantown Cemetery Company , a Marshallville, New Jersey-based outfit specializing in green burials that owns numerous cemeteries across the country. A Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas judge signed off Monday morning on a tentative agreement that would see Steelmantown take possession of the property from a careholder organization and potentially end a multi-year legal saga to control the fate of the forlorn burial ground.
 First founded in 1856, the cemetery was once a final destination for well-to-do Philadelphians, including several actors from the Barrymore family. Yet, over the last half century, it has flirted with dereliction as the cemetery's most recent owner failed to maintain the property. Its various monuments still tell the tale of a prosperous past–one is a 25-foot high decorative pyramid carved by Belgian sculptor G. Geef in 1864–but the wild foliage and overgrown pathways that surround them are emblematic of its more recent history.
 The gatehouse of Mount Vernon Cemetery was built in 1858 and designed by John Notman, the architect who designed Laurel Hill Cemetery next door and the Athenaeum of Philadelphia on Washington Square. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The cemetery’s downward trajectory led a collection of preservationists and concerned citizens to launch a successful effort to use Pennsylvania’s Act 135 to gain control of the property in 2020. Under that statute, a judge can appoint a conservator organization to work to find a new buyer of a derelict property against the owner’s wishes, as long as there is a coherent plan to restore and reuse the property in a beneficial way.
 Those knowledgeable of the situation say over the past year just such a plan was formed to bring in Steelmantown as a new owner and rejuvenate the cemetery. In recent months, court hearings on the matter were delayed as the conservator organization, the Philadelphia Community Development Coalition (PCDC), worked out the final details. However, on March 31 the PCDC filed legal documents asserting they had signed off on the plan. Following a court hearing on Friday, Common Pleas judge Ann M. Butchart authorized a sale to Steelmantown to move forward.
 In an interview, Steelmantown founder and owner Edward Bixby said he was excited about Mount Vernon’s future. While legal and logistical hurdles remain, Bixby envisions a significant transformation of the property by the end of 2026, with a fully realized vision coming to fruition over the course of the next decade. Ultimately, he plans a Mount Vernon where existing markers and plots are restored in a traditional manner for the benefit of visiting kin of the deceased, but also where a significant portion of the property is transformed into a more natural setting akin to a park. "It's like you're owning an art museum in the middle of a garden setting. It's mindblowing,” Bixby said. “What we want to be able to do is give access to the people, to be able to walk through there, to be able to enjoy the property, a recreational jog, whatever. Go have a walk and learn about the history of Philadelphia.”
 The Resting Place of Tens of Thousands 
 Thaddeus Squire, a philanthropic management professional with a special interest in historic preservation, said Mount Vernon was originally founded in the 1850s to compete with the adjacent Laurel Hill Cemetery. The cemetery is currently believed to contain the remains of about 33,000 people, its main historical clientele wealthy German-Americans, a customer case that proved to be particularly important following the Black Tuesday stock market crash of 1929.
 With the cemetery’s finances on the ropes, the families of the interred turned to Joseph Murphy, counsel to a large brewery supply company in Philadelphia. Murphy became involved in the cemetery’s operations, and, as board members and shareholders began to pass away, consolidated stakes until he became the outright owner. Eventually, Murphy passed on the property to its most recent owner, his son, Joseph Dinsmore Murphy.
 This stereograph from 1875 shows the marble, pyramid-shaped Gardel Monument at Mount Vernon Cemetery. The monument was built in 1864 and commissioned by French teacher Bertrand Gardel for his wife, Julia Hawks Gardel, who died while touring Damascus, Syria. | Photo courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 For a time, Squire said the younger Murphy believed himself a responsible caretaker of the cemetery. Yet, to those who cared about the cemetery locally, Murphy, a lawyer based in Washington, D.C., was an absentee owner under whose watch Mount Vernon fell into disrepair. In a 2021 Philadelphia Inquirer article , a woman named Regina Miller retold a journey that began with her contacting Murphy simply to gain access to the cemetery to visit her grandparents’ graves. Murphy in turn asked Miller for help sifting through records. After becoming involved, she wound up with the unexpected delivery of cremation ashes for two people on her doorstep. Turns out they were individuals with burial rights in the cemetery, but that operations were too defunct to follow through.
 “He told me to hang on to them,” Miller said of Murphy. According to Squire, Murphy at one point made contact with the late University of Pennsylvania professor and historic preservationist Aaron Wunsch , admitting he no longer felt capable of running the cemetery and wanting to hand it off. Squire said both groups retained attorneys to hash out the paperwork and were close to settling several times, but that Murphy “dithered and dallied,” leading their group to lose pro bono legal representation. “After we lost our second counsel, I had kind of had it at that point,” Squire explained. “That’s when I said, ‘We need to 135 this.’”
 A vandalized mausoleum and broken asphalt greet visitors to the 169-year-old cemetery. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Squire said he, Wunsch, and other interested parties worked to convince the Philadelphia Community Development Coalition, a nonprofit focused on remediating blight, to act as conservator and initiate legal proceedings. After the court recognized PCDC as conservator in 2021, the organization spent $200,000 stabilizing the cemetery's gatehouse and employed workers to provide for some care of the property. However, much of the regular maintenance of the grounds has fallen to the Friends of Mount Vernon Cemetery, an all-volunteer group led by coordinator Brandon Zimmerman.
 Squire and others stood up their own nonprofit in an effort to eventually take ownership of the cemetery, but ran into fundraising difficulties. The property settled into a new limbo until Bixby arrived.
 Still, there are loose ends to be sewn up both before and after Bixby takes possession, currently scheduled for 35 days from the judge’s order. At Friday's hearing, Judge Butchart asked PCDC and Bixby to produce financial records indicating that his company has financial capacity to restore the cemetery. She also asked for further documentation to ensure that the roof of the cemetery’s gatehouse was to be properly restored. Neither Bixby nor PCDC objected.
 Areas of Mount Vernon have been cleared of overgrowth, while others await maintenance after decades of neglect. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Also raised at the hearing were some concerns over historic documents belonging to the cemetery. While PCDC said the vast majority are being temporarily housed at the University of Pennsylvania and would become property of Bixby’s company, missing from the archives is a master ledger book useful in establishing who has been buried in the cemetery and where. Zimmerman and PCDC alleged they believed the book to be in possession of Regina Miller, something they said she denies.
 Regardless, Zimmerman said he anticipates the Friends group transitioning from primarily landscaping activities to research, record-keeping, and grant writing. He said some 30,000 index cards exist that can be tediously reviewed to recompile an understanding of who is buried in the cemetery, although they do not include records from the first 20 years of the cemetery’s operation.
 Butchart said regardless of sale, the court will continue to hold regular hearings on the cemetery to ensure a successful transition.
 Bringing the Green 
 Bixby, a former South Jersey real estate developer, came into the cemetery business by accident. His family has roots in the state dating back centuries and in the 1700s started a family burial ground in Steelmantown, a small rural neighborhood in Cape May County. The property was eventually passed into the hands of Upper Township, then a private funeral company which opened up the cemetery for public interrment.
 Yet, when Bixby went to visit his brother’s grave there in 2007, he found the cemetery in a state of disrepair with trash strewn about the property. When he complained to the 87-year-old proprietor, the man asked Bixby if he wanted to buy the cemetery for $1. Bixby said yes and had an instinct to do something different.
 “We are located adjacent to Belleplain State Forest, which is beautiful. I said to my family, all of the history of the township lies within this cemetery, but nobody knows it’s there,” Bixby said. “So I put in about a mile walking trail so people could come out and enjoy the property.”
 Steelmantown Cemetery in the Pine Barrens of New Jersey features moss-covered nature trails flanked by wooded green burial sites. | Photos: Kate Bixler
 That launched a second career in which Bixby has come to own 15 different cemeteries across the country. He said he typically works to identify down-and-out properties like Mount Vernon that he feels can be restored to glory. Along the way, he also fell into a green burial niche after reading a story about it in the Press of Atlantic City . In its simplest form, a green burial just means burying an individual in a basic wooden box without the use of embalming fluid or other chemicals. Historically in the United States, Bixby said that was viewed as an ignoble end for those without means or loved ones. Now, it is surging in popularity, including more deluxe options that can bury an individual at the base of a tree or shrub.
 Bixby said his first order of business is to secure the property against vandalism and trespass. He has already installed a network of security cameras to help keep a watchful eye on the place. After that, he anticipates needing about a year to do the heavy lifting of removing the worst of the overgrowth from the cemetery. Ultimately, he envisions a “hybrid” cemetery that includes traditional, landscaped areas, while leaving a significant portion as a more park-like setting for the enjoyment of the greater community.
 One of historic Mount Vernon's many ornate monuments sees the light of day after years of being entombed in weeds and underbrush. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 While there is some question as to how much space is left in the cemetery for burials, Bixby said he doesn’t view that as a major risk. In some cemeteries he has taken over there was believed to be very little room left. Yet, after transforming the properties and removing roads and other obstacles, he was able to free up much more space to make it pencil out. He also anticipates offering cremation and other services to support his bottom line.
 Bixby speaks in glowing terms of Mount Vernon, which he said represents a unique opportunity nationally to combine public art, history and nature in a major urban setting. "You know, 99.9 percent of anyone in my business would have looked at Mount Vernon and said, ‘You're insane,'" said Bixby. "But I thought this could be something magnificent, something for the ages. As ridiculous as it may sound, I really mean that."
 Tags: abandoned Act 135 East Falls historic cemeteries 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Restoration Role Model: The Bellevue
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 The Bellevue Hotel’s Pearl Room features 36-foot ceilings adorned with glass domes and grand balconies offering spectacular views of the city skyline. Hanging pearls give the room its name. Photo courtesy of The Bellevue
 South Broad Street’s grand dame, the Bellevue, designed in 1904 by George and William Hewitt, has undergone an extensive renovation by owner Lubert-Adler. Extant Magazine spoke with Tony Machado, head of design for LUCID, the in-house design and construction studio for Highgate, a leading hotel management, investment and development company, about how the project restored the “original glory” of the hotel, while creating newly designed rooms, residences, offices and event spaces.
 Extant Magazine (EM): What was most important to preserve in the Bellevue restoration?
 Tony Machado (TM): The Bellevue is an architectural treasure not only for Philadelphia, but for our nation. It’s shocking to see that these grand dames are still being taken down around the country. We just lost the Hotel Pennsylvania in New York City.
 At the Bellevue, many architectural features had been lost to time. Fortunately, there was much left to celebrate. It was important for us to preserve everything we could and stay flexible enough that, if we were to discover something under the layers, we could change our course.
 EM : What was the original vision for the restoration? Did it change over time?
 TM : The building had suffered years of neglect. Even in its state of decay, we knew we had something special. There were many attempts to modernize over the years. Our vision was to return the Bellevue to her original glory, celebrate her heritage and give her back to the community. It seems everyone you bump into in Philadelphia has a Bellevue memory.
 The Grand Belle Ballroom, which has hosted illustrious personalities and countless Philadelphian memories. | Photo courtesy of The Bellevue
 EM : What was the biggest preservation challenge?
 TM : Many of the Bellevue’s architectural features had been preserved by neglect. This was fortunate for us. We were able to phase the main public space preservation and restoration, while keeping the building open for business–both the hotel and office components. This was one of our biggest challenges.
 EM : Did you look to any role models for inspiration or at an example in Philadelphia or elsewhere?
 TM : We were fortunate to have a great number of materials available to us for historical reference: photos, floor plans, and a very helpful book, The Bellevue-Stratford Hotel , written by Roger S. Lucas. This book became our go-to guide. It helped us understand the original layout, circulation corridors, and where there were actual voids behind walls that could potentially be restored. We were very happy to have that book.
 EM : What was the project’s biggest surprise (good or bad)?
 TM : While pulling back the layers of past renovations, we found some of the original decorative wall coverings. In an effort to celebrate the building’s heritage, we salvaged what we could and framed it for our guestroom artwork. This helps reinforce our narrative of providing spaces that have evolved over time with a subtle nod to history.
 Tags: Broad Street Center City hotel Renovation Restoration Role Model 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Places to Save: Spring 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 The Sprucemont 
 Location : 257 South 16th Street
 Built : 1916
 Threat : Vacancy
 The Sprucemont, a Beaux-Arts masterpiece, rises 16 stories in the heart of Philadelphia’s Rittenhouse-Fitler historic district. It was built in 1916 by architect Frederick Webber, known for his grand apartment houses and hotels, including the Touraine at 1520 Spruce Street.
 Despite its local designation within the Rittenhouse-Fitler historic district and its structural soundness, the Sprucemont now stands vacant and decaying. In 2019, developers purchased the building with a multimilliondollar redevelopment plan to transform the building into 61 modern rental units. Escalating costs and extensive system updates derailed the project. The developers defaulted on a $14 million loan, halting all work in 2022. Legal disputes and bankruptcy filings caused the developers to lose control of the building in November 2023. The Court of Common Pleas approved a request to place the building in receivership while financial matters are worked out in court.
 Now, with windows shattered and graffiti creeping up the elevations, the property continues accumulating violations from the Department of Licenses and Inspections. Originally conceived as a hotel and later converted into apartments, the Sprucemont has the potential to meet Philadelphia’s housing needs once again. With its ideal location and historic character, it could attract residents seeking the unique charm of the city’s landmark buildings.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Old Main 
 Location : 3 Seminary Avenue, Upland, Pennsylvania
 Built : 1858
 Threat : Neglect
 Old Main, on the Crozer-Chester Medical Center campus, was built in 1858 by industrialist John P. Crozer to house Upland Normal Institute, which provided education to underserved children. Samuel Sloan designed this three-story, stucco-coated stone building with an F-shaped layout, central cupola and geometric pilasters that exemplifies mid-19th-century institutional architecture.
 During the Civil War, it served as an Army hospital, treating more than 6,000 casualties from both sides and leaving behind soldiers’ names etched in its iconic cupola. In 1868, it was converted into the Crozer Theological Seminary, where it nurtured many leaders, including Martin Luther King Jr.
 King’s years at Crozer profoundly shaped his philosophy of nonviolence and social justice. Living and studying at Old Main, he embraced the Christian social gospel, was elected student body president and graduated valedictorian in 1951. The building’s serene surroundings fostered his intellectual and spiritual growth, preparing him for the transformative leadership he would later embody.
 Added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1973, the building has been underutilized for years. Ongoing financial and operational instability within the Crozer-Chester Medical Center system has added to its precarious state. Crozer-Chester Medical Center’s struggles have drawn the attention of the Pennsylvania state government, which has intervened to stabilize the health care provider. However, Old Main remains at risk, with no clear preservation plan in place.
