The Preservation Alliance is consulting with the Friends of Old Main to help raise awareness of the building’s significance and advocate for its preservation.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Joe Frazier’s Gym 
 Location : 2917 North Broad Street
 Built : 1895
 Threat : Neglect
 Joe Frazier’s Gym is steeped in cultural, historical, and social significance. Built in 1895 as a warehouse, it became a gym in 1968 where “Smokin’ Joe” Frazier, Olympic gold medalist and World Heavyweight Champion, prepared for legendary bouts, including his 1971 “Fight of the Century” against Muhammad Ali.
 Following his 1975 retirement, Frazier trained boxers at the gym, including Golden Gloves Heavyweight Champion Duane Bobick, Bert Cooper, and Olympic medalist Terrance Cauthen. More than just a training facility, the gym served as a community hub for more than 25 years, offering mentorship and opportunity to North Philadelphia’s youth. Through the gym, Frazier empowered generations of boxers and instilled values of hard work and perseverance.
 Financial hardship forced Frazier to sell the building in 2008. Since his passing in 2011, a series of neglectful owners have left the gym vacant and in disrepair with mounting Department of Licenses and Inspections violations and unpaid taxes. Listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2013, it is protected from demolition, but faces an uncertain future.
 In December 2024, the building was listed for sale at a prohibitive asking price, hindering efforts to find a preservation-minded buyer. A committed buyer can restore this landmark, celebrating its pivotal role in Philadelphia’s boxing history and inspiring future generations. Saving Joe Frazier’s Gym is more than preserving a structure. It is an opportunity to honor the legacy of a man who inspired a city and a nation.
 For a deeper understanding of the importance of Joe Frazier's Gym, listed below, listen to episode 3 and episode 4 of season 2 of Song of Philadelphia , Hidden City's podcast, available on Spotify and Apple .
 Tags: Center City Joe Frazier's Gym North Broad Street Places to Save suburbs

title: Windows into History and Inspiration
author: Starr Herr-Cardillo
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 A rose window created by noted stain-glass artist John LaFarge for First Unitarian Church, 2125 Chestnut Street. It was installed when the house of worship was erected in 1891. | Photo: Joseph E.B. Elliott
 Sunlight streaming through stained glass has a magical, immersive quality that conjures the celestial and divine, tapping deep into some essential part of the human imagination. I remember being transfixed by stained-glass windows as a child–not at church, but at the planetarium I used to visit on the way home from middle school. The mid-century building featured a wall of them, made from chunky, textured and vibrantly hued glass. They drifted through an abstract gradient of colors and, when struck by the low angle of the afternoon sun, were absolutely mesmerizing.
 In 2020, I visited Beyer Studio, a stained-glass studio in Germantown for an Extant article on traditional building crafts. As we talked and wandered around the studio, Joe Beyer raised a gorgeous piece of cobalt blue glass up to the window and remarked that no medium is as “potent” as glass. When I recently prompted him with the memory, he laughed and said, “I still feel that way, whenever I see a really nice piece of red flash. There’s no medium that really matches it. The daylight is really a major ingredient.”
 A Timeless Quality 
 In the early 12th century, stained glass became the primary conduit for channeling “divine light” in ecclesiastical buildings as Gothic architecture came into its own. Large, faceted, pictorial windows were a defining feature of the style, linking the earthbound to the celestial. Historically, stained glass specifically meant leaded windows that had been painted, often with silver oxide, and fired to literally “stain” the glass. Today, stained glass is used as a catchall term to refer to an assemblage of cut glass pieces, often colored or textured, held together in lead channels to create a window or two-dimensional pane. Architectural glass is ornamental glass that may be colored or clear and is often patterned glass, meant to enhance the design and function of a building (think leaded glass transoms or textured glass in bedroom doors or bathrooms). Art glass is another key term that can apply to any glass panel made with opalescent, iridescent or patterned glass.
 There is a timeless quality to stained glass, perhaps because the medium as a whole has not deviated much from its medieval roots. When I asked Beyer how the process had changed, he joked that now the soldering irons plug in. To make glass, at least back in the medieval days, sand and wood ash were melted down to a liquid form and various metals were added to the glass in its molten state to create colors. The molten glass would then be blown into a long, cylindrical shape, sliced open and coaxed to lay flat. Or it might be blown into a bulb, opened at one end and then spun high in the air into a plate-like disk to make crown glass, creating the distinctive “bullseye” glass, the thicker, round section at the point where the glass adheres to the iron.
 Joe Beyer holds up one of the thousands of pieces of stained glass imported from Europe that his studio keeps in stock both for repairing antique windows and making new ones. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Some glass is still made this way today, although the number of producers has been dwindling over the past several years. Specialized companies in Germany, France, and the United States still produce mouth-blown sheet glass, known as “antique glass.” Beyer, a self-described “glass snob,” stocks his studio with European antique glass, which is what you’ll likely find in historic church windows and other higher-end pictorial glass pieces. Many of the stately homes along Broad Street and early suburban developments in West Philadelphia, Chestnut Hill, and Mount Airy featured leaded and stained-glass embellishments, intricate woodwork, and other flourishes. Beyer said much of this glass was industrially produced. Cathedral glass or textured window glass manufactured in the United States was made from molten glass that was rolled out and impressed with textures and patterns in a manner that was easier to mass produce.
 Yet, there is another type of very highly prized glass that was frequently used throughout Philadelphia: the pearly and opalescent art glass made by Louis Comfort Tiffany of Tiffany Studios. Inspired by Roman and ancient glass during a trip to London in 1893, Tiffany began experimenting with glass production, mixing metallic oxides with molten glass, mixing glass colors and embracing irregularities. The result defined the studio’s signature style, called Favrile glass, patented by Tiffany in 1896.
 Illuminating Philadelphia 
 Stained glass production in the United States intensified around the mid-to-late 19th century, when Victorian and Gothic Revival churches and residential architecture proliferated. The hundreds of ecclesiastical buildings that rose across Philadelphia between 1890 and World War II incorporated stained glass based on earlier European styles and techniques. Often, congregations would import mass-produced stained-glass windows out of Europe. In the late 1890s, Philadelphia was home to both the Willet Stained Glass Studios and D’Ascenzo Studios, two renowned studios whose works are featured in prominent buildings across the country. By the turn of the 20th century, stained and leaded glass were being mass produced and were widely available, with designs for decorative architectural glass windows appearing in catalogs and residential designs throughout the U.S.
 A scene from D'Ascenzo Studios circa 1925. At the time, it was arguably the most well-known stained glass workshop in America.| Photo: D'Ascenzo Studio Archives collection via Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 In an ecclesiastical setting, pictorial stained glass serves multiple purposes. It evokes an emotional response, shifting the mood of a space throughout the course of a day. It’s also often didactic, highlighting scenes and stories of biblical figures. These windows carry significance and meaning from a sociological perspective, too, reflecting the tastes, values and economic circumstances of communities at particular points in time. Beyer used to offer a Center City tour that deciphered the stylistic influences of stained-glass windows in churches. The windows, often funded by donors, reflect stylistic preferences, tastes and technologies of their time. Center City offers what Beyer calls a “cornucopia of glass” in churches such as Frank Furness’s First Unitarian, John Notman’s Church of the Holy Trinity, and Isaac Purcell’s Evangelical Lutheran Church of the Holy Communion.
 Yigdal Raphael soldering together pieces of stained glass at Beyer Studio. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 “The space can speak to us,” said Reverend Carolyn Cavaness of the historic Mother Bethel African Methodist Episcopal Church. “It is the embodiment, the hard work of not just labor, but resources, collective genius, creative genius, and community creating a space to gather.” That carries symbolic weight. Mother Bethel, founded in 1791 by Reverend Richard Allen, located in what is now known as Society Hill, occupies the oldest continuously Black-owned parcel of land in the nation. “For the African American community, where we have so few structures and places that are ours, that’s really powerful.”
 Worshippers at Mother Bethel African Methodist Church on a recent Sunday. The Stained-glass windows in the main sanctuary were made by the Century Art Company and installed when the church was built in 1890. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 The current late Victorian-style building dates to 1889 and features a gorgeous assemblage of large, arched figurative windows and ornamental glass windows throughout the sanctuary. Those windows, Cavaness said, were funded by people who had been systematically disenfranchised by slavery, coming together with whatever they had to esteem God and their community. “In the midst of darkness, these windows are shining bright,” she said. “They help to center us, and they come as a testament to past generations.”
 Other Stained-Glass Jewels 
 Stained glass wasn’t limited to Philadelphia’s ecclesiastical architecture. A number of the city’s commercial buildings also hosted impressive works of glass art. Horn & Hardart automats featured stained-glass windows designed by Nicholas D’Ascenzo as a way to add a sense of grandeur and elegance to the dining experience. Sadly, none of them remain, but one of the windows from the 16th and Chestnut Streets location was restored in 2022 by stained glass artisan Chandler Coleman of Cathedral Stained Glass Studios in Cheltenham after it was rescued during demolition in 1966 and donated, years later, to the Woodmere Art Museum.
 The Dream Garden , a mural gracing the lobby of the Curtis Building at 6th and Walnut Streets, was designed by Philadelphia native Maxfield Parrish and fabricated from hundreds of thousands of iridescent Favrile glass tesserae by Tiffany Studios in Queens, New York. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Another masterful public work of glass art is Maxfield Parrish’s “The Dream Garden,” installed in the Curtis Publishing Building in 1916. Not technically stained glass (the mural is not illuminated from behind), the work consists of hundreds of thousands of opalescent Tiffany glass tesserae that form a glowing garden scene that gives the illusion it is lit from within.
 Carrying on the Craft 
 When three of the historic ornamental stained-glass windows at Mother Bethel were damaged by vandalism in February 2024, the Preservation Alliance helped lead a fundraising effort for their restoration. Glass artist Owusu Ansah, of Owusu Studio in Germantown, removed the broken panes and beautifully restored them. These particular windows were a simple design of offset rectangles of colored glass, making them a straightforward fix. Ansah, a Nigerian-born master glass artist who studied at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, has restored and designed new stained-glass windows throughout Philadelphia and the East Coast. The Mother Bethel congregation gathered to bless the new windows after they were returned.
 “What stained glass does for a community of worshippers is that it’s supposed to inspire the best in us, so that when we come in to worship, we look up at the windows, they open up our imagination,” Reverend Mark Tyler, former pastor of Mother Bethel, told CBS News.
 Philadelphia is lucky to have a number of skilled stained glass specialists practicing in the area, but, overall, traditional craft and knowledge associated with historic buildings is dwindling. The skill is typically learned in other countries through a formal apprenticeship process. “There are currently no programs in the United States at a four-year university level to teach stained glass,” said Stephen Hartley, associate professor of the practice at Notre Dame’s School of Architecture. Hartley, who used to head the now-defunct Building Arts program at Bryn Athyn College, said there hasn’t been an official apprenticeship program for stained glass artists since the 1970s. Many practitioners will train with a professional for years, often referred to as apprenticing. But the key difference is that a traditional apprenticeship, as various trade unions offer, implies a pathway to employment and a standardized curriculum and skill set.
 In February 2024, a vandal through rocks through Mother Bethel's 134-year-old stained-glass windows costing the church roughly $20,000 in damages. The Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia ran a fundraising campaign that helped the congregation fully cover the costs.| Photo: Michael Bixler
 Today, the outlook for stained glass as a craft isn’t bad, Hartley said. According to the Stained Glass Association of America, there are roughly the same number of firms offering stained glass services as there were 100 years ago. The work has changed. Much of it is new commissions for secular architecture and restoration work, but there is still demand.
 Another notable difference is that the younger generation taking up the craft today tends to come from a background in fine arts rather than building or applied arts. The artistic sensibilities and skills–such as color selection and painting ability–translate well but in service of a different end, said Hartley. “Stained glass is an applied art and not a fine art. You’re taking your artistic ability and applying it to a profession.” Students in his class, Painting with Light, get a taste of this distinction, learning the tools, art history, deterioration, and conservation techniques for stained glass. At the end of the semester, they perform an assessment for a house of worship in need.
 Conservation, Restoration, and Care 
 Stained-and-leaded-glass windows, while beautiful, are trickier to maintain than regular windows and periodically require specialized maintenance. They can sag and stretch, causing the window to bow. Individual glass pieces may break or crack from the pressure of bowing and go missing, causing the window to become drafty. Surface painting may become scratched or otherwise damaged. There are some key points to be aware of if you’re looking to embark on stained glass maintenance or restoration to ensure that windows aren’t damaged in the process.
 First, understand what you’re dealing with. Stained-glass windows involve multiple different materials that age and deteriorate, from wooden frames to steel supports, lead cames, glass pieces, and copper foil. A professional can help you understand how your window was made and identify the key issues that need to be addressed. This is an absolutely essential step for congregations or folks dealing with larger scale, decorative historic windows that may be highly valuable.
 In spring 2023, Emmanuel Christian Center, the new owners of the 1901 St. Paul’s Presbyterian Church in West Philadelphia, sold what they thought were two grimy, old stained-glass windows to a salvager for $6,000. The large rose windows turned out to be Tiffany and were sold at auction for $250,000. The unfortunate situation made national news and left church clergy feeling foolish and neighbors and historic preservationists frustrated and dismayed that the windows had been lost.
 The rose windows from St. Paul's Presbyterian Church, at 50th Street and Baltimore Avenue in Cedar Park, were sold at auction in 2024 from $20,000 plus $52,000 in auction fees. The church has been sold recently, and the new pastor sold these windows, along with many others, to an architectural salvage dealer without realizing they were made by Tiffany Studios. | Photo: Freeman's | Hindman
 Second, never try to repair in place. Given the lack of knowledge about stained glass, Beyer said it can be easy for congregations to fall for salespeople pitching quick fixes. Once the window has been examined by a professional, it will likely need to be removed in order to be repaired properly. Despite what some smooth sales pitches might suggest, there are very few issues that can be solved in place. Stained glass needs room to expand and contract as different components of the windows react with environmental temperatures. After a certain amount of time, some components–often the putty and, in extreme instances, the lead cames–simply need to be replaced, a straightforward and relatively quick fix for an experienced professional. Beware of anyone offering to re-cement windows in place. This will likely yield sloppy results and will raise the cost of a properly done restoration later. Another consideration is exterior window protection. If you have the resources, Beyer said, go with glass storm windows versus plexiglass, which will discolor and become foggy over time.
 Congregations looking to replace a stained-glass window that isn’t protected by historic designation should look into the Sacred Window Rescue Project, an initiative at Beyer Studio that seeks to match salvaged stained-glass windows with faith organizations around the world that can provide permanent homes for them. The goal of the project, which Beyer said has been running for decades, is to keep sacred windows out of the antiques market and ensure they end up somewhere where they will be shown respect. Over the years, it has helped more than 1,000 church windows–primarily from Philadelphia–find permanent homes.
 Where to View Glass Art in and Around Philadelphia 
 Bryn Athyn Cathedral : 900 Cathedral Road, Bryn Athyn, PA 19009
 The jewel-toned stained glass was inspired by Gothic French cathedrals and was fabricated at Bryn Athyn’s studio (equipped with its own glass furnace) from 1916 into the 1940s.
 Calvary United Methodist Church : 801 S. 48th Street, Philadelphia, PA 19143
 Designed in 1907 by New York architect William R. Brown, the church features Tiffany stained-glass windows.
 Curtis Building : 699 Walnut Street, Philadelphia, PA 19106
 Maxfield Parrish’s “The Dream Garden” graces the east lobby of the former Curtis Publishing Company, which is open to the public daily.
 Mother Bethel AME Church : 419 S. 6th Street, Philadelphia, PA 19147
 The church’s figurative and decorative stained-glass windows were funded by parishioners and fabricated by Century Art Company in 1890.
 United States Min t: 151 N. Independence Mall E, Philadelphia, PA 19106
 The lobby features seven Favrile glass mosaics depicting the process of coin production. The mosaics were commissioned for the Mint’s former location at 1700 Spring Garden Street in 1901 and were moved to the current location.
 One of two 26-foot-tall stained-glass windows at Calvary Church, 48th Street and Baltimore Avenue. They are the largest Tiffany-signed stained-glass window ensembles in Philadelphia. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Washington Memorial Chapel : 2000 Valley Forge Park Rd, King of Prussia, PA 19406
 Located in Montgomery County, the chapel features great works of the American Arts and Crafts movement, including ironwork by Samuel Yellin and 13 windows by Nicola D’Ascenzo inspired by the Chartres Cathedral in France.
 Fisher Fine Arts Library : 220 S. 34th Street, Philadelphia, PA 19104
 Designed by Frank Furness and completed in 1890, the library features elaborate textured, clear leaded-glass windows adorned with aphorisms selected by the architect’s brother, Horace Howard Furness, a Shakespeare scholar.
 First Presbyterian Church in Philadelphia : 201 S. 21st Street, Philadelphia, PA 19103
 The 1872 landmark by Henry Augustus Sims features works from various studios including Willet, Tiffany and smaller studios from the late 19th to late 20th century.
 First Unitarian Church of Philadelphia : 2125 Chestnut Street, Philadelphia, PA 19103
 Features brilliant stained-glass windows, including a seven-sided rose window designed by John La Farge, a contemporary of Louis Comfort Tiffany who also patented early opalescent glass-making techniques.
 The McClatchy Building : 10 S. 69th Street, Upper Darby Township, PA 19082
 This Egyptian Revival spectacle at 69th Street in Upper Darby features a multistory stained-glass window by D’Ascenzo Studios that can be viewed from inside the H&M store.
 Tags: Conservation historic churches windows 
 About the Author
 Starr Herr-Cardillo is a freelance writer and historic preservation professional working in the nonprofit sector. She holds a master’s degree in historic preservation from the University of Pennsylvania.

title: A New Public Park Brings Bridesburg Back to the River
author: Ann de Forest
bodyText:
New landscaping and reclaimed nature converge at Borski Park in Bridesburg. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 On a balmy evening in early May, lifelong Bridesburg resident Stacy Schwab sat with a group of neighbors on the side steps of the Bridesburg Recreation Center. “There’s a river right there,” she waved over her shoulder in the direction of the playground, “and you would never know it.” Bridesburg curves into the Delaware River on maps of Philadelphia, a gentle cape in the lower northeastern edge of the city. Because it recedes on approach, it was once called Point-No-Point. Frankford Creek flows, or channeled now, seeps into the Delaware there, a confluence that made the area attractive to tanneries, which dominated the riverfront in the 18th and 19th century. The waterfront also featured the double-decker Bridge Street Pier, which some very old timers remember as the dock for a ferry from Center City, as well as a popular fishing and swimming spot. 
 By the mid 20th century, however, industry had usurped the riverfront with Rohm and Haas’ chemical manufacturing and the Philadelphia Coke Company, known locally as Cokie’s, the largest of several factories that occupied the Delaware River. The Bridge Street Pier, primarily a loading dock for shipments of hazardous materials, was closed to public access for safety reasons in the 1950s. These factories provided jobs for the working-class neighborhood of mostly German and Polish immigrants. They also spewed smoke into the air, leached chemicals into the soil, and toxic runoff into the water. The concrete factory once located at the end of Orthodox Street dumped its excess production into the river at the close of every day. “I worked at a place that murdered the river,” said longtime resident Alexis Macool, with characteristic bluntness. A degree in biochemistry landed her a job at Cokie’s, virtually in her backyard, where every week took water samples from the Frankford Creek effluent. “There were fish kills,” she recalled.
 All along the waterfront of Northeast Philadelphia, the Delaware received similar disregard and mistreatment. “This is where the city has put its garbage dumps, its prisons, its manufacturing facilities,” says Stephanie Phillips, executive director of Riverfront North , the nonprofit environmental organization that has built 11 miles of trails along the Delaware Avenue in the past decade.
 The Philadelphia Coke Company factory in 1970 and the Rohm and Haas chemical plant in 1979. | Photos courtesy of the Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Today, though, the Delaware River is cleaner than ever, and under Riverfront North’s initiative, Bridesburg is on the verge of taking the river back. July 11 marks the official opening of Borski Park , a brand new 10-acre city park built as a collaboration between Philadelphia Parks and Recreation (PPR) and Riverfront North on the restored site of the former concrete plant.
 The neighbors gathered last May on the rec center steps were not just shooting the breeze. The steps were the site of a monthly meeting of the Friends of Borski Park (FBP) , a group formed by Riverfront North under the guidance of community engagement manager Gina Craigo. She formed FBP to tap into the energy, local knowledge, and neighborhood pride of Bridesburg’s famously tight-knit community as Borski Park, planned and promised for 20 years, was about to become a reality.
 With two months to go before the opening, members of FBP that evening had decisions to make about the festivities–food, music, games, and other logistics. Craigo reviewed her checklist. Should there be a cake for the ribbon cutting on July 11? “That’s in my wheelhouse,” said volunteer Stacy Schwab, FBP's secretary, and immediately began texting her contacts. What about food for the Borski Splash on July 12? “You can’t go wrong with barbecued chicken,” said FBP president Jennifer Allen, another longtime resident, who also co-leads the Bridesburg Community Action Alliance. Another friend commented on a local food purveyor. “His brisket is good too.”
 The conversation isn’t all focused on cornhole boards and volleyball nets. FBP talks about their hopes for what Borski Park will bring to a community not only deprived of a waterfront, but of green spaces. After Rohm and Haas and the coke factory shut down, the brownfields and Superfund site they left behind had reverted to woodlands, paradoxically giving the neighborhood of tightly-knit rowhouses an illusion of parklands. Now, several mega-warehouses for data logistics and other uses occupy that compromised land. The hulking boxes are surrounded by asphalt parking lots, fenced off and gated on Richmond Street, Bridesburg’s main drag, and Bridge and Orthodox Streets, which are the only access points in and out of the neighborhood. “I was reading that being in nature is the prescription for anxiety, for depression," said Jackie Kasprzak. "I’m happy to get green space. [Until now] my green space was walking through the cemetery.”
 Bridesburg Bathing Beach on the Delaware River circa 1900s. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 At the same time, many in Bridesburg doubted the park would ever happen and still remain skeptical. Tight-knit in Bridesburg can also mean insular and manifest as distrust, especially of City and other government intervention. Riverfront North understood the importance of community involvement in planning Borski Park from the get go. Phillips characterizes the general attitude as “’This decision was made without me, and my way of life doesn’t matter.’” She and Riverfront North understood the importance of community involvement in planning Borski Park from the get go. A community grant received from the William Penn Foundation led to her hiring Craigo to ensure the new park would respond to local needs. Craigo's mother grew up on the outskirts of Bridesburg, a section now severed by I-95, which instantly gave her some community cred, she said. Along with establishing a board of directors and the friends group, she hangs out at I Knead Coffee every Tuesday for Trail Talks, her low-key office hours for people to ask questions, get the latest updates on the park’s planning, or even complain.
 When Craigo first came on board, the William Penn funding also supported exploratory excursions for the board to experience how other cities design parks that encourage play, engagement with nature, and build community in innovative ways. For Craigo, the goal was to spark imaginations and expand definitions of what a park can be. “For most people,” she said, “you say ‘park’, and they think ‘ballfield.’ “
 There will be no ballfields or play equipment at Borski Park. Instead, a grassy area known as The Lawn, planted over the former factory’s slab foundation, presents a blank canvas for a panoply of activities, programmed and unprogrammed. Morning yoga, volleyball, picnics, and story hours are among the possibilities, though Craigo is on the lookout for imaginative ideas that she and her volunteers may not have considered yet. On a rise beyond The Lawn lies The Meadow, where invasive species have been removed to cultivate a native pollinator garden. A nature trail wends through the meadow and into a woodland that grew up in the abandoned Philadelphia Coke Company site. A family of deer already inhabits the woods. A gnawed tree trunk attests to to the presence of beavers not far away.
 The first photo shows Borski Park's concrete wasteland before construction began. The second view shows what the park looks like today. | Photos: Riverfront North and Michael Bixler
 This property’s industrial past is both evident and hidden. The factory’s daily dump of excess concrete created a tough and jagged tundra of a shoreline, striated grey swirls that look like petrified soft-serve ice cream swirls. To cultivate trees at the edge of the lawn, holes have been drilled into a concrete trench that functions as a cross between a planter and a rain garden. Even the gentle slope that leads from lawn to meadow is artificial and speaks to an industrial past. “We’re walking on history,” explained Craigo. Buried underneath are the remains of Bridge-Pratt Terminal in Frankford, torn down in 1986 to make way for the renovated Frankford Transportation Center. The debris was deposited on what was then an abandoned post-industrial site and is now owned by the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation (PIDC). Although not part of the park property, the ruins of Cokie’s dock, a collapsing structure reminiscent of Graffiti Pier in Port Richmond, can be glimpsed jutting out into an inlet beyond the woods.
 “It’s a place that has a past,” said Leigh Ann Campbell, deputy commissioner of planning, property, and strategic engagement for the PPR. “I love being able to see a part of history in that concrete sledge at the edge. It tells a story without telling the story directly.”
 Concrete debris left by the Philadelphia Coke Company factory blankets the shore of the Delaware River. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 That story, when the park opens next week, is worth celebrating. It is a hopeful story of reclaiming and transforming degraded land into a place that celebrates the beauty and wildness of the Delaware River, a woodland and meadow with a stellar view of the Betsy Ross Bridge and a glimpse of the Center City skyline. Campbell, Craigo, and Phillips hope that story will be accessible not just to the residents of Bridesburg, but for other Philadelphians as well. While Borski Park answers a very local need for water access for a community long deprived of their river, for Riverfront North, the park also represents the culmination of an integrated system of parks along those 11 miles of trail that parallel the Delaware River from just north of Center City up to Glen Foerd on the city’s northeast corner. “Basically, these are jewels along the necklace,” said Campbell, “[Borski Park] is part of a larger vision to connect these jewels of space, a suite of amenities, along the trail.” Both PPR and Riverfront North are looking at the upper Delaware River in Philadelphia wholisticly, she added.
 Renderings of Borski Park show the trailhead and lawn upon completion. | Images: Ground Reconsidered
 The source of that wholistic vision is Robert A. Borski Jr., known to all as Bob, the former congressman for whom the park is named. As representative of the Northeast from 1982 until 2002, he served on the House Transportation Committee and co-sponsored the Intermodal Surface Transportation Efficiency Act of 1991. “ISTE opened up tremendous doors, because it expanded the definition of transportation beyond just highways," said Borski. He explained the transformative legislation one morning at I Knead Coffee. The concept of “rails to trails” grew out of ICT, and, he said, “funded the conversion of disused rail lines into trails and linear parks all over the U.S.”
 That funding is responsible for many trail networks across Philadelphia, as well as the East Coast Greenway . It also led to the founding of Riverfront North. For Borski, however, trails were just part of a much larger vision. As a member of the Transportation Committee, he had the opportunity to travel to cities around the world to study their transportation infrastructure. What struck him the most was how cities drew on their waterways as assets available to everyone. “Every other place in the world celebrates its rivers,” Borski said. He was determined to give his constituents the same connection. “We actually have a real river here. The Delaware is one of the great rivers of the world.” On July 11, at a ceremony honoring Borski for his enthusiasm, vision, and support, Bridesburg will be reunited with that great river that has been disregarded and invisible for so many years.
 Riverfront North will host a dedication ceremony at Robert A. Borski, Jr. Park, 3101 Orthodox Street, on Friday, July 11 from 10 a.m. until 12 p.m. Register for the event here: https://www.eventbrite. com/e/robert-a-borski-jr-park- dedication-ceremony-tickets- 1382787276969?aff= oddtdtcreator 
 Borski Splash!, a family-friendly day of summertime activities, will take place on Saturday, July 12 at the park between 10:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m. See event details and register here: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/borski-splash-a-community-celebration-of-the-new-borski-park-tickets-1397052695219?aff=oddtdtcreator 
 Tags: adaptive resuse Bridesburg Delaware River industrial history Northeast Philadelphia public parks public space 
 About the Author
 Ann de Forest writes frequently about design, architecture, and the built environment. She is co-editor of Extant, the magazine of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. Her short stories, essays and poems have appeared in Coal Hill Review, Unbroken, Noctua Review, Cleaver Magazine, among others. She is the editor of Ways of Walking, an anthology of essays published by New Door Books in 2022, a project inspired by her having walked the entire perimeter of Philadelphia twice.

title: Historic Guardhouse in FDR Park Primed for New Life as a Welcome Center
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
Normally, an ornate animal stable housing police-trained horses and dogs would seem a more interesting use of space than a row of public restrooms, but an exception to that rule can now be found in South Philadelphia. Philadelphia Parks and Recreation (PPR) has officially completed the adaptive reuse of a century-old guardhouse in the northeast corner of Franklin Delano Roosevelt (FDR) Park. Over the past several years, the three-part, 18,000-square-foot structure has undergone extensive renovations for new use as a Welcome Center, led by the nonprofit Fairmount Park Conservancy (FPC), as part of a larger $250-plus million overhaul of the park.
 An original three-story guardhouse, built circa 1919, is set to become dedicated office space for PPR as well as multiple nonprofits who operate in the park. On the other end of the property, a cavernous former auto garage has been converted to an event space large enough to hold wedding receptions for 200 people.
 FDR Park's former guardhouse received a faithful renovation and a new use as a welcome center. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 Yet, the main attraction for everyday visitors to FDR will undoubtedly be a collection of modern bathroom facilities, an amenity currently, and glaringly, lacking in the 348-acre park. And they're making a show of it: the restrooms will be accessible through a large barn door entranceway into an open-air courtyard, replete with Romanesque-archways in restored historic brickwork. As visitors make their way down an adjoining corridor, they will also pass by reused stable gates, recalling the space's previous function as a home for police horses. 
 Architecture firm WRT provided the project's design. Renovations by construction contractor Keating were completed in May. A date for public opening is not yet set. During a recent tour of Architecture firm WRT performed the design.the facility, FPC staff who worked on the $12 million project said they were excited to soon bring new life to the building, particularly one that will see its doors open to visitors for the first time. “At the time planning began, this building wasn’t really accessible to the public, it didn’t have a public use,”said Allison Schapker, FPC's chief operations and projects officer. “So [the goals were] to make sure we provide good amenities to park users, adaptively reuse a historic building, and make sure that the building welcomed the public.”
 A Stroll Down Memory Lane 
 A map of League Island from 1897. | Image: World Maps Online
 Ever since its original development, the land on which FDR Park now sits has been a place for the people. Maps of Philadelphia in the 18th and 19th centuries show little happening among its substantial acreage, save for Hollanders Creek running through what is now the heart of the park, as well as a few isolated residences. Indeed, the low-lying area was referred to as primarily swampland in public records as late as 1895.
 However, it was in that year that City officials planned for a different future. Articles in the Philadelphia Inquirer and other newspapers record that City Councilmember Edward A. Anderson was by that time championing conversion of the land into a “League Island Park,” its name derived from an adjacent island of that name, which is now referred to as the Philadelphia Navy Yard. Anderson and other supporters of the idea noted that Fairmount Park, which had been protected over the course of the prior century, was miles away from this rapidly densifying part of the city and advocated that South Philadelphians too should have access to parkland.
 “Don’t cut down the size of the park whatever you do,” argued Councilmember Stratton during one hearing on the proposal. “Give the boys and girls a playground. Things have now come to the point in this city where a boy can’t stick his nose outside of a door, if he has a ball in his hand, but a policeman has him and marches him off to a station house.”
 The Olmsted Brothers' 1913 plan for League Island Park. | Image: Fairmount Park Conservancy
 Yet, the park’s initial development faced a rocky road. Objections from some councilmembers over the price tag were overcome when an ordinance was passed and signed by then-Mayor Edwin S. Stuart in 1895. Still, maps from the first decade of the 20th century show little development. Indeed, a history compiled for FDR’s successful 2000 nomination to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places notes an original design wasn’t made by the City until 1908, and, even then, construction was stalled for several years by “politics and economics.”
 Help arrived in the form of the Olmsted Brothers. In 1912, the nomination states, the City’s Department of Public Works approached the seminal landscape design firm to redesign the park. This time, the plans were realized and the modern landscape of FDR was constructed, complete with “picturesque curving roads, walks, lakes, and tree planting,” characteristic of the ethos of progenitor Frederick Law Olmsted, Sr. “[Olmsted] believed that landscape design could affect society, especially promoting a sense of community,” the nomination recorded. “He believed that scenery could have a powerful psychological effect on people. He was convinced that the open, rolling terrain of his parks provided a specific, medical antidote to the artificiality, noise, and stress of city life.”
 FDR Park's gazebo, or tempietto (small temple), was built in 1914. The park and structures within were placed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2000. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Work to develop the park began in 1914, and the original guardhouse on the property is thought to date to about 1919, according to educational materials provided by the City (the architect is unknown). The park’s historic register nomination defines the building as a contributing to the historic value of FDR. “Flemish-bond brown brick Arts & Crafts building,” and states it was later used as the headquarters for the Philadelphia Police Department’s Mounted Police training and Services unit. “This space is where park guards used to live and work,” said Schapker. “When they were on shift they may have stayed overnight here. Their offices may have been here.”
 Adjoining stables believed to be a part of the original construction had room for 25 horses and were also later used for the Philadelphia Police Department's K-9 Corps Kennels. Then, in the 1980s, a large auto garage was built to the rear of the property on its western flank. In eecent history, many of those functions fell away, leaving limited use for anyone besides sparse PPR staff. When FDR came up for redevelopment in 2018, it set the table for new life.
 Welcome to FDR 
 The future Welcome Center is located near FDR Park’s main entrance at Broad Street and Pattison Avenue and just a 3-minute walk away from the popular Anna C. Verna Playground. | Photo: Albert Yee, Fairmount Park Conservancy
 When conducting community surveys for the park redesign, FPC staff said a few amenities came through loud and clear. They weren’t particularly fancy. “Places to use the restroom, get something to eat. Places to sit down, you know, be in the shade and take a break,” Schapker said.
 However, reconnecting with historic infrastructure was also a request that popped up. Planners saw the former guardhouse as a place to scratch multiple itches. The former stable area will become a central focus, with the large exterior barn door at the far end of the courtyard rolling open each morning to allow the public into the space. The center of the courtyard has been converted from asphalt to permeable pavement and features a small rain garden to help infiltrate stormwater, as well as three enclosed stalls for concession vendors. One side of the courtyard will allow public access to the restroom facilities, while the other will provide private entry into the rear of the former guardhouse.
 The Welcome Center's outdoor courtyard features space for food vendors and a public area for dining . | Photo: Albert Yee, Fairmount Park Conservancy
 "The idea is if you come to FDR Park, you should be able to get an ice cream cone, a chicken wing, a cookie… something to make you want to relax and extend your stay,” Schapker said, adding they envision proceeds from the vendors helping to pay for long-term maintenance of the building.
 Inside the former guardhouse, FPC staff envision office and meeting space for their organization, along with PPR and other park users such as the nonprofit Discovery Pathways, which hosts regular, free canoeing opportunities for South Philadelphia schoolchildren.
 The future information counter can also support concession sales. The Fairmount Park Conservancy's preservation efforts throughout the project included restoration of glazed brickwork like that shown here. | Photo: Albert Yee, Fairmount Park Conservancy
 The large former auto garage, which features a high, pyramid-shaped roof sloping to a skylight, will be used as an all-purpose event space. A terrace off the garage offers immediate line of sight to an adjacent and recently re-landscaped lagoon, connecting the built and natural environments.
 For each part of the renovation, FPC staff said historic preservation was taken into account. Minutes of the Philadelphia Historical Commission from earlier planning phases indeed note wrangling over the minutiae of historic windows, doors, and other materials. FPC staff said in total they restored 99 sashes and replicated five others, restored several interior doors, and repaired a pair of large decorative urns flanking the entranceway of the guardhouse
 Public restrooms are a crucial amenity for a park that welcomes over 4 million visitors annually. | Photo: Albert Yee, Fairmount Park Conservancy
 Of particular interest is the courtyard of the former stables, where staff said they removed concrete in-fills within numerous glazed orange brick archways ringing the space. They also kept and refinished the original floor of the garage.
 In a nod to the future, the renovation elevated the building’s mechanicals to the third floor of the guardhouse, where they will hopefully be protected from any flooding in the low-lying parkland. The first few feet of the event space, which is closest to the park’s water bodies, is also constructed with materials meant to withstand flooding. The overall design of the building earned a LEED gold certification.
 Tags: adaptive resuse Department of Parks and Recreation FDR Park Olmsted Brothers Renovation South Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Illegal Windows and Building Additions Abound at Historical Commission's Monthly Meeting
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Philadelphia Historical Commission did not add any new properties to the local register at its meeting on July 11. Instead, it reviewed and approved a variety of requests to construct additions onto buildings under the department's legal protections, while navigating the challenges to maintaining the character of historic architecture.
 St. Peter's School's main 19th century building and approved addition proposals in Society Hill. | Photo: Michael Bixler | Renderings: Atkin Olshin Schade Architects
 St. Peter’s School at 317 Lombard Street received approval for a three-story addition. The main building was constructed in 1873 and is a contributing asset to the Society Hill Historic District, which was established in 1999. The brick and composite paneled addition will attach to the west façade of a 1983 addition, attempting to recall the massing of several large, three-story rowhouses that formerly occupied the space. It was noted that the addition will not have a basement, so it will not require significant excavation, removing the possibility of disturbing any potential archaeological resources.
 A proposal to construct rear additions and restore the windows, doors, shutters, and stoops of the front facades of seven rowhouses in the 100 block of N. Mole Street was granted in concept. The mid-19th century buildings were added to the historic register in 1967.
 Another rear addition, on the house at 800 S. 5th Street in Queen Village, was also approved. The corner home was built in 1835 and designated historic in 1975. As with most requests for additions to historic buildings, the Historical Commission weighs in on how much they might be visible to the public, as well as assuring that historic materials and features will not be destroyed and new materials are compatible with the originals.
 800 S. 5th Street in Queen Village. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The owners of a contributing building tucked into a corner of the Victorian Roxborough Historic District will be allowed to build a two-story garage addition to the 1868 house at 4567 Fleming Street and a separate two-story building on the site. Both are modern in design and will be clad in dark composite wood siding, although the landscaping and grade of the parcel will prevent visibility from the street.
 In another historic district, the French Village in Mt. Airy , a one-story addition was approved for 7321 Elbow Lane. The home was designed in 1925 by architecture firm Willing, Sims and Talbutt, who were commissioned for a number of large homes for the wealthy.
 7321 Elbow Lane in Northwest Philadelphia's French Village. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The owners of 2024 Delancey Place , which was built in 1870 and is both individually designated and contributing to the Rittenhouse Fitler Historic District , received permission to construct a garage and rear deck.
 While these requests were either approved without changes or approved with final review to be done by Historical Commission staff, another proposal did not proceed. The owners of the building at 614 Pine Street , a contributing asset to the Society Hill Historic District, sought to construct a rear addition and roof deck, but was remanded back to the Architectural Committee owing to incompleteness.
 Other matters regarding alterations included a demolition request and a petition to retroactively legalize windows installed in a historically designated building.
 Two one-story buildings at 700 S. 2nd Street in Queen Village were approved for demolition. | Photo: Google Street View
 For the former, the Historical Commission approved the demolition of two one-story buildings on the parcel at 700 S. 2nd Street which will be replaced with two four-story buildings. Another structure on the lot, from the 18th century, is individually designated. The other two are not. Plan revisions addressed concerns about the buildings’ massing owing to their height and facade materials.
 The current owners of the 18th Street Methodist Episcopal Church at 1730 Wharton Street sought to legalize aluminum-clad windows that had replaced many of the original wood-framed marbled blue glass without the Historical Commission's approval nor a building permit from the Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I). The church was designed by architect J. Franklin Stuckert, and completed in 1888. It was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1988.
 1730 Wharton Street in Point Breeze. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In 2020, following a change in ownership, the Historical Commission approved a plan to restore the building’s exterior as part of a conversion to multi-unit residential use, contingent upon the marbled blue glass windows being retained, restored, or replicated in the front facade openings. Window plans were approved the following year by the Historical Commission staff, but not executed, and the current windows windows were installed earlier this year. A subsequent Stop Work Order issued by L&I led to the owner’s request for legalization. It was denied by the Historical Commission at Friday's meeting and remanded to the Architectural Committee, pursuant to the Department of the Interior’s Standard 6, which stipulates that “deteriorated historic features will be repaired, rather than replaced. Where the severity of deterioration requires replacement of a distinctive feature, the new feature will match the old in design, color, texture, and, where possible, materials.”
 In historic designation news, the long-awaited nomination of Piers 38 and 40 at 775 S. Columbus Boulevard was granted another continuance to the September 2025 meeting of the Historical Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation.
 Tags: Department of Licenses and Inspections historic churches Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Historic Willow Steam Plant Swiftly Heading For New Life as Apartments
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
After decades hanging in limbo, the former Willow Street Steam Generation Plant is primed for a revival as a 73-unit apartment building. Current owner James Maransky, a real estate developer and president of construction firm E-Built, has undertaken the monumental project. This may have the sound of a story told before: new life has been promised for the building for many decades, most recently as an apartment building under prior owner John Wei just two years ago. However, that was before E-Built purchased the building at 411-419 N. 9th Street from Wei for a cool $8.8 million. Maransky said this time it is for real.
 Extensive remediation work on the building has been completed. Work framing out the interior and restoring the exterior of the historic building has begun, activity that recently caught attention of onlookers posting on social media. If things go according to plan, Maransky explained it won’t be long before the building fully leaves behind its days as a steam generation plant and transforms into something new. “We are fully rocking and rolling,” said Maransky, adding that he predicts a mid-2026 opening.
 Willow Street Steam Generation Plant in Callowhill, one of Philadelphia’s most distinctive industrial landmarks, is currently being converted into apartments. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Willow Steam's iconic three stacks are staying, albeit with refinishing. Workers are also currently rappelling from the building’s 7th story roof to pressure wash and otherwise touch up its primarily red brick and steel facades.
 Skeptics may find some comfort in Maransky’s priors. Perhaps most apropos is E-Built’s recent development of the 10-story Gotham Silk Hosiery Company factory in Kensington into upscale apartments and retail space, an effort that won a 2022 award from the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. Other notable projects are the buildout of the Bok Bar roof and redevelopment of the Engine 29 firehouse on 4th Street near Girard Avenue, which received a 2025 Preservation Alliance award.
 Maransky’s plans for Willow Steam have also won support from local community organizations. “I'm excited to hear that this building will be preserved and have a new life,” Vincent DiMaria, zoning co-chair for the Callowhill Neighborhood Association, wrote in an email. “I hope that construction goes quickly and smoothly, and I look forward to welcoming new neighbors to this area.”
 Running Out of Steam 
 Built in 1927, the Willow Steam Plant is a vestige of a relatively unique heating system still in use in some parts of Center City today. As the United States began to electrify in the 1880s, the Edison Electric Light Company set up shop at 908 Sansom Street, burning coal to generate electricity to sell. However, an add-on quickly followed, as steam from the plant’s machinery was repurposed to heat a nearby home.
 That method grew into an extended network, with additional plants like Willow Steam popping up nearby to push steam through dozens of miles of underground pipelines and heat buildings throughout Center City and into West Philadelphia. Willow Steam was originally constructed by the Philadelphia Electric Company (PECO). The building fell into disuse by the 1970s and was then sold and resold many times over, all while deteriorating further into disrepair.
 A view inside Willow Steam from 2012. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 A few ideas for reuse were floated, but never came to fruition. One proposal was to convert it to a facility to burn trash and create steam. Another was the site for huge, wraparound advertising. Eventually, the building came to be owned by Quyen V. Tran. Incensed by its continued deterioration, a pair of Bella Vista residents and attorneys, Joel Palmer and Jeff Goldman, filed a state Act 135 petition against the property. As chronicled in a 2016 Philadelphia Inquirer article, the pair sought to take conservatorship of the property through their nonprofit, Scioli Turco Inc.
 That never came to pass after Chinatown developer John Wei purchased the building and began a remediation process that ultimately appeased a judge overseeing the matter. Wei then sought and obtained permits to convert the building into a 69-unit apartment building with ground-floor commercial space. But Wei, who public records indicate has encountered financial hardship , later sold the building to E-Built.
 Knocking the Rust Off 
 As part of the deal, Maransky said Wei agreed to finish the bulk of the remediation process prior to the sale in return for a premium on the price. “The interior is totally clean,” he said, adding that the only hurdle that remains is monitoring groundwater wells required by state standards.
 Willow Steam's renovated brick and metal facade at ground level. | Rendering: E-Built
 Because Wei had already received new use permits, there were few permitting hurdles left to clear. Maransky did file some modifications with the City, changing the number of units from 69 to 73 and eliminating the ground floor commercial space. E-Built’s development team, at the direction of Lizzy McGowan, is also rehabbing the property’s basement and vault to include a swimming pool, sauna, gym, theatre room, and golf simulator. “We liked [commercial], but at the same time it’s not the best,” Maransky said. “Traffic is tough to get. 9th Street is cut off. There’s no direct flow from Center City. There’s not a ton of parking as well.” Another amenity will be a large rooftop deck with Center City skyline views and space for pets. Two elevators were installed. Plans call for 14 parking spaces.
 On the exterior, architectural renderings show existing metal features of the building painted dark gray. Red brick is restored and so are many of the building’s copious original windows, which Maransky explained will be done in line with historic standards. Inside the building will be market rate apartments including studio, one-bedroom, and two-bedroom units with high ceilings and exposed brick walls.
 A bird's eye view of Willow Steam's iconic stacks and forthcoming roof decks. | Renderings: E-Built
 Maransky said the building’s historic nature was an attractive attribute. He filed for and received recognition for the building on the National Register of Historic Places in January, which will allow E-Built to access some tax credits and other financial incentives. He said the company is also uniquely equipped to financially handle such a project given that it has both development and construction arms, cutting down on overhead. Maransky noted that the building’s sturdy construction as one that would be prohibitively expensive to build in today’s market.
 Beth Grossman, managing director of reBuilding Blocks, the nonprofit successor of Scioli Turco, said the news that Willow Steam is finding an adaptive reuse is an ideal example of how the Act 135 process, originally initiated by her organization, is supposed to work. “Any time a historic property can be reconfigured and put back into productive use, it thrills us,” she says. “We are very happy.”
 Tags: adaptive resuse Callowhill industrial architecture Renovation Willow Street Steam Generation Plant 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: University Parking Garage
author: Alan Jaffe and Bryan Mckinney
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Summer 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 University Parking Garage 
 Location : 3201 Walnut Street
 Architects : Mitchell/Giurgola Associates
 Built : 1963
 Brutalism is having a moment. The Oscar-winning, Philadelphia-set film, The Brutalist , casts a spotlight on the mid-century architectural movement characterized by the use of poured, raw concrete. Some hate the style. President Donald Trump isn't a fan. On his first day in office, Trump issued an executive order calling for “classical” architecture in federal buildings. In Philadelphia, an internationally renowned Brutalist building, the Police Administration Building (aka theRoundhouse) , lost its bid for designation on the city's historic register in November 2024.
 Outstanding examples of Brutalist architecture deserve protection in Philadelphia, including a garage. The University Parking Garage was designed by partners Ehrman Mitchell and Romaldo Giurgola, whose work can be found and has been honored around the world. Diagonal, light-colored concrete trusses form the pattern of the exterior. Purple brick-clad walls rise over the Walnut Street side, intended for an addition that was never built.
 Newer neighboring buildings on the University of Pennsylvania's campus complement and seem to be inspired by the bold geometry of the Mitchell/Giurgola garage. Its style, which evokes powerful emotions one way or the other, certainly deserves preservation and appreciation on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 Tags: Brutalism Midcentury Modern modernism parking garage Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Unlisted Philadelphia

title: Rittenhouse-Fitler Historic District Celebrates 30th Anniversary
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Rittenhouse-Fitler Residential Historic District , one of the first historic districts to be added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places , is celebrating its 30th anniversary. Although it district was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1983, it wasn’t until 12 years later that the district was recognized locally as well.
 A historic district is a group of buildings, archaeological resources, or other properties that are deemed historically or architecturally significant by a local, state, or the federal government. Within the boundaries of a historic district, individual buildings, structures, and sites are usually classified as either contributing or non-contributing to the district.
 They can range from a handful of properties, as in the recently created Northwest Apartments Thematic Historic District , which comprises 30 apartment buildings in Germantown and Mt. Airy, to neighborhoods that contain thousands of properties, as with the Rittenhouse-Fitler district.
 A 1955 ordinance created the Philadelphia Historical Commission and gave it authority to designate individual properties as historic. “Since it only allowed individual designations, preservationists felt that wasn’t sufficient to preserve streetscapes,” recalled David Brownlee, who served on the Historical Commission for many years beginning in the 1980s.
 “In the early 1980s, the historic preservation ordinance was rewritten to grant new authorities,” explained Jon Farnham, executive director of the Philadelphia Historical Commission. “It was given the power to deny demolitions, and another big change gave it the authority to create historic districts.” Before that, the Historical Commission had created informal historic districts in Old City and Spring Garden by approving hundreds of individual designations in those neighborhoods.
 The Center City Residents Association (CCRA), which had been instrumental in securing the National Register designation, then submitted a nomination to the Philadelphia Register as well. “Rittenhouse was high on everyone’s mind,” said Brownlee. “When I became chair of the Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation, I knew one of the first things I had to do was to bring up the Rittenhouse District.”
 The Bradbury Bedell Residence at 2134 Chestnut Street. Built in 1889, designed by Wilson Eyre Jr. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The district is outlined by a jagged perimeter that includes and excludes various blocks and individual properties, extending roughly between Walnut, South 15th, Pine, and South 25th Streets. The neighborhood has maintained its status as an elite enclave longer than almost any other in Philadelphia, which has helped preserve its architecture from decline and redevelopment.
 It contains a diverse range of architectural styles, including along the eastern edge, Greek Revival brick townhouses with marble bases, mid-19th century Italianate homes west of 17th Street, and large Victorians with Gothic details west of 20th Street. The small streets like Panama and Cypress that lie between the main streets feature smaller houses, originally for the workers in the large mansions. Development after World War I saw the building of apartment towers that replaced many of the original mansions, particularly on the square itself.
 The pedigree of many homes in the district represents a veritable who’s who of important Philadelphia architects of the 19th and early 20th century, including Thomas U. Walter, Samuel Sloan, Theophilus Chandler, Wilson Eyre Jr., John Notman, Furness and Hewitt, and Cope and Stewardson.
 In addition to residences, numerous historic churches and institutions are within the district’s borders, such as the Gothic Revival St. Mark’s Protestant Episcopal Church at 16th and Locust Streets (Notman 1847), the Romanesque Holy Trinity at 1900 Walnut Street (Notman 1856-9), the Swedenborgian Church of the New Jerusalem at 2129 Chestnut Street (Chandler 1881), the First Unitarian Church of Philadelphia at 22nd and Chestnut Streets (Furness and Hewitt 1885), and the College of Physicians of Philadelphia at 9 South 22nd Street (Cope and Stewardson 1907), to name a few.
 As one of the first nominations under the revised ordinance, the Rittenhouse-Fitler district experienced a number of struggles and setbacks owing to some vagaries in the law’s language, misinterpretations by property owners, and a lawsuit that worked its way up to the State Supreme Court twice. As a result, although nominated in February 1987, it was finally added to the Philadelphia Register in February 1995.
 To commemorate the district’s 30th anniversary, the CCRA is holding an event at Trinity Memorial Church, 2212 Spruce Street on Sunday, May 11 at 2 p.m. The event will begin with a panel discussion with former Philadelphia Historical Commission members David Brownlee and David Hollenberg and former Philadelphia Historical Commission staff members Sally Elk, Lori Salganicoff, and Laura Spina, who helped with the creation of the district. They will discuss the challenges and successes in creating the district 30 years ago as well as CCRA's involvement in advocating for the district's nomination. Walking tours will leave from Trinity after the panel. For more information about the event see the CCRA website: https://members.centercityresidents.org/atlas/events/join-us-for-a-talk-and-tour-celebrating-the-30th-anniversary-of-the-rittenhouse-fitler-historic-district–42/details 
 Tags: historic district Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Rittenhouse Square 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: "A Pretty Good Track Record of Resisting"
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Kaia Chau looks on as the lion dances to chase evil spirits away from Chinatown | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 "This, my friends, is the sound of Philly resilience," observes Hidden City's Song of Philadelphia podcast host Julien Suaudeau in the second part of season two's first episode, "Following the Suns." Here, Julien spends the Lunar New Year with young activist Kaia Chau and her mother, the long-time Chinatown community organizer Debbie Wei. Amidst drums and firecrackers, on an ecstatic nighttime tour of the neighborhood, Chau and Wei recount the many fights to protect Chinatown since the 1980s. 
 Listen to part-two of Kaia's story on Song of Philadelphia, out today from Hidden City on Spotify and Apple .
 http://hiddencityphila.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Kaia-2-final.mp3 
 "We're pretty resistant," says Wei, describing some of the organizations and businesses that have taken hold in Chinatown North since the defeat of the proposed Phillies stadium in the late-1990s. 
 "Pretty good track record of resisting," adds her daughter, a leader in 2024's fight to stop the Sixers arena, 76 Place, from being built.
 The second floor Karaoke room of Little Saigon Cafe on N. 10th Street, where the No Arena campaign was headquartered | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Chau and Wei introduce Suaudeau to "Uncle Sam," the Vietnamese owner of Little Saigon Cafe and, like Wei, a longtime Chinatown activist. They go upstairs to the Karaoke room Sam turned into a campaign office for No Arena organizers. In the words of Julien Suaudeau, "This is where history was made." 
 Tags: Chinatown Chinese New Year Development immigration No Arena Song of Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Nathaniel Popkin Hidden City Daily co-founder Nathaniel Popkin’s latest book is To Reach the Spring: From Complicity to Consciousness in the Age of Eco-Crisis.

title: Fmr Pro Boxer Kevin Dublin On Why Joe Frazier's Gym Matters: The Latest from Song of Philadelphia Podcast
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Kevin Dublin in his fighting stance outside Joe Frazier’s Gym | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Song of Philadelphia heads from Chinatown to North Broad as host Julien Suaudeau brings Joe Frazier's Gym alum and fierce advocate, Kevin Dublin, to the podcast. In this first of a two-part episode, Dublin recounts how Frazier recruited him to the gym and gave him the support he needed to become a professional pro boxer. "Joe ran up on me fighting… He said, ‘Wow, man, you can get paid.' So I'm looking at him, like, that's Joe Frazier, world champion." 
 "One thing stays with Kevin," observes Suaudeau, "Joe's voice."
 "Kevin has a few things to say about the neighborhood where he grew up, the gym that used to be there, and the man whose name is still on the building and that Kevin calls Smoke," says Suaudeau, who spent days, microphone in hand, fighting this spring's high winds to bring listeners the voice of a Philadelphian who has dedicated himself to Joe Frazier's legacy of helping others.
 "I just thought this man was like a Superman," says Dublin, about the father-figure who drew him off the streets not once, but twice, and taught him how to fight for his life.
 Kevin Dublin and old friends on Cambria Street, where he grew up | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 You can listen to the entire riveting episode, "Let Me See What You Got," right here, or on our podcast page , or on Spotify or Apple .
 http://hiddencityphila.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Kevin.mp3 
 Tags: Joe Frazier Joe Frazier's Gym North Philly Song of Philadelphia
