 Nathaniel Popkin Hidden City Daily co-founder Nathaniel Popkin’s latest book is To Reach the Spring: From Complicity to Consciousness in the Age of Eco-Crisis.

title: Preservation Advocates Raise Alarm on $158M in Proposed Trump Funding Cuts
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The Battery, developer Lubert-Adler Real Estate Funds' $153.6 million mixed-use project that recently transformed Delaware Generating Station, received $21 million in federal historic tax credits to help finance the project. The 108-year-old power station was listed on the National Register in 2016. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In 2024, an obscure Pennsylvania government office in Harrisburg assisted owners of historic properties across the state secure federal tax credits to help pay for about $335 million in rehabilitation work. By next year, such support for historic properties could all be gone, shuttered by a Trump administration plan to axe a comparatively paltry $1.5 million in federal funding that helps pay for staffing at the office. 
 The program in question is the Pennsylvania State Historic Preservation Office (PA SHPO), which is housed within the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission. Those familiar with the office say it plays an important, but behind-the-scenes role in the historic preservation ecosystem. It is a state office staffed by state employees, but it performs a federally-mandated function to, among other tasks, review applications to list buildings on the National Register of Historic Places. In turn, the office is then able to help developers interested in rehabbing or adaptively reusing historic properties obtain federal tax credits to do so. 
 All states and territories in the U.S. have a SHPO office . Because their responsibilities are federally mandated, Congress has seen fit to provide the offices with federal funding to carry them out. Advocates say such funding is actually at zero cost to the taxpayer as it originates from a federal fund whose revenue is generated by royalties from federal offshore oil and gas leases. 
 However, at the behest of President Donald Trump, the current Republican-controlled Congress may get rid of it anyway. A draft federal budget bill introduced by a House committee on May 12 seeks to zero out the National Park Service’s Historic Preservation Fund (HPF) starting next year, which is a primary source of funding to state SHPO offices. At the moment, specifics about what would happen next are unavailable, including where revenues from the oil and gas leases would go instead. 
 “Many historic preservation projects have matching funds from state, local, and private sources, rendering the Historic Preservation Fund highly duplicative,” the Trump administration claimed in its proposal to cut the fund by $158 million next year. “Further, the projects are often of local, rather than national, significance.” 
 Developer Eric Blumenfeld and Live Nation's extensive $56 million renovation of The Met on North Broad Street received financing through the federal historic tax credit program. The former Metropolitan Opera House was placed on the National Register in 1972. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Already, this year’s HPF funding has been frozen since early in the Trump administration in what opponents say is part of a wider, unprecedented executive branch policy of withholding funds already approved by Congress. In recent weeks, Ohio’s SHPO office laid off 12 employees after about $1.5 million in funds allocated for this year were frozen, multiple local media outlets have reported , a development that has spooked Pennsylvania-based advocates into thinking the same fate could be in store for the Commonwealth. 
 Coupled with similar cuts to staff at the National Park Service, the loss of funding presents a potentially “devastating” scenario, said Mindy Crawford, executive director of the nonprofit Preservation Pennsylvania. “The concern is if we’re laying off National Park Service workers, and we have to lay off state historic preservation workers, that means there is no one to review the National Register nominations and there is no one to review the state historic tax credit,” Crawford explained. “The building doesn’t happen because that money is needed to make it work.” 
 Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, likened the budget proposal to a four-alarm fire. “Preservation projects will stop. Properties could be lost. Projects will be suspended. And that will have negative, perhaps irreversible impacts on historic landmarks, on cultural sites, and archaeological sites. All of the things the SHPOs do,” said Steinke. 
 Megan McNish, eastern region community preservation coordinator for PA SHPO, said that as of mid-May no staff have been laid off and no decisions have been made about what may happen in the future. As a state employee, McNish cannot advocate for any policy measures. However, she noted that the federal funds for PA SHPO are supplemented by $1 million from state coffers, which are currently providing extra funds to cover the federal freeze. Her office is reaching out to various lawmakers to ensure they are educated on the office and its work. “Our budget is not entirely reliant on federal funds. However, they do add significantly to our overall funding,” McNish said. “There is a lot of uncertainty at the moment.” 
 Advocates say they believe it is ultimately the Trump administration’s goal to shift all of the costs of the program onto other sources, particularly state governments. That fear is leading them to take action. Preservation Pennsylvania last week sent out an “advocacy alert” to its supporters to ask their congressional representatives to support HPF and other measures designed to support historic preservation. Local interest groups like the Preservation Alliance are amplifying the message to its supporters as well. 
 The Importance of Tax Credits 
 Arguto Oilless Bearing Company was listed as contributing within the Wayne Junction Historic District when it was approved for placement on the National Register in 2012. Developer Ken Weinstein is using federal historic tax credits to help fund his redevelopment of the former industrial site. | Photo: Michael Bixler 
 Ken Weinstein , a Northwest Philadelphia-based developer whose Philly Office Retail firm specializes in adaptive reuse of historic buildings, said federal tax credits for historic preservation and PA SHPO’s role in obtaining them are often essential elements to redevelopment. Weinstein spoke to Hidden City in his capacity as a private developer, but he is also a commissioner of the Pennsylvania Historical & Museum Commission. “Needless to say, discussions are happening and this is something Pennsylvania needs to deal with,” he said. 
 Weinstein explained he is most worried about impacts to historic preservation in areas of low-to-mid income and property value. Historic renovation often comes with a price premium compared to new construction, he said. The numbers work better in “hot” neighborhoods where developers can command higher rent or sales to offset the costs. Yet, the tax credits become essential to make the numbers pencil out in other areas, especially the economically-challenged towns and communities that dot much of the interior of Pennsylvania. “It’s not just Philadelphia and Pittsburgh. There are rural areas around the state where the rents just aren’t there, where historic tax credits are most needed,” said Weinstein. 
 Locally, he offered an example of 147 W. Berkley Street in Wayne Junction, the site of a former Arguto Oilless Bearing Company factory. Weinstein said he relied on historic tax credits to make the math work on an ongoing plan to convert the building to a groundfloor cafe run by the adjacent Attic Brewing Company, with office space above. “Those are already locked in,” he said. “But it’s the type of project where the budget is very tight. If we did not receive the historic tax credits, both federal and state, we would not be doing those projects.” 
 Even in neighborhoods closer to Center City, the tax credits can play a large role. Former owners of the Willow Street Steam Generation Plant in Callowhill have for decades discussed various new uses, including conversion to an apartment building as recently as 2023. New owner James Maransky said he intentionally worked to add the building to the National Register last year, unlocking federal tax credits. Conversion of the building into apartments is now moving forward with a target opening of next year. Maransky’s team was uncertain of the potential impact of a loss of federal funding to historic redevelopment in general, but predicted it could lead to layoffs at PA SHPO and subsequently longer review times. 
 Willow Street Steam Generation Plant's new owner, James Maransky, worked to have the building placed on the National Register in 2024. The long-abandoned site was added to the list in January. The developer will partially finance the residential conversion of Willow Steam with federal historic tax credits. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In PA SHPO's most recent annual report the office reported that, in 2024 alone, it helped developers complete rehabilitation work on 22 properties across the state and also obtain $5 million in Pennsylvania historic tax credits. It reviewed 485 properties for inclusion on the National Register and listed 29. The office also reviewed thousands of submissions for other projects requiring various forms of federal and state review. 
 In addition to the loss of funding, another major concern among developers is the lack of certainty, Weinstein said. Will the HPF funding be completely eliminated? If so, will there in fact be a reduction in staff at PA SHPO? What would that mean for the ability of developers to obtain the federal tax credits? All are questions currently eating at developers, he said. “We can deal with change. We can deal with different funding priorities,” Weinstein said. “But when you don’t know day-to-day what’s happening or what’s going to be funded it freezes your activities… you can’t work in an environment like that.” 
 It may be some months until a final answer is rendered. The congressional budget bill remains in committee and is expected to be subject to ample negotiations both within and between the House of Representatives and the Senate. The bill can be passed in both chambers with a simple majority, but that still means Republicans can only afford to lose a handful of defectors from their party. With no Democrats expected to vote for the bill, if there are even half a dozen Republican lawmakers willing to stand their ground on the HPF, the funding could be restored, at least partially. Congressional leadership is currently aiming for final passage on the bill some time in July. 
 Advocates must contend with similar dynamics in the Pennsylvania State House, where budget negotiations also are underway and could prove critical if federal funding indeed disappears. Crawford said preservation groups are encouraging supporters to reach out to all of their state and federal representatives and voice support for the funding. Specifically, Preservation Pennsylvania recommends contacting a congressperson and voicing support for the immediate release of 2025 HPF funds, funding the program at $225 million for 2026, and co-sponsoring of HTC-GO (H.R. 2941/ S.B. 1459), a bipartisan bill to “modernize” historic tax credits. “Our voices have to be loud enough to get something to happen,” said Crawford. 
 Tags: adaptive resuse Donald J. Trump federal government historic tax credit Renovation 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Places to Save: Summer 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Name : Francis R. Strawbridge House
 Location : 5710 Wissahickon Avenue
 Built : 1906
 Threat : Vacancy
 The Francis R. Strawbridge House in Germantown is a significant example of early 20th century Georgian architecture. Built between 1905 and 1906, the house was designed by the esteemed firm Brockie & Hastings for Francis R. Strawbridge, son of the co-founder of Strawbridge & Clothier , one of Philadelphia’s most prominent department stores.
 Recognizing its architectural and historical significance, the Keeping Society of Philadelphia successfully nominated the Strawbridge House for inclusion on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2015. This designation protects the building from demolition and inappropriate alterations. However, it does not obligate the owner to maintain the structure beyond the basic safety and security standards enforced by the Department of Licenses & Inspections. As a result, the house has remained vacant and is decaying, raising serious concerns about its long-term preservation.
 In 1957, Alden Park Apartments purchased the property to expand its holdings, encompassing the neighboring former estate of Justus C. Strawbridge. While the three 1926 Jacobean-style apartment towers of Alden Park have been carefully maintained and restored over the years, the Strawbridge House, the last physical remnant of the Strawbridge family’s presence in the area, has been neglected.
 To draw attention to its plight, the Young Friends of the Preservation Alliance have been advocating for the building’s preservation. In February, members decorated the house with Valentine’s Day hearts, symbolizing the community’s love for this historic structure and the need for action.
 Photo: Bradley Maule
 Name : Wanamaker Building
 Location : 1300 Market Street
 Built : 1910
 Threat : Vacancy
 The Wanamaker Building, an iconic Center City landmark, faces significant challenges following Macy’s announcement to close this location in March. The building was designed in 1910 by Daniel H. Burnham, with later renovations and expansions carried out to accommodate its evolving use as a retail space.
 Macy’s closure raises concerns about the future of the building, particularly its Grand Court, which houses the renowned Wanamaker Organ and the bronze eagle statue. The Grand Court’s historical importance is safeguarded by its inclusion on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, which the Preservation Alliance nominated in 2017. Notably, it’s one of only five interior spaces in Philadelphia with such protection, including City Hall’s Council Chambers and the Family Court Building. This designation ensures that any alterations to the Grand Court require approval from the Philadelphia Historical Commission.
 TF Cornerstone, the current owner of the first through third floors of the building, has expressed a commitment to preserving these historic features. Recognizing the organ’s cultural significance, the company assures that it will remain a central element within the space. TF Cornerstone is also in the process of purchasing floors four through seven, which they plan to convert to residential use. However, the future of the retail areas remains uncertain, with discussions ongoing about their adaptive reuse.
 As plans for the building’s future unfold, it is crucial to balance redevelopment with the preservation of its historic elements, ensuring that the Wanamaker Building remains a cherished Center City landmark.
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 Name : 17 Elliott Avenue
 Location : 17 Elliott Avenue, Bryn Mawr, Pennsyvania
 Built : 1900
 Threat : Demolition
 The house at 17 Elliott Avenue in Bryn Mawr was designed in 1900 by renowned architect William Lightfoot Price in the Arts and Crafts style. It embodies Price’s vision for human-scaled, high-quality suburban design and represents a pivotal moment in his career, bridging his early suburban commissions with his later utopian communities like Rose Valley. The original materials of the house retain remarkable integrity, making it a rare surviving middle-class residence by Price. Additionally, the home features the region’s first attached car garage, an architectural innovation reflecting the dawn of the automobile age.
 Beyond its architectural value, 17 Elliott Avenue holds deep historical significance related to women's history and LGBTQ+ history . The original owner, Helen Sleeper Pearson, was a pioneering educator at local girls’ schools and one of Smith College’s earliest graduates. She shared the home with Dr. Helen Dean King, a groundbreaking biologist whose research advanced the field of genetics. Their story highlights the often overlooked contributions of women in science and academia at the turn of the century.
 Despite its importance, the home faces an uncertain future as Lower Merion Township commissioners are actively debating its historic designation. With nearby historic homes already lost to commercial expansion, preserving 17 Elliott Avenue is crucial to maintaining the township’s architectural and cultural heritage. Listing the property on Lower Merion’s Historic Resource Inventory as a Class I resource would ensure its survival, protecting an irreplaceable link to the past and honoring the pioneering women who lived there.
 Tags: LGBTQIA+ History Strawbridges suburbs Wanamaker's Women's history 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Historic District Protections and Destruction Challenge the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Philadelphia Historical Commission approved the designation of the Blakemore Street Historic District at its meeting on Friday, August 8. The district, nominated by Oscar Beisert of The Keeping Society of Philadelphia , is located on a block that gently curves to follow the line of the Chestnut Hill East railroad tracks in Mount Airy. It is comprised of a set of Tudor Revival twins. The homes were constructed in the 1920s as apartment buildings during a time of significant dense residential growth in the neighborhood along the train lines.
 In an area with many examples of the Tudor Revival style, the Blakemore Street buildings stand out for their thorough treatment on all sides, with second-floor faux half timbering in a variety of motifs, steeply pitched roofs, and extensive use of Wissahickon schist on shared courtyards and steps. At the rear of the buildings there is a large swath of green space that spans the length of the block.
 Tudor Revival apartments that make up the Blakemore Street Historic District. | Photo: Google Street View
 The Historical Commission staff recommended approval of the district. While they were in the process of sending notifications to the property owners, the buildings at 6657 and 6659 on one end that had been owned and left to decay by Germantown Settlement were taken over by the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority (PRA) and demolished. PRA stated it intends to build affordable housing on the site and objected to its inclusion in the proposed historic district.
 When the Committee on Historic Designation reviewed the nomination, it recommended designation, with the properties at 6657-59 Blakemore Street classified as non-contributing and the shared stairs and courtyard between it and 6655 Blakemore Street classified as contributing. At today’s Historical Commission meeting, staff reversed their recommendation and supported the exclusion of the lot from the district, citing a previous, similar case that resulted in a court order.
 After much discussion of keeping the shared steps and courtyard in the district, including a request from the owner of the adjacent property, the Historical Commission voted to remove the entire parcels of 6657 and 6659 from the Blakemore Street Historic District.
 1730 Wharton Street in Point Breeze. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Earlier in the meeting, the long saga of illegally replaced windows at 18th Street Methodist Episcopal Church at 1730 Wharton Street finally reached a resolution. The owners will be able to proceed with converting the 1888 building to 14 residential units.
 Top: 148, 150, and 152 N. 2nd Streets are listed as contributing to the Old City Historic District, which was added to the National Register in 1972 and to the Philadelphia Register in 2003. The legally protected buildings, including a home that dates back to 1755, are now slated for demolition with the exception of the facades. The small, single story commercial building next door will be razed and the entire lot will be used for new construction. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 The owner of a row of six parcels on the west side of North 2nd Street, between Race and Quarry Streets, received approval in concept for a construction project. A 2 1/2 story house built in 1755 at 150 N. 2nd Street and a two-story building at 148 N. 2nd Street were individually designated in the 1980s. They were also designated as contributing to the Old City Historic District , along with the three-story building at 152 N. 2nd Street, which dates to the 1920s.
 The other three parcels consist of two vacant lots and a one-story commercial building to the south of the other three and are non-contributing to the historic district. The project will partially demolish the three contributing buildings while maintaining their facades and demolish the non-contributing building. A six-story, mixed-use building will fill out the conjoined parcels.
 Tags: demolition Historical Commission Meeting Report Northwest Philadelphia Old City Philadelphia Historical Commission 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: "Banners of Liberty" Exhibition Gives Warning to the Dangerous Erosion of National Unity
author: Mickey Herr
bodyText:
Flag of the United States of America, Unidentified Maker, 1800-1825 . This flag, made over 20 years after the conclusion of the Revolutionary War, is one of the earliest examples of the "Stars and Stripes" known to exist. | Photo courtesy of the Museum of the American Revolution and Jeff R. Bridgman Antiques, Inc.
 The United States is gearing up to celebrate our Semiquincentennial, otherwise known as the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence. This forthcoming celebration leaves me extremely conflicted. Local historic sites, museums, and archives have been making plans to mark the occasion for months, even years. As an active volunteer at several historic sites, I have paid close attention to the various “250” committees that have formed both locally and statewide. I even wrote a grant for a women’s history project that was successfully funded through the Philadelphia Funder Collaborative for the Semiquincentennial. Yet, even in the waning months of 2024, and before we watched the countless Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) and National Endowment for the Humanities (NEH) grants disintegrate before our eyes these past few weeks, it has all felt a bit like rearranging the deck chairs on the Titanic. The closer we get to July 2026, the more squeamish I become. I wonder, what exactly are we celebrating?
 Case in point. In mid-April I was invited to attend the private opening of Banners of Liberty: An Exhibition of Original Revolutionary War Flags at the Museum of the American Revolution (MoAR). It is billed as the largest gathering of rare and significant Revolutionary War flags in more than two centuries. The public opening date of April 19th was specifically chosen on the 250th anniversary of the “shot heard round the world” which preceded the Battles of Lexington and Concord. Of the estimated 30 surviving Revolutionary War era flags carried into battle, this exhibition features 17, including MoAR’s prized possession, the Commander-in-Chief Standard, which helped General Washington’s troops track his movements through the smoke of the battlefield. As Scott Stephenson, MoAR’s president and CEO, evocatively stated in his opening remarks “The soldiers marched under these banners into the mouths of cannons for the promise of the American Revolution.”
 It's heady stuff. Especially if you add in this quote from The Pennsylvania Mercury published on June 9, 1776, which presumably served as the inspiration for the exhibit’s title. “The aged, as well as the young, daily march out under the banners of liberty, and discover a determined resolution to maintain her cause even until death.”
 The Nation Makers, 1902 by Howard Pyle. | Image courtesy of The Brandywine Museum of Art
 Likewise, the exhibit’s graphic imagery featuring Howard Pyle’s The Nation Makers from 1902, a painting from the collection of the Brandywine Museum of Art, heightens the sentiment. Pyle, part of the notable Brandywine School of Artists, was the master of elaborate hyperrealistic illustration. He recreated the fanciful worlds of Robin Hood, King Arthur, a plethora of swashbuckling pirates, and, of course, the battles of the American Revolution. Like most Colonial Revival mythmakers, his battle scenes were meant to convey optimism and a faith in the goodness of America. Pyle’s quiet influence should never be understated.
 Which brings us back to the point of the Banners of Liberty exhibit. Here we see various groups of individuals—colonies which are not yet a nation—working to create a persona which might also foster a political identity. Each flag has a message. The symbology represented has been well-debated. It’s where our mythmaking begins.
 During the usual round of introductions and remarks from staff and supporters at the base of MoAR’s grand spiral staircase, I found myself reflecting back to a mere two years prior. That evening in February 2023 was a different opening event and a visibly different tone. The opening celebration of Black Founders: The Forten Family of Philadelphia had been such a revelation. I needed to write about it and did. It felt like real progress in expanding history beyond the concept that the American Revolution is more than a single moment in time, beyond that “shot heard round the world,” and the once more into the breach-of-it-all. That seismic shift I felt back then suddenly felt ephemeral. The optics and the difference in energy of this opening night as compared to the previous one could not be denied. We live in a different world. And as Amy Cohen reminded us in her recent op-ed published by Hidden City, " Philly Must Fight the Erasure of Black History ," we are all responsible for protecting the progress made in integrating African American history into the mainstream whole. Our history is, after all, a singular story with many viewpoints.
 This flag, sewn by Boston milliner Fanny Johonnot Williams, features the motto “The Glory Not the Prey.” It was sent to England as a war trophy after the Battle of Hubbardton in 1777. It was returned to the United States and was donated to New Hampshire Historical Society in 1913. | Photo courtesy of the Museum of the American Revolution
 This was not an opening full of Forten exuberance. It was reserved. The audience cared deeply about that singular moment in time. Was I judging too harshly? When I made my way into the exhibit space, there was yet another noticeable shift. A hush. A reverence. The energy of a thousand individual stories of sacrifice woven into each flag. To be fair, there was also some excitement. Several members of the Society of the Cincinnati of New Hampshire, who had funded the conservation work of one of the two flags on loan from the New Hampshire Historical Society, were exuberant in seeing their flag and meeting the woman who did the conversation work. They were proud. This flag, paid for in 1777 by the New Hampshire Committee of Safety, was sewn by a Boston milliner named Fanny Johonnot Williams, from blue silk provided by her brother Nathan Blodgett. A man named Daniel Rea Jr., painted a heraldic motto, “The Glory Not the Prey,” in red and gold. The British union was stitched in its canton. This flag was captured just months after completion by the British 9th Regiment of Foot and sent to England as a war trophy until it was donated to the New Hampshire Historical Society in 1913. Had it not been captured would this painted silk flag survived?
 While standing in front of Pulaski’s Legion Standard I met a man whose life work is recreating flags for museums and film. If you have seen the movie Glory , you have witnessed his work in action. We bonded over a double-sided, circa 1778 red silk and silver flag with fringe and appliques, which also featured ornate flaming bombs on each corner. Casimir Pulaski was a Polish volunteer who was commissioned as a commanding officer. Among his ranks where British, Irish, French, Polish, and Hungarian volunteers. When granted congressional permission to raise his own legion, he turned to the Moravian Single Sisters of Bethlehem who created this masterpiece. One side features the Latin phrase Unita Virtus Forcior (United Valor is Greater), and the verso features God’s all-seeing-eye with the words Non Alius Regit (No Other Governs.) We both stood in awe admiring the handiwork of the Moravian Single Sisters.
 Commanding Officer Casimir Pulaski’s Legion Standard flag from 1778. The highly ornate, double-sided flag features flaming bombs on each corner and the latin phrase Unita Virtus Forcior (United Valor is Greater). On loan from the Maryland Center of History and Culture. | Photo courtesy of the Museum of the American Revolution
 Flags and their symbolism have become a flashpoint of conflict. I know I am not the only one who wonders what it says when a person flies a simple American flag outside their home. Does it make you a patriot? What do our American symbols even represent at this point? Apparently, the appropriation of symbols was an American thing before we were a United States. Take Benjamin Franklin’s “Join, or Die” political cartoon published in 1754. In the context of the French and Indian War, the dissected snake featured was Franklin’s editorial on the “disunited state” of the colonies. According to The Charleston Museum website, a man named Christopher Gadsden presented a similar coiled snake with the words “Don’t Tread On Me” to the commander of the newly established U.S. Navy in 1775 and a second time to South Carolina’s state congress in 1776. The snake became an emblem of true courage as an attribution to as Franklin states it “never begins an attack, nor, when once engaged, ever surrenders.” It’s all about respect.
 Imagine my surprise when I recently discovered a bright yellow envelope featuring the Gadsden flag inside my mailbox. It was junk mail, but I was too curious to simply toss it into the recycle bin. “Dear Fellow Patriot…” began the letter signed by the president of The Heritage Foundation, which was followed by two pages of double-speak on liberty and “heritage” education. Included was an authorization form that would guarantee me my own Gadsden flag for a $35 contribution. I felt the need for a shower after I read the rhetoric. I later reread the letter in the hopes I might decipher the double-speak. What is liberty? Everything changed after our most recent presidential inauguration. I am now a middle-aged white woman who feels less safe and free than I have in my entire lifetime. I just reread the letter again as I write this. I burst out in laughter after reading this line. “The Gadsden Flag is an inspiration for all who are sick of Washington trampling the Constitution and catering to corporate lobbyists and radical leftists.” What happens if we substitute that very last word? Nothing means what you think it does. It’s not just me, right?
 Details of “Gadsen Flag Delivery Authorization” mailing from The Heritage Foundation. | Photo: Mickey Herr
 We Americans are great at looking back. Yet, as we approach our 250th anniversary of declaring our independence, might we serve ourselves better if we look forward instead. When someone asks me to pick a time-travel era, I always think about going back. It never dawns on me to visit the future. The Centennial Exposition held in Philadelphia in 1876 is a time and place high on my go-to list. It was when the world came together to not just commemorate the Declaration of Independence, but to celebrate cultural advancements in all realms. To celebrate progress through inventions like the typewriter, the sewing machine, and the telephone. I want to see all those people and all those buildings that populated Fairmount Park in full-swing. The Sesquicentennial Exposition in 1926 also holds some curiosity. After fighting to gain their right to vote, this was a moment when women were working to further assert their authority. There was also a resurgence of white supremacy which helped push forward the American Eugenics Society movement. Yet, these women weren’t looking forward, but rather finding their authority by connecting to their patriot ancestors by creating a Colonial Revival "High Street" village. You could visit a recreation of Sulgrave Manor, the English ancestral home of the Washington family. Or you could have a meal in the Indian Queen Tavern. However, these meals could only be enjoyed by white attendees. Was this progress?
 Apparently, all American flags are not created equal. The Atwater Kent Collection at Drexel University recently announced that their IMLS grant, to conserve the American flag carried by Commodore Mathew Perry when he visited Japan in 1854, had been cancelled. The flag had been displayed at the 1876 Centennial Exposition. The IMLS grant would have paid for a textile conservator to bring the flag back to its original glory. The reason cited by the federal agency, under the direction of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), was that the proposed work was “no longer consistent with the agency’s priorities and no longer serves the interest of the United States.” Then, just as suddenly, a late-night email arrived informing staff the grant had been restored. An internal review by the IMLS determined conserving this flag did further “the President’s agenda.”
 Commodore Mathew Perry's 1845 American flag was aboard the the USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay during the Japanese surrender ceremony on September 2, 1945. | Photo courtesy of the Digital Collections of The National WWII Museum
 When we look back at American history, are we truly seeking lessons so that we might not repeat our mistakes? Or are we merely looking to venerate our patriot ancestors? This seems to be where the dividing line currently falls. I am less interested in celebrating a flag for its representation of liberty, but more interested in the moments behind these flags. Tell me more about the Boston milliner Fanny Johonnot Williams. Tell me more about the Moravian Single Sisters. Tell me more about Pulaski’s second-in-command, the Hungarian cavalryman Mihály Kováts de Fabriczy. What liberties were they afforded after they put their lives on the line during the American Revolution?
 Maybe this time of political turmoil has arrived precisely when it was supposed to. Perhaps, 250 years later, we are back to where we started. It took a dozen years for our newly-minted nation to figure out what came next. In January of 1790, George Washington wrote to Catharine Sawbridge Macaulay Graham after the establishment of the United States Constitution. “The establishment of our new Government seemed to be the last great experiment, for promoting human happiness, by reasonable compact, in civil Society.” Is it time for our great experiment to come to an end? Is this question where my growing queasiness resides? The historian Heather Cox Richardson has said, “The past has its own terrible inevitability. But it is never too late to change the future.” I remain conflicted about celebrating Revolutionary era flags, but, apparently, I took something away from spending time with them.
 Banners of Liberty: An Exhibition of Original Revolutionary War Flags is now on view at Museum of the American Revolution, 101 S. 3rd Street, until August 10. See the museum's website for hours of operation and special events: https://www.amrevmuseum.org/exhibits/banners-of-liberty-an-exhibition-of-original-revolutionary-war-flags 
 Tags: art exhibition Donald J. Trump National Museum of the American Revolution Revolutionary War 
 About the Author
 Mickey Herr lived in many places until her heart settled in Philadelphia. She has led the development and communications efforts for several significant nonprofit cultural institutions in the city. Current interests involve elevating the hidden histories of women. She is at work on a novel and gives tours for Hidden City Philadelphia, both of which are allowing her to research incredible untold stories of women. She believes in ghosts, synchronicity, and taking chances. Read her writing on Philadelphia, history, and geneology at mickeyherr.com.

title: 150,000 Artifacts From West Shipyard Go To a New Home
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
A parking lot at Columbus Boulevard and Callowhill Street covers the former site of West Shipyard, a long-lost piece of 17th century maritime history along the Delaware River waterfront. AECOM concluded an archeological study that began in 2019. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In 2019, archaeologists with AECOM excavated a portion of the parking lot at 300 N. Columbus Boulevard. They were searching for materials related to the 17th century shipyard that had been located there in advance of a planned development project for the site by the New York firm the Durst Organization. Six years later, 150,000 artifacts have been identified, conserved, and are now on their way to a new home in Harrisburg with the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission (PHMC).
 James West founded his shipyard in 1676, before the founding of the city, at the foot of the Water Street steps, which at that time was the Delaware River waterfront. “During the ship building period, most of the building occurred on the water’s edge and some of it on wharves,” noted Joel Dworsky, archaeologist with AECOM. In 1987, the parcel became the first archaeological site added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 The site was an active shipyard until about the mid-18th century. “It represents the very end of a pre-industrial, almost medieval craft of shipbuilding. I was interested in the larger economics of shipbuilding at that time. There was a large market for Philadelphia-built ships in Europe, so a lot of those that were built here were for export,” explained Dworsky.
 This lithograph from 1830 shows the Penny Pot Tavern, with the bow of a ship at the West Shipyard to the right. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 “After the shipbuilding period, the site was a center for the Philadelphia salt trade, which was vital for the preservation of food,” he continued. “In the late 18th century, there was a run of several salt warehouses along Vine and Water Streets. It grew out of the Revolutionary period, when the British blockaded the salt trade coming from the Caribbean and South America.”
 An archaeological dig proceeded vertically, with the first layers yielding items from the most recent occupation of the site. “Because of the nature of the structures being built on top of older things, we study, document, remove to see what’s underneath. Usually by the time we’re down to just the soil, there’s nothing more to see.”
 Eventually the waterfront was extended further into the river, although the former shipyard site remained fairly wet. “It’s the best organic preservation I’ve seen. Most of the material we found was in deep fills in the water. Once we pulled them out, we kept them in water to avoid them drying out,” said Dworsky. “The water-logged conditions are a double-edged sword. It’s a hard environment to work in, but the artifacts like wood, leather, and bone are well-preserved.”
 Eventually, the total number of artifacts that they excavated reached an astounding 150,000. By comparison, Dworsky noted that an excavation of a typical domestic household might yield around 10,000.
 Archaeologist with AECOM, the engineering firm leading the dig, unearthed artifacts like pieces of a shoe (pictured here), redware pottery, and a pipe among other items. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Many of the finds were relics of the site’s shipbuilding past, including a measuring tool called a shipbuilder’s bevel gauge, with the numbers etched in the brass still visible. A more ominous item is a pewter syringe that was used to treat venereal disease aboard ships by injecting mercury into the patient.
 “Because it was a workplace, there really weren’t a lot of people in residence there,” Dworsky explained. “But the fill-in material yielded household refuse from several city blocks, like a wine bottle that still had a wax seal on it and with the initials J.M. in it. We tried really hard to narrow down who it was.”
 “It also includes artifacts attributed to the Penny Pot Tavern (c. 1690), which provides a rich array of early colonial table wares,” added a PHMC spokesperson. Other domestic and personal items include a number of engraved tobacco pipes with maker’s marks and nearly 40 pairs of shoes from the 17th and 18th centuries.
 One artifact that was unearthed surprisingly intact is one of Dworsky’s favorites. “It’s a piece of bone, with the carving ‘a trifle from Philadelphia’ on it and a waterfront scene,” he explained. “It’s a little bigger than a silver dollar in size. We called it a sailor’s love token.”
 An etched, bone trifle, what AECOM archeologists call a "sailor’s love token," was found during the dig. | Photo courtesy of the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission
 As painstaking as an archaeological dig is, the subsequent work of conservation, inventory, and documentation is equally so. “An archaeological collection is more than just the artifacts,” explained the PHMC spokesperson. “It also includes all the documentation from the excavation, such as artifact inventories, photographs, field notes and sketches, and a report.”
 “All the leather, wood and metal material have been conserved, so it’s now a stable, preserved collection,” noted Dworsky. Metal objects such as a padlock were also x-rayed so their inner workings could be studied. The work was done at the Maryland Archaeological Conservation Lab along the Eastern Shore, part of Maryland’s State Museum of Archaeology.
 Beyond the artifacts, the structures they unearthed, such as wharves, were generally mapped, photographed, studied, and then left in place. The exceptions were any structures they encountered in areas of the parcel where building might take place, which were removed.
 The work continues in Harrisburg, where PHMC curators are reviewing the materials and its documentation, accessioning it into their collection of over 14 million artifacts, and transferring it to a new home in a climate-controlled storage location. “We have no immediate plans for the collection,” said the PHMC spokesperson. “Artifacts are available for study. They may also be borrowed for exhibit by another museum.”
 “The hope is to bring at least a portion of the collection back to Philadelphia for display,” said Dworsky. “It was sent to PHMC, so there’s a definite repository for it and it is integrated into the state system.”
 A padlock found at the site is examined, x-rayed, and catalogued. | Photo courtesy of the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission
 The future of the planned development for the 1 ½ acre site is less clear. In 2021, the Durst Organization obtained zoning and building permits to construct a 25 story, 360-unit building with ground floor commercial space on the site. Zoned CMX-3, the plans included height bonuses for mixed income housing, stormwater management, green building, public space, a trail, and public art, bringing the total height to 322 feet.
 Although permits for plumbing, electrical, and excavation were issued in the following year, construction has not begun on the parcel and all have expired. A spokesperson for the developer told Hidden City , “The Durst Organization is currently restoring and reopening two sidewalks along Vine Street and North Water Street. They’re reopening the sidewalks for the community.” In a press release, they further noted, “While the challenging financial market and escalating construction costs have paused the development timeline, the company continues to maintain the property and evaluate future development opportunities.”
 In addition to the former West Shipyard site, the Durst Organization also owns parcels across the street, at 319 and 410 N. Columbus Boulevard, collectively called Pier 24.
 Although archaeologists may not have a say in development plans, Dworsky noted, hopefully, “The buildings will likely be sited on the southern half of the parcel because that’s where we found the fewest artifacts. The idea was to minimize the impact on the archaeology.”
 Tags: AECOM archaeology Delaware River waterfront West Shipyard

In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: SEPTA Crisis: The Opposite of Growth is Decline
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Late-80s message boards that also now display next to arrive train information | Photo: Nathaniel Popkin
 On Monday afternoon, for various unimportant reasons, I flew into Newark Liberty. Found my way to the AirTrain, two stops to the New Jersey Transit/Amtrak station, and down to the platform. The southbound train was just arriving. Unsure how quickly I would make it through the airport I had booked a later train, which I explained to the Amtrak conductor. “But there’s no ticket counter here,” I said, “so I can’t change it." He said I needed to call 1-800-USA-RAIL to book a different train.
 I huffed a little and then shrugged. The next train was the one I had booked. It would come in an hour. So what? I wasn’t really in any rush.
 Then something almost magical happened. The conductor called me over. “Where are you going?” he asked.
 “30th Street.”
 “Get on.”
 It was only two stops to Philly.
 I crossed the weird maze of traffic islands and over to the L station, content with the knowledge that in a year or so, once renovations to Amtrak's 30th Street/William H. Gray Station are complete, it will once again be possible to get there underground.
 When SEPTA’s 30th Street L and trolley station reopened last year, then SEPTA chief Leslie Richards said it was the new model for service amenities. Well-lit, clear signage, clean tiling, almost disorientingly modern. There, you can find a full range of SEPTA’s elegant updated maps, showing bus frequencies and graphics, and line maps that suggest how easily the so-called Metro network might function.
 SEPTA's excellent new line maps and graphics | Photo: Nathaniel Popkin
 The greatest gift of the afternoon, however, was the real-time information available: the circa-1989 message boards displaying next train arrivals. Accurately, too, which hadn’t been the case as SEPTA began to implement this messaging about a year ago—several decades after most other transit systems.
 Two minutes until the next eastbound train! No more than seven or eight minutes and a free transfer later I was on the 47 bus heading south, walking in my door in less than an hour-and-a-half from boarding the train at Newark.
 All this to point to what’s at stake, as Pennsylvania Senate Republicans hold funding for mass transit in the Commonwealth hostage: the potential for Philadelphia to actually perform, even dazzle, and therefor grow. What will happen, should lawmakers fail to do their duty to serve the needs of the people, forcing SEPTA to cut entire train and bus lines and reduce service by 45 percent? Quite likely a new age of decline. Think Detroit, think Baltimore, think St. Louis. Because no dense, legacy city can fulfill its potential without adequate public transit.
 When I was an urban studies student back in the era when SEPTA installed those rectangular digital signs in L and trolley stations, we used to talk about the advantage old cities had over the likes of Denver, LA, Phoenix…because we already had so much transit infrastructure in place, the grand legacy of the streetcar and railroad age. Those other cities could never afford to create it new. But, in fact, they’re doing so, particularly in the west, spending tens of billions on public transit, because they have to. Otherwise, they too will stop growing.
 In Philadelphia, should the PA Senate force SEPTA to dismantle this inheritance, discontinued train lines will begin to deteriorate immediately, meaning they will become even more expensive to restore (all the more reason why the ploy to use capital funding for operations is so cynical).
 So this is an existential moment. Which is why I find the radio silence from Mayor’s Office odd. A mayor who evidently possessed positive relationships across the aisle with legislators in Harrisburg hasn’t bothered to articulate to them why this matters, not in public, anyway. Hasn’t bothered to organize the business community, the tourism industry, the eds and meds, to deliver a unified message. Hasn’t shown up for transit advocates who very clearly see the writing on the wall.
 5th Street L Station | Photo: Nathaniel Popkin
 Philadelphia has been here before many times, as Hidden City reporter Kyle Bagenstose pointed to in his excellent contextual piece on the transit funding crisis . But possibly the best analog to this moment isn’t a time when SEPTA scrambled to preserve barely adequate support, but the moment, in the second decade of the 20th century, when various machine politician mayors abandoned a carefully engineered plan for 60 miles of subways across more than a dozen lines, a plan meant to dazzle the urban imagination. What happened next, after it took twenty more years to complete just one line, the Broad Street Subway, was urban stagnation (with various intermingling causes, of course): Philadelphia essentially stopped growing. And the opposite of growth, in an urban context, is decline.
 Tags: Mass Transit public transit SEPTA 
 About the Author
 Nathaniel Popkin Hidden City Daily co-founder Nathaniel Popkin’s latest book is To Reach the Spring: From Complicity to Consciousness in the Age of Eco-Crisis.

title: A Flatiron, a Firehouse, and a Fine Set of Victorian Twins Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The former George Institute Library at 1461-65 N. 52nd Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At its meeting on June 13, the Philadelphia Historical Commission added three properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places and approved significant alterations to two previously designated buildings.
 The George Institute Library at 1461-65 N. 52nd Street was constructed in 1914 and designed by architect E. Allen Wilson in the Federal Revival style. The library was founded in 1872 through a bequest of Quaker philanthropist Jesse George . The Hestonville building's flatiron shape is a prominent fixture in the five-way intersection at Lancaster Avenue, 52nd Street, and Bible Way. In 1927, it became part of the Free Library of Philadelphia system, which closed the branch in 2001 and turned the building over to the City.
 The Engine House of Truck Company F at 4027-31 Haverford Avenue. | Photo: Google Street View
 The Engine House of Truck Company F at 4027-31 Haverford Avenue was built in 1884 as one of the first fire houses to serve the growing neighborhood of West Philadelphia. The station reflects the early history of the City’s municipally controlled fire department, which replaced the volunteer companies that served various neighborhoods.
 The final historic designation was for two contrasting Victorian twins, now listed as one parcel, at 1439 N. 15th Street . The homes were built for prominent 19th century industrialists during a period when lower North Philadelphia was being developed as a wealthy enclave. One home, originally owned by carpet manufacturer William Ivins, was designed in the Chateauesque style. The other, built for Hamilton Disston of the Disston Saw Works, is an example of Second Empire style.
 Victorian twins at 1439 N. 15th Street. | Photo: Google Street View
 In 2018, the former Green Hill Market House at 1632 Poplar Street was added to the Philadelphia Register as an example of market houses that were built in the mid-19th century to replace open-air street markets. In 2023, the owner, The Church of the Living God, The Pillar, and Ground Truth, unsuccessfully sought to have the designation rescinded and now plans to convert the property into an apartment building. As a result, the church requested permission to remove the structure's roof and stone veneer and add a fourth-floor addition, roof deck, and pilot house. Following the advice of the Historical Commission’s Architectural Committee, the plans had been revised to further set back the addition to reduce its visibility from the street. The proposal was approved in concept. The developer is required to work with Historical Commission staff for final approval of the plans.
 The former Green Hill Market House at 1632 Poplar Street. | Photo: Richard Gonzalez
 Another request for alterations came from a much more prominent building. The Drexel Company Building at 1435-41 Walnut Street was built in 1927 by the architectural firm Day & Klauder, whose other works included Franklin Field at the University of Pennsylvania and the Germantown branch of the Free Library of Philadelphia in Vernon Park. The Center City building was added to the local register in both 1971 and 1973.
 The current owner maintained that its imposing facade, with windows that “look out, but do not allow looking in,” was befitting of the private bank it was built for, but is problematic for today’s Walnut Street shopping corridor. They requested permission to remove the masonry sills from seven windows along Walnut and S. 15th Streets to enlarge the windows.
 Proposed window alterations at 1435-41 Walnut Street. | Rendering: ARX Solutions
 The owner said the removed stone panels would be stored, should they be needed for reinstallation at a later date. In September 2021, the Historical Commission denied the application, owing to the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties and Guidelines, which stipulate that “new additions, exterior alterations, or related new construction shall not destroy historic materials that characterize the property.” After the owner filed an appeal with the Board of License & Inspection Review, they arrived at an agreement with the City’s Law Department to remand it back to the Historical Commission for another review. Although the proposal was essentially unchanged from four years ago, the Historical Commission staff recommended approval, while the Architectural Committee voted to deny the application in its original review in 2021, suggested altering fewer windows would maintain more historic fabric.
 While sympathetic to the owner’s difficulties in finding a tenant for the building’s first floor, some Historical Commission members were uncomfortable with granting the request based on the speculation that it would attract a tenant. Others appreciated the offer to salvage and preserve the removed masonry, but this raised the concern that its oversight would not be realistic, as was evident recently in the case of the now-demolished St. Laurentius Roman Catholic Church in Fishtown, where architectural elements were not saved and stored, even though it was a requirement of the Historical Commission’s demolition permit. In a roll call vote, the Historical Commission approved the proposal to cut the seven window sills, install new windows, and preserve and store the removed materials.
 Tags: fire house Historical Commission Meeting Report libraries Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Victorian architecture

In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Oral History Project Seeks Black Voices from the Delaware River Waterfront
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
The stories that go unheard the longest often resonate the loudest when they are finally heard. This sentiment is the core driver of Independence Seaport Museum’s (ISM) new oral history project, Breaking Uncommon Ground on the Delaware River . The initiative is an extension of the museum's ongoing exhibition, Tides of Freedom: The African Presence on the Delaware River . The neew oral history project will focus exclusively on three distinct groups of people: Black people who worked in labor unions along the Delaware River, Black women who did work connected to the Delaware River, and anyone who lost their home or business to demolition when I-95 was built along the waterfront. The organizers of the new project are hoping that people on both sides of the Delaware River will contribute their personal stories from now until May 2026 for a prospective launch in the fall of 2026.
 Unlike Tides of Freedom, which has a broader scale and focuses on Philadelphia’s role in the slave trade, Revolutionary War era, Civil Rights movement, and the turn of the 20th century, Breaking Common Ground zeroes in on events that transpired from the 1950s to 2015 with local, generational stories centered on the Delaware River.
 According to Peter Selbert, ISM's president and CEO, the new project is “not only central to the Seaport Museum’s core purpose, but personally important to me and the staff.” These stories are part of a bigger effort to tie into the people and events that have shaped the waterfront and will create not only personal connections, but a time capsule that future Philadelphians can draw upon, learn about, and hopefully add onto at a later date. This is exemplified by the staff of Paul Best, the project's director, which includes three local high school students and two students from Temple University and the University of Pennsylvania who have assisted with the data collection and canvassing for the project.
 Project director Paul Best and the Breaking Uncommon Ground Ambassadors on the banks of the Delaware River conducting research on Alice of Dunk's Ferry. | Photo: Independence Seaport Museum
 Best, a transplant from Gary, Indiana, who also serves as a museum educator at the Penn Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology and is the founder of the storytelling troupe Black Boys Makin’ Noise, explained that his grandfather was the first certified Black electrician in Philadelphia. This is what prompted his interest in the new project. By offering an opportunity for “learning the everyday Black history that we kind of overlook whether it is not being shared or covered,” Best hopes to get people interested in not only sharing their own stories, but engaging with the physical exhibit or through the audio/visual part of the project that will be made available on ISM’s YouTube channe l and at the J. Welles Henderson Research Center.
 Thus far, the most difficult part of the project has been finding stories related to the construction of I-95, which took place between 1959 and 1985. Best revealed that this difficulty is due to people who were personally affected either passing away or not wanting to dredge up memories they would rather forget. Nevertheless, the fallout from I-95 is a part of local history, especially in terms of urban renewal and the people who were displaced. Their voices and stories are an essential part to telling the entire story.
 The collected oral histories so far are about 14 Black women who worked as the merchants and artists to build the communities along the riverfront. One of these stories is about the world-renowned bassist Lady Fingers, whose real name is A. Marcy Francis. She has performed along the waterfront with an all-Black female percussionist group, Women’s Shekere Ensemble . Another story is about Denise Valentine with the Middle Passage Ceremonies and Port Markers Project , whose annual event recreates the arrival of enslaved Africans to Philadelphia. The event is commemorated by the Pennsylvania slave trade marker outside ISM.
 The contributions of four Black labor union members who's work was connected to the river have already yielded the story of Janet Elam. She has the distinction of being the first female member of the International Longshoreman’s Association Local 1291, a title she earned in the 1990s despite facing adversity due to her gender. Another story is about Marcus Cooper who waited for four months outside the Longshoreman’s hiring center hoping for employment until he was vouched for by a veteran member who also sponsored him. This was a hiring procedure that was unknown to Cooper at that time.
 Eddie Sherman, an employee of F.A. Urie Produce Company on Dock Street, holds a box on his shoulder while smoking a cigarette in 1959. | Photo courtesy of the Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 While being appreciative of the stories already gathered, Best said that “We need to realize that the real history of any people lies in their stories and how they get by.” This includes the stories of friendships, the day-to-day work, and the dock workers, plumbers, welders, and other groups who were categorized as “essential workers” throughout the pandemic and either have worked or continue to work along the Delaware River.
 “I believe that the only limit to our success with this project is time," said Selbert. "With every obituary that appears in the newspaper, the stories of the African American community in the last quarter of the 20th century are lost forever.” This sentiment is shared by Best who added, “History sits in our homes, in our neighborhoods, and within our communities.” He noted how people often think that history is only made by the people who are highlighted and that there are so many people who are or were longshoremen that have either purchased or fought for their homes, paid for their children’s schooling, made long-lasting friendships, or brought some entertainment or levity to the lives of others. All of these stories intersect at the Delaware River and deserve to be heard and recorded.
 If you or someone you know fits into any of these groups–African Americans who worked in labor unions along the Delaware River, Black women who did work connected to the Delaware River, and anyone who lost their home or business when the I-95 highway was built in Philadelphia—feel free to contact Paul Best, director of Breaking Uncommon Groun t, at (215) 315-3242 or pbest@phillyseaport.org and share your stories. More information on the oral history project can be found here: https://www.phillyseaport.org/breaking-uncommon-ground/ 
 Tags: African-American history Archives Delaware River I-95 Urban Renewal 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Archeological Wonder or Heartbeat of North Philly? Find Out in Episode 4 of This Season's Song of Philadelphia Podcast
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Kevin Dublin with George Gee and some of the GDGU Boxing and Mentoring Program participants | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 "So what we have here is two layers of personal history on top of one layer of Philly boxing history," observes Julien Suaudeau, the host of Hidden City's podcast, Song of Philadelphia. This spring, Suaudeau has been interviewing Joe Frazier protege Kevin Dublin. As today's episode begins, the two men are inside the Be Well (Behavioral Wellness) Center at Girard (formerly Girard Medical Center), where Dublin is a social worker. It's also where he got clean in 1991 and where, twenty years before, Joe Frazier recovered from fighting Muhammed Ali in the Fight of the Century. Back then, this was St. Luke's Hospital.
 Fitting for a podcast that, in form and function, reveals the sonic layers of Philadelphia's past and present. 
 You can listen to the fourth episode of Song of Philadelphia season two, "The Heartbeat of North Philly," right here, or on Spotify or Apple .
 http://hiddencityphila.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/Kevin-2.mp3 
 "An archeological wonder, if you ask me," says Suaudeau.
 "It's an amazing place," adds Dublin. "My decision to walk away [from drugs] was [Frazier], my parents, I had children…I had more than what other people wish they had, so I'm not gonna mess this up…I walked in the door in that building." 
 Kevin’s workplace at 8th and Girard is a Philly archeological wonder | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Dublin recounts his path from being addicted to counseling others. When the receptionist asked why he'd come inside the treatment center the day he decided to get clean, in 1991, she wondered if he was running from someone. The truth was he was running toward Joe Frazier, who had always been a kind of guardian angel. He sat down in the waiting room and there was Frazier on the television. "When you see ‘Smoke' on the screen, it's like telling you, okay, this is the place where you need to go."

title: Historic Wyck House In Germantown Gets a Facelift
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
Wyck Historic House and Garden. | Photo: Heritage Conservation Collective
 Wyck Historic House and Garden at 6026 Germantown Avenue was home to nine generations of the Jansen-Wistar-Haines family dating back to 1690. It is among Philadelphia’s oldest homesteads. Recognized as “one of the most architecturally innovative buildings in Germantown,” Wyck is undergoing extensive conservation of its exterior, including historic windows, shutters, doors, and trellis, along with the building stucco. Challenges include windows that are made with glass from the 18th century, doors that date back to 1824, and stucco first applied in 1799.
 The project is being carried out by Heritage Conservation Collective (HCC), with Andrew Fearon, the firm's principal architectural conservator, at the helm. Claire Donato from Mark B. Thompson Associates is the architect, and Dan Bosin Associates is serving as the owner’s representative.
 Conservation technician Bob Donahue in the steam room. | Photo: Heritage Conservation Collective
 Work began in April with the house’s 44 windows. Conservators remove them from the building, then place them in a steam cabinet for about an hour to soften the paint and glazing. They carefully remove the glass and scrape the paint and putty off the wooden sashes by hand. Then they prime and paint the sashes with linseed oil-based paint. “The house is an untouched survivor with an early chronology of windows that still retain some hand blown crown glass typical of the 18th century, as well as an abundance of early cylinder glass of the 19th century,” said Fearon. “For this reason the project calls for a conservation approach to carefully employ gentle steam to soften the window putty and later layers of paint to ensure that the original glass and early stratigraphy is saved. We are also using traditional linseed oil paint and putty so the conservation work uses all natural materials. The linseed oil paint is imported from Sweden and we are also using hand blown cylinder glass imported from Germany to replace the broken panes.”
 The wood is in remarkably good condition, according to Cyrus Yerxa, HCC architectural conservator and on-site project manager . When the sashes are ready, Yerxa and his team will re-install the panes of glass. “The original window sash construction and shutters alone are a testament to quality and performance of traditional craft and materials used at Wyck, and for the most part, have survived in excellent condition,” noted Fearon. After work on the windows is completed “the stucco will be repaired using a traditional lime mortar render mix of naturally hydraulic lime and sand, then given a final traditional lime wash to protect it from years of weathering to come.” 
 Methods and Materials Tested 
 Once work on the exterior is finished, planning will begin on restoring the interior and the outbuildings. The last significant restoration project at Wyck took place from 1995 to 1996, “but in the last few years we restored the East Wall (2017) and the Kitchen Arbor (2018) as test projects for the larger restoration,” said Kim Staub, executive director of the Wyck Association, which is the custodian of the estate. “These projects tested methods and materials that are guiding the work today. One of the challenges to this building is the fact that we have no singular period of interpretation, as the family's residence at Wyck lasted 283 years," said Staub. "The family used, adapted, and altered portions of the house at different times, so there is a large variance across the house on when things were added, restored, and altered.”
 A pane of old window glass. | Photo: Heritage Conservation Collective
 “The work at the Wyck has very specific challenges in that we rarely come across windows that retain early crown glass, and must be extremely careful in handling them and re-setting them,” said Fearon. “We are also working in direct contact with some of the rare and early species of roses grown on the house exterior walls and at the perimeter of the building, so we are very cautious with our scaffolding, containment, and selection of environmentally friendly materials and procedures. The reason the Wyck is so special is that it retains these early materials and plantings and has escaped the over-aggressive restorations so common in the past.”
 Funding for the $1.23 million exterior conservation and preservation is coming from the Historic Preservation Fund administered by the National Park Service, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, Roy E. & Elizabeth C. Hock Foundation, McLean Contributionship, and individual donors.
 The House Evolves 
 “It’s not certain just when Hans Millan came to Germantown, but it was probably around 1686,” wrote Randal L. Whitman in an essay for Germantown Monthly Meeting . “A widower, he brought with him two children, Margaret and Matthias.” Hans purchased lot #17 West from Francis Daniel Pastorious, the founder of Germantown. By 1690, he built a log cabin on the property, located near the current intersection of Germantown Avenue and West Walnut Lane. The log cabin no longer exists, but the oldest extant portion of the house dates to 1736. A three-bay stuccoed stone structure, it sits close to Germantown Avenue and comprises what is now referred to as the front parlor and hallway.
 A separate, four-bay stuccoed stone section was completed in 1773–west of the smaller building and on the site of the original log cabin–and eventually connected to the front building. The most significant improvements came in 1824, when Philadelphia architect William Strickland remodeled the first floor of the house.
 The Wyck property in 1934. | Photo courtesy of Prints & Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 Strickland, known for designing the Second Bank of the United States and Merchants’ Exchange, removed the windows that faced Germantown Avenue, added windows along the north wall open to the garden, rearranged the interior to allow more natural light, and installed innovative doors that let residents switch between closed rooms and an open floor plan.
 Outbuildings include the coach house and smoke house (both late 18th century), ice house (1836), and greenhouse (1914). Dating to Colonial times, and greatly expanded in the 1820s, Wyck’s rose garden reportedly is the country’s oldest in its original plan, featuring historic, exotic, and hybrid varieties. “Several roses in cultivation today had been thought lost until they were discovered growing at Wyck,” according to the Wyck Association. “All specimens of these varieties in commercial trade today descend from Wyck plants.” Wyck was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1971 and designated a National Historic Landmark in 1991.
 Generations 
 Wyck also is notable for its nine generations of Quakers, “leaders in science, education, glassmaking, brewing, and horticulture,” noted the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission. Hans Millan’s daughter, Margaret, married Dirk Jansen, a Quaker from Germany. Their daughter, Catherine, married Caspar Wistar, a successful button maker, glass-maker, and land investor. The Wistars, members of Philadelphia Monthly Meeting, used the 1736 building as a summer home. Their daughter Margaret married Reuben Haines, a prominent brewer and merchant of English descent.
 Jane Reuben Haines in 1905. | Photo: Wyck Association
 “Their son, Caspar Wistar Haines, continued the family business and married Hannah Marshall, a member of another prominent Quaker family,” according to a history compiled by Wyck Association. The property passed to their son, Reuben Haines III and his wife Jane, who used it as a summer home before moving there permanently in the early 1820s. “He conducted experiments in scientific agriculture, led school reforms, and helped to found the Academy of Natural Sciences, Franklin Institute, and Pennsylvania Horticultural Society.”
 It was Reuben who commissioned William Strickland to turn the house into a Greek Revival country villa. “With similar zeal, Reuben’s wife, Jane Bowne Haines, joined organizations promoting education for the poor, prison reform, and the abolition of slavery. She also transformed Wyck’s garden in the 1820s into the magnificent display of roses still enjoyed today.” It was around this time that the homestead became known as Wyck. “The name comes from an English estate named Wyck that was owned by a man named Richard Haines,” said Staub. “In the early 19th century, Haines family members here mistakenly believed they were related to that Haines family. Later, they discovered there was no relation, but the name stuck. It means ‘village’ or ‘long-inhabited place,’ so it fits the Haines family that lived here for nine generations.” 
 The rose garden at Wyck. | Photo: David Owen Bell
 Rueben and Jane’s youngest daughter, Jane Reuben Haines, lived at and cared for Wyck until her death in 1911. Her niece, Jane Bowne Haines II, founded the Pennsylvania School of Horticulture for Women (now Temple University’s Ambler campus), one of the first schools of its kind in the United States. The last family owners of Wyck, Mary and Robert Haines, used it as a winter home when they weren’t growing fruit on orchards in Berks County. In 1973, they donated the 2.5 acre property, including the house and its contents, outbuildings, and garden, for preservation under the care of the Wyck Association.
 With two full-time and two part-time staff, along with a corps of volunteers, the Wyck Association also sponsors tours, workshops, lectures, concerts, and special events, including the annual Food and Seeds Community Expo, Celebration of the Roses, and Philadelphia Honey Festival. The grounds are open to the public Tuesday through Friday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Walk-in tours are available on Thursday through Saturday from April through mid-November, all subject to temporary disruptions during construction.
 Tags: Conservation Germantown historic houses 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: "I See a Spark" Larry Robin's Philadelphia Life, Now on Sound of Philadelphia Podcast
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Larry Robin, still on 13th Street with his books | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 "I think industrialization was a mistake," says Larry Robin, the former bookseller and co-founder of Moonstone Arts, in front of a shuttered factory near Lehigh Avenue. "They'd hire ten year olds and work 'em to death."
 But isn't that a kind of contradiction? wonders Song of Philadelphia podcast host Julien Suaudeau. For a Philadelphian, someone so identified with the city, to look askance at the legacy of industry in the once and forever Workshop of the World means doubting the nature of the very place you love.
 Robin, whose eponymous bookstore on 13th Street closed in 2012, shrugs. "Contradiction is the essence," he says. That's the title of this new episode of Song of Philadelphia .
 Larry Robin next to a former textile mill near Lehigh Avenue | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 The man, like his city, contains multitudes. So many multitudes…which emerge in this long-form episode, as Julien follows Larry from his apartment above the old bookshop to the formerly Jewish neighborhood where he spent his earliest years near Mifflin Square to the Jewish Quarter that's now Society Hill and ultimately to industrial North Philly, where Larry recounts his encounters with the back-to-nature philosopher Scott Nearing.
 Wide-ranging—and deeply personal—describes this fifth episode of the second season of Hidden City's podcast. Larry reflects on his own back-to-nature experiments, the creation of Moonstone Arts, the tendency to become more conservative with age, his powerful guiding principle of self-sufficiency, and how he works with writers and artists. "I see a spark and I'm going to blow on it," he says.
 Song of Philadelphia from Hidden City is available on Spotify and Apple . You can also listen to this episode right here.
 http://hiddencityphila.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Larry.mp3 
 Julien will be back soon with a writer's tribute to Larry Robin, the last episode of season two. Stay tuned!
