title: Stories of Pride That Won't Be Erased
author: Starr Herr-Cardillo
bodyText:
Editor’s Note : A version of this story was published in the Summer 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 National Park Service sign at the Stonewall National Monument in the West Village neighborhood of Lower Manhattan, New York City. | Photo: Kaitlin Pomerantz
 In 2016, the Stonewall Inn, on a small stretch of Christopher Street in New York City, and the small triangular park in front of it was designated a national monument by President Barack Obama, making it the first national monument commemorating LGBTQIA+ history . The Stonewall Uprising–a series of clashes and demonstrations in June 1969 in response to police raids at Stonewall–is widely regarded as a pivotal moment in the fight for LGBTQIA+ rights, and the area has become a sort of pilgrimage site.
 However, on February 13, 2025, the National Park Service scrubbed the “T” and “Q” in LGBTQIA+, as well as the words “transgender” and “queer,” from its webpage about the Stonewall National Monument and from several other Park Service webpages referencing LGBTQIA+ history. Almost immediately, mementos were left at the site that reflected a definitive stance: The contribution of trans individuals in Stonewall’s history would not be so easily erased.
 “As a preservation movement, we say in no uncertain terms that LGBTQ+ history is our history, and it needs to be amplified and celebrated. We choose not to remain silent while attempts are made to deny the existence of trans people, both past and present. Revising the historical record for political purposes is dangerous and unacceptable.” — PRESERVATION LEAGUE OF NEW YORK STATE
 Since February, more than 100 queer and transgender stories have been erased from Park Service websites. The agency’s seminal 2016 LGBTQIA+ context study, “ LGBTQ America: A Theme Study of Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender and Queer History ,” an oft-cited and thorough reference document, was also removed. The shocking act of erasure was said to have been done in compliance with an executive order issued by President Donald Trump on January 20 called “ Defending Women from Gender Ideology Extremism and Restoring Biological Truth to the Federal Government .”
 A screenshot of the National Park Service website taken in April 2025 shows that the "T" (trans) and "Q" (queer) initials have been removed from what had previously read "LGBTQ."
 The removals have deeply disturbed many of those working for the agency and in the broader fields of history and historic preservation. The stunning about-face makes one thing clear: Preserving LGBTQIA+ histories and stories is more important than ever.
 Fortunately, historians, artists, and citizens in Philadelphia’s LGBTQIA+ community have been doing so in powerful and creative ways for decades. While recognition takes different forms, Philadelphia’s landscape is rich with sites connected to the ongoing fight for LGBTQIA+ rights, like the 1965 Dewey’s lunch counter sit-in , an important precursor to Stonewall, where young, gender-nonconforming patrons protested being denied service, or the Reminder Day pickets that were held annually during the latter half of the 1960s outside of Independence Hall to advocate for gay rights.
 LGBTQIA+ History Is Philadelphia History 
 A historical marker is kind of like a tweet, said Rami George, an interdisciplinary artist whose work draws on archival material and found imagery. George’s point is that with the limited character count available on a marker, the narratives told, the language used, and who is included and who is not add other layers of meaning. “I am interested in social events, uprisings, solidarity, and wanted to see which of those events get commemorated,” George said. The diner at 17th and Chancellor Streets where the Dewey’s lunch counter sit-in occurred in 1965 later became the beloved Little Pete’s. In 2017, the building was demolished by New York developers who built a hotel in its place. A year later, the site was commemorated with a historic marker. However, George noted, there was some opposition to the marker within the community because any language about gender nonconforming individuals was omitted, even though they had been integral participants in the action.
 The public presentation of history–what is emphasized, what is included, what is excluded–constantly evolves and is a barometer of a society’s outlook, priorities and values.” — ORGANIZATION OF AMERICAN HISTORIANS 
 While there are few physical sites or buildings that are listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places specifically for their association with LGBTQIA+ history (the first, the Camac Baths building at the corner of Camac and Chancellor Streets, was listed in 2019), thousands of historical events have taken place across the city, and the influence of the community continues to play a significant role. Events like the Dewey’s sit-in and annual reminders are recognized by physical historic markers. There are currently only 12 state- recognized markers in Philadelphia that highlight LGBTQIA+ history. Yet, for many events that are not recognized, chances are good that Bob Skiba has mapped them.
 Skiba is prolific in his dedication to sharing the stories of LGBTQIA+ Philadelphia. He leads popular walking tours of the Gayborhood, runs a blog called The Philadelphia Gayborhood Guru , teaches a course called “Queer Community and Culture” at Thomas Jefferson University, and serves as the curator of collections at the William Way Community Center . In addition to all of that, Skiba has spent years curating the Philadelphia LGBT Mapping Project , an initiative of the William Way Center, which “celebrates sites in the Greater Philadelphia area that are important queer history and community.”
 The LGBT Mapping Project created by Bob Skiba.
 The LGBT Mapping Project now includes more than 1,100 sites in the Philadelphia area and paints an incredible picture of Queer Philadelphia–marking layers of history, from cornelia Chapin’s Giant Frog sculpture that has graced Rittenhouse Square since 1940 (according to the map, Chapin lived with fellow sculptor and “close companion” Marion Sanford for 40 years) to the West Philadelphia location of Adodi International, an “intergenerational Brotherhood of Black Same Gender Loving (gay) Men across the African Diaspora” and Philadelphia’s oldest continuously operating Black gay group, founded by therapist Clifford Rawlins in 1986.
 Last year, for Black History Month, activist and historian Gary Hines gave a talk titled “Black and Queer in Philadelphia: From the 1930s to Today” at the Free Library of Philadelphia. Hines has worked closely with Skiba, filling in gaps specifically related to the Black queer scene. In his talk, Hines highlighted social clubs like the Gelede Sisters, Mox Nix, and the Philadelphia Gourmets, who coordinated gatherings in private homes or at establishments that were known to be safe and queer-friendly. Documents and history related to these groups can be hard to come by.
 “Gay and lesbian African Americans in Philadelphia were often caught between the racism of white male gay bars in [Center City] and the homophobia of Black neighborhood bars,” said Hines. In the 1960s to the 1990s, he said there were many prominently Black gay bars on South Street, north of Market Street, and in West and North Philly. Hines named some of the spots and shared photos from them in his talk–“The Ritz, Pep’s, The Fuel Pump, The Smart Place.” Yet, bars and nightclubs are inherently ephemeral. None of them still exist today. They are documented, however, on the LGBT Philadelphia map.
 Of the National Park Service erasures, Hines said, “I think it’s absolutely horrible that all of this is being erased. Particularly for me as a Black gay man, it’s twofold: The Blackness and the gayness is being targeted.” If anything, it has reinforced his dedication to this project. “If the Smithsonian, Stonewall, and other places are going to change their narratives, we are going to need these other outlets,” Hines said.
 Insights from the Archives 
 As Hines’ and Skiba’s work attest to, queer archives are a crucial resource. Traditional archives don’t represent everyone and tend to be skewed to reflect those with status, money, and power. People who didn’t conform to social norms or weren’t well-resourced, or communities that have had to keep a low profile due to fear of harm or suppression are often represented poorly or not at all. Dedicated LGBTQIA+ archives, like the John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives at the William Way LGBT Community Center , are amazing resources that seek to preserve those stories.
 Selection from the Archives, a 2023 exhibition by artist Rami George, who searched for underrepresented voices in the John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives at William Way LGBT Community Center. | Photo courtesy of John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives
 A 2021 Pew Fellow, George has spent a significant amount of time exploring the John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives, first when they were conducting research for their MFA and now as the first artist in residence. George said that before starting graduate school at the University of Pennsylvania, they had an idea of what archives could offer, but hadn’t spent much time in any. After meeting John Anderies, who serves as director there, George struck up a relationship and became more familiar with the contents of the archive. “I knew I was scratching at the surface of a lot of histories,” George said.
 During their fellowship, George dug in, searching for underrepresented stories of lesbian, POC, trans and nonbinary, and disabled people. The work evolved into the creation of a visual finding aid, which was part of the exhibition “Selections from the Archives.”
 AMong the objects George selected to display was the photo album once owned by James E. Hardyway, a member of the Black social club Mox Nix in the 1970s and 1980s. | Photo courtesy of John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives
 “Archives have a lack of POC representation,” said George. “I know there is some [representation], and I want to mark it so that people can go see it and are invited to add to it.” George has also explored reimagining elements of historical markers in their installations, applying fonts and graphic design choices to make temporary pop-up signs of sorts highlighting quotes from archival material. In connection to their own activism, their current line of research focuses on queer anti-war activism through the ages.
 A few years ago, Hines encountered a community member who had held onto a stack of photo albums once owned by James E. Haryway, a member of the Black gay social club Mox Nix in the 1970s and 1980s. Hines arranged to have the photos donated to the William Way Center archive, where they will live on, illuminating an era of Philly’s Black LGBTQIA+ social scene for future generations.
 Straight from the Source 
 LGBTQIA+ history is inseparable from present-day activism. Because the struggle for rights is ongoing, oral histories from members of the community who are engaged in the fight are a powerful tool to preserve those stories. “Philadelphia has a very rich and queer history,” said David Acosta, an activist, poet, writer, curator and cultural organizer. Acosta was deeply involved in the Philadelphia chapter of AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power (ACT UP) in the 1980s and 1990s, helping plan actions, including a demonstration protesting President George H.W. Bush’s visit to the Bellevue Stratford on September 12, 1991.
 Hundreds of AIDS activists from ACT UP Philadelphia blocked Broad Street in front of the Bellevue Stratford when President George H.W. Bush visited Philadelphia during his reelection campaign in 1991. | Photo: Au Courant , a gay newsweekly, courtesy of John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives
 “Philadelphia’s ACT UP was interesting in the sense that some of us were activists that were really cognizant of intersectionality work before that was en vogue,” said Acosta. “Part of that was because some of us were people of color and we were in ‘leadership’ positions,” he continued. Acosta noted that there were no formal leadership roles, but a momentum kept up by dedicated members, including nights spent Xeroxing and organizing until the wee hours of the morning, often after a full workday. “We were extremely organized. We didn’t do things haphazardly.”
 With the protest of Bush’s visit, “we really wanted to go and connect the dots around what was then a Republican assault on so many fronts,” Acosta said. “Much like now, except now, of course, it’s much, much worse.” In preparation for the action, ACT UP built a broad coalition with other communities who were working on interconnected issues, like labor unions, housing organizers, censorship issues, and more. Groups like the National Organization of Women, the National Abortion Rights Action League, local union employees, and others were in attendance. “The day of the demonstration, we had several thousand people–it was massive.” During the protest, ACT UP dropped a prop coffin (the group often used such props to draw attention to the number of people dying from the AIDS crisis). According to news reports, protestors pushed against the police barricades, and the police responded with violence, using barricades to push the crowd, hitting multiple protestors with nightsticks, spraying tear gas, and bringing in more officers on horseback.
 Front cover of the October-November 1969 issue of The Ladder showing Annual Reminder Day protests in front of Independence Hall. Barbara Gittings was the editor of the publication, which was a widely circulated lesbian journal. | Photo courtesy of Outhistory.org
 When asked how he would like actions like these to be commemorated, Acosta said that they live on in the memories of the activists who took part and their stories, recorded in the form of oral histories. While physical plaques are helpful, alternative websites, QR codes that can link to photographs and accounts, interviews and writing are all useful ways to ensure the true depth and complexity of the stories are preserved, he said.
 While working on his dissertation at the University of Pennsylvania in the early-to mid-1990s, history student Marc Stein conducted and transcribed oral histories from dozens of interviews for the Philadelphia LGBTQ History Project, 1940-1980. The interviews with major players in the activism scene like Barbara Gittings, Kiyoshi Kuromiya, and Tyrone Smith formed the basis of his book, but the transcriptions of the oral histories are all available in an online archive via OutHistory.
 Another impactful oral history project by Sharon Hayes, a Philadelphia-based artist and chair of fine arts at Penn’s Weitzman School of Design, recorded group conversations with elders in queer communities in Philadelphia, Tennessee, and Los Angeles. The piece, which was featured in the 2024 Whitney Biennial, is a two-channel video installation of these conversations stitched together, as members in each group reflect on their personal history, relationship to the queer community and activism.
 The Fight Continues 
 “I’ve seen so much in my life and as a queer historian,” Skiba said. “I don’t think there’s been this much pushback against queer people since the 1950s. They’ve gone for the most vulnerable part of the community, and they’re kicking them while they’re down.” In Skiba’s mind, this means it is even more critical to keep talking, keep writing and keep stories alive.
 Thanks to an intergenerational dedication to this work, there’s solidarity and hope–even at Stonewall. The Stonewall National Monument Visitor Center, run by the independent nonprofit Pride Live, issued a statement in response to NPS actions, which currently sits on its website’s landing page: “Pride Live is a nonprofit organization founded on the principle of advancing the fight for full LGBTQIA+ equality. Through the creation of the Stonewall National Monument Visitor Center, we’re unwavering in our effort to protect and preserve Stonewall’s legacy and history. Our space is inextricably linked with and honors the brave pioneers, especially transgender and gender-nonconforming individuals, who led the Stonewall Rebellion. Independently-owned and -operated, and 100 percent supported by donations, we will continue our mission to ensure that every person has access to learn about and see themselves in history.”
 Some Key LGBTQIA+ Figures in Philadelphia 
 Kiyoshi Kuromiya (1943-2000): Kuromiya was a Japanese American LGBTQ+ rights activist and author. Born in an internment camp in Wyoming after his family was forcibly relocated, Kuromiya was involved with several social movements throughout his life, including HIV/AIDS activism, the anti-war movement and the fight for civil rights. In 1969, he was a founding member of Philadelphia’s Gay Liberation Front. Kuromiya embraced the intersectionality of the fight for civil rights: He served as an openly gay delegate to the Black Panther Convention, marched in Selma, and supported many other causes through his work.
 Barbara Gittings (1932-2007): Gittings was a major player in the early LGBTQ+ civil rights movement. Though Gittings was based in Philadelphia, she started the New York chapter of the Daughters of Bilitis, the first lesbian civil rights organization in the United States founded in San Francisco in 1955. Gittings also organized the Annual Reminder marches, the first public demonstrations for gay and lesbian equality in the U.S., which took place in front of Independence Hall. Gittings was integral to the fight to declassify homosexuality as a mental disorder, disrupting the annual meeting of the American Psychiatric Association in 1971 and organizing a panel in 1972, recruiting Dr. John E. Fryer to give his famous Dr. Anonymous address.
 Dr. John E. Fryer (1937-2003): Dr. Fryer was a psychiatrist and gay man, working at a time when being gay was considered a mental illness. A nontenured professor at Temple University, in 1972, Fryer delivered a speech at the annual convention of the American Psychiatric Association, where he talked about the experience of closeted gay psychiatrists, in disguise. Fryer delivered the speech as Dr. Henry Anonymous, wearing a Richard Nixon mask, wig, oversized suit and a voice-distortion microphone, and received a standing ovation. The following year, homosexuality was removed from the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, a major step toward reducing legal bases for discrimination. Fryer’s former home at 138 West Walnut Lane was listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2022.
 Tyrone Smith (1943-2025): Smith was a community organizer who was deeply involved in Philadelphia, specifically as a champion of the Black LGBTQ+ community. Smith co- founded Unity Inc., a community organization that was one of the first toaddress the issue of HIV and AIDS for Black gay men in Philadelphia. He also served in several capacities, including as a social services adviser to former mayors Wilson Goode and John F. Street. He was involved with the Minority AIDS Council, served as a community adviser to the Center for AIDS Research at the University of Pennsylvania, and served on the boards of We the People, the William J. Craig Foundation and the Colours Organization Inc.
 Charlene Arcila (1963-2015): Arcila was a transgender woman who founded the Philadelphia Trans-Health Conference in 2001. The conference, which takes place annually, is centered on transgender health and wellness and is the largest free trans- focused conference in the world. Arcila was also at the forefront of a movement to ban M/F gender markers on SEPTA passes.
 Tags: civil rights Donald J. Trump LGBTQIA+ History 
 About the Author
 Starr Herr-Cardillo is a freelance writer and historic preservation professional working in the nonprofit sector. She holds a master’s degree in historic preservation from the University of Pennsylvania.

title: Two Exhibitions Mine the Archives for Hidden Black History
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
Charting a Path to Resistance , an interactive mural by artist Talia Greene, is on permanent display at Philadelphia City Archives. | Photo courtesy of Talia Greene
 When I was in 11th grade my classmates and I were required to research the history of our homes. To complete the assignment, I retrieved deeds from City Hall, pored over maps at the Free Library, and examined city directories at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. I was astonished by how readily I could obtain specific information using materials preserved from the past. That early fascination with tangible historical sources has stuck with me through undergraduate and graduate degrees in history, my career as a social studies teacher who assigned archival research, and my current position as an author and a contributor to Hidden City .
 Today, much archival material has been digitized, making primary source research much more accessible and far less site-specific. I strongly believe, however, that there is still value in digging into physical archives and not just relying on what has been deemed worthy of online existence. Indeed, in America's current political environment, the ability to uncover truthful information about the past has never been more important. Recent visits to a permanent installation at the Philadelphia City Archives and a temporary exhibit at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania illustrate this point.
 A Mural to be Seen and Experienced 
 J.M. Brewer's map from 1934 lists color-coded sections of the city by race. Areas populated by Black (red), Italian (green), and Jewish (blue) people were considered risks for investment. | Image courtesy of Map Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 Charting a Path to Resistance is an interactive mural that was unveiled in 2018 at the Philadelphia City Archives as part of the Percent for Art program. Artist Talia Greene created a wallpaper-like artwork that begins in the lobby and wraps around the public research room. The mural is more than an attractive wall covering. It is meant to be experienced using either a tablet available at the front desk or a free downloadable cellphone app called Resistance: Philadelphia .
 On a morning in late June, Greene and I viewed and engaged with her work which tells stories of abolition and housing discrimination from the city’s beginnings through 1964. Documents and images appear and reappear, in some places obscured by a redlining map and in others they are fully revealed.
 Greene referred to the redlining map frequently during our time together. I was confused. I have researched and written about redlining in Philadelphia , and I am familiar with both the 1934 J.M. Brewer map and the 1937 Home Owners’ Loan Corporation (HOLC) map. The images I was seeing in the mural did not correspond with either of these brightly color-coded sources. The Brewer and HOLC maps gave low ratings to Black neighborhoods and those facing “Negro encroachment.” Yet, areas with high concentrations of foreign born in general and Jews and Italians in particular were also categorized as high risk for investment.
 A Racial Map of the City of Philadelphia was prepared by the City's Department of Engineering, Surveys, and Zoning in 1944. | Images courtesy of Philadelphia City Archives
 Greene explained that her work was inspired by a map she happened to see when touring the archives prior to earning the mural commission. She asked the archivist to bring it out for me to see. The map that Greene used was prepared in 1943 and delivered to the City’s chief of Engineering, Surveys, and Zoning in 1944. It is simply entitled A Racial Map of the City of Philadelphia . More an atlas than a map, it contains page after page of Philly neighborhoods breaking each city block into one of four categories: All White Occupancy, All (Black) or Mixed in 1932, All (Black) or Mixed since 1932, and All (Black) or Mixed in 1943. In other words, the spread of the Black population into specific blocks and neighborhoods was something to monitor closely, at least in the mind of the City official who had commissioned the map’s creation.
 In 1944, African American men in uniform, albeit in segregated units and often doing the most menial tasks, were overseas fighting against fascism. Yet here in “the birthplace of liberty,” their very existence was seen as a threat to real estate values. I knew from my earlier research that Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal legislation, which excluded domestic and agricultural workers from key programs such as social security, had the effect of “whitening” previously outsider groups. By 1944, overt anti-Semitism had become less acceptable as news of the Holocaust filtered into the United States. Racism, however, was clearly alive and well.
 Community as Curators 
 With my head spinning as I thought about this atlas of white supremacy, I headed over to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) to check out the Voices in the Community: Local Black Preservation exhibit. In late April I had participated in a Black history teach-in at HSP where panelists shared a plethora of examples of how deep dives into archives can uncover forgotten, ignored, and hidden history. The exhibit, like the teach-in, underscores a recent democratization of historical research. High interest in genealogical research, particularly among African Americans, along with the widespread availability of digitized documents, have opened archives to people whose determination and passionate interest in a given topic can lead the way to important discoveries.
 Association for the Study of Negro Life and History. Negro History Week Booklet, 1934 PAM E 185 .A84 1934. | Image courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 The Voices of the Community exhibit showcases how archival sources inform the work of several local entities. Genealogist Shamele Jordan’s curated documents about Lawnside, New Jersey, from its founding as an important stop on the Underground Railroad to its emergence as a vibrant Black community that appeared in the Negro Motorist Green Book . The local branch of the Association for the Study of African American Life and History created a display that exemplifies the mission of the organization, founded in 1915 by Carter G. Woodson, to both preserve and disseminate information about Black history. Faye Anderson , preservationist, activist, and founder of All that Philly Jazz set up a collection of materials that illustrate varied aspects Black musical traditions.
 A Disturbing Connection 
 One segment of Anderson’s musical exhibit includes sources related to the Pyramid Club, a mid-20th century private club for elite Black Philadelphians where entertainers like Marian Anderson, Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, and Billie Holiday performed for adoring crowds. I was thunderstruck when I came upon the 1944 Pictorial Album of the Pyramid Club. The cover contains a photograph of four Black men in uniform with the caption, “Training for Victory.” My mind immediately flashed back to the Racial Map that had astounded me hours earlier.
 The juxtaposition of the Racial Map and this photo of Black men serving in the military is a clear, undeniable, and devastating exemplar of structural racism. The servicemen pictured would return to a country and a city where they would find it nearly impossible to access aspects of the GI Bill related to housing. The Federal Housing Administration favored loans for new construction, but burgeoning neighborhoods like Northeast Philadelphia and Levittown were closed to Black buyers.
 The 1944 cover of Pictorial Album of the Pyramid Club. | Image courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 Additionally, the redlining that resulted when banks consulted the Brewer, HOLC, and, one can assume, the Racial Map , presented additional obstacles to securing financing. As I noted in my previous article on redlining in Philadelphia, “as many white and newly ‘white’ Americans bought homes, often with government support, Black families were thwarted in their attempts to partake in this wealth-producing aspect of the American Dream. Between 1945 and 1959, only two percent of government backed mortgages were issued to African Americans.”
 It is remarkable that the Racial Map still exists. When Greene’s mural was brand new, the City’s commissioner of records, James Leonard, told the Philadelphia Inquirer , “It’s relatively rare to find an original map. A lot of them were destroyed, perhaps for obvious reasons. They are not exactly things people are proud of given what they were used for in terms of discrimination.”
 Archives are essential, and unfortunately, archives that specialize in Black history materials are under particular threat . No matter what version of flag-waving history the current federal administration tries to foist upon the country, dedicated and honorable historians, both professional and amateur, know that the truth lies in the sources that have been preserved from the past.
 Voices of the Community: Local Black Preservation will be on display at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, 1300 Locust Street, through September 26, 2025.
 Charting a Path to Resistance can be viewed at the Philadelphia City Archives at 548 Spring Garden Street.
 Tags: African-American history Archives Donald J. Trump 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Poquessing Trail of History Brings Awareness to Byberry's Past
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
One of the furthest corners of the far Northeast holds some of the oldest historical sites in Philadelphia. The former Byberry and Moreland Townships were a longtime home of a significant Lenape population, the location of Byberry Friends Meeting, one of the oldest Quaker meetings in Philadelphia, as well as an important abolitionist site and an early Black burial ground.
 Now, a project coordinated by the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia aims to knit these sites together under a unified theme, the Poquessing Trail of History , named after the creek that forms a boundary between Philadelphia and Bucks County. “Assets that have been protected and stewarded are finally getting some attention,” said project coordinator Aislinn Pentecost-Farren.
 Detail of a map in Thomas Companius Holm’s Short Description of New Sweden, published in 1702 and based in part on Peter Lindestrom’s journal of his 1654-1655 survey of the region. “Poanpissing” (Poquessing) Creek is at mid-left, on the right bank of the Delaware River. The map is oriented with north on the bottom; the Poquessing Creek, shown on the right side of the river in this map, is on the west side. | Image and text courtesy of Poquessing Trail of History
 “People in this area are used to being overlooked in the historical narrative,” noted project director Jack McCarthy. “In general, the Northeast hasn’t gotten a lot of attention, so it’s fun to bring it to life.”
 The project connects a number of stakeholders in the Byberry neighborhood: historic preservation groups, a religious congregation, a state park, a city park, and a Native American tribe. “Everybody was enthusiastic and supportive. Everyone saw the value of working collectively,” recalled McCarthy. “There were a few logistical challenges, like working at a distance with the Delaware Band, based in Oklahoma. And some pacing differences: things work slower in city government. With smaller groups, some are nimble, others working with volunteers can be slower.”
 Several of the sites are within the boundaries of Benjamin Rush State Park, including the location of the birthplace house of Benjamin Rush , the colonial physician and signatory to the Declaration of Independence. Built around 1690, it stood until 1969 despite efforts that were underway to restore it. Now, the Poquessing Trail of History project will construct a representation that will consist of an outline marking the original structure, with interpretive signage, much like the President’s House on Independence Mall and Franklin’s Court. “The construction of the Benjamin Rush House representation will be a high point for me,” said McCarthy. “So many people were devastated 50 or so years ago when it was demolished . At that time, the restoration architect John Milner had been working on its restoration, so now we’ve engaged him and his firm to reconstruct it.”
 The birthplace of Benjamin Rush circa 1950s. | Photo: Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 The next stop on the trail will be an interpretive memorial to the Lenape. “This is one of the most challenging parts of the project,” explained Pentecost-Farren. “Unlike the other components, there is no one site, because the whole area is representative of the Lenape.”
 Unlike other areas where Native Americans were displaced quickly by settlers, in Byberry the two groups coexisted for a long time, possibly owing to the large amount of land relative to the sparse population. "There were Lenape in this area into the early 18th century. A group would come back and stay for the summer, into the late 1700s,” noted McCarthy. “There was a good bit of interaction between Lenape and settlers. There was a sort of cooperative spirit, with the Lenape helping the newcomers, but eventually the waves of settlers put pressure on resources like water and land and forced out the Lenape.”
 “For the Lenape, land ownership wasn’t a cultural concept,” said Pentecost-Farren. “There are theories now that they might have been thinking the treaties were more of a sharing agreement. But as more settlers arrived, the Lenape were displaced.”
 Byberry Friends' Meeting House circa 1920. | Photo courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 Another significant population in the area is represented in a site located at the very edge of Benjamin Rush State Park. The Byberry Township African American Burial Ground was founded by Byberry Friends Meeting in 1780 when a member of the meeting donated the land to establish the graveyard.
 In 1980, Byberry Friends sold the site to the City. The Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation, the economic development corporation created by the City of Philadelphia and the Chamber of Commerce for Greater Philadelphia, subsequently sold a parcel that included the graveyard to a private firm that developed much of it into an industrial park. Now, it will be formally transferred to the state to become part of Benjamin Rush State Park. “The saving grace was that the burial ground was on the very edge of the tract and didn’t get developed,” said McCarthy. It was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2015.
 Although its location has been known, there are no headstones and no burial records save one. Nevertheless, Victoria Best, acting president of the Society for the Preservation of Philadelphia African American Assets (SPPAAA) was moved when she visited the site. “It felt like a space that was near and dear. It was a place for African Americans. Being in that state park, we didn’t often see Black folks. Being there [at the burial ground] felt like, we’re still here,” Best reflected. “It became a spiritual place. It reminded me that wherever I walk in the city, there’s layers of the past, the people all around.”
 Detail from 1843 Map of the County of Philadelphia by Charles Ellett, showing the location of the burial ground for Blacks that Byberry Meeting established on Thomas Townsend’s land near Poquessing Creek, about a mile from the Byberry Meeting House. | Image and text courtesy of Poquessing Trail of History
 Archaeological consultants using ground penetrating radar have identified disturbances that could be grave sites and have been taking measurements in an effort to estimate a count of how many people could be buried there.
 The project has engaged a landscape architectural firm to design a renovation. “Byberry is an important mission for us. To not let it be forgotten,” said Best. “We want the site permanently identified with markers. To make it a place of rest where we can honor the people that are there, even if we can’t identify those individuals. So that it becomes a more significant asset for African American history.”
 “It’ll be so satisfying for this overgrown plot to be turned into a landscaped burial ground,” agreed Pentecost-Farren. “The burial ground is so inspiring for me, making sure that Black history is included in Philadelphia’s history.”
 Another site with ties to Byberry Friends Meeting is Byberry Hall. Built by Robert Purvis in 1847 on land adjacent to the meeting, it hosted lectures and discussions on abolitionist and women’s rights topics. Both the meetinghouse and Byberry Hall were added to the local historic register in 1974. Now owned by Byberry Friends, the building will be renovated and developed into a local history center.
 Byberry Hall in 2024. The original stone building was completed in 1847. The rear and front wooden additions were added in the late 19th and early 20th century, respectively. | Image and text courtesy of Poquessing Trail of History
 Collectively, the four sites cover centuries of the area’s history and are linked by a trail through Poquessing Creek Park, a city park that follows the creek. “Along the trail that people use there will be interpretive signage, and the project website has a virtual interpretive walking tour,” noted McCarthy.
 In addition to self-guided walks, the project participants are planning several public programs to highlight the history of the sites, beginning this month and continuing throughout 2026. The inaugural offering is on September 13, when Lenape elders from the Delaware Tribe of Indians in Oklahoma will visit Byberry Friends Meeting to share stories, songs, and teachings.
 Byberry’s Underground Railroad history will be commemorated on October 18, the 175th anniversary of a meeting at Byberry Hall that protested the 1850 Fugitive Slave Act.
 Prominent Philadelphia abolitionist Robert Purvis (1810–1898). | Photo courtesy of Boston Public Library
 Another program will honor the Byberry Library Company, which was established by the meeting in 1794. Like the Library Company of Philadelphia, it was supported by subscriptions from its members including Robert Purvis . On November 15, visitors to the meeting will learn what Purvis was reading. “We have the circulation records, so we know which books he checked out,” McCarthy explained. “We’ve found most of them for this program, so people will be able to hold the actual books he held and read.”
 Future aims for the Poquessing Trail of History project include an ongoing roster of programming and investigating the possibility of extending the trail to the Delaware River at Glen Foerd.

 About the Author

title: Latinos and Preservationists Celebrate Saving Teatro Puerto Rico
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The former Diamond Theater, home to Teatro Puerto Rico from the 1960s until 1985, at 2119-2123 Germantown Avenue. Asociación Puertorriqueños en Marcha plans to reactivate the storied neighborhood landmark. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 When Lorna Cruz-Pierce returned to the theater of her childhood at 2119-2123 Germantown Avenue in North Philadelphia this summer there was no use trying to hold back the tears. This was the Teatro Puerto Rico, her grandfather’s theater, where she spent the nights and summers of the 1960s ushering, sweeping, selling candy–a teenage girl doing whatever needed doing. Yet, here was that same theater, a shell of what it once was, but still familiar and brimming with the possibility of returning to glory.
 “I got there, I cried. I cannot even tell you the emotions I felt walking back in. I was embarrassed, but ecstatic,” Cruz-Pierce said. “ I wanted to walk around every crevice.”
 Here, also, was the irrefutable evidence of the value of historic preservation: Exhibit A in the case for saving the past for future’s sake. Only a year ago, admirers of this century-old theater on Germantown Avenue northeast of Temple’s Main Campus–built 1922 as The Diamond–were fearing the worst. Worn down and on the market, there was word an out-of-state developer was eyeing the property for a demo-and-condo job, the latest casualty on the frontlines of Temple University and Kensington development's northward advance.
 Original ornamentation can still be seen on the century-old theater's facade. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 That turned nearby indy rocker Andy Molholt into an activist, teaming up with experienced preservationist Oscar Beisert to successfully nominate the building to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places last November. Later, word came that the developer had walked. Then the even bigger news arrived this summer: Asociación Puertorriqueños en Marcha (Puerto Ricans on the Move, or APM), a community services nonprofit with a long history in the neighborhood, had purchased the former theater to serve as an anchor space in a wider redevelopment plan for the Germantown Avenue corridor. The announcement electrified Molholt, who said experienced preservationists he spoke with called the dramatically rapid change in fortunes extremely rare. “This never happens,” Molholt said.
 In August, the plans went public when APM hosted a kickoff event at the theater, offering Cruz-Pierce, Moholt, and anyone else interested a chance to walk its interior one last time before a dramatic conversion, or perhaps reversion, into a treasured community space began. Nilda Ruiz, president and chief executive officer of APM, said she views the theater as a critical anchor property on a four-block stretch of Germantown Avenue currently undergoing a master planning effort. Specifics are yet to be worked out, but streetscaping, affordable housing, and improved commercial and cultural destinations will all play a role, perhaps none more exciting than the theater. “One thing I do know for sure is that I want to bring it back to a performance hall where we can show movies, we can have independent plays, we can maybe preserve the culture,” Ruiz says. “We’ll probably just call it ‘Teatro.’”
 A Center of Puerto Rican Life 
 The Diamond Theater in 1945. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 In a Hidden City article detailing efforts to save and the history of the theater published last year , its time as a touchstone of the Puerto Rican experience in Philadelphia received little more than two paragraphs. Historical records, at least in the English language, are simply not robust. Yet, Cruz-Pierce’s oral history, combined with research performed by Beisert as part of his historic nomination of the building , can fill in the blanks.
 After its 1922 opening, the theater spent less than 30 years as an English-language venue before a woman named Josephine Trilla applied in 1950 for a permit to convert it into the “Diamente Theatre,” Spanish for Diamond. A decade later, Felix Sampayo Rodriguez, Cruz-Pierce’s grandfather, purchased it and shortly thereafter restyled it as the “Teatro Puerto Rico.” As Beisert noted, this coincided with the “first great period” of Puerto Rican migration to Philadelphia between 1950 and 1970. “While there were certainly a handful of Puerto Ricans in Philadelphia in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, this specific Latino community did not have a large population in the Quaker City until the mid-20th century,” Beisert wrote in his nomination. “After the Second World War, the largely agrarian Puerto Rican economy was industrialized, ultimately leading some Puerto Ricans to migrate to Philadelphia.”
 This migration actually began in the late 1940s, Beisert noted, and by a decade later Puerto Ricans were said to have been the largest Latino group in Philadelphia, located predominantly in North Philadelphia. Cruz-Pierce explained that her family’s history goes deeper still: her parents, still living, date the arrival of Felix Sampayo Rodriguez and his wife Rosamaria to 1941. “They worked in the fields originally,” said Cruz-Pierce, recalling her grandmother’s stories of working in blueberry and strawberry fields likely in New Jersey.
 However, Felix had an entrepreneurial mind and began his social climb. First there was a little bodega he opened to sell items to fellow workers. Then a service shuttling people to and from the airport. Eventually, he came to own night clubs in Philadelphia and the greater region, then theaters, including several in the city. “He had one in Camden called the Parkside. He had another one a little further up the street on Germantown that he called the San Juan. He had the Century on 6th and Erie, and the Ruby on York,” Cruz-Pierce recalled. “But the Teatro Puerto Rico was the only one that did live shows. That was like the flagship theater.”
 The re-opening of Teatro Puerto Rico circa early 1970s. The first photo captures owner Felix Sampayo Rodriguez engaged in a celebratory toast. The second photo shows the massive crowd that gathered to welcome back the beloved theater. | Photos courtesy of Lorna Cruz-Pierce
 Cruz-Pierce grew up nearby, on Howard then Front Streets, before later relocating to New Jersey. She worked at the Teatro from childhood until she married at age 25 and her grandfather sold it in 1985. While under his ownership the theater served as an institution in the neighborhood and Puerto Rican community, showing both Spanish-language films and live performances, including from famous actors in the films. She added these were marquee attractions, with the theater getting first crack at exciting new Spanish language films in a time before Univision and Telemundo were able to provide native speakers with in-home entertainment.
 “Wednesday was always the new run. I used to drive up with my grandfather to New York early in the morning, pick up the films, load them up, and then drive to Philadelphia, put them in the theater, have the film ready when the cameraman came, go home, eat dinner, get dressed, and then come back. That was my Wednesday,” Cruz-Pierce said.
 Then, crowds would go “crazy” when actors and singers such as Vicente Fernández, Sandro (de América), and Sabu arrived for live performances. Wrestling matches were also performed in the space, which Cruz-Pierce recalled as a 600-seat theater with a steep, sloped seating arrangement and stage. She also holds many more mundane, but still important memories, such as deep friendships she made with other girls her age as they worked the theater and sold from the candy stand. Yet, none are perhaps more indelible than a grand re-opening. Following a fire in the theater, the exact date unknown, it had to close for a time for repairs. On the night it reopened, she remembers a packed theater with a line out the door. Everybody seemed to want to show their support. A photograph she still keeps shows patrons toasting her grandfather, decked out in a suit while raising his drink in turn. “I was overwhelmed by the amount of people,” Cruz-Pierce said. “You could not walk in there.”
 Down, But Not Out 
 Teatro Puerto Rico circa 1960s. | Photo courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 The theater’s history since Rodriguez sold it in 1975 is somewhat hazy. Cruz-Pierce said the next owner had plans to turn it into a hotel, a vision that never appears to have materialized. 36 years then passed until a church, Iglesia Ministerio Maranatha Pentecostal, purchased the property in 2011, worshipping there until a few years ago.
 Newspaper records suggest a record shop and nuisance bar may have operated at the address prior to the church’s ownership, although it is unclear whether such functions utilized the actual theater space. By the early 2000s, Google Street View images show a shuttered and nameless facade that persisted until at least 2012, followed by some restoration work and signage denoting the church’s occupancy by 2014. Evidence of upkeep continued until the “for sale” sign went up sometime in 2023 and the threat of demolition that followed.
 What is clear is that the building has endured substantial physical transformation, particularly of its interior. An early photograph from its time as The Diamond shows a cavernous theater space with ornate flourishes flanking the stage and a pair of faux-balconies replete with arches and columns. Cruz-Pierce believes much of that was damaged by the Teatro-era fire. Photographs from its reopening show what appear to be new wood paneling and light fixtures on the walls. “When we fixed it up, we ended up putting curtains and paneling to cover what was damaged,” said Cruz-Pierce.
 Upon her return to the theater this summer, she took note of nearly wholescale changes, including a faux/drop ceiling and a leveling of the floor in the main theater space that appeared to have been made at some point to convert it to a more traditional event room. The property historically included two smaller shops and storefronts flanking the main entrance,which Cruz-Pierce noted had also been converted.
 2119-2123 Germantown Avenue in 2019, which as last owned by Iglesia Ministerio Maranatha Pentecostal. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 APM has engaged Antonio Fiol-Silva, architect and founding principal at Center City-based SITIO architecture+urbanism, to lead the redevelopment of the theater and the creation of a master plan for the surrounding commercial corridor. APM previously received grant money to start the process for both and more recently received a $650,000 implementation award from Wells Fargo’s Regional Foundation to begin performing work. The nonprofit has also kicked off a $10 million fundraising campaign to complete the vision.
 Both Ruiz and Fiol-Silva say exactly what will take place inside the theater–renovation or restoration–will be dictated by what they find as they begin to chip away at the layers added to the space over time. The vision is indeed to convert it back to a theater, a concept Fiol-Silva is familiar with as lead architect of FringeArts’ theater in Old City, a former pump house. “This will be more of a black-box type of performance space that can be used in different iterations: to have events, to have educational activities, and to have performances, primarily,” Fiol-Silva explained.
 The greater challenge could come from revisioning the neighborhood. Fiol-Silva is currently working with APM to flesh out a master planning document for a four-block stretch of Germantown Avenue from Berks to Dauphin Streets. The Teatro and Cousin’s Supermarket at 5th and Berks Streets will serve as currently existing-anchors, while plans for a market-style food court and centralized food truck destination could also serve as primary points of interest. From there, APM hopes to bring new commercial development along the corridor while beautification efforts add to the experience. “As Germantown Avenue cuts through [on a diagonal], it creates these very odd triangles and kind of semi-dangerous intersections,” said Fiol-Silva. “So part of this also will be to rescue some of those little triangular parklets or open spaces and put them to some kind of utility and make crossings easier, not unlike what has happened on Passayunk Avenue where all those little parks have grown trees and fountains and become little nodes.”
 Affordable housing also remains a priority as large-scale condominium and apartment development continues to press in from Kensington and Temple University's campus. Fiol-Silva and Ruiz explained that the plan is to try and engineer the development of dense, but affordable housing, numbering 400 to 900 units, on empty lots in the district, potentially through the creation of an overlay with the City or other rezoning measures. "This was a neighborhood where nobody wanted to come and now it’s getting gentrified. Definitely a neighborhood of choice,” Ruiz said. “I like the idea of mixed use, you know, mixed income.” Ultimately, Ruiz said the hope is that they can welcome, but also guide new development, while largely keeping the neighborhood and its importance to the Puerto Rican community intact.
 Tags: adaptive resuse Hispanic heritage Historic theaters North Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Song of Philadelphia Concludes Second Season with Poets' Tribute to Larry Robin
author: Nathaniel Popkin
bodyText:
Larry Robin listening to a poetry reading at Fergie's Pub | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 "This room is filled with poets," someone observes just before Larry Robin takes the stage at a weekly Moonstone Arts Center reading at Fergie's Pub. In Song of Philadelphia's season two conclusion, host Julien Suaudeau brings his mic to record the sound of this now beloved Wednesday night event.
 Listen to the final episode of season two of Song of Philadelphia, "Is this loud enough?" on Apple and Spotify .
 "I tell people I love the words," Robin, the former bookseller and longtime director of Moonstone Arts, explains as he introduces the eleven poets who will read. "You can write a 300-page novel, a three-page poem, a three-line haiku. How are you going to make people feel what you feel? See what you see? That's the magic of poetry."
 Larry Robin in front of Fergie's Pub, Sansom Street | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 What follows on the podcast is exactly that, the sound of magic produced by Philadelphians wrestling with their city and their memories, and it's Robin who has given them space to reflect on and sometimes of dream of changing the world. "You have to recognize the world around you and hopefully you come up with a solution," says Robin, who before taking over his family's bookstore was a union organizer. "We're on the verge of a civil war. How do you learn to talk to each other again?"
 If you ask the poets interviewed at Fergie's the answer is, be like Larry. "Amplify other voices." "His example is his mentorship." "He doesn't try to be that person. He just is." "Forever energetic." "He loves other people."
 Larry mostly ignores the praise. Listeners are invited to bask in it, a loving tribute to Robin and poetry's place in the life of a city.
 You find every episode of seasons one and two of Song of Philadelphia on Hidden City's website . Look for more this coming winter as Julien Suaudeau explores how David Lynch invented his cinematic language of fear and strangeness in Philadelphia. And Julien solves a very Philadelphian Lynchian mystery.
 Tags: Fergie's Pub Moonstone Arts Poetry Song of Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Nathaniel Popkin Hidden City Daily co-founder Nathaniel Popkin’s latest book is To Reach the Spring: From Complicity to Consciousness in the Age of Eco-Crisis.

title: Restoration Role Model: YouthBuild Philadelphia Charter School
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2024 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 The front facade of the YouthBuild Philadelphia Charter School in its fully restored state. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 While searching for a new, permanent home, the YouthBuild Charter School chose a vacant, but historically and architecturally significant building in North Philadelphia. Extant spoke with representatives of the school and Atkin Olshin Schade Architects about the excellent rehab and adaptive re-use project, which engaged its students and received a 2025 Preservation Achievement Award from the Preservation Alliance.
 Extant Magazine (EM) : What was the building’s original use?
 Atkin Olshin Schade Architects (AOSA) : The building at 2309-2313 N. Broad Street was constructed in 1930 and designed by noted architect John T. Windrim. It originally served as a Philadelphia Electric Company (PECO) showroom and North Philadelphia district office. At the time, PECO still sold appliances in addition to providing electric service to residents, and the building served as a retail location. PECO sold the building in the 1970s, and it subsequently changed hands multiple times. Although the building was not protected by any historic registrations, the limestone façade, bronze storefront and prominent Philadelphia Electric Company name on the upper faccade had remained intact.
 EM : What was most important to preserve?
 AOSA : Preserving the exterior was a top priority to maintain the building as a prominent landmark on Broad Street. The project team saw this as an opportunity to honor the legacy of the Windrim-designed PECO building while ensuring its continued presence as a symbol of Philadelphia’s history. At the same time, renovations were carefully planned to modernize the building’s functionality, aligning it with the evolving needs of this vital institution.
 EM : What was the client’s original vision? Did it change over time?
 AOSA : The original vision was to secure a space that truly reflected what YouthBuild students and educators deserved. Initially, YouthBuild Philly hoped to find and purchase an existing school building that could serve as a permanent home. However, after exploring dozens of properties, it became clear that the school’s unique facility needs–along with its commitment to remaining in North Philadelphia–called for a building rehabilitation and adaptive reuse project instead. The vision for this new space was co-created with YouthBuild students, graduates, staff, Board members and the design team. While plans for this new space evolved throughout the process, YouthBuild Philly’s core vision for how the space would be used remained strong and consistent.
 Top: Google Street View from 2019 showing the spandrels and front door surround before they were stolen. Bottom and left: The main showroom’s terrazzo floors on the first floor were the only original interior feature that was retained. Detail showing the replacement spandrels and surround that were fabricated to look as close to the original as possible. Photos: Peter Woodall
 EM : What was the biggest preservation challenge?
 AOSA : Preservation challenges arose due to the building’s prolonged period of vacancy and lack of climate control, as well as vandalism that had damaged or removed elements of the facade. Careful coordination and planning were required to retain as much of the original structure as possible while upgrading the building’s envelope performance, integrating new systems and accommodating the client’s program. While the masonry façade remained largely intact, exposure to the elements and water infiltration had corroded the window lintels, necessitating their replacement. Additionally, shifting and cracking masonry required repairs and stabilization. The most complex challenge was adapting the remnants of the existing bronze storefront to accommodate a new thermally broken glazing system. This required addressing structural stability issues, reinforcing missing elements and meticulously recreating lost architectural details. Adding an additional story to the building to meet programmatic needs was an additional challenge that required both deference to the historic Broad Street façade and an acknowledgement of 21st century materials and energy efficiency goals.
 EM : Did you look to any role model for inspiration or as an example?
 AOSA : The inspiration for this building came directly from YouthBuild students and graduates, who expressed a need for a space that was open longer, safer and better suited for learning. Many contributed thoughtful ideas about what the building should include and how it should be designed. YouthBuild Philly looked at examples like the recently built Cristo Rey School facility in North Philadelphia . However, YouthBuild’s unique need to balance education and career training spaces sets this project apart. With only a handful of YouthBuild programs nationwide owning their own buildings, this effort was both ambitious and groundbreaking.
 EM : What was the project’s biggest surprise (good or bad)?
 AOSA : During the design phase, much of the historic bronze facade remained intact. However, just before construction began, the building was vandalized, resulting in the theft or severe damage of significant portions of the Broad Street facade metalwork. This unexpected loss created both scope and budget challenges. Initially, the plan was to preserve and restore the bronze facade while constructing a new thermally insulated system behind it. Due to the extent of the damage, the approach shifted to integrating new, matching aluminum storefront components within the remaining original bronze framing. New bronze elements were fabricated to replace missing pieces, and the entire assembly was refinished to ensure a seamless blend of old and new components.
 Although the loss of the double-hung windows, acanthus leaf ornamentation, entry surround, brackets, and other decorative elements was unfortunate, it provided an opportunity to enhance the thermal performance of the system. The situation also became a valuable hands-on learning experience for students. By partnering with Legacy Atelier, a local caster in Germantown, students gained firsthand experience in the process of casting new bronze elements and assembling the replacement acanthus detailing, which now adorns the restored facade.
 Tags: Adaptive Reuse North Philadelphia PECO Renovation Restoration Role Model 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Calder Gardens Debuts on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Calder Gardens. | Photo: Iwan Baan. Artwork by Alexander Calder © 2025 Calder Foundation, New York / Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York
 The long-awaited opening of the new site dedicated to the work of artist Alexander Calder has finally arrived. With the addition of Calder Gardens, the Benjamin Franklin Parkway will now feature works by all three generations of the illustrious Philadelphia family of sculptors. It joins grandfather Alexander Milne Calder’s sculpture of William Penn atop City Hall and father Alexander Stirling Calder’s Swann Fountain on Logan Circle, although Alexander Calder’s mobile entitled Ghost has enjoyed a place of honor in the Great Stair Hall of the Philadelphia Museum of Art for decades.
 Located on a City-owned tract of land on the south side of the Parkway between 21st and 22nd Streets, Calder Gardens sits directly opposite the Barnes Foundation, which is providing administrative and operational support for the new enterprise.
 Alexander Calder in his Roxbury, Connecticut studio, 1941. | Photo: Herbert Matter. © 2025 Calder Foundation, New York / Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York
 The artworks and their curation, however, will be the province of the New York-based Calder Foundation, whose president, Alexander S. C. Rower is Calder’s grandson. Juana Berrío has been named the senior director of programs. She was previously a curatorial advisor at the Whitney Museum in New York City.
 Alexander Calder was born in 1898 in Lawnton, Pennsylvania, near Harrisburg. His sculptor father and portraitist mother discouraged him from pursuing a career in art, so an early interest in mechanical devices led to his enrollment at the Stevens Institute of Technology in New Jersey, earning a degree in mechanical engineering. Although he found engineering work unsatisfying and went on to study art in New York City, his technical background would prove instrumental in his artwork.
 The materials utilized by his father and grandfather–stone, plaster, and bronze—never appealed to Calder. He first devised three-dimensional wire figures in the 1920s, later developed his distinctive mobiles, and, beginning in the 1950s, created large outdoor sculptures from bolted steel plates. He has been likened to Leonardo da Vinci, as both were interested in “problem solving, experimenting with materials, mechanical systems, and devices.” according to Joan Marter, professor emeritus of art history at Rutgers University, in her 1991 book Alexander Calder .
 Inside Calder Gardens. | Photo: Iwan Baan. Artwork by Alexander Calder © 2025 Calder Foundation, New York / Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York
 In April 2022, the City of Philadelphia approved a 99-year lease for the 1.8-acre site, in exchange for $1.00 in rent, although noting that all the construction, operating and maintenance costs would be borne by the institution. The Calder Foundation worked with a coalition of philanthropists to raise the required funds.
 The site features a building with indoor galleries, designed by Pritzker Prize–winning architects Herzog & de Meuron, who also designed the Tate Modern. The garden of native and flowering species is the work of landscape designer Piet Oudolf, whose credits include New York’s High Line.
 Reluctant to call it a museum, the Calder Foundation views the site as a contemplative oasis to appreciate both the art and the changing seasons reflected in the landscaping. “We want to be a welcoming place for introspection,” Berrio said. “I think that’s what Calder would want us to do. To pause, contemplate what’s around you, and notice how things are impermanent.”
 An aerial view of Calder Gardens. | Photo: Iwan Baan. Artwork by Alexander Calder © 2025 Calder Foundation, New York / Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York 
 By eschewing a permanent collection, Calder Gardens sees itself as sharing the artist's interests in experimentation, impermanence, and cross-media practice. For its opening, Rower has selected works across the phases of his grandfather’s career. “The exhibits will reflect different moments in his life,” said Berrio. “Some of them have never been shown before because they’re in private collections. Other works have never been seen in the U.S.”
 In addition to presenting works by the Calders and other important artists on a rotating basis, staff anticipates using the site for concerts, lectures, performances, and other events. “We want to activate the space with programming,” explained Berrio. “We plan to commission works by artists in time-based work, such as performances and concerts.”
 Calder Gardens is open every day, except Tuesday, from 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. with a members-only (Calder Gardens and Barnes Foundation) hour at 10:00 a.m. each day.
 Tags: Alexander Calder Benjamin Franklin Parkway museums sculpture 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Abuse of Power in the 1700s Ignited a War Between Washington and the Editor of the Philadelphia Aurora
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
The year was 1795, the president was George Washington, and the newspaper was Philadelphia’s own Aurora General Advertiser . The pro-Jefferson Aurora was relentless in its written attacks on Washington, John Adams, and their fellow Federalists, who responded by harassing the paper’s editors, eventually charging them with seditious libel. Much like ongoing controversies over policies of the Trump administration , the clash between Hamiltonian Federalists and Jeffersonian Democratic-Republicans tested the limits of the First Amendment, due process, executive power, and actions taken by the federal government in the name of national security.
 An extant copy of the November 17, 1794 edition of the Aurora General Advertiser. | Photo: Ebay
 We see historic parallels in which the party in power engaged in voter suppression, demonized critics, persecuted foreigners deemed undesirable, imposed restrictions on opposition journalists, leveled trumped-up criminal charges against enemies, plotted to prevent the other party’s candidate from becoming president by disqualifying their electors, and encouraged, condoned, or ignored acts of violence committed by supporters against political opponents. The 18th century targets included the offices and editors of the Aurora .
 Beginnings 
 Soon after the death of Benjamin Franklin in 1790, Benjamin Franklin Bache (pronounced “beech”) used the printing press he inherited from his grandfather to establish the General Advertiser, and Political, Commercial, Agricultural, and Literary Journal . This coincided with the beginning of Philadelphia’s 10-year tenure as the nation’s capital. By 1794, the newspaper had evolved into the Aurora and General Advertiser and became a staunch critic of Washington and the Federalists. Bache’s work eventually would get him barred from the halls of Congress.
 A rare, undated portrait of Benjamin Franklin Bache. | Image: World History Encyclopedia
 Founded by Alexander Hamilton, the Federalist Party promoted the interests of wealthy bankers, merchants, and landowners who favored and benefited from a strong, centralized federal government, according to American History Central: The Encyclopedia of American History (AHC) . The Democratic-Republican Party of Thomas Jefferson and James Madison stood for strict adherence to the Constitution, limits on federal powers, an egalitarian society, an economy based on agriculture, state and individual rights, and an alliance with France, rather than Great Britain.
 Initially supportive of the nation’s first president, “As early as 1791, the Advertiser sometimes published opinions chiding what some saw as the trappings of monarchy in Washington’s presidency, [and] articles expressed distaste with the notion of making Washington’s birthday a holiday,” Delia Titzell wrote in a column for the George Washington Presidential Library. “By Washington’s second term, Bache was leveling accusations of corruption and bad character. [He] also began publishing and selling forged letters claimed to have been written by Washington during the war that made his motives for taking his commission appear self-interested. The Aurora berated Washington’s ownership of slaves , expressing disgust that ‘Liberty’s Apostle should be seen with chains in his hands, holding men in bondage.’”
 Corruption and Impeachment 
 In October 1795, the Aurora published a letter, presumed to be written by Bache or one of his staff, but attributed to “A Calm Observer,” claiming that the Comptroller of the Treasury and President Washington violated Article II, Section 1 of the Constitution by granting and accepting, respectively, several thousands more than the $25,000 annual salary allocated by Congress. The charges resulted in a lively and sometimes acrimonious printed exchange between the paper and Oliver Wolcott, then Secretary of the Treasury and the former Comptroller in question, who admitted to and defended the payments to Washington, noting that although made, had not been requested.
 Citing the impeachment clause, the Aurora warned Wolcott, “I know of no crime or misdemeanor against the Constitution and the laws greater than that which you have severally committed.” It drew nationwide attention at the time, but the controversy eventually fizzled out, except for Bache. On the occasion of Washington’s retirement from office in 1797 he noted,” The name of Washington from this day has ceased to give currency to political iniquity and legalized corruption.”
 A lithograph by Nathaniel Currier, published in 1852, depicts George Washington in 1787 speaking to his slaves at Mount Vernon. | Image: Public Domain
 Some of the charges Bache leveled at Washington over the years were true, others were mere opinion, still others were blatantly false. Of course, Washington was no fan of Bache, calling his paper “outrages on common decency” and concluding, “If you read the Aurora of this city… you cannot but have perceived with what malignant industry and persevering falsehoods I am assailed in order to weaken, if not destroy, the confidence of the Public.” He expressed his reluctance to seek a third term to Alexander Hamilton, citing a “disinclination to be longer buffeted in the public prints by a set of infamous scribblers.”
 In a letter to Wolcott, Washington concluded, “That Mr. Bache will continue his attacks on the government, there can be no doubt.” Writing to Secretary of State Timothy Pickering, Washington characterized Bache’s “continual attacks” on the administration as “indecent as they are devoid of truth and fairness. Under these circumstances, it would be wished that the enlightened public could have a clear and comprehensive view of facts, but how to give it lies the difficulty. I see no method at present.” Benjamin Rush, noted Philadelphia physician and signatory to the Declaration of Independence, speculated that Bache’s writings in the Aurora induced Washington to retire.
 A Step Too Far 
 Enactment of the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798 heightened the divide between the two political parties of the day. They were passed by the Federalist majority in Congress and signed into law by President John Adams, supposedly in the interest of national security at a time when war with France was considered likely. “The Acts were met with opposition and criticism from Thomas Jefferson and the Democratic-Republicans, who argued they were unconstitutional and violated Freedom of Speech and Freedom of the Press,” noted The National Archives.
 The Sedition Act restricted freedom of speech and of the press by imposing fines or prison for anyone who criticized the president, Congress, or government in print or speech. The Naturalization Act targeted immigrants, who tended to favor the Democratic-Republican Party, by making it more difficult for them to become citizens, thus suppressing potential votes by anti-Federalists. The Alien Act and the Alien Enemies Act provided for the expulsion of non-citizens deemed dangerous during times of peace and of war, respectively.
 This political cartoon from 1798 satirized a fight in Congress concerning the Alien and Sedition Acts of 1798. Federalist Congressman Roger Griswold (at far right) attacks Jeffersonian Republican Congressman Matthew Lyon with a cane. Lyon retaliates with fireplace tongs. | Image courtesy of Print and Picture Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 Out of the four, the Alien Enemies Act is the only one to remain in effect today. The Trump administration cites it as the legal basis for deporting hundreds of people to El Salvador for imprisonment without due process. “In the end, widespread anger over the Alien and Sedition Acts fueled Jefferson’s victory over Adams in the bitterly contested 1800 presidential election, and their passage is widely considered to be one of the biggest mistakes of Adams’ presidency,” according to History.com .
 “The only journalists prosecuted under the Sedition Act were editors of Democratic-Republican newspapers,” noted AHC . The Act expired in 1800, but not before Bache and his successor, William Duane, were charged.
 Arrests and Other Shenanigans 
 Soon after Bache printed a letter supporting France’s position in a diplomatic disagreement with the United States, the June 27, 1798 edition of the Aurora reported, “The editor was yesterday arrested on a warrant from Judge Peters of the Federal Circuit Court on the charge of libeling the President & Executive Government in a manner tending to excite sedition.” The arrest came more than two weeks before Adams signed the Sedition Act into law. Bail was set at $4,000, ahead of a court date that October. Bache went back to work at the Aurora, but, before he would stand trial, Benny, as he was known, became a victim of the yellow fever epidemic sweeping the city. He was 29 years old.
 “After Bache’s untimely death, there were rumors of Federalist attempts to buy out the Aurora , but his widow, Margaret, retained and continued to publish her husband’s newspaper, with William Duane at the editorial helm,” according National Park Service historians. “William and Margaret married in 1800 and successfully continued the newspaper through the year 1822.”
 Carrying on Bache’s war of words led to Duane’s arrest for seditious libel in 1799 for articles he published suggesting Britain’s undue influence on the U.S. government. He avoided prosecution after producing a letter in which Adams had expressed similar concerns. Ahead of the 1800 elections, the Federalists tried to pass a bill authored by Senator James Ross of Pennsylvania, legislation that would have let their allies block electors pledged to Jefferson.
 A portrait of William Duane by artist Charles Balthazar Julien Févret de Saint-Mémin. | Image courtesy of National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution
 “The Ross bill itself was a stealth measure, since the Senate’s debates were not then open to the public or reporters,” Bernard A. Weisberger wrote in his book, America Afire . A sympathetic senator passed the details of the bill to Duane, who published them in the Aurora . “The Senate called Duane before a quickly created Committee on Privileges to answer for the sin of printing ‘false, scandalous, defamatory, and malicious assertions.’”
 To avoid seizure by the Sergeant-At-Arms for contempt, Duane went into hiding until Congress adjourned. The Ross bill failed “after Federalist hard-liners, of all people, could not agree on a final version.” The Federalist reign ended with the election of Jefferson in 1800, and when he took office the following year, Jefferson dismissed a federal case against Duane.
 Over the years, the Aurora and its editors were the targets of physical violence. Federalist sympathizers assaulted Bache more than once, and Duane and his son were beaten severely by federal agents over his refusal to reveal the source of an article. The March 5, 1798 edition reported, “The front window of the office of the Aurora was, on Friday evening, successfully assaulted by three stones the size of a man’s fist or larger. Several panes of glass were consequently broken, and this is the third attack of the kind for which Mr. Bache has been indebted to the friends of regular government .”
 Legacy 
 “With the U.S. Capital residing in Philadelphia from 1790 to 1800, the Aurora became the voice of opposition against the perceived (and sometimes real) pro-British sympathies of the Washington and Adams administrations, as well as their Federalist allies in Congress,” according an account by the National Park Service. “With the tacit support of Thomas Jefferson and open support of other Democratic-Republicans, the Aurora mercilessly attacked the federalists and helped shape the character of two-party politics in America.”
 A reproduction of the original Aurora General Advertiser sign. | Photo courtesy of Mount Vernon Ladies' Association
 Time and history generally have been kind to George Washington (think “Cherry Tree” and “Father of his Country”). Writing through the tumult of his era, Bache was in the thick of history, but lacked the perspective of time. “As a strong critical voice against the Federalist Washington and Adams administrations, Bache’s Aurora was the most popular and well-known Republican newspaper of the early 1790s,” Titzell concluded. “At its peak, the Aurora had 1,700 subscribers, more than three times the average periodical of the day. Although often dismissed as a man on the wrong side of history, Bache has enjoyed renewed interest in recent years, celebrated as an early champion of freedom of the press and for his uncompromising idealism and outspokenness.”
