 In the very first issue of the General Advertiser Bache wrote, “The freedom of the press is the bulwark of liberty. If the people are enlightened the nation stands and flourishes, thro' ignorance it fails or degenerates.”
 Tags: Donald J. Trump free press George Washington newspapers political history 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: The Forgotten Cemetery
author: George deBenneville Bell, Jr.
bodyText:
It was almost dusk when I decided to jump the gate. Looking up and down the street I saw no one. This was going to be easier if I didn’t have to explain myself. The canopies of trees, lush in the June air, leaned over the surrounding walls like graceful fans slowly collapsing over the property. Securing a foot on the gate, I hoisted my other leg up, but the chain lock gave way, already broken, and the old wrought-iron gate, like a door to the afterlife, swung open. I had every reason to believe I was the first relative to enter our family burial ground in over 100 years.
 The deBenneville Family Burial Ground at North Broad Street and Green Lane. Major work to clean and preserve the cemetery began in 2024. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 One glance told me the property in West Oak Lane had been neglected in the most abject way. Syringes, sandwich wrappers, and condoms were strewn through the waist-high grass. Jagged bits of glass glinted with menace as the street lights came on. Vines as thick as your arm overgrew the shattered walls. I stumbled on a dead cat, hard as a cinder block. The headstones, many drowning in overgrowth, could be seen listing this way and that, as if for years they had been gasping for life in a losing battle with nature and time. Some had fallen over. I was rapt as I pulled away weeds to read the inscriptions of my family members from 200 years and more ago. The shallow chiseling of names and dates, faint with age, or entirely illegible, was thrilling to me. Alone in the burial ground, I felt the mystic touch that often comes from unexpected connections.
 Also, I was puzzled. Why such squalor where my ancestors lay next to Broad Street, Philadelphia’s most famous thoroughfare? The neglect was so vile that it made me want to turn away and be grateful to exit the graveyard without injury. It was not at all what I had expected to find. I had travelled from my home in Boston to see the cemetery for myself, to see if this hidden place five miles north of the city’s center was indeed the little gem I had discovered from my research on the web. The old pictures I had found showed an intact, if slightly overgrown, burial ground. My sense of hopeful discovery quickly curdled to anger.
 The little graveyard in West Oak Lane is 267 years old. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 High on one stone wall was a plaque, not yet reached by the rioting green beneath it. It read: The deBenneville Family Burial Ground. Established 1758.
 I hadn’t lived in Philadelphia since high school, and, yet, I knew immediately that I had to get to the bottom of this. What to call it? An affront? A desecration? Half a dozen rowhouses overlooked the cemetery. In my righteous dismay, I knocked on doors to see what I could learn. No one answered, although in one or two windows I could see wary faces peering out at this impatient stranger.
 An Enlightened Ancestor 
 The idea for a family burial ground, along with a gift of $500 for its “perpetual” maintenance, came from Dr. George deBenneville, my 7th great-grandfather and the first preacher of Universalism in America. He was the first of my deBenneville ancestors to migrate to the Philadelphia area before purchasing 132 acres of farm land in the Oley Valley, some 50 miles northwest of the city. Later, he b ought a farm in Branchtown, now part of the West Oak Lane section of Philadelphia , and allocated a half-acre for a burial ground. His instructions hinted at the strange immortality that attends cemeteries: AND WHEREAS I have set off from my said plantation on the Old York Road which I purchased from Joseph Spencer a small piece or strip of ground three perches wide and twenty perches in depth for the purpose of a graveyard or burial place for myself and family and have marked or fixed the boundaries thereof by three stones. Now my will and desire is that this strip or piece of ground shall not be sold by my executors but always exempted and reserved out of the sale of the plantation and be and remain the property of my family to and for a burial place forever and to and for no other use and purpose whatsoever. 
 deBenneville was born to an aristocratic family. Remarkably, his mother produced nine children in five years, four sets of twins, successively, and then died giving birth to the youngest, George, in 1703. To escape King Louis XIV’s movement of religious suppression, the deBennevilles, well-to-do Huguenot (Protestant) landowners, had fled to London shortly before George’s birth. His father soon died as well, and his godmother, Queen Anne, agreed to raise him in the Royal Court. Anne had recently ascended to the throne as Queen of England, Scotland, and Ireland. She was married to Prince George of Denmark and had 17 known pregnancies. Her oldest child, Prince William, survived only for 11 years and died in 1700, so deBenneville may have been a stand-in for the sons she bore who never grew old. From early accounts, he was an unruly handful. W hatever sentiments the Queen may have had, young deBenneville wasn't around for long. From his autobiography: When arrived at the age of twelve years, I was very wild, believing myself to be of a different mass from mankind in general. As it was designed that I should learn navigation, I was sent to sea in a vessel of war belonging to a little fleet bound to the coast of Barbary with presents, and to renew the peace with Algiers, Tunis, and Tripolis. 
 A sketch portrait of Dr. George deBenneville. Date and artist unknown. | Image courtesy of North Texas Unitarian Universalist Congregations
 Thus dispatched, he was trained and worked at sea in the British maritime service, sailing the Barbary Coast of North Africa. The crew’s mission was to renew trading status with the most important territories still under Ottoman control in the early 18th century. After four years at sea, deBenneville returned to England in 1719. He fell into a year-long depression, which he described, But God who always seeks to convince and save his poor creatures, did not leave his poor wandering sheep; for some time after my return home, being present by invitation at a ball, and having over-heated myself. I ordered my servant to prepare linens for me to change, and as I was putting it on, I fell into a fainting fit, and had a vision of myself, burning as a firebrand in hell, and coming to myself; again, I cried out, ‘I am damned! 
 From his depression he was roused by a sudden epiphany, a mystical call from God, and he began preaching at the age of 17. The Calvinist Church in England roundly rejected him as a heretic. His sermons found no better reception when he tried his luck in France, where he was condemned to death for his unorthodox beliefs. King Louis XV’s last-minute pardon, citing deBenneville’s royal upbringing, reached the executioner’s scaffold in time to prevent his hanging. He decamped to Holland and then Germany, where he studied herbal remedies for several years and was certified as a doctor, even as he continued to preach radical ideas that routinely got him thrown out of churches.
 I suspect all of this would be lost to time, but for what happened next. In Germany, he came down with a fever and was pronounced dead and placed in a coffin. Almost two days later, he revived, claiming to be possessed by a new vision, a gospel of “boundless love for the entire human race.” Over time, he pieced together the notion of universal forgiveness largely from other religions and his own b eliefs , a nd emerged as the spiritual founder whose history the Universalists sought to preserve.
 The headstone of Dr. John deBenneville, the grandson of Dr. George deBenneville. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In addition to several historical monographs, his autobiography was translated from French posthumously, with the publisher’s introduction: “A true and remarkable account of the life and trance of Dr. George de Benneville, late of Germantown, (Pennsylvania) who departed this life in March, 1793, aged nearly ninety years. : Including what he saw and heard, during a trance of forty-two hours both in the regions of happiness and misery….”
 deBenneville may have had a back-from-the-dead, fevered energy about him, but none of his new sermons on universalism (“Honor the ocean of love…”) were well received. With the means to continue pursuing the messages of his trance, he took his steamer trunk of beliefs and rejections to America, bearing an inchoate view of forgiveness, and arriving in Philadelphia in 1741. He married Jean Bertolet, from a similarly high Huguenot family. He befriended many Native Americans and learned their healing methods, which depended on local herbs and plants. Opening an apothecary in Philadelphia, he preached and continued to practice medicine. His marriage produced eight children, some of whom are buried with him in the family plot.
 The Path of a Family Name 
 The deBenneville name entered my family through my great-great-grandmother, Esther deBenneville Keim (1827-1889). My father, George Bell, was given deBenneville as his middle name and passed it down to me. He never mentioned the existence of a family burial ground. Nor did my grandfather, John C. Bell, Jr., who was Chief Justice of the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania for many years and the shortest-termed governor in state history, serving 19 days. Nor did his brother, my great-uncle, deBenneville “Bert” Bell, one of the first commissioners of the NFL and owner of the Philadelphia Eagles. The Maxwell Memorial Football Club still awards the Bert Bell Trophy annually to the NFL’s most outstanding player. These prominent men, along with other de Benneville relatives, were in and out of the city throughout their lives. Many went to the University of Pennsylvania, worked downtown, and likely passed by the family burial ground many times. All are gone now, each buried in their favored churchyards, a few miles from one another, with members of their own families. I’ve convinced myself that they knew nothing of the cemetery because I don’t want to believe that they turned their back on it. This sweet, hidden place.
 The badly overgrown deBenneville Family Burial Ground in 2023. | Photos: George Bell
 On my visits I am drawn to the walls and the headstones of children. One in particular is low to the ground in a half-moon shape and marked only "Little Hettie." The rocks in the walls and the gravestones age with puzzling variety. It’s like trying to understand time itself. The most recent stone was set 114 years ago, marking Anna deBenneville Michener. No deBenneville has been buried here since then. Concerned about the cemetery’s upkeep, she left $2,000 for its maintenance. In 1925, a deed records the sale of the western portion of the burial ground, although it's not clear how much was paid for that land. That sum, and Michener's gift, were the only additions to the initial $500 bequest that deBenneville had tendered at its inception over 150 years before Michener was buried there. Two deBenneville relatives who never knew each other, now separated by 20 yards, both silently bearing a family legacy forward. Since then, just the churn of time. The quiet of the most recent 114 years, the city growing louder and more populous around it as cars became more common, their emissions eating into the marble, though not the granite gravestones. The beautiful border walls of Wissahickon schist, bright with flecks of mica, have, in places, dulled to the color of dust. With my finger I scrape at the weakest parts and come away with a hunk of powdery stone. Many times, I imagine, my ancestors must have passed by the tallest border wall abutting North Broad Street by car and never looked up. In our family not a word was passed down. Not a mention of the burial ground at Thanksgiving, or on a weekend car ride, or when we attended services to bury other relatives in other places.
 Nothing suggests their ignorance was willful in the way that forgetting needn’t be willful. Enveloped by the same silence we so revere at funerals, failing to be carried on in family stories, the burial ground simply stopped being discussed. It went mute, rarely visited, the tombstones mere relics from a forgotten age that disappeared under the weight of other things.
 Taking Control of the Burial Ground 
 I had never pondered the question of who owns cemeteries, but I became determined to take control of my own family burial ground. I learned surprising things. Hundreds of years ago, graveyards could fill up fast. Although families were large, life expectancy was short, with high child mortality rates. We have yet to find the deed to the burial ground, this quarter-acre that holds the remains of 124 deBennevilles, although George deBenneville’s will does exists. There is a market for cemetery mergers and acquisitions, with its own network of lawyers, surveyors, and tax specialists. For a time, it seemed, Laurel Hill Cemetery , the 265-acre national historic landmark, was interested in buying the deBenneville burial ground. By law, the cemetery is overseen by the court of Common Pleas, Orphans’ Court Division, because it is a private cemetery with no known heir serving as its trustee.
 The cemetery's walls, built with Wissahickon schist, are now visible and clear of overgrowth after years of abandonment. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Two trusts govern the burial ground: Dr. George deBenneville's and Anna deBenneville Michener's. The first holds his land and his $500 gift. The second holds her $2,000 gift. I learned that Wells Fargo bank had inherited sole trusteeship of both trusts many years ago after a series of mergers. In my cemetery notebook, I recorded the shorthand of it: deBenneville invests his $500 bequest in Philadelphia city water bonds in 1758. A few generations later, no family member stands as trustee, and The Pennsylvania Company for Insurance on Lives and Granting Annuities is appointed as such. Bank mergers and name changes tumble forward through the next 150 years. More recently, the passing of authority reads like a corporate family tree: First Pennsylvania Bank, Core States, Wachovia, and First Union, in succession, all held the trustee roles for the two trusts. Today, 267 years later, Wells Fargo is the surviving trustee with authority over the burial ground.
 So it was Wells Fargo I needed to contact, but what would I say if I could navigate my way to the relevant trust officer? Please cut the grass? I already knew I had my answer in the condition the cemetery had lapsed into. Wells Fargo had lost its interest in caretaking.
 The North Philadelphia graveyard in 1986. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 A picture from 39 years ago shows a fairly tidy burial ground with several benches for reflection, although the walls were overgrown with ivy and encroached upon by nearby trees. Given the dereliction of the grounds today, I assumed there was no money left in either trust. Yet, as with so much else related to this project, I underestimated the divergent power of time to grow and to destroy. It turns out, if a bank takes a fee for trust administration and another fee for investment oversight annually, and allows significant problems to go untended–trees, walls, fences–and can’t be bothered to cut the grass for years, then voila, you may find $300,000 slumbering comfortably in a line in a spreadsheet in a small corner of your banking empire. For Wells Fargo, this is a speck. No more than a nickel under the couch cushion. When I petitioned the Orphans’ Court to take over both trusts, the bank didn’t object. Especially when I volunteered to show them recent pictures of the cemetery. Out of stubbornness and not wanting to spend a dime of the assets on anything but cemetery improvements, I represented myself legally throughout the year it took to gain the trusteeships. By the time the accounts came under my control, the transferred sums were less. The bank’s lawyers and accountants took their piece, but there was enough to begin the substantial work of repairing and revitalizing the burial ground.
 The story of the past ends there, giving way to the long work of restoration. Repairs will take several years. I am learning about insidious root systems, forensic gravestone experts, and how granite and marble headstones age differently from one another. I had the great luck of meeting David Rowland, the president of the Old York Road Historical Society who has been an invaluable partner in this journey. Based on researching birth and death certificates, the Society has amassed the only comprehensive list of those entombed in the burial ground. My cousin Baker Bell, who bears the same relationship to deBenneville as I do, has been enlisted for his wisdom and for the fact that he is one of my last remaining relatives in Philadelphia. For 30 years Shirley and Ed Parks hav e lived across the street from the cemetery in one of the rowhouses on Green Lane. On a subsequent visit to the burial ground, Rowland and I knocked on their door. “Damn,” Ed said, “You mean someone’s finally going to care about this?” His family had enjoyed the view and lamented the decline of the stones and the crumbling walls. He said the grass used to be cut regularly, but in the last few years no one had shown up to do anything.
 The resting place of British soldiers General James Tanner Agnew and Lieutenant Colonel John Bird. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The gravestones are oddly distributed. At the east end of the property lay all the deBenneville stones, gathered haphazardly as a clan might if they stood together informally, leaning this way and that, reminding me of the way families depend on one another. deBenneville’s is a large, flat slab flush with the ground. The middle of the cemetery is given to open space, and then, to the west, lie two graves that differ from all the others. Here are the resting places of General James Tanner Agnew, one of only four British Generals from the Revolutionary War period buried on American soil, and Lieutenant Colonel John Bird, also felled in the Battle of Germantown on October 4, 1777. The two soldiers were first interred in Germantown’s Lower Burying Ground, but a year later, British General Sir William Howe, fearing the desecration of their graves after the British withdrew from Philadelphia , secured a secret agreement with deBenneville to move the bodies to the family burial ground. It was known that deBenneville cared for the wounded on both sides, true to his belief about universal love and forgiveness. “Deeds, not creeds,” he had often preached.
 Today, a day care center and an auto repair shop share the northern border of the cemetery. It is a dreary landscape of chain-link fences and barbed wire, and despite some early improvements, the cemetery contributes to the melancholy. I think to myself, we have a long way to go to bring it back to what my 7th great-grandfather envisioned. Of all the things that might occupy this spot, a historical cemetery must be among the most unlikely. Yet, it has survived hundreds of winters, the blight of the industrial age, and the exhaust from the traffic that runs ceaselessly along North Broad Street on its eastern border. It occurs to me that it's done so by turning its back on everything but its own dignity and existence. It speaks to me of patience even as I wonder how to preserve it structurally, legally, and spiritually for another 267 years. I hadn’t expected to gain much from simply wanting the cemetery to look less lousy. Yet, already, it has given me a greater capacity for forgiveness and a reminder of the twin forces of silence and time. There is still time to make it right, I remind myself whenever I visit. There’s still time.
 Tags: historic cemeteries longform article North Broad Street North Philadelphia West Oak Lane 
 About the Author
 George deBenneville Bell, Jr. is an Emmy Award-winning writer and producer of wilderness and adventure documentaries, a multiple-time public company CEO of technology and software companies, and is currently Senior Partner at Archer Capital Group.

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: Fairmount Park Welcome Center
author: Alan Jaffe and Bryan Mckinney
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Fairmount Park Welcome Center 
 Location: 1501 John F. Kennedy Boulevard
 Architect: Harbeson, Hough, Livingston & Larson
 Built: 1960
 Like a flying saucer from a 1950s science fiction film, the circular building originally commissioned as the Philadelphia Hospitality Center landed on the southwest corner of the public square across from City Hall in 1960, 16 years before Robert Indiana’s sculpture inspired the name LOVE Park. Designed by the firm Harbeson, Hough, Livingston & Larson–former students of Ben Franklin Parkway designer Paul Cret –the $300,000 midcentury modern visitors center offered 360-degree views of the heart of Center City through floor-to-ceiling windows and a wrap-around terrace under a projecting cornice.
 The building served as the Fairmount Park Welcome Center for more than 50 years until a dramatic park redesign began in 2016. The underused structure was threatened with demolition , but a “Save the Saucer” campaign led by the Young Friends of the Preservation Alliance helped rescue it. The City spent $5.6 million in 2021 to renovate the building, and a restaurant tenant was onboard until COVID-19 dashed those hopes.
 Vacant for a decade, the building was utilized this year for a public arts project celebrating Philadelphia’s immigrant roots, and the Department of Parks and Recreation is again seeking proposals for this modernist survivor. Until a visionary entrepreneur or organization realizes its potential, the City needs to show the building some LOVE by adding it to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places .
 Tags: Fairmount Park Welcome Center Love Park Midcentury Modern modernism Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Unlisted Philadelphia

title: Places Saved: Summer 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Summer 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. 
 The former Trinity Reformed Church at 3601-07 N. Broad Street was built in 1912. It will reopen as a community impact and medical center in 2026. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Reverend Leon Sullivan Community Impact Center 
 Location : 3601-07 N. Broad Street
 Built : 1912
 In February, a groundbreaking ceremony marked the start of construction on the Reverend Leon H. Sullivan Community Impact Center , a transformative project revitalizing North Philadelphia’s Nicetown-Tioga community. The center will be housed in the historic Zion Annex, originally Trinity Reformed Church, a Gothic Revival structure designed by Carl P. Berger in 1912. When the congregation relocated in 1969, Zion Baptist Church and its pastor, Reverend Leon Sullivan , acquired the stone masonry and stained-glass building, renaming it the Zion Educational Annex and transforming it into a hub for education, social services, and job training.
 A towering figure in the civil rights movement, Reverend Sullivan was a champion for Black economic empowerment and social justice. As the longtime pastor of Zion Baptist Church, he spearheaded initiatives like the Opportunities Industrialization Center (OIC), which provides job training to marginalized communities. The annex reflected his mission, hosting after-school programs, flea markets, career training, and cultural events. Structural issues forced the annex to close in 2014. The once-vibrant building has since suffered water damage, vandalism, and theft.
 Now, thanks to a public-private partnership that has secured more than $18 million, the 27,000-square-foot building will once again serve the community. Slated for completion in 2026, the revitalized building will feature a community arts center, café, and bookstore along with the Department of Family and Community Medicine at Temple University, continuing Reverend Sullivan’s legacy of empowerment and opportunity.
 Carriage Car Lofts at 4100-12 Haverford Avenue. Built in 1876. Revived with reuse in 2025. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Carriage Car Lofts 
 Location : 4100-12 Haverford Avenue
 Built : 1876
 The West Philadelphia Passenger Railway Company (WPPRC) trolley car barn in Haverford North played a crucial role in the city’s streetcar industry, transforming West Philadelphia into a thriving streetcar suburb. The car barn served as an assembly and repair building at the western reaches of the line. Despite its utilitarian function, the building features ornate late-Victorian detailing, blending Queen Anne and Neo-Grec influences. Constructed entirely of red brick, its primary and side elevations are distinguished by polychromatic, patterned brickwork and decorative limestone belt courses.
 The building ceased operations as a car barn in the 1920s and was then used as a garage, car wash, and storage. It symbolizes the technological and social advancements of late 19th-century Philadelphia as the last remaining structure of the once-extensive WPPRC complex. The building is listed on both the National Register and Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 After decades of neglect, structural deterioration, and vandalism, the car barn underwent a comprehensive historic tax credit rehabilitation project, transforming it into a mixed-use development known as Carriage Car Lofts. The project included the addition of two new interior floors, creating distinctive loft-style residences and dynamic commercial spaces on the ground floor. The developer, MM Partners , retained the original brickwork, industrial features, and historic roofline, ensuring the building remained a cornerstone of West Philadelphia’s identity. The car barn now serves as both a testament to Philadelphia’s transit history and a blueprint for future preservation efforts.
 Tags: adaptive resuse African-American history Leon Sullivan MM Partners Nicetown North Philadelphia Places Saved 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Love Park's "Flying Saucer" Lands on the Local Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Philadelphia Hospitality Center, 1962. | Photo: Lawrence Williams, courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 At its meeting on October 10, the Philadelphia Historical Commission added four new properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, including an iconic, midcentury modern landmark in Center City.
 The Philadelphia Hospitality Center (aka the "flying saucer") at 1501 John F Kennedy Boulevard has been a distinctive feature of Love Park for over 60 years. It was designed in 1959 in the International Style by architect Roy F. Larson, a founding principal of Harbeson, Hough, Livingston & Larson . He greatly influenced modern architecture in Philadelphia during the period of urban renewal, especially in Center City, under Mayor Richardson Dilworth. Although vacant for many years and labelled as “endangered” by both the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia (the nominator) and Preservation Pennsylvania in 2014 and 2015, the City-owned structure underwent major renovations in 2021 and appears ready for a new use.
 Two churches added to the local register were nominated by their owners. The first, Providence Baptist Church of Germantown at 87-91 East Haines Street , was designed by architect Maurice Rosenthal in the Gothic Revival style using Wissahickon schist. Originally a nomadic congregation, the historically Black community financed, planned, and constructed the church building over a period of four years.
 The former Presbyterian Church of the Evangel at 1800 Tasker Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The second church, at 1800 Tasker Street in Point Breeze, is owned by Dane Jensen who has plans to repurpose the building. It was designed in the Gothic Revival style by Theophilus P. Chandler, an important Philadelphia architect in the late 19th century, with later modifications by Duhring, Okie & Ziegler, another notable local firm. It has been a visual anchor in the neighborhood since its construction in 1886 as the Presbyterian Church of the Evangel and later the home of the Second Nazareth Missionary Church.
 In February 2025, Jensen received a zoning permit “for partial demolition of an existing structure; for erection of the third-floor addition, chimney, and stair tower enclosure in an existing structure.” He has stated a desire to repurpose it as a community gathering place, although it is currently zoned RSA-5, residential single family attached.
 The former Tacony Savings Fund Safe Deposit Title & Trust Company at 4900 Longshore Avenue was also added to the Philadelphia Register. Architect John Ord designed the building with a mixture of Romanesque and Italianate details, characteristic of Victorian bank design in the late 19th century. Built in 1893, it was a significant financial institution in the development of Tacony, having been operated by two sons of Henry Disston who, with his Disston Saw Works, developed the neighborhood into a sort of company town.
 The item that occupied much of the meeting was a proposed amendment to 2018’s Ridge Avenue Roxborough Thematic Historic District , which includes 186 historic buildings along Ridge Avenue between the Wissahickon Creek and Northwestern Avenue. The nominator, the Ridge Park Civic Association, requested the addition of 14 more properties scattered between 6600 and 8113 Ridge Avenue that had not been included in the original thematic district.
 A 200-year-old home at 6649 Ridge Avenue was razed prior to a demolition moratorium bill introduced by Councilperson Curtis Jones in 2017. A mid-rise condominium complex was built in its place. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The nominators expressed their concern that historic properties not included in the historic district were at risk of demolition and replacement by large multifamily and commercial units. Emphasizing that they were not against this type of development, but rather felt it could be done without removing the historic buildings. They gave examples of developments that had restored historic buildings and constructed multifamily units behind them and contrasted them with large developments that had been built on the sites of demolished historic buildings, such as the 200-year-old house formerly at 6649 Ridge Avenue.
 Two property owners contested their inclusion, at 6807 Ridge Avenue and 7615 and 7617 Ridge Avenue, one claiming his buildings were not constructed during the period of significance of 1681-1908 and the other disputing the history of his parcel as contained in the nomination.
 After much deliberation, the Historical Commission voted to add all the proposed properties except the one at 6807 Ridge Avenue.
 A 6th nomination was not approved, although with a caveat. The Conchy-Leech Tenant House at 5831 Yocum Street in Kingsessing was nominated as an example of the formerly rural character of Darby Road, now called Woodland Avenue. A two-and-one-half story frame building constructed around 1805, it had been extensively altered between March 2023 and March 2024 without receiving permits from the Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I). While the Historical Commission felt the building still maintained much of its original integrity beneath the additions and siding, and therefore was worthy of designation, it declined to do so at this time owing to L&I’s concerns about the unpermitted alterations, which were likely to be pursued.
 Tags: Fairmount Park Welcome Center historic churches Historical Commission Meeting Report Midcentury Modern modernism Philadelphia Historical Commission 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: When a Philadelphia Hostel Provided Refuge for Victims of Internment Camps
author: Zachary Matusheski
bodyText:
Philadelphia has earned its moniker as the "City of Brotherly Love" at key moments in national history. The establishment of a hostel for recently imprisoned Japanese Americans during World War II was one such moment. Current efforts to establish a historical marker for the now-demolished Philadelphia Hostel at 3228 Chestnut Street, spearheaded by Robert Buscher, Connor Nakamura, and the University City Historical Society, has brought renewed attention to this important part of the city's history as a place of refuge.
 Rows of desert living quarters at the War Relocation Camp in Poston, Arizona. | Photo courtesy of the National Science Foundation
 After the Pearl Harbor attacks, President Franklin D. Roosevelt ordered the removal of 120,000 Japanese Americans from their homes on the West Coast to prison camps inland. This dark moment in U.S. history violated Japanese Americans’ right to due process, stripped many families of wealth, and caused great hardship. Some in Philadelphia supported the move. In a two-article run, celebrated Philadelphia Inquirer reporter Ivan Peterman mocked Japanese Americans and referred to them as “transplanted Orientals” unable to become loyal Americans. The Evening Bulletin agreed, noting the forced removal was the product of a “natural, and in many cases, justified prejudice.”
 However, others in the Philadelphia region disagreed with the policy. Driven by a commitment to justice and pacificism, the region’s small, but influential community of Quakers stepped up to help. Philadelphian Quakers, like civil rights activist Henry Patterson, joined the federal agency, the War Relocation Authority (WRA), to shape the policy from the inside. Another group, the Philadelphia-based American Friends Service Committee (AFSC), provided food and other forms of aid. City residents outside of the Quaker community also dissented. In an interview, Buscher, a lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania (Penn), shared that city residents resisted the imprisonment of Japanese Americans they knew personally. According to Buscher, Edward G. Budd , a wartime contractor constructing anti-tank rockets and other wartime supplies, put his large war contracts at risk when he advocated on behalf of one of his employees, Penn graduate Yosuke Watanbe Nakano. Other city residents tried to protect their Japanese American friends as well.
 A pamphlet from the 1940s advocating for the creation of a place in Philadelphia to resettle Japanese Americans recently imprisoned by the federal government. | Image courtesy of the University City Historical Society
 Part of the resistance to displacement of Japanese Americans included finding ways to get them out of the camps. In May 1942, the AFSC convinced the federal government to approve the establishment of the National Japanese American Student Relocation Council. This organization, based in Philadelphia, helped Japanese American students leave the camps to go to universities. Swarthmore, Bryn Mawr, and other local universities provided a place for displaced Japanese American students. This move transformed lives. In a private letter to his parents, George Inouye wrote that the opportunities afforded at Swarthmore and the friends he made there convinced him of “a God who watches us and takes care of us.” Other Japanese Americans had positive experiences. Many, including George’s brother William, made Philadelphia their home after the war.
 The successful integration of Japanese Americans on college campuses supported the argument for a large-scale effort to vet and let them resettle around the country. Breaking up Japanese American neighborhoods and dispersing Japanese Americans were goals for Roosevelt and his administration, who looked at the East Coast and Midwest, where there were smaller groups of the population, as places to push Japanese Americans toward. To this end, the WRA opened an office in Philadelphia in July 1943 with Henry Patterson at the head.
 This map, taken from promotional materials for the hostel, demonstrates the emphasis organizers placed on Philadelphia’s strengths as a transportation hub. | Image courtesy of Special Collections, Swarthmore College Libraries
 Philadelphians wasted no time in launching a plan to help ease Japanese Americans into the community. They decided to establish a modest hostel for individuals that were newly released from the camps. On August 16, 1943, members of the Women’s International League for Peace and Freedom, The Philadelphia Federation of Churches, the Catholic community, the Jewish community, civil rights activists, and others met at Patterson’s office to organize. The group designated artist Henry Lee Willet, owner of a stained glass studio, to serve as chair. It also resolved to be careful of “too much advanced publicity” because the group anticipated resistance from some in the city.
 Willet, Patterson, and their allies were right to be concerned. A few days after their meeting, a congressional committee attacked the WRA. A protest at the Tule Lake prison camp in November 1943 led the Philadelphia Inquirer to criticize the WRA for “namby pamby tactics” and argued that the agency should be replaced by the Army. Distrust of Japanese Americans continued into 1944.
 Philadelphia Hostel at 3228 Chestnut Street circa 1940s. | Photo courtesy of the University City Historical Society
 This, along with wartime housing shortages, delayed the project. In one February 1944 letter, Mildred Scott Olmsted, a Delaware County-based peace activist and Quaker, wrote that the group lost multiple chances to sign a lease for reasons including that “neighbors objected to any kind of boarding house coming to the neighborhood, but particularly one that would bring in Japanese Americans.” In time, the effort to establish a hostel’s fortunes would improve, and the groups supporting the hostel signed a lease for 3228 Chestnut Street. Organizers hoped that this location’s proximity to both 30th Street Station and the Baltimore–Ohio Railroad would ease Japanese American integration into the city and region. With a location selected, Women’s International League leader Katherine Arnett began organizing the work required to furnish and open the hostel. As a leading peace activist in the city, an alum of Bryn Mawr College, and a member of one of the families who helped found the Philadelphia Orchestra, Arnett had connections to the city’s faith communities and other sources of volunteers. Thanks to her and other’s efforts, the hostel opened in April 1944.
 Members of the Dewey Wright Quintette of Philadelphia sing for the residents of the hostel in July 1944. | Photo courtesy of The Bancroft Library, University of California-Berkeley
 African American support for the hostel, then located in a predominantly Black neighborhood, eased the path for many Japanese American arrivals. African American Pastor William Stevenson, an alum of West Philadelphia High School, pledged support and provided an invitation for Japanese Americans to worship with his congregation in the welcoming materials for those arriving at the hostel. Stevenson was quoted in a pamphlet, “We understand well the difficulty one encounters when confronted by race prejudice.” Penn lecturer Buscher noted many others in the African American community near the hostel understood that the decision to imprison Japanese Americans “had to do with racism in the context of the institutional decisions of the United States government." In the spirit of fellowship, an African American choir visited the hostel. It received favorable coverage in the Philadelphia Tribune in September 1944.
 The Inouye family rests on the steps of the Philadelphia Hostel. Saburo and Michiyo Inouye are standing with their daughter, Miyoko. William and George Inouye are seated. William stayed in Philadelphia after World War II, serving as a full professor of surgery in the Penn School of Medicine. A faculty award is named in his honor at Penn today. | Photo courtesy of The Bancroft Library, University of California-Berkeley
 A key staffing choice also helped the hostel thrive. Early on the hostel hired Inouye’s parents, Saburo and Michiyo. The Inouye family had lived in Sacramento for more than nine years when they were forcibly removed from their home and put into prison camps. In an interview, Penn student Nakamura characterized Saburo and Michiyo’s role in the Philadelphia hostel as “house parents” or comforting family figures. Saburo and Michiyo later became permanent residents of Philadelphia, celebrated years after the war not only for their service to the Japanese American community, but also for the help they gave to many college students and others in West Philadelphia.
 Recent Japanese American arrivals walk through Fairmont Park in August 1944. Pictured in the front are Toshio Ino and Virginia Yanagisako. In the back are Lucy Yoshioka and Jack Fujiki. Jack Fujiki organized social events at the hostel to welcome new arrivals. After the war, he lived in Mount Ephraim, New Jersey and worked at Philadelphia’s Farm Journal. | Photo courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 Those who came through the hostel or received help from the Inouye family provided the best evidence of why the hostel mattered. Grayce Uyehara, later a resident of South Jersey, recalled that coming to the Philadelphia Hostel marked “a turn in the direction of my life” because it was during that experience that she got involved in supporting the Japanese American community. Uyehara would go on to be an important leader in the movement for the government to compensate and apologize to those Japanese Americans the government displaced during World War II. Herb Horikawa, a young child during the war, recalled that when his family moved to Philadelphia, they “met and became friends of virtually all members of the [Japanese American] community here,” including the Inouye family at the hostel. This sense of community helped the Horikawa family find a home in the Philadelphia region.
 A flyer advertising the Philadelphia Hostel. Date unknown. | Image courtesy of the University City Historical Society
 In the end, more than 1,100 Japanese Americans came through the hostel. Resettlement increased the Philadelphia region’s population of Japanese Americans to a few thousand from less than 300 before World War II. In the years after the war, Willet successfully convinced Arnett and others to provide a loan to the Inouye family to help them buy property to continue to run the hostel. They later forgave some of this loan. Redevelopment of West Philadelphia led to the tearing down of the old hostel building. The effort to put a marker at the hostel’s old address would, if approved, be a reminder of a moment when people in Philadelphia came together to help persecuted and displaced Americans in need.
 Tags: Asian American history Immigrants Japanese Americans West Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Zachary Matusheski is a historian born and raised in the Philadelphia region. He earned his PhD in American history from Brandeis University. Matusheski's writing on the intersections of U.S. political and military history has been published by Marine Corps History, Ohio Valley History, and other venues.

title: Plan to Auction Historic Home and Andrew Wyeth Studio Riles Chadds Ford
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
Painter's Folly at 1421 Baltimore Pike in Chadds Ford. | Photo: Edward Worteck
 In a bucolic stretch of countryside along the Delaware and Chester County borders–once the site of the Battle of Brandywine during the American Revolution–sits a 170-year-old home whose moniker is finally catching up to it: Painter’s Folly.
 In a bizarre accumulation of coincidences, that name now has three connotations. The first was bestowed critically by neighbors upon the 1857 construction of the robust, three-story Italianate home, by farmer Samuel Painter in Chadds Ford, for its lack of cohesion with the modest Quaker community of the time.
 The second came at the turn of the 20th century, when the property helped birth an artistic movement that made it dear to famous American painters such as Howard Pyle and Andrew Wyeth.
 The third act has seen the name come full circle again: a home in limbo, still beloved by artists, but viewed as a financial albatross by the current leaders of Chadds Ford Township, which purchased the property with open space funds in 2018. In recent months, the township’s Board of Supervisors has telegraphed their intent to sell Painter’s Folly at public auction sometime in the not-too-distant future, an idea that, even with planned facade and landscape protections, is opposed by some preservationists and historians.
 Inside the historic home. | Photo: Edward Worteck
 The dynamics of this debate simmering about 20 miles southwest of Philadelphia will ring familiar to proponents of historical preservation in the city proper. On one hand, township officials say they are responsible owners who have done the best they can, but that they have been unable to find outside help and simply can no longer afford the upkeep. On the other are those who believe financial or political expediency is getting in the way of the best possible outcome for a historic property. “Their transparency is misleading,” said Emma Leuschner, a member of the Heritage Commission of Delaware County, of the township’s efforts to publicly make their case for the auction.
 A Landscape for Painters 
 Most of the indisputable facts of Painter’s Folly, listed on the National Register of Historic Places, lie in the past. It was originally constructed by Painter, who was not an artist, but a prosperous Quaker farmer with a taste for architecture beyond his denomination’s social norms, according to a history compiled by the Painter’s Folly Preservation Alliance (PFPA), a group advocating against the township’s current plans. Having already been disowned by his Quaker meeting for other reasons prior to his construction of the home, Painter apparently only leaned in further to his ostracism. The home has 16 rooms and is adorned both inside, with “high, molded plaster ceilings and carved woodwork,” and out, featuring a “towering cupola, sprawling piazzas, and distinctive green shutters,” according to PFPA.
 Samuel Painter lived there only about a decade before selling to an attorney named Joseph Turner, whose wife Eliza Sproat Turner was a published author, women’s club founder, suffragette, and abolitionist. In line with her obvious passion for civic improvement, she turned the country home into a summertime destination for disadvantaged children from Philadelphia. Her work as a suffragette led her to a relationship with the Drexel Institute, employer of artist Howard Pyle. By 1898, Joseph and Eliza had officially leased Painter’s Folly to Pyle, who also happened to be the nephew of Samuel Painter. The artist then used it as a launching point for his Brandywine School of Art.
 Pyle, a Wilmington native enamored with the countryside of Chadds Ford, began a competitive program among top Drexel art students to come to Painter’s Folly for an immersive summer experience. “Applicants were required to study with Pyle for two years before the summer course. Pyle accepted many women into his program, which likely pleased suffragette Eliza L. Sproat Turner when he began renting her property,” PFPA’s historical account states.
 The Nation Makers , 1902, by Howard Pyle. | Image courtesy of The Brandywine Museum of Art
 Among the many students accepted include Newell Convers “NC” Wyeth, who would later go on to become a famous artist and illustrator of Scribner’s fame. He is also father of Andrew Wyeth and the grandfather of Jamie Wyeth, both renowned 20th century painters. The arrangement with Drexel and Painter’s Folly lasted just a few years before Pyle left to launch his Howard Pyle School of Art, later the Brandywine School, nearby.
 However, the seeds of an influential American artistic moment had been sown at Painter’s Folly, Leuschner explained. Pyle and his students would model for each other and went so far as to dress up in colonial garb. Pyle, obsessed with the American Revolution, in 1902 used the arrangement to paint The Nation Makers, one of his most famous works and a depiction of the Battle of Brandywine. This focus on American history and landscapes, along with an emphasis on illustration and commercial success, defined the Brandywine School. “All of his students were learning to immediately sell their work to publishing houses and magazines. All of those things really made the Brandywine School of Art unique,” Leuschner said.
 Soon after Pyle’s departure, the home would be sold again, passing through the hands of several prominent families before a 1975 purchase by George and Helen Sipala. The couple were real estate professionals and had no inclination to use the property for artistic purposes until 1989 when they found a man on their property sketching the house in the middle of a snowstorm. It was none other than Andrew Wyeth, then later in his career, but still appreciative of the buildings and landscapes of his native Chadds Ford. The encounter sparked a 20-year relationship between the couple and Wyeth in which he regularly used Painter’s Folly’s cupola for painting and its many rooms for socializing. In 1991, a photo for the cover story of National Geographic captured Wyeth climbing out of the cupola.
 Marriage , 1993, by Andrew Wyeth features George and Helen Sipala. The couple were friends of the artist and former owners of Painter's Folly. Helen still lives on the property. | Image courtesy of The Brandywine Museum of Art
 “Wyeth often retreated to Painter’s Folly to escape the press, prying neighbors, jealous models, and even his own family,” PFPA notes in its collected history. “Wyeth left materials, studies, and paintings in Painter’s Folly and used a bedroom on the third floor as a private studio. Soon enough, others from Wyeth’s world, such as model Helga Testorf, figured out where he was stowed away and would burst into the house to search for him.”
 At Painter’s Folly, Wyeth painted several dozen works until his death in 2009 including the notable work Marriage , which depicts the Sipalas asleep in their bed, as well as several others he made of the home and its cupola, including the appropriately titled Painter’s Folly . Helen Sipala, who served as model for some of his works and is now 91, still lives in an auxiliary structure on the property. The home and land itself, however, are owned by Chadds Ford Township.
 Chadds Ford’s White Whale? 
 Those at the center of Chadds Ford’s 2018 purchase of Painter’s Folly for $625,000 are no longer in charge. The township’s three supervisors and manager have turned over since, some several times. Generally, the belief is that former Supervisor Chairman Frank Murphy was instrumental in purchasing the property for $625,000 after learning about its history. Township officials said the Sipalas had put it up for sale and the price had dropped several times, and Murphy worried it could fall victim to a developer’s bulldozer. “This [Chadds Ford] is possibly the most historic seven miles around,” news site Chadds Ford Live quoted Murph y saying in 2018 as he pushed for more historical preservation efforts.
 Current officials say their read was that the purchase of the property was a well-intended move, but that it lacked a formal plan and ultimately didn’t pan out. “The house was purchased with all good intent, but is a white whale. It’s a dinosaur,” claimed Thomas Bradley, a member of the township’s planning commission and retired real estate developer and general contractor. “None of this was well thought out.”
 Exactly how much the township has spent on the property, beyond the initial $625,000, is somewhat unclear. In an interview, Township Supervisor Vice Chair Kathleen Goodier and manager Lacey Faber declined to offer a total, instead referring to financial documents made available on the township’s website. Those appear to show operating and maintenance losses of about $214,000 in the six years since 2019, most of which occurred in 2023 when repairs to the roof and masonry cost nearly $100,000.
 Widow’s Walk Study , 1990, by Andrew Wyeth gives an exterior view of the cupola and roofline of Painter's Folly. | Image courtesy of Wyeth Foundation for American Art
 That squares with the assessment of Bradley, who said the township has spent a total of about $800,000 on the property. Bradley believes Painter’s Folly had several hundred thousand dollars of deferred maintenance when the township purchased it and that mounting costs are too much to afford. “The roof was leaking, the windows were leaking, the paint was peeling, the plaster was wet and coming apart,” Bradley explained. “It’s failing because we didn’t get all of the problems, and now there are new problems.”
 Goodier and Faber further defended the township’s stewardship and decision-making. Faber said the township obtained a $20,000 grant and chipped in another $12,000 perform a feasibility study for best uses of the property in 2021, which described the property as being in “very good condition.” Nevertheless, the study found that its sloped landscape and problematic entrance off a busy Baltimore Pike “ruled out all retail and business uses.” Instead, the report recommended sustaining uses as a bed and breakfast or artists studios, the latter of which it noted had “the strongest community support.”
 Indeed, the township moved forward with what Faber described as a pilot program in 2023 to rent artist studios. That year the township took in about $26,000 in rent between the studios and the carriage house in which Helen Sipala lives, a figure greatly exceeded by the expensive operations and maintenance costs of that year. In January 2024, the township held a public meeting to discuss expanding the program. “The conversation centered around restructuring the program to expand studio space, offer rotating exhibits, host classes and youth programming, and expand public access and tours—all to better serve the community and increase engagement with the historic site,” the township’s records indicate.
 Renfield , 1999, by Andrew Wyeth shows the interior of the home's cupola. | Image courtesy of Wyeth Foundation for American Art
 It was determined that in order to expand, upgrades would need to be made to meet ADA compliance. The township was awarded a $100,000 Keystone Historic Preservation Grant to make the upgrades, but officials said the funding would only be unlocked if the township contributes $217,000 from its own coffers and makes a 10-year ownership commitment. After Murphy’s passing last year, Faber said, Goodier and other supervisors decided to perform a comprehensive review. “We said, ‘We need to stop and reevaluate."
 In August 2024, the township held another public meeting on the topic. While it received a diversity of feedback, “about half of the residents” thought the township should put protections on the building and sell it, explained Farber. An online survey conducted later garnered feedback that the township should instead try to find a preservation partner. Officials maintain they have made numerous such overtures to outside organizations including the Brandywine Conservancy and Museum of Art, the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, and Delaware County to seek financial support or advice, or even entertain offers of a sale, but that no dynamic-shifting support has materialized.
 While speaking with the North American Land Trust, Faber said the parties originally talked about the prospects of a sale. Yet, that evolved into an idea for the township to instead place conservation easements to maintain the exterior of the property and forbid subdivisions, which North American Land Trust would maintain in perpetuity even after a sale of Painter’s Folly. Faber said the township is currently pursuing that option and applying for grants to pay for the development of the easements. “[Former chairman Murphy] did not want to see development or anything like that,” on the property, said Goodier. “And I think these easements are the answer to that. This property was purchased to be preserved. Let’s do it. Once these easements are in place, this will never be townhouses.”
 Painter’s Fury 
 Opponents of a public auction are painting a different picture. Edward Worteck, a retired professor of art history at Yale and Goucher College who lives in Chadds Ford, said he believes the township has never actually come up with a “coherent plan” during its ownership of the building. He cites a lack of “basic historical practices,” giving an example of himself and other preservationists taking it upon themselves to fundraise to record an oral history from Helen Sipala . He is also “puzzled” why the Brandywine Conservancy hasn’t been more involved, and says he recently notified the township of a grant opportunity at the Wyeth Foundation for American Art. “It doesn’t seem like the township has pursued anything” for the grant, said Worteck. “The lack of interest in local institutions is surprising.”
 Worteck had previously been appointed by the township’s supervisors as liaison for Painter’s Folly, granting him access to the property and ability to photograph its interior. But he says he was recently told he was no longer permitted to do so, and has been unable to determine whether he still officially holds the title.
 He also doubts the level of hardship to the township. Both he and Leuschner said they believe a reluctance to invest more in the property is driven primarily from the township’s general political conservatism. Worteck also believes the township has mischaracterized the level of support for its plan thus far. Instead, he said, it was his impression at a July public meeting on the topic that most were concerned about the preservation of Painter’s Folly than selling it. He also believes the artists’ studio plan was abandoned prematurely after one resident complained about possible mold in the house.
 Painter's Folly in the snow evokes Andrew Wyeth's painterly winter visions of Chadds Ford. | Photo: Edward Worteck
 Leuschner also thinks the township threw in the towel too early. “Outside of the preservation plan study from 2022 there really hasn’t been any documented efforts to try and look into other solutions or possible uses.” She believes that, while the township has met to some degree with various organizations, it has not been forthcoming about the content of the discussions.
 She said the township first floated the idea of a public auction in January 2025, prior to discussing it publicly or “calling for help” from preservations or other outside groups Materials from the township’s August 2024 meeting show some audience members expressing support for a sale, but do not indicate whether officials first raised or supported the possibility. Leuschner said she would actually welcome the township divesting itself of the property, but not in the manner it is planning. The conservation easements being discussed would only protect the exterior of the building, and Leuschner thinks it should remain open to the public. She fears a private owner will come in, completely renovate the interior, and keep its doors closed. “This building is so significant to Chadds Ford’s identity and would directly bring in tourism dollars. It adds to the vibrancy of the arts tourism in the area,” said Leuschner. “If you have a public auction you run the risk of it being closed forever. In my opinion, it belongs to the public. It belongs to the creatives.”
 Opponents of a public auction have created a Change.org petition which has garnered several hundred signatures. The primary ask: “Encourage Chadds Ford Township to share a sense of a timeline, request that ample time be given to explore preservation partnerships, and provide regular, two-way updates to the community.”
 Township officials said they do not believe any public auction will be imminent and that they expect the process of obtaining funds for and developing easements will take at least many months. They haven’t closed the door on another arrangement as well, even as the property progresses toward an auction. “We’re still meeting and looking into potential partnerships,” explained Faber.
 Tags: Delaware County Philadelphia artists suburbs 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Recalling and Celebrating the Often Hidden Stories
author: Bob Skiba
bodyText:
Inside the stacks of the John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives at William Way LGBT Community Center. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 From the moment I walked into the LGBT archives at the William Way Center, I was in love. I pored over everything–the newspapers, the political buttons, the posters, the T-shirts, and even all of the corporate records. What I found most compelling, however, were the small, personal collections that documented the lives of everyday LGBTQ+ folks in the Philadelphia area. They showed me how, even when America was the most unwelcoming toward anyone who was outside the norm, when gay people were portrayed as “deviants who lived miserable lives in the shadows,” queer Philadelphians were creating loving relationships, strong, supportive communities, and claiming urban spaces as their own. For historians, uncovering and celebrating these stories and these spaces means dealing with unique problems.
 Queer history is often intentionally ignored, destroyed, denied, or hidden, even by queer people themselves in their effort to remain hidden and safe. Gay spaces can be invisible to the general public. In 1962, Philadelphia Magazine was the first mainstream publication in the country to publish an article about its city’s “gay ghetto” (the term “Gayborhood” wouldn’t appear for another 30 years), with its bars, hangouts, and cruising spots. The article took the form of an exposé called “The Furtive Fraternity,” its title emphasizing the fact that LGBTQ+ Philadelphians inhabited a hidden parallel urban landscape that was mostly invisible to those not in the know. Queer people learned about these spaces by word of mouth, from friends or from printed gay guidebooks that began appearing as early as the late 1950s. These guides would tell the traveler or local who was welcome where–much of the city’s “gay ghetto” was seen as a white male enclave that excluded women and people of color.
 Top: Standing room only. The crowd at Woody's celebrating the gay bar's 3rd anniversary in 1983. Bottom: Dancing the night away at Mamzelle's, a lesbian nightclub located on the second and third floor above The Bike Stop on Quince Street. | Photos courtesy of the John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives at William Way LGBT Community Center
 The Philadelphia Magazine article was groundbreaking for the Quaker City. Unlike New York tabloids, which loved to print lurid stories about “debauchery and perversion,” genteel Philadelphians tolerated such goings-on here. They just didn’t talk about them. An exception was the sporadic queer content that appeared in Black newspapers like the Philadelphia Tribune , something the Philadelphia Inquirer wouldn’t touch. This hyper-discretion in the Philadelphia press means a lot of reading between the lines and decoding for LGBTQ+ researchers and historians.
 Often overshadowed by its bigger and louder sibling, New York, Philadelphia’s queer accomplishments shine.
 Every year on the Fourth of July, from 1965 to 1969, Philadelphia hosted the Annual Reminders in front of Independence Hall. These were the first planned annual demonstrations for gay rights in the country. In the early 1970s, activist groups began pushing for a city gay rights amendment, which would finally pass in 1982 and be amended to include gender identity in 2002. The 1970s also saw the proliferation of LGBTQ+ activist groups. In 1976, the award-winning Philadelphia Gay News began publishing, and the Gay Community Center of Philadelphia opened its doors on Kater Street off of South Street.
 A jean jacket donated to the John J. Wilcox, Jr. Archives displays buttons from The Blue Parrot, The Bike Stop, Westbury Bar, The Post, and other local LGBT bars. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Gay-owned bars and businesses proliferated–along Spruce and Locust Streets from Rittenhouse Square to 11th Street, along South Street on both sides of Broad Street, in Old City, in Queen Village, and with a string of Black gay bars along Filbert and Arch Streets where the Pennsylvania Convention Center sits now.
 In the 1980s, the community pulled together to fight the AIDS epidemic. Grassroots activists formed dozens of organizations to fight a threat that the federal, state, and local governments were doing nothing about. In 1988, the Philadelphia chapter of ACT UP was formed to protest that lack of governmental response.
 In 2002, the city saw its first Trans Health Conference and, in 2011, its first Trans March. In 2007, the City put up 36 rainbow street signs in the Gayborhood to mark it as a place of diversity and inclusivity.
 Today, when many gayborhoods across the country seem to be disappearing, Philadelphia’s Gayborhood is thriving thanks to the unflagging political action of its LGBT community.
 Tags: Archives Gayborhood LGBTQIA+ History 
 About the Author
 Bob Skiba is the curator of collections at the John J. Wilcox, Jr. LGBT Archives at the William Way Center and gives fun, engaging tours of the Gayborhood. He has co-authored two books on Philadelphia history and teaches a class about Philadelphia’s queer culture and community at Jefferson University. He has given lectures on Philadelphia queer history for universities, corporations, libraries and museums all around the region. Bob loves to cook and has just taught himself how to crochet.

title: Cultural Institutions Mobilize as Trump's Executive Order Deadline Approaches
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
The monument The President’s House: Freedom and Slavery in the Making of a New Nation on Independence Mall was dedicated in 2010. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 A touch of irony pervaded the September 3 gathering of the Avenging The Ancestors Coalition (ATAC) at the Zion Baptist Church. It came from the Trump Administration's executive order, " Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History," that is attempting to erase African American history under the pretense that difficult truths about the Black experience in the United States are actually dismantling “Western foundations” and “interrogating institutional racism.” The order is something that the church's founder, Reverend Leon Sullivan , and many other civil rights activists in attendance that evening have worked against and assumed that this chapter of their lives had concluded.
 On Wednesday, September 17, the National Park Service (NPS) and Independence National Historical Park (INHP) are scheduled to remove any and all signs and imagery involving slavery that, according to a mid-August review, have been flagged as “inappropriate.” According to a recent article published by the Philadelphia Inquirer , not only will items from the President's House be removed, but also items from the Benjamin Franklin Museum, Edgar Allen Poe House, The Second Bank of the United States, and other unnamed sites.
 In response, ATAC board members Roz McPherson, who is the former project director of the President’s House, and attorney Michael Coard led a discussion with community members, historians, tour guides, politicians, and representatives from various organizations, such as Visit Philly, Preservation Alliance of Greater Philadelphia, Asian Americans United (AAU), and Mother Africa, speaking on behalf of Mumia Abu-Jamal, were in attendance to offer suggestions and support.
 Feedback given during the discussions ranged from affirmations to frustrations with proposed digital displays and signage with QR codes in proximity to Park Service sites explaining to visitors that they can “find the truth here.” One of the more poignant points raised came from Pennsylvania State Senator Sharif Street, who recounted that under his father, former Mayor John F. Street who was in office during the reconstruction of the President's House, a condition of this reconstruction was that the “City only agreed to it if it would include the history of those enslaved individuals.” Senator Street also recounted that former Mayor Street refused to move forward without that stipulation and “that at the minimum constitutes an agreement between the City and the federal government constituting a contract.” He went on to state “ removing it [mentioning of the enslaved] violates allowing the President's House to exist.”
 Although the NPS serves as part of the visitors’ experience, it is not the totality of it. Reaching out to various museums, sites, and interpreters who also work within the Olde City, I wanted to learn how each group will respond to the impending changes. Off the record, various NPS rangers stated that the content covered in their individual tours depends on their discretion. Some explained that they will continue discussing all facets of American history until they are let go or mandated to do otherwise. Dr. Ashley Jordan, president and CEO of the African American Museum in Philadelphia (AAMP) stated “Part of what makes America great is its history, and the experiences and contributions of Black Americans are an important part of that history. Our hope is that the AAMP can lead thoughtful discussion about how we preserve and support the vital role that history plays in the great American story.”
 The Trump Administration has ordered National Park Service staff at Independence National Park to remove this interpretive sign display about slavery in the United States by September 17. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Dr. R. Scott Stephenson, president and CEO of the Museum of the American Revolution released the following statement: “On the eve of America’s 250th birthday, it is important to remember that the American Revolution is an ongoing experiment in liberty, equality, and self-government. A mature and confident nation like the United States should be able to celebrate the optimism and transformative power of our ideals and achievements while also acknowledging the ways that we have sometimes failed to embody our values as a people. The most powerful story of America that we can share is one that is self-reflective, self-aware, and self-confident.”
 The 1838 Black Metropolis Project that currently serves as “Pennsylvania’s second official extension of the NPS Reconstruction Network” and a training tool for independent and corporate tour guides stated, “We are used to being in a space and verbally recreating the people and the space with words—as is our oral history tradition. If the panels are there or not, we will keep speaking life into the space and keep speaking the truth of our past and our ancestors. Energy never dies.” Robert Branch, a present-day interpreter of Bishop Richard Allen, said on his own behalf that the removal of the mentions of slavery and those enslaved at the President's House would be “a great distortion of the history” and that he has never encountered any visitors who felt devisive about any of the content marked for removal.
 At this time, ATAC is in discussions with NPS officials as part of a process to return the earmarked items if they are removed. “We still have a relationship with them,” McPherson relayed to the audience and informed everyone that their feedback will be expressed as part of their communications. She also advised that “Many in the park service are being forced to make recommendations,” and reminded everyone where the appropriate finger should be pointed. Fellow ATAC board member and attorney Michael Coard went on to add that there is a legal aspect that they are pressing, but they are currently not at liberty to give details.
 The Trump Administration's executive order states, “This revisionist movement seeks to undermine the remarkable achievements of the United States by casting its founding principles and historical milestones in a negative light.” Regardless of the statements and actions taken, the impending deadline has motivated various tour companies and parties to prepare by sharing more stories of the enslaved and the many periods of local history that involve historically disenfranchised groups. The Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides (APT) has begun offering complimentary tours to City Council and Pennsylvania state representatives to highlight “the true, complicated history” of the city. A teach-in is also planned for September 20 around Independence National Park to inform visitors about unrepresented history. The (In)Visible Architects of Freedom Walking Tour and related research are still available to educators and NPS staff on the agency's website.
 Tags: African-American history Donald J. Trump Independence Mall National Park Service The President’s House 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: A New Exhibition Pays Homage to the Spirit of 1776
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
On October 18 the Museum of the American Revolution (MoAR) will open its most ambitious and timely exhibition to date. The Declaration’s Journey will feature manuscripts and printed documents that have drawn inspiration from the Declaration of Independence within the United States and internationally. Coinciding with the 250th anniversary of the signing of the document, the event seeks to bring back to the forefront the questions regarding “people’s natural right to equality,” “inalienable rights,” and other promises inherent within the document when it was published in July 1776.
 A stone engraving of the Declaration of Independence created in 1823. | Image courtesy of the National Archives
 Commencing with the American Revolution, the Declaration’s path of influence will be traced from Philadelphia to highlight the individuals who questioned and challenged what independence means. In line with events within the United States will be others that feature Haiti, Mexico, Korea, Czechoslovakia, India, and similar countries that were influenced by the Declaration.
 According to Matthew Skic, director of collections and exhibitions for the museum, the exhibition has been five years in the making. On hand will be docents, interpreters, and virtual tours to assist participants who cannot visit in person. WHYY will partner with the MoAR for a 10-episode video series, commencing in the fall, that will feature insights from museum staff, historians, and curators.
 Among the 100 featured individuals, documents, and items will be the story of Jewish Philadelphia merchant Jonas Phillips who, in 1776, sent a letter in Judeo-German and the John Dunlap Broadside print of the Declaration to Amsterdam. Both the letter and Dunlap Broadside will be featured along with notes from Phillips regarding the promises made by the Declaration.
 Many other notable items will be featured, and on loan from various institutions, including Thomas Jefferson’s Windsor chair, which is believed to have been used by him while writing drafts of the Declaration of Independence, a rare surviving broadside printed in January 1777 by Mary Katharine Goddard of Baltimore, the only woman who operated a newspaper under her own name in the United States, and a petition signed and sent to Congress in 1799 by Absalom Jones, Richard Allen, and 71 other free Black Philadelphia men who condemned the slave trade and hoped to abolish the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793.
 A civil rights petition signed by 71 free Black Philadelphians, including Absalom Jones, and Richard Allen, sent to Congress in 1799. | Image courtesy of the National Archives 
 Other figures highlighted in the exhibition include Harvey Milk, Eleanor Roosevelt, Abraham Lincoln, Marquis de Lafayette, Jean-Jacques Dessalines, Philip Jackson, Tomas Masaryk, Vincente Guerrero, and many more.
 Present-day politics of book bans and the skewing of history and facts will be at the forefront of many visitors’ minds while viewing the exhibits. According to Skic, the intention behind the production is meant to be encouraging and an inspiration to recommit to the nation’s ideals of equality and to foster a “deeper examination of the United States’s relationship with its founding document.”
 Kenneth Morris Jr., a descendent of both Frederick Douglass and Booker T. Washington of the Frederick Douglass Family Initiative, said The Declaration’s Journey "will help more Americans understand the diverse people and viewpoints that contributed to our founding and to where we are today as a nation.” When asked why Douglass’s words still resonate so long after his passing, Morris elaborated, “We’re still dealing with the same struggles and challenges that he faced.”
 Skic hopes that a lot of the content will be new to visitors and that they ask questions. “This is a document that has been challenged by many people over generations. It has been fought over, contested, celebrated, and that will continue as long as we believe in the United States.”
 The Declaration’s Journey opens on October 18 and will be on view until January 3. See the Museum of the American Revolution's website for more details: https://www.amrevmuseum.org/exhibits/the-declaration-s-journey 
 Tags: American Revolution art exhibition Museum of the American Revolution

 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: A New Book Views Philadelphia From Above
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
"View of Philadelphia City Hall." | Photo: Daniel Moreno
 Several years ago, Trope Publishing, a Chicago-based company, began a series of coffee table books called “Above & Across,” with each volume devoted to aerial photography of a particular city. After producing editions for Chicago, London, San Francisco, and Atlanta, they have now released one of Philadelphia. 
 11 photographers captured the city from above via helicopters, observation decks, and drones. One of them, Philadelphia resident Luke Cuccurullo, works exclusively with the latter.
