Although he’s been a professional photographer for a long time, he only began using a drone less than a year ago. “The aerial view, with its different angle, has been really interesting,” he said. “Philadelphia is pretty flexible when it comes to what you can do with drones. In places like New York City, there are a lot more restricted areas.”
 "Above Independence Hall and Independence National Historical Park." | Photo: Brett Gross
 Drones are programmed to avoid entering restricted areas, such as airports and military installations. Those for recreational use must weigh less than 250 grams, slightly less than nine ounces. Drones for commercial use can be larger, but require a license from the Federal Aviation Administration to operate.
 The book’s Chicago-based editors did their homework, assembling a list of the iconic images they wanted and locating Philadelphia-based photographers by trawling Instagram. “I asked them, ‘what do you not have?’ They sent a checklist of about 20 sites and gave me a week to shoot them,” Cuccurullo recalled. “It was tough, a week of bad weather, but I got it done.”
 "Looking down on Lincoln Financial Field." | Photo: Luke Cuccurullo
 How did they get Philly to look so good? Admittedly, most of the images are iconic: famous historic sites, modern skyscrapers, sports stadiums. Cuccurullo explained that a lot of it has to do with the time when the photographs are taken. “You mostly try to shoot during the ‘golden hour.’ Around an hour before sunset or an hour after sunrise. 15 minutes or so on either side is ideal.” The array of photographs in the book also captures how attractive Philadelphia’s four seasons can be.
 As Executive Director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia and native son, Paul Steinke often extols the city’s walkability and streetscapes. Nevertheless, he appreciates this different vantage point and contributed a foreword to the book. “These different views from the sky show Philadelphia is in best light.”
 In this book series Philadelphia is number five. However, the city actually holds a historic first in aerial photography. In July 1893, witnessed by a crowd of thousands in Fairmount Park, photographer William Nicholson Jennings and three others attempted a hot air balloon excursion to Atlantic City. The trip was not completed, but it earned Philadelphia the distinction of being the first city in the world to be photographed from a balloon. The images were exhibited in Europe and the United States and were used in a series of popular postcards.
 "View of the Merchant Exchange Building and Walnut Street." | Photo: Brett Gross
 One of the challenges of obtaining pristine photographs of iconic Philadelphia sites is having the subject in the clear from any distractions or extraneous objects, a difficult situation with some of our most beloved tourist destinations. “My shot of the Art Museum steps with the Eagles banners after they won the Superbowl was tough to get,” Cuccurullo admitted. “I had to wait a long time for people to leave and then still had to edit a few out of the final image.”
 A particularly intriguing shot is of Eastern State Penitentiary, where architect John Haviland’s design, with the cellblocks radiating out from a central hub like the spokes of a wheel, is in full view. “I probably wouldn’t have shot Eastern State Penitentiary if they hadn’t asked me to do it,” Cuccurullo noted. “Now, it’s one of my favorite contributions to the book.”
 "View of the Victory Building." | Photo: Trevor Adams
 Another of his favorites is the aerial view of the Packer Avenue Marine Terminal along the Delaware River. “Driving over the Walt Whitman Bridge, I always like to look at all the colors of the shipping containers.”
 A few of the descriptions are indicative of out-of-town editors. That aerial shot of the Packer Avenue Marine Terminal is simply labelled a “look down on the Delaware River.” Another photo of the tall ship Moshulu, which contains a restaurant, is called “a restaurant on the Delaware River,” and one of Kelly Drive near the Ellen Philips Samuel Memorial sculpture garden is labeled “Lemon Hill Park.” Yet, they still allow us to claim as our own a shot of the battleship New Jersey on the Delaware River, in Camden, and Subaru Park, where the Philadelphia Union play, in Chester.
 "View of the Philadelphia Skyline." | Photo: Nathaniel Bayona
 On the other hand, the photographic record in the book serves, and will continue to serve, as a historical marker as Philadelphia’s built landscape changes. A stunning shot of the USS United States provides a memory of the ship that had been anchored along the Delaware River for so long.
 With an abundance of grand historic buildings, sleek modern skyscrapers, and big sports stadiums, the book belies our image of a city of neighborhoods, images of which are in short supply here. Despite that, Above & Across Philadelphia is a breathtaking collection of stunning photographs, which will appeal to visitors and potential visitors, as well as Philadelphians who appreciate the architecture of our iconic sites.
 Tags: aerial photography book review 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: A New Book Explores the Origins and Outcomes of Exclusive Urban Planning
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
In Race, Real Estate, and Education: Inventing Gentrification in Philadelphia, 1960-2020 , published by Temple University Press, author Edward M. Epstein reveals the policies and practices that have shaped Philadelphia in general, and West Philadelphia in particular, over the past 60 years. Epstein focuses on the role of the University of Pennsylvania, with which he has long been affiliated, in controlling its surroundings. He is especially interested in initiatives related to K-12 education that have been used to attract primarily white, affluent, university-connected families while displacing economically challenged Black residents.
 Six Degrees of Edmund Bacon 
 Any book seeking to describe the development of post-World War II Philadelphia has to include quite a bit about city planner Edmund Bacon and his vision for a post-industrial urban utopia. Epstein compares Bacon’s plans for Society Hill, where a colonial-era neighborhood was mostly preserved and then gentrified, with what happened in the newly named University City area in which the Black Bottom neighborhood , a place Bacon deemed “a band of blight,” was razed.
 These topics have been covered elsewhere, but Epstein sheds fresh light. For example, he documents how the myth of the “urban pioneer,” the young, upwardly mobile, white idealists with a passion for city living and old houses, was intentionally constructed, first by the Old Philadelphia Development Corporation in Society Hill and later by the West Philadelphia Corporation (WPC). The book includes images from Elaborations on Living in West Philadelphia , a 1963 WPC booklet that showcases the aspirational lifestyle of young families earnestly rehabbing Victorian homes.
 The WPC, a consortium representing the interests of West Philadelphia’s universities and hospitals, was founded in 1959 and became the prime mover in shaping University City and other Penn-adjacent neighborhoods. The University of Pennsylvania was the main funder of the WPC, and Gaylord Harnwell, the president of Penn, was also the organization’s board president. According to Epstein, “there was no wall between Penn elites and Philadelphia’s city planning apparatus.” Penn also had strong connections to the City’s Redevelopment Authority and to individuals who controlled federal urban renewal funds. As a consequence, Epstein indicates that by the end of Harnwell’s administration in 1970, Penn’s physical plant had tripled in size.
 The Role of Schools 
 The WPC vision of creating stable neighborhoods inhabited largely by university-affiliated individuals and families depended on the accessibility of the types of schools deemed desirable by this mainly white, highly educated cohort. Thus, the development of progressive, integrated, neighborhood public schools became the Holy Grail of the Universities-Related Program (URP), the education arm of the WPC.
 Epstein documents the lofty plans and disappointing failures of a variety of initiatives. The Lea Learning Lab, an experimental school within a school at the Henry C. Lea Elementary School, was designed by educated white parents. The program featured mixed age groupings, open classrooms, and other educational trends that were in vogue in the late 1960s and early 1970s. Although the Learning Lab attracted a number of affluent white families, it ultimately functioned as part of a racial tracking system. The broader Lea population saw little benefit, and most white families eventually chose other, usually private, schooling options.
 As also described in Laura Wolf Power’s University City: History, Race, and Community in the Era of the Innovation District , University City High School was conceived as a science and math magnet school with an innovative curriculum that would be enhanced by access to Penn and Drexel. Resistance by the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers and insufficient support from the universities doomed the project from the beginning.
 Lessons Learned 
 By the 1990s, federally subsidized urban renewal had given way to neo-liberal, market-based development strategies. It was in this economic environment that plans for yet another contender to become a progressive, integrated, neighborhood public school were launched. Under the leadership of Judith Rodin, the Sadie Tanner Mossell Alexander University of Pennsylvania Partnership School, dubbed Penn Alexander, was created with a recognition of past mistakes. The School District of Philadelphia was brought in as a full partner, and Penn’s financial and academic commitment to the school were firmly established.
 Epstein, like many other educated, progressive, white Philadelphians, moved his family to a home that would enable his children to attend the new school. When Penn Alexander opened in 2001, eligible students were drawn from a carefully mapped catchment area that was both racially and economically diverse. The school succeeded in achieving the decades-long goal of keeping university-affiliated families in the neighborhoods directly west of Penn. It also led to skyrocketing home and rental prices that eventually pushed less well-off, mostly Black families out of the Penn Alexander catchment zone. As the school’s academic reputation soared, its socioeconomic diversity and percentage of Black students nosedived.
 Conclusions 
 One can walk away from either Epstein’s book or this review with the conclusion that the end result of six decades of urban policy and educational social engineering in West Philadelphia has been gentrification. Yet, that oversimplification is not the full message of Race, Real Estate, and Education . Epstein presents a nuanced, textured history that is enriched by personal accounts, informative maps, and wonderful, vivid illustrations. In clear prose and with thorough documentation, he fleshes out the many ways that good intentions, naivete, and idealism have combined with greed, concentrated power, and racism to shape West Philadelphia.
 In writing my master’s thesis in 2001, I came across Philadelphia: Neighborhoods, Division, and Conflict in a Postindustrial City (Temple University Press, 1991). Written by a group of Temple professors, the book explains how the interaction of economics, politics, urban policy, housing, and neighborhood demographics shaped Philadelphia from the 1940s through the 1980s. I have come back to that book repeatedly for its clarity in connecting seemingly disparate dots. I notice many other local authors, including Epstein, refer to it as well. I view Race, Real Estate, and Education as a successor to that fine work in that it also creates a framework of understanding that explains where we are and how we got here.
 Edward M. Epstein will discuss his new book, Race, Real Estate, and Education: Inventing Gentrification in Philadelphia, 1960-2020 at The Rotunda, 4014 Walnut Street, on October 28 at 5 p.m. See details here: https://www.therotunda.org/event/book-talk-and-discussion-on-race-real-estate-and-education-inventing-gentrification-in-philadelphia-1960-2020 
 Charles Library at Temple University will host a book talk with Epstein on November 19 at 2 p.m. More information here: https://library.temple.edu/events/2063 
 Tags: Black Bottom book review Urban Renewal 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Strengthening "National Trust" Through Preservation and Public Lands Advocacy
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
As the United States faces a list of crisis-level challenges–among them income inequality, environmental degradation, and a dearth of affordable housing–the National Trust for Historic Preservation wants to be acknowledged as a player in the solutions. “When people hear ‘historic preservation,’ they often think it means ‘keep things just as they are,’ instead of all the things that preservation creates—experiences, jobs, revitalized neighborhoods,” claimed president and CEO Carol Quillen. “Preservation can be a tool to address national environmental, economic and social challenges. We want to shift the narrative from what stays the same to what can be.”
 The National Trust was created by Congressional charter in 1949. It is a privately funded nonprofit organization which supports historic preservation through education, granting, and advocacy. Its granting programs include the African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund (AACHAF) and the National Fund for Sacred Places .
 Powel House at 244 S. 3rd Street in Society Hill is included in the National Trust's Distinctive Destinations program. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The organization has different ways to interact with sites. Here in Philadelphia, it owns and operate Cliveden, the historic estate in Germantown, while Joe Frazier’s gym on North Broad Street receives technical assistance through the National Trust’s AACHAF. Two other local sites that it has added to its Distinctive Destinations program illustrate the National Trust's wide reaching interest in America’s history: Powel House, the 18th century home of early Philadelphia mayor Samuel Powel and his wife Elizabeth, both of whom had significant influence on the founders of the nation, and Philadelphia’s Magic Gardens, which houses many of the exuberant 20th century mosaics of Isaiah Zagar.
 Since 1988, the National Trust has published an annual list, America's 11 Most Endangered Historic Places . “The selection is based on the urgency of the threat and the viability of the plan the community has to save it,” Quillen explained. Local sites on the list have included Philadelphia’s Chinatown in 2023, Azikiwe-Nkrumah Hall at Lincoln University in 2016, Joe Frazier’s Gym in 2012, the Boyd Theater in 2008 (demolished in 2015), Valley Forge National Historical Park in 2000, and Independence National Historical Park in 1991 and 1992.
 Joe Frazier’s Boxing Gym was placed on the National Register and the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2013. Advocates working to preserve the local Black landmark at 2917 N. Broad Street receive technical assistance from the National Trust's African American Cultural Heritage Action Fund. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 Like most preservation advocates, staff of the National Trust envision new uses for historic buildings. “How should we talk to non-preservationists about preservation? We have to talk about what it creates,” Quillen said. In particular, she sees the nation’s supply of historic buildings as an economical asset to address housing needs. “The first question should be, ‘How do we use what we have instead of tearing it down?’ We’re working hard at the National Trust with our partners to create the right policy, with incentives to think about converting vacant or underused buildings into affordable housing. When you consider the cost of demolition and disposal, the greenest building is the one that already exists.”
 However, she acknowledges that preservation can sometimes exacerbate gentrification. “The key is working with the local community to have their input on development. Preservation is about giving people who live in a community a say in what happens there.” That can be seen as rather optimistic, to suggest residents have much power with zoning codes and private developers.
 Willow Street Steam Generation Plant’s new owner worked to have the building placed on the National Register in 2024. The long-abandoned site was added to the list in January 2025. The developer will partially finance the residential conversion of Willow Steam with federal historic tax credits. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 A popular and effective incentive has been the Federal Historic Tax Credit, administered by the National Park Service and the Internal Revenue Service and applauded by preservationists. The program provides a 20 percent federal tax credit on qualified expenses incurred in the rehabilitation of historic commercial or income-producing properties. Since its creation in 1976, it has assisted in the rehabilitation of more than 50,000 historic properties nationwide. “Both federal and state historic tax programs are crucial. It’s important for how it creates jobs and leverages private investment. It’s often what makes the deal possible,” Quillen noted. “There is a lot of support in Congress for the Historic Tax Credit and possibly strengthening it."
 As a tax credit, it doesn’t involve the outlay of federal dollars, so it is not on the Trump administration’s list of programs to be reduced or eliminated. However, the Historic Preservation Fund, which supports several grant programs as well as the federally-mandated preservation offices in every state and territory, is slated to have its $158M annual appropriation removed from next year’s federal budget. 
 Quillen is earnest and upbeat when discussing the economic and social benefits of historic preservation. When the conversation shifts to their other advocacy focuses, like history and public lands, she is more circumspect, in the face of an administration that often has a hostile view of them.
 The National Trust owns and operates the Cliveden, the historic 18th century estate at 6401 Germantown Avenue. | Photo courtesy of Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress
 Perhaps the work of the National Trust that is most fraught today is their advocacy of the country’s historical record, with the current administration pushing hard to elevate its narrative of U.S. history and to eliminate other stories, events, and figures that might contradict it.
 A historian with a Ph.D. from Princeton University, Quillen affirmed the importance of acknowledging history, but when we spoke over the summer she avoided commenting on recent actions such as the removal of Native names or the restoration of the Confederate names of military bases. In early September, however, the National Trust’s Cliveden joined 43 other Philadelphia institutions—including Hidden City– in a letter to Doug Burgum, the Secretary of the Interior , expressing opposition to the President Trump's Executive Order to remove “descriptions, depictions, or other content that inappropriately disparage Americans past or living (including persons living in colonial times), and instead focus on the greatness of the achievements and progress of the American people or, with respect to natural features, the beauty, abundance, and grandeur of the American landscape,” and which specifically cited the President’s House in Independence National Historical Park. 
 “We’re committed to telling the full American story. Even places that hold the most complicated stories, we need to confront them, not erase them,” Quillen stated. “We want to honor the people who fought for what we have—freedom, equality. All Americans deserve to see their history in their built environment. Preservation can create a sense of belonging for all of our people.”
 Tags: African-American history Donald J. Trump historic tax credit interview National Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Hiding in Plain Sight: Bird Studio
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
Bird Studio's artistry is everywhere . The Four Seasons, The American Academy of Music, Comcast, and not just in Philly. So how come you've never heard of it?
 Maybe because Bird Studio is hidden away in a maze of factories in East Falls, rather than maintaining a glitzy showroom at the Design Center. Or because, prior to 2018, the studio was a pop-up, renting temporary space until it found a permanent home at 2800 Roberts Avenue. More to the point, Bird Studio's founder Zachary Bird is too busy orchestrating a tsunami of projects to take credit for his many accomplishments. His work often goes unsigned.
 Bird, 55, credits his career choice to genetics. "I'm a fourth generation artist," he said. "My dad, Bill Bird, was a graphic designer. So was my mother. My grandfather, William Bird, was one of Philly’s leading scratch board illustrators. My great grandfather was an artist as well." Bird also lays claim to a French-American great great uncle, Victor Nehlig, (1830-1909) who inserted himself into the historical painting, Pocahontas Saving John Smith (1870).
 However, genetics alone will not open doors. So Bird, like generations of aspiring artists, enrolled at the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts (PAFA). "It was clear to me and my parents by the end of my second year that PAFA was not in any practical way preparing students for commercial success," he said. "Tuition was high, and I needed an income." His situation is one that all art students face whether they complete their degree or not. Unless they major in architecture, graphic design, or education, the majority of fine arts grads work in fields unrelated to their major. In retrospect, Bird caught on to something decades ago that PAFA only recently realized. In January 2024, PAFA announced that it was eliminating its degree programs due to "rising costs" and "dwindling enrollment," ultimately closing in August 2025. The University of the Arts folded last May.
 Zach Bird creating gilded signage for Friday, Saturday, Sunday restaurant. | Photo courtesy of Bird Studio
 Bird was lucky. He discovered that his skills were in demand. A friend told him that The Palm Restaurant was looking for artists to paint faces on the walls of their restaurants in Philadelphia and elsewhere. It wasn't the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel, but it was a paying gig. "The caricatures were a ‘Who's Who' in politics, business, and the arts," Bird said. He continued working with the Palm Management Corporation for 20 years.
 "Back in the mid 1990s, Palm Restaurant was expanding," said Bird. "I felt the historic brand was diminished by the newness of their sites and suggested that they would be far more interesting if they reflected the grungy feel of their original NYC restaurants. Management agreed, so I began experimenting with aging and scenic techniques." The result helped catapult The Palm into an international franchise. It also expanded Bird's expertise and client base.
 While many of his peers viewed computers as the antithesis of art, Bird was an early adapter. In 1992, as an art director in advertising studios in Atlanta, he embraced the latest photo editing technology: Adobe Photoshop. "I found it could be implemented as a powerful digital art rendering tool," he said. "I was invited by Adobe, with other design professionals, to assist their tech team in developing rendering capabilities of the Photoshop platform."
 When 9/11 happened there was global market uncertainty, and many businesses pulled back, including The Palm. "They stopped ordering murals. But catastrophe equals opportunity," said Bird. "I started doing conservation work for them. I was hired to perform delicate cleaning and conservation of 100 year-old original cartoon illustrations that adorned the walls of the Palm on Manhattan's Upper East side." Once again, Bird's ability to continually adapt his skills to new materials and processes allowed him to expand his creative services.
 Jacintha Kruc, a conservator at Bird Studio, works on a mural. | Photo courtesy of Bird Studio
 Bird worked closely with conservation experts from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the University of Delaware's Art Conservation Department to complete the project. During the process he discovered that his knowledge of art materials and techniques applied to this new kind of work in exciting ways.
 "Zach Bird is incredibly talented," said Marie Bender, a local painter whose career path mirrors Bird's. After graduating with a degree in fine arts from Tyler School of Art and Architecture, Bender worked as a calligrapher, sign painter, decorative plasterer, muralist, and substitute teacher. Whatever it took to pay off student loans and keep a roof over her head until she was able to focus entirely on painting. "I understand why Zach does all these things and does them all so well," Bender said. "He loves to work with his hands."
 This is Bird's comfort zone: constantly upgrading his skills and taking on new challenges. When Provenance, a new restaurant in Society Hill, presented a design by Stokes Architecture that involved a space entirely made up of curved edges, Bird Studio was able to create a system of overlapping insulation that resulted in a seamless smooth plaster space in the restaurant that lowered the noise level.
 "Everything we do is site and client specific," said Bird. That includes murals at Suraya, faux marble columns at the Bellevue, and 24 carat gold vintage signage in the window of Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
 Zachary Bird and Nicolo Gentile discuss a work in progress. | Photo courtesy of Bird Studio
 If you walk into Bird Studio, a no-frills space that could pass for a shipping container, you might find a conservator from PAFA perched on a scaffold meticulously painting a 19-by-40-foot mural. "We trowel a layer of plaster on the muslin first, then paint the mural on the plaster. That makes it easy to make changes later, just by using sand paper," said Bird. The technique creates the appearance of a faded relic that was excavated from an archaeological site.
 Which is what restaurateur Stephen Starr wanted for his new Italian restaurant, Borromini. "I found a Pompeii fresco in an art book and worked with New York architectural designer Ian McFeely of Paisley Design on a mural that would work well in the space,” said Bird.
 Bird doesn't work alone. "It's a team effort," said Mari Elaine Lamp, Bird's studio manager who holds a 2017 MFA degree from PAFA. Nicolo Gentile, the studio's
project manager, has an MFA in sculpture from Tyler School of Art and Architecture and is an internationally exhibited artist. Ultimately, the side gig that Bird embarked upon 30 years ago to pay off art school debt has grown into a full service design business that has generated employment for many other Philly artists over the years.
 Tags: artist studios East Falls murals 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: Op-Ed: Save the Wave and Reanimate the Robinson Building for FIFA 2026
author: Jason Lempieri
bodyText:
The Robinson Building's wavy facade at 1020 Market Street in 2015. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Philadelphia will be in the spotlight in 2026. The city is hosting numerous large-scale sporting events, including the MLB All-Star game, March Madness games, and, most noteably, six international soccer matches for FIFA’s World Cup. The world’s eyes will be on Philadelphia, and every aspect of our culture, history, and built environment will be on display, faults and all.
 Recently, HBSE, a sports and entertainment venue management company, which owns most of the 1000 block of Market Street, declared that a portion of the block will be demolished on Tuesday, November 11. This is the same Sixers/Comcast billionaire group that played the City with its arena proposal across the street. Located within that block, and slated for demolition, is the Robinson Building at 1020 Market Street. It was designed in 1947 by Victor Gruen, who is most famous for being the first architect to propose and design shopping malls. The “cresting wave,” as the Inquirer’s architecture critic Inga Saffron referred to the iconic building in her 2015 article , is the last standing edifice Gruen developed for the chain of Robinson department stores. For 78 years, the near monolithic building has stood out on Market Street. For many of those years it has been in a state of neglect. 
 Vacancy and deferred maintenance is often the preferred method of demolition for urban developers. Significant buildings are permitted to decay, and the public becomes anesthetized to the structures’ slow death. In this way, people are lulled into thinking that there is no value in retaining an historical edifice. Philadelphia has a long history of this approach. Yet, the Robinson Building, with its unique form, scale, history, and site, still has much to offer.
 The Robinson Building's sign illuminated at night circa 1950s. | Photo: Prints and Photographs, Library of Congress
 The real jewel of the Robinson Building is its north-facing facade. Behind decades of grime and soot lies a mosaic of tiny, variegated purple tiles that once served as an undulating backdrop to a neon cursive sign for Robinson's. The electric night lighting was something to behold: American commercial architecture at its 1940s best. The mosaic turns outward at the cornice and then curves inward above the ground level, floating the whole remarkable, multi-story, monolithic composition above what was glass casework. Although the ground-floor casework is long gone, the impressive character of the monumental facade is still extant. A power-washed Robinson Building exterior could be a powerful main attraction on Market Street.
 Preservationists have fought, and are likely continuing to fight, to preserve the Robinson Building. They may balk at a facadectomy, which is the process whereby the exterior of a building is retained and the remainder of the building is removed. It is accomplished by installing a reinforcing structure behind and then integrating the facade into a new complex, thereby retaining a semblance of historical value, while preserving contemporary development opportunities beyond. It is a careful operation, and detailed integration is the key to its success. One of Philadelphia's finest examples of a facadectomy is the Penn Mutual Life Insurance building at 510 Walnut Street. There, the Egyptian Revival marble exterior designed in 1836 by noted Philadelphia architect John Haviland was preserved and masterfully showcased by the elegant 1970s modernist tower designed by Mitchell/Giurgola. Facadectomies have their critics because they are often seen as a poor last resort of preservation as suggested in Starr Herr-Cardillo’s 2018 op-ed for Hidden City . However, applying this method to the Robinson Building would result in a thick, well-reinforced poche akin to the heft of a castle wall and a dramatic entry to the site.
 It is unclear what HBSE will do with a partially razed Market Street block, which is concerning given Philadelphia developers’ history of tearing down buildings only to have the lots sit empty for decades. One plan that the company recently floated is to use the empty space to host pop-up events in connection with the 2026 sporting festivities. Here is where the Robinson Building and its distinctive facade can be an asset: as a monumental gateway to a FIFA World Cup Fan Zone.
 The Robinson Building's facade reimagined as a gateway to Market Street's FIFA World Cup Fan Zone. | Rendering: Jason Lempieri
 The World Cup is a spectacle like no other. People travel from all over the world to support their teams. Some can afford the tickets to attend the games, but many others come to party with their compatriots, tour local sites, and watch the games at designated outdoor venues. The City plans to host a Fan Fest at Fairmount Park's Lemon Hill, but that site is challenging to reach using public transportation and unusable in the inevitable summer thunderstorm.
 Once the other buildings slated for demolition in the 1000 block of Market Street are cleared, the Robinson Building facade, festooned with temporary FIFA-related regalia, would stand tall as a gateway to a Center City Fan Zone. Like I.M. Pei's Louvre pyramid in Paris, but in Moderne style, the facade and its supporting structure would serve as a memorable entry to the site. Along with fencing displaying the flags of the competing countries, the Robinson facade would help to secure the site, which has ample space for concessions, bathrooms, games, and a multi-story game screen to show the soccer matches. This plan fits perfectly with the sports-oriented mission of its developers and could be a “mea culpa” for the Sixers arena fiasco that consumed so much of our legislators’ and citizens’ time. Once again, the Sixers would have the chance to preserve an historic asset rather than destroying a significant element of our city’s cultural history.
 After the games, the storied Robinson Building facade can be a portal for a new, large-scale development, and Philadelphia can shake off its history of demolition by neglect in favor of preservation by reincarnation.
 Tags: adaptive resuse Market East Midcentury Modern modernism Robinson Department Store Victor Gruen 
 About the Author
 Jason Lempieri has a Bachelor of Architecture degree from Pratt Institute and a Master’s degree in Industrial Design from the University of the Arts. A devout urbanist and city resident, he is the principal and owner of the design firm RethinkTANK and the brand Tombino. Lempieri has taught architecture and design at local universities including the University of Pennsylvania and the former Philadelphia University and UArts. He is a long-time contributor of architectural criticism to Hidden City.

title: Temple Contemporary Takes Viewers Inside the Pyramid Club
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
Matthew Jordan-Miller Kenyatta is ideally suited to his job. He is the curator and director of exhibitions and public programs at Temple Contemporary, an exhibition space and public programming site located on the first floor of Tyler School of Art and Architecture on Temple University's Main Campus. The 3,400-square-foot gallery is open to the public as befits its mission to “serve as a beacon for art, architecture, and community imagination.”
 Kenyatta, who goes by "Dr. Matt," has a unique and impressive resume that includes a B.A. in urban studies with an African/African American studies minor from Stanford, a M.A. in city planning from M.I.T, and a Ph.D. in urban planning from USC. Fortunately for Philadelphia, he came to the Stuart Weitzman School of Design at that University of Pennsylvania in 2018 where he served in a variety of roles and became a member of the Philadelphia Arts Commission.
 Pyramid Club: 1937-2035 is currently on view at Temple Contemporary until December 19. | Photos courtesy of Temple Contemporary, Tyler School of Art and Architecture, Temple University
 In taking on his new position at Temple Contemporary in 2024, Dr. Matt brought with him his multidisciplinary academic background, his expertise in urban placemaking, and his passion for Afro-futurism, a movement based on the interplay between Black history, culture, and science fiction. Think Wakanda in the Black Panther movie series. In making the decision to leave Penn for Temple, it didn’t hurt that he would be significantly reducing his commute time. Dr. Matt and his husband Malcolm Kenyatta, North Central Philadelphia’s representative in the Pennsylvania General Assembly, call the neighborhood home.
 The first exhibition at Temple Contemporary under Dr. Matt's leadership, Pyramid Club: 1937-2035 , opened in September of this year. The Pyramid Club was a social club for Philadelphia’s Black elite that opened in 1937, a time of widespread segregation in the city. Initially meeting in the basement of the Christian Street YMCA, the club was founded for “the cultural civic and social advancement of Negroes in Philadelphia.” In 1940, the club moved to 1517 W. Girard Avenue where the building remains and a historical marker attests to its past glory.
 A photograph by John W. Mosley of artist Samuel J. Brown at a Pyramid Club cookout circa 1950s. | Photo courtesy of Charles L. Blockson Afro-American Collection, Temple University Libraries
 The first room of the exhibition highlights the prestigious Pyramid Club art shows that were organized by artist and curator Humbert Howard from 1941 to 1957. These juried exhibitions displayed the works of artists both white and Black and helped catapult the careers of African American artists such as Romare Beardon, Jacob Lawrence, and Dox Thrash . The pieces on display at Temple Contemporary come from the collection of Dr. William Dodd, a dentist who has acquired numerous works from mid-20th century Black artists. Dodd spent 20 years collecting these works and used to run a gallery in Center City called Art Around.
 The middle room contains photographs by John W. Mosley , the official photographer of the Pyramid Club and a prolific chronicler of Philadelphia’s Black experience. The display was curated by Leslie Willis Lowry, an archivist with the Charles L. Blockson Afro-American Collection in collaboration with Philadelphia artist Shawn Theodore. It features images of fashionable Black people engaged in leisure pursuits as well as portraits of many of the celebrities who visited the Pyramid Club including Marian Anderson, Dizzy Gillespie, Pearl Bailey, Sidney Poitier, Langston Hughes, Duke Ellington, Eartha Kitt, and Mahalia Jackson.
 Woman With a Green Hat , 1940, by Dox Thrash and Trap Saint , 2017, by Shawn Theodore. | Photos courtesy of Temple Contemporary, Tyler School of Art and Architecture, Temple University
 The final room is dedicated to Shawn Theodore’s avant-garde photography and several of his multi-media installations. Theodore, who is represented by Paradigm Gallery + Studio, is interested in “Afromythology,” a term he coined to encapsulate his exploration of Black cultural identity and community.
 Although the exhibition is divided into three distinct spaces, there are several common threads. One is the Egyptian motifs designed by Theodore that were inspired by the décor of the Pyramid Club. Another is that each of these spaces poses different aspects of the same question about the Pyramid Club that guided the development of the exhibition, “What if Philadelphia’s legendary cultural space had never closed.” This question is crucial to Dr. Matt who sees Temple Contemporary as playing a vital role in a revival of the North Broad Street corridor as an arts and culture hub. 
 Dr. Matt’s language often reflects his numerous degrees and his visionary inclinations. He uses words like “Afroprismatic” and “speculative timeline” in casual conversation. Toward the end of our tour, however, he shared a succinct summary of the exhibition’s aims. “It is an exploration of how art can help make history a blueprint for the future.” For me, this simple explanation made all the beautiful paintings, historical photographs, and exemplars of Afromythology come together in a cohesive whole.
 Pyramid Club: 1937-2035 is on view at Temple Contemporary until December 19. See the gallery's website for more information: https://tyler.temple.edu/happening-tyler/temple-contemporary-gallery 
 A community forum will be held on Wednesday, November 12 at Temple Contemporary from 5:30 to 7:30 p.m. The event will feature living descendants of Pyramid Club members and people connected to the art exhibited at the Pyramid Club.
 Tags: African-American history art exhibition Dox Thrash Temple University 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: The Myth and Measure of the Shackamaxon Elm
author: Tim Kerner
bodyText:
The great, great, grandchild of the Great Elm Tree, propagated at Haverford College and planted in 2010. | Photo: Michael Froio
 When we think of family relationships we often visualize a tree, but when we consider a tree we seldom think of its family. One exception is the Great Elm of Shackamaxon. Its grandchildren reside at the University of Pennsylvania and Haverford College, but its great, great grandchild has returned to its ancestral roots on the Kensington Waterfront. The young tree stands as a living connection to the city’s creation and symbolizes the founder’s principles of virtue and justice, although these ideals were eventually betrayed.
 The cultural significance of the Great Elm stems from the influential representation of Philadelphia’s founding myth , Penn's Treaty with the Indians . The nine-foot panorama painted by Benjamin West in 1771 portrays the moment, 90 years earlier, when Penn and friends, just off the boat, secured land from the Lenape under the branches of the Great Elm. The composition brings two contrasting worlds together into balanced visual harmony.
 William Penn's Treaty with the Indians , Benjamin West, 1772. | Image courtesy of Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts
 At the center of the canvas, European merchants present a bolt of white cloth to Chief Tamanend who is enrobed in similar fabric. Penn frames this interaction with open arms, and a cluster of Quakers stand about in drab attire and black hats. Behind them are houses under construction, boats floating on the river, and goods being hauled ashore. The Lenape warriors have laid down their arrows and gaze at the fabric with interest. They are muscular and lightly clothed with accents of colorful feathers. Further back is a shadowy group of natives and wigwams and then, impenetrable darkness. In the foreground, a breastfeeding mother and child accentuate the peacefulness of the scene. One group has just stepped out of the deep forest, while the other has crossed the ocean with bright offerings. They meet under the Great Elm whose branches form a space of mediation and bear witness to the profound meeting.
 As a Neoclassical painter, West drew on Enlightenment philosophy and emphasized formal clarity, compositional stability, and heroic nobility. His bold innovation was to paint contemporary scenes in a classical manner, breaking from the tradition of only representing the ancient world. West’s dramatic portrayals of events in the English colonies impressed the court, and in 1772, he became the official “History Painter to the King” for George III.
 The painting was displayed in the 1772 Royal Gallery Exhibition in London and struck a resonant chord with the public. Engravers from England, Scotland, Italy, Germany, France, America, and Mexico created reproductions for distribution. Various renditions were produced over the next century and could be purchased as framed pictures, on dishes, candle screens, painted trays, window curtains, whisky glasses, and bed quilts. The Treaty Tree is present in every version, even accompanying Penn to an undefined tropical location.
 Transfer-printed plate by Thomas Goodwin, c. 1850, with William Penn under a palm tree. | Photo: Live Auctioneers
 Penn’s Treaty associates the colonization of America with virtuous intentions. As West described, “The great object I had in forming that composition was to express savages brought into harmony and peace by justice and benevolence, by not withholding from them what was their right, and giving to them what they were in want of.” His attitude reflected the typical European view of Indigenous people confronted through colonial conquest: their primitive lives would obviously benefit from contact with modern society.
 The darker side of this scene is that it portends the devastating impact the colonists would inflict on Native Americans. When Penn arrived, the Lenape inhabited New Jersey, southern New York, and eastern Pennsylvania in a loose, nonhierarchical network of tribes. Their lives revolved around the waterways, and they fished, hunted, farmed, and lived relatively free of disease. Within a century of contact with the Europeans, their numbers were decimated by exposure to smallpox, measles, and influenza. Disease, death, and colonial expansion accompanied by violence pushed the remaining Lenape westward, away from their lands and manner of living.
 Penn’s intentions were different from those who gained territory through armed confrontation and intimidation. As he wrote prior to his departure from England in a letter addressed to the Kings of the Indians in Pennsylvania , "I am very sensible of the unkindness and Injustice that hath been too much exercised toward you by the People of these Parts off the world, who have sought themselves, and to make great Advantages by you […] and caused great Grudgings and Animosities, sometimes to the shedding of blood, which have made the great God Angry. but I am not such a man, as is well known in my own Country: I have great love and regard towards you, and I desire to win and gain your Love and friendship by a kind, just and peaceable life."
 The Quaker principle of nonviolence required Penn to maintain peaceful relationships with the Native Americans. In his 1681 Concessions to the Province of Pennsylvania he wrote that disputes between the Lenape and the colonists would be resolved through discussion among six members from each society. This was a radical proposition in the history of international conflict resolution. Penn earnestly sought peace, but his colony’s expansion eventually pushed the Lenape from their homeland as much as the colonies that did not claim such love-affirming principles.
 Frontispiece to William Penn’s Own Account of the Lenape or Delaware Indians. Artwork by Fritz Eichenberg, 1937. | Image: Public Domain
 The common interpretation of West’s painting is that it represents the moment when Penn first arrived in America in October of 1682. However, before he met with the Lenape, Penn rushed about attending to affairs with other colonists. His first stop was in New Castle, in present day Delaware, where he gathered the inhabitants to assure them of their rights. Over the next month, he inspected the site of future Philadelphia, went to New York to help mediate a political dispute, visited the governor of New Jersey, attended a Friends Meeting on Long Island, and convened the first meeting of the Pennsylvania Assembly in Chester.
 The earliest Pennsylvania land treaties were arranged in the months before Penn arrived. The treaty documents include a description of the boundaries to the land that was “Bargained Sold & Delivered […] unto the Said William Penn his Heirs & Assignes forever.” The treaties also included a long list of items given to the Lenape in exchange, such as kettles, guns, coats, shirts, stockings, axes, knives, glasses, shoes, copper boxes, scissors, combs, fishhooks, needles, tobacco, rum, and beer. 
 Penn was 38 when he arrived, far younger than the portly gentleman portrayed in West’s painting, and there is no record of him meeting with the Lenape in Shackamaxon. Although Chief Tamanend has a primary role in the painting, he also was not part of the Shackamaxon land deal. Tamanend signed a treaty for land further up the river between Neshaminy and Pennypack Creeks. The arrangements for that treaty took place in the recently constructed Friends Meeting House in Philadelphia. After the conference, Tamanend and the other chiefs stayed overnight and attended worship with Penn the next day. Clearly, West intended his painting to be allegorical rather than a historical representation.
 The scene was invented, but the setting was real. The Great Elm was over 150-years-old at the time of the treaty and 250-years-old when the scene was painted. The tree was a well-known figure on the riverfront and stood in the area known to the Lenape as Shackamaxon, which has been translated as both “the place where the chiefs meet” and “the place of eels."
 Lenape villages of Shakamaxon and Coaguannock in the area of Philadelphia before Penn’s arrival, as depicted in a map by the Works Progress Administration in 1934, note the Great Elm on the waterfront at the center of the image. | Image: Public Domain
 In three years, Penn and his deputies assembled enough land through treaties to form the counties of Philadelphia, Bucks, and Chester. In 1684, Penn was compelled to return to England to support his claim over the Lower Counties (future Delaware) which was disputed by Lord Baltimore. The treaty arrangements halted shortly after Penn’s departure and did not resume until after his death in 1718.
 Pennsylvania land treaty boundaries and their dates. | Image: Wikipedia Commons
 Penn administered his colony from England for the next 15 years and expressed frustration in his many letters that his “holy experiment” was not sufficiently lucrative. In 1699, he traveled to Pennsylvania a second time, but it was just two years until legal problems again forced his return to England. These did not subside. To add to his misfortunes, Penn suffered a stroke in 1712 and was largely incapacitated until his death six years later. During much of that time, his wife, Hannah, made the proprietor’s decisions for his colony.
 After Penn’s death, Thomas, the second son from his second marriage, took over the leadership of the Pennsylvania enterprise, but only after years of legal wrangling with the offspring of Penn’s deceased, first wife. He finally arrived in Philadelphia in 1732 to great fanfare and set to work on his primary objective, which was to extract as much money as possible to pay the staggering family debt. Thomas’s conversion to Anglicanism simplified the undertaking for it liberated him from Quaker principles when dealing with the Lenape.
 Thomas had his sights set on unsold land in the Lehigh Valley, but the Lenape were not cooperating with his plans. To overcome their resistance, in 1737, he and James Logan presented a questionable draft of a 1686 treaty, which described an exchange of land that extended northwestward the distance a man could walk in a day and a half from a point in Bucks County (current Wrightstown). Historians consider the 60-mile run of the “Walking Purchase,” the subsequent northeasterly extension of the treaty’s boundaries, and the resulting 1.2-million-acre land transfer to have been an elaborate scheme of fraud which displaced the Lenape without their consent.
 The relationship between the Pennsylvania Assembly and Thomas soured over his efforts to decrease their power and increase his own. He returned to London after 10 unpleasant years and continued to administer the colony from afar. In 1757, the Assembly sent Benjamin Franklin to London to persuade the government to abandon the proprietary arrangement and place Pennsylvania under direct control of the crown. Their complaints about Thomas included the inefficiencies of his distant control, the imposition of unjust financial penalties, the vetoing of Assembly bills, and the tax-exempt status of the proprietor’s land.
 Franklin was unsuccessful, but his attempt to unseat the proprietor explains the context in which Thomas commissioned Benjamin West to paint his famous scene. The painting would serve to reinforce the family’s claim on the colony and West was the obvious choice for the job. He was born in Pennsylvania and moved to London after touring Italy to study the masters of the Renaissance. He was a founding member of the Royal Academy of Art and served as its second president. The influence of West’s depiction of Penn’s Treaty under the Great Elm endured, but the proprietorship did not. In the early 1770s, land sales in Pennsylvania were finally bringing wealth to the family, but it all came to an abrupt end when the Assembly voted to join the other 12 colonies and declare independence from England and the Penns.
 The City and Port of Philadelphia on the River Delaware from Kensington , William Birch & Son, 1810. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 Meanwhile, the Great Elm flourished. Its canopy was 150-feet in diameter, and the circumference of its trunk was 24 feet. An 1800 engraving by Thomas Birch portrays the tree at its full extent. The print served as the frontispiece of the first comprehensive visual guide to the city, William Birch & Son’s The City of Philadelphia, in the State of Pennsylvania North America . Other pages depict “the buildings, of any consequence […] and the street-scenes all accurate as they now stand,” but for the introductory image, the Birches chose the famous tree standing on Kensington’s industrial waterfront.
 Sadly, this graceful giant was violently uprooted by a storm in 1810. As reported by Poulson’s American Daily Advertiser , “During the tremendous gale of Monday night last, the Great Elm Tree at Kensington […] was torn up by the roots. The celebrated tree […] is at length prostrated to the dust!” Over the next month, the story of the tree’s demise was circulated in newspapers from Maine to South Carolina. The fallen tree attracted onlookers and souvenir hunters who harvested its wood to make chairs, picture frames, and gift boxes. Cuttings and seedlings were planted at the Pennsylvania Hospital, the University of Pennsylvania, and Haverford College. Through the tree’s mythical participation in an iconic episode of constructed memory, the relics and its living descendants were imbued with the values of peace and justice.
 Commemorative Box, “Made from the Treaty Tree, a relic of Unbroken faith of William Penn with the Indians 1682.” | Image courtesy of Haverford College
 In 1827, the Penn Society erected an obelisk, “to mark the site of the Great Elm Tree,” which was inscribed into the stone. Unfortunately, industrial activities prevented it from being placed at the tree’s original location. Changing circumstances in the surrounding lumber, coal, and marble yards forced at least one other relocation. The inappropriate conditions of the site of the famous treaty and its lost tree disturbed civic leaders. The Philadelphia Inquirer complained that “The Penn treaty grounds are a wharf property which is a scene of dirt, old carts, stray chickens, broken-down fences, [and] a shanty or two…”
 The desire to create an appropriate setting for the associated memories gathered momentum and City Council voted to place Penn Treaty Park on the city plan in 1892. They allocated $85,000 to condemn and purchase two acres of land and plans were drawn up for site improvements. On October 28, 1893, thousands crammed into the new park to watch an enactment of Penn sailing up the river to land on the banks and meet Chief Tamanend.
 Monument to the “Great Elm Tree,” Penn Treaty Park. | Photo: Michael Froio
 The timing of the park’s creation was fortuitous.It offered a compromise solution to a very large Penn problem. In 1894, City Hall was ready for the mounting of Alexander Milne Calder’s 36-foot statue of William Penn. The architectural drawings prepared 20 years earlier by John McArthur and Thomas U. Walter oriented the statue squarely north, which they considered the building’s primary facade. However, one of City Hall’s peculiar attributes is that it has four fronts, and Calder insisted the statue should face southward so it would be illuminated by the sun. If not, he wrote in a letter to the Philadelphia Times , it would, “Instead of being a graceful statue of William Penn […be] a monument to the indifference and shortsightedness of everyone in charge.”
 The City Commissioners refused Calder’s request, but devised a slight compromise. They rotated Penn one-eighth of a turn eastward to face the newly created park up the river. His gaze would forever memorialize the mythical location of Penn’s Treaty under the Great Elm. Although the summer morning sun would almost illuminate his statue, Calder was not appeased. Neither was the Philadelphia Inquirer , which declared the Commissioner’s decision to be “a farce to those who have the intelligence to understand the difference between the right and wrong way of doing a thing.” 
 City Hall Tower with William Penn looking northeast. | Photo: Tim Kerner
 The angular rotation of the founder’s figure is a source of puzzlement to city visitors. One explanation to offer is that the founder’s non-orthogonal orientation references the time of Penn’s arrival, prior to the urban grid, when the land was forested and inhabited by the Lenape. This could be compared to the diagonal streets, such as Passyunk Avenue, that are remnants of ancient Lenape pathways. Penn’s gaze toward the mythical site of his colony’s founding reflects his initial intentions and an alternate history in which peace is prioritized, treaties are maintained, and Indigenous people are respected. It is a world that remains disappointingly elusive.
 West’s painting is a powerful cultural artifact with contradictory associations. It is a memorialization of Penn’s desire to form a society guided by virtue and justness, and a powerful piece of propaganda that masks the shameful treatment of Native Americans. Although the story of the Lenape and Quakers meeting under the tree is largely fictional, the Great Elm of Shackamaxon remains a symbol of peaceful intentions. The fall of the tree in 1810 echoed the unraveling of Pennsylvania’s founding myth, but the tree’s descendants maintain the meaning associated with their ancestor. These living connections to pre-colonial times remind us how nature quietly bears witness to human values and actions, and their consequences.
 Tags: Lenape longform article Native Americans William Penn 
 About the Author
 Tim Kerner, AIA is principal of Terra Studio LLC and an adjunct professor of architecture at Temple University.

title: Can Smart Design Save a Historic Manayunk Mill From Floods and Father Time?
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
4050 Main Street in Manayunk. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 Main Street Manayunk is a place where powerful forces are colliding. There is the tension between the past and the present, with the historic mills of yesteryear and vestiges of a blue collar community more and more giving way to upscale condominiums and nightlife. Then there are the physical dangers posed by the Schuylkill River, which has long overflown its banks and flooded the district, and is expected to increasingly do so as the Earth’s changing climate brings ever heavier rainfall.
 Can smart building design help Main Street navigate this perilous transition? Jeremy Avellino, an architect and owner of Philadelphia-based firm Bright Common , is out to prove it.
 Avellino recently hosted a tour of 4050 Main Street, a 27,000-square-foot, two-story historic factory on the far eastern end of Manayunk’s commercial strip, at the intersection of Shur’s Lane. The building dates back to around 1850 and housed a variety of industrial and commercial uses over its lifespan before falling vacant over the past decade.
 The upper floor of the old mill will serve as Citylight Church's sanctury. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 Now, it is in the process of rebirth, both physically and spiritually. In 2022, Citylight Church , a growing congregation of the Christian and Missionary Alliance denomination based in Manayunk, purchased the building as its first permanently-owned location. Working with Bright Common, the church agreed to a plan that will leave the first floor of the former factory designed to intentionally flood and then quickly rebound, with primary use limited to a parking garage. The second floor will then be effectively sealed from below, designed to minimize water intrusion or other resulting damages. At the time of tour, the renovation was still under construction, but completion is anticipated later this year.
 Avellino said his firm has also designed the renovation to bring congregants in through the river side of the building to enter as opposed to the street, so that they can contemplate its place in space and time. “We wanted to bring people in procession on their way to Sunday workshop, to nature, to remember, not just to care for the Earth, but remember this place flooded,” Avellino explained.
 A Life by the Water 
 Records of the Philadelphia Historical Commission date the building at 4050 Main Street to 1850, which would place its establishment squarely in the midst of Manayunk’s first transformation from natural landscape to industrial boomtown.
 Scull and Heap’s 1750 map of “Philadelphia and Parts Adjacent” show little happening in that part of what is now Northwest Philadelphia, save for a ferry in the vicinity of present day Wissahickon Station (later referred to as Jones Ferry), and, a few miles to the northwest, the homestead of the Levering family. This rural character continued in the decades that followed, as an 1808 map depicted development along what is now Ridge Avenue, but nothing save a variety of streams and creeks closer to the river’s banks.
 Roxborough Mills on Shurs Lane is featured in Hexamer General Surveys, Volume 27 published in 1892. | Image courtesy of Greater Philadelphia GeoHistory Network
 That would change with the arrival of the Schuylkill Canal system and the Manayunk Canal in the early 1800s. Soon, numerous mills and other industrial operations began to populate along what is now Main Street, taking advantage of the new access to copious hydropower. By the mid-19th century, dozens were in operation , spinning out everything from cotton, to paper, to nails.
 The exact context of the construction of what is now 4050 Main Street is difficult to discern. The building was added to the city’s historic register in 1983 as part of the Manayunk Main Street Historic District . Yet, details about the building in the nomination are limited to a short physical description of its Italianate facade and an original name of Roxborough Mills.
 Many 19th century materials reference a Roxborough Mills location on Shurs Lane further up Manayunk’s slope, although an 1862 atlas of the city does depict structures and a steamboat landing near the present day location and lists the name of “Roxborough Mills” at a larger structure nearby at the site of the present day Manayunk Brewing Company.
 The building’s middle history is easier to track down. By the late 19th century it is clearly depicted on maps and titled the “Fidelity Machine Works.” An 1891 ad in The Philadelphia Inquirer lists a need for the services of a good pattern maker for textile machinery at the location. By 1898, a notice in the same paper announced the factory would become the new location of the Wilson Childs Wagon works, a nationally-renowned company originally founded in Philadelphia in 1829 . Historical records show the company made what would be millions in today’s dollars selling wagons and parts to the Union during the Civil War, but in the decades that followed, transitioned to a focus on Cuban and South American marketplaces.
 An advertisment for Wilson, Childs & Co. from 1883. | Image courtesy of University of South Carolina Libraries
 “The firm will make a speciality of building Cuban cane wagons and patent iron hub wheels for the South American trade,” the Inquirer notice revealed. “The first floor will be used as a machine shop and the second floor for body making.”
 In time, 20th century records revealed the factory’s use by various textile and chemical companies. In 1983, longtime-owner Gary Gevurtz purchased the building for use as a furniture store , which continued through its closure in 2018. The year prior, the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved a plan to redevelop the building and three adjacent historic homes into new residential. However, the plan never came to pass. Damaged by flooding in 2020 and 2021, the homes were demolished and the plan abandoned.
 Building an Ark 
 For some, redeveloping such a parcel would feel treacherous. For Matt Cohen, lead pastor of Citylight Church, it is exciting and feels “a little bit like purchasing a time machine.” Cohen started his congregation in Manayunk in 2011. The church currently rents space at a nearby synagogue. He said its membership is young and growing, buoyed by transplant graduates of Penn State University’s main campus, where the denomination has a previously-established church. Once his congregation raised enough to purchase its own space, they wanted to look no further than Manayunk and its immediate neighborhoods, Cohen said, and found relatively limited options. The old factory at 4050 Main Street ended up checking most of the boxes and the church purchased it in late 2022.
 A rendering showing an aerial view of the former mill and its proximity to the Schuylkill River. | Image: Bright Common
 Avellino said his team quickly realized that the first-floor space would largely not be suitable for regular use due to its propensity to flood and resulting regulations. He described working with various federal, state, and city agencies, from FEMA to the Historical Commission, as arduous. “They don’t really talk to each other,” he said of the various entities.
 As part of the previous agreement to allow the demolition of the adjacent three houses and build new residences at the site, the Historical Commission asked prior ownership to restore their facades upon new construction. However, the agency ultimately canned that requirement upon the request of Citylight. The footprint of the former residences will now be used as part of the church’s entranceway, including allowing vehicular access into the first-story parking garage.
 Still, Avellino framed this as an unfortunate reality of a plan that would at least give new life to the kind of industrial age building steadily disappearing from the Manayunk waterfront. Cohen, too, sees the benefit in maintaining not only the building’s physical structure, but also an element of urban fabric beyond apartments and restaurants on the strip. “Someone comes off of Main Street. It’s sort of symbolic of life is busy, life is crazy. And then now they’re walking toward this river and up to worship,” Cohen said.
 Then, there is the matter of flooding. Avellino said he realized early on in the planning process that the building’s first floor would not be usable for regular programming, adding that the project was one of the first to go through a new Philadelphia floodplain management guide. That more or less cut in half the amount of usable space Citylight had envisioned for all of its needs, including worshipping, children’s rooms, offices, food prep, and other uses. “Hurricane Ida flooded the bowl here in Manayunk,” Avellino said. “We took it on immediately after a natural disaster. So that was a pretty prescient moment.”
 Renderings of Citylight Church's entryway and sanctuary. | Images: Bright Common
 Yet, Avellinio said the church wasn’t spooked and instead embraced his firm’s vision of a facility that would stand the test of time. He described the building’s steel and timber bones as “big and beefy,” well suited to supporting a planned 500-seat worship space, with restored historic windows looking out on one end onto Main Street and the other over the Schuylkill River.
 To protect the building from floods, Avellino said the underside of the second floor had to be waterproofed to “submarine” level standards. The ground floor sits about 33 feet above sea level, but design flood elevation rises to just under the first-floor ceiling. That is the approximate location where Ida’s waters reached, the highest level in Philadelphia’s recorded history. The new design will incorporate perforated metal gates at the entrance of the garage and cinderblock-sized cutouts from the walls, which will be waterproofed. The idea is to allow the space to intentionally flood and then release waters with minimal damage to the first floor.
 “The original design wasn’t to put a parking garage here. That’s rather anti-urbanist,” Avellino said. “But after a long series of hard conversations, we just realized that we’re at that moment. I don’t know if you want to call it resiliency or managed retreat or adaptation, but we realized as designers we were at this moment of, what to do with a building that probably shouldn’t be renovated, but is part of the historic fabric and narrative and culture of the city.”
 Along with the flood protections, Avellino said the building is also being designed to passive house standards. “We just pitched it hard and said, ‘Why don’t we just go with resiliency and design an ark that’s net zero energy?’” Avellino said. “The clients, to my wonderment and surprise, said definitely, let’s do this.”
 Tags: adaptive resuse climate change Manayunk Renovation Sustainability 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: National Register Nominations Sail Through Local Review
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on September 12, the Philadelphia Historical Commission commented on four Philadelphia nominations to the National Register of Historic Places, reviewed restorations and renovations to a historic Center City block, and approved the final event in the long and unhappy saga of Fishtown’s St. Laurentius Church.
 In May, the Historical Commission approved the construction of eight three-story townhouses on the site where St. Laurentius Roman Catholic Church had stood at East Berks and Memphis Streets. The church was built in 1885 and designed by renowned ecclesiastical architect Edwin Forrest Durang. It was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2015 in an effort to save the beloved neighborhood landmark as it deteriorated during a battle between neighbors and the developer who purchased the church from the Archdiocese of Philadelphia. Ultimately, the building was declared unsafe by the Department of Licenses and Inspections and demolished in 2022 by the developer who ignored the Historical Commission’s requirement to either retain the front facade or salvage historic elements for incorporation into a new building. As part of its approval of the townhouses, the Historical Commission required the creation of a public display commemorating the St. Laurentius church building.
 St. Laurentius Roman Catholic Church in Fishtown was demolished in 2022. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 The applicant proposed a commemorative display consisting of a bronze cast of the front section of the church building, to be fabricated from a scan taken before demolition and set on a masonry base, which would include a plaque and cornerstone salvaged from the church. It would be accompanied by a marker that resembled the blue metal plaques of the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission. Both would be located in front of the St. Laurentius Catholic School at 1608 East Berks Street, adjacent to the site where the church building had stood at 1600-06 East Berks Street. Both would be financed and maintained by the church. After hearing concerns about securing the bronze cast and plaque from thieves, and what might become of the display if the Archdiocese divested itself of the school building, the Historical Commission approved the project.
 Final approval was granted to restore the front facades and construct rear additions to eight rowhouses on the 100 block of North Mole Street. Built between 1835 and 1850, the entire block received individual designation in 1967. The applicant stated they own seven of the properties with options to buy more from a family trust that has held many of them since 1939.
 The last item on the meeting’s agenda was to comment on nominations of Philadelphia properties to the National Register of Historic Places. These nominations are overseen by the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, which must solicit comments from the appropriate local government, which must also offer an opportunity for public comment. The Historical Commission speaks on behalf of the City of Philadelphia in historic preservation matters. Members commented favorably of all four nominations.
 The Philadelphia Macaroni Company Factory at 11th and Catharine Streets. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Philadelphia Macaroni Company Factory at 1101 Catharine Street was built in 1933 and designed by architect Isadore W. Levin. The industrial landmark is historically significant as the largest and most important manufacturer of macaroni and pasta in Philadelphia for much of the 20th century. The building still serves as the company’s corporate headquarters. It is not listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 The Morse Elevator Works Historic District includes several properties in Fishtown on Frankford Avenue, East Wildey Street, Shackamaxon Street, and Sarah Street. The location was home of one of the largest and most important elevator manufacturers in the United States during the late 19th century. Founded as Clem & Morse around 1877, the company played a major role in the development of early elevator technology. Several of the properties in the proposed district are listed on the local register: 1101-03, 1105-09, and 1111-13 Frankford Avenue and 1045-40 Sarah Street.
 Morse Elevator Works at 1105-09 Frankford Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Another site related to historical industry, the BIOSIS Headquarters Building at 2100 Arch Street, was nominated for its association with the largest database publisher for the life sciences. Also known as Biological Abstracts, it was founded in 1926 and was significant in the abstracting and indexing of millions of scholarly articles focused on life sciences and biology in the United States, a process critical to the sharing of information among institutions and researchers.
 Bethel Presbyterian Church at 1900 West York Street was also nominated. It was designed in the Late Gothic-Revival style by architect Charles W. Bolton. Its period of significance, beginning around 1947, reflects the social history of the neighborhood, as the church transitioned from the white congregation that built it in 1904 to a Black population. The church is not listed on the Philadelphia Register.
 Tags: Historical Commission Meeting Report National Register of Historic Places Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places St. Laurentius 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Woodmere Art Museum Defies Odds With Major Expansion
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Frances M. Maguire Hall for Art & Education in Chestnut Hill is now open to the public. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At a time when many arts institutions are reeling from federal funding cuts and patron numbers still below pre-pandemic levels, the Woodmere Art Museum in Chestnut Hill has just completed an audacious project that will double its gallery size. This month it celebrated the opening of Frances M. Maguire Hall for Art & Education, which had been known as St. Michael’s Hall when it was owned by the Sisters of Saint Joseph, the founders of Chestnut Hill College.
 The museum is named after Frances M. Maguire, an artist and benefactor to Woodmere and other arts institutions. The former location of the Barnes Foundation in Merion was also named after her when it was acquired by St. Joseph’s University.
 The house, located at the corner of Germantown and Sunset Avenues in Chestnut Hill, was built in 1853 for William Henry Trotter, a partner in the metal importing and manufacturing firm of Nathan Trotter & Company. It was founded by his father in 1817 and today is thought to be the oldest continuously operated metals company in the United States. In 1868, Trotter sold the property to Henry Latimer Norris, also an industrialist in his family’s firm, the Norris Locomotive Works.
 9001 Germantown Avenue when it was the home of J.M. Geary. Date unknown. | Photo courtesy of the Chestnut Hill Conservancy
 The third owner, Alfred Craven Harrison, bought the estate from Norris in 1884 and owned it for the next 40 years. Harrison was one of the richest men in Philadelphia in the late 19th century from the sale of his family’s Franklin Sugar Refining Company.
 A brief ownership by a developer saw some its acreage subdivided to build houses. In 1927, the house and remaining four acres of land were purchased by the Convent of the Sisters of Saint Joseph. It was first used as a school, later for student housing, and most recently as a residence hall for nuns.
 The stone house, the work of an unknown architect, was built in the Gothic Revival style. Alfred C. Harrison commissioned Cope & Stewardson to add two large Italianate style wings in 1899. Among other features, an elaborately carved staircase was the work of Edward Maene, a woodworker and stone carver who contributed to many Philadelphia churches, as well as the University of Pennsylvania's Quadrangle dormitories and the Washington Memorial Chapel at Valley Forge.
 William Valerio, the director and CEO of Woodmere Art Museum. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 When the Sisters of Saint Joseph announced their intent to sell the property in early 2021, alarms were raised in Chestnut Hill about its future. The property had been included as a “significant” property in the Chestnut Hill National Register Historic District, but it is not listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. The former does not protect a property from demolition, while the latter requires oversight by the Philadelphia Historical Commission.
 Community concerns were replaced by hopes when the next-door neighbor, the Woodmere began talks with the Sisters about their interest in acquiring the property. “We engaged in a quiet campaign and people stepped forward,” said William Valerio, the director and CEO of Woodmere. “A $10 million gift from the Maguire Foundation made the project a reality.” After a $2.2 million purchase in October 2021, renovations began in the spring of 2023.
 Local architect Jeff Krieger assisted the lead architects, New York firm Matthew Baird Architects and Philly-based Andropogon Associates were enlisted as the landscape architects.
