Much of the work involved the removal of interior walls that had been added to create numerous smaller bedrooms where salons had originally been. The architects reopened the front porch, which had been closed in, and commissioned new window grillwork to harmonize with the originals on the front door.
 A contemporary gallery on the ground floor. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 When finished, the project yielded an additional 17,000 square feet of space, with 14 new galleries, a dedicated children’s art and education space, event spaces, as well as four acres of preserved greenspace.
 “Our overall vision for Maguire Hall is to showcase Woodmere’s permanent collection,” explained Valerio. With a large portion of their holdings in storage, it wasn’t difficult to fill the new galleries.
 The center front hall is staged as a tribute to Frances M. Maguire, with her portrait and some of her work hung alongside paintings by some of her teachers and classmates at Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts. An Art Deco chandelier that originally hung in the mezzanine of the Boyd Theater now graces the front hall gallery. “ The Friends of the Boyd salvaged anything they could,” said Valerio. “They gifted the chandelier, a painted mirror, and 12 Saturn lights to us.”
 Light fixtures salvaged from the Boyd Theater are featured in Maguire Hall's dining room. | Photo courtesy of Woodmere Art Museum
 Another gallery on the first floor serves as a bit of a reality check. “Here we have art that depicts some of the harder aspects of living in Philadelphia and also some pieces about healing,” noted Valerio, gesturing towards paintings by Charles Searles, Bo Bartlett, Marta Sanchez, and others.
 “For each gallery we picked a main piece and then added related works, such as by the artist’s colleagues, students, or with similar themes,” said Amy Ferracci, Woodmere’s director of marketing and communications.
 A second-floor gallery is dedicated to the work of American Impressionists from Philadelphia. The paintings are complemented by a patterned wallpaper in rich colors. “When renovating this room we found fragments of the original wallpaper,” explained Valerio. “From it, we created a kaleidoscopic pattern to design a new wallpaper.”
 The American Impressionists gallery features recreated wallpaper inspired by the original. | Photo courtesy of Woodmere Art Museum
 The former breakfast room, in the Cope and Stewardson addition, serves as a sculpture gallery. Edward Maene’s original carved wooden paneling remained, but the ceiling and upper portions of the walls had been painted over. “We were able to recreate the original deep red paint, which is actually now available at Kilian’s Hardware Store here in Chestnut Hill, as ‘Woodmere Red,’” Ferracci said.
 The basement level had been used by the Harrisons for the safe keeping of silver and jewels, so the Woodmere staff decided to continue that use by exhibiting contemporary jewelry artists.
 In the midst of the thoughtful renovations and compelling thematic galleries, is the crown jewel of the project, the room which houses the 18 murals comprising The Building of the House of Wisdom by Violet Oakley as they were originally staged in the mansion of Charlton Yarnall on the northeast corner of 17th and Locust Streets, which was built in 1908 and designed by architect Frank Miles Day. “It had been on the third floor, looking down onto a music room on the second,” said Valerio. In building the installation, they recreated the skylight of painted glass that had been designed by D'Ascenzo Studio .
 The Building of the House of Wisdom by Violet Oakley has an entire room to itself. | Photo courtesy of Woodmere Art Museum
 Oakley created a series of 43 murals in the Pennsylvania State Capitol building in 1902, the first American woman to receive a public mural commission. Other of her works in Philadelphia include the Great Women of the Bible murals at the First Presbyterian Church in Germantown and Life of Moses , commissioned by Samuel S. Fleisher in 1927 for the altar piece for the sanctuary of the Fleisher Art Memorial on Catharine Street in South Philadelphia.
 Woodmere became the repository for the Yarnall murals in 1973 after a series of sales of the house endangered their preservation. Edith Emerson, an artist, Woodmere’s director, and Oakley's life partner, stepped in and brought the murals to Chestnut Hill.
 With the museum’s expansion into a second building, the original site next door at 9201 Germantown Avenue has been christened Charles Knox Smith Hall, after its founder who transformed his home, Woodmere, into a showcase for his art collection.
 The acquisition of an additional four acres has also enabled Woodmere to expand its sculpture garden. In addition to a couple dozen artworks, the grounds include a pollinator garden, an outdoor amphitheater, hundred-year-old trees, and native plants.
 Tags: adaptive resuse Chestnut Hill museums Philadelphia artists Renovation Woodmere Art Museum 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Mid-Century Modern Home of Philadelphia's First Licensed Female Architect to be Demolished
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
4024-34 Apalogen Road in East Falls. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Philadelphia Historical Commission added two properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places at its meeting on November 14. It also rejected the nomination of a culturally and architecturally significant midcentury modern house, a decision that clears the way for the building's demolition.
 Tulipwood, a mid-century modern home at 4024-34 Apalogen Road in East Falls, was designed in 1954 by Elizabeth Fleisher , the first woman architect licensed in Philadelphia, and her husband, landscape architect Horace Fleisher, for their home. At its meeting on October 15, the Historical Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation found that the property satisfies criteria for designation based on its association with Elizabeth Fleisher and as an example of Modernist architecture.
 Tulipwood was completed in 1954. It was designed by architect Elizabeth Fleisher and landscape architect Horace Fleisher for the couple's home. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 The nomination was contested by the recent purchasers of the property, Valerie Safran and Marcie Turney, celebrated restauranteurs of the “Midtown Village” revival, whose establishments include Barbuzzo, Darling Jack’s Tavern, Marcie Blaine, Bud and Marilyn’s, Open House, Verde, and Little Nonna’s, plus four residential and office properties on the 1300 block of East Passyunk Avenue. They plan to demolish the house to build something new on the 2.4-acre lot, saying they had already spent about $400K on the redevelopment before receiving notification of the nomination. 
 Like most nominations, this one was limited to the building’s exterior. Nevertheless, the owners’ attorney referenced their removal of interior craftwork, including a Wharton Esherick cabinet and fireplace surround and cabinetry by Paul Evans and Phillip Lloyd Powell, suggesting respect for the building’s history. However, when she frequently said they “sold” the items she then amended herself to say “repurposed.” According to Freeman’s Auction House, the gross proceeds of the sale were nearly $100,000.
 After contentious public comment, the Historical Commission voted, with one abstention, to recognize that Tulipwood satisfies several criteria for designation, but they ultimately declined to vote in favor of protecting the building from demolition. The home can now be razed for new construction.
 419 West Clapier Street in Fernhill Park. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 A nomination of four service buildings for an adjacent former estate was not approved for listing on the local register. A gardener’s cottage, garage, solarium, and a stone building at 419 West Clapier Street were associated with the house at 5000 McKean Avenue, the home of James Mapes Dodge, his wife Josephine Kern Dodge, and their son Kern Dodge, who were impactful in the fields of engineering and children’s literature. The gardener’s cottage was designed by John Linerd Conarroe in 1923. The Historical Commission ruled that the nomination lacked sufficient evidence that the buildings on their own merit designation, but some members suggested a proposal of a small historic district with the main house, which is not individually designated, would be more convincing.
 5001-11 Lancaster Avenue in Cathedral Park. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Lutheran Publication House Manufacturing Building at 5001-11 Lancaster Avenue was added to the Philadelphia register. It was built in 1930 by the firm Harris & Richards, Architects and Engineers, who were known for designing industrial and institutional buildings during a time when Philadelphia had a significant religious printing industry.
 723 Church Lane in East Germantown. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The house at 723 Church Lane , a Victorian cottage constructed in 1866 with Gothic and Italianate architectural elements and Wissahickon schist, was also designated historic. It was the home of Lt. Col. T Ellwood Zell, a Civil War officer and publisher, one of many prominent Philadelphians who built suburban homes in Germantown in the late 19th century. The property's half-acre lot also may contain archaeological resources from the 1777 battle of Germantown. A 1910 newspaper article noted that 20 skeletal remains of Revolutionary War soldiers were discovered during the building of the house. The site has remained largely undisturbed since then.
 Tags: Elizabeth Hirsh Fleisher Midcentury Modern modernism Women In Architecture Women's history 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: An Underutilized Landmark on Lincoln Drive Receives Some TLC
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
Wissahickon Hall in East Falls turned 176 years old this year. The impressive, and forlorn, former creekside inn that motorists pass while navigating the twisty turns of Lincoln Drive is also getting a numerically-appropriate birthday gift: an injection of $776,000 in funding from owner Philadelphia Parks & Recreation (PPR) to buoy its aging facade and mechanical systems. 
 Earlier this year, passersby may have noticed scaffolding going up around the hall’s two-story, gallery-style porch, along with construction vehicles and equipment. PPR has confirmed this is part of a two-phase, $608,000 project to repair or replace numerous aspects of the building’s structure and facade, including framing members, historic columns, gutters, porch decking, a marble plinth, and windows. That work is about 40 percent complete and should be finished next spring. It has also performed additional interior repairs, including repointing and infilling stone walls–strengthening the building’s foundation–and then replastering. 
 The work was needed, a PPR spokesperson said, to follow up on issues found during engineering assessments in 2008 and 2014. Such concerns were amplified when a car crashed into the building in 2015 and Hurricane Ida flooded its first floor in 2021. “PPR takes the building’s preservation seriously and has, for over 140 years of City ownership, maintained the building to the best of our ability,” the spokesperson said, adding that PPR also paid $168,00 in 2023 to replace the hall’s boiler system. 
 But to what end? Parks and Recreation said that its Street Tree Management unit, which inspects and monitors 130,000 street trees throughout Philadelphia, has operated out of the building since 2008. Yet, even before the current construction project, activity appeared scant. Is there a better use? 
 Wissahickon Hall at Lincoln Drive and Gypsy Lane. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Alex Bartlett wonders. The Northwest Philadelphia native and curator and archivist at the Chestnut Hill Conservancy has driven by Wissahickon Hall countless times in his life. He has always been enamored by its historical significance as one of two remaining historic inns along the Wissahickon Creek, the Valley Green Inn being the other. The hall is listed on the National Register of Historic Places within the Wissahickon National Register District. It is not listed for legal protections on the Philadelphia Register. 
 Bartlett has been inside Wissahickon Hall just once, when he got into a fender bender in the 1990s and exchanged information at the hall, which was then the headquarters for the Philadelphia Police Department’s 92nd District. He was taken aback by the condition of the interior of the building, where large chunks of plaster were missing from the walls. “Clearly, at the time, nothing had happened in that building for decades, any kind of repairs,” Bartlett said. 
 Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, noted that PPR is responsible for the maintenance of over 200 historic structures in the city’s park system, a monumental task for the cash-strapped department. For some buildings, PPR will eventually find a way to achieve great things, with Steinke pointing to last summer’s rehabilitation of a former guardhouse in FDR Park as a prime example. Yet, others fall into and remain in disrepair, with little to no information from the City about when they’ll be repaired or reused. “They’ve got a lot on their plate,” Steinke said. 
 Both Bartlett and Steinke acknowledge the problematic reality of achieving a better use for Wissahickon Hall: location, location, location. Unlike Valley Green and its cozy cocoon of trees, ducks, and pedestrians along Forbidden Drive, Wissahickon Hall is just a few feet from the de facto speedway of Lincoln Drive, where southbound lanes are unable to legally access the property. Instead, most vehicular traffic would likely have to wind through East Falls to ingress and egress into auxiliary parking areas along Gypsy Lane. That’s a detour that curbs the enthusiasm of even an aficionado like Bartlett for something like a restaurant. “How sustainable is that? I don’t really know what the tourist [potential] is. I’ve worked or lived here all my life. Would I go there? Probably not,” said Bartlett. 
 A “Palace” Along the Creek 
 Long ago, Wissahickon Hall didn’t have to worry about a lack of foot traffic. Built in 1849, it originated at a time when Wissahickon Valley was making the transition from an industrial workshop to a recreational destination–what the nonprofit Friends of the Wissahickon calls the valley’s “ Road House Era .” 
 In the early 19th century, FOW retells , improvements in river navigation along the Schuylkill River began to draw more interest to what is now Northwest Philadelphia. In 1826, rocky outcroppings near the nexus of the Wissahickon Creek and Schuylkill River were blasted away to allow better access and a series of road improvements began along present day Lincoln and Forbidden Drives. Visiting writers, Edgar Allen Poe perhaps most famous among them, began to sing the creek’s praises. Increased public interest followed. In 1840, Nicholaus Rittenhouse III built the first road house, the Log Cabin Inn, as a gathering place for fellow Whig party members to cavort. Six more roadhouses followed along the creek through the start of the 20th century. “I've also assumed that the Wissahickon got a major boost in popularity because of the Centennial Exposition of 1876,” said Bartlett, noting that visitor guides highlighted the valley. “The [inns], especially after 1876, had a pretty decent boost in popularity.” 
 The reputations of the inns varied widely. Valley Green Inn started as a “temperance hotel,” while the Log Cabin Inn was famous for gang fights and a menagerie of live wildlife. Resident black bears were trained to pop champagne bottles. Wissahickon Hall, the closest to the city, was instead known as an “elegant” inn that catered to wealthy patrons arriving by sleigh and carriage, with a later owner of the nearby Log Cabin Inn likening it to a “palace.” 
 Wissahickon Hall in 1915. | Photo courtesy of Germantown Historical Society
 According to City records, Wissahickon Hall was built by entrepreneur Henry Lippen and originally consisted of the main, two-and-a-half story structure, along with two ice houses, a carriage house, and horse sheds. The enterprise benefitted greatly from its location along the creek. Steps originally ran down from the drive to the creek, where there was a boat launch. As with many other nearby inns, Wissahickon Hall specialized in waffles with catfish , then abundant in the creek. However, the real money maker was the ice. Benefitting from the damming of the Wissahickon just downstream, Lippen ran a large ice business that could hold 1,000 tons of inventory at a time, supplying Manayunk, Germantown, and Philadelphia in a time well before electric refrigeration. “There’s no question of its historical significance,” Steinke said. “It’s one of the few surviving roadside inns that are still standing and a nice one architecturally to look at–an amazing survivor down through these decades.” 
 Yet the building has encountered its share of hardships. Newspaper records suggest flooding has been a persistent problem for Wissahickon Hall, with reports of a rising creek swamping its lower floor in October 1869. The year before, an act of the State Assembly established the Fairmount Park system, and Philadelphia began to take control of the Wissahickon Valley. That spelled greater disaster for many of the inns, as the Fairmount Park Commission’s regulations also forbade the sale of alcohol. By the early 1870s, several road houses, including the Log Cabin Inn, were closed and demolished. 
 Wissahickon Hall held on, with newspaper records showing Charles Lippen, son of Henry, fighting the agency into the mid-1880s over the taking of the property and proper compensation. However, by 1885 he was out. The Fairmount Park Commission offered to rent the property to him for $2,000 a year, providing he gather ice “for family purposes only.” When he countered for $1,000, the commission evicted him from the building his father had built. 
 Adrift 
 It was clear from the get-go that the Fairmount Park Commission wasn’t quite sure what to do with Wissahickon Hall. Newspaper records published shortly after Lippen’s eviction noted squabbling among powerbrokers. Former Mayor William S. Stokley advocated selling “light refreshments” from a stall on its lower floor, according to an Inquirer account from March 1885. A man named David W. Sellers opposed this idea during a “humorous” floor speech, the newspaper reported, instead advocating for fare that packed more of a punch for what he counted as 75,000 visitors a year to the valley. “Full grown men over 40 years don't take long drives to eat ice cream or drink soda water, and the people who go out there should not be deprived of their particular refreshments,” Sellers said. “There should be established in the park a respectable tavern, inn, restaurant, or cafe where the people who are not cold water drinkers could get the refreshment they desired.” 
 What happened next is somewhat unclear. Newspaper records suggest the Fairmount Park Commission ultimately determined that Wissahickon Hall should be leased as a restaurant and received several applications. Yet, accounts are few and far in between afterward. A PPR spokesperson said its records reflect the hall was leased to a Nicholas Hayes under agreement that no alcohol be sold. However, an 1890 Inquirer article suggested that Hayes was indeed selling liquor at the hall without a license, benefitting from lawmen looking the other way. 
 Scant accounts of some flooding and repair work followed in the decades after until a 1912 newspaper notice suggested a "Duran" family had taken up residence. In an email, a PPR spokesperson said the department’s records indicated the hall continued to be used as an inn during the early 20th century before transitioning at some point to use as a Fairmount Park Guardhouse. Indeed, a 1927 Inquirer article detailing a “badly damaging” fire at the hotel identifies the “Dorns” as caretakers of the building, with the park guards stationed on the first floor. PPR said that use continued until 1972, when park guards were absorbed into the Philadelphia Police Department (PPD). Officers in turn were stationed there until 2008, when the PPD moved on from the building following budget cuts and PPR moved in. 
 Wissahickon Hall in 1964 when it was Fairmount Park Guard house. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 More damage ensued. In March 2008, a large tree fell during a storm and hit the building causing structural damage to the roof and rear of the hall. A Daily News piece from the following year reported the City was spending about $240,000 to repair and rehab the “stucco-stone-and-frame structure,” including a new roof, gutters, brick paving, and interior ceiling repair and electrical upgrades. “The exterior and interior are getting a new coat of paint based on historical paint analysis,” the article noted. 
 PPR said the hall underwent an additional engineering assessment in 2014 that discovered “structural damage to the south rubble stone wall of the building.” The hall’s porch was then “severely compromised” when a Jeep crashed through its southwest pillar in 2015. 
 “While measures were taken to repair the issue at the time, this accident caused considerable unseen damage to the porch as time went on,” said the PPR represenative. “Over the years water that used to be collected at the corner of the porch through the downspouts and gutter system seeped into the porch woodwork and framing members.” 
 The damage, amplified by Ida flooding in 2021, led to the current round of repairs, the most significant in the building’s recently documented history. 
 A Different Future? 
 Could something different be in store for Wissahickon Hall? For the record, PPR said it does “not anticipate any changes to use of the building” and asserts parks staff continue to use it “While there have been some changes to the building over the years (it no longer has its rooftop cupola for instance), much of its character-defining features have survived and Wissahickon Hall remains a park cultural icon." 
 The FOW also appears content with the present arrangements. “We’re deeply grateful to PPR for its ongoing commitment to preserving this iconic structure, which adds lasting value to the community and the park,” said Sarah Marley, interim executive director of the nonprofit. 
 But, the City’s ongoing ownership and management of the hall leaves Steinke a little uneasy, given the long-term maintenance backlog across all of its properties. “It’s not ideal, because they are overwhelmed and they can’t keep up,” Steinke explained. In a perfect world, more money would regularly flow to historic properties in the park system like Wissahickon Hall, Steinke said, adding that he is hopeful there might be some improvements through new leadership and fundraising campaigns by the Fairmount Park Conservancy, the City’s primary nonprofit partner in the park system. 
 Wissahickon Hall is currently undergoing $776,000 in repairs and stabilization. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Yet, either way, he added, there are no obvious alternative uses for Wissahickon Hall. Like any historic property, Steinke explained, a best use could be determined by a thorough and thoughtful analysis, such as by a consulting design firm. He said that can yield surprising results, citing past instances in which preservationists learned of the particular fragility of certain historic buildings and had to set aside dreams of robust public use. Thus it’s hard to speculate about Wissahickon Hall, but Steinke said it is clear that local road infrastructure is not presently conducive to a high-traffic use. “You can’t reconfigure or re-orient Lincoln Drive very easily,” he said. 
 Bartlett also struggles to confidently offer suggestions. There’s a little-used hiking and biking trail on that side of Lincoln Drive tracking a ridge in the woods behind Wissahickon Hall. Could that be a draw? Lincoln Drive also has a brief break in its center median just in front of the hall, presumably so emergency vehicles can connect to southbound lanes when needed. Bartlett noted some online commentators have suggested that placing a traffic light there and allowing turns onto Gypsy Lane could solve the access issue. “I do think that somehow, you know, there is an opportunity here,” he said. 
 Tags: Department of Parks and Recreation Fairmount Park Lincoln Drive Northwest Philadelphia Renovation 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Places to Save: Fall 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Conkling-Armstrong Houses 
 Location: 2224-26 West Tioga Street
 Built: 1898
 Threat: Deterioration
 The Conkling-Armstrong Houses are a striking, but endangered pair of Chateauesque twins, rich in architectural and industrial history in Nicetown-Tioga. Built in 1898, the homes were designed by architect Edward V. Seeler, who trained at the École des Beaux- Arts, as a showcase for the Conkling-Armstrong Terra Cotta Company. The houses’ facades drip with ornate terra cotta details that once exemplified the company’s mastery of the material.
 The homes, commissioned by company founders Ira L. Conkling and Thomas F. Armstrong, were not just showpieces, but their personal residences located minutes from their factory. Unfortunately, after the industrial heyday, the houses fell into deep disrepair. The buildings have suffered from vandalism, theft, and ongoing deterioration.
 In 2019, the buildings were listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places , offering protection against demolition and inappropriate alteration. But preservation requires more than designation status. In 2021, new ownership emerged with plans to restore the crumbling structures. Permits were filed, early repairs began and optimism briefly bloomed. Yet the work has since come to a halt.
 Today, the homes are in peril. Without immediate intervention, Philadelphia risks losing some of its most distinctive industrial-era residences, an architectural catalog in miniature and a physical link to the city’s once-booming terra cotta industry.
 Photos: Peter Woodall
 Closed National Park Service Units 
 Location: Various
 Built: Various
 Threat: Lack of funding
 While Philadelphia boasts an unparalleled collection of historic sites under National Park Service (NPS) stewardship, many remain closed to the public–some temporarily, others indefinitely. These closures limit access to critical chapters of American history and raise pressing questions about long-term stewardship, funding, and public interpretation.
 Among the most prominent shuttered sites is the First Bank of the United States, which has been closed to the public for years while serving as NPS offices. However, it is now being restored and transformed into a museum of the early American economy. Nearby, the Portrait Gallery in the Second Bank of the United States is also closed, despite recent restoration work. Other sites, such as the Bishop White House, Dolley Todd House, Declaration House, Pemberton House, and New Hall Military Museum, remain closed, with their public interpretive programming suspended indefinitely. Outside of Center City, the Germantown White House (Deshler-Morris House) has also been closed since 2015 and is currently undergoing a renovation project.
 These closures reflect a broader crisis in preservation and public access, one fueled by chronic understaffing and deepening federal funding cuts. NPS has faced staffing losses of up to 40 percent at some sites over the past decade, and recent federal budget proposals include more cuts to the agency. Without significant reinvestment, these historic buildings risk further decline and the loss of key narratives in American history.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Church of the Assumption 
 Location: 1123-33 Spring Garden Street
 Built: 1849
 Threat: Sale
 After two decades of vacancy, the Church of the Assumption , a architectural landmark in Callowhill, is again facing an uncertain future. Built in 1849 by the prolific ecclesiastical architect Patrick Charles Keely, the church is the oldest surviving example of his 600-plus works nationwide. Its copper spires and unaltered Gothic Revival design earned it a place on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2009. It also holds deep spiritual and cultural significance as the baptismal location of St. John Neumann and St. Katharine Drexel.
 Although protected by local designation, the church has faced numerous threats. In 2010, the then-owner filed for demolition citing financial hardship. The Philadelphia Historical Commission narrowly approved the request in a controversial tie vote, broken by the chair. Community members, led by the Callowhill Neighborhood Association, mounted a legal challenge and ultimately won a reversal of the demolition permit in 2011. This major preservation victory kept the church standing, but not out of danger.
 The building’s current owner, who purchased the property in 2012, also pursued demolition before pivoting to a failed hotel conversion plan. Due to the owner’s defaulting on the mortgage, the church is slated for a sheriff’s sale following foreclosure.
 Still, there is reason for hope. Zoning reforms now ease the redevelopment of historic nonresidential buildings. The sale is a chance for new ownership to stabilize and revitalize the site. With vision and investment, the Church of the Assumption could be preserved and adapted to a new use.
 Tags: Church of the Assumption Conkling-Armstrong Terra Cotta Edwin Forrest Durang National Park Service Places to Save 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Some Philly-Area Malls are Changing, While Others Are Dying. Is Anything Worth Preserving?
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
As director of the Philadelphia-based Partners for Sacred Places, Rachel Hildebrandt works to preserve some of society’s most hallowed grounds: the churches, synagogues, mosques, and other religious buildings whose cultural value often far outpaces whatever the “marketplace” says they are worth. Yet, as a kid growing up in East Oak Lane, it was massive structures specifically focused on profit that were the recipients of Hildebrandt’s affection: sprawling American shopping malls. In her teenage years, Hildebrandt would regularly hop on a SEPTA bus to the Cheltenham, Neshaminy, and Willow Grove malls, sometimes going even further afield to the Oxford Valley Mall in Bucks County or Montgomery Mall in North Wales. “Growing up in the 90s, that was like, the thing,” Hildebrandt said. “I’d grab a friend, and we’d sit on the bus for an hour and half because we were just so excited to go shopping.”
 King of Prussia Plaza opened in 1963. J. C. Penny was one of the mall's original anchor stores. | Photos: Reddit
 As the Delaware Valley’s malls have been swept up in the e-commerce wave wiping out many malls across the country, Hildebrandt’s preservationist antennae have started to tingle. Just how perilous the moment is for malls is subject to debate. “U.S. malls are dying, and there may be just 150 left in 10 years,” blared a headline in Business Insider, while CNN Business claims “ The U.S. Mall is not dying .” However, go shopping for statistics and the numbers seem to speak for themselves. In the 1980s, there were about 2,500 malls in the United States, according to Atlas Obscura , while the estimated number today ranges from about 750 to 1,150, which some analysts predict could drop to into the low hundreds by 2032.
 Some of the discrepancy may come from exactly what constitutes a mall, a taxonomic challenge complicated by an era in which many malls are reinventing themselves, some closing for years before reopening as casinos, entertainment centers, with residential and commercial conversions, or with a mix of uses.
 Franklin Mills in Northeast Philadelphia opened its doors in 1989. | Photos: Reddit
 Even still, it begs a question for Hildebrandt: should anything be done to preserve some essence of the golden era of the American shopping mall? She admits it’s a challenging question. First, there are considerable logistical issues in attempting any kind of traditional, large-scale preservation effort of a mall. Furthermore, as she knows firsthand working for Sacred Places, there is already a mismatch between the number of high value targets for preservation and the resources to make it happen, without adding such a heavy lift to the list.
 Yet, perhaps the most difficult hurdle to overcome is skepticism within the preservation community that shopping malls are worth honoring, especially given their role hollowing out urban centers and indeed imperiling buildings already denoted as historic (Exhibit A: Center City’s Wanamaker building). Still, Hildebrandt wonders. “My personal take is that the American mall is significant, but it was also so prolific, right? It’s like, how do we decide which were the significant ones? Which ones do we really want to invest in and keep? Which are we OK seeing close?” said Hildebrandt. “I most definitely think there are historic malls out there. Convincing the public at large that that is the case seems like an uphill battle.”
 The Birth of the American Shopping Mall 
 Jeffrey Hardwick is public programs director for the National Endowment for the Humanities, one of the largest funders of important museums and historic sites across the country. So, the fact that he wrote a book on shopping malls, Mall Maker: Victor Gruen, Architect of an American Dream , may seem a little incongruent. Not so, Hardwick said, adding he thinks there is enough “there” there to add some malls to the lexicon of spaces in America worth protecting, or at least recognizing. “You know, Postmodernists looked to Las Vegas and the layout of casinos for their inspiration. There’s so much [conversation to be had around] popular architecture and its value. I do think preservationists end up fetishizing a little too much, you know, an 1800s Greek Revival thing with its balusters intact,” explained Hardwick. “That was one of the things I ran into doing the research.”
 Cherry Hill Mall opened on October 11, 1961. It was designed by architect Victor Gruen and was the first large enclosed mall on the East Coast. | Images: Ebay
 Hardwick acknowledges that malls have a problematic history. These were spaces built for a “99 percent white” clientele during the era of white flight and segregation, leading to major economic decline in urban areas and deep-seated sociodemographic problems that continue through today. “Critical aspects need to be taken into account,” he said, but also doesn’t believe them to be disqualifying.
 Hardwick said early forms of the modern American mall began to arise in the 1930s and 1940s from a combination of factors. Suburbanization was underway and early experiments in commercial development there were waylaid by the Great Depression, leading to blighted buildings that were viewed as a drag on land values and the bucolic ideal of the suburbs. So post War World II, planners began zoning off specific parcels of land for commerce, then burying them behind treelines and topography so as not to upset the locals. “The shopping mall ends up strangely as this kind of planning idea that you’re going to put a giant commercial center in the middle of domestic suburbia. You’re going to hide it behind large mounds of soil. You’re not going to have signage or anything. You’re not going to see it from the road,” Hardwick said. “Then you bring in all of the retailing needs for a community.”
 Moorestown Mall was built in 1963 and designed by John Graham Jr., the architect behind the Space Needle observation tower in Seattle. The mall has undergone a number of character-altering interior renovations beginning with a wide-scale redesign in the mid-1980s. | Images: Ebay
 Enter Victor Gruen . A Jewish, Vienna-born architect, Gruen fled an occupying Nazi regime following Kristallnacht in 1938 and landed in New York City. A showman and prolific writer of books and essays, Gruen positioned himself as a leading visionary of the American shopping mall. He wasn’t the first to build a modern shopping mall, Hardwick said, but was certainly the most influential architect in the space. Of the dozens of malls he designed in the mid-20th century, the Southdale Mall in suburban Minneapolis is often referenced first as the country’s first fully enclosed shopping center, opening in 1956. Regionally, Gruen designed the Cherry Hill Mall.
 “One of his big problems is financing, and he figures out a way to convince the department stores that they’re going to be the main developers of these shopping malls,” Hardwick said. “They don’t realize that once they put in the suburban shopping malls that they’re going to kill their downtown flagship.”
 Economics aside, Gruen’s ethos and designs may be surprising to some. Openly Socialist for a time, Gruen had a certain egalitarian instinct, and in other corners of his career argued that downtowns should be people and not car-centered places. Indeed, his vision for the shopping mall was as a sort of “European town square in a soulless wasteland” of suburbia, Hardwick said. Design features often included fountains and gardens, and Gruen aimed for a diverse mix of tenants. “He imagines the shopping mall is going to be a mixed-use space, so it’s not going to be solely devoted to retail,” said Hardwick. “Libraries, a childcare center, a post office. You’re going to have office buildings and apartments. Some of that is actually at Cherry Hill.” While Hardwick said Gruen is sometimes criticized as an architect, he thinks Gruen is undeniably important historically, noting that modernist architect Philip Johnson applauded his work and called him the most influential architect of the era.
 Church on the Mall at Plymouth Meeting Mall was established in 1966. The congregation, made up of three merged churches, worshiped in common spaces within the mall when it was closed on Sundays. Its permanent home was built in 1972. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Further complicating the image of the American shopping mall as a soulless monstrosity, Hardwick said, are “amazing” images of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and Duke Ellington performing at malls in suburban Chicago, and court cases arguing that protests at malls should be protected by the First Amendment, given their station as the central public gathering point in suburban communities. “The mall does become a community focal point,” Hardwick explained.
 Hildebrandt sees similar dynamics locally. One of the spaces she finds fascinating in the region is the Church on the Mall , a Presbyterian congregation that relocated to the Plymouth Meeting Mall in the 1960s and continues to worship there today, in a purpose-built space replete with stained glass windows and a faux-spire cross.
 Hildebrandt said it was an intentional choice for the congregation to follow the flow of the American populace into a mall. As far as she knows, it was the first of its kind anywhere in the country. “It was about being where the people are, from a mission perspective,” she said. All of this leaves a lingering question of whether some part of our history would be lost should such a place slip into the past without recognition.
 The Rise and Fall of Philly’s Malls 
 Hardwick’s history of malls can be traced in the Delaware Valley. In 1927, construction began on Ardmore’s Suburban Square, a campus of several buildings designed to include a variety of commercial and entertainment uses along with department stores. “Local residents were concerned about the traffic and the decline of property value,” noted the Lower Merion Historical Society in a history of the mall. “Ardmore business owners feared a drop in revenues, but building moved forward.”
 A drawing of an early proposal for The Gallery on Market Street by architect Romaldo Giurgola. | Image courtesy of Mitchell/Giurgola Collection, The Architectural Archives, University of Pennsylvania
 However, it is Gruen’s Cherry Hill Mall, opened in 1961, that has the claim of the area’s first modern, enclosed shopping mall–a claim also exists that it was the first east of the Mississippi River, but that butts up against similar claims such as Maryland’s now-demolished Harundale Mall, opened 1958. The King of Prussia Mall came next in 1963, Plymouth Meeting Mall in 1966, Oxford Valley Mall in 1973, Montgomery Mall in 1978, the Willow Grove Park Mall in 1982, and Franklin (Mills) Mall in 1989. Center City Philadelphia’s long-running struggle to compete began with the opening of The Gallery in 1977, now called Fashion District Philadelphia.
 The health of all of these institutions varies. The Pennsylvania Real Estate Investment Trust (PREIT) owns Cherry Hill, Willow Grove, Plymouth Meeting, Exton Square, and Moorestown malls, but declined an interview. Mario Ventresca, chief financial officer for PREIT, did speak with WHYY in November 2024 and put forth generally good vibes, despite the company having filed for bankruptcy twice in the past five years. The station’s reporting noted that some malls, such as KOP and Cherry Hill, continue to attract both tenants and customers, while reinventing themselves with dining and entertainment experiences that can’t be purchased online, as well as adding residential and healthcare uses. Others, like Willow Grove and Exton, appeared to be falling short, with the latter in the process of being sold by PREIT to the Abrams Realty & Development company, WHYY reported.
 The Easter Bunny rides an escalator at The Gallery during its heyday in 1985. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 The malls within Philadelphia proper appear to be tipping toward that end of the spectrum. As of 2023, the Fashion District had a tenancy rate of 80 percent, tracking significantly below that of KOP, Cherry Hill, and even Willow Grove. About a third of its square footage was set to be demolished for the 76ers arena before the plug was pulled, leaving an open question of what happens next. Franklin Mall has undergone a series of name and ownership changes in recent years, most recently seeing a name change from Philadelphia Mills after private investment group Jones Lang LaSalle purchased it over the summer. The company has yet to reveal any further plans to try and reinvigorate the site.
 This shifting nature of malls presents a challenge to any potential efforts to preserve or historically recognize them. As Hildebrandt pointed out, architectural integrity is often a valued trait in a preserved building, and malls inherently are constantly shapeshifting. “There aren’t a lot of malls out there that are preserved in amber,” she says.
 Given that there’s no immediate signs of demolition for any area malls, Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, doesn’t see much reason to act. “I don’t think there’s much of a clamor for preserving malls, but there is a new desire to find new uses for the real estate,” Steinke said. Looking at the bigger picture, Steinke also expressed some skepticism. He doesn’t see much love for the architecture of malls among preservationists, and while he understands there is a community of people devoted to remembering the golden era of the American mall, he cops to personally not being particularly enamored by them. “I wouldn’t care if Franklin Mall went away, but there are some people who might be devastated and speak out for preservation in some way,” opined Steinke
 The old entrance of The Gallery at 9th and Market Streets readies for its reinvention as The Fashion District in 2017. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 What would that look like? At the grandest scale, the first thought Steinke had was of the Smithsonian Museum of American Industrial History in Bethlehem, which is located on the site of a former Bethlehem Steel property, amongst its hulking, rusting stacks and dilapidated factory buildings. Yet, that appears to be without precedent. Hardwick said he is aware of some efforts to preserve the signage, layouts, and some buildings of smaller predecessors of the modern mall, but nothing approaching the full-scale preservation of a shuttered mall, especially the behemoths that dot the Delaware Valley.
 Hildebrandt noted that there are already robust online communities dedicated to collecting memorabilia from malls that have been demolished or are heading that direction. Perhaps these groups might be the best thing we’ve got for commemorating the American shopping mall, whatever its value. “There are some unbelievable postcards out there of the Cherry Hill Mall when it opened,” Hildebrandt said. “Beautiful, beautiful. Like lush, with plants, very classic midcentury. But it doesn’t look like that anymore.”
 Tags: malls shopping 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Planning Commission Applies the Brakes on Controversial Squilla Bill
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
A fast-moving City Council bill that would dramatically alter the process for adding properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places will receive further scrutiny and input over the next several weeks.
 Bill No. 251030 was introduced by Councilmember Mark Squilla on November 20. He represents the 1st District, which includes much of Center City and stretches along the Delaware River from South Philadelphia to Port Richmond. He was also on the Historic Preservation Task Force , convened by former Mayor Jim Kenney in 2017 and whose final report the following year included sweeping recommendations to improve historic preservation in the city. 
 Currently, when a nomination for designation is submitted to the Philadelphia Historical Commission , the staff reviews it for completeness and issues notification to the owner of record with 30 days' notice of a public hearing to review the nomination. At that time, the property is under the protection of the Historical Commission until the final decision.
 The bill would add a second step to the process, requiring the full Historical Commission to vote on allowing a nomination to be reviewed, triggering another 30-day notice.
 Another change would allow the Historical Commission to reject a nomination simply because the owner had submitted an application for a demolition or alteration permit, rather than having already received the permit. It would also compel the Historical Commission to allow demolition or alteration permits if the owner had development designs or contracts at the time they were notified of the proposed nomination.
 The bill would eliminate the work of significant landscape architects as a qualifying criterion for designation and would also weaken the ability to designate for archaeological reasons.
 Reactions from preservation and community organizations were swift and largely negative. Suzanne Ponsen, president of West Central Germantown Neighbors, said the Philadelphia Crosstown Coalition, an organization of 30 Registered Community Organizations, wrote a letter of opposition to Councilmember Squilla.
 "We oppose the bill as written,” stated Hanna Stark, director of policy and communications at the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. “It doesn’t have anything to benefit preservation.”
 The Philadelphia Historical Commission denied placing 4024-34 Apalogen Road on the local register in November despite publicly recognizing that the home satisfies several criteria for designation. Tulipwood was completed in 1954 and designed by architect Elizabeth Fleisher, Philadelphia's first licensed female architect. The home's new owners have conceptual plans, but, according to the Department of Licenses and Inspections, have not attained any permits to raze the building and redevelop the property. Bill No. 251030, as it is currently written, would eliminate protections put in place for historic nomination submissions. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 David Gest, executive director of the Chestnut Hill Conservancy, which advocates for historic preservation and landscape conservation in Northwest Philadelphia, agreed. “Our main take on this bill is that it’s proposing many sweeping changes that warrant further discussion.”
 The most alarming portion of the bill was the addition of the second step in the nomination process. “By creating a new type of public meeting before the property is under protection creates a potential loophole for owners to obtain a demolition permit or zoning changes,” explained Gest.
 Some preservationists felt that, after several months of discussion with Squilla while the bill was being written, their suggestions were not included. “What was surprising to me is that I thought we were in agreement,” said Squilla.
 “Tiered historic districts are a priority of ours,” said Stark, as an example. “The Historic Preservation Task Force had recommended them as well.” Advocates say that by having more than one type of historic district, the Historical Commission could offer a more nuanced way to preserve neighborhoods by providing different levels of oversight, depending on the significance and assets of the proposed district.
 A process for tiered historic districts had been originally included in the bill, but Squilla said he took it out because he felt it was written too broadly and did not explain well how it could be applied. However, with discussions set to continue, “We want to have that added in, but we need to flesh out the process,” saif Squilla.
 The bill was next presented to the Philadelphia Planning Commission at their meeting on December 4. It was slated to be an action item on the agenda, but at the recommendation of their staff, the Planning Commission voted to place a 45 day hold on it to allow sufficient time for review. “It’s a good idea,” said Squilla. “It’s their language, so they need to be on board.”
 The next step for the bill would be to go before City Council’s Rules Committee. It had not been introduced with enough time to be included on their most recent committee meeting agenda on December 3. “February will probably be the earliest for hearings,” noted Squilla, adding that talks will continue, and he anticipates changes will be made to the bill’s language. “It’s a matter of trying to get everyone on the same page.”
 With preservationists and developers generally having different interests and aims, is it possible to create a process that would satisfy both parties? “It’s doable,” said Gest optimistically. “We think there are ways to dive into these policies and come up with procedures that satisfy both.”
 Tags: demolition Development Philadelphia City Council Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Textile Bank In Kensington to be Added to the National Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Textile National Bank building at 1801 E. Huntingdon Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At its meeting on December 12, the Philadelphia Historical Commission reviewed several requests to make alterations to properties on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. It also reviewed a nomination to the National Register of Historic Places for the Textile National Bank building at 1801 E. Huntingdon Street in Kensington.
 Nominations of Philadelphia properties to the National Register are overseen by the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, which must solicit comments from the appropriate local government, which in turn must offer an opportunity for public comment. The Historical Commission speaks on behalf of the City of Philadelphia on historic preservation matters.
 Top: Architect Herman Miller designed the sculptural panel in the tympanum on the building's west elevation and contracted Conkling-Armstrong Terra Cotta Company to create it. Bottom: Massive Corinthian columns flank the entryway of the bank while an ornate clock keeps time from above. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 The Textile National Bank building was designed in the Classical Revival style in 1904 by architect Herman Miller who specialized in bank buildings. It was one of several neighborhood banks that helped fuel the textile industry in Philadelphia. Two other banks of the same era, the Industrial Trust, Title & Savings Bank and Ninth National Bank , stood at 1952-1958 N. Front Street, but were demolished in June 2023 after decades of neglect.
 In 2012, the Textile National Bank was included in the Kensington Textile Historic District on the National Register of Historic Places as a contributing property and was added to the Philadelphia Register in 2017. The Historical Commission offered comments in support of the nomination.
 A photograph of Textile National Bank circa 1900s. | Photo courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 Each month, the Historical Commission reviews and votes on exterior alterations to properties on the local register after a review by the Architectural Committee. The rules and regulations call for Commission approval before the work is done. However, this requirement is sometimes ignored by property owners. If discovered, the owners appear before the Historical Commission to request the legalization of the work. In 2025, this happened at more than half of the Commission’s meetings, including this one. Most frequently, windows and doors inappropriate for the historical nature of the building had been installed. At the meetings, the owners are reminded that they could have enlisted the advice of the Historical Commission and its staff in selecting appropriate materials.
 No new properties were added to the Philadelphia Register during December's meeting.
 Nominations are first reviewed by the Historical Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation, which meets less frequently than the full Commission. The Committee does not meet in November, and its December meeting has been cancelled. In January, the Committee on Historic Designation meeting is scheduled for two weeks after the Historical Commission’s meeting, so the next time new nominations can be considered by the Commission will be at its February 13, 2026 meeting. The Committee on Historic Designation has six meetings scheduled for 2026. In 2025, it had eight meetings scheduled, although two were cancelled.
 National Marine Engineers Beneficial Association Office at 428-34 N. 4th Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 On the Historical Commission’s website, three nominations that have each been continued over time are listed as “under consideration.” The list includes the National Marine Engineers Beneficial Association Office at 428-34 N. 4th Street (nominated January 2025), Piers 38 & 40 South at 775 S. Christopher Columbus Boulevar d (nominated October 2021), and Jewelers' Row Historic District (nominated March 2017).
 The nomination for 428-34 North 4th Street was submitted on January 8, the property owner was notified on January 17, 2025, and at that time it came under the protection of the Historical Commission as if it was already designated. On May 21, i t was reviewed by the Committee on Historic Designation, which voted to recommend designation owing to the building’s distinguishing characteristics of the New Formalism architectural style, representing the post-war turn to Modernist architecture in the United States, and as part of the Callowhill East Redevelopment Project, exemplifying the economic and political heritage of the community in the era of urban renewal. Committee members also noted how the building is representative of Philadelphia’s labor history as well as the historic location of the city's port along the Delaware River waterfront before operations moved to South Philadelphia in the 1960s. The Committee also complimented the nominator for their thorough research.
 A rendering of 428-34 N. 4th Street from the 1960s. | Image courtesy of Misha Wyllie via MEBA Archives
 In a letter dated December 15 , Richard Hasz, president & CEO of Gift of Life Howie’s House, the owner of an adjacent property at 401 Callowhill Street, requested that designation of 428-34 N. 4th Street be denied, stating that the organization had “recently entered into an agreement of sale.”
 When asked about the three nominations, a spokesperson for the Historical Commission responded that the Marine Engineers building will be reviewed at the January 2026 meeting and Piers 38 and 40 is potentially slated for that meeting as well. “The Jewelers' Row Historic District – continued indefinitely,” they noted in an email. “During the continuance, the district is treated as though it is designated. The Historical Commission is reviewing all building permit applications for properties in the district.”
 Tags: Historical Commission Meeting Report Kensington Kensington banks Midcentury Modern modernism National Register of Historic Places Philadelphia Historical Commission Piers 38 and 40 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: History Repeating Itself: What Market East’s Original Urban Planner Thinks About the Beleaguered Corridor
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
In the 1960s, John Gallery was just a whippersnapper fresh out of Harvard’s architectural program when he went to work for the Philadelphia Planning Commission under influential executive director Ed Bacon . That would launch an accomplished career that saw Gallery help create and lead the City’s Office of Housing and Community Development before leaving public service to head up private and nonprofit enterprises focused on historic preservation.
 Gallery, now 85, retired about a decade ago. Yet, from his 8th-floor apartment overlooking the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, he still keeps an eagle’s watch over Philadelphia’s land use. A thick stack of papers on his dining room table constitute his unpublished memoir, and tabs mark the places Gallery sees history repeating itself. Particularly, that is, along Market East.
 The City of Philadelphia has 1000-46 Market Street in its crosshairs for redevelopment, yet there is no definitive master plan nor any conceptual ideas currently in the works. | Photo:Michael Bixler
 Gallery’s first assignment after arriving in Philadelphia in 1964 was to try and effectuate redevelopment plans along the corridor, stretching along Market Street from City Hall to 9th Street. Power players in the city–the executives of then-dominant department stores such as Strawbridge’s and Gimbels, as well as some politicos–had been trying for the better part of a decade to successfully adapt to changing demographics and consumer preferences. Ideas about better transportation planning, open streets for pedestrians, major new construction, and even the possibility of a sports stadium were being cast about. Yet, little, it seemed, was getting done. Sound familiar?
 I recently sat down with Gallery to discuss his tenure working on Market East for the City, what he makes of recent developments along the corridor, and what lessons from the past he thinks might be valuable for the present day. This resulting interview has been edited for length and clarity.
 1000 Market Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Kyle Bagenstose (KB): Tell us about what challenges Market East faced when you first got started.
 John Gallery (JG): In the 1950s there was a median in the middle of Market Street with buses running down lanes on either side: NJ Transit, Trailways, Greyhound, city buses, lots of cars. So, the concern of the merchants was not making it a better retail area, but that there was a lot of congestion on the street. The first plans were to remove the buses and do something to help get rid of the cars. In 1957, Wilhelm von Moltke develops a plan to put in a parking garage and a bus terminal and four office buildings with little courtyards in-between. The idea was that the parking garage and bus terminal would be linked to the Vine Street Expressway by ramps running though Chinatown–the Planning Commission didn’t recognize the existence of Chinatown at the time. The plan had a lot of detractors. There were reports the bus terminal was not economically feasible, and there was no market for office development.
 There was also a proposal to build a commuter rail tunnel and demolish all the buildings along that route including Reading Terminal, which remained sort of the primary plan up until 1963. Edmund Bacon was severely criticized for not hiring Louis Kahn to be consultant, so he hired him in a token gesture kind of way. They didn’t get along.
 The property owners on Market Street were not happy with these plans, so they formed their own committee under the old Philadelphia Development Corporation, consisting of the presidents of Strawbridge’s, Lits, Gimbels, Wanamaker’s, and PSFS bank. They hired Victor Gruen , who was the most famous shopping center architect in the country. He proposed closing Market Street, making it a pedestrian mall, and having the north-south streets bridge over Market, which, of course, was ridiculous. The clients rejected that plan immediately in early 1963, but Bacon felt very threatened by this idea of them going off and doing their own plan.
 KB : It’s interesting they bring in Gruen, who is sort of the father of the American shopping mall, which by that point is already starting to gut urban department stores. They really weren’t worried about their competitiveness in a changing market?
 JG : At that point, I would say the interest starts to shift. All of these plans continue to have parking and bus terminal facilities, but increasingly the focus becomes the retail shopping complex and what that was going to be. If you think about a regional shopping center, usually there is a department store at both ends and a lot of little stores in between. So here you have Wanamaker’s on one end and Strawbridge’s, Lits, and Gimbels at the other. Market Street worked very well that way.
 KB : On your dining room table here you have a timeline printed out counting nine total plans for Market East between Von Moltke’s in 1957 and the Fashion District in 2019. There are other big names who take a stab at it like Romaldo Guirgola. The fourth plan that you made, in 1964, gets modified, but ultimately approved, and basically becomes The Gallery of the 1970s through 2010s. Tell us about that legacy and whether you view it as successful.
 JG : What seemed fairly obvious to me was, if you want a continuous pedestrian shopping mall, you put it one level below the street and connect it to this new train station (now Jefferson Station). The department stores approved this. The Planning Commission approved this. It was the first plan that everyone agreed to.
 At the time of the first phase (1977), it was the most economically successful urban shopping complex in the United States. So, there was pressure to do a second phase. I had moved to Texas in-between, but for the second phase I returned. Mayor Frank Rizzo asked me to come back. People do not like to give Frank Rizzo credit for anything. He may have been a controversial police commissioner, but without Rizzo Market East would never have been accomplished. He got behind the plan and convinced Nixon to give federal funds necessary for the first phase. There was a signing of agreements in 1979 for the second phase.
 The problem is that (next Mayor) Bill Green sat on it and started questioning it. Eventually it got built, but a second courtyard was eliminated and there was no major entrance on the west end. The commuter tunnel opened in 1984 and, in a certain way, that was the end until the Fashion District.
 One thing that I think contributes to its failure [The Fashion District redesign] is that they changed it so that you don’t go down into anything. You come in at street level, you walk down the mall, and when you get to the end, instead of being able to exit back onto Market Street, you exit onto Filbert Street. Why would anyone want to do that? The fact that there’s no real entrance to the mall part, it’s always made it a strange plan to me.
 1010-18 Market Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 KB : So, overall, success or failure? Did Market East accomplish the redevelopment vision of 60 years ago?
 JG : Even when they closed The Gallery, it was economically profitable. It wasn’t like it was losing money. It was like, “We want something different. We want something like Plymouth Meeting Mall.” So, planning what could happen on Market East, I think you really have to think, "Where are the important customers?" It’s not just bringing people from Chestnut Hill. What would make East Market Street meaningful to the communities that are closest to it?
 [At this point in the interview, Gallery sketches a map showing the connectivity of public transit between Market East and West Philadelphia via the Market Street subway line, and North Philadelphia via the Broad-Ridge subway spur, which lets out at 8th and Market].
 The clientele for Market East was principally the Black community. Some people might say it was a failure, but it was relevant to a large group of people and still made money for the owners.
 KB : Let’s talk about power players and how big land use and planning decisions like these get made. Who called the shots in your day, and how does that compare to now?
 JG : One thing that’s changed is that almost all of these plans were done during a period where there was a substantial amount of federal funding for rebuilding cities. An important piece of the funding was a program called Urban Development Action Grants, which were federal grants leveraged by private investment. The City was obviously in a strong role since it was the only one that could get access to those funds, but it needed to have partnerships with the private sector. This no longer exists, so it’s not like the mayor can come in and say, “Well we’ll apply to HUD for $20 million to do XYZ, if you’ll do ABC.” There’s a different financial climate than existed during the era of all those other plans up to the Fashion District.
 And you have many more actors now. Center City District has its own ideas about some things. A 60-member task force is a large number to be a real decision-making body. When we created the Market East Development Corporation, I think it was like 10 members on the board. Something you could fit everyone around a table and make decisions.
 KB : Help us understand the motivations for Market East property owners to tear down buildings when there’s no plan for what comes next? It seems that is what happened with the Disney Hole and now we risk repeating history.
 JG : People always refer to the Disney Hole, and that somehow gives the impression that it was because of something related to Disney that the parking lot is there, which is not true. As soon as Gimbels got a new building built, they demolished their old building [on the site]. Yes, it’s unfortunate that there wasn’t something over all these many years that came along to be developed there, and I don’t know what the real explanation for that is, but it wasn’t that the Disney idea failed and then we got this vacant lot. It was that Gimbels moved.
 But private property owners can demolish anything they want anytime they want. They don’t have to have future plans for it. If you don’t have property on the land, you don’t have a real estate property tax on it. If they demolish it, ongoing expenses are probably less, right? They don’t have to worry about maintenance and vandalism. It’s hard to say you should wait until there’s a plan from their economic point of view.
 What I would say, and get myself in trouble, is that it’s been many years since the City Planning Commission did any planning. Many years. And that’s a handicap. It’s not that they could have anticipated the whole issue with the Sixers. But because the Planning Commission doesn’t think in planning terms–I mean, it's a reactive agency–then I think you are in a more difficult situation dealing with private property owners. If you had an effective Planning Commission, and someone there did go to a [landowner] and told them to wait a year to demo, if you were Frank Rizzo you could probably convince them to do that. Mayor Parker?
 1020 Market Street (aka the Robinson Building) | Photo: Michael Bixler
 KB : At the end of the day, this is all still a question of figuring out how to use Market East, which is something you’ve been thinking about for 60 years. Is there a way to revitalize it?
 JG : I don’t know the answer to that.
 Two things. One, take a walk on Walnut Street from 16th to 19th Street. Crowded with people. Are they all people living in Center City? I doubt it. So, obviously people will come to Center City if things are attractive.
 Streetscaping and walkability is a very important ingredient that I don’t think is discussed a whole lot. Frankly, I think you go back to 1957. Get the buses off the street, transform the street, make it an exciting environment, then, I think, many of these buildings along the way may adapt. For example, Market Street between 10th and 11th Streets–it’s all these glass walls that you can’t see anything through. The stores are big stores, it’s like three stores on the whole block. If you were on Walnut Street, there’d be 20 stores on the whole block and everyone would have a display window. And right now, the Marriott, I mean it’s a great facility, but walking down Market Street it’s like a blank wall. With Reading Terminal Headhouse, you’ve got Hard Rock Cafe on the corner and nothing else.
 But there is another side to it, which is maybe the east side of Market Street can’t be that again. Maybe the only thing you can do is build an apartment building with a couple of stores on the ground floor and not expect it to be a big, vital shopping district the way it was before. You look at photographs from the 1950s and the streets were packed with people,but there were no regional shopping centers.
 Again, the clientele for Market East was principally the Black community, so it may be that you can’t go back to the past. And maybe it doesn’t regain that functionality, but maybe it has a different function. You could change the composition of stores in the Fashion District that might make it more meaningful, but thinking we’re going to make it back into an equivalent of West Walnut Street–maybe that is the wrong direction.
 Tags: Development Edmund Bacon John Gallery Market East Victor Gruen 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: A Sweet New Space In Old City Completes Confectioner’s Row
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
The Cacao Pod at 104 Market Street. | Photo courtesy of Neal Santos
 Upon entry to The Cacao Pod , the new event and production space by owner Eric Berley of Franklin Fountain, Shane’s Confectionary, and Franklin’s Ice Cream Bar, beautiful antique elements fill the majority of the main room. Neo-Baroque oak panels and Solomonic columns engage the eyes. They were once interior features of a Main Line mansion during the late 19 th century before being removed in the 1950s. The carved oak counters were originally used in a Victorian confectionery shop on East Girard Avenue in the 1880s. Hanging overhead is a caramel slag glass ceiling that was originally installed by Zipf’s Candies in Reading, Pennsylvania. Wooden trays on the bathroom walls were once used to cool and transport chocolates. A church pew transported from Wallingford Presbyterian Church sits off to the side, and was stained to match the interior of 104 Market Street. 
 100 Block of Market 
 The theme of reusing and saving historic spaces and materials is not only established within the interior of The Cacao Pod, but almost the entire 100 block of Market Street, which currently has the distinction of being continuously utilized as store fronts since their original construction in the late 18th century.
 Immediately connecting the space to what was once known as Publisher’s Row, of which Benjamin Franklin’s own shop existed on what is currently the westbound entrance of the Market Frankford Line's 2nd Street Station, is a historical marker for printer and bookseller Robert Aitken, which sits right outside of 104 Market Street. Aitken was given approval by Congress to print the nation’s first English Bible in 1782. 
 By 1795, the first half of the block consisted of a number of shops which transitioned from Front Street to then High (current day Market) Street. According to the Philadelphia Directory, merchants James Stokes’ and Saddler and John Marr shared the lot at No. 16. Fruiterer Jacob Ernst occupied No.18. Samuel Read owned a shoe warehouse at No. 20. R. Aitken & Son, a printer and , bookbinders conducted business at No. 22.
 A lithograph from 1830 of London Coffee House. | Image: From Annals of Philadelphia by John Fanning Watson via Independence National Historical Park
 The following year the property on the southeast corner of Front and Market Streets, which included the London Coffee House, was extended to Aitkens' lot on High Street and was up for sale by Israel, Charles, and Joseph Pleasants. The property was noted as “a valuable lot of ground,” according to a Philadelphia Inquirer article dated September 8, 1796. The listing mentions Stokes having spent many years occupying “the merchants coffee house” and a proposal to divide the plot for future use as multiple store fronts. Having purchased the property, Stokes converted the site into both his home and a store.
 Throughout the first half of the 19th century, a number of shops came and went such as the shoe store of John H. Broetigan, suspenders maker James Davis, Jonathan Squier and Company's hat warehouse, and tailor John Horgbin.
 By the late 1850s going into the following decade, the lot at 104 Market served multiple roles as a restaurant owned by James Pollett, a home to blacksmith William Milligan, and Joseph Rau & Brothers', clothing store. 112 Market Street was a confectionary supply business owned by Samuel Herring, which later extended into a family run confectionary shop at 110 by 1863. At this point 100 Market Street is now occupied by Ulrich & Brother’s Tobacco & Segar Store, followed by Phillip Hunt’s clothing store for boys now adjacent to William Umberger’s merchandise shop at 102 Market Street. By 1883, the site on the southwest corner was razed and subdivided to be replaced by what is currently 100 Market Street.
 Confectioner’s Row 
 104 Market Street was last used by Uzu Sushi. | Photo courtesy of Neal Santos
 The sushi restaurant that was the previous occupant of 104 Market Street vacated in 2024 leaving behind grease-soaked under flooring, an ice bin, dropped ceilings, and the possibility that the downstairs space could be structurally altered.
 “We moved the chocolate cafe from the back of Shane's over to 104 Market Street for more visibility," said Berley. “In the end-we settled on a hybrid space model of production and catering private events. Preservation of historic properties is central to the Berley Brothers and the brands we created. Adaptations and reuse are organically driven by the changing needs of both our company and guests' desire.”
 Eric Berley, co-owner of The Cacao Pod, Franklin Fountain, Shane’s Confectionary, and Franklin’s Ice Cream Bar serves up the sweet stuff. | Photo courtesy of Neal Santos
 The Berley Brothers currently have four locations in Old City: The Cacao Pod (104 Market Street), Shane’s Confectionary (110 Market Street), Franklin’s Ice Cream Bar (112 Market Street) and Franklin Fountain (116 Market Street). The idea to make the 100 block of Market Street a "Confectioner’s Row" had been floated to form a connection to past confectioners who also worked and lived in the area like Benjamin Jackson and August Jackson (no relation) who both created their own style of sweet treats while living in Philadelphia.
 The 100 Block of Market street in 1982. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 Jumping back to the later half of the 20th century, the possibility of the block's current outcome would have been unfathomable. As throughout the period the 100 block went through a decline that by the late 1990s left much of it abandoned. Old photos from the early 1980s reveals a number of merchants including a Cheese shop (108 Market Street) staple Shane’s Candy Company (110 Market Street) then owned by the Shane family, Feitig’s A New/Used Discount Office Furniture Co (112 Market Street), what appears to be a Independence Franklin Cream (116 Street), Wagner’s Meats (118 Market Street), Youngs Restaurant Supply Shop, and a unnamed Sign Shop (122 Market Street), Hendler’s Radios, Tires, and Appliances (124 Market Street), Arrow Drugs (126 Market Street), and Agency Furniture & Appliance store, and a money for loan shop (128 Market Street). 120 Market Street appears to be abandoned while the photo quality of 114 shows a store front but the signage is too low quality to read.
 Although The Cacao Pod will be closed to walk-in traffic, the Berley Brothers have partnered with Historic Philadelphia to establish a tour program. It will allow small groups to experience an immersive deep dive into historic confectioners and recipes that have been reproduced and sold at Shane’s to allow visitors to sample a variety of offerings.
 Tags: adaptive resuse bars and restaurants Old City 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: "Roundhouse Reimagined" Explores New Uses for a Modernist Landmark
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
South elevation. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott
