 After nearly four years of sitting vacant, the former Police Administration Building, aka the Roundhouse , is receiving attention again with new ideas for repurposing the iconic modernist building at 7th and Race Streets. The Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia and Docomomo US/Greater Philadelphia (DocomomoPHL) have teamed up to present a half-day symposium to present a handful of responses to a call for concepts they issued last month.
 “The idea of the symposium is to shine a spotlight on the building, to keep it in the forefront of people’s minds,” explained Dan Macey, president of DocomomoPHL.
 When it was planned in 1959, the new Police Administration building was intended to be a symbol of the aspirations for the City of two progressive mayors, Joseph Clark and Richardson Dilworth, the first Democrats elected in over 70 years. They chose a young local architectural firm, Geddes Brecher Qualls & Cunningham (GPQC) to design a new home for the police department, along with a new image after decades of corruption. David Geddes, son of the late Robert Geddes of GBQC, said the mayors’ plans matched his father’s outlook. “He was at heart an idealist. That’s why he related to Richardson Dilworth’s ideas for the city. The building was to be emblematic of community service and welcoming to the public.”
 Looking east from rooftop. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott
 The subsequent mayoral administration of former Philadelphia Police Commissioner Frank Rizzo bestowed a different image on the Roundhouse, as the police department became notorious for brutality, especially among Black citizens.
 A department move to 400 N. Broad Street in 2022 raised the question of what to do with the Roundhouse. The City hosted a lengthy series of community engagement forums , noting that it was the first time they’d done so prior to offering a request for proposals to developers. Of the responses they received, two of the most frequent were to use the building for some form of community benefit and to acknowledge, rather than try to erase, its history.
 Later that year, the Preservation Alliance and DocomomoPHL submitted a nomination for the Roundhouse to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. In November, 2024, it was rejected by the Philadelphia Historical Commission under the order of Mayor Cherelle Parker .
 First floor, main lobby, looking west from south entrance. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott
 Today, although the Roundhouse is vacant and unused, it remains a potent and distinctive architectural landmark. “It was detailed very simply, but very nicely. For its time, it was an architectural marvel,” remarked Jack Pyburn, an architectural historian at Georgia Technical University who has extensively studied the building.
 “It was very striking at the time,” recalled Geddes. “Though the exterior isn’t clean now, back then at night it would be a luminous presence. It was a beacon.”
 The Roundhouse is so striking that both its exterior and interior appeared recently in the HBO series Task in the role of the Philadelphia headquarters for the FBI.
 It remained one of Robert Geddes’s favorite projects. “In the last 10 or 12 years, my father had decided he wanted a webpage, ” Geddes said. “I think he had worked on 300 or 350 buildings during his career. For the webpage he picked three: the Moore School of Electrical Engineering’s Pender Labs at the University of Pennsylvania [since demolished], the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, and the Police Administration Building.”
 First floor, auditorium. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott
 After the Historical Commission’s refusal to acknowledge the building's architectural value, advocates were determined to keep the building and its fate in the public eye. “We’re in the process of submitting an Historic American Building Survey to the Library of Congress for the Roundhouse,” noted Macey. “We’ve taken photos in the format they require and are now working on the submission.”
 The symposium aims to generate interest and support both in architectural, design, and historic circles as well as the general public. “I think the exercise for ideas was most valuable in engaging people with the building,” Pyburn said. “That’s distinguished from determining the best use of it.”
 “We put out an open call for ideas. We felt it was important to not limit who could respond,” explained Hanna Stark, director of policy and communications at the Preservation Alliance. “And we’re going to record the symposium so it can reach a wide audience. We want it to be impactful and start a conversation.”
 Second floor, corridor connecting east and west areas of building. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott
 A Q&A webinar with 60 attendees yielded 31 submissions this summer. A jury of architects and design professionals selected six to make presentations at the symposium. “We also named nine ‘honorable mentions’ and offered them an opportunity to display a poster presentation of their ideas,” said Stark. “There were some common themes and some uses that a lot of people were thinking about.”
 The six presentations will be from the Design Advocacy Group, Ian Smith Design Group, KieranTimberlake, Parallel Architecture Studio, RVA Architecture, and SSPJ Design.
 In addition to the presentations of selected concepts, the event will include remarks by David Geddes and Philadelphia Inquirer architecture critic Inga Saffron, a keynote address by Alan Greenberger, former chief city planner and currently the vice president of real estate and facilities and a professor at Drexel University, and a panel discussion moderated by David Brownlee, professor of the History of Art emeritus at the University of Pennsylvania.
 Third floor, executive office outer reception area and executive office. | Photos: Joseph E. B. Elliott
 Although not one of the presenters on the agenda, representatives from the Philadelphia Chinatown Development Corporation will be participating. The group has long advocated for the building to be reused to benefit their neighborhood, which is immediately to the west and whose growth had been thwarted by the construction of both the Pennsylvania Convention Center and the Vine Street Expressway.
 The producers of the symposium had hoped to offer a tour of the Roundhouse that would include visiting the interior, but as of press time, they had not received permission from the City. A tour of the building’s exterior will be led by William Whitaker, curator and collections manager of the Architectural Archives of the University of Pennsylvania Weitzman School of Design.
 Having collaborated on the Roundhouse nomination to the Philadelphia Register, DocomomoPHL and the Preservation Alliance are now working on its nomination to the National Register of Historic Places. The first step is to submit it to the State Historic Preservation Office of the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission by its next deadline in December. “We believe the building has national significance,” said Stark. “But to see how it presents itself elsewhere, we are working with readers from other states.”
 Lower level, prisoner holding area. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott
 The symposium producers see the event as a first step to move the City’s seemingly stalled process forward. “The last we heard, the City was planning to do some sort of RFP on it. But they don’t seem to be planning anything very soon,” said Macey. “While the City is deciding on an RFP, the building is in good shape and still viable for immediate use.” An attempt to reach representatives from the City’s Department of Public Property was unsuccessful.
 “We hope the City will see the submissions and get an idea or two to include in any RFP,” Macey added.
 “Maybe this will spark some interest by a developer to repurpose it and put the rest of the lot to good use,” said Geddes. With its 2.6-acre parcel zoned CMX-4 Center City Commercial Mixed-Use, Stark feels it can address the Parker administration’s priority of creating affordable housing. “The parking lot should be developed for more density in housing. We hope to demonstrate that this can be well positioned to increase affordable housing.”
 Overview, looking northwest from Federal Reserve Bank. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott
 Although lacking any real agency with regards to the building’s fate, advocates for the Roundhouse remain hopeful and enthusiastic. “In a sense, time is on its side," said Pyburn. “The more people learn about it, the more they appreciate it.”
 “It would be great to invigorate the space with more access,” said Stark. “Having it be a welcoming open space would be important.”
 Roundhouse Reimagined: A Symposium Looking at Reusing, Repurposing and Reinvigorating the Modern Marvel will be held on Wednesday, October 29 from 1 p.m – 6 p.m. at WHYY Studios, 150 North Sixth Street. Purchase tickets here: https://preservationalliance.com/all_events/roundhouse-reimagined/ 
 Tags: adaptive resuse Brutalism Midcentury Modern modernism Police Administration Building 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: A Symposium Explores Anna Wilstach and the Fine Art of Philanthropy
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
Philadelphia's Gilded Age is synonymous with wealthy industrialists and the opulence left in their wake. Most people can rattle off the names: Wanamaker, Drexel, Elkins, Widener, et al. What about Anna Wilstach? If you have never heard of her, you are not alone.
 Wilstach had all the trappings of her privileged class. A rich husband, a mansion on Rittenhouse Square, servants, and an art collection valued in the millions in today's currency. While her life was not remarkable in the elite circles in which she traveled, Wilstach's philanthropy was exceptional by any standard. She helped launch the Philadelphia Museum of Art (PMA), and her endowment continues to underwrite PMA's purchase of important acquisitions.
 Dr. Brian D. Seymour, associate professor of art history at Community College of Philadelphia, traces Wilstach's legacy to a pivotal event. "In 1864, there were very few places in the United States to see art. A Civil War Union Army fundraising event, the Great Central Fair , was held in Logan Square featuring a big art gallery with paintings stacked to the sky," Seymour explained. President Abraham Lincoln attended the fair, as did Philadelphia's elite, including Anna and her husband William P. Wilstach, and the general public. No one had ever seen such a display of European art in the United States. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City would not exist for over a quarter of a century.
 A daguerreotype portrait of Anna H. Wilstach taken circa 1846. | Photo courtesy of The Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 That same year, William, a saddlery hardware manufacturer, retired. The couple embarked upon building a European art collection which eventually anchored PMA. It may well have been at this time that Anna first grasped the concept that viewing fine art could enhance quality of life for the general public. Yet, her name is not to be found anywhere in the museum she helped create.
 "The original Wilstach Collection of 381 objects and endowment belonged to Anna's husband William H. Wilstach who predeceased her by 22 years," said Jennifer Thompson, curator of European art and sculpture at PMA. "During those years, Anna invested wisely, doubling the value of her husband's estate. More importantly, she constantly and methodically revised her will to reflect, not just her husband's wishes, but her own. Leaving her name out of her bequest was typical in the Victorian era," said Thompson.
 In other ways, Anna was ahead of her time. According to his will, William thought visitors to his proposed museum should buy a subscription. Anna's bequest made it clear that the Wilstach Collection was "for the enjoyment and benefit of the public… for free." This was a radical concept in the late 19th century when there were no public art museums in the city. Visiting the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts required a subscription well above the means of the average citizen. While William only gifted funds to a handful of institutions, Anna's will endowed 50 Philadelphia organizations, including hospitals, schools, churches, and charities.
 Bust of William P. Wilstach , 1870 by artist William Henry Rinehart. | Image courtesy of Philadelphia Museum of Art
 However, Anna adhered to her husband's wishes that the collection was to be displayed in Memorial Hall, the Beaux Arts building in West Fairmount Park that served as a gallery of industrial art for the 1876 Centennial Exposition and is now the Please Touch Museum. "At the time of her bequest, half the gallery housed the Pennsylvania Museum of Decorative Arts and the Wilstach Collection was to be displayed in the other half, giving the city its first collection of European paintings," said Thompson. When the Philadelphia Museum of Art opened in 1932 the Wilstach Collection moved there along with its endowment.
 Most of the original collection is no longer at PMA. "Anna and her husband collected what was contemporary art in 1870s. Victorian taste was sentimental, and she was aware that taste changed. She wanted it to be a living collection reflecting the best and highest art," Thompson explained. "We have a dozen works from the original collection that remain on view, but we have sold things and reinvested those funds which allow us to buy extraordinary art. She left a robust endowment with specific wishes how it adds to the culture richness of City of Philadelphia. Anna's bequest in 1892 has enabled us to buy 16,000 acquisitions over the years, starting with The Annunciation by African American artist Henry Ossawa Tanner in 1899, Cezanne's The Large Bathers in 1937, and Ruben's Prometheus Bound ," said Thompson.
 Trinity Memorial Church hosts an annual concert series in its sanctuary. | Photo courtesy of Trinity Memorial Church
 Another act of generosity undertaken while Anna was still alive continues to directly impact the quality of life in Philadelphia. Following the untimely death of her 16 year-old daughter, and, later, her husband and only surviving daughter, Anna was bereft. Rather than closing herself off from the world, she opened herself to the needs of others. In memory of her late daughter, Anna purchased land on the southwest corner of 22nd and Spruce Streets for $50,000 and paid for the construction of Trinity Memorial Church. It was designed by architect James P. Sims. When Trinity Memorial opened, three years after Anna Wilstach's death in 1895, it was not just another church, but a mission that offered classes for immigrants and where anyone could worship without paying for a pew. Anna, who spent over $1,000 for her own pew at The Church of the Holy Trinity four blocks away, knew what she was doing.
 "Anna Wilstach followed a familiar Victorian pattern in which grief was turned into civic engagement," said Michael J. Krasulski, historian of the Episcopal Diocese of Philadelphia. "That little church, which she built and endowed, became a powerhouse for social justice. Although it is one of the smaller Episcopalian churches in Philadelphia, Trinity Memorial became an early center of progressive ministry," he explained. "Starting in the 1960s, it took the lead in the ordination of women and outreach to the LGBTQ+ community,"
 On Saturday, October 18, Trinity Memorial Church will host The Power of Generosity: Celebrating the Enduring Legacy of Anna Wilstach in Philadelphia at 2212 Spruce Street. The symposium, part of the church's 150th anniversary celebration, is free and open to the public. Register for the event here: https://sites.google.com/trinityat22nd.org/celebratingourfounder/home 
 Tags: Events historic churches Women's history 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: AIA Philadelphia Sets Sail for the Avenue of the Arts
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
AIA Philadelphia is changing its location. "We have been at 1218 Arch Street for 17 years. We love the space," said Danielle DiLeo Kim, AIA board president and founder of DDK Urban Consulting. So why the move? A substantial amount of AIA's income came from renting event space and leasing its basement to a printing company. When the organization lost its main tenant, and the pandemic slammed the brakes on events, the numbers did not crunch.
 In February 2025, AIA voted to sell its building, not knowing where they would land. "We wanted to get out of the business of owning and managing an event space so we could better focus on serving our professional membership and our mission to serve the public," said DiLeo Kim.
 As the second oldest AIA chapter in the nation, as well as one of the largest, representing 250 architectural firms and 1,500 architects, AIA Philadelphia does not make sudden moves. Founded in 1869 on the third floor of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia, AIA waited almost 100 years before relocating in 1966 to the Architects Building, 117 S. 17th Street, a 24-story Art Deco office tower built in 1930 (now the Hotel Palomar). The alluring AIA bookstore/gift shop at 17th and Sansom Streets did a thriving business. It would be 42 years before AIA moved to 1218 Arch Street.
 Meanwhile, Lindsey Scannapieco, founding partner of Scout Urban Design, the firm behind the creative and successful repurposing of Bok Technical High School, was bidding on former University of the Arts buildings . She was hoping to reproduce Bok's success on Avenue of the Arts, but the competition, including a Miami residential developer, had deep pockets.
 Hamilton Hall at 320 S. Broad Street was built for The Pennsylvania Institute for the Deaf between 1824-26 and designed by John Haviland. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 "We've known Lindsey for a long time and were following her on social media," said Rebecca Johnson, AIA executive director. "We were afraid the historic UArts buildings would be turned into condos. We advocated and supported Lindsey's bid to win the property in bankruptcy court."
 With political support from City Council, and a $8+ million bridge loan from an unknown investor, Scout's $12.25 million bid succeeded. AIA didn't waste time. A tour of Hamilton Hall at 320 S. Broad Street, motivated AIA to become one of its first tenants of the Village of Industry & Art (VIA).
 "The buildings were in remarkably good shape," said DiLeo Kim. Scannapieco isn't doing a full gut renovation. Other than repairing, reopening, and installing signage, they are matching tenants with existing spaces. Architects bringing VIA up to speed include Jules Dingle, the co-founding partner of DIGSAU, and Sam Olshin, a principal at Atkin Olshin Schade.
 Two of AIA's nonprofit partners are also moving to VIA: DesignPhiladelphia and Community Design Collaborative. Other organizations moving to VIA include Monument Lab, BlackStar Projects, and the Stained Glass Project.
 The atrium of Hamilton Hall. | Photo courtesy of Mike Persico via Village of Industry & Art
 "This move was about synchronicity. In 2024, when UArts shut down, we had no idea we would end up there. We looked at a few other spaces. VIA was an organic solution," explained DiLeo Kim. "Our space on the first floor of Hamiliton Hall is large enough to host 50 people for a lecture. Plus, there are four larger spaces that will be available to us, including a huge atrium. We did a space analysis, and 95 percent of events we did on Arch Street we will be able to do here." The central location at Broad and Pine Streets, along with AIA being on the first floor, will be a natural draw for public engagement.
 The right fit isn't just about the floor plan. It's the concept at the heart of VIA–converting over 110,000 square feet and 1.9 acres into maker studios and spaces, plus affordable housing for artists. The housing program realigns with Furness Hall’s original purpose as a dormitory. In addition, ceramic, woodworking, plaster, and metal shops will be available for leasing.
 "It's going to be great for our staff to work with so many creatives," said DiLeo Kim, who envisions a communal retail space on the first floor showcasing VIA's makers and creatives and perhaps a small cafe to loiter over a book or croissant. While it will not be a return of AIA's legendary and much missed bookstore, it will give visitors a glimpse into the diversity of the VIA's tenants.
 In retrospect, Scannapieco could have developed a Bok spin-off in many other parts of the city like Fishtown to University City. Her interest in the almost 200 year-old former UArts building was, in part, due to its similarity to the Bok, a former vocational school. Both were schools that closed due to declining enrollment and budget cuts. Like the Bok, the potential of Hamilton and Furness Hall as a home for nonprofits, makers, small retailers, artists, exhibitions, and special events is obvious. There is a strong sense of continuity in converting a former art school into a community of arts-driven organizations.
 Furness Hall at 15th and Pine Streets was built in 1875 and designed by Frank Furness. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Hamilton Hall, where AIA will set up shop, was originally designed for The Pennsylvania Institute for the Deaf between 1824-26 by John Haviland, and later expanded by William Strickland, with an addition in 1887 by Frank Furness. It became the Pennsylvania Museum and School of Industrial Art in 1893 and was renamed Philadelphia College of Art in 1964. It became University of the Arts in 1987. Thanks to the vision of Scannapieco and the presence of AIA, Philadelphia's oldest extant building on Avenue of the Arts will not only be preserved, but will continue its 133-year role as a center for the arts.
 “We were thrilled when AIA Philadelphia decided to come on as one of our anchor tenants for the Village of Industry & Art," said Scannapieco. "As one of the city’s most important conveners across architecture and design, they exemplify exactly what we’re building here—a community of people who could be anywhere in the city, creating their own worlds and centers of gravity, but want to be in a place energized by potential collaborators, partners, and colleagues," she explained. "We are united by a belief that in communities like these, the whole can truly be greater than the sum of its parts. We are so glad they are joining us at the beginning of our journey to help set the tone.”
 Chances are you have walked by Hamilton Hall on your way to the Kimmel, Suzanne Roberts Theatre or the Arden. Maybe you sent your kids to Saturday classes at UArts or watched the Mummers Parade from its marble steps. Now, you have a reason to explore what's inside and see what the excitement is all about.
 Tags: adaptive resuse AIA Philadelphia University of the Arts

Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local.
