title: Op-Ed: How Philadelphia Is Streamlining Capital Projects Under One Roof
author: Aparna Palantino
bodyText:
Months after being sworn into office, Mayor Cherelle Parker established the Capital Program Office (CPO) through an executive order with one big goal: to help the City deliver capital projects more effectively and efficiently. Mayor Parker identified this as a priority need because nearly every City department relies on public facilities—from libraries to fire stations—and safe, functional spaces are key to delivering high-quality services to residents.
 Capital planning is the process cities use to plan, fund, and manage investments in public infrastructure. Effective planning ensures that public facilities are functional and aligned with community priorities, while balancing limited resources and long-term sustainability. The creation of a centralized office enables us to take a holistic view of what is working, and what isn’t, across the hundreds of capital projects the City manages.
 Our mission is straightforward in concept, yet challenging to execute: complete capital projects on time and within budget, while ensuring a meaningful community impact. Our team manages individual project budgets, oversees design and construction, helps shape the capital budget, and develops strategies to accelerate project completion.
 Cobbs Creek community members gathered on September 12, 2025 for a community planting day at Johnny Sample Recreation Center. Neighbors and City officials gathered to plant over 2,000 native plant species. | Photo courtesy of Capital Program Office
 Why CPO Is a Necessary and Critical Department in the Parker Administration 
 Big wins don’t come from one bold move, but from small, steady improvements that help us achieve bold goals over time. That is the mindset we are bringing to how our team manages public projects.
 Philadelphia is an old city with aging infrastructure. Over the years, our city faced significant obstacles in maintaining its public facilities, including its wealth of beautiful historic buildings. These buildings are a tremendous asset, but a historic budget shortfall for maintenance and capital improvements has created deep and lasting challenges. There is no single fix, but by identifying small improvements at every step–from planning to expediting internal processes–I believe we will see real progress.
 That is why Mayor Parker created CPO. Not to promise the impossible, but to bring subject matter experts from across City government together to focus on the unglamorous, often hidden work that keeps projects on track.
 Scaling Impact Across the City 
 Among the city’s most impactful investments are those in our shared public spaces—recreation centers, libraries, and parks.
 Rebuild , launched under former Mayor Jim Kenney's administration and funded by the beverage tax and a $100 million gift from the William Penn Foundation, represents a $500 million investment in 72 neighborhood spaces, most in Philadelphia’s highest-need communities.
 Rebuild’s early years weren’t without challenges, from pandemic delays to slow construction timelines. Mayor Parker established the Capital Program Office, not to gloss over the challenges faced by Rebuild and other City capital projects, but to confront them head-on to carry forward what works and fix what doesn’t.
 By taking a high-level view of all City construction projects, we’re doing exactly that–identifying bottlenecks, finding opportunities for collaboration, and implementing standardized practices across all projects to address delays. When projects fall behind or exceed budgets, CPO works with departments to develop corrective action plans and realign resources.
 In the first six months of 2025, Rebuild alone celebrated five ribbon cuttings and two groundbreakings, representing a $64 million investment in Philadelphia communities. The department as a whole celebrated 22 completed projects and five groundbreakings, totaling $96 million invested in public space.
 This incredible momentum reflects the dedication of City staff, past and present, community partners, and project funders.
 With roughly 200-plus active construction projects in our portfolio at any given time, our challenge now is to take every project as an opportunity to build trust, increase transparency with communities, expand economic opportunity, and deepen partnerships with those who share our vision of a safer, cleaner, greener city with access to economic opportunity for all.
 The Riverview Wellness Village: Addressing Critical Community Needs 
 The Riverview Wellness Village exemplifies CPO's comprehensive approach to the mayor’s One Philly, A United City agenda. This 127,000-square-foot, 336-bed facility offers housing, healthcare, workforce development, and other support services for individuals transitioning from treatment to recovery. What would have taken 14 months under normal conditions, construction and renovations were completed in just 90 days.
 One of several renovated courtyards within the grounds of Riverview Wellness Center, originally designed by Cornelia Oberlander, a trailblazing landscape architect who was the first woman to graduate from Harvard’s landscape architecture program. | Photo courtesy of Capital Program Office
 CPO's management of Riverview’s design, construction, and opening demonstrates our ability to deliver projects that address urgent community needs. The interdepartmental coordination required for this success–bringing together health services, housing, and facility management experts from a variety of City departments–illustrates how centralized management can expedite projects that meet these needs.
 Reviving a Community Hub: The Vare Recreation Center Transformation 
 The renovation of Vare Recreation Center is a powerful example of how strong strategic partnerships can help supercharge public investment in community spaces. This $21 million project brought together the City, the William Penn Foundation, Make the World Better Foundation, the Philadelphia Eagles, and Southwest Philly residents to reimagine a facility that has served the Gray’s Ferry neighborhood for over a century.
 In partnership with the Make the World Better Foundation, we introduced upgrades that elevate the standard for recreation facilities. We transformed a city block with a new building and outdoor areas featuring playgrounds and recreation space. Support from partners like the Philadelphia Eagles, who funded the key athletic field improvements alongside contributions from the Rosenthal Foundation and state agencies, showcases how diverse partners can amplify public investment.
 The new and improved Vare Recreation Center in Gray's Ferry. | Photo courtesy of Capital Program Office
 Vare Recreation Center is now Rebuild’s largest completed project to date and was the first recreation center in the city to receive high-speed fiber optic internet. Vare is setting a new standard for what community-centered, tech-forward, and inclusive spaces can look like when collaboration is at the heart of the work. 
 Creating Economic Opportunity 
 CPO's mission extends far beyond physical construction. Through Rebuild's comprehensive Workforce Development Program and strategic contracting, the office creates meaningful, long-term economic opportunities throughout Philadelphia. The results speak for themselves. Nearly 55 percent of contract dollars flow to small businesses– concrete evidence of the City's commitment to ensuring public investment strengthens local communities and drives local economic growth.
 The impact reaches deep into Philadelphia's workforce. Through Rebuild's Skilled Trade Academies , more than 170 residents have been trained in trades like carpentry and masonry; over 70 percent secured union apprenticeships or full-time jobs.
 Business development forms another critical pillar of this strategy. Rebuild's Emerging Vendors Program has supported 74 small businesses, many of which expanded their capacity to bid on public contracts through City-sponsored training and mentorship.
 This integrated approach–leveraging capital investment to create new pathways into the skilled trades for residents and opportunities for businesses to develop–positions CPO as catalysts for economic opportunity in Philadelphia.
 The One Philly Vision in Action 
 The collaborative approach at Vare Recreation Center and Riverview Wellness Village, and the economic opportunities offered through our workforce development and business support programs, exemplify the mayor’s "One Philly" vision. These projects and programs show what’s possible when City departments, community partners, and funders work together towards a shared goal.
 For CPO, the "One Philly" approach means bringing together City departments, community stakeholders, and experts to solve problems and accelerate progress. Creating economic opportunities for residents alongside physical improvements. Identifying and addressing challenges early to ensure projects stay on track
 Yet, our commitment doesn’t end when the ribbon is cut. We invite residents to stay involved. Join your local park’s friends group, attend a community engagement meeting, register for the Skilled Trades Academy, or sign up to volunteer with Love Your Park.
 A better city isn’t built by government alone. It takes all of us working together.
 To learn more or connect with our office, drop us a line at CPO@phila.gov
 Tags: Department of Parks and Recreation Mayor Cherelle Parker op-ed Rebuild 
 About the Author
 Aparna Palantino Before taking the helm of the City of Philadelphia’s Capital Program Office Aparna Palantino served as a Deputy Commissioner for Capital Infrastructure in the Parks & Recreation Department. A public servant with more than 24 years of experience in the design and construction of municipal facilities, Palantino was born in India and has made her home in Philadelphia for the last 25 years.

title: Reuse Plan for Wanamaker's Grand Court Gets the Go-Ahead
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The John Wanamaker Department Store's Grand Court was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in July 2018. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At its meeting on January 9, the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved some of the first steps in the planned reuse of the John Wanamaker Department Store building at 1301-25 Chestnut Street. Designed in 1910 by the architectural firm of Daniel H. Burnham & Co., the iconic Palazzo-style building has been an object of concern after Macy’s closed its outpost there last year. Located just east of City Hall, it is considered a landmark anchor for the Market East corridor.
 The building was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1973, to the National Register of Historic Places in 1978, and has also been listed as a National Historic Landmark. The first-floor Grand Court was designated in 2018 —one of only five interiors on the local register, preceded by the bronze eagle statue within it, which was designated a historic object in 2001.
 A rendering showing new pockets of retail spaces for the Wanamaker Building's Grand Court.| Image: JKRP Architects
 The Historical Commission approved several changes to the building as part of its transition from a department store with offices to a mixed-use retail and residential building. The ground floor retail area will be divided into smaller individual retail spaces by the addition of bronze and glass storefront partitions. New entrances based on the building’s historic doorways will be inserted into the exterior window openings on the Market, Juniper, Chestnut, and 13th Street facades, and exterior tenant signage will be added. Two rooftop additions, a roof deck, and a pool will be constructed and will not be visible from the street.
 The Historical Commission also reviewed the beginning stages of the renovation of a pair of designated houses in Nicetown-Tioga. The Conkling-Armstrong House at 2224 and 2226 W. Tioga Street were designed in 1898 by architect Edgar Viguers Seeler, the architect behind the Curtis Publishing Building at 6th and Walnut Streets and the Real Estate Title & Trust Company Building at Broad and Chestnut Streets. The twin buildings were constructed as the homes of Thomas F. Armstrong and Ira L. Conkling and served as a showcase for the terracotta architectural ornaments created by their Conkling-Armstrong Terra Cotta Company, which was located at Wissahickon Avenue and Juniata Street.
 The Conkling-Armstrong House in February 2019. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 After sitting vacant and neglected for many years, the pair were purchased in 2021. The new owner received permission by the Historical Commission to shore up the buildings by demolishing the interiors. The third-floor mansard roof and dormers on the rear ell were also demolished, but with the condition that these elements would be reconstructed. The proposal includes reconstruction work along with preliminary plans for a three-story addition at the rear to create 12 apartments.
 Top: The entrance and rotunda of Overbrook School for the Blind at 6333 Malvern Avenue. Bottom: Wynnewood Hall apartments is slated for demolition to make way for new campus amenities.| Photos: Michael Bixler
 The Overbrook School for the Blind at 6333 Malvern Avenue was added to the local register in 1970 owing to its original buildings designed by the architectural firm Cope & Stewardson between 1897 and 1900. At the meeting, the school received permission from the Commission to demolish two non-contributing buildings constructed in the 1960s in order to build a new dining hall and assembly place and improve vehicular traffic flow through the campus.
 St. John’s Baptist Church at 1601 S. 13th Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Two other agenda items each involved the challenges sometimes posed by the need for historically appropriate materials when altering designated properties. The first was a review in concept for the conversion of St. John’s Baptist Church at 1601 S. 13th Street into 26 apartments. The East Passyunk landmark was built in 1892 as the Church of the Reconciliation and designed in the Romanesque Revival style by architects Samuel Hall Day and Charles E. Oelschlager. It was added to the local register in 2020. The original grey slate roof appears to have reached the end of its useful life, and the project proposed replacing it with asphalt shingles, citing the high cost of a new slate roof. The Historical Commission advised that slate-like materials are available and would be more appropriate than asphalt shingles.
 Victorian twins at 4221-23 Pine Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In the second case, the owner of a twin Victorian home at 4221 Pine Street requested the legalization of the removal of slate roofing and its replacement with brown fiberglass asphalt shingles on the mansard, which had been done without Historical Commission approval or a building permit. The property is part of a larger development row on the 4200 block of Pine Street, all of which historically featured slate mansard roofs and were designated in July 2024 as part of the Southeast Spruce Hill Historic District . The Commission denied the request, stating that the brown fiberglass asphalt shingles do not match the old in design, color, texture, or materials, a requirement of the standards set by the U.S. Department of the Interior for the treatment of historic properties.
 The Historical Commission did not review any nominations for designation at this meeting. The nomination of the National Marine Engineers Beneficial Association at 428-34 N. 4th Street , originally scheduled for this meeting, has been continued to the Historical Commission meeting on February 13.
 Tags: Conkling-Armstrong Terra Cotta Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission Wanamaker's 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: One Million Abolitionists Project Puts Empowering Words in Children's Hands
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
Frederick Douglass is currently one of the most culturally relevant intellectuals in American history. This observation prompted J. Justin Ragsdale of the Lest We Forget Museum to introduce his goddaughter Nicole Ross, president of the Hands Across Philadelphia organization, to Kevin Douglass Greene, who is the great-great grandson of Douglass and the spokesperson for the Frederick Douglass Family Initiative (FDFI). The encounter occurred in 2018 at the African American Civil War Memorial and Museum in Washington, D.C. and has led to a relationship working to bring Douglass’s works via the One Million Abolitionists Project to school-age Philadelphians during a rapidly changing political view of book bans.
 Hands Across Philadelphia’s partnership with FDFI helps with an ongoing transformative initiative to inspire local area youths to find and develop their work skills in an effort to keep them out of the crosshairs of gun violence. This is a goal that continues the legacy of another organization founded in the 1970s with the same name. According to Ross, the murder of another individual named Ross [no relation] in the early 1970s inspired the original group to become activists and work to end violence. Taking inspiration from the story’s originators, Carlette and Kenneth Brooks, the new group adopted the same name in 2008 with about 12 members who continued this legacy.
 Since then, they have been working with other organizations and businesses, such as the NAACP, the Pennsylvania Legislative Black Caucus, and Brown’s Shop Rite, to host ongoing and one-off events like The Hands Across Philadelphia Black History Essay Contest, which was made available to high school students in 2014. About 25 students have won various prizes including $100 and $50 gift certificates to Brown’s. Additional activities included the almost yearly 5K peace walks along 52nd Street and Woodland Avenue to Jefferson Street.
 Portrait of Frederick Douglass taken by George Kendall Warren in 1876. | Image: Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 Greene visits Philadelphia yearly to assist and speak at events scheduled around Douglass’s birthday on February 14. The One Million Abolitionists Project began in 2018 in honor of the 200th anniversary of Douglass's birth in 1818. Since it’s inception, the goal has been to get one million copies of a special bicentennial edition of The Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, and a special Douglass Family Edition republished by Forefront Publishing and Simon & Schuster, into the hands of young people to inspire and empower them. Co-founder of FDFI, Kenneth B. Morris Jr., a descendant of Douglass and Booker T. Washington, said that about 50,000–70,000 books were distributed quickly, largely due to grants from foundations, corporate sponsorships, and individual donors.
 Morris said the resurgence of book bans “energized and ignited us to get this book into the hands of students, even if the book was being banned, anywhere that students gather: churches, organizations, and youth groups. We get the books into their hands any way we can.”
 Book banning is not an issue that Ross encounters in Philadelphia and the surrounding area. Instead, the book has reached around 870 students in schools such as Einstein Science Technology Leadership Academy, Strawberry Mansion High School, East Norriton Middle School, John Hartranft School, School of the Future, Norristown High School, several more.
 Although funding is an issue—most of it comes from donations and the pockets of board members—the group said the benefits have made the project worth it. Both Ross and Greene recounted a visit to Norristown High School where a teacher approached them stating that he had received a copy of Douglass’s book years earlier and how it was an inspiration to his teaching career.
 In Douglass’s 1872 speech, "Self-Made Men," he stated, “Properly speaking, there are in the world no such men as self-made men.” The comment was made during Reconstruction and just prior to his taking on the role of president of the Freedman’s Bank. His self-development was due in part to the people in his life, including his wife, Anna Maria Douglass, whose story not only inspired him to achieve his own freedom prior to their marriage, but it also supported the creation of the Underground Railroad.
 Ross added that the speech serves as a reminder about the work that Hands Across Philadelphia is doing. Board members have grown frustrated with children remarking on all the violent deaths that they witness in the city. This has prompted the organization to expand its programs to include drone training, cyber security education, coding, and AI automation to assist in keeping young people out of trouble and focused on their prospective careers. There is also a noncombat sports initiative “emphasizing fitness and focus without physical sparring” with boxing drills, footwork, jump rope, and mindfulness sessions with support from boxers Tim Witherspoon, Nate Miller, Jarron Ennis, and others. They host group trips to Muhammad Ali’s former training camp in Deer Lake, Pennsylvania where Ross helps children “fight for their future—not with fists, but with focus.”
 Kevin Douglass Greene, the great-great grandson of Frederick Douglass, poses with pageant winners at a Juneteenth celebration. | Photo courtesy of the Frederick Douglass Family Initiative
 There is no strict criteria for how local area schools are selected to participate in the One Million Abolitionist Project. They either reach out to Ross as a local representative of the project or through her connections or they contact school administration and teachers who may be interested. Most schools are eager to receive the literature, especially since the books are free.
 Morris said that the continuing inspiration for this project is the smiles of the children affected by it. He recounted a story about a 10-year-old girl he met who was anxious for his attention during a school visit. Morris said the girl had learned that her “[four greats] grandmother was born into slavery and taught herself to read and write in secret. After getting her freedom, she became a businesswoman and a philanthropist. ‘This all means that I have greatness flowing through my veins,’ she said.”
 Tags: African-American history book Fredrick Douglass 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Sailing to Freedom with the Runaway Navy
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
“The most common—and the most important—means of transportation to freedom was the ship,” according to Marcus Rediker, author of the recently published book, Freedom Ship: The Uncharted History of Escaping Slavery by Sea. 
 “The metaphor ‘underground railroad’ has, from the late 1830s onward, pointed us in the wrong direction, limiting most historical investigations to the landed routes by which people traveled northward to freedom," Rediker explained. "Thousands of people escaped slavery by sea, leaving behind voluminous documentation, yet the history books have had little to say about them. We have been ignorant not only of the mass of maritime escapes, but of their rate of success, which was likely much higher than those attempted by land.”
 The enslaved escaped from dozens of ports. “They arrived throughout the Northern states that had abolished slavery, but mainly to Philadelphia, New York, New Bedford, and Boston,” noted Rediker. A graduate of the University of Pennsylvania (M.A. and Ph.D. in history), he is the Distinguished Professor of Atlantic History at the University of Pittsburgh and has written extensively on slavery and maritime subjects, along with biographies of Benjamin Lay, the fierce Quaker abolitionist who spent his last years in Philadelphia City and County.
 With its proximity to slaves states, a relatively large population of free African Americans, and a strong abolitionist movement, Philadelphia was the first stop for many escaped slaves making their way to northern states or Canada. Also, the opening of the Chesapeake and Delaware Canal in 1829 facilitated maritime traffic from the slave states of Virginia and Maryland. 
 Exhaustively researched, Freedom Ship documents the systems of escape by sea Rediker calls “the Runaway Navy.” It included slaves and free African Americans who worked on East Coast waterfronts, white ship captains and crew members, free black sailors, and networks of supporters in southern and northern ports, where communities of free Black citizens and their friends provided shelter, food, clothing, and other assistance.
 “The port of Philadelphia was a major site in the Atlantic system of maritime escape,” Rediker said. “The Quaker tradition and living legacy of anti-slavery, coupled with the presence of sailors, dockworkers, and market women, along with Robert Purvis and the abolitionist Vigilance Committee, made the city a magnet for freedom-seekers.”
 Philadelphia’s Vigilance Committee played a key role in welcoming, housing, and providing aid to runaways. Founded in 1837 by abolitionist Robert Purvis , the committee reorganized in 1852 with William Still as chairman. The son of former slaves, Still interviewed hundreds of escapees upon their arrival in Philadelphia and kept a written record of their lives in captivity and in flight. After passage of the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, possession of such records put both the escapees and their helpers at grave risk. Purvis reportedly burned his, and during the Civil War, Still hid his journals in a cemetery. In 1872, he published them in The Underground Railroad. A Record of Facts, Authentic Narratives, Letters, &c. 
 Schooners, Steamboats, and Skiffs 
 A lithograph by John William Hill and Benjamin Franklin Smith shows the Philadelphia waterfront in 1850. | Image courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 Rediker’s meticulous analysis of The Underground Railroad concluded, “Still’s notations made it abundantly clear that the most common—and the most important—means of transportation to freedom was the ship. For the 283 people whose means of escape he noted, two-thirds (67.4 percent) did not so much run away from bondage as sail, steam, or row away from it, depending on the kind of vessel they boarded in their home port. Arrivals by sea were thus more than twice as common as all other noted means of travel combined.”
 The steamer Pennsylvania made at least six voyages with fugitives in 1854 and 1855, according to Rediker. The steamship City of Richmond brought runaways from Virginia to Philadelphia “on at least thirteen voyages between August 1853 and November 1854, each time carrying someone who was usually hidden near the scorching hot boiler in the engine room.”
 One of the City of Richmond fugitives was Clarissa Davis, a 22-year old woman who escaped bondage in Portsmouth, Virginia. She boarded the ship disguised as a man and hid in a box during the voyage to Philadelphia. Given a new name and Underground Railroad passport by the Vigilance Committee, she eventually was reunited with her brothers and sister in New Bedford, Massachusetts.
 The S.S. City of Richmond at sea by American painter Antonio Nicolo Gasparo Jacobsen. | Image courtesy of Bonhams
 While almost one-quarter of runaways who landed in Philadelphia came by steamship, roughly two-fifths (42.4 percent) arrived on a schooner—one of the many two-masted sailing ships commonly used in the coastal trade. One of these was under the command of Captain James Fountain, who reportedly carried 57 people from Virginia and North Carolina to Philadelphia and Wilmington, Delaware between June 1855 and November 1857. “Of course, the number of fugitives he transported was no doubt greater and the time span of his efforts much longer,” noted Rediker. “Fountain family lore had it that the captain had assisted more than a thousand.”
 Not all attempts were successful. In 1848, Captain Daniel Drayton, a New Jersey native who spent most of his adult life in Philadelphia, was caught smuggling 77 men, women, and children from Washington, D.C. to freedom in the Quaker City. “Drayton, his two crewmates, and the freedom seekers were captured and returned to the nation’s capital, where police held at bay an angry mob eager to lynch Drayton,” Rediker wrote. Drayton was convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison. He served four years before being pardoned by President Millard Fillmore.
 A drawing of Lear Green being smuggled in a sailor’s sea chest. | Image from The Underground Railroad. A Record of Facts, Authentic Narratives, Letters, &c. by William Still
 William Still counted 18-year old Lear Green among “the heroic women of the nineteenth century.” Bonded to a butter dealer in Baltimore, Green wanted to marry her fiance, William Adams, as a free woman. Green, Adams, and his mother concocted a plan to smuggle her to freedom in a sailor’s sea chest. They had the loaded sea chest brought aboard one of the Ericsson Line steamers to Philadelphia as cargo. A free woman, “Adams’s mother would accompany the chest on the voyage, knowing that the racist policy of the shipping company required all people of color to remain on deck, which was exactly where she wanted to be, near the chest that carried Green,” explained Rediker.
 After the 18-hour voyage, Green and the sea chest were brought ashore, eventually to Still’s home, where “she remained several days under the protection and care of the Vigilance Committee.” Green made it to Elmira, New York, where she married William Adams, but, sadly, died just three years later. “The chest in which Lear escaped has been preserved by the writer as a rare trophy, and her photograph, taken while in the chest, is an excellent likeness of her and, at the same time, a fitting memorial,” Still lamented.
 ‘A Sharp Contest with Pursuers’ 
 William Still assisted nearly 1,000 men, women, and children along the eastern branch of the Underground Railroad as they fled enslavement. | Photo courtesy of Swarthmore College
 The Underground Railroad remains widely available in print and online. It features vivid accounts of the cruelties escapees endured as slaves, along with detailed narratives of actual trips by people seeking freedom on schooners, steamboats, and small craft.
 One of these narratives describes how, in 1860, Thomas and Mary Ann Sipple, Henry and Elizabeth Burkett, John Purnell, and Hale Burton decided to make a run from captivity in Worcester County, Maryland. “In considering what way would be safest for them to adopt, they concluded that the water would be less dangerous than any other route,” reported Still. They purchased an old bateau for six dollars and planned to cross the Delaware Bay to New Jersey. Not far from shore, “they were attacked by five white men in a small boat. The parties speedily came to blows. One of the white men dealt a heavy blow with his oar upon the head of one of the black men, which knocked him down, and broke the oar at the same time. The blow was immediately returned by Thomas Sipple, and one of the white men was laid flat on the bottom of the boat.
 “The white men were instantly seized with a panic and retreated. After getting some yards off they snapped their guns at the fugitives several times, and one load of small shot was fired into them.” Four of the escapees were hit, “but the shot being light, none of the fugitives were seriously damaged. Some of the shot will remain in them as long as life lasts. The conflict lasted for several minutes, but the victorious bondmen were only made all the more courageous by seeing the foe retreat.”
 Six escapees battle violent white pursuers while fleeing Maryland for New Jersey. | Image from The Underground Railroad. A Record of Facts, Authentic Narratives, Letters, &c. by William Still
 They made landfall not far from the Cape May lighthouse, exhausted and without resources or knowledge of their location. “After walking about one mile, they came across the captain of an oyster boat. They perceived that he spoke in a friendly way, and they at once asked directions with regard to Philadelphia. He gave them the desired information, and even offered to bring them to the city if they would pay him for his services. They had about twenty-five dollars in all. This they willingly gave him, and he brought them according to agreement.” Upon arrival in Philadelphia, “They greatly needed food, clothing, rest, and money, which they freely received.”
 “Still assiduously recorded information about fugitives who passed through his office,” noted Rediker. “He wrote down the names of the self-emancipated and for many of them, noted details such as age, physical appearance, where their escape began, why they decided to run, and how they made their getaway, by land or by sea. Still listened sympathetically as the veterans of bondage told chilling tales of murder, flogging, rape, and other cruelties that staggered the imagination. [He] understood the historic nature of what he was witnessing and its importance for posterity.”
 Likewise, in Freedom Ship , Rediker makes a valuable contribution to the history of what Still called the Underground Railroad. Covering the waterfront from Savannah to Boston, Freedom Ship is a ground-breaking , deeply researched, fascinating look into the long-neglected role of the maritime trade in enabling countless runaways to achieve freedom.
 Tags: abolitionist history African-American history Delaware River waterfront slavery Underground Railroad 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: Preserving The ‘Full Story of American History'
author: Kevin Riordan
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 As the nation prepares to celebrate the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, the pushback against the Trump administration ’s efforts to de-emphasize, or perhaps minimize, the subject of slavery at Independence National Historical Park seems unlikely to subside.
 The president’s executive order, " Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History ," seeks to rewrite, remove, or restore exhibits and other elements at national parks, monuments, and institutions across the country to stop what the president calls the spread of a “divisive” ideology largely focused on race. Also in the president’s sights: “descriptions, depictions or other content that inappropriately disparage[s] Americans” living or dead.
 The monument The President’s House: Freedom and Slavery in the Making of a New Nation on Independence Mall was dedicated in 2010. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At Independence National Historical Park, targets are reported to include depictions of the lives of enslaved people , as well as acknowledgements of slavery’s existence, at the President’s House, Independence Hall, the Liberty Bell, the Benjamin Franklin House, and the Second Bank of the United States.
 While these historic and widely recognized buildings and places in Philadelphia are at the heart of the nation’s struggle for freedom, less well-known locations across the city also offer opportunities to more deeply appreciate the bravery, resilience, and accomplishments of African Americans . These include landmark sites such as Mother Bethel AME Church, founded in 1794 by the formerly enslaved Bishop Richard Allen, the William and Letitia Still House , a former Underground Railroad station operated by Black abolitionists, the Dinah Memorial at Stenton , and the Camp William Penn Museum.
 Telling the ‘Whole Truth’ 
 The recreated President’s House at 6th and Market Streets has long raised the ire of some observers. The original dwelling was torn down in the 1830s after serving as the official residence of President George Washington between 1780 and 1788. Philadelphia was then the temporary capital of the United States, and the president and his wife, Martha, had a live-in staff that included nine enslaved people. The president rotated the enslaved workers between his Philadelphia and Virginia homes every six months to exploit a loophole in Pennsylvania’s then-groundbreaking “gradual abolition” law.
 According to historians and community advocates, President Donald Trump’s executive order would likely enable a shift in the narrative focus at the house and the other Philadelphia sites. Candor about slavery and similarly complex matters will be truncated or eliminated, while simpler, more traditional paeans to the Founding Fathers will be elevated, they said.
 “I disagree with their approach of cherry-picking in order to highlight more positive elements and making that a protocol,” said Alan Spears, a regional director at the National Parks Conservation Association, an advocacy organization. “Talking about slavery in ways that are positive? I’m not sure that’s possible,” Spears said.
 What is at stake in Philadelphia and elsewhere, Spears and others believe, are scholarship, community engagement, and continued progress toward inclusion of long-overlooked, under-researched individuals and events in the larger American story. Deeply documented, nuanced narratives centered on the experiences and contributions of enslaved and free Black people, as well as Indigenous and other people of color, are at risk of being officially disappeared.
 At the President’s House site, Mijuel K. Johnson, guide for The Black Journey, explains how President George Washington used a legal loophole while living in Philadelphia to retain the people he had enslaved. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 “All this is symbolic of a larger campaign to erase Black history and dehumanize Black people,” said Michelle Flamer, co-founder and board chair of the historical organization 1838 Black Metropolis. A Pennsylvania Abolition Society census counted nearly 19,000 free Black people living in Philadelphia in 1838. Black Metropolis researches, documents, showcases, and offers tours of locations of African Americans, enslaved and free, living in Philadelphia during the first half of the 19th century. The sites include the Northern Liberties neighborhood, where networks of Black families, tradespeople, and entrepreneurs established businesses, schools, and churches long before the Civil War.
 At the southwest corner of 6th and Race Streets, where the American College of Physicians now stands, Pennsylvania Hall –built to house abolitionist meetings–was attacked by a mob and set on fire on May 17, 1838. Educator and civil rights advocate Octavius V. Catto , a monument for whom now stands on the south apron of City Hall, was assassinated outside of his South Street home on October 10, 1871.
 “On the eve of the 250th, if you want to say you love America, you need to know the truth, the whole truth and nothing, but the truth. No whitewashing. No censorship,” said Michael Coard, a founding member of the Philadelphia-based Avenging the Ancestors Coalition (ATAC). Launched in 2002 to advocate for the President’s House project, ATAC also sponsors educational programs and community events that elevate awareness of Black heritage.
 Coard was optimistic that the pushback was having an impact, citing how September 17, 2024, thought to be a “D-Day” for action by the administration, came and went without tangible steps to remove exhibits. The government shutdown in the fall also seemed to pause implementation. “It’s too early to declare victory,” Coard said. “But we have moved the champagne bottle from the refrigerator to the table.”
 ‘Strongest Possible Opposition’ 
 Black Metropolis and ATAC are among the 49 members of a coalition organized by the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia in response to the president’s initiative. “We thought it was important for historical preservation advocates and advocates from the community to speak with one voice,” explained Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance. “We wanted to defend the accuracy of the scholarship that led to the creation of the exhibits at Independence National Historical Park,” he said. “We’ve been overwhelmed by the amount of support we’ve received from the community.”
 Michael Coard, founder of the Avenging the Ancestors Coalition, led a protest in September 2025 against potential changes to the President’s House exhibit by the Trump Administration. Coard was one of the driving forces behind the National Park Service’s decision to highlight the lives of the enslaved people who labored for the Washington household at the President’s House site. | Photo: Paul Steinke
 The coalition expressed the “strongest possible opposition” to altering content in a letter sent in September to Doug Burgum, director of the U.S. Department of the Interior, which oversees the National Park Service. “These exhibits, including those honoring the lives of the nine individuals enslaved by President George Washington, are the result of a long, hard-fought endeavor to tell the full story of American history,” the letter said in part. “History is not mythology … [and] removal or replacement of the interpretive panels, exhibits and signage under the guise of eliminating anti-American ideology is ahistorical and un-American." 
 First White House Is Also a Slavery Memorial 
 Information about slavery-related elements at certain Independence National Historic Park sites was brought to the Trump administration’s attention after park employees were encouraged to submit comments, the Philadelphia Inquirer reported in July. Flagged materials include an interactive display of information about Benjamin Franklin’s views on slavery, as well as a proposed Independence Hall exhibit featuring versions of foundational documents such as the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution. The Inquirer reported that park staff members who submitted comments also flagged six displays that collectively include 13 items, all of them touching on slavery, at the President’s House. In appearing to single out that site, Coard said, the administration “poked the bear. And the bear is roaring back in black and white.”
 The interpretive design of the President's House exhibit by Eisterhold Associates included the site's history of enslaved residents. | Images courtesy of Eisterhold Associates
 20 years ago, ATAC galvanized community and political support to ensure that a slavery narrative would be front and center as the house site–a long and unmarked stretch of grass surrounding a public restroom–was being excavated, envisioned, and built. An estimated 300,000 people watched from a platform as the four-month archeological dig uncovered foundations of additions to the original dwelling.
 Built with the help of a $3.5 million donation from the Delaware River Port Authority, $3.6 million from the federal government, and $1.5 million from the city, the $10.5 million project, officially named “The President’s House: Freedom and Slavery in the Making of a Nation,” opened in 2010. The National Park Service website describes it as telling “the story of the paradox of liberty and enslavement in one home–and in a nation.” Coard and others refer to the site as a Slavery Memorial and President’s House.
 Washington’s Legacy Is… Complicated 
 “It’s hard to believe the Park Service had left that site uninterpreted for decades,” said Ed Lawler, a local historian in Philadelphia. It was Lawler’s exhaustive research into the architectural history of the house that brought to light the accurate number of enslaved people who lived there and details about their lives. He culled the information from letters written by Washington and archived at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. Publication of his article in the Pennsylvania Magazine of History and Biography in 2002 helped energize efforts to do archaeological and other research at the site.
 “The fact that Washington was an enslaver in Virginia was well known, and the fact of his having brought enslaved people to Philadelphia was known by the park, but not by the public,” said Sharon Ann Holt, a Philadelphian who as editor of the Pennsylvania magazine published Lawler’s article. “The fact that we now had names and stories about these enslaved people, nine human stories, was absolutely dazzling,” she said.
 A lithograph depicting George Washington the farmer speaking to his slaves at Mount Vernon. Nathaniel Currier, 1852. | Image: Public Domain
 A watercolor painting titled The Residence of Washington in High Street, 1795-6 by artist William Breton. | Image courtesy of The Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 Not everyone was dazzled: “Trashing the President’s House” was the headline on an architectural review in a 2011 issue of Commentary magazine in which critic Michael J. Lewis characterized the site as offering too much slavery and too little presidential history.
 “The President’s House site today is not all that it could have been, not by a mile,” Holt wrote in an op-ed the Inquirer published in August. “But it remains one of the most prominent monuments in the nation to openly acknowledge how much American liberty depended on African slavery,” she wrote.
 ‘Trying to Erase Me’ 
 Mijuel K. Johnson is a guide for The Black Journey, a commercial tour operation in Philadelphia that focuses on a wide range of sites in the Independence National Historic Park and in the 7th Ward. Tours cover portions of the Society Hill, Washington Square West, and South Street West neighborhoods that were the residential, economic, professional, cultural, and spiritual hub of Black Philadelphia in the 19th and early 20th centuries. “This is the first stop on most of our tours,” said Johnson, sitting on a bench in the President’s House. A landmark at the park’s western gateway, the site is mostly outdoors and includes a viewing area of subterranean foundation portions of additions to the original house. “For me, slavery is personal history,” said Johnson, 34, who was born, raised and lives in Philadelphia. “Slavery is part of my own family’s history like it is for a majority of Black people in this country. So, if you’re trying to erase my ancestors, you’re trying to erase me.”
 Black Journey owner Raina Yancey established her business in 2019 and is deeply concerned about White House-ordered alterations to Independence National Historic Park sites. “But we are independent and we don’t answer to the federal government,” she said. “So, we will continue to bring tours to the President’s House and talk about the struggle and the triumphs [of Black people].”
 William and Letitia Still’s former home at 625 South Delhi Street (far right) in Bella Vista. The Underground Railroad landmark, built in 1850, was placed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 2018. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 While some houses and other buildings included on the tours have been altered or razed, the sites nonetheless illustrate often-overlooked stories about Black institution-building, as does the former home of the Institute for Colored Youth, the predecessor of Cheyney University, which still stands at 9th and Bainbridge Streets.
 Yancey said the latest tour offers a look at the history of Black medical education and Black-operated health care facilities in Philadelphia. Key sites include two pioneering hospitals–Douglass at 15th and Lombard Streets and Mercy at 17th and Fitzwater Streets. Black Journey is also developing a food-related tour that will include the site of Cyrus Bustill’s bakery near 2nd and Arch Streets in 1780. Bustill baked bread that helped nourish Continental Army troops during the Revolutionary War. “We can’t let these stories go untold,” Yancey said.
 Michiko Quinones, who co-founded Black Metropolis, said Northern Liberties was a center of Underground Railroad activity that brought thousands of Black people from slave states north to freedom in Philadelphia. The Black tradespeople, residential property owners, and clergy of Northern Liberties also created a nexus of advocacy for abolition and civil rights. Nearly all of the people and events of this period were ignored by historians of the era–and beyond. The “intentional whiteout of Black history” by white historians and others itself has a long history, explained Quinones. Even when the history mirrors the against-the-odds ethos of the overall American story. “People came out of enslavement and built all this in Northern Liberties,” she said. “What’s not to like?”
 Providing a Full Perspective 
 Marianne Ruane, board president for the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides, said members are encouraged to “tell the true stories, warts and all. No matter what the administration does.”
 Johnson and two other tour guides said they make it a point to talk about slavery during stops at the President’s House.
 “When I take tourists to the President’s House, I tell them it’s not going to be a Hallmark Channel tour,” said Jim Murphy, 80, who lives in Society Hill and blogs about Philly history.
 Tour guide Bob Branch at the President’s House site on Independence Mall, performing in the role of Bishop Richard Allen, founder of the African Methodist Episcopal Church (AME), the first independent Black denomination in the United States. He was participating in an Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides initiative undertaken in response to President Donald Trump’s directive for the National Park Service to remove “divisive” displays from historic sites. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 “I’ve never had anyone get angry at me, even when I tell them how George Washington legally went after Ona Judge [who had escaped to freedom].” Bob Branch is known for doing presentations while in character as Bishop Richard Allen, the founder of Mother Bethel AME. “I’m not about interpretations of history that say white people are evil,” the 72-year-old Philadelphia native said.
 However, if the content at the President’s House and the other sites is altered, Branch added, “what would be lost is a full perspective that includes enslavement and racism. “When they made plans for the President’s House, they intentionally made it a priority not to hide what happened there, and that [approach] is good,” he said. He also noted that Allen, who had been enslaved, offered a eulogy for George Washington from the pulpit of Mother Bethel in 1799 because the former president had “intended to free his slaves.”
 Edward Stierli, the mid- Atlantic senior regional director for the National Parks Conservation Association, said Philadelphia has been “a model for what community pushback could look like.”
 Mathew Palmer, a guide for The Black Journey tour company, talks about the history of Mother Bethel AME church at Sixth and Bainbridge, which sits on land that has been owned by Black people longer than any other property in the United States. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 “The City and the community are calling out the fact that this [move by the administration] is an effort to rewrite history and would be a betrayal of trust with the community that would be an ominous precedent,” he said. “Philadelphia, more than any other place, has drawn the line as far as the story the community wants to be told there. And I believe that story will continue.”
 Editor's Update: On January 22, 2026, all exhibition panels relating to the history of slavery at the President's House were removed by National Park Service staff in accordance with an executive order issued by the Trump Administration. The City of Philadelphia has since filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Department of the Interior and National Park Service Acting Director Jessica Bowron. Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro filed an amicus brief in support of the lawsuit on January 27.
 Exhibition panels at the President's House that honored the enslaved were removed on January 22 by the National Park Service under an order from the Trump Administration. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 During an injunction hearing on January 30, U.S. District Judge Cynthia Marie Rufe ordered the Park Service to safely store the exhibits while the suit plays out in court. She also issued an order prohibiting the Trump Administration from any additional removals or changes to the President's House until a ruling has been made. 
 Avenging the Ancestors Coalition will hold a "Rally to Restore the Truth" on Tuesday, February 10 at the President's House on Independence Mall. The demonstration begins at 3:30 p.m. See details here: https://www.facebook.com/photo/?fbid=941864205178925&set=a.118244644207556 
 Tags: African-American history Donald J. Trump Independence National Historical Park National Park Service slavery The President’s House 
 About the Author
 Kevin Riordan is a longtime Philadelphia-area journalist. He grew up in North Adams, Massachusetts, earned a degree in journalism at Syracuse University, covered Camden for South Jersey's South Jersey's Courier-Post , and most recently worked as a columnist and business writer on the staff of the Philadelphia Inquirer .

title: John T. Morris Takes Pictures of Port Richmond with His Kodak. It’s 1889.
author: Joyce H. Munro
bodyText:
It is fair to say that John T. Morris was an early adopter of technology in the 80s. The 1880s, that is. His willingness to embrace new ideas and adapt to change, whether in business, architecture, travel, or horticulture, is well documented. For example, consider Morris' investment in a start-up steelworks using the “Mitis process” to combine aluminum with wrought iron, thus making it more flexible and lighter weight. Investing in this Swedish innovation was a brave move that could have a negative impact on his foundry business, but a risk he was quite willing to take.
 Photograph negatives taken in 1889 by industrialist John T. Morris with a point and shoot Kodak camera. | Photo courtesy of Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives
 At the time, Morris was president of I.P. Morris & Co ., the long-standing Port Richmond ironworks known for forging massive machines like boilers, turbines, and steam engines. Morris Iron Works was the kind of industry that had to be at the leading edge of technology. Their machines powered ships, refineries, mines, and factories across the nation.
 All sorts of modern machines were designed and tested at the ironworks, but, in one instance, the machine was not made by Morris. It was his new camera, the first “point and shoot” Kodak . Unlike his cumbersome field camera, it was small, lightweight, and easy to use. So, it was no problem for him to take the Kodak to work, step out the front door of his office, and point the camera toward the street.
 A horse-drawn milk wagon passes 2254 Richmond Street. Judging by the open window, it’s too warm on the third floor. | Photo: John T. Morris, courtesy of Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives
 Simply press the button and voila! —the 2200 block of Richmond Street is captured on film, probably for the very first time. Morris may have thought he was just practicing with this novel camera. It didn’t matter what he pointed to. Little did he know his photos would be published online for the public to view many decades later.
 A dray horse minces its way around coiled ropes at the edge of the I.P. Morris pier. | Photo: John T. Morris, courtesy of Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives
 The camera Morris used to take the Port Richmond pictures was a simple wooden box covered in leather and weighed less than two pounds. At a cost of $25, the Kodak was a good investment. It was also convenient. All Morris had to do was take the exposed film to a photography company in Center City for developing, a labor-saving innovation for the amateur photographer in the 1880s.
 A lanky boy strides up the sidewalk in front of 2254 Richmond Street leaving his little sister behind. | Photo: John T. Morris, courtesy of Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives
 A few days later, the company would send Morris a small paper envelop containing 19 Kodak negatives, each bearing the number of the job order and written by an employee during processing. 14 negatives from job #67 have survived. What happened to the other five is anyone’s guess.
 A steam-powered tug moves ahead down-stream across from Petty Island. | Photo: John T. Morris, courtesy of Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives
 In 1887, Morris and his sister Lydia established a country estate named Compton in Chestnut Hill. In 1932, the estate was bequeathed to the University of Pennsylvania and renamed Morris Arboretum.
 Streetcar No. 13 makes haste on Richmond Street, passing the Western Union Telegraph office, conveniently located near the utility pole. | Photo: John T. Morris, courtesy of Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives
 Sometime before 1968, the superintendent of the Morris Arboretum rescued Morris' Kodak negatives from the Compton mansion prior to its demolition.
 A huge boiler on a rail flatcar is ready to be hoisted onto a waiting ship at Morris Pier. | Photo: John T. Morris, courtesy of Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives
 Morris likely took the Port Richmond photos in early October 1889. At the end of the month, Morris, Lydia, and their travel companion, Louise Kellner, went on a nine-month trip around the world. Morris took the Kodak with him. No photos of that trip survived.
 A three-masted ship, its sails furled, rides low in the water. | Photo: John T. Morris, courtesy of Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives
 The three row houses on Richmond Street across from I.P. Morris & Co. were demolished at the turn of the century when the street was widened to accommodate the expansion of Cramp’s shipyard.
 Author's Note : This essay was made possible by records at the Morris Arboretum and Garden Archives and with the assistance of Mark Osterman, an expert in the technical evolution of photographic processes. 
 Tags: industrial history Morris Arboretum photo essay Port Richmond 
 About the Author
 Joyce H. Munro is a lecturer and former dean of the School of Graduate Studies at Chestnut Hill College. Her articles and literary essays on the Morris Arboretum and Gardens can be found in Hidden City Philadelphia, Broad Street Review, Philadelphia Stories, Poor Yorick, Seasons, and Morris Arboretum: Private Estate Era.

title: Places Lost: Fall 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2023 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 United Missionary Baptist Church 
 Location: 2500 West Thompson Street
 Built: 1892
 In February, a devastating fire swept through the United Missionary Baptist Church in Brewerytown, reducing the 133-year-old architectural and spiritual landmark to ruins. Although no injuries were reported, the blaze caused the roof to collapse, and the loss of the historic building sent shockwaves through the community it had long served.
 Originally built in 1892 as Hebron Memorial Presbyterian Church, the building stood at the corner of 25th and Thompson Streets as a striking example of modified Gothic architecture. Designed by Franklin J. Stuckert, the structure featured marble and Indiana limestone trim, as well as stained glass by C.H. Postel & Co., and could seat 450 worshippers. It began as a mission of Olivet Covenant Presbyterian Church and evolved into its own congregation, later renamed the Robert Graham Memorial Presbyterian Church in honor of its long-standing reverend. In 1965, the congregation voted to disband and sold the building to the United Baptist Church.
 Since then, the United Missionary Baptist Church has remained a cornerstone of North Philadelphia’s religious life. For almost 70 years, the congregation has been led by members of the Williams family, most recently Dr. Chandra I. Williams, the church’s fourth overall and first female pastor, who succeeded her father in 2012. The fire not only destroyed a building, but also dealt a blow to a community deeply connected to its history. The congregation remains active and continues to meet at other local churches.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Greater Church of Philadelphia 
 Location: 2017-23 East Allegheny Avenue
 Built: 1884
 In March, a devastating fire marked the end of one of Kensington’s oldest houses of worship. Built in 1884, the former East Allegheny Avenue Methodist Episcopal Church was a wooden-framed sanctuary behind a commanding stone facade. Over the years it changed names and congregations, most recently known as the Greater Church of Philadelphia, which served generations of faithful in the heart of this working-class neighborhood.
 The blaze spread rapidly through the walls of the vacant and deteriorated structure, causing the roof to collapse, and sections of the stone facade gave way, crumbling into the street. Thankfully, no injuries were reported, but the damage was irreversible. The structure was quickly deemed unsafe and torn down in the days following the fire.
 Once a neighborhood anchor, the church had already suffered years of neglect. Ownership passed through several hands in recent decades, with visible deterioration preceding the fire. The congregation vacated the premises in 2016, and, since then, the developer who owns the site allowed it to further deteriorate. The cleared lot is for sale, but no redevelopment plans have yet materialized.
 These losses underscore the growing vulnerability of Philadelphia’s ecclesiastical architecture. The buildings, once supported by large and well-funded congregations, are now aging with limited and often inadequate financial resources required for proper upkeep. Their part-time occupancy and high maintenance costs make them particularly susceptible to deterioration and fire. As these sacred spaces disappear, so does the architectural and spiritual history they hold.
 Tags: demolition historic churches Places Lost

title: Restoration Role Model: The Spence Building
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2023 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 The Spence Building has been brought back to its former glory. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 The Spence Building is an important historical landmark in the heart of West Chester, but the 1890 building had fallen into a state of disrepair and was in need of extensive restoration. Extant spoke with the owner, Zukin Realty, and PZS Architects about their process of revitalization, which began in 2022 and focused on maintaining the integrity and character of the original structure. The meticulous restoration earned a 2025 Grand Jury Award from the Preservation Alliance.
 Extant Magazine (EM) : What was the building’s original use?
 Zukin Realty (ZR): Built in 1890, the Spence Building served as a residential space and dining establishment under the ownership of James Spence, the first African American to own a liquor license in Chester County. When the Zukin family purchased the building, it was being used as apartments above a ground-level bakery.
 The Spence Building in the 1920s. | Photo courtesy of Chesco250
 EM: What was most important to preserve?
 ZR: The most important aspects to preserve were both the historical integrity of the building’s exterior and the legacy of James Spence. Restoration efforts focused on ensuring the Spence Building complemented the adjacent historic fabric of West Chester. The facade and slate roof were carefully restored, and the stucco exterior was removed to reveal the original cut sandstone. Original features, such as the interior access stairway and railing, and the curved entry door and windows on the first floor were restored. The roof was replaced with historically accurate slate and copper.
 Equally important was honoring the story of the building’s original owner. We achieved this by preserving the building’s original character and ensuring its integrity for many more years.
 EM: What was the client’s original vision? Did it change over time?
 PZS Architects (PZS): The client’s original vision was to honor the historical vernacular of Gay Street through the building’s exterior restoration, while upgrading the apartments and common areas and ensuring compliance with current building codes. Initially, the plan was to save the facade and 15 to 20 feet of the existing building and add a new modern structure behind it. However, as the project evolved, the value of full preservation became clear. The vision shifted to saving the entire building, restoring the front and a portion of the rear facade and constructing an addition at the rear, all while maintaining the character of the original structure.
 The Spence Building and others along Gay Street in the 1960s. | Photo courtesy of Chesco250
 EM: What was the biggest preservation challenge?
 PZS: Preserving the building’s historical features in order to meet the requirements of the State Historic Preservation Office and obtain historic tax credits was a challenge on this project. One of the most difficult aspects was restoring the facade, which required careful attention to historical accuracy. Designing modern apartments within the existing structure, while preserving key elements like the original hallway, posed some additional design and construction challenges.
 EM: What was the project’s biggest surprise (good or bad)?
 PZS: The original intent was to re-stucco the building, which was peeling off and had a faux- brick finish. We had received permission from SHPO to re-stucco, and when we started to prep the building for new stucco, we made an important discovery–the building’s original sandstone had been covered for more than 70 years. We removed the stucco and cleaned, restored, and repointed the sandstone, bringing the exterior back to its original appearance.
 Tags: Restoration Role Model suburbs 
 About the Author

title: Circle Theater and Sugar Loaf Orchard Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on February 13, the Philadelphia Historical Commission added two properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, declined one nomination, and continued two other nominations to future meetings.
 The Circle Theater at 4648-62 Frankford Avenue. | Photo courtesy of the Philadelphia Historical Commission. Architect's rendering courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia.
 The Circle Theater at 4648-62 Frankford Avenue was built in 1929 for the Stanley Company of America and represents a trend in neighborhood movie theaters in the early decades of the 20th century. The architects, the Hoffman-Henon Company, designed over 100 such theaters, with more than 40 in Philadelphia, including the Boyd and the Mastbaum. The firm was also known for designing Catholic buildings such as the West Philadelphia Girls Catholic High School at 4501 Chestnut Street and St. Carthage Church at 6213 Cedar Avenue.
 The main house of Sugar Loaf Orchard at 29 and 31 W. Bells Mill Road. | Photo courtesy of Kevin McMahon
 Five buildings at 29 and 31 W. Bells Mill Road , collectively named Sugar Loaf Orchard, were added to the local register. The parcels include a 1917 cottage, a 1919 main house, a 1924 tool house, a garage, and a barn, all designed in the Colonial Revival style, typical of early 20th century country-style domestic architecture. They were built by the Philadelphia architectural firm Martin & Kirkpatrick, which designed a number of similar houses, as well as the Girard College Chapel.
 419 W. Clapier Street in Germantown. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 The Historical Commission rejected the nomination for four buildings at 419 W. Clapier Street in Germantown. The parcel includes a gardener’s cottage, chauffeur’s cottage, barn and greenhouse dating to the late 19th-and early 20th centuries that were originally service buildings for the adjacent large house at 5000 McKean Avenue, formerly the home of noted engineer James Mapes Dodge. Last October and November, both the Historical Commission and its Committee on Historic Designation ruled that the nomination did not sufficiently prove the property satisfied any criterion for designation. This second nomination was submitted on November 23, 2025. However, the owner submitted a demolition permit application to the Department of Licenses and Inspections on November 19. In the nine day period between the Historical Commission’s rejection on November 14 and its receipt of a new nomination, the property was not under the Commission’s protection. With a valid demolition permit on the property, the Historical Commission voted against designation.
 Another nomination was continued amid procedural concerns. The property at 7001-09 Greenhill Road in Overbrook was built between 1916 and 1919 by the architectural firm of Mellor, Meigs & Howe in the Colonial Revival style. The stone house is attached via a twin garage to the property at 6953 Greenhill Road, which is a mirror twin of the house and the subject of its own nomination. The two properties were a result of the early 20th century subdivision and development of Green Hill Farm by the Wistar Morris Estate in West Philadelphia.
 The stone home and garage at 6953 Greenhill Road. | Photo courtesy of the Keeping Society of Philadelphia 
 The property at 6953 Greenhill Road was purchased in February 2025 by Chabad of Penn Wynne, Inc., which has been granted a continuance of the nomination to the July meeting of the Committee on Historic Designation. Historical Commission staff raised concerns that, given the identical nature of the two properties, a designation today of one of them could be a de facto designation of the other before the owner had an opportunity to contest it. Despite the urging of the owner of 7001-09 Greenhill Road and the nominator, the community group Greenhill Farms Preservation Club to rule on the nomination, the Historical Commission continued it to the July meeting of the Committee on Historic Designation.
 A one-month continuance was given to the nomination for the interior main banking room in the Fidelity-Philadelphia Trust Company building at 123 South Broad Street , Unit 1. Other nominations that have been continued include the National Marine Engineers Beneficial Association at 428-34 N. 4th Street to the April meeting, and Piers 38 and 40 at 775 S. Christopher Columbus Boulevard , nominated in October 2021, but currently without a specific continuance date.
 Tags: Historic theaters Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Places Saved: Winter 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Frankford High School 
 Location: 5000 Oxford Avenue
 Built: 1914
 Frankford High School in Northeast Philadelphia reopened in time for the 2025-2026 school year after an extensive $29.9 million renovation preserved the historic main building and addressed critical environmental hazards. Founded in 1910 as the northeast branch of Central High School, the current building was designed by Henry deCourcy Richards in 1914 in the late Gothic Revival style.
 The building was closed in April 2023 after inspections identified damaged asbestos materials throughout the structure. While asbestos is not inherently dangerous, disturbed materials can release harmful fibers, requiring careful management and remediation.
 Following the closure, several options were considered to meet the needs of students and staff. The chosen plan combined safety upgrades with comprehensive renovations, allowing the school to reopen in time for its 115th birthday celebration. Key measures included removal or repair of asbestos materials, installation of new windows, and upgraded educational technology in all classrooms. Floors were refinished, ceilings upgraded, and AC units installed throughout. The auditorium, gymnasium, and cafeteria received significant improvements, including new furniture, lighting, and flooring.
 Historic features were carefully preserved, including murals, artwork, and architectural details. Routine asbestos inspections will continue every six months, and further maintenance, including roof repairs, is planned. Through this investment, Frankford High School has been revitalized as a safe, modern, and inspiring educational environment.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Willow Street Steam Generation Plant 
 Location: 411-19 North 9th Street
 Built: 1927
 After decades of uncertainty, the former Willow Street Steam Generation Plant is poised for a new life as an apartment building. Built in 1927 by the Philadelphia Electric Company and designed by prominent local architect John T. Windrim, the plant once powered a unique underground steam network, providing efficient heating to our dense urban fabric. By the 1970s, the building had fallen into disuse, changing hands multiple times and steadily deteriorating.
 The rehabilitation project, led by the construction firm E-Built, began with extensive remediation work to stabilize the historic structure. Renovation of the exterior and interior is now underway, preserving the building’s industrial character, while adapting it for modern residential use. Recently added to the National Register of Historic Places , the project benefits from historic rehabilitation tax credits.
 Inside, the building will feature studio, one-bedroom, and two-bedroom apartments with high ceilings, exposed brick walls, and polished concrete floors. Lofted units occupy the first and second floors, taking advantage of ceilings more than 16 feet high. Residents will enjoy amenities including a swimming pool, sauna, gym, theater room, and golf simulator in the basement, as well as a rooftop deck with Center City views.
 Slated to open in mid-2026, the Willow Street project demonstrates how historic industrial buildings can be thoughtfully repurposed, blending preservation with contemporary living.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Cathedral Flats 
 Location: 1030 North 48th Street
 Built: 1872
 Our Mother of Sorrows Church, located in West Philadelphia, has been thoughtfully adapted for contemporary residential use. Established as a parish in 1852, its origins trace to 1849 with the creation of the adjacent Cathedral Cemetery, which spurred Catholic settlement in the area.
 The church’s Romanesque Revival structure, designed by prominent ecclesiastical architect Edwin Forrest Durang and completed in 1872, was later enhanced with twin spires in 1891-92, making it a landmark along Lancaster Avenue. For nearly a century and a half, Our Mother of Sorrows served as the spiritual and social center of a large and diverse congregation. The parish supported multiple schools, a convent and extensive charitable programs.
 By the early 21st century, however, declining attendance led to the parish’s 2017 merger with St. Ignatius of Loyola, leaving the complex vacant and vulnerable to redevelopment pressures. Recognizing the site’s architectural and cultural importance, the Preservation Alliance successfully nominated Our Mother of Sorrows for local historic designation in 2018, ensuring its protection under the city’s preservation ordinance.
 Today, the church has been sensitively converted into Cathedral Flats, a residential complex that preserves the grandeur of Durang’s design. The adaptive reuse maintains the church’s signature 12-foot ceilings, stained-glass windows, and monumental masonry while incorporating modern interiors and amenities. The project exemplifies how historic religious buildings can be reimagined to meet contemporary needs.
 Tags: Callowhill Edwin Forrest Durang Northeast Philadelphia Places Saved West Philadelphia Willow Street Steam Generation Plant 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: The Sunken Cathedral: Philadelphia's Lost Gothic Masterpiece
author: Thomas H. Keels
bodyText:
As America approached the apogee of the Gilded Age in 1900, its Episcopal elite appeared to undergo a major meltdown. Their position seemed unassailable. Numbering only 720,000, Episcopalians represented less than one percent of the United States population of 76 million. Yet, they controlled much of the nation’s corporate wealth, political power, and social status. Their mansions lined Upper Fifth Avenue in New York, Rittenhouse Square in Philadelphia, and Beacon Hill in Boston. The Social Register dripped with such Episcopal names as Astor, Vanderbilt, Cabot, Lodge, Biddle, and Cadwalader.
 However, American Catholics, bolstered by waves of European immigration, numbered 12 million in 1900, making them the largest religious denomination in America. Catholics’ vast numbers and growing financial power, along with their fervent religious devotion, had manifested itself in the construction of magnificent cathedrals. A cathedral was not only the principal church of a diocese where its bishop was seated, but a highly visible statement of economic and social status.
 Cathedral Basillica of Saints Peter and Paul was built between 1846-64 and designed by Napoleon LeBrun, John Mahony, and John Notman (and many others). Placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1971. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In New York City, “the Cathedral” meant St. Patrick’s Cathedral. Completed in 1879, its Gothic spires towered above the Episcopal enclave of Fifth Avenue. In Philadelphia, “the Cathedral” referred to the Cathedral Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul, which had dominated Logan Square since 1864. Its stately dome overshadowed not just the colonial steeples of Christ Church and St. Peter’s, but 19th century Holy Trinity and St. Mark’s. Where were the great Episcopal cathedrals, the New World counterparts to majestic St. Paul’s in London?
 As if to reassert their religious dominance, American Episcopalians embarked on a wave of cathedral building unmatched since the Middle Ages. On December 27, 1892, the cornerstone was set for the massive Cathedral of St. John the Divine in Upper Manhattan. On September 29, 1907, Episcopal President Theodore Roosevelt laid the cornerstone for a National Cathedral atop Mount St. Albans, the highest point in Washington. Nominally a “house of prayer for all people,” the structure would serve as headquarters for the Episcopal Diocese of Washington, reflecting the marriage of the national power structure and the Episcopal faith. Before long, Baltimore, Boston, and San Francisco announced plans for their own Episcopal cathedrals.
 Philadelphia, birthplace of the Protestant Episcopal Church in the United States of America, was slower to join the Cathedral Crusade.
