Ozi William Whitaker, Episcopal Bishop of Pennsylvania from 1887 to 1911, was adamantly anti-cathedral. He preferred to use an existing institution like Christ Church, where the Founding Fathers had worshipped, as the bishop’s seat for the Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania, which is composed of Philadelphia, Bucks, Chester, Delaware, and Montgomery Counties.
 The George W. South Memorial Church of the Advocate, Philadelphia’s first Episcopal Cathedral, as it appeared shortly after its completion in 1897. | Photo courtesy of Church of the Advocate
 When the George W. South Memorial Church of the Advocate opened its doors at 18th and Diamond Streets in 1897, Philadelphia’s Episcopalians seemed to have found their cathedral. Designed by Charles Marquedant Burns, the Church of the Advocate was the largest and most elaborate Episcopal church in the city. Measuring 170 feet long and 110 feet wide at its transepts, and seating 1,500, the church was considered the de facto Episcopal Cathedral of Pennsylvania.
 Nevertheless, the lure of a custom-built, Center City cathedral continued to tempt Episcopalians. By 1910, the North Philadelphia neighborhood around the Church of the Advocate had become a congested, working-class community. Philip M. Rhinelander, Whitaker’s successor as Episcopal Bishop, was sympathetic to a new cathedral, especially as St. John the Divine took shape in Manhattan.
 In 1913, Bishop Rhinelander met with members of Philadelphia’s Episcopal elite, including George Wharton Pepper, Samuel Frederic Houston, and Eli Kirk Price II, to form a Cathedral Foundation. A charter was drawn up for the “Protestant-Episcopal Cathedral Church of Christ.” In 1916, the Fairmount Park Commission, under the direction of Eli Kirk Price, allotted a site for the cathedral on the north side of the Fairmount Parkway between 21st and 22nd Streets, the site of the current-day Rodin Museum.
 A cross-section of the Episcopal Cathedral on the Fairmount Parkway, 1917, as envisioned by the office of Jacques Gréber. | Image courtesy of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Library and Archives
 A grand Episcopal Cathedral was an integral factor in the Fairmount Parkway (today the Benjamin Franklin Parkway), laid out by Paul Philippe Cret in 1907 and later modified by Jacques Gréber. Before the Parkway opened in 1918, Cret and Gréber had drafted plans depicting it as Philadelphia’s Champs-Elysées. Lined with neoclassical buildings housing the city’s major institutions, the Parkway would culminate in a palatial museum of art atop Fairmount Plateau.
 Among its landmarks would be the Episcopal Cathedral. Gréber’s elevations depicted a structure in the Byzantine style, flanked by a soaring campanile. Its elongated dome evoked the new Basilique du Sacré-Coeur de Montmartre in Paris. From 1917 through 1924, outdoor summer church services were held on the site, attracting between 200 and 400 worshippers each Sunday.
 In 1923, Thomas J. Garland succeeded Rhinelander as Bishop. While Garland supported the cathedral, he was less enthusiastic about its proposed location. The rise in automotive traffic meant increasing noise and congestion along the Parkway. More importantly, affluent Philadelphians, including many Episcopalians, were fleeing Center City for outlying enclaves like Chestnut Hill and the Main Line.
 The architect’s model for the Cathedral Church of Christ and campus in Roxborough. This model, which cost $10,000 to construct in 1929, later vanished. | Image courtesy of St. Mary’s Episcopal Church
 On December 2, 1926, the Philadelphia Inquirer announced the Episcopal Diocese had acquired over 100 acres in rural Upper Roxborough from the Henry H. Houston estate. The new cathedral site was bounded by Hagys Mill Road on its west, Ridge Avenue on the east, and Manatawna Avenue on the north. Garland explained that while the site was currently meadow and woodland, suburban expansion would make it the geographic center of the Diocese within a decade.
 More importantly, the proposed Chestnut Hill-Bryn Mawr Boulevard would run along the southern edge of the site. This road would originate in Ardmore, cross the Schuylkill River, Upper Roxborough and Wissahickon Creek, and traverse Chestnut Hill before connecting with Bethlehem Pike and Lincoln Drive. Nicknamed “the Social Highway,” the boulevard would link nearly every upscale community west of Center City, from the Main Line to Old York Road. It would provide the perfect conduit for the affluent Episcopalians Bishop Garland hoped would finance and fill the pews of his cathedral. Designed by Paul Philippe Cret, the boulevard was under consideration by the Philadelphia City Council with approval expected soon.
 The sale was a coup for Samuel F. Houston, who owned thousands of undeveloped acres throughout Upper Roxborough. In 1921, he had lobbied unsuccessfully for Philadelphia to use these lands for the 1926 Sesquicentennial International Exposition. Houston, a leader in the Cathedral Chapter, donated the four acres of land on which the Cathedral proper would stand. The remaining 96 acres cost the Episcopal Diocese approximately $500,000.
 : Thomas J. Garland, Episcopal Bishop of the Diocese of Pennsylvania, leads the first open-air worship service on the Roxborough Cathedral site on May 22, 1927. | Photo: Newspapers.com via The Philadelphia Inquirer 
 Houston was the son of Pennsylvania Railroad executive Henry H. Houston, the largest landowner in Northwest Philadelphia. After convincing his railroad to extend a line to the western side of Chestnut Hill in the 1880s, Henry created the model suburb of St. Martin’s, complete with Episcopal church, private school, cricket club, and dozens of upscale homes. Samuel Houston had hoped to emulate his father’s accomplishment in Upper Roxborough with minimal success to date. Yet, the realization of both the cathedral and the Social Highway would surely transform his fields and forests into a second Chestnut Hill.
 On May 22, 1927, the first open-air worship service was held in Roxborough. A crowd of 4,000 heard Bishop Garland envision “a noble and majestic cathedral crowning a lofty eminence, its stately spires silhouetted against the sky.” Standing 400 feet above sea level, the cathedral would anchor a vast campus containing dozens of ancillary buildings. A traffic circle at the intersection of Ridge Avenue, Henry Avenue, and a new Cathedral Avenue would channel worshippers into the beautifully landscaped grounds.
 The firm of Watson, Edkins & Thompson, specialists in ecclesiastic architecture, was engaged to design the project. In 1929, they unveiled plans for the world’s biggest Gothic cathedral. The cruciform structure with an exterior of local Wissahickon schist would extend nearly 1,000 feet along its east-west axis. A square bell tower would soar 300 feet over the central crossing, visible for miles, while a 220-foot tower would rise above the apse.
 Paul Philippe Cret’s proposed Bryn Mawr-Chestnut Hill Boulevard is the pink line running from the Main Line at left to Chestnut Hill at right in this 1927 map. The section in purple at right center indicates the Cathedral site. | Image courtesy of University Archives and Records Center, University of Pennsylvania
 In June 1932, ground was broken for the Cathedral Church of Christ. Construction began at once on St. Mary’s Chapel, the smallest section at the eastern end of the apse. This unit had been funded by a bequest from the estate of Annie Masden Vaughan Watson as a tribute to her mother. Watson, wife of a U.S. Congressman, had left over $100,000 to build a memorial chapel in South Philadelphia when she died in 1915. Bishop Garland had persuaded her heirs to donate the funds to the Roxborough Cathedral instead.
 If not for the Watson bequest, nothing might have been built on the site. By 1932, the Great Depression had paralyzed the nation. Even the mighty Episcopal Church struggled to remain solvent. Bishop Francis M. Taitt, who succeeded Thomas Garland in 1931, recommended the cathedral project be shelved for 20 years. However, construction continued, and the first service of Evening Prayer was held in St. Mary’s Chapel on December 8, 1933. It was a candlelight service, since the electricity was not yet working.
 In 1935, the Cathedral Building Committee issued a new design reducing the size of the structure by nearly one-half. The revised format eliminated most of the surrounding buildings and apse tower, and replaced the square central tower with a lower octagonal lantern modeled on Ely Cathedral. By this time, the church had defaulted on its mortgage and forfeited 34 acres back to the Houston estate, reducing the size of its property to roughly 70 acres.
 Left: architect’s conception of St. Mary’s Chapel at the far eastern end of the Cathedral (behind the apse tower), ca. 1929. Right: St. Mary’s Chapel as completed, 1932. | Images courtesy of St. Mary’s Episcopal Church
 Work ground to a halt after the construction of St. Michael’s Chapel on the south side of St. Mary’s Chapel in 1938. America’s entry into World War II guaranteed that nothing would be built “for the duration.” The western end of the truncated structure was walled in with a temporary facing of corrugated steel that would remain in place for four decades. Despite its fragmentary status, the structure was still referred to as "the Cathedral." Before long, it became the final resting place of Bishops Thomas Garland and Francis Taitt. 
 When prosperity returned after World War II, the original cathedral developers were either elderly or dead. Plans for the Social Highway had been suspended, and would be scrapped in 1959. Only a one-mile stretch named Cathedral Road was built between the cathedral property and Wissahickon Valley Park. On the east side of Ridge Avenue, Cathedral Road was surrounded by a suburban development originally called Cathedral Hills, but later named Andorra.
 In the 1950s, there was discussion of resuming construction, and a Chapter House was erected on the north side of St. Mary’s Chapel. Yet, the Episcopal Church was shifting its focus from cathedrals to social reform. In 1977, the Diocese announced plans to build a $22 million retirement community named Cathedral Village on the land surrounding St. Mary’s Chapel. “The retirement village means that the cathedral never will be completed,” a diocesan spokesman confirmed. “We feel we can do much more for mankind by taking care of its needs.”
 Architect’s conception of the condensed Cathedral design from 1936, showing the one central lantern tower. | Image courtesy of St. Mary’s Episcopal Church
 During the same period, the Episcopal Diocese sold the western half of its property above Hagys Mill Road to private developers. Roughly 100 homes were constructed along a network of ecclesiastically named streets including Steeple Drive, Belfry Drive, and Prelate Circle.
 In 1987, Edward R. Watson of Mirick Pearson Batcheler redesigned St. Mary’s as a parish church seating 50. The metal shield on its west end was replaced with a tinted glass wall, and a temporary narthex used as the main entrance was demolished. A large assembly room named Cathedral Hall was constructed between the cathedral and the main entrance to Cathedral Village, along with covered walkways connecting the church and retirement home.
 Following the latest trends in church design, St. Mary’s traditional altar, baptismal font, and pews were replaced with modern furnishings. The clear windows of the sanctuary were exchanged for contemporary designs by Charles Z. Lawrence of Willets Stained Glass Studio. Architect Watson discovered that in the haste to finish the chapel in the 1930s, some stones of the vaulted ceiling had been laid in place with wadded newspapers instead of mortar. For nearly 50 years, St. Mary’s parishioners had been at risk of being crushed by falling masonry.
 The front of the Cathedral ca. 1955, showing the temporary entrance (with the red doors traditional to Episcopal churches) and the sheet metal covering the unfinished western end. | Image courtesy of St. Mary’s Episcopal Church
 In 1992, the Episcopal Diocese of Pennsylvania established its current cathedral at the former Church of the Saviour at 38th and Chestnut Streets in West Philadelphia. The Romanesque Revival brownstone church, originally designed by Samuel Sloan, opened in 1855, but was substantially rebuilt after a 1902 fire. Supported by the wealthy Drexel family, the church interior boasted elaborate murals, decorated walls, and a baptismal font of translucent Mexican onyx.
 Since its designation, the Episcopal Cathedral has courted architectural controversy several times. In 2001, then-cathedral Dean Richard Giles undertook a radical “re-ordering” of the interior. The altar, pews, and other furnishings were replaced by modern fittings, while many of the murals and wall decorations were concealed. A decade later, the cathedral sold its parish house and rectory, listed on both the National and the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. The properties were replaced by a 25-story luxury apartment tower, 3737 Chestnut, which included facilities for diocesan use. Proceeds from the sale were used to repair and stabilize the cathedral’s bell tower.
 The western facade of St. Mary’s Episcopal Church as it appears today. | Photo: Thomas H. Keels.
 Today, St. Mary’s Episcopal Church in Andorra ministers to the Episcopal community of Upper Roxborough. Besides its Gothic exterior and older stained-glass windows by D’Ascenzo Studios, a few traces of the cathedral-that-might-have-been linger in corners of the church. Outside the building's eastern end, a massive bell weighing over a ton hangs from a steel girder. Seven smaller bells rest in the basement. All were cast at the Whitechapel Bell Foundry in London, where the original Liberty Bell was cast in 1752. They are part of a chime of 12 bells that once hung in the tower of the Episcopal Church of St. Matthias at 19th and Wallace Streets. When St. Matthias relocated to West Oak Lane in 1943, the congregation gifted their bells to St. Mary’s, hopeful that they would one day ring out from the tower of the finished cathedral.
 A stained-glass window depicts St. Michael defeating Satan inside St. Michael’s Chapel. | Image courtesy of St. Mary’s Episcopal Church
 The beautiful detailing of St. Michael's Chapel gives some indication of how the entire cathedral might have appeared had it been finished. A stained-glass triptych showing St. Michael defeating Satan dominates the space. An intricately carved stone altar fills the eastern end, while gilded and enameled bosses shine from the ribs of the vaulted ceiling. The crypt stones of Samuel F. Houston (died 1952) and his second wife Charlotte (died 1940) take up most of the floor.
 Across the road, a portrait of Samuel Houston by Alice Kent Stoddard hangs in a corner of the lobby of Cathedral Village. Damaged and worn, the Houston portrait goes unnoticed by most Village residents. It serves as an apt analogy for the entwined social and religious aspirations of Philadelphia’s vanished Episcopal elite, who a century ago dreamt of raising the greatest Gothic cathedral in the world high above the Schuylkill River.
 The author wishes to thank the Reverend Peter Carey, Rector of St. Mary’s Episcopal Church, for his generous help in researching this article. 
 Tags: historic churches Roxborough 
 About the Author
 Thomas H. Keels is a historian, lecturer, and commentator specializing in the history and architecture of the Philadelphia region. He has written or co-authored seven books, including "Forgotten Philadelphia: Lost Architecture of the Quaker City" and "Sesqui! Greed, Graft, and the Forgotten World's Fair of 1926" both published by Temple University Press. His next book, "Sinners and Scandals of Laurel Hill Cemetery," will be released by The History Press in Autumn 2026.

title: A Three-Book Set Offers Philadelphia "a New History for the 21st Century"
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The year 2026 promises to yield a plethora of projects centered on United States history for the Semiquincentennial, and Philadelphia is positioning itself to be the epicenter of the celebrations. The University of Pennsylvania Press has gotten an early start, in a big way, with a three-volume set of books on Philadelphia history.
 Subtitled A New History for the Twenty-First Century , the books have been curated in collaboration with the online site, The Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia (EGP), with additional content. EGP resides at the Mid-Atlantic Regional Center for the Humanities located at Rutgers Camden. “When we went to curate the books, we looked at what we had in the digital site,” said Charlene Mires, professor emerita of history at Rutgers Camden and a co-founder of EPG. She was the leader of the book project and co-editor of Volume Two.
 Rather than being arranged chronologically or alphabetically, each of the three volumes places Philadelphia in a geographic framework. With the first book, The Greater Philadelphia Region , Mires explained, “We were thinking about how Philadelphia relates to New Jersey, Delaware, and southeastern Pennsylvania, at how they’re connected.” The second volume is titled Greater Philadelphia and the Nation , and the third expands outward with Greater Philadelphia and the World .
 Within those geographic contexts, each book examines the city’s history, culture, institutions, and politics, past and present. “We saw that we had groups of topics with not only historical events, but also showing how the nation continued to evolve,” said Mires.
 The more than 100 contributors are historical scholars, archivists, public historians, journalists, and cultural commentators. Yet, despite the roster of authors being weighted somewhat towards Ph.D. historians, the content is remarkably accessible to a general readership, while still holding the interest of those with a deeper knowledge of the city.
 Even the editors found themselves learning new things. “I co-authored an essay on Center City, working with Catharine Dann Roeber. I learned why we call it Center City,” Mires recalled. “At the city’s founding, it was just ‘Philadelphia.’ In the aftermath of consolidation, a new reference was needed for what it was called. It became Central City and, eventually, Center City. It was fun for me to figure out that transition.”
 “We wanted to write them in ways that are not too technical,” she continued. “We set out to have accessible essays grounded in the latest, best scholarship, including content that might have been contained in academic publications, but not widely known.”
 Howard Gillette, professor emeritus of history at Rutgers Camden and co-editor of The Greater Philadelphia Region , noted that all the essays, regardless of the authors’ credentials, underwent the same rigorous fact-checking and editing that more academically-oriented work will experience.
 While it is common practice for non-fiction publications to include a reading list to encourage more learning, these books take it further. Each chapter ends with an “Explore More” section that highlights places and collections to visit, as well as suggested readings, following the lead of EPG. “That’s always been fundamental in our work,” said Mires. “We’ve always asked our authors to encourage readers to get out and actually see the places they’re reading about.”
 The editors followed their own advice when sourcing visuals for the books, seeking out Philadelphia’s wide collection of archives and institutions to assemble photographs and images of maps, portraits, and documents to support the writing.
 The University of Pennsylvania Press received funding to provide a set of the books to all Philadelphia public schools and each of the 55 branches of the Free Library of Philadelphia and for the editors to offer workshops in the schools.
 At a time when portions of the nation’s history are under siege by the Trump administration , which aims to erase negative events, it is noteworthy that the authors in these volumes have instead acknowledged that history in a straightforward, objective manner. Volume 2, Greater Philadelphia and the Nation , opens with an essay by co-editor Jean R. Soderlund entitled “Challenging the Nation’s Paradox,” a clear-eyed discussion of the contradictions contained in the Declaration of Independence’s assertion of “all men are created equal” when it was written in 1776.
 “I look at these books as being a legacy of scholarship. They were finished before that [executive order],” explained Mires. “They reflect on all aspects of Philadelphia and U.S. history. These books speak to that history. We hope that by doing so will inspire the next generation of scholars.”
 Tags: book review Semiquincentennial 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Philadelphia Was David Lynch’s Room To Dream
author: Julien Suaudeau
bodyText:
Laura Dern as Diane Evans in David Lynch's Twin Peaks: The Return . Most of the people the author talked to at the Philadelphia Film Society’s The Return Marathon agreed that Diane is Philly.
 Author's Note : Episodes 1 and 2 of Song of Lynchadelphia (Season 3 of Hidden City's Song of Philadelphia Podcast ) focused on the creative big bang that took place during David Lynch’s time in Philadelphia, between 1965 and 1970. Episode 3, available today on Spotify and Apple Podcasts , examines the wild ways in which the city—Lynch’s impression of the city—manifests itself in Eraserhead, Mulholland Drive, and the Twin Peaks universe .
 I don’t think David Lynch owes everything, as an artist, to the years he spent in Philadelphia. I have no doubt he would have pursued the “art life” anywhere—his soulmate Jack Fisk told me the drive to do so existed in his friend long before Lynch followed Fisk to study at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. I don’t think Philadelphia is Lynch’s only influence either. The personal memory of the picket-fence, lots-of-woods, lots-of-chrome world of his childhood in the Northwest plays a key role in Blue Velvet and the Twin Peaks universe. Hollywood ghosts haunt the character names in the first two seasons of the TV show: Billy Wilder’s Sunset Boulevard (Lynch’s Gordon Cole double) and Otto Preminger’s Laura (Laura Palmer, Waldo Lydecker), among others. In Twin Peaks , Lynch also inserts playful nods to people who had a major impact on him early on: a mentor in the arts ( Bushnell Keeler), a high school sweetheart ( Judy Westerman), a Germantown printmaker who gave him work when Lynch dropped out of PAFA (Roger LaPelle, whose last name means “shovel” in French, turns into a rant in Dr. Amp’s online videos in The Return , Lynch’s 2016 reboot of the original show).
 But Philadelphia, as Lynch put it himself multiple times, was his greatest influence. Although the city is visible only in a couple of shots in his entire filmography (the Liberty Bell in Twin Peaks: Fire Walk With Me and the William Penn statue on top of City Hall in The Return ), it finds a spiritual way onto the screen. Philadelphia exists in Lynch’s cinema as an aura, not as a physical presence. Take Eraserhead , Lynch’s “Philadelphia story.” Not only does the film recreate the sights and sounds that Lynch experienced while he lived here, but it also offers a cinematic translation of powerful personal memories attached to the city: the memory of the “fear,” the “violence,” the “corruption,” and the “insanity” that Lynch identified as the fabric of Philly in the second half of the 1960s; the memory of sleep deprivation as a young father (Lynch was 22 when his daughter Jennifer was born).
 The daily grind of parenting, seen from the perspective of a man who has other desires to pursue, takes monstruous proportions in the film. When they started working on Mulholland Drive , Lynch told Fisk that the original idea for the film came to him after a frightening encounter in the back of an L.A. diner.
 Early in the film, two men with no apparent connection to the main plot sit at a diner called Winkie’s. They are there because one of them has had two bad dreams about the place. In the dreams, the man says, “there’s a man in the back of this place. He’s the one who’s doing it.” The dreamer wants to get rid of that “god-awful feeling.” When they go outside to make sure it was just a dream, a soot-covered creature appears in front of them. The dreamer collapses and becomes unresponsive. How is that a trace of Philadelphia? Soot. In two interviews of Lynch that I have used extensively in the Lynchadelphia season, Lynch mentions that Philly was a filthy place when he lived here. “The buildings were soot-covered.” “The walls were covered with a black soot.” In his imagination, soot is both a plot signal that something bad is happening or about to happen, and a Philadelphia memory. It is the artist processing the negativity of what he experienced in the city and turning it into art, painting it on film.
 When the Woodsmen appear to David Lynch’s Gordon Cole character in The Return , they are standing on a staircase that looks straight out of a Philly row house
 In Twin Peaks: The Return , the characters known as the Woodsmen are soot-covered. Gordon Cole describes them as “dirty bearded men,” while his sidekick Albert Rosenfield says one “looked like a homeless man.” When three of them appear in a vortex to Gordon Cole, they are standing on an old staircase that looks straight out of a Philly row house. Lynch’s character strangely waves to them, as if he wanted to be sucked into the Philadelphia memory. Albert grabs him by the arm and holds him back just before the Woodsmen take him away.
 Another character in The Return , Diane, is widely seen in the Philly Lynch fandom as a personification of the city’s mood. Diane is a chain-smoker. She drinks large amounts of coffee and liquor. When Cole and Rosenfield visit her in her Philadelphia apartment (the outside shot of the façade is of a New York brownstone), Diane makes it very clear that they are not welcome. “Fuck you, Gordon… Fuck you too, Albert.” Most of the people I talked to at the Philadelphia Film Society’s The Return Marathon agreed that Diane is Philly. George Griffith, the actor who plays Ray Monroe in The Return , is from Philly. In high school, at the end of the 1980s, he was obsessed with Twin Peaks . When he met Lynch, years later, he introduced himself as “George Griffith from Philadelphia.” Together, they invented a character whose “playfulness when approaching menace” is a reminder of Philadelphia.
 A Philadelphia apparition in LA: Bonnie Aarons (who plays the figure behind the dumpster) and David Lynch on the set of Mulholland Drive 
 In Twin Peaks: Fire Walk With Me , the FBI has its headquarters in Philadelphia. You could see that as just a funny reference to Lynch’s time here. I think it is much more than that. The scene, which Lynch replays in The Return (“I saw myself, from long ago, in the old Philadelphia offices”), is the center of the Twin Peaks mythology. It is also connected to the Mulholland Drive diner scene: a character tells another about a dream they had, and something epically bad happens. What’s going on? Who’s the dreamer?
 I think Lynch himself is. Philadelphia is the name of the dream place where he is giving us unrestricted access to his creative mind, while hinting that it’s all a dream, and that we too live inside the dream. We share the “powerful, uneasy feeling” that comes over Gordon Cole as we become aware of the possibility that we too may be characters, shadows pretending to be real.
 At the end of the day, this is what Philadelphia is in the Lynch universe: both the origin of the art life and the realization that life is but a dream. What I love most about Lynch and his characters is that they reach deeper into the dream even after the suspension of disbelief has been shattered. And we’re invited to reach along. It’s one of the most powerful contradictions I’ve experienced in front of any art form, and it’s a legacy of Lynch’s time in Philadelphia.
 Tags: David Lynch Eraserhood Song of Lynchadelphia Song of Philadelphia Twin Peaks 
 About the Author
 Julien Suaudeau Julien Suaudeau is a French-American writer, documentary filmmaker, and podcaster. He was born in Evreux, Normandy, grew up in Paris, France, and moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 2006. He teaches French and Film at Bryn Mawr College. In 2024, he launched Song of Philadelphia, Hidden City's podcast.

title: 339 Manumissions Project Honors Those Enslaved by Quakers
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
If you ask Wanda Avis McClinton of the 339 Manumissions and Beyond Project to define manumission, her immediate reply will be that it is “okey doke,” which is a slang term that means “to go along with something until you are in a position to get your way.” In this case, the enslavers used manumission, according to McClinton, as a “tool of slavery to keep [slaves] in line and obedient” instead of as it was intended to be a promise to deliver “freedom to the enslaved, either immediately or at a later date.”
 The 339 Manumission Project is a reparative, genealogical search to find, acknowledge, and provide closure to the formerly enslaved of the Pennsylvania Quakers–and over time, North America–who gained their freedom from the abolishment of slavery within the Society of Friends. The project hopes to identify and tell their stories instead of leaving them lost to time. The project’s board, or “A-Team," is comprised of Quakers and non-parishioners: Dennis Gregg, Stephanie Leonard, Catherine Nnoka, Brittany Lewis, Kitty Mizuno, David Lopez, and McClinton. The group are determined to repay “a debt that is owed to those people and their descendants.”
 McClinton said that “God told her to go to the Upper Dublin Meeting House on the hill.” After visiting the location, she had meetings where she was told about the burial ground and the enslaved buried there. It was at that moment she had her “epiphany” about finding all of the formerly enslaved who were once owned by Quakers. To her and the other members of the restorative project, it has become a passion project that they hope finally tells the stories of the Quakers and their enslaved ones.
 Wanda Avis McClinton. | Photo: 339 Manumissions and Beyond Project
 Commencing in 2022, Haverford College intended to find additional information about the individuals within their Quaker archives, which are composed of collections from Abington, Exeter, Gwynedd, Haverford, Philadelphia, Blackwater, and both the Northern and Southern Districts’ Meeting Houses. McClinton was asked to join due to her 2013 work that helped established a historical marker at the Upper Dublin Meetinghouse for the unnamed enslaved and Quaker Hannah Atkinson buried in their cemetery. Since then, the project has become more than only McClinton who, over time, reached out to friends and other individuals who also feel strongly about the research on a personal level.
 Mizuno, formerly from the Haddonfield, New Jersey Friends Meeting, learned through the project that her ancestors signed two manumission documents. Nnoka was born and raised in Nigeria to a Nigerian father and Swedish American mother who was a Quaker. She finds the work to be a “priority to help make it possible for those descended from the enslaved to have access to their family tree.”
 Manumission of Celia, an enslaved woman, from 1779. | Photo: 339 Manumissions and Beyond Project
 Who were these enslaved individuals? Thus far, the most complete story goes to Dinah, her daughter Bess, and her grandchild Cyrus from Stenton, which was the home of James Logan, the colonial secretary to William Penn. Dinah recently received a monument to her memory. Some of the other individuals found within the records include Cesar, who was enslaved by the Evans family, Jack, enslaved at age 11 and freed at age 21 by Benjamin Mather of the Abington Meeting House, and Phebe, whose age of enslavement and freedom are unlisted, but she was owned by Rebecca Steel of the Northern District. The list continues with James, Ann, Rose, Cicely, Robert Venable, Violet London, Sancho, Hagar, Cassandra (Cassy), Eleanor Sneed, Mary Amy, Exeter, Glasgow, and others all making up the initial 339 found in the manumission records. To date, the number is close to 400 and climbing as the research scope expands to encompass New Jersey, Maryland, and Delaware.
 Gregg explained that “the 339 is the beginning.” Over time, the project members plan to increase the scope to include everyone who was manumissioned by Quakers across the United States. This end goal is likely to outlast the A-Team, but team members hope that the project is continued by the B-Team consisting of historians, researchers, academics, history majors, retirees, enthusiasts, and any other interested persons.
 Genealogist Shamele Jordon and a volunteer searches the archives for information on Dinah, who was enslaved at Stenton, and her children. | Photo: 339 Manumissions and Beyond Project
 At the moment, the biggest obstacle is gaining access, reviewing, and finding all the records related to the formerly enslaved. This task is made even more difficult due to census records not fully acknowledging Blacks until about 1870. McClinton added how “unique the reparative research is” and mentions that the Quakers had remarkable records and resources that detail names, slave ships, the companies who insured them, and their destinations in Africa. “Paper, paper, paper. All of these papers are in these archives somewhere, and no one has looked at them and decided to try and make order of it all,” McClinton remarked on how long it has taken for a project such as this to take form. The group has faced obstacles from other Quakers and institutions that feel that the past should stay there. In response, McClinton stated that they are not assigning blame to anyone, and it is important to remember that history of the enslaved is interwoven with Quakers history. Doing something like the project is long overdue.
 The collected works will be gathered and made digital at Howard University’s newly-minted Center for an Equitable and Sustainable Society (E2S2). The collaboration will allow the work to be easily accessible to future generations.
 For now, the focus is on finding researchers and funding because the work is being done voluntarily. The project would like to change that status to help staff devote more time to conducting research. Until then, the volunteers are relying on support from the Friends Fiduciary, but they plan to apply for a PEW research grant in the near future.
 Tags: African-American history Quakers slavery 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Places Saved: Fall 2025
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Fall 2025 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Laurel Hill Gatehouse 
 Location: 3822 Ridge Avenue
 Built: 1836
 Laurel Hill Cemetery , founded in 1836 along the banks of the Schuylkill River, was the first cemetery in the United States to be designated a National Historic Landmark. At the forefront of the rural cemetery movement, it offered a new vision for burial: one that reflected changing cultural attitudes toward death and merged natural beauty with personal remembrance.
 At the heart of this vision stands the gatehouse, the cemetery’s last remaining original building. Designed by Scottish American architect John Notman , the gatehouse served as a formal threshold to a landscape shaped by scenic design, elaborate monuments, and botanical collections. Although modest in size, the gatehouse has long played a significant role as both a symbolic and functional entry point.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Mount Vernon Cemetery 
 Location: 3301 West Lehigh Avenue
 Built: 1856
 Hope is on the horizon for one of Philadelphia’s most overlooked historic cemeteries. Just up the hill from Laurel Hill Cemetery, Mount Vernon Cemetery , a 26-acre burial ground in Allegheny West, is preparing for a long-overdue revival after decades of neglect thanks to a new era of collaborative stewardship.
 Founded in 1856 as a direct competitor to Laurel Hill, the cemetery was part of the rural cemetery movement, offering beautifully landscaped grounds and architect-designed monuments, including a stunning marble archway attributed to John Notman. The site is also home to the Gardel Monument, a pyramidal tomb by architect Napoleon LeBrun, adorned with marble figures by Belgian sculptor Guillaume Geefs.
 After years of ownership disputes, a Philadelphia judge approved the transfer of the property to Steelmantown Cemetery Company, a national leader in green burials, the conclusion of an Act 135 conservatorship process. The Friends of Mount Vernon Cemetery, who have stewarded the site for the past four years, will continue and expand their role, overseeing public access, community engagement, and preservation efforts.
 The plan is to create a “hybrid” cemetery model that combines green burials with historic restoration, cultural programming, and accessible green space. Security cameras have already been installed, and invasive overgrowth is being cleared. By 2026, pathways and structures are expected to be stabilized, and the site will be reopened to visitors and mourners alike. Mount Vernon is preparing a comeback, one rooted in memory, ecology, and renewed community connection.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Lansdowne Theater 
 Location: 31 North Lansdowne Avenue, Lansdowne
 Built: 1927
 The Lansdowne Theater stands as a stunning example of 1920s movie palace architecture. Designed in 1927 by renowned theater architect William H. Lee, it showcases the Spanish Revival style with an ornate interior that includes hand-painted ceilings, a grand chandelier and intricate plasterwork. For decades, it served as a vibrant cultural anchor, hosting films, live performances, and community events.
 The theater closed in 1987 due to an electrical fire and the rise of alternative entertainment options. Years of vacancy and neglect led to significant deterioration, with water damage and deferred maintenance placing the building at risk. Fortunately, the Historic Lansdowne Theater Corporation and local advocates recognized its cultural and architectural value, launching an ambitious restoration campaign.
 Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the theater has benefited from generous public and private support. A multiphase rehabilitation effort is now nearing completion, preserving original features such as the vaulted auditorium ceiling, ornate stage proscenium, and iconic marquee, while modernizing the building for its new life as a live music venue.
 The theater’s reopening marks a major milestone for Lansdowne, restoring a cherished landmark as a hub for arts and entertainment. Once again, it will host nationally and internationally recognized performers, drawing an estimated 100,000 annual visitors. The revitalization is expected to stimulate the local economy, generate new jobs, and reaffirm the theater’s role as a dynamic centerpiece for the community.
 Tags: historic cemeteries Historic theaters John Notman Laurel Hill Cemetery Places Saved 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Gilded Age Home at 16th and Girard May be Saved From Dereliction
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
Three years ago, the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia included a Gilded Age home-turned-church on Girard Avenue on its quarterly Places to Save list. That served as a warning of its potential demise more than as an honorific. Yet, either way, the preservation gods may have been listening.
 Ferat Ferko, a plumber and part-time developer operating in Philadelphia, said he purchased the French Gothic Revival building at 1609 W. Girard Avenue last fall with the intention of restoring it–or at least its handsome front facade–and converting the interior into apartments. During an interview in January, Ferko was unaware of the structure’s history. Some scholars believe it was designed by notable architect William Lightfoot Price and constructed in 1895. The once well-to-do residence is listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. It later became home of the Mount Sharon Baptist Church in 1970, which maintained active ownership of the property until about 2017. Ferko expressed intrigue, asking for more information and stating he had no intention of seeking a demolition or otherwise materially altering the structure, which has fallen on hard times over the past decade. “We’re going to keep it the same in the front,” Ferko said. “I’ll fix it nice.”
 1609 W. Girard Avenue. | Photo: Peter Woodall
 He confirmed prior reports that the building’s roof is significantly compromised. He also said there are structural issues to the rear of the building, which extends to a depth of about 100 feet from the facade. He's recently had an architect in to begin drafting repairs for the roof and rear walls and is working to close Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I) violations with the City over the building’s derelict status and exterior sanitation issues.
 Ferko has a track record nearby, stating that he restored the adjacent 1613 Girard Avenue, a three-story rowhouse built in the 1860s that is also listed on the local register. City property records and visual evidence indeed indicate that Ferko worked to rehab the property.
 This all sounds like good news to Hanna Stark, director of policy and communications at the Preservation Alliance. She is the author and researcher behind the 2023 Extant magazine article on 1609 W. Girard Avenue. Last Stark had heard, the home's future was tied up in a messy Act 135 process–a legal remedy allowing third-parties to take charge of historic buildings with absentee owners. Now there is new hope for what she called a “very distinct” late 19th century home. “That was what caught our eye, was the fact that it was so unique. You don’t really see these types of loggia porches on Girard, very atypical from the standard rowhouse, even from a time when West Girard was very desirable and fashionable,” Stark explained. “And it comes at a very interesting point in Price’s career, after he had already done some of his suburban Arts and Craft style.”
 A Gilded Beginning 
 Who was the original owner of 1609 W. Girard Avenue? Stark’s research points to Ferdinand Keller, a "significant importer of antiques to Philadelphia” in the late 1800s. That would appear to make sense. During the Preservation Alliance’s research for a nomination of the nearby Pyramid Club , Keller’s name was linked to architect Price, whom he hired to renovate that property at 1517 W. Girard. A late 19th century construction of 1609 W. Girard Avenue by a prominent architect would also fit thematically, occurring at a time when wealthy Philadelphians were populating the corridor and building grandiose residences, none more so than the Widener Mansion at Broad Street and Girard Avenue which was built 1887.
 Keller would appear to have fit in with that crowd. “Keller was the largest importer of Old World antiques to Philadelphia for roughly a half-century, from around the time of the Centennial until the 1920s,” the Preservation Alliance noted in its nomination. “It is likely that Keller supplied at least some of the antiquities that filled Woodmont and Price’s other mansions along the Main Line. What is clear is that Price was himself a great admirer of the kinds of antiquarian objects that Keller collected and sold.”
 What isn’t clear is whether Keller was indeed the owner and commissioner of 1609 W. Girard Avenue. The Preservation Alliance cites a 1985 nomination of the Girard Avenue Historic District to the National Register of Historic Places by Dr. George Thomas of the Clio Group, which attributes the “wonderful French Gothic house” as being designed by Price for Keller.
 A portrait of architect William Lightfoot Price from Philadelphia and Notable Philadelphians , 1901. | Photo courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 However, other records call that into question. Bruce Bohri, a spokesperson for the Department of Planning and Development, said its files on the property are scant. However, a clipping it holds from the 1891 Philadelphia Real Estate Record and Builders Guide states that a construction firm called Geo. Watson & Son was to build a residence with a “brownstone front” for Dr. B.F. Betz at 1609 Girard Avenue. The snippet makes no mention of Keller or Price, although it does not specify the architect.
 Contemporary newspaper records point in a similar direction.The first reference to a 1609 W. Girard Avenue dates to 1861, when a Philadelphia Inquirer article lists for sale a “well built three-story” brick dwelling at the address without further description. Other records suggest occupancy by a George Stuckert eight years later, and then a Dr. Betts, a “prominent homeopathic physician,” by 1882. In 1891, the same year as the clip housed in the City’s files, a notice in The Philadelphia Times also notes that “George Watson” had been retained to perform a “front and interior alteration” at 1609 Girard Avenue. Dimensions are listed as “30×15 feet,” which appears to match the approximate size of the building’s current limestone porch. Again, the notice did not specify the architect of any alterations and appears to contradict the Builders Guide snippet from the same year, which suggested a brand new construction.
 Additional newspaper records suggest continued residency at the address by the Betts family into the early 20th century until, at some point, passing into the hands of a Hill family until 1949. Then, the building changed uses. Records show it was purchased by Lewis James Howell, once head of Temple University’s vocal department, for use as a music school. Howell, also once president of the Philadelphia Music Teachers Association and founder of the Pennsylvania Music Teachers Association, started a “Duo Music Club” at 1609 Girard Avenue and advertised music study sessions in local papers until his death in 1956.
 Rise and fall of Mt. Sharon Baptist Church 
 The more recent history of 1609 W. Girard Avenue as the home of the Mt. Sharon Baptist Church is clearer. Newspaper records indicate the congregation first purchased the property in May 1972 and owned it until its recent 21st century dereliction.
 Stark, in her 2023 Extant article, said the congregation was founded in 1949 by Reverend Berkley Hall, who preached racial justice and equity until his death in 1960. The congregation continued to grow after his death, necessitating the purchase of 1609 W. Girard Avenue, which it converted into a worship space. Eventually, Hall’s daughter, Prathia, who served as a field organizer with the Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee in the South, took over as pastor until her own death in 2002.
 Prathia, according to her 2002 obituary in the Philadelphia Daily News , was shot and jailed in separate incidents in Georgia in 1962 as she organized civil rights demonstrations. She showed further bravery in becoming one of the first female preachers in the “male-dominated Baptist church, when men sometimes walked out on a woman minister,” her obituary reads. Prathia would later move to Boston, where she held the Martin Luther King Jr. Chair in Social Ethics at the Boston University School of Theology.
 “Thinking about changing demographics of the neighborhood, it’s interesting that [1609 W. Girard] was kind of built for the new industrial class, and then the neighborhood becomes predominantly African American,” Stark said. “It’s an interesting duality of this space.”
 1609 W. Girard Avenue in 1968. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 Following Prathia's death, her sister Betty Hall took stewardship of 1609 W. Girard Avenue. It was then that the building began to deteriorate and rack up L&I violations, even as Hall and Pastor Clarence Smith launched an unsuccessful capital campaign in 2017 to repair the building. Stark said that in 2020, the Calcutta House, a nonprofit occupying another distinct nearby property at 1601 W. Girard Avenue, initiated the Act 135 process to attempt to save the building from dereliction. However, a dispute over ownership of Mt. Sharon Baptist Church (Stark believes Betty Hall passed during the pandemic ) and the Calcutta House’s own closure in the following years threw the effort into disarray.
 Regardless of the mysteries swirling around the property’s distant and recent past, Stark said she is glad to see new ownership and hopes it is restored. During walkthroughs during the 2010s, Stark said collegues described the building as in very poor condition, with significant water damage likely taking place for at least a decade. Still, she said the building’s significant history from the Gilded Age through Civil Rights era, and its unique facade, are indeed worth saving. “It’s a stunning building,” said Stark. “I think the fact that a developer is willing to take on rehabilitation shows that a building is never too far gone.”
 Tags: Act 135 William Lightfoot Price 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Preservationists Worry of a Demolition Loophole in Squilla Bill
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The Powelton Village Historic District in West Philadelphia was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in November 2022. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In late November, City Councilmember Mark Squilla introduced legislation that would alter the City’s regulations on protecting historic properties. Most notably, Bill No. 251030 would modify the initial stages of the nomination process to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places , giving property owners at least a 30-day heads up between when a nomination is made and an initial hearing in front of the Philadelphia Historical Commission . Proponents of the measure–primarily representatives of real estate development interests–call that fair notice. However, preservationists worry it amounts to a demolition “loophole” that will lead to the destruction of culturally-important buildings and spaces by giving property owners a chance to get a head start on demo permit applications before historic protections can go into place.
 As previously reported by Hidden City, another change would allow the Historical Commission to reject a nomination simply because the owner had submitted an application for a demolition or alteration permit, rather than having already received the permit. It would also compel the Historical Commission to allow demolition or alteration permits if the owner had conceptual development designs or contracts at the time they were notified of the proposed nomination. Finally, it would eliminate the work of significant landscape architects as a qualifying criterion for designation and weaken the ability to designate for archaeological reasons. 
 Although these provisions caught some by surprise, they didn’t come out of nowhere. Across five interviews, with Squilla and four key stakeholders, two each from the preservation and development communities, it becomes clear that the proposed policy changes arrive during a period of heightened acrimony between the interests and political jockeying that has picked up over the last year.
 The Logan Theater at 4732-42 N. Broad Street in Wyoming was was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in March 2025. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 On one side, preservationists like Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, see an overall backsliding on citywide policy. He feels that helpful recommendations from former Mayor Kenney's Historic Preservation Task Force compiled just six years ago have been left by the wayside, replaced by Squilla’s recent “surprise” introduction of the proposed amendments. “These [policy ideas] do not reflect the letter or spirit of the task force, and we think they would significantly weaken the City’s historic preservation ordinance,” Steinke said.
 On the other side, allies of developers like Sarina Rose, president of the Building Industry Association (BIA) of Philadelphia, claim current nomination practices are unfair, creating a system where historic preservation is financially hindering not just deep-pocketed interests, but homeowners and working class Joes, while also tying bureaucratic machinery in knots. “That one arm of the City accepting our money for [permit] approval, and then the other is working to stop a project, is kind of inappropriate. Really, due notice is important and fair,” said Rose.
 In the middle–ostensibly–is Squilla, who fashions himself a neutral arbiter interested in hearing arguments from both sides, while hinting that he may intentionally be cracking eggs to make an omelet. “I know it got off to a rough start. I think sometimes that’s good–not everybody understanding the full intent of the legislation,” Squilla said. “Maybe by bringing those concerns to light, that gives us an opportunity to look at it closely and make a difference.”
 All parties agree that Squilla, whose district stretches from Port Richmond to Old City and South Philadelphia, has long been engaged on matters pertaining to the historic preservation ordinance. Yet, they add that momentum behind introducing a substantial change has picked up in the last year or so, and that there is a sense that the time for discussion is coming to a close. “My understanding is that Councilman Squilla is taking very seriously all the input from stakeholders and weighing that input,” said Rose, “but, that he wants to get this done pretty soon.”
 The Backstory 
 The Paul Robeson House and Museum at 4949-51 Walnut Street in Walnut Hill was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in August 2023. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Squilla was elected to office in 2011 after an earlier public sector career as a systems analyst. By 2017, former Mayor Kenney had announced the formation of a Historic Preservation Task Force to bring together the contentious array of interests and come up with changes to the City’s ordinances. Squilla wanted in and became City Council’s representative in its membership.
 “My district has a lot of historic properties in it,” explained Squilla. “So anytime something comes out, whether it’s the Historic Commission or Planning or whoever, they look to me to say, ‘Hey, would you be interested in introducing this legislation?’”
 The Task Force spent several years producing a final report of recommendations , released in April 2019, before disbanding. From Steinke’s perspective, precious few of those recommendations have been enacted. In an interview this month, Steinke at first said none had, but later agreed with Squilla’s office that a pair introduced shortly after the Task Force, allowing for more commercial and residential reuses of historic properties , had passed.
 Still, Steinke said other major recommendations have sat on the shelf. Given Squilla’s position as the primary councilmember active on historic preservation policy, Steinke said his group and other preservationists have continued to interface with his office behind the scenes, as well as the City’s planning agencies. In fall 2024, Steinke's group approached the City’s Department of Planning and Development with policy recommendations for creating a Preservation Trust Fund, a city-wide historic resources inventory, a reintroduction of independent reviews of financial hardship applications to circumvent protections, and the creation of a tiered system of historic preservation regulations. Steinke said his group then took the recommendations to Squilla last March. “We weren’t getting much traction with Planning and Development, and so we went to Squilla. He said he was open to those ideas, and to send him a bill."
 In July, Steinke said someone from the Planning Commission called the Preservation Alliance and said they were getting started on writing a policy and asked for their recommendations again. However, Steinke learned that other draft policies were also being circulated by the development community. “We were being told by Planning and Development that they didn’t really think those ideas [from the developers] had much traction, and so it gave us some comfort,” said Steinke, adding that he was then surprised to see them included in the bill Squilla ultimately introduced in November.
 The Dr. Oscar James Cooper House at 1621 Jefferson Street in Cecil B. Moore was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in October 2023. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Rose refers to a similar timeline, saying that the BIA’s membership asked its leadership sometime in late 2024 to begin speaking with Squilla about what they felt were unfair mechanisms in the city’s historic nomination process. “There were projects that owners had spent money on: design professionals, approvals, or permits… and at the same time there was either a third party or the Historic Commission working on a nomination they had no idea about,” Rose said, adding that in some instances a property owner would be working with one City office on pulling permits, while another office unbeknownst worked to take actions that would invalidate them. “And so it was in everybody’s best interest to explore that and make sure the property was looked into before tax dollars were spent nominating [it].”
 Rose said that her group indeed met with the Historic Commission regarding a “disclosure” bill and provided text, but that City staff ultimately produced something substantially different, which wound up in the Squilla bill. That description largely squares with Squilla, who says his office received language from the BIA and other members “of the community,” but that City staff had issues with it. So, Planning staff created their own text that ultimately appeared in the bill. In an interview, Squilla also appeared to be surprised at some elements of what was included in his own bill. “I’m hearing some other consternation too about removing landscape architecture [from the list of considered protections]. About why that was removed–I’m still not sure why that was removed from the designation or nomination part of it,” Squilla said.
 He added that he thinks disclosure issues are important to address, particularly because of percolating legal challenges. Yet, Squilla also said he understands and even has supported the idea of a tiered designation process, which was in the Task Force report and continues to be a top priority for preservationists. Language creating a tiered system–which would create less onerous regulations for certain historic properties than others–was actually in a draft of the current bill at one point before being removed, he said. Concerns over how that provision was written and recent pushback from some residential groups on the creation of historic districts caused him to pull it, he added. “[A two-tiered system] was initially in this legislation that came from the Planning and Historic Commissions,” Squilla said, adding that he removed it out of concerns it lacked specificity. “We need to have some sort of guard rails and regulations in place.”
 David Gest, executive director of the Chestnut Hill Conservancy, which is opposing the bill as it is currently written, has also been involved in stakeholder meetings. He believes the bill primarily represents policies championed by development interests. However, Gest said he believes City staff also have concerns over current “technical issues” with the existing ordinance and the perceived legal vulnerabilities borne from them, and that there is a need to respect input from homeowners.
 A spokesperson for the City’s Department of Planning and Development did not respond to questions about the agency’s role in the bill’s formation.
 Disagreements Over Severity of the “Loophole” 
 Wharton Hall at 1268 S. 26th Street in Point Breeze was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in June 2023. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Squilla bill provision getting the most attention is the so-called 30-day “demolition loophole,” which Steinke said may stretch to as far as 60 days depending on how the calendar falls. In essence, it requires that the Historic Commission notify a property owner as soon as a nomination is made or received and provides a 30 or 60-day gap prior to the Commission’s consideration of its merits at a public meeting.
 Currently, Historic Commission staff review the merits of a historic nomination privately and make a determination as to whether they will recommend approval to the full Historical Commission. If they do, the property owner is notified and temporary prohibitions against issuing demolition or alternation permits go into effect. The full Commission then considers the application in a public meeting and weighs any hardship or other arguments set forth by the property owner or other interested parties before making a final determination.
 Steinke said “the fear” around a change is that the advanced notice will give property owners a heads up and time to apply for demolition and hardship permits. If they are able to obtain one, or perhaps even just apply for one, it could provide a winning argument against the application at the first hearing. “If there’s going to be a battle, it would happen at that first meeting,” Steinke said. “And that’s a standard the Commission has used all along: ‘Well, if a demolition permit was applied for before the nomination was determined complete and correct, then the demolition permit prevails.’”
 American Trust, Loan, and Guaranteed Investment Company at 684-86 N. Broad Street in Fairmount was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in February 2024. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Steinke is also concerned about paperwork issues, asserting that the Historic Commission receives many half-baked nominations that it rejects or asks an applicant to improve. Issuing notices to owners and holding a hearing for every application regardless of its merits risks gumming up the works, he said. “All of a sudden the system would be clogged up with, potentially, a whole bunch of trash nominations: having to hold hearings and the Commission has to come together [for all of them],” Steinke said.
 Matthew McClure, a zoning and land use attorney for Ballad Spahr who has been involved in policy conversations with Squilla’s office, said he believes concerns about a demolition loophole are “a little overblown.” McClure noted that the City tightened its regulations on demolition permits after the deadly 2013 Salvation Army Collapse at 22nd and Market Streets. Now producing an application, he said, often requires the engagement of engineering and legal professionals. He views it as unrealistic that a property owner will accomplish that in time, particularly if the building is presently occupied. “I have never seen anyone be able to put together a demolition permit application within 30 days,” claimed McClure.
 Rose is a little less absolute, saying she also doesn’t believe the changes will cause demolitions not already planned, but that she “could see someone pulling a demo permit for negotiating purposes.” However, both she and McClure said the provision would prevent real-world scenarios they actually are seeing, where property owners who have already sunk significant investment into the redesign of a property are blindsided by a nomination that nullifies it. “It’s a private homeowner, and they spent their nest egg on architectural fees, and they’ve already submitted for a building permit,” Rose offered as a scenario. “Then [the home] is nominated, there’s an automatic stay on the property, meaning they can’t pull their permit. Now they have to come up with a brand new design, and the Historic Commission might want it to look like the property next door.”
 What Comes Next? 
 Running through the background of the debate around new ordinances is a sense that the dynamics are exactly that: an ongoing debate. The week after Squilla introduced the ordinance, his office organized a conference call that included many of the key players, multiple attendees said. Squilla explained that the meeting provided a “surfacing of the issues,” on both sides, and mainly focused on the notification provision.
 The Philadelphia Historical Commission denied placing 4024-34 Apalogen Road in East Falls on the local register in November despite publicly recognizing that the home satisfies several criteria for designation. Tulipwood was completed in 1954 and designed by architect Elizabeth Fleisher, Philadelphia’s first licensed female architect. The home’s new owners have conceptual plans, but, according to the Department of Licenses and Inspections, have not attained any permits to raze the building and redevelop the property. Bill No. 251030 (aka the Squilla Bill), as it is currently written, would eliminate protections put in place for historic nomination submissions. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 The bill was slated to be an action item at the Planning Commission’s December 6 meeting, but was punted after staff requested a 45-day review period. At least one more stakeholder meeting then followed in mid-December, Gest said, adding that more are expected in the months ahead. Squilla said he sees at least one more private stakeholder meeting happening in January before a public Planning Commission meeting in February where the bill could be considered. A series of Council procedures and votes would then follow. “I don’t see this happening until March at the earliest,” he said. “Until we get to the point where people feel mostly comfortable with the language.”
 All parties believe the bill arrives at a time when tension over historic preservation regulations has reached a fever pitch. Preservations see a city that is losing historic buildings year-after-year as policy recommendations sit on a shelf, while developers, and some residential groups, have felt stung by what they consider overreaches under the current system of nominations. Regardless, some hope for compromise remains. “What I’ve tried to do in the meetings I’ve been in with [Squilla] and others is to just sort of carefully and continuously emphasize that these are very complex issues that require a lot of discussion and flushing out,” said Gest. “I’m cautiously optimistic that we’re going to be able to get to something that works.”
 ***
 Kimberly Haas contributed reporting to this article. 
 Tags: demolition Development Mark Squilla Philadelphia City Council Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: A New Docuseries Spotlights Women Who Helped Define the United States
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
Despite recent attempts to revert to simplistic and sanitized historical interpretations, Americans will continue to be exposed to an inclusive, nuanced depiction of the nation’s founding. Scholars will not accept the whitewashed narratives that the Trump administration is purveying. Equally important, an invisible army of genealogists, grassroots activists, and historians lacking academic credentials will continue to comb archives, special libraries, databases, and burgeoning online resources to uncover diverse and complex stories of the past. The toothpaste cannot be put back in the tube. 
 A film still from For the Common Good shows Laura Adie as Elizabeth Coates Paschal. | Image: You'll Never Forget Productions
 There is no better example of this dynamic than For the Common Good: The Women Who Shaped Our Nation , a multi-part docuseries which tells the vivid stories of nine pioneering Pennsylvania women who made important contributions to the founding of the United States. Creation of the series was spearheaded by the National Society of the Colonial Dames of America in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania (NSCDA/PA), an organization of women who have proven lineage to an ancestor who provided “service to the colony” prior to July 5, 1776.
 21st century Dames recognized that this all-female group focused almost exclusively on the lives of Colonial-era men who held office or signed key documents. The NSCDA set a goal of adding the names of 250 women to their Register of Ancestors in honor of the America 250 celebration. National efforts have exceeded this goal, while Pennsylvania alone added 73 women, nine of whom are subjects of the For the Common Good films.
 The Mother of Germantown 
 One of these women is Elin Kunders, among the first German Quakers to settle Germantown. When she and her husband Thunes left Krefeld, Germany for Pennsylvania in 1682 they were already parents of three children. Elin became pregnant en route. Their daughter Sarah was the first child born in Germantown. The Kunders’ home was one of the first buildings constructed in Germantown, and they labored with their neighbors to cultivate flax that was spun into thread and woven as cloth.
 Shelby Hightower and Faith Kelly (Elin Kunders) during shooting of For the Common Good. | Photo: Nathaniel Popkin
 Trips to Philadelphia to sell this cloth revealed to the German Quakers a shockingly different society. Many 17th century British Quakers in Philadelphia relied on enslaved labor. Horrified by what they observed, in 1688, Germantown Quakers penned British North America’s first anti-slavery document. Their reasoning included high-minded ideals about the equality of all people and more practical considerations such as the fear that slavery would deter more immigration from Germany.
 Although only men signed this anti-slavery petition, the new film imagines Elin's centrality to its creation. Women were the planters of flax, spinners of thread, and sellers of cloth who witnessed slavery in Philadelphia firsthand. The 1688 document was signed at the Kunders’ home, and Quaker communities were open to women’s voices. Furthermore, archival research done by the For the Common Good team revealed the extent of Elin's kin networks among the Germantown Quakers. Elin, who went on to have three more Pennsylvania-born children, can be considered the “Mother of Germantown.”
 Discovering Dinah 
 Dinah, another colonial ancestor newly registered by the NSCDA/PA, is also one of the women profiled in the For the Common Good series. Dinah was a formerly enslaved woman credited with saving Stenton during the Revolutionary War. Stenton, former home of the prominent Logan family , has been stewarded by the NSCDA/PA since 1899. The Dames played a pivotal role in the development of a memorial to Dinah that was unveiled in 2024.
 Piecing together life stories of individual 18th century women is challenging. The undertaking is much harder when the woman was enslaved, illiterate, and did not even have a recorded last name or date of birth. Despite the difficulties, researchers from Stenton found sporadic mentions of Dinah in records kept by women in the Logan family that owned and later employed Dinah. Likely inspired by her encounters with free Blacks and pervasive talk of universal rights, Dinah requested and was granted freedom in April 1776. Her manumission papers were found in the vast collection of the Haverford College Library , a treasure trove of Pennsylvania Quaker history.
 Dinah (Demi Davis) parlaying a British Soldier (Randell Spackman) at Stenton October 30, 2026 during shooting of For the Common Good. | Photo: Nathaniel Popkin
 Karin Wulf, the director and librarian of the John Carter Brown Library and a professor of history at Brown University, served as an advisor to the For the Common Good project. Wulf drew a parallel between slavery, in which the condition of the child depended on the status of the mother, and the use of genealogy among elite families to determine birthrights and connections. She refered to both practices as employing a similar “infrastructure of inheritance.”
 In Wulf’s view, the For the Common Good series will be a “powerfully interstitial” complement to Ken Burns’ recent miniseries The American Revolution . “These films highlighting women’s lives are really illuminating, and they will catch people’s attention if they get the chance,” said Wulf. She describes the docuseries, as well as the Colonial Dames’ efforts to expand the Register of Ancestors, as “brave and bold.”
 Documentaries as Tools of Public History 
 The nine short films in the For the Common Good docuseries were created by You'll Never Forget Productions led by director Andrew Ferrett, writer Nathaniel Popkin , and producer Eva Roben. This trio were key members of the team that created Philadelphia: Great Experiment and other Mid-Atlantic Emmy Award winning films for History Making Productions . As in the earlier documentaries, these films feature carefully researched reenactments, vivid primary sources, and commentary by well-spoken experts. Ferrett and Popkin’s most recent project for History Making Productions, In Pursuit: Philadelphia and the Making of America, premiered last month and will be screened throughout the region in coming months.
 Cinematographer Isaak Popkin with Melanie Rosenthal and Rehina Solodovnik (Eliza Hudson) at Pennsylvania Farmstead in Ridley Park during shooting of For the Common Good . | Photo: Nathaniel Popkin
 A key aspect of the For the Common Good project will be curated conversations scheduled across the Commonwealth during 2026. The first of these discussions will take place on Wednesday, March 18 at the Museum of the American Revolution (MoAR) following a screening of three of the films. A panel including Wulf, Popkin, and Mickey Herr , executive producer and NSCDA/PA member, will be moderated by Adrienne Whaley, the museum’s director of education and community engagement. Whaley was an advisor to the Dinah project at Stenton and is one of the experts featured in the Dinah film.
 According to Whaley, there is a strong alignment between the goals of For the Common Good and the MoAR’s mission to “uncover and share compelling stories about the diverse people and complex events that sparked America’s ongoing experiment in liberty, equality, and self-government.” As she explained, “People think about Founding Fathers, but not of a founding generation. Two and a half million people lived in British North America. It is ridiculous to say that only 56 of them matter.” Whaley commended the Dames for lifting up women’s stories and showing that women were active participants in the American Revolution. Fortunately, the MoAR is a private museum and thus immune to federal initiatives to erase complexity and diversity in American history.
 Sowing the Seeds of Women’s History 
 In addition to her official job at MoAR, Whaley is an avid genealogist and a past president of the African American Genealogy Group. She is passionate about the role of dogged family researchers in revealing hidden histories that become a part of the broader historical narrative. At the beginning of the Dinah film, there is a voiceover from Whaley in which she says: “When we are able to find a story of a woman, and research it deeply, and pull out the documents that can be found, piece together every mention of them that you can find, you’re creating something that’s really rare and special, and you have an opportunity to think about, for this one flower that you’ve helped to grow, this one story of a woman’s life, maybe if you can help enough of those flowers to grow, you’re going to end up with something that is lush and full and beautiful and green and has the opportunity to grow even more.”
 The inspiration for For the Common Good was a silhouette made by a young participant of Stenton's History Hunters education program.| Photo: Mickey Herr
 For the Common Good: The Women Who Shaped Our Nation is a strong start to growing this imagined garden of women’s history as we celebrate the United States Semiquincentennial. Herr was inspired by the reflections of a schoolgirl who came to Stenton as part of the History Hunters education program. When asked to express her hopes the future, the young visitor wrote in the thought bubble of a silhouette “That one day women will be treated and thought of the same way as men.” According to Herr, “Before For the Common Good was created, that little girl and her silhouette became my north star. I took a photo so I wouldn’t forget. It made me want to create a world where young girls and women could find themselves in our founding narrative. I am lucky to be a Pennsylvania Dame and part of an organization—this group of women—who want the same thing. We believe we are planting seeds for the future.”
 A screening of For the Common Good: The Women Who Shaped Our Nation will take place at the Museum of the American Revolution on Wednesday, March 18.
See details and reserve tickets here: https://www.amrevmuseum.org/events/amrev-presents-women-s-history-night 
 Learn more about future For the Common Good: A Year of Curated Conversations events here: https://www.nscdapa.org/common-good 
 Tags: American Revolution Dinah documentary Quakers slavery Women's history 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Grand Banking Hall on Broad Street Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The ornamental plaster coffered ceiling in the banking hall of the former Fidelity-Philadelphia Trust Company Building at 123 S. Broad Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Meetings of the Philadelphia Historical Commission are often dominated by frequent and predictable matters, like the review of proposed windows on a historic building or alleviating an owner’s concerns about a nomination to the historic register. At its meeting on March 13, 2026, however, the Historical Commission included a rare item on its agenda: the nomination of a building interior to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places.
 While the local register includes over 10,000 building exteriors, the Main Banking Room of the former Fidelity-Philadelphia Trust Company Building at 123 S. Broad Street has become only the 6th interior designation in the register’s 70-year history.
 Built in 1928, the exterior was added to the Philadelphia Register in 1973, followed by the National Register in 1978. It currently houses a branch of Wells Fargo Bank. The architects, Simon & Simon, specialized in public and commercial buildings, but also designed the Rodeph Shalom synagogue on North Broad Street.
