 The Main Banking Room is a significant example of the Classical Revival style typical of banking institutions in the early 20th century. It features stained glass windows by the studio of Nicola D'Ascenzo, including the large piece, History of Philadelphia , which depicts historical figures and events, and sculptural elements by the noted New York City firm Piccirilli Brothers, including a female and a male figure, representing night and day, framing a large clock on the east wall.
 The marble knee walls and teller stations were listed as "non-contributing" to give the owner future flexibility in adapting the space. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The owner did not object to the designation, but requested that the marble knee walls and bronze registers along the north and east wall, and the marble teller stations along the south wall, be classified as non-contributing. The nominator, the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, was amenable to the request.
 Historical Commission members, however, expressed concern about the “non-contributing” label, and struggled to find language that would allow flexibility for the use of the space, while still providing some protection to the elements in question, acknowledging that they are in fact part of the design of the interior. It was also pointed out that, owing to the designation, their removal would require repairs that would need to be reviewed by the Historical Commission.
 The nomination was approved, with the exclusion of the knee walls, bronze registers, and marble teller stations, but with the caveat that their removal would require documentation that would include photographs and measurements, and salvage, if possible.
 The remainder of the meeting was taken up with requested changes to three historic properties.
 The National Liberty Museum at 321-23 Chestnut Street sought approval to install five murals on several infilled window openings on its east facade, which would “highlight the museum’s mission and values.” The 1905 building was designed by architect Theophilus P. Chandler Jr. for the E. W. Clark Bank. It was individually designated in 1970 and listed as contributing to the Old City Historic District in 2003.
 The museum’s proposed method was to paint the murals on parachute cloth and attach them with a gel adhesive. The Architectural Committee had raised concerns that, because the removal method would be mechanical, it could risk damaging the historic facade. It recommended painting the murals on panels that could be attached to the infill. The Historical Commission approved the latter method, although public comment expressed concern that it opened up the possibility of other historic buildings asking to use their walls for promotion.
 St. John’s Baptist Church at 1601 S. 13th Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The owners of the former St. John’s Baptist Church at 1601 S. 13th Street returned with a revised request to convert the 1892 building into residential units. At issue had been the choice of roofing material and the size, number, and style of dormers to be added, with the Historical Commission concerned about their compatibility with the building’s architecture and the owner seeking increased interior space and financial viability. After the applicant presented another revision addressing the concerns, the Commission gave an in-concept approval.
 In Chestnut Hill, the owners of 8226 Germantown Avenue proposed the construction of a four-story mixed-use building and parking spaces on an open portion of the quarter-acre lot. The proposal does not alter a 1760 stone house on the parcel, known as the Detwiler House. Designated in 1957, it is thought to be one of the oldest extant buildings in the Chestnut Hill historic corridor.
 The plans require a change in zoning, from the current RSA-3 (Residential Single Family) to CMX-2 (Neighborhood Commercial Mixed-Use) to allow for three residential units above a ground floor commercial space. A hearing at the Zoning Board of Adjustment, and a meeting with the Chestnut Hill Community Association, the Registered Community Organization, are both scheduled for this month. After addressing Architectural Committee concerns about the building’s size and materials, the applicant received in-concept approval from the Historical Commission.
 Tags: Historic Banks historic interiors Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission South Broad Street 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Places to Save: Winter 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Edward Worteck
 Painter’s Folly 
 Location: 1421 Baltimore Pike, Chadds Ford, Pennsylvania
 Built: 1857
 Threat: Sale
 Located in the heart of the Brandywine Valley, Painter’s Folly is one of the most intact and distinguished examples of mid-19th-century Italianate architecture in Chester County. Although built after the Battle of Brandywine, the property was part of the original land that housed the Continental Army encampments and Gen. Washington’s headquarters. Listed on the National Register of Historic Places, the house is closely tied to southeastern Pennsylvania’s architectural, cultural, and artistic legacy.
 Howard Pyle, founder of the Brandywine School of Art, operated a summer art school there from 1898 to 1903. Pyle’s students included luminaries such as N. C. Wyeth, Jessie Willcox Smith, and Maxfield Parrish. Painter’s Folly also later served as an art studio and inspiration for Andrew Wyeth, who produced numerous works featuring the house and its surroundings.
 Despite its distinguished history, the future of Painter’s Folly is uncertain. Purchased by Chadds Ford Township in 2018, the property is currently closed to the public, and evaluations have revealed significant preservation needs. While pilot programs and public outreach efforts have explored expanded access, ADA improvements, and programming opportunities, the costs and long-term feasibility of sustaining the building as a publicly owned property is under review.
 Regardless of whether the property remains public or is returned to private ownership, it is essential that preservation restrictions be placed on the site to ensure the community does not lose this landmark. The township should continue to carefully consider all viable public uses and meaningfully engage community stakeholders before making any final decisions about its future.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Swann Fountain 
 Location: 19th Street and Benjamin Franklin Parkway
 Built: 1924
 Threat: Disrepair
 Swann Fountain, also known as The Fountain of Three Rivers, is a public artwork located in Logan Square. Designed collaboratively by architect Wilson Eyre Jr. and sculptor Alexander Stirling Calder, the fountain features three bronze Native American figures reclining amid jets of water, representing Philadelphia’s three main waterways, the Delaware and Schuylkill Rivers and Wissahickon Creek. Calder’s figures, complemented by bronze frogs, turtles, and a 50-foot central jet, blend classical allegory with regional geography. It was commissioned to celebrate the vision of Dr. Wilson Cary Swann and the Philadelphia Fountain Society, whose 19th-century work provided drinking water to humans and animals and promoted civic welfare.
 For a century the fountain has been a beloved civic feature, opening to crowds dancing the tango in 1924 and serving as a vibrant centerpiece for the Benjamin Franklin Parkway. Yet, in 2023, repeated acts of vandalism damaged the fountain’s pumps, cutting off the majestic central jet and other water features. A complete pump failure in September 2025 required draining the basin and suspended all water activity. Philadelphia Parks & Recreation has committed to restoring the fountain by spring 2026, but the repairs involve major system work and are expected to cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 University Avenue Bridge 
 Location: 3401 Grays Ferry Avenue
 Built: 1930
 Threat: Neglect
 The University Avenue Bridge, a double-leaf bascule span crossing the Schuylkill River, connects West Philadelphia with 34th Street in Grays Ferry. Designed as part of the City Beautiful movement , the bridge was a collaboration between engineer Stephen H. Noyes, mechanical engineer John A. Vogelson, and renowned architect Paul Philippe Cret , whose Neoclassical vision can be found in numerous landmarks elsewhere in Philadelphia and in Washington, D.C. Cret’s design features octagonal operators’ houses topped with stylized porpoise reliefs, bronze lanterns adorned with seahorse motifs, and a monumental draw span that arches over the river. The bridge opened in 1933 and was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1994.
 Today, however, the bridge faces significant threats. Its architectural features are neglected, with broken windows, missing mortar, graffiti, and debris accumulating. The operators’ houses are derelict, and the ornate cast bronze doors were recently stolen. Despite its historic importance, no restoration work is currently planned by PennDOT. Without intervention, these unique design elements risk permanent loss.
 The bridge’s vulnerabilities have gained increased visibility due to more pedestrian and bicycle traffic along the newly expanded Schuylkill River Trail, which passes by the southern portion. Immediate attention and long-term investment in restoration are critical to safeguard the bridge’s role as both a historic landmark and an urban gateway across the Schuylkill River.
 Tags: Benjamin Franklin Parkway historic bridges Paul Cret Places to Save suburbs University Avenue Bridge 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Remembering the Philly Women Who Programmed the First Computer
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Computer programmers Betty Jennings and Frances Bilas prepare ENIAC for Demonstration Day in February 1946. | Photo: Army Research Laboratories Technical Library
 The world entered the computer age right here in Philadelphia. It is fairly well known that the modern computer’s birthplace was in 1946 at the Moore School of Electrical Engineering at the University of Pennsylvania, with ENIAC, the Electronic Numerical Integrator And Computer. What is less well known is that its first programmers were a team of six women, four of whom were native Philadelphians.
 At that time, the Moore School was male-only, a stipulation of the 1923 endowment from Alfred Fitler Moore, whose family business produced wire for use in telegraphs, telephones, and electricity. In the 1940s, the term "computer" meant a person who solved mathematical equations by hand. The United States Army was a major employer of computers, for calculating thousands of ballistics trajectories, which varied with the type of gun used, and even the climate in which it would be fired. A human computer would take about 30 hours to calculate a trajectory using differential calculus equations. The ENIAC’s mechanical precursor, the Differential Analyzer, could do the same work in about 15 minutes, but required cross-checking for accuracy by a human computer.
 Although women were often employed as computers in some fields, this military work required not only skills in using a desktop calculator, but also a knowledge of higher math and physics. As the United States entered World War II, men educated in those typically male dominated fields were in short supply, so opportunities for women opened up.
 Philadelphia was chosen as a site for the Army’s Ballistic Research Labs (BRL) as it was not too far from the Aberdeen Proving Ground (APG) in Maryland where the weapons were tested, and it was a major city with several large universities, plus several women’s colleges.
 After employing dozens of women calculators, six were ultimately chosen to move on to the ENIAC project. Kay McNulty [later Antonelli] grew up in Chestnut Hill, graduated from John Hallahan Catholic Girls’ High School at 311 N. 19th Street, and earned a degree in mathematics from Chestnut Hill College. Fran Bilas [later Spence] grew up in South Philadelphia, graduated from South Philadelphia High School for Girls, and also earned a degree in mathematics from Chestnut Hill College, where she met and became friends with McNulty. Marlyn Wescoff [later Metzler] grew up in West Philadelphia, graduated from West Philadelphia High School, and earned a degree in mathematics from Temple University. Betty Snyder [later Holberton] was born in Philadelphia and raised in Narberth. As the daughter and granddaughter of astronomers, she was encouraged to pursue her ability in mathematics, but was discouraged at the University of Pennsylvania by a professor who felt women shouldn’t be in the field, and so she studied English and journalism instead.
 Two other mathematicians moved to Philadelphia to join the project: Ruth Lichterman [later Teitelbaum], with a degree from Hunter College in New York City and Jean Jennings [later Bartik], a graduate of Northwest Missouri State Teachers' College.
 ENIAC’s former home at 200 S. 33rd Street. Date unknown. | Photo: Public Domain
 ENIAC’s home was in the basement of the Howard E. Pepper Building at 200 S. 33rd Street, now called the Moore School Building. Originally designed by the architects Morris & Erskine for the Pepper musical instrument company, in 1926, Alfred Bendiner, an architect employed by the firm of Paul Phillipe Cret, provided alterations and the building was officially occupied by The Moore School.
 ENIAC was a modular computer employing 18,000 vacuum tubes and with individual parts performing different functions via inputs and outputs of IBM punch card technology. It occupied a 50 by 30-foot area of the building, with 40 computing panels arranged in a U-shape along three walls. It weighed 30 tons and used 150 kilowatts of power to operate. ENIAC used a base 10 system. Its designers, J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, initially thought about using base 2, like today’s computers, but decided it would be too difficult and time consuming to convert. Base 10 is the major reason why ENIAC needed so many vacuum tubes in its circuitry.
 The ENIAC programmers’ job was far more laborious than that of today’s computer programmers. With no programming language or operating system, they had to figure out how to interface with it and then hand-wire the computer with cables and switches to create numerous very small steps that ENIAC could perform, to ultimately calculate a complicated mathematical problem. Now, instead of 30 hours to complete by hand, a ballistic calculation could be done by ENIAC in a few seconds.
 ENIAC was introduced to the public on Valentine’s Day, 1946. On its front page the next day, The New York Times described “an amazing machine,” calling it “the new electronic speed marvel.” It went on to report about the ceremonies and dinner to be given to “a group of Government and scientific men” following a demonstration of the machine. Although the demonstration was given by Marlyn Wescoff and Ruth Lichterman, none of the six programmers were invited to the other events.
 Wartime ballistics trajectories were the impetus for creating ENIAC, but supply chain delays caused it to be completed after the end of the war. However, the contract between the Army Ballistic Research Labs and the Moore School “called for ENIAC to be delivered with a working ballistics trajectory program,” according to the Times article. ENIAC was moved to Aberdeen, Maryland in 1949 and was in use until October 1955.
 After World War II, women were encouraged to leave their wartime jobs in factories and on farms to free up employment for returning soldiers. Yet, in the case of ENIAC, there was no one else who knew how to program it, so the six were encouraged to stay on.
 Corporal Irwin Goldstein sets the switches on one of the ENIAC's function tables as two unidentified female programmers work in the background. | Photo: U.S. Army via a 8×10 transparency courtesy of Harold Breaux
 Later, Eckert and Mauchly left the Moore School to start their own company, were joined by Holberton and Jennings, and together developed UNIVAC, one of the first commercial computers. Holberton is credited with creating the first software that allowed a computer to be operated by keyboard commands instead of switches.
 Eckert and Mauchly are firmly ensconced in the standard narrative of the history of computers, but, until recently, the programmers were hardly mentioned or omitted altogether, as in the 2013 book The Smithsonian’s History of America in 101 Objects . The chapter on ENIAC describes the costs, dates, and numbers of components, but the only names included are those of Eckert and Mauchly. In his history comic book series from the 1990s, Pennsylvania Profiles , author and illustrator Patrick Reynolds includes a chapter on ENIAC and again mentions the two men, but not the programmers, even though his illustration portrays two women operating the computer.
 More recently, other outlets have taken steps to correct the omission, such as University of Pennsylvania's Engineering School, the IT History Society, Wikipedia, a few authors and documentary filmmakers, and the organization Workforce Innovation, Trust, and Influence, which sponsors the Women in Technology Hall of Fame, where the “ENIAC 6” are inductees.
 In October 2023, the Army Research Laboratory Supercomputing Resource Center had a public dedication of new supercomputing systems. According to an Army press release, “The five new supercomputers, with a sixth one coming online next year, are named after the original six programmers of the world's first general purpose scientific computer, the ENIAC, which stands for Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer. It began operation on Aberdeen Proving Ground in 1947. The original six programmers were: Jean Jennings, Marlyn Wescoff, Ruth Lichterman, Betty Snyder, Frances Bilas and Kay McNulty.”
 Parts of ENIAC are ensconced in various museum collections around the country. The University of Pennsylvania has on display four of the original 40 panels of the ENIAC on the ground floor of the Moore School Building. Other repositories include the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History, the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, the Computer History Museum in Mountain View, California, and the U.S. Army Ordnance Museum in Aberdeen.
 Tags: military University of Pennsylvania Women's history

title: Plans for Major Renovation of Germantown Town Hall Met with Community Concerns
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
As one passes through Germantown, the vibes shift is palpable. Just a little further toward Philadelphia’s core is the familiar landscape of seemingly endless rowhouses. To the northwest are the more suburban environs of Mt. Airy and Chestnut Hill. In between, the Colonial era buildings and streetscapes of Germantown Avenue and towering former department stores on Chelten Avenue suggest a place unto itself, as if the traveler has suddenly transported to some other city in some other place.
 Of course, that’s precisely what Germantown once was, and in many ways still continues to try to be, even long after the city of Philadelphia subsumed it during a massive expansion to its current borders in 1854. Perhaps no structure is as emblematic of this history than Germantown Town Hall , the century-old, Classical Revival landmark at 5928 Germantown Avenue.
 Aggressively unused since the City of Philadelphia vacated the property in the late 1990s, the three-story, clock-tower-capped structure now appears slated for a new lease on life. During a community meeting held nearby on February 26, Anthony Fullard, president of the West Powelton Development Company, presented a team and plans to execute a $13 million renovation of the building. The bottomline: a full-scale interior and exterior restoration of the 25,000-square-foot structure for use as a charter school, food service, and community space, with completion and grand opening date of fall 2028.
 Germantown Town Hall looking west. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott courtesy of Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS), Library of Congress
 “The building is beautiful. It looks like it was just frozen in time,” Fullard told an audience of several dozen community members. “We’re not trying to change any of that. Our focus is to bring this building back online for the community and for the utilization of tenants.”
 Indeed, at face value, Fullard’s plans appear to be a preservationist’s dream come true. He was joined at the meeting by Sam Olshin, an architect with local firm AOS Architects, who was behind the transformative Metropolitan Opera House’s restoration. Olshin noted he will be working on the renovation of Germantown Town Hall with Domus Inc, the general contractor that restored both The Met and nearby Divine Lorraine Hotel.
 “Very much like The Met, the town hall has amazing bones,” Olshin said, expressing excitement about being a part of its restoration. “I’d see this building year after year, and say, ‘What is this? And how in God’s name can it be left here like this?’”
 Fullard and Olshin said they plan to restore the town hall, built 1925 and listed on both the Philadelphia and National Register of Historic Places, with a keen eye for preservation. Previous news reports indicate that copper and bronze features, railings, and other elements have been stripped away over time. Yet Olshin said the building’s captivating, three-story, open rotunda remains as a centerpiece, replete with memorials of Germantown’s war dead that will be restored.
 Rear elevation, looking northeast. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott courtesy of Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS), Library of Congress
 Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance of Greater Philadelphia, said an 1828 clock that once was hung in Independence Hall, and a contemporaneous bell cast by John Wilbank in the same shop as the Liberty Bell, also remain onsite. “The Preservation Alliance is glad to see some movement on repurposing this long-neglected historic landmark,” Steinke wrote in an email.
 Despite the excitement over reactivating this abandoned landmark, proud Germantowners have something of their own to say. During Fullard’s community meeting, a voluntary engagement outside the normal RCO process yet to come, numerous neighborhood locals in attendance raised concerns about details of the redevelopment plan, both known and unknown. Many were residents who remember the building as an inviting center of community life in the late-to-mid-20th century, with open-door City offices, a military recruiter, and even a successful boxing gym in the basement. How could a closed-off charter school, which poster boards at the meeting depicted taking up the entirety of the second and third floors, comport with that history, several wondered. “That was a central point for the community for decades, forever, and when it all boils down to it, it seems you’re trying to block the property off so you can make money,” said a person who who identified themselves as James. “This property is really on sacred ground.”
 Past Meets Present 
 A review of the property’s history indeed reveals its long use as a public space. Germantown was founded in 1683, a year after Philadelphia. Maps through the mid-19th century show development aligned mostly along the Germantown Avenue corridor, including along the block where Germantown Town Hall now sits. In the 1850s something changed: the arrival of a “Germantown Hall” near the intersection of that thoroughfare and Poorhouse Lane, now Rittenhouse Street.
 Germantown was one of many independent municipalities that spent as much money as possible prior to the 1854 consolidation , knowing that the City would assume all existing debts. Seeking to build a monument to the community’s outgoing independence, leaders erected an original, wood-framed town hall designed by architect Napoleon LeBrun. When that building was declared structurally unsafe in 1920, according to a 22011 preservation studio study at the University of Pennsylvania's Weitzman School of Design, it was torn down and replaced by the current one as part of then-Mayor J. Hampton Moore’s "campaign promise to relocate all City agencies" to City-owned buildings. "Furthermore, the move was an outgrowth of the reformist Decentralization Movement, which took hold in early 20th century public policy with the purpose of distributing City services to remote residential neighborhoods,” the report states.
 A building material advertisement from 1925 features Germantown Town Hall. | Image courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 The current building, designed by City architect John Penn Brock Sinkler, was modeled after William Strickland’s Merchant’s Exchange building on 3rd and Dock Streets in Old City. Upon its opening in 1926, the building was used for all municipal functions in Germantown and later as one of three emergency operation centers in the city. Yet, by the 1980s, the City began to pull out due to waning demand of services and deteriorating finances before leaving entirely in 1998 and passing control to the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation (PIDC).
 The building has sat vacant ever since, increasingly forlorn and open to the elements and trespassers. Fullard said several years ago he tried to put together a mixed-use plan centered around residential use, but it didn't “pencil out.” His current plan envisions assembling $3 million from the state Redevelopment Assistance Capital Program, $5.6 million in new market and historic tax credits, and about $4.4 million in debt financing, which he says his team feels “very confident that we can handle” with the building’s prospective anchored tenants. He maintains a memorandum-of-understanding with the PIDC, has key support from local political leaders, and said current plans can be executed by-right.
 Interior view, rotunda. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott courtesy of Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS), Library of Congress
 Fullard would not disclose the name of the prospective charter school, citing ongoing contractual obligations, frustrating some community members. Several descriptions of the school suggest it may be, or be similar to, YouthBuild Philadelphia Charter School, a nonprofit that aims to steer at-risk young people ages 17 to 20 toward careers in fields like healthcare, culinary arts, and the building trades. Fullard also serves on the Board of Trustees of YouthBuild, and Olshin’s firm designed a 2023 restoration of the school’s current location in a former PECO building on North Broad Street.
 Fullard said the charter school at Germantown Town Hall would serve about 140 students and it would be an expansion of an existing school, not a relocation. His team would add an elevator, handicap access, new wiring and mechanicals, and the building’s first-ever air conditioning system.
 More details were available about a prospective culinary use in the town hall’s basement. Tarik Ryant, a South Philly-based restauranter nicknamed "Chef Reeky," was on hand to identify himself as a future tenant. Ryant said he planned to install a high-end commercial kitchen to service a "cuisine hub" with potential uses including a staple diner or cafe, but also for the use of local food entrepreneurs or nonprofits steering youth toward culinary careers. “My vision for this beautiful space would be to have the basement as a hub for community, other entrepreneurs, so we can lose this sort of food desert concept in Germantown and bring some really, really good craft cooking,” Ryant said.
 Fullard also teased a third tenant, which he is close to signing an agreement with, whom would anchor a space on the first floor and bring the building to 100 percent utilization. He hinted that it would be a community-focused use and something he thinks the community will be “very, very happy with.”
 Interior view, second floor, looking southwest. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott courtesy of Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS), Library of Congress
 Yet, that level of detail wasn’t good enough for some in the first public audience to hear of Fullard’s plans, who continued to raise concerns about what’s coming down the pike. Among the questions: where would cars park, would students loiter after school, would the public not be able to access the building during school hours, why not make space for uses like artists studios, where was the community benefits agreement, and would there be green space?
 In the most heated moments, things became personal between Fullard, a Germantown resident for 63 years, and other long-term residents, over the purity of his plans. Fullard asserted he intended to do right by his community, offering opportunities for local residents and tradespeople, and insisting there was still flexibility to implement the public feedback that he was receiving, especially for community-focused uses in common spaces like the rotunda.
 Yet, while it appears Fullard has successfully laid the groundwork for a major physical renovation of Germantown’s historic Town Hall, it is evident he still has work to do to fully win over the community that calls it home. “I’ve known [Fullard] a long time. He is from Germantown. We used to play when we were kids,” said a man who identified himself as Sam. “I know he’s put his heart and soul into this project. I just wished that your team would have reached out to the community a little bit sooner, and hopefully not everything is written in stone.”
 Tags: abandoned buildings Germantown Germantown Town Hall Renovation 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Where to Find David Lynch in Philadelphia
author: Julien Suaudeau
bodyText:
Author’s Note : Episodes 1 and 2 of Song of Lynchadelphia (Season 3 of Hidden City’s Song of Philadelphia Podcast ) focused on the creative big bang that took place during David Lynch’s time in Philadelphia, between 1965 and 1970. Episode 3 examined the wild ways in which the city—Lynch’s impression of the city—manifests itself in Eraserhead, Mulholland Drive, and the Twin Peaks universe . Episode 4, available today on Spotify and Apple Podcasts , explores the Lynchian happenings in Philly .
 Dennis McNett's mural, "There is Trouble ‘Til the Robins Come," 1025 Hamilton Street (on Buttonwood Street side of Love City Brewing) | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Over a beer and a glass of white wine, Hidden City co-founder (and Song of Philadelphia supervising producer) Nathaniel Popkin told me about Salvador Dali’s method for locating one’s center of the universe.
 “In your case," Nathaniel said, "you would measure the distance between your house and David Lynch’s house when he lived in Philly.”
 The idea made sense: Lynch’s work on the screen and the canvas can be seen as an extension of the surrealist canon. But it raised a practical issue: between the end of 1965, when he joined Jack Fisk at 21st and Cherry, and 1970, when Lynch moved out of the house he’d bought with Peggy Reavey at 2416 Poplar, he lived in four different places in Philadelphia—not to mention where he studied (the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts), worked (Roger LaPelle’s fineprinting shop in Germantown), or bought second-hand clothing and objects (the Goodwill at Broad and Girard).
 Which one of those locations was I supposed to pick to figure out where the center of my universe was? How could I think geographically, even in a poetic or symbolical way, given the number of portals in the Lynchverse?
 In this episode, I tell you about four gateways to the David Lynch dimension in Philadelphia. First, there is PhilaMOCA , at 12th and Spring Garden, where Eric Bresler has been cooking up Lynchian events since 2012, including the annual Eraserhood Forever festival. Watching Laurel Near perform The Lady in the Radiator’s In Heaven with a chamber orchestra there feels like an immersion in the radiator, in Philadelphia.
 PhilaMoca, 521 N. 12th Street | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Josh Hitchens loves Eraserhead as much as Bresler. This past January he screened the movie at the Starr Garden Recreation Center, as part of his Monday Macabre film series. Before the event, Hitchens told me about the phone interview he did with David Lynch in 2022. At the end of the interview, which you will hear in the episode, Lynch wishes all the best to his interviewer and to Philadelphia. More than half a century after he left, his love for the city feels more than intact. It comes through as bigger than any other source of inspiration.
 Flyer for Monday Macabre at Starr Garden, hosted by Josh Hitchens
 Love and tenderness for Lynch’s work is what drove Dennis McNett to create the mural-memorial that sits on the back wall of Love City Brewing, 1025 Hamilton Street (the mural is on Buttonwood). With the support of the Mural Arts program, he imagined a scene filled with Easter eggs: Lynch himself with the Eraserhead haircut, the Blue Velvet ear and robins, the Mulholland Drive blue key, the Twin Peaks floors, curtains, blue rose and Judy symbol.
 Dennis McNett's There's Trouble ‘Til the Robins Come, 1025 Hamilton Street (mural on the Buttonwood Street side of Love City Brewing) | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Because things like that only happen in Philadelphia, a creepy figure that looks just like Judy stands behind the window of a building down the street.
 Who's that in the upper window? 445 N. 11th Street | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Lynch and his lifetime friend Jack Fisk, who studied at PAFA with him and was production designer on Eraserhead , The Straight Story and Mulholland Drive , came back to Philly 15 years ago to look up locations for Lynch’s unmade "Ronnie Rocket" project. What Lynch was after was the “decay and destruction” that had made such a powerful impression on him in the second half of the 1960s. Much to his dismay, he found none of it in present-day Philly. The film was abandoned, and Lynch made Twin Peaks: The Return instead. At the end of the blue rose dialogue in Part 4 of The Return , Lynch’s Gordon Cole character asks his sidekick if he still knows “where she lives.” 
 “I know where she drinks,” Albert answers. She is Diane. Not only does she drink in Philly; she is the embodiment of Philly in the Twin Peaks universe. 
 That upper window…445 N. 11th Street | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Although this is my personal favorite in Lynch’s entire body of work, I wish I could have walked around with him and Fisk as a decay and destruction consultant. I can think of a couple places that would have swayed the decision.
 Tags: David Lynch Eraserhood PhilaMOCA Song of Lynchadelphia Song of Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Julien Suaudeau Julien Suaudeau is a French-American writer, documentary filmmaker, and podcaster. He was born in Evreux, Normandy, grew up in Paris, France, and moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 2006. He teaches French and Film at Bryn Mawr College. In 2024, he launched Song of Philadelphia, Hidden City's podcast.

title: On the One-Year Anniversary of David Lynch's Death, Welcome to Lynchadelphia
author: Julien Suaudeau
bodyText:
Jack Fisk and David Lynch, 1967, near 19th and Chestnut | Photo: C.K. Williams
 When I was 15 years-old, in Paris, I found out about Twin Peaks . Actually, Twin Peaks found me.
 I remember exactly what I felt and who I was when I watched the show for the first time, thirty-five years ago. A very very different person. It may sound cheesy, but it’s true: falling into the David Lynch universe as a teenager changed my life. That experience shaped my taste in film, music, fashion, people—and just about everything else. It felt like an invitation.
 I don’t think I would have moved to Philly without all that weird stuff showing me the way. And you know what? I had no clue Lynch had lived here during his formative years as an artist. I was aware of the references to Philly in Twin Peaks and Fire Walk With Me . But it’s not until much later, when I was already living here, that I realized Lynch would have been a different Lynch without Philadelphia. He would have made different films. And I would have been someone else. [Read " David Lynch called Philadelphia one of ‘the sickest, most corrupt, fear-ridden’ cities. That’s what makes it Lynchian " from the Inquirer .]
 The new season of Hidden City's podcast Song of Philadelphia with Julien Suaudeau is Song of Lynchadelphia
 For the first anniversary of his passing, I built a sound portal between Lynch’s dreamworld and my adopted city. Here’s Song of Lynchadelphia—how David Lynch dreamed up his cinema in Philadelphia. The third season of Song of Philadelphia will have six total episodes:
 E01 : Smiling Bags of Death, Part One January 15 [Listen: Apple / Spotify ], Part Two January 29
 E02 : Fuck You, Gordon Part One February 19, Part Two March 5
 E03 : Lynch Memories March 19
 E04 : We are like the Dreamer April 16
 In the Fireman’s words to Agent Dale Cooper: "Listen to the sounds.”

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: Mighty Mick’s Gym
author: Alan Jaffe and Bryan Mckinney
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Mighty Mick’s Gym/Lost Time Brewing Company 
 Location : 2145 North Front Street
 Architect : Unknown
 Built : 1910
 The flatiron building wedged into the nexus of Front Street and Susquehanna Avenue in Kensington exemplifies the Philly accolade of “gritty.” The 115- year-old, three-story brick structure preceded the construction of the adjacent Market–Frankford Line. In recent decades, it was a Dollar Plus store and is now a mixed-use apartment building with a microbrewery and taproom called Lost Time Brewing Company on the ground floor.
 Yet, the building’s well-deserved reputation is that it served as the exterior of the fictional Mighty Mick’s Gym in the 1976 film Rocky and reappeared in several sequels. (A storefront across the street that was used as the location of the pet shop where Rocky wooed Adrian was razed in 2017.)
 The recent installation of another Rocky statue at the Philadelphia International Airport may be more than some residents feel the city requires. Yet, for all of the fans and tourists who make the pilgrimage to the base of the steps at the Philadelphia Museum of Art for a photo with Rocky, this building in Kensington, a genuine, if quirky, relic of our cinematic heritage, is worthy of a listing on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places , particularly as the original movie marks its 50th anniversary in 2026. Yo!

title: Cunningham Piano Gives a Final Goodbye to Philadelphia
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
For the first time in 135 years, Cunningham Piano Company will not have a physical presence in Philadelphia. Its last outpost, 24-26 E. Coulter Street in Germantown, has been put up for sale and will soon have new owners. The sale also marks the end of piano making in the city of Philadelphia, which in the 19th century was home to 80 companies. 
 For Cunningham Piano, it’s a change that has been in the making for a while. In 2016, its showroom was moved to King of Prussia, opening auxiliary locations in Cherry Hill and Delmar, Delaware, while keeping its piano restoration business in Germantown. “Restorations are still a part of the business, though the demand has decreased,” explained co-owner Tim Oliver. “We’re always going to restore pianos, because we love it.”
 Although he said consolidating made good business sense, it wasn’t without emotion. “It was especially hard for my partner [Rich Galassini], who’s worked for the company for almost 40years,” he said, adding wryly, “I’ve only been here for 28.”
 Cunningham Piano Company's old ghost sign on the rear wall of its former restoration facility at 24-26 E. Coulter Street. Mural Arts completed recreations of the building's advertisements in 2016. | Photo: Joseph E.B. Elliott
 The company was founded in 1891 by Patrick Cunningham, an Irish immigrant and woodworker, who established a factory at 4946 Parkside Avenue, and a showroom at 1105 Chestnut Street. Later properties included a factory at Poplar and North 41st Streets and an additional showroom and company headquarters at 1312-14 Chestnut Stree t as “Piano Row” expanded westward. The move to Germantown came after World War II and included a showroom at 5423 Germantown Avenue , the former Germantown Masonic Hall.
 On East Coulter Street, the four story, 20,000 square foot building is a landmark along the Germantown Avenue corridor, enhanced by the signage emblazoned on a side wall. Today, the fresh appearance of the two signs belies the building’s age, but that is owing to an initiative from 11 years ago called Vital Signs. It was a collaboration between Mural Arts and Temple Contemporary, involving Tyler School of Art students, to revive a few of the many “ghost signs” left on Philadelphia’s commercial buildings.
 “We had been asked to touch up a few ghost signs. Their rejuvenation brought attention to the city’s industrial buildings,” recalled Jane Golden, executive director of Mural Arts. “This was a way to respect the architecture and the history. To shine a light on the past and also think about the present.”
 A restorer in Cunningham Piano's workshop in 2014. | Photo: Joseph E.B. Elliott
 The ghost sign project was part restoration and part original mural. Lead artist Brad Carney oversaw the restoring of the old promotional sign along the rear of the building side, that reads “Cunningham Piano Co. New & Used Pianos • Bought • Sold • Exchanged / Buy Direct From Factory / Entrance on Coulter St.” in yellow and white lettering on a bright red background. They then added a new mural near the front, replicating the iconic “Cunningham Piano Co.” logo over the image of a grand piano.
 Some of the restorations done through the Vital Signs program are no longer in existence. Besides Cunningham, those still standing include Honest Lou’s Exterminating at 3905 Lancaster Avenue and Photo Process Screen Manufacturing Co., a screen-printing company run by the Oteri family, at 179 West Berks Street.
 “I am aware that the entire neighborhood loves that artwork,” said Oliver. “It’s part of the neighborhood.” In addition to questions about the fate of the building itself, he said that many neighbors asked him whether the murals would be saved.
 The company's facility on Coulter Street has been sold to a Germantown couple, and the building will be converted for residential use. | Photo: Joseph E.B. Elliott
 Oliver thinks the neighbors and preservationists will be relieved to learn about the new owners. “They are Germantown people, a couple, and they intend to live in the building,” he explained. “They’re involved in the movie set industry, so they were excited to have the space and use some of the equipment we’re leaving behind, like work benches and some finishing equipment.”
 And as for Cunningham Piano going forward without Philadelphia? Over the years the company has added rentals, music lessons, tunings, and organ sales to its roster of services. Its sales catalog has changed with the times, with digital pianos accounting for roughly half of the 500 or so instruments they sell in a year.
 The manufacturing of pianos still holds a place, although it has changed since the company’s founding. “We don’t make pianos beginning to end here in Philadelphia anymore. Parts come from elsewhere and we mostly do the finishing work,” noted Tim Oliver. “It’s currently the only piano on the market that says ‘Philadelphia’ on it. And the logo on the soundboard is still in Patrick Cunningham’s handwriting.”
 Tags: Cunningham Piano Company Germantown industrial history Philadelphia music history 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: New Book Reveals Hidden Stories of Fairmount Park's Performance Venues
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The enormous profiles of the Robin Hood Dell East and its younger sibling the Mann Center for the Performing Arts are major, familiar landmarks in Fairmount Park on their respective sides of the Schuylkill River. They have held court there for so long, few Philadelphians ever consider how they got there. Now, historian and archivist Jack McCarthy reveals the origin stories of the legendary performance venues in a new book, A Century of Music Under the Stars: A History of the Mann Center for the Performing Arts and Robin Hood Dell published by Temple University Press.
 A publicity picture from 1950 shows two female patrons posed in front of a male ticket agent at the Robin Hood Dell's box office. | Photo courtesy of Print and Picture Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 In the late 1920s, the Philadelphia Orchestra wanted to have a summer venue, and many civic-minded individuals wanted to make the orchestra accessible to everyone and more affordable than its regular season at the Academy of Music. To keep up with orchestras in other cities such as Chicago and Boston, an outdoor venue was envisioned.
 When the fundraising for the project began in earnest, it faced competition from other major campaigns by the Franklin Institute and Settlement Music School. Not to mention the launch date of early 1930, mere months after the 1929 stock market crash. “If it had happened a year or two later, it never would have gotten done,” noted McCarthy.
 Despite the headwinds, the Philadelphia Bureau of Music, which was a department of municipal government, and the Orchestra’s board of directors spearheaded the effort, securing a location with the Fairmount Park Commission and enlisting everyone from the musicians’ union to various women’s clubs, which used their social networks to sell subscriptions. “It’s a real Philadelphia story,” McCarthy said. “To build and run these places took incredible ingenuity and efforts by all these people, from the political realm, philanthropic, the musicians—all played critical roles in making these places possible," he said. "They faced a lot of challenges, but they got it done.”
 At the center of it all, from the earliest plans for the Robin Hood Dell right up to the building of the Mann Center for the 1976 Bicentennial, was the powerful figure of Fredric Mann. “He was such an outsized figure in Philadelphia society and politics,” explained McCarthy. “He was a huge Democratic donor. He was such a politically engaged figure who wielded such influence. The Dell was his passion.” That power was on display in 1959 when the peaceful soundscape of the Dell was interrupted by increased commercial jet traffic. Mann, who was the City’s director of commerce at the time, had the airport reroute flights around the venue during concert times.
 Although both amphitheaters are familiar sights in Fairmount Park, their architecture was not always beloved. Walter H. Thomas designed the Robin Hood Dell while serving as City's architect. All its seating was open-air, so bad weather necessitated the postponement of concerts. The Mann Center, on the other hand, had about a third of its seating under a roof, leaving the lawn seat attendees to grapple with the elements. The latter, designed by New York architects John MacFadyen and Alfredo DeVido, whose credits also include the Saratoga Performing Arts Center and the Wolf Trap Center, was criticized for its aesthetics and charged with elitism owing to the two-tiered seating arrangement.
 McCarthy's book is full of remarkable narratives throughout the history of the two venues, which sheds a great deal of light on Philadelphia politics and society as well. It’s a virtual who’s who of the city in the mid 20th century: philanthropists, industrialists, artists, arts promoters, and more than a dozen mayors.
 A couple from Bella Vista have a picnic before a concert at the Mann Center in 1981. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries 
 Indeed, the fortunes of the two sites mirror those of the city, such as when it evolved from a strictly classical music entity to include rock and pop musicians as audiences changed and later, laboring under a large deficit during the Ed Rendell years.
 “One of my favorite stories is how the musicians’ union in 1930 agreed to the payment arrangement for the opening seasons of the Dell. The building’s planners said they could raise the money to build the Dell, but didn’t have the funds to pay the musicians, so the union allowed them to be paid based on attendance,” McCarthy recalled. “I learned that, in the late 1920s, the national musicians’ union was promoting live music because recording technology had been improved and recorded music sales were taking off. The union led a campaign against ‘canned music,’ feeling they needed to combat this infiltration that was threatening their livelihood. So they were eager to help a new live concert series.”
 McCarthy had previously conducted research for the Mann Center, writing blog posts and creating a backstage timeline display of the history of the venue, which was completed in 2021. “The book was originally envisioned as a coffee table book, with lots of pictures, but not much text. Yet, as I researched it, I realized there were stories that were important, but largely unknown.”
 Jack McCarthy will give an author's talk about his new book, A Century of Music Under the Stars: A History of the Mann Center for the Performing Arts and Robin Hood Dell, on Tuesday, April 14 at Falls of Schuylkill Library. See event details here: https://libwww.freelibrary.org/calendar/event/161335 
 Tags: book review Fairmount Park Philadelphia music history 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Places Lost: Winter 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Google Street View
 6657 Blakemore Street 
 Location: 6657-59 Blakemore Street
 Built: 1927
 The corner building at 6657-59 Blakemore Street in East Mount Airy has been demolished. Constructed in the 1920s during a period of dense residential growth along the Chestnut Hill East railroad line, the two-story, four-unit, semidetached apartment house was designed and constructed by Eugene K. Davis–one of 30 buildings in a coordinated development of Tudor Revival structures.
 Constructed primarily of Wissahickon schist with steeply pitched roofs and half-timbered upper stories, the development’s design created a cohesive, yet visually rich streetscape opposite the Stenton Station. At the ends of the block, the U-shaped corner buildings at 6601 and 6657-59 Blakemore Street served as architectural anchors. Larger and more elaborately composed than their rectangular counterparts, these bookend structures articulated the rhythm and human scale of the entire terrace.
 After a fire and years of deferred maintenance under prior owners, the property was acquired by the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority in 2020. Despite the submission of a historic district nomination for Blakemore Street by the Keeping Society of Philadelphia in April, City officials applied for a demolition permit one day after the nomination was filed. The building was razed before the Philadelphia Historical Commission could assume jurisdiction in August. The corner lot was ultimately classified as non-contributing and excluded from the newly designated district, resulting in the loss of one of the development’s defining anchor buildings and diminishing the architectural cohesion of the block.
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 Lawnside 
 Location: 4641 East Roosevelt Boulevard
 Built: 1859
 Lawnside, the 1859 Superintendent’s House on the historic Friends Hospital campus, was lost to arson in September after a long and contentious fight to save it. Designed in coursed fieldstone and built amid the hospital’s park-like setting, Lawnside stood as a rare surviving example of mid-19th century institutional housing and was recognized as a contributing structure in the National Historic Landmark District designation of Friends Hospital, the nation’s first private psychiatric hospital, founded by Quakers in 1813.
 In July 2023, the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved the building’s demolition to make way for a new public health center, despite strong community opposition and a robust case for preservation advanced by the Preservation Alliance. Nevertheless, the Historical Commission deemed demolition to be “in the public interest,” and appeals to the Board of Licenses and Inspections Review and the courts were not successful. 
 Before the final appeal to Commonwealth Court concluded, disaster struck. On September 4, the vacant structure was set ablaze by an unknown person. The fire rendered the building unsalvageable, and Lawnside was entirely demolished within weeks. Its loss marked not only the destruction of a 166-year-old historic building, but also the end of a prolonged preservation effort that sought to balance public needs with Philadelphia’s architectural fabric.
 Tags: demolition Mount Airy National Register of Historic Places Northeast Philadelphia Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Places Lost 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Are you Ready to Party Like it’s 1976, 1926, or 1876?
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
“Ring it on!” urged Mayor Cherelle Parker recently with City officials promising that Philadelphia’s celebration of the 250 anniversary of the Declaration of Independence will bring “economic and cultural investments..[that] aim to boost civic pride, strengthen neighborhood economies, and create lasting impact well beyond 2026.”
 That all sounds great, but history isn’t on our side. While intending to promote the city and its many virtues, Philadelphia's celebrations of the Centennial, Sesquicentennial, and Bicentennial were dogged by their respective issues of the day: elitism, racism, sexism, corruption, fiscal and operational mismanagement, and, of course, politics.
 The 250 anniversary of the Declaration of Independence, variously known as the Semiquincentennial, Bisesquicentennial, Sestercentennial, America250, and locally, Philadelphia250, comes at a time when the populace is bitterly divided over the character of the nation and what it means to be an American.
 Minority and immigrant populations are currently being targeted by federal law enforcement, as persistent systemic economic, racial, ethnic, and gender inequalities continue to challenge the very premise and implied promise of the Declaration of Independence, that “all men are created equal.” This certainly was true in 1976, when urban renewal, civil rights, unemployment, and the recently-ended Vietnam War cast shadows over Bicentennial celebrations.
 Leftist Radicals 
 The July 4th Coalition demonstration parade on July 4, 1976. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Protest groups, including the Gay Activists Alliance, Rich Off Our Backs Coalition, and Vietnam Veterans Against the War, came together in Philadelphia under the umbrella of the July 4 Coalition to stage demonstrations and a march designed to call attention to issues of concern. “Puerto Rican socialists, Vietnam veterans, women’s rights advocates, Black liberation groups like the Black Panthers, and unemployed workers joined into one march that proceeded west along Lehigh Avenue and into Fairmount Park, ending with a sprawling concert and cookout on the fairgrounds built for the 1876 Centennial,” wrote Ella Comberg in an article published by Monument Lab . “The protest came after weeks of fear-mongering by Philadelphia Mayor and former police commissioner Frank Rizzo, who requested 15,000 federal troops to combat ‘a substantial coalition of leftist radicals’ he anticipated would violently disrupt the Bicentennial with acts of terrorism. Federal authorities rejected the baseless request, and the protest went on peacefully.”
 Rizzo was attempting to “deflect attention away from the city's budget woes and the demands for his recall,” according to Edward Duffy, author of Philadelphia Celebrates : Three Great Anniversaries 1876, 1926, 1976. In the end, media attention to Rizzo's unwarranted warnings of violence likely had the effect of curbing attendance.
 Philly Bicentennial street scene. | Photo: Don Hudson via Flashbak.com
 “The total number of visitors to Philadelphia in 1976 was estimated to be between 14 and 20 million, which fell far short of the planners’ expectations,” noted an essay published by Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia. Unlike the Sesquicentennial and Centennial that preceded it, Philadelphia’s Bicentennial celebration was not an official national commemoration or World’s Fair. Operation Sail in New York Harbor was considered to be the main event.
 “Mayor Rizzo, for his part, hoped to use the Bicentennial as an opportunity to further criminalize poverty and assert control in the regulation and use of public space in an era thought to be defined by its lawlessness,” noted Comberg. “After the uprisings of the late sixties and in the wake of the Vietnam War, the Bicentennial came at the right time for bureaucrats to assert an alternative to counterculture and disruption; they meant to re-inscribe the values of family and patriotism that had been challenged in the preceding years. In contrast, the protesters understood the city’s fatal flaw not as its lack of order but as antagonism from an unsupportive state.”
 "A Crumbling, Sodden, Bankrupt Mess" 
 A 80-foot illuminated Liberty Bell was placed over Broad Street near Marconi Plaza in South Philadelphia during the Sesquicentennial International Exposition of 1926. | Photo: Public Domain
 If Philadelphia’s Bicentennial celebration was a disappointment, the Sesquicentennial that preceded it was a disaster. The International Exposition of 1926, held in South Philadelphia, “was meant to be the greatest world’s fair since the 1876 Centennial,” according to Thomas Keels, author of Sesqui!: Greed, Graft, and the Forgotten World's Fair of 1926 . “Thanks to political corruption, greed, egotism, and the wettest summer on record, it became a crumbling, sodden, bankrupt mess. When the Sesqui opened on May 31, 1926, in the remote, muddy swamps of South Philadelphia, the fair was unfinished, with a few shabbily built and mostly empty structures.”
 In his book Duffy notes that “The fair was not ready for opening and the grounds resembled a construction site with many exhibits either half finished or not even begun. Some that had been built did not yet have their displays installed. Exhibits continued to open as late as a month before closing,” The much-ballyhooed, 175-foot Tower of Light never was completed.
 A lithograph poster by Dan Smith advertising the Sesqui-Centennial Exposition of 1926. | Image courtesy of Tennessee Virtual Archive
 On opening day “a torrential rainstorm struck the city, engulfing the low-lying South Philly fairgrounds in a sea of mud and washing out recent plantings of flowers and shrubs,” Sandy Hingston wrote for Philadelphia Magazine . “Only 250 visitors arrived in the first hour. In the opening ceremonies in the Municipal Stadium, there were only 20,000 spectators.” 5,000 of them were members of the chorus.
 Two events later in the year each drew more than 100,000 people to the stadium: a Catholic mass and a boxing match between Jack Dempsey and Gene Tunney. Renamed the John F. Kennedy Stadium in 1964 , the facility was demolished in 1992. 
 Highlights of the Sesqui included an illuminated 80-foot tall replica of the Liberty Bell that arched across Broad Street, international displays, reproduction of colonial High Street, Treasure Island amusement area, and the Palaces of Agriculture, Liberal Arts, Machinery, and Education, to name a few.
 ‘Scars in the Psyche’ 
 Philadelphia Mayor Freeland Kendrick and Senator William Vare in 1927. Undeveloped marshland in South Philadelphia controlled by Vare's political machine became the troubled fairgrounds for the Sesquicentennial International Exposition. | Image courtesy of the Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia via Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 “The event attracted only a small fraction of expected visitors and closed with a $4 million deficit, which the City had to absorb, transferring funds earmarked for other projects,” according to Duffy. These included upgrades to the water supply, subway and rapid transit extensions, and a convention center, to name a few. “Given the miscellaneous appropriations and special loans pushed through by City Council surreptitiously, and the money distributed clandestinely in countless insider deals, the true cost of the fair will never be known.”
 Low attendance throughout the run of the Sesqui contributed to the deficit. “Even if they lost money, most world’s fairs attracted tens of millions of visitors,” noted Keels. “Sesqui planners expected between 40 and 50 million guests: fewer than five million paying visitors actually attended the fair during its six-month run.” In comparison, the 1876 Centennial counted 9.8 million paid admissions, even with a fraction of the national population, and before the era of autos, airplanes, electric streetcars, and radio.
 Much like the Bicentennial, the Sesquicentennial reflected the biases of its time. “Philadelphia women tested their new-found political muscle, African Americans struggled to keep their voices from being stifled by a callously racist white establishment, [and] Jewish leaders generously contributed their money and talent, only to be vilified by anti-Semites,” according to Keels, who noted a City-approved attempt by the Ku Klux Klan to hold its national convention at the Sesqui. The plan failed in the face of opposition by African American, Catholic, and Jewish leaders.
 The 1926 Sesquicentennial half dollar featuring the profiles of George Washington and then-president Calvin Calvin Coolidge. | Photo: NGC / CoinWeek
 A precedent set in 1926 is likely to be rediscovered in the next few months. For the first and only time (so far), the likeness of a sitting United States president appeared on official, legal-tender currency. The 1926 half dollar commemorative coin featured profiles of George Washington and then-President Calvin Coolidge. Meant to sell for $1 each, one million of the coins were struck at the Philadelphia mint, “but sales fell far short of expectations,” according to an article in Coin Week magazine . Eventually, “859,408 half dollars were returned to the mint and melted.”
 All in all, the Sesqui is considered to be a product of corruption and ineptitude—culminating in a summer marked by alternating rain and scorching heat. “Besieged by lawsuits, the City spent the rest of the decade trying to clean up the financial wreckage of the fair,” Keels concluded. “The Sesqui left deep scars in the psyche of the City.”
 Progress and Nostalgia 
 An aerial view of buildings constructed in Fairmount Park for the Centennial Exposition of 1876. | Image courtesy of the Library Company of Philadelphia
 In general, Philadelphia’s celebration of the 1876 Centennial was considered a success. Staged in West Fairmount Park, and officially named The International Exhibition of Arts, Manufactures, and Products of the Soil and Mine, it was the country’s first world’s fair. “The fair had twin goals: first, to celebrate a century of freedom; and second, to show the world how far America had progressed, from a rural, agricultural nation to a grand, industrialized country that stretched from the Atlantic to the Pacific,” Wendy Moonan wrote for ANTIQUES magazine. 
 Highlights of the Centennial included the arm and torch of the yet-to-be erected Statue of Liberty, the first public demonstration of Alexander Graham Bell’s telephone, the massive Corliss steam engine, the 35-acre Main Hall, the largest building of its time, displays of new inventions, such as typewriters and sewing machines, a liberty bell made from tobacco plugs, a portrait of George Washington made from the hair of Simon Bolivar, and the local introduction of popcorn, root beer, and bananas.
 Barely a decade after the Civil War, the Centennial was an attempt to portray unity and progress, along with nostalgia for colonial and revolutionary times. Still, it “represented incremental advances in women’s rights even as its displays perpetuated stereotypes of African Americans and North American Indians,” noted John L. Puckett in a series of essays for the West Philadelphia Collaborative History project. 
 Women Assert Themselves 
 The Woman's Pavilion at the Centennial Exhibition of 1876. | Image: Public Domain
 Led by Elizabeth Duane Gillespie, head of the Women’s Centennial Exposition Committee (WCEC), and great-granddaughter of Benjamin Franklin, women were credited with raising much of the funding necessary to stage the event. The Committee was promised space in the main building for its exhibit, but 11 months before opening day, was told there would be no room, though the women were welcome to erect their own building if they could secure the funds.
 “Mrs. Gillespie decided to go ahead and raise the money for a separate women’s pavilion,” Lynne Cheney explained in American Heritage . “In a little more than three months she and her workers had acquired a sufficient sum. “On opening day Empress Theresa [of Brazil] pulled a cord in the Women’s Pavilion, activating various machines attended and invented by women.”
 Inside the Women's Pavilion. | Image: Public Domain
 “The Women’s Pavilion was a popular Exposition attraction, with demonstrations of women’s contributions to the arts, sciences, education, and industry,” wrote Puckett. “These progressive women broke new ground in advancing women’s rights, first by putting American women’s formidable intellectual and material achievements on international display, second by publishing the New Century for Women , a weekly paper printed on site and financed by the Women’s Centennial Committee." Edited by Sarah Hallowell of Germantown, the journal advocated for women’s rights in the home and marketplace, including equal pay for equal work, humane working conditions, and greater financial and social autonomy.
 Overall, the organizers of the Centennial Exhibition were pleased with the results. More than 100,000 people witnessed opening day and there were nearly 10 million paid admissions during its six-month run. “Philadelphia’s Fairmount Park was lined with pavilions, hosting exhibits that demonstrated the new industrial and technological advancements of the age,” concluded an article published by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania . “The Centennial Exhibition celebrated America’s birthday by introducing the country as a world power.”
 Few Buildings Remain 
 Memorial Hall in Fairmount Park, the only surviving structure from the Centennial Exposition of 1876, in 1972. | Image courtesy of Prints & Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 Although the Centennial prompted construction of more than 200 buildings of various sizes, just four survive. Memorial Hall opened on May 10, 1876 with more than 4,000 works of art from around the world on display. It has been home to the Please Touch Museum since 2008.
 Two small brick comfort stations built for the Centennial currently are used for storage, according to Jon Caroulis’ account for WHYY . “Almost immediately after the Centennial closed, most physical remains were removed, either taken elsewhere or broken down and sold for parts. Of the 27 states that sent houses, only the one from Ohio is still standing. Made of marble and other stones culled from 21 quarries in the state, each quarry placed a stone with its name engraved in it on the house.” Ohio House now is home to the Fairmount Park Conservancy. In 2025, The Preservation Alliance of Greater Philadelphia awarded the Conservancy its Grand Jury Award for the building’s restoration and adaptive reuse.
 With the exception of Municipal Stadium, after the Sesqui closed, its buildings were sold off “for pennies on the dollar,” Keels told a meeting of Friends of Northeast Philadelphia History earlier this year. The incomplete Tower of Light sold for $1,050, and the replica of the Liberty Bell, along with its 60,000 light bulbs, fetched just $60 at auction, only to be demolished for scrap.
 The Bicentennial Bell at Whitechapel Bell Foundry in London, England circa 1976. | Photo courtesy of the National Park Service
 Relatively little was built for the Bicentennial. “Some famous structures around town were reconstructed or refurbished, including the second floor of Independence Hall, the Second Bank of the United States, Old City Hall, and City Tavern,” noted Caroulis. “The Liberty Bell was moved from Independence Hall to its own pavilion on the mall.”
 A full-size replica Liberty Bell, known as the Bicentennial Bell, was sent as a gift from the British people to the people of the United States. Presented and dedicated by Queen Elizabeth II in Philadelphia on July 6, 1976, the bell was cast at the same London foundry as the original. On display at 3rd Street between Walnut and Chestnut Streets until 2013, it was removed and put into storage to make way for the Museum of the American Revolution. In 2024, the bell was installed and re-dedicated in the Benjamin Rush Garden at 3rd and Walnut Streets. 
 The Living History Center at 6th and Race Streets was completed in 1976 and designed by Mitchell/Giurgola. | Photo courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 A notable exception to the paucity of new construction was the $11.5 million Living History Center (LHC) at 6th and Race Streets. “It had dozens of multi-media exhibits, 10 color television monitors, computers that gave quizzes, a state of the art IMAX theater, a restaurant, and a history themed rooftop playground for the kiddies,” according to local historian and tour guide Bob Skiba in a public Facebook post. “What it didn’t have was visitors.”
 The LHC was meant to outlive the Bicentennial and support itself through paid admissions and rentals, but “Attendance was poor from the beginning and only got worse over time.” It closed in June 1978, a little more than two years after it opened. A deal was reached to turn the building over to public television station WHYY, Skiba noted. “In 1999, WHYY tore down most of the original Living History Center to build the headquarters and studios it occupies today.”
 Reaching All Neighborhoods and Residents 
 Semiquincentennial logo for Philadelphia 250.
 “Philadelphia truly is a city of neighborhoods,” Duffy told Chestnut Hill Local in a review of his new book . “Getting everyone behind a massive celebration requires necessary effort. This effort happened during the Centennial. However, there was not so much preceding the Sesquicentennial and hardly any before the Bicentennial. The lesson to be learned from the Sesquicentennial and Bicentennial is to encourage local celebrations that neighborhood folks can identify with.”
 In that vein, the Philadelphia Visitor Center, organizer of Philadelphia250, is touting “a Semiquincentennial celebration that reaches all neighborhoods and residents,” with block parties, tours, cultural festivals, attractions, and experiences that “celebrate Philadelphia’s diverse communities.” In addition to museums and historical organizations, community groups are playing key roles in planning and staging events throughout the city.
 Philadelphia's semiquincentennial mascot, Libby the PHL-Belle. | Photo: @ libbythephlbelle via Instagram 
 The Philadelphia Historic District 250th Committee is offering 52 Weeks of Firsts , a year-long, city-wide celebration of innovation. Every Saturday in 2026, from January 3 through December 26, there will be a free event featuring an invention or innovation created in Philadelphia.
 The Neighborhood Gateways program will feature neighborhoods that are associated with Colonial and Revolutionary War heritage, immigrant communities, and African American history. For example, events in Germantown and West Philly “will honor local Black artists and entrepreneurs, their historical impact, and contemporary achievements,” according to the program's press release. Each gateway is invited to create its own time capsule with contributions from residents that reflect the spirit of their community. “Local talent will take center stage, from musicians and storytellers to artists and culinary experts. Festivals will feature homegrown entertainment, ensuring celebrations reflect the voices and creativity of Philadelphians.”
 Tags: Bicentennial Centennial Exposition Frank Rizzo Sesquicentennial Women's history 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: At Ginger Arts Center, Chinatown Youth Take Inspiration from Local History
author: Kathryn Rice
bodyText:
Ginger Arts Center, a vibrant community hub for young Philadelphians, is nestled into this nondescript stretch of Chinatown North. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Ginger Arts Center is tucked into a modest storefront in a section of the city known as Chinatown North. The name of the neighborhood, like much of its land, has been the subject of dispute between residents and real estate developers, who often market the area Callowhill. Once a hair and nail salon, the space is now painted light green and decorated with protest signs, polaroid photos, and hanging plants. This is where Kaia Chau spends most of her time, working without pay, to give Chinatown youth something she says she wished she’d had growing up: a safe place outside home and school to hang out. (Editor's note: Kaia Chau is the subject of episodes 1 and 2 of season two of Hidden City's Song of Philadelphia Podcast hosted by Julien Suaudeau .)
 As a student at Bryn Mawr College, Chau co-founded Students for the Preservation of Chinatown (SPOC), a coalition of college students that organized against the development of the 76ers arena in Chinatown, with her childhood friend Taryn Flaherty. After the 76ers withdrew their plan to build the arena, Chau reflected on what she would prefer to see built in its place. “It’s really important to oppose the things that you don’t want in your neighborhood,” said Chau. “But, at the same time, it’s equally important to think about ways you can sustain and nourish your community.”
 What Chau and Flaherty wanted to build most was a “third space” for youth, who, Chau said, have few safe spaces to hang out due to the lack of funding for after school and library programs in Philadelphia. Under the guidance of mentors from Asians Americans United, the pair teamed up with three other SPOC members to secure a grant from the Leeway Foundation and launched Ginger Arts Center in June of 2024. They added the word "ginger" to the name of the center because it is a yellow plant and they wanted to pay homage to the Yellow Seeds, a group of student activists based in Chinatown in the 1970s whom Chau wrote her college thesis about.
 “I really credit them [the Yellow Seeds] with being the catalyst of this really long line of history of organizing in Chinatown,” Chau said.
 Vivian Chen, Claire So, Kaia Chau, Celina Seck, and Will Chan at Ginger Arts Center in Chinatown. | Photo: Kathryn Rice
 The old axiom that history repeats itself is truer in Philadelphia's Chinatown than most places. Community members have fought development projects for decades that threatened to displace residents—including proposals for a prison, stadium, casino, and arena—for most of the neighborhood’s 150 year history.
 The community has nurtured a proud tradition of community organizing since 1966, when activists, including the Yellow Seeds, organized against the expansion of Vine Street into an interstate expressway—a project that severed Chinatown North from the rest of the neighborhood. This tradition is Chau’s inheritance. Some of her earliest memories include attending protests with her mother, the activist Debbie Wei, who organized against the proposal to build a stadium in Chinatown in 2000 and helped found Chinatown’s only public school, Folk Arts-Cultural Treasures Charter School (FACTS). Chau has also known Mary Yee, one of the Yellow Seeds founding members, since she was a child.
 “Something we talk a lot about at the center is intergenerational learning,” said Claire So, who volunteers as a graduate student mentor at the Ginger Arts Center. “Kaia is an individual who really holds that true to her value and her heart.”
 The September 1973 issue of Yellow Seeds community newspaper. | Image courtesy of Tending Our Roots, Coalition for Asian Pacific American Community Development
 The Yellow Seeds ran a community center that included a bilingual library, tutoring sessions, and a ping-pong table. They also published a newspaper for Philadelphia's Asian community. “We were able to build some very good bonds with the people of Chinatown, so much so that they donated a good amount of money to Yellow Seeds,” Yee said in an oral history recorded by Asian Americans United (AAU). The Yellow Seeds also received in-kind donations including a projector, folding chairs, and food for October 1st celebrations.
 Those descriptions bear a striking resemblance to the Ginger Arts Center, which is furnished with found and donated items—including two bookshelves that once belonged to a Yellow Seeds member. Renovating the space was a community effort. “We had kids coming in and volunteering their time to just sand the walls,” said Chau. “From the beginning, the space has really been a real labor of love.”
 The end result is a place that feels more like a home than a nonprofit agency. Instead of desks or cubicles, the space is furnished with a couch, armchairs, and a giant red bean bag. Like the Yellow Seeds center, there is also a library, volunteer tutors, and a ping pong table.
 "Kai Wong teaches English to two young women from Hong Kong in the Yellow Seeds Center at 1006 Winter Street in the Chinatown section of Philadelphia in 1973." | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries 
 Framed posters and screen printed signs on the walls reflect the center’s dual commitment to art and activism. “Something that has really driven how we have run the center is the role of art and resistance,” said Celina Seck, who leads the center’s art and media cluster.
