 Chau said that the center hosts four to five programs per month including workshops, teach-ins, and tutoring sessions, but a core part of its mission is simply to offer teens a space to hang out. “The most important moments are the times that we’re kind of doing nothing, the times when we’re here after protests,” said Chau. “Hanging out is very revolutionary in a way I didn’t really think about before being a part of Ginger Arts.”
 On a Saturday afternoon at the Ginger Arts Center last fall, Joey Zhou, 17, lounged on the couch before beginning a one-on-one tutoring session with Will Chan, one of the center’s graduate student mentors. “There’s just so much support here,” said Zhou. “They do tutoring, they do workshops, like, so much love, and it’s just a space to hang when you need it to.”
 Staff of Ginger Arts Center protest the Philadelphia 76ers' plan to build an arena in Chinatown. November 2024. | Photo courtesy of Ginger Arts Center
 The staff at Ginger Arts are mentored by AAU, an advocacy organization that Wei helped found nearly 40 years ago. For Vivian Chang, the executive director of AAU, investing in Ginger Arts is a part of a deliberate strategy to protect the neighborhood from future development threats. “A part of the way you defend it [Chinatown] is by building things in the place,” said Chang. “Ginger Arts is literally like putting a little kind of frontier, a little boundary on Chinatown to be like, it’s also north of Vine Street.”
 Chau pointed out that the interagency collaboration between the Ginger Arts Center, AAU, and other local organizations is reflected in the center’s name—ginger is a root system. “Ginger Arts Center in a lot of ways wouldn’t have existed without the founding of FACTS and the founding of the Asian Arts Initiative,” said Chau. “Those institutions showed us that we can build something for ourselves.”
 At 24, Chau is eager to pass on the wisdom she’s received from older mentors to younger activists like Seck and Zhou. “I feel indebted to my parents and the older generation for fighting to preserve this community,” said Chau. “For the young people I’m working with now, same thing. I feel a duty to them, to continue fighting.”
 Tags: Asian American history Chinatown 
 About the Author
 Kathryn Rice is a freelance journalist based in Philadelphia and a graduate student at The Columbia School of Journalism.

title: Lawsuits and Legal Wrangling Seek to Undermine Philadelphia's Historic Districts
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
A block of well-maintained Victorian twins leads by example within the Powelton Village Historic District. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 To date, there are 45 historic districts on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places . While the first, the Main Street Manayunk Historic District, dates back to 1984, the majority of them have been created within the last decade.
 Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia, believes there’s a reason for the increase. “In many cases, the nominations are put forth by neighbor associations that are concerned about development," he noted. “The neighbors turn to the Historical Commission to help manage these changes.” Recent examples include the Powelton Village Historic District , nominated in 2022 by the Powelton Village Civic Association and the Victorian Roxborough Historic District , nominated that same year by the Central Roxborough Civic Association.
 The extensive nomination process for a historic district requires a map of the proposed district’s boundaries, written descriptions and photographs of all its built and natural environments and characteristic streetscapes, an inventory of every property, a bibliography of the major references cited in the nomination, and a statement of significance that references at least one of the 10 criteria for designation as listed in Section 14-1004(1) of the Philadelphia Code, such as representing a significant era in the city’s history, or association with a significant architect or historic person. For a historic district nomination, the presentation can easily run to many hundreds of pages.
 Designations, for either an individual property or a historic district, are occasionally contested, but the Philadelphia Historical Commission usually prevails. That is not surprising, given the exhaustive research that goes into a successful nomination and the Historical Commission’s multi-step review. In early March, however, a judge in the Court of Common Pleas overturned the 2024 designation of the Washington Square West Historic District in a lawsuit filed by three properties owners and subsequently joined by others.
 The owners cited concerns that the designation would inflict burdensome expenses on them. “In general, I think the complaint about cost is not unfounded, but it is overblown,” said Steinke. “It’s not the case that some preservation police will force you to change your property to bring it up to some kind of historic standard.”
 Judge Christopher Hall’s brief ruling stated the nomination “was not in accordance with law,” and that the decision to designate the district “was not supported by ‘substantial evidence.’” With over 1,000 properties in the district, the nomination for the Washington Square West Historic District unsurprisingly contained nearly 1,500 pages of documentation.
 The leadership of the William Way LGBT Community Center recently announced that the organization will demolish its longtime home at 1315-1317 Spruce Street for new construction. Public outcry has ensued. The historic building sits within the legally-protected Washington Square West Historic District, a designation currently embroiled in litigation. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At the time of the designation, the nominators had argued, and the Historical Commission had agreed, that the district satisfied six of the criteria for designation, as it is representative of the development and heritage of the city, features several distinctive architectural styles by significant architects, and in addition to the built features, may yield archaeological history. More than half of the properties in the district had already been individually designated.
 “What underlies the judge’s decision is something of a mystery. It seemed like the judge was treating it like a judicial proceeding,” said Steinke. “The Historical Commission is an executive function. They’re not judicial, and because of that, they’re not set up as a court.”
 The City’s Law Department appealed the decision to the Commonwealth Court, which restored the designation during the appeal. At the same time, the Preservation Alliance, which did not participate in the first set of hearings, petitioned the Court of Common Pleas to reconsider the appeal with the Preservation Alliance treated as an appellee.
 On March 30, 2026, the court granted the petition and vacated its order. It granted appellee status to the Preservation Alliance and the Washington Square West Civic Association, the co-nominators, directing all the parties to file new briefs. While a hearing for new oral arguments has not yet been scheduled, the district remains under the jurisdiction of the Historical Commission until the court’s review and ruling.
 That protection will extend to the building at 1315-17 Spruce Street, the former Engineers Club, classified as “significant” to the Washington West Historic District. Its current owner and occupant, the William Way LGBT Community Center, has announced its plan to demolish the 1917 building and replace it with a six-story facility to include affordable senior housing on the upper floors.
 Meanwhile, lawsuits are also pending against two other historic districts.
 An appeal of the designation of the Southeast Spruce Hill Historic District in West Philadelphia was filed by several property owners and denied by the Court of Common Pleas in December 2025. The appellant has appealed the denial to the Commonwealth Court.
 Cresheim Valley Apartments at 7200-04 Cresheim Road were built in 1914 and designed by Henry DeHoff. The complex is listed as contributing to the Northwest Philadelphia Apartment Thematic Historic District. An individual property owner is currently challenging the legality of the entire district. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Designated in January 2025, the Northwest Philadelphia Apartment Thematic Historic District comprises 30 apartment buildings along the Chestnut Hill West Regional Rail Line in Germantown and Mt. Airy. The nomination proposed, and the Historical Commission agreed, that collectively the buildings, constructed between 1910 and 1940 with suburban-like features such as lawns and landscaped courtyards, transformed the area into a suburban-like, middle class enclave. During the Commission’s review of the nomination, the owner of one of the properties had asked to be removed from the district’s inventory. When that request was denied, they then filed an appeal of the entire designation to the Court of Common Pleas. Oral arguments are to be held after June 5.
 Recently, there has been an uptick in proposed historic districts, with six potential nominations currently at various stages, including four—Tulpehocken, Wissahickon, Yorktown, and Pelham in the Northwest, one in East Falls, and a Chestnut Street West Historic District in Center City. How the Washington Square West ruling will affect these nominations is not clear, but Steinke is optimistic about the Preservation Alliance’s nomination for Tulpehocken. “The circumstances are different, and the neighborhoods are different,” he explained.
 While possible cost concerns are frequently a reason for appeals of designated properties, another pushback comes from an impression that historic preservation somehow hinders the housing development needs of many cities, including Philadelphia. “I feel like preservation is under the gun today, everywhere,” noted Peg Breen, president of New York Landmarks Conservancy, a non-profit organization dedicated to preserving New York City’s architectural heritage through financial and technical support and advocacy. “There is enormous pressure for housing and there’s a perception that preservation gets in the way.” She sees that misunderstanding coming from the public and office holders alike, referring to a statement put out by Brooklyn Borough president Antonio Reynoso that he would not support the creation of any more historic districts.
 Preservationists believe the numbers don’t support that view. For example, New York City has around 157 historic districts, ranging in size from a couple of blocks up to very large neighborhoods. Despite that seemingly big number, Breen pointed out, “Altogether, our historic districts take up about five percent of the city’s land area.” Similarly, the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places represents 4.4 percent of all buildings in the city.
 Locally, the Preservation Alliance issued a report last year, Growing Through Preservation: The Economic Impact of Historic Preservation in Philadelphia , demonstrating that in the past decade, rather than hindering the creation of housing, the number of housing units in historic districts actually increased at more than twice the rate of the rest of the city.
 The authority to designate historic districts was added to the City’s historic preservation ordinance in the early 1980s. When it was created in 1955, the Historical Commission’s power was limited to the designation of individual properties. “Preservationists felt that wasn’t sufficient to preserve streetscapes,” recalled David Brownlee, who served on the Historical Commission for many years beginning in the 1980s. Since then, historic districts have become an important tool to preserve the distinguishing character of neighborhoods.
 Tags: historic district LGBTQIA+ History Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places William Way Center 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Philadelphia Was David Lynch’s Surface, Not His Source
author: Julien Suaudeau
bodyText:
Peggy Reavey and David Lynch outside the home of Reavey’s parents in Philadelphia in 1968 | Photo: Bernard V. Lentz
 Author’s Note :  Episodes 1 and 2 of Song of Lynchadelphia (Season 3 of Hidden City’s  Song of Philadelphia Podcast ) focused on the creative big bang that took place during David Lynch’s time in Philadelphia, between 1965 and 1970. Episode 3 examined the wild ways in which the city—Lynch’s impression of the city—manifests itself in  Eraserhead, Mulholland Drive,  and the  Twin Peaks  universe . Episode 4 explored the Lynchian happenings in Philly. Episode 5 is the first part of a long interview with Philadelphia’s own Peggy Reavey, who married Lynch at 20-years old, in 1968, and is the mother of Jennifer Lynch. Available today on  Spotify  and  Apple Podcasts , this episode interlaces Reavey’s memories with Jack Fisk's and soundscapes from David Lynch's films and shows, as Reavey explains how Lynch projected his deepest terrors on his living environment at the time. 
 “Philadelphia, Pennsylvania was a filthy city.” During his final years, David Lynch repeated those words like a mantra in interviews near and far. When he lived here from 1965 to 1970, he said, the city was filled with fear. Violence, corruption, insanity. You know how the chorus goes.
 When I set out to produce the Song of Lynchadelphia season for the first anniversary of Lynch’s death, I had no reason to doubt him. I even explored a personal theory that Lynch had been traumatized by Philly and that his entire body of work, on screen as well as on canvas, could be seen as a form of catharsis. Although I came to nuance this initial view with other factors—how young Lynch was when he came over, the city’s artistic effervescence at that time—I still believed that, as he put it, Philadelphia had been his greatest influence.
 And then, I talked with Peggy Reavey, Lynch’s first wife and the mother of their Philly-born daughter, Jennifer. And listening to Peggy Reavey made me realize how I little I knew—how superficial some of my assumptions had been. Now I wonder if Lynch’s mantra could have been both a crowd pleaser and a form of personal revisionism. According to Reavey, when Jack Fisk introduced her to Lynch in early 1966, Lynch had just arrived in town with a luggage full of fear. The fear, Reavey told me, was inside him. He projected it on things to create his art.
 Peggy Reavey Lynch in David Lynch's 1969 film The Alphabet 
 As a twenty-year old man who had just received a student deferment that allowed him to avoid being drafted during the war in Vietnam, Lynch had a lot to be fearful about. He was afraid he would disappoint his parents, and at the same time he was afraid he wouldn’t be able to live the “art life” he was meant for. He was worried about not getting the money he needed to produce the films he was dreaming up. Most importantly, he was terrorized of failing as an artist—as all artists are. Not all artists get to become David Lynch.
 “We were there,” Peggy told me. “We didn’t know what was going to happen.” The David Lynch we know in 2026, the master, the genius, the icon, was anything but a foregone conclusion. Sixty years ago, when Lynch and Reavey started dating in Philadelphia, there was an infinity of futures ahead of them in which he did not become what he aspired to. I have no idea how close he came to giving up in the face of that adversity, but I am convinced that not giving up demanded tremendous willpower, endurance, and resilience, emotionally as well as artistically. 
 2429 Aspen Street, the house where The Alphabet was shot | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Contemplating the worlds in which my all-time favorite filmmaker, the artist who changed my life when I was a teenager, does not exist, is a most humbling and thrilling experience. Thanks to Peggy Reavey, who witnessed first-hand how all those parallel universes folded back into nothingness, and whose presence helped forge Lynch as we know him, I now know a lot more about where the present version of me came from.
 Tags: cinema David Lynch Eraserhood Fairmount Lynchadelphia Song of Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Julien Suaudeau Julien Suaudeau is a French-American writer, documentary filmmaker, and podcaster. He was born in Evreux, Normandy, grew up in Paris, France, and moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 2006. He teaches French and Film at Bryn Mawr College. In 2024, he launched Song of Philadelphia, Hidden City's podcast.

title: A New Exhibition Encourages Visitors to Get Their Minds Into the Gutter
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The idea of subterranean Philadelphia captures the imagination. Walking down Broad Street, the roar of a passing subway rumbles up from the grate underfoot and invites questions: What’s down there? Where does it go? Who built it all? Why? How? 
 If there is a demogorgon lurking in this sprawling upside down world beneath Philadelphia’s streets, it lives in the combined sewers. For the uninitiated, these are 19-century engineering works that entombed many of the city’s creeks and streams, turning them instead into sewers, carrying away both sewage and stormwater. They’re now a major, and majorly expensive, problem for the city. The Philadelphia Water Department (PWD) is spending billions to try and rectify the fact that these sewers end up dumping billions of gallons of sewage-laden water into the city’s two rivers each year. How best to solve the puzzle is a bit of a controversial topic . Yet, PWD historical consultant Adam Levine is keeping his eye on the bigger picture. 
 In “ Lost Creeks of Philadelphia: Burying the Streams, Building the City ,” a special exhibition at the Athenaeum of Philadelphia, Levine and collaborating photographer Joseph Elliott place the city’s combined sewer system within a greater context, exploring the why and the how of their creation, while also examining the role they played in shaping the above-ground landscape of the city. 
 This photograph taken on June 7, 1900 shows the Aramingo Canal Sewer under construction near Girard Avenue. | Photo courtesy of the Philadelphia Water Department Historical Collection
 Indeed, the scale of their impact is vast. Combined sewers comprise the majority of the city’s 3,000 miles of sewage pipes, with some reaching 20 feet in diameter and running for miles. In the two centuries between the 1760s and 1960s, Levine noted, 73 percent of the city’s streams and creeks were buried, leaving only 118 linear miles of exposed waterways today out of an original 283 miles. That contributed much to the flattening, and graying, of the city’s once surprisingly complex landscape. 
 Levine, who also manages the resource-rich WaterHistoryPHL.org , sat down with me to discuss his exhibit, now open to the public through May 16, and how his decades of research has shaped his perspective on combined sewers. 
 Kyle Bagenstose (KB) : I recently read that combined sewers are actually what got you into the PWD historian role back in the 1990s. Tell me about that and why they caught your fascination. 
 Adam Levine (AL) : I was taking care of a community garden in West Philadelphia in the 1980s, and I was told there was a creek (Mill Creek) that had undermined the two houses on either side of the vacant lot that the garden was on. I considered myself an environmentalist and couldn’t understand why anyone would want to bury a stream. Nine years later, I was freelance writing for City Paper and suggested a story on Mill Creek, and the editor said, why not a story on the whole combined sewer system? 
 So, I contacted the water department, and they took me down into a sewer. The article was not like most articles about infrastructure these days, which are all, you know, saying how bad it is and how everything is falling apart. I was impressed by the idea that the water department was able to manage 3,000 miles of sewers. The [PWD’s] Office of Watersheds had just formed, and they wanted to know more about the history, so they hired me to start doing research. I’ve now been consulting since 1998. 
 A painting from 1871 shows 8th Street and Indiana Street. In the foreground is an upstream reach of Gunner’s Run, a stream that once flowed into the Delaware River in the Kensington neighborhood. In the 1840s the downstream portion of this stream was converted into a canal, which was, in turn, converted into a sewer around 1900. | Image courtesy of the Philadelphia Water Department Historical Collection
 KB : Of all the City agencies and institutions that could probably use a historian, PWD is an interesting one to actually have one. What do you think the value is? 
 AL : You know the water department is 225 years old. We started delivering water in 1801. We need to keep records because we have infrastructure that is very old that we need to keep track of. A lot of those records have now been digitized, and engineers are primarily focused on keeping the drinking water flowing and safe and properly treating the waste of the city. They don’t necessarily need a historian. 
 But I think it’s good for morale. Everybody likes feeling like they’re part of something bigger than themselves, and there is a long history here. It’s also been a really good way to engage neighborhoods where we’re doing big projects. To give them some idea that there is a larger vision that not only goes into the future, but stretches back 200 years. It’s part of a continuum. 
 KB : Let’s talk about the Athenaeum exhibit. Tell our readers how it came about and what they’ll see if they go there. 
 AL : The exhibit was really supposed to coincide with the release of my upcoming book with Joe Elliott, with a working title of The Lost Landscapes of Philadelphia . But as it became clear it was not going to happen as soon as we thought, we figured an exhibition was a way to jumpstart the process. The show covers a piece of the book on combined sewers, which hasn’t really had a big exhibit before. 
 What we try to do is take people through a history of their creation. We start with pictures showing the landscape of the city as it was. Then, there are watercolors that show some of the changes in the landscape as the city was being leveled out for development. We have items from the Historical Society of Pennsylvania, the Penn Museum, and from the water department’s own collection. There is artwork, drawings, watercolors, lithographs, and plans showing really amazing draftsmanship from the 19th century. Joe’s original photography. We also have artifacts–drafting tools, some things I dug up in an excavation of a filled area. 
 An ink, pencil, and watercolor rendering from 1879 of a sewer at 13th Street and Snyder Avenue. | Image courtesy of the Philadelphia Water Department Historical Collection
 KB : I understand you’re a sucker for the draftsmanship. Tell us about that. 
 AL : Personally, I can’t even draw a stick figure. So, to see these drawings, the detail is just amazing. Sure, they’re just drawing sewers to carry the waste of the city. But they delineated every brick, every stone. I’m curious how they fixed their mistakes, because they can’t have been perfect. But they’re not all blotchy, you can’t tell where they’ve erased. Maybe they were just that careful. 
 KB : Let’s talk about the landscape. There is a geologic thing happening in Philadelphia, where you have a flat coastal plain in the old city and then piedmont to the west and north. But looking at some of the old topography maps, it’s clear that large parts of the city look much different now than they used to. Tell us what roles combined sewers played in transforming the landscape. 
 AL : The building of the city, period, involved a lot of cutting and filling. Cutting down high ground, filling in low ground. Forget sewers, just to get it so the streets would drain properly. [Engineers] also wanted a sort of leveling out. But we do still have elevation changes in Philadelphia: zero at the river, to about 250 feet at the Pennypack and West Philly, up to 400 in Chestnut Hill. They also didn’t level out every valley. 
 What’s missing is about 150 miles of streams. When you look at the historic streams map and compare it to what’s on the surface now, it’s shocking. Shocking that they had the hubris to do that, but also sort of awe-inspiring, just to think of the amount of work that was involved, especially since a lot was done by manual labor. 
 KB : Explain how combined sewers were actually built. Did they just put an archway over the stream, so there’s still a natural stream bed? Or somehow divert flow into a full pipe? 
 AL : The engineering is usually to build a solid pipe so that all the water is carried away. You build up the bottom first and then go section by section, diverting the creek as each section is finished. They wanted everything to be carried to where they were dumping it, whether that was to the river, or ultimately now the city’s three sewage treatment plants. If there were any springs or little tributaries to these larger creeks, they wanted to capture them, too, in smaller pipes, and create a whole sewer system. 
 It was variable enough that it’s hard to generalize. There are some streams–Mill Creek is one–that definitely still has a flow outside the city. It flows on the surface and when it reaches the city at Overbrook Train Station, it enters a pipe–it sort of ceases to be a creek and becomes a sewer. And at Dock Creek (in Old City), they actually walled it first, then did just put a big arch over it, so there’s no bottom to that particular sewer. 
 A photograph taken on September 19, 1913 shows a break in Cohocksink Creek Sewer on Thompson Street, west of 8th Street. The sewer broke and overflowed many times in the 19th and early 20th centuries. This truck, sunken into one of those collapses, was clearly parked in the wrong place at the wrong time. | Image courtesy of the Philadelphia Water Department Historical Collection
 KB : Dock Creek brings up another point as one of the oldest to be buried. I thought combined sewers were made primarily to protect public health, but your research suggests they were also convenient to further real estate development. How much was it one or the other? 
 AL : Pollution was a reason. Dock Creek, Peggs Run (Northern Liberties), Cohocksink Creek (Kensington) were creeks flowing into the Delaware River that got badly polluted early by industry, which at the time were basically slaughterhouses and tanneries making leather. Then, as the city grew, in rural areas, creeks became the only way they knew to get sewage out of neighborhoods. So, instead of having a big open sewer going along, they figured, we’ll put it into a pipe. Why? Some of the engineers in the 19th century are not the best writers, so you have to sort of surmise their logic. When they started doing this in the 1850s, they still believed that odors were causing disease, not bacteria. So they thought it was much better to flush this out to the river. 
 Development was also an important part. When you have a stream meandering through a neighborhood, when you have hill and dale, you can’t really develop it on a grid, and Philadelphia is really big on the grid. So, you have to sort of level it out. 
 A third reason streams were put into sewers was because there’s really no other way to dig a channel that would flow by gravity. They had steam engines that could do some digging, but to dig a trench that flowed by gravity in the same way as a stream would have just been way too expensive. The city didn’t have to develop this way, but in the 19th century, engineers felt it was their duty to create as much real estate as possible to get as much tax revenue as possible. It was like a sort of micro manifest destiny. 
 Frankford Creek, looking downstream from Castor Avenue bridge. This artificial concrete channel, meant to prevent flooding of adjacent neighborhoods, replaced the stream’s natural bed in a project that began in the late 1940s. | Photo: Joseph E. B. Elliott
 KB : How does all of this make you think about the contemporary challenge for the PWD? I’m thinking of a line from one of the Daniel Craig's James Bond movies: “You’re a kite dancing in a hurricane, Mr. Bond.” It’s wild to think this one City agency that’s just trying to keep the water clean has to grapple with an engineering challenge of this vintage and magnitude. 
 AL : The historical context is important because we [PWD] didn’t just start dealing with pollution. Until 1952 the water department wasn’t in charge of the sewer system–the Public Works Bureau of Surveys was doing sewers before a city charter change. Even before, the water department was interested in keeping pollution out of the rivers, because the rivers were the source of our drinking water, and we were killing people with that water in the 19th century. 
 The city from 1914 to the 1950s had a plan to collect, intercept all that sewage flowing into the rivers, and then treat it. It took until the mid-1950s before the three sewage treatment plants that we still have today were built, and we really made a huge dent in the pollution of the rivers. That was a huge step, and then the federal government finally got involved with the Clean Water Act and EPA in the 1970s to try and stem industrial pollution. 
 The rivers are much cleaner now, but it’s hardest to get the last little bit of pollution no matter what you’re doing. From my point of view, it’s actually a very small problem now. It’s not unimportant, don’t get me wrong. I understand the importance. Most people alive today have never experienced the horrible pollution before the 1950s. Today, we expect that when we have a body of water that we feel safe being near it. 
 KB : I think I can understand that perspective. The water department has long been the agency kind of tasked with confronting the sins of our past. Scientists develop germ theory, and suddenly it’s incumbent on the water department to overhaul all the engineering. Combined sewers are just another example. 
 AL : It’s not only the sins of the past. It’s the sins of the present. Plastics in the river, chemical spills in the water. The water department is the one responsible to try and make the final product safe. 
 “Lost Creeks of Philadelphia: Burying the Streams, Building the City” is on view and open to the public through May 16. The Athenaeum of Philadelphia is free to visit and is located at 219 S. 6th Street. Adam Levine and Joseph Elliott’s book detailing the historic development of Philadelphia’s landscape is scheduled for release in fall 2027 by Temple University Press. 
 Tags: art exhibition Athenaeum of Philadelphia Philadelphia Water Department sewers 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: In Philadelphia, David Lynch Tuned Into The City's "Deep Frequencies"—Episode Two of Song of Philadelphia Podcast's "Lynchadelphia" Is Out Now
author: Julien Suaudeau
bodyText:
Peggy Reavey and David Lynch outside Reavey’s parents’ home in Chestnut Hill, 1968 | Photo: Bernard V. Lentz
 Editor's Note : Today, Hidden City published the second episode of season 3 of Song of Philadelphia Podcast. This season is "Song of Lynchadelphia" and it's dedicated to the ways Philadelphia influenced the work of David Lynch, throughout his entire career. You listen to the episode right here on Hidden City's Podcast page , on Spotify , and on Apple Podcasts . Here, host and creator Julien Suaudeau reflects on Lynch's idea of the "art life," which he cultivated in late-1960s Philadelphia. 
 It’s not just about Philadelphia’s “filth.”
 Granted, when looking back on his early years, David Lynch often emphasized “the violence, the insanity, and the corruption” he had witnessed in the city when he came from Alexandria to study at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. He would lean fully into the idea that he’d been both terrified and delighted during his time
here, and that Philly had left a powerful “impression” on him. Philadelphia, he said, was his greatest influence.
 I have no mind to argue with my favorite filmmaker. Still, I think it’s worth nuancing and investigating beyond the trauma sublimation theory I explored "in Smiling Bags of Death," Song of Lynchadelphia’s season opener.
 According to Jack Fisk, Lynch’s roommate during those years, PAFA classmate, best man, brother-in-law, and lifetime collaborator, two lesser-known, Philly-centric factors also came into play.
 When Lynch arrived in Philadelphia, he was just twenty years-old. “It’s crazy what you do when you’re young,” Fisk told me. “Everything’s new, and it’s all kind of vibrating inside of you, and it affects you for the rest of your life." Youth, as the power to see beauty in anything. Like Arthur Rimbaud, another precocious seer, Lynch tuned in to the deep frequencies of his living environment. He allowed himself to be moved by Philly, and he allowed Philly to become part of him. Years, decades later, his subconscious was still processing and translating that experience in works that we’ve come to recognize as masterpieces: Eraserhead , Twin Peaks , Mulholland Drive , Twin Peaks: The Return .
 David Lynch and his best man, Jack Fisk, at the party following Lynch’s marriage to Peggy Reavey, 1968 | Photo: Peggy Reavey
 And then, there was the vibrant artistic scene of late 1960s Philadelphia, at the Academy and beyond. Bruce Samuelson, who studied at PAFA at the same time as Fisk and Lynch, said they were part of a very special close-knit group, in which people showed each other their work and discussed their influences, such as Francis Bacon. That effervescence emboldened Lynch to explore across media—drawing, painting, sculpture—and eventually led him to film, a collective craft. But, Samuelson said, “he never gave up painting.”
 What strikes me the most about the three films Lynch made in Philly is how deeply their fabrication is woven in the fabric of his personal life. Lynch and Fisk cast each other’s faces on the screen of Six Men Getting Sick (Six Times) . The cries of Jennifer, the baby Lynch had with Peggy Reavey, yet another PAFA alum, are
present on the soundtrack of The Alphabet , which was shot on the third floor of the “Father, Son, and Holy Ghost” trinity house, at 2429 Aspen Street, where Lynch lived with Fisk and Reavey. The Grandmother was shot entirely at 2416 Poplar Street, the home Lynch and Reavey bought after getting married. A neighborhood boy plays the lead.
 David Lynch in the "Father, Son, Holy Ghost house" – 2429 Aspen St – 196 7 | Photo: C.K. Williams
 Lynch and Fisk referred to their time in Philadelphia as the "Art Life." But art is the most fragile process—anything in life can derail it. There are so many things that could have prevented that life from happening. Both friends had the drive and the resilience to pursue their dreams, and both eventually made it big in Hollywood. Yet, they never forgot about Philadelphia. “The fact that we were there together the whole time,” Fisk said, “bonded us in a way that lasted for sixty years.”
 Tags: David Lynch Eraserhood Fairmount Song of Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Julien Suaudeau Julien Suaudeau is a French-American writer, documentary filmmaker, and podcaster. He was born in Evreux, Normandy, grew up in Paris, France, and moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 2006. He teaches French and Film at Bryn Mawr College. In 2024, he launched Song of Philadelphia, Hidden City's podcast.

title: Train Station Designed by Frank Furness Listed on the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Mount Airy Train Station at 119 E. Gowen Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Philadelphia Historical Commission added four properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places at its meeting on April 10. The nomination of Mount Airy Train Station at 119 E. Gowen Avenue elicited a surprised reaction from the Historical Commission. Members were taken aback by the fact that the station was not already on the local register. It has been listed on the National Register of Historic Places since 1977. The building was designed in 1875 for the Philadelphia & Reading Railroad by renowned Philadelphia architect Frank Furness in the Queen Anne Stick Style. The station is associated with the railroad’s president Franklin Gowen, who had it built at a location near his home. The commuter station contributed to the development of the Mount Airy neighborhood. Although it is owned by SEPTA, the building has been leased to developer Ken Weinstein , as part of an adaptive reuse plan for five shuttered train stations along the Chestnut Hill East and West Regional Rail lines.
 In East Oak Lane, the Carl Metz House at 601 W. Godfrey Avenue was designed in 1927 by architect Carl E. Metz and built by his father, real estate developer Carl Metz. It is an exemplary example of the Spanish Colonial Revival style that was popular in Philadelphia at the time. 
 The Carl Metz House at 601 W. Godfrey Avenue in 2022. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 The Andrew Nebinger Jr. House at 1018 S. 2nd Street was designated. Its early history is associated with Dr. Andrew Nebinger, Jr., a prominent Civil War-era physician who cared for Union soldiers while the head surgeon of the Cooper Shop Hospital.
 The Andrew Nebinger Jr. House at 1018 S. 2nd Street. | Photo courtesy of the Philadelphia Historical Commission
 Since 1898, it has been the location of the Cieplinski Funeral Home, reflecting a significant social aspect of Southwark’s heritage of neighborhood-based, family-operated funeral establishments. The current owner, Henry A. Cieplinski, attended the meeting and showed Commission members 19th century a few artifacts he has discovered on the property.
 The fourth property that was designated at April's meeting is Blue Bell Mission, located at 701 W. Johnson Street . The one-story wood frame building on a schist foundation was built in 1879 as a Methodist mission chapel. It was originally located at 6244 Wissahickon Avenue and moved to its present location in 1922. 
 Blue Bell Mission at 701 W. Johnson Street. | Photo: Google Street View
 The church in 1960. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 Although a cupola that had adorned the front of the main roof has been removed, the building retains its religious character with its rectangular shape, steep gabled roof, and a brick vestibule entrance. As one of the few surviving examples in Philadelphia of a mission chapel, a church building style not intended to be permanent, it served as a significant religious and community centerpiece of the surrounding neighborhood.
 Earlier in the meeting, the Historical Commission reviewed various requests for alterations to designated buildings. One proposal in particular raised a challenging issue in interpreting the Commission’s rules. The owners of 2027 and 2029 Brandywine Street , two adjoining rowhouses in the Spring Garden neighborhood, planned to demolish the buildings’ flat roofs and rears and construct an addition with a gable roof spanning both to convert them into one dwelling. The two properties are contributing assets to the Spring Garden Historic District .
 Amid remarks about the visibility from adjacent 20th Street and the proposed gable roof interrupting the flat rooflines of the rest of the block, the question arose of whether the alterations were so extensive that they would be a de facto demolition. Concerns were raised that, if granted, it would set a precedent for property owners to demolish a building under the guise of renovations. The Historical Commission can grant a demolition permit for several reasons, such as after a review by the Commission’s Committee on Financial Hardship or if a property is deteriorated to the extent that it raises safety concerns. In this case, the Commission determined the property would not meet their criteria to grant a permit and denied the proposal.
 Tags: Frank Furness Historical Commission Meeting Report Mt. Airy Oak Lane Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: The Woman Who Was There at the Beginning of David Lynch
author: Julien Suaudeau
bodyText:
Peggy Reavey’s portrait of David Lynch, c. 1970 | Courtesy of the Artist
 Author’s Note :  Episodes 1 and 2 of Song of Lynchadelphia (Season 3 of Hidden City’s Song of Philadelphia Podcast ) focused on the creative big bang that took place during David Lynch’s time in Philadelphia, between 1965 and 1970. Episode 3 examined the wild ways in which the city—Lynch’s impression of the city—manifests itself in  Eraserhead, Mulholland Drive,  and the  Twin Peaks  universe . Episode 4 explored the Lynchian happenings in Philly. In episode 5, Philly’s own and Lynch’s first wife Peggy Reavey recalled how he projected his own fears on the city. Available today on Spotify and  Apple Podcasts , episode 6 is the second part of Reavey’s interview. As she reflects on her contributions to The Grandmother, Lynch’s third short, and remembers how she was replaced “by a whole staff” on the set of Eraserhead, we come to realize that each film originated in a bundle of dreams, experiences, people, and places that could not be ascribed only to the person known as the author. 
 Peggy Reavey took a long breath, thinking about the best way to phrase what was on her mind. “It was his thing,” she said, “but I knew what it was.” 
 She had married David Lynch back in 1968, when they were both in their early twenties and lived in Philadelphia. Five decades after their divorce, in Lynch’s final years, they zoomed at least once a month for a couple of hours with their daughter Jennifer, who was born in Philly on April 7, 1968. During those conversations, Lynch often brought up the home they’d bought that year at 2416 Poplar Street and how lucky they’d been to find such a big house.
 Peggy Reavey and David Lynch in Philadelphia, c. 1967 | Photo: EO Omwake
 As Reavey recalled how the two of of them had worked on The Grandmother , Lynch’s third short and the last film he made in Philly, on the top floor of 2416 Poplar, I heard an undertone of nostalgia for their beginnings in adulthood, love for her first husband, and pride to have been there with him. On a lower frequency, I also heard something more tender: the regret of having not always stood her ground in their artistic relationship and the desire not to be reduced to a footnote in film history. 
 “I showed him a painting I had done,” Reavey told me. “It was a nude of myself painting with a muse above me. He said: ‘Well, I don’t know, Peg, that’s kind of weird.' And I have to say that, unfortunately, I did not have the confidence to tell him to shut up. If he said something wasn’t good, it really set me back. I was a girl. Obviously, I didn’t have that kind of confidence as a painter at all yet. I got it eventually, but it took me a lot longer.”
 When Lynch wrote The Grandmother script, he borrowed details from Reavey’s personal life, as he had done with his second short, The Alphabet , shot at 2429 Aspen Street. “David never wet the bed,” Reavey told me. “I did and my brother did. My brother’s name is Martin, and we called him Mart. In the film, the father yells ‘Mot!' when the boy wets the bed. David never had a scary, angry father. I did and my brother did.”
 As an artist, Reavey knows that art takes from life all the time. She’s not out to claim shared authorship over any of Lynch’s works. As thoughtfully as the blind spots of art history allow, she is just demanding a more complex and nuanced understanding of Lynch’s creative process—and about how David Lynch became the artist we know. For instance, she recalls him wondering how he could make the wet bed in The Grandmother look like a wet bed. “This whole thing is like a cartoon,” she answered. “Just paint it bright yellow. A big yellow circle.”
 The wet bed, still from The Grandmother (1970)
 Listening to Reavey, I thought about Chloe Zhao’s Hamnet and about all the women who lived with a male artist and who disappeared in the shadow of the artist’s greatness once that greatness was established by the canon. Putting the emphasis on the artist implies a self-driven narrative that typically acknowledges artistic influences but often minimizes the impact of loved ones: we basically choose what and who is worth remembering. That’s why I think the politique des auteurs , as formalized by the French New Wave, is both a conceptual scam with its focus on the creator and a misogynistic world view because a lot of the people that get pushed on the sidelines happen to be women. 
 Peggy Reavey was a key enabler for David Lynch. She’s not the only one—in the previous Song of Lynchadelphia episodes, we talked to Jack Fisk, we discussed the mentoring role that Bushnell Keeler played during Lynch’s teenage years, as well as the creative explosion that happened when Lynch discovered the work of Francis Bacon. But, from 1967 to 1970 in Philadelphia, she is the person who lived with Lynch on the good and the bad days, through the eureka moments, the doubts, and the anxieties. She was there for all of it. 
 It’s always the people who are there all the time that we end up unseeing. They become part of the artist’s habitat, and whatever agency they had in the making of the artist takes on a form of invisibility too.
 In this episode, I don’t mean to diminish the merits of my favorite filmmaker. My intention is to find a way back to that lost agency. Who was Peggy Reavey as a 20-year old? What did she dream about? How did she find a balance between life and art, between Lynch’s art and her own? What did she give away to support the man she loved?
 “I went away for one weekend,” Reavey told me. “When I came back, he was sitting inside the entryway, waiting for me to come through the door, smoking cigarettes. And he just said he couldn’t do anything.” That doesn’t mean Lynch was helpless by himself. But he had to constantly be in conversation with Reavey to translate his ideas into sounds and motion pictures. He needed her close to make art. They were romantic, emotional, and creative partners.
 That ability to create together came to an end when they moved to California and Lynch started working on Eraserhead. “I wasn’t needed anymore,” Reavey said. “I was replaced by a whole staff.” The marriage ended soon after, but the complicity never disappeared. Twenty-five years later, when Lynch was working on the production design of Lost Highway , he bought three paintings from Peggy Reavey and hung them on the wall of Fred and Renée Madison’s living-room.
 Peggy Reavey's paintings hanging in a scene of David Lynch's Lost Highway (1997)
 I see that gesture as a way to let his first wife know that she was still in his heart and that her art had been an organic part of his the whole time.
 Peggy Reavey and David Lynch at the opening of Reavey’s exhibition at 478 Gallery, 2022 | Photo: 478 Gallery
 Tags: David Lynch Eraserhood Fairmount Lynchadelphia Peggy Reavey Philmadelphia 
 About the Author
 Julien Suaudeau Julien Suaudeau is a French-American writer, documentary filmmaker, and podcaster. He was born in Evreux, Normandy, grew up in Paris, France, and moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 2006. He teaches French and Film at Bryn Mawr College. In 2024, he launched Song of Philadelphia, Hidden City's podcast.

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: Philadelphia Macaroni Company
author: Alan Jaffe and Bryan Mckinney
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Philadelphia Macaroni Company 
 Location : 780 South 11th Street
 Architect : Isadore W. Levin
 Built : 1933
 The Italian Market broke ground in the 1880s along 9th Street, a still-thriving piazza that has given Philly much of its culinary character, including hoagies, water ice, soft pretzels, and cheesesteaks. On the fringe of the market, a three-story brick and block-glass building, designed by residential and industrial architect and engineer Isadore W. Levin, rose on 11th Street in the 1930s, where the factory churned out American-made pasta products–and they called it macaroni.
 The Philadelphia Macaroni Company, founded in 1914 by the Antonio Marano family, produced a variety of noodles, including the shapes used in Campbell’s SpaghettiOs and Alphabet Soup. Pasta production shifted long ago to other facilities, and the company, which had grown into a national entity, was sold in 2024.
 Plans are now cooking for conversion into a 47-unit apartment building, with an additional floor, at the convergence of the bustling Bella Vista and Hawthorne neighborhoods. The 38,000-square-foot old factory, which is being nominated to the National Register of Historic Places , certainly deserves local appreciation as well on the Philadelphia Register.
 Tags: Italian Market Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Unlisted Philadelphia

title: The Greenhill Estate: From Quaker Settlement to National Scandal to a Place for Friends
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
Peaceable Kingdom , 1834 by Edward Hicks. | Image courtesy of National Gallery of Art
 Quaker minister and artist Edward Hicks painted Peaceable Kingdom over one hundred times in the mid-19th century to commemorate the transfer of thousands of acres of Lenape land to William Penn. His most famous version, now in the permanent collection of the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts (PAFA), depicts ferocious beasts lying down with lambs and little children. In the far distance, on the banks of the Schuylkill River, colonists and Lenape gather under a tree. This idyllic image, based on Quaker pacifism and the Bible, mythologized the founding of Pennsylvania . A more realistic painting would have shown Penn's agent, William Markham, in 1692, purchasing all of what is now Montgomery County in exchange for bars of lead, guns, and an assortment of tools.
 Quaker Aristocracy 
 A mapp of ye improved part of Pensilvania in America, divided into countyes townships and lotts. Surveyed by Thomas Holme for William Penn. The Welsh Tract is featured left of center. | Image courtesy of Geography & Map Division, Library of Congress
 Thomas Lloyd, a Quaker from an aristocratic Welsh banking family, purchased a sizable portion of the 40,000-acre Welsh Tract from Penn in 1692, covering parts of present-day Montgomery, Chester, and Delaware Counties. The tract enabled Welsh Quakers to have a community where they could speak their own language and live by their own laws. Lloyd's property, which became known as the Greenhill Estate, was bordered by Lancaster Avenue (known then as Lincoln Highway) to the north, Haverford Road to the south, the Indian Creek Water Basin to the west, and what is now City Avenue to the east. 
 Educated at University of Oxford, Lloyd quickly rose through the ranks of local politics, becoming deputy governor for Pennsylvania under William Penn until 1693. As a committed pacifist, Lloyd opposed the introduction of a militia into the province and was the most powerful and popular leader in the state during this period. Following his death, 118 acres of his land were sold to David Price who built a stone house, known for 269 years as the Old Homestead. Price added adjacent land until he owned 300 acres, including what is now Morris Park and Overbrook on the Philadelphia side of City Avenue, which he leased to farmers. Greenhill Estate became known as Greenhill Farms Plantation. At its peak, it contained 2,000 acres, extending across City Avenue and into what is now Overbrook.
 Elites Flee the City 
 The Israel Wistar Morris residence. Date unknown. | Photo courtesy of Lower Merion Historical Society
 When millions of impoverished immigrants started to arrive in Philadelphia in the late 19th century, the city's elite cast an eye on farmland just outside the city limits with little interest in growing crops. Israel Wistar Morris, a wealthy broker and merchant, relocated his family from Philadelphia to Greenhill Farms. In the spirit of Marie Antoinette, Morris and his family maintained a mansion while leasing out their farmland. The family had indentured servants and enslaved people in the 18th and early 19th centuries. Morris' son, Wistar Morris, who served as director of the Pennsylvania Railroad, president of the Board of Pennsylvania Hospital, and trustee of Haverford College, built a large stone mansion 300 yards west of the Old Homestead. 30 years later, a mansion was no longer enough. 
 In the 1890s, Wistar Morris erected an unreasonable facsimile of a Scottish castle designed by Mantle Fielding. Morris wasn't alone in his embrace of the Gilded Age. Industrialist Henry C. Gibson had recently moved an entire castle, brick by brick, from Scotland to Wynnewood. Meanwhile, hundreds of Welsh Quakers transitioned to the Anglican Church, which allowed them to swap simplicity for flamboyant displays of wealth. When Morris died in 1891, he donated Morris Park to the City of Philadelphia. The original Overbrook Golf Club, founded in 1900, was located on 90 acres leased from the Wistar Morris Estate. Around that time, portions of the Green Hill Estate began to transition into the middle class suburban community of Penn Wynne. 
 Roaring Twenties 
 A postcard from the 1920s showing Greenhill Farms Hotel. Built in 1919, designed by Horace Trumbauer. | Image: CardCow.com
 Charles Morris Wood, the great, great grandson of the devout Israel Morris, took the former Quaker enclave to a new level of glitz when he erected and managed the Greenhill Farms Hotel in 1919. Designed by architect Horace Trumbauer , the Colonial Revival hotel was a high end residential hotel for the Blue Book crowd. It became a fashionable place for tea, dinner, dancing, and private parties. 
 Champagne flowed freely at the hotel through Prohibition, as did scandal. It was here that a stockbroker, the 1920s version of Bernie Madoff, was whisked from his hotel room in silk pajamas to Sing Sing Correctional Facility after embezzling over $1 million from New York society women. In 1931, the hotel made national headlines again when a guest defended his sister's honor with a 12-gauge, double barreled shotgun. Following his acquittal, MGM made a movie based on this sensational murder, Unashamed, starring Robert Young. Warner Bros. released its own version, Two Against the World , starring Constance Bennett. 
 The End of an Era 
 Greenhill Estate's "castle" is now home to Friends Central School. | Photos: Stacia Friedman
 The original Welsh Quaker founders of the Greenhill Estate would have been horrified, but not surprised, at the moral and financial failings of their descendants. Forced to sell off their assets, the "castle" was sold to Friends' Central School for $1 (plus a hefty mortgage) in 1925. Greenhill Farms Hotel was bought by the Eastern Baptist Theological Seminary in 1939 for $550,000. In 2015, it became a luxury residential apartment complex, The Palmer, preserving Horace Trummbauer's design. The Overbrook Golf Club was sold for $500,000 in 1940 to the developer of Lankenau Hospital. In 1962, the Old Homestead was demolished to make way for The Greenhill Apartments which were built on a 22-acre tract that date back to the original land grant. The eastern part of the estate, from 66th Street to 72nd Street in Philadelphia, was developed throughout the 20th century with a mix of homes, leaving only a small portion of the original estate intact. 
 However, if the original Quaker founders of Greenhill Farms were to visit today, they would be relieved to discover their faith is alive and well at Friends' Central. The school uses its ornate mansion, built in the Victorian era, as the main building of its 28-acre campus of their Middle and Upper School which includes an arboretum, nature trail, and a pollinator garden. Students and faculty enter though a porte cochere.
 The mansion's main staircase features Tiffany stained glass. | Photo: Stacia Friedman
 While the historic mansion's opulence is a far reach from traditional Quaker values, there is no denying its architectural significance. Students and teachers are surrounded by authentic Tiffany leaded glass windows, vintage chandeliers, beamed ceilings, carved wooden walls, and original tiled fireplaces. "We light two of the fireplaces in the front hall in the winter to provide warmth on cold days," said Grant Calder, Friends' Central history instructor and archivist. Raised in the Quaker tradition, Calder is not surprised that Jewish students form a substantial and influential minority in Quaker schools in and around Philadelphia for over the last half century. "Quakerism and Judaism have a lot in common," he said. "Both share core values, emphasizing the importance of community and the pursuit of peace and social justice, as well as not requiring an intermediary between the individual and God."
 If you go, visit Morris Park at Woodcrest Avenue and 66th Street, which has been fully restored by the Friends of Morris Park. It contains branches of Indian Creek, part of the Cobbs Creek Watershed, and currently has picnic areas and two miles of safe and maintained trails for hiking, biking, and bird and wildlife watching.
 The author would like to thank the staff of Lower Merion Historical Society and Friends' Central School for their assistance with researching this article. 
 Tags: Horace Trumbauer mansions Overbrook Quakers 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: A New Exhibition Immerses Visitors in a Living History of the "No Arena" Campaign
author: Kathryn Rice
bodyText:
As America’s 250th birthday approaches, cultural institutions across Philadelphia are gearing up to host special events celebrating the history of American democracy. The Walnut Street Theatre will run 1776 The Musical . Tempeste di Mare, Philadelphia’s Baroque orchestra, will perform songs popular during the American Revolution. Multiple museums will run exhibits on early American history.
 At the Asian Arts Initiative in Chinatown, the celebrations focus on a more recent historical chapter. The arts center’s splashy new exhibition, No Arena: Making a Movement , spotlights the grassroots campaign that fought the Philadelphia 76ers’ push to build an arena near Chinatown from 2022 to 2025.
 “We were trying to figure out what we would like to put forward in a moment when we weren’t feeling really celebratory about American democracy,” said Dave Kyu, director of programs at Asian Arts Initiative. Kyu and his colleagues decided the No Arena campaign, which organized people across the city in a fight against a powerful corporation, should be spotlighted during America’s semiquintennial as a local example of democracy in action.
 The exhibition, which features protest art and archival materials from the campaign, reflects what Kyu called the “messiness of organizing.” Colorful protest signs, handwritten postcards, photographs, and slightly wrinkled No Arena t-shirts are arranged on the walls in playful disarray. A piece of butcher paper, covered in sticky notes, invites guests to share their memories of the movement. The back wall is covered with a floor-to-ceiling photograph of protestors linking arms and awaiting arrest.
 Photo courtesy of Constance Mensh, Asian Arts Initiative
 Rather than moving chronologically, the show carries visitors through the emotional ups and downs of the campaign, with spaces that evoke joy, confrontation, and, ultimately, transformation. In a neighborhood rattled by Donald Trump’s immigration policies, the exhibit offers community members a chance to feel hope and pride. “I think it’s really important, especially at a time where there’s so much happening and there’s a lot of negative news to have this moment of hopefulness,” said Lauren Lowe, an organizer with Asian Americans United, one of the organizations co-presenting the exhibition.
 The 76ers withdrew their proposal to build an arena in Market East just eight days before President Trump began his second term in office. Many of the community organizers who had fought the proposal dove immediately into anti-ICE organizing, leaving them with little time to reflect on their historic win. “It ended so abruptly,” Lowe said. “There was a little bit of whiplash.”
 Some of the organizers, including celebrated activist Debbie Wei, approached Kyu asking if the Asian Arts Initiative could host an exhibit on the No Arena movement that would honor the many people across the city who had participated in the campaign. Kyu was interested, but he thought the Asian Arts Initiative would need to partner with other community groups to make the exhibit happen. Asian Americans United, Asian Pacific Islander Alliance, and the Philadelphia Folklore Project signed on as co-presenters.
 “It always needed to be kind of a community that came together to present the exhibition,” Kyu said. “We could draw within our network, like, ‘oh this person still has this art piece in their basement.’” The group assembled a rich trove of art works, most of which were made with help from volunteers. Of the roughly 100 of works on display in the exhibition, Kyu said only nine were attributed to a professional artist. He said the rest “resisted attribution” because they’d been made in community settings. “It was like, we rolled out the banner,” Kyu said. “Yes, there was somebody that thought about the outline and made the format, but then 12 people came together and executed that.”
 Photo courtesy of Constance Mensh, Asian Arts Initiative
 Vivian Chang, the executive director at Asians Americans United, explained that for community members who worked on the pieces on display, the experience of seeing their work in an “elevated setting” was affirming. “People definitely feel like, ‘Oh wow, this stuff belongs in a museum,'” she said. There’s “that sense of ‘this is so official, and we get to be here too.'”
 On a recent Thursday evening, a group of people huddled around a table in the center of the gallery space. A grinning dragon with shiny gold scales slithered along the wall to their left. Hand painted banners draped from the ceiling. A floor-to-ceiling collage of photographs and painted faces covered the wall behind them. It was a colorful, eye-catching display that Kyu aptly described as “maximalist in the best way.” But for the moment, no one was gazing at the art on the walls. They were too busy making their own.
 The people seated at the table were participating in a poetry workshop with David Acosta and Mabel Lee, local writers who participated in the No Arena campaign. In the back of the building, other groups were busy singing movement songs and turning old cereal boxes into protest signs.
 The event, Art for Resistance, was one in a series Asian Arts Initiative is hosting in tandem with the exhibition. The events serve as a kind of bridge between the present and recent past, creating a space for organizers to reflect on the No Arena campaign while bringing new activists into the fold.
 Photo courtesy of Constance Mensh, Asian Arts Initiative
 Many of the people who attended had not participated in the No Arena protests. Some were learning about Chinatown’s long legacy of community organizing for the first time.
 Mark Baek said he had recently “gotten into organizing” through the Ginger Arts Center. He described the exhibition as educational, saying he had not been aware that Chinatown community members have fought development projects throughout much of the neighborhood’s history.
 Juny Ardon recently moved to Philadelphia from Los Angeles, where she felt inspired by the anti-ICE protests. As a graphic designer, she came to the event looking to receive advice from other artists involved in activism. “I took so many gems of wisdom from people that are doing the work,” she said after listening in on a panel discussion with artists who participated in the No Arena movement. “I am really grateful I’m here.”
 At the end of the evening, the workshop participants fanned out in a large circle to share what they’d created. Three friends shared signs they’d decorated that said “Migration is beautiful.” Members of Son Revoltura, a collective that performs Afro-Indigenous folk music, led a group through a protest song.
 Photo courtesy of Constance Mensh, Asian Arts Initiative
 Katherine Antarikso read a poem she composed earlier in the evening. Antarikso was an active participant in the No Arena campaign, attending protests and hearings at City Hall. She was excited to see an exhibition so soon after the No Arena campaign had ended. “Usually you see these things 10 years or 20 years later, and then it’s hard to find some of the materials for the archives,” she said. “They’ve done such an amazing job keeping everything.”
 Given Chinatown’s history, Antarikso said she expects the neighborhood will face other development threats in the future. She hopes the next generation of activists will draw inspiration from the No Arena exhibition. “I love that there is an archive and an exhibit so that we can show the future generation that this is probably going to happen again,” she said. “We were able to fight it now. In the future you can fight again.”
 Tags: art exhibition Chinatown Immigrants protest 
 About the Author
 Kathryn Rice is a freelance journalist based in Philadelphia and a graduate student at The Columbia School of Journalism.

title: Photo Exhibition Shines a Different Light on Wissahickon Valley Park
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
A photography exhibit invites viewers to see a favorite part of Fairmount Park in a different light, literally. Forbidden Light , now on view at Space Art Gallery in Bella Vista , showcases 31 images of the Wissahickon Valley Park captured using infrared film photography.
 “A lot of the photos are measuring light that we cannot see,” explained photographer Dale McCarthy. Along the electromagnetic spectrum, infrared light begins with waves that are longer than those of red light, the longest waves in the visible spectrum. Hence, infrared light is invisible to the human eye. The results are at once familiar and otherworldly. Several shots capture recognizable structures and vistas, but the portrayals are different, with dark skies and foliage that glows white.
 Cresheim Creek Bridge. | Photo: Dale McCarthy
 McCarthy’s process involves using high speed 35mm infrared film, a Leica M6 rangefinder camera, and a deeply opaque filter that blocks out visible light while allowing infrared light to pass through. Working with infrared film is a challenge, as it must remain frozen until use, and many manufacturers, including McCarthy’s choice, have discontinued production. He ruefully admits that he’s stockpiled a stash of it in his freezer.
 It is all in keeping with McCarthy’s overall approach to his photography, which includes developing his negatives by hand and creating most of his prints in his personal darkroom. “The traditional analog process is generally how I’ve made my photos. It allows me to take in different things,” he noted. “With digital photography, you’re making an exact replica. Analog methods can sometimes take an abstract spin.”
 Andorra Meadow. | Photo: Dale McCarthy
 The choice of the Wissahickon Valley Park fed another fascination. McCarthy was interested in the opportunity the park offers for a contemplative encounter with nature, yet within an urban environment. “I called it ‘Forbidden Light,’ because it suggests the possibilities when we set aside areas like this,” he said. “The possibilities of how people will use it and relate to it.” It is expressed in a gentle play on words in the exhibition's title, referencing Forbidden Drive, which has been closed to vehicular traffic for more than a century and also the infrared light that humans are not able to see. McCarthy took around 500 photos. “I go through a process of revisualization, imagining what the printed photo will look like, with its highlights and contrasts.” In the end, he narrowed it down to the final 31 in the exhibition.
 McCarthy took the photographs at various times during the spring and summer of 2022. “It needed to be at a time when there were leaves on the trees,” he said, explaining that foliage reflects infrared strongly, but the trees’ bark and wood do not. The effect is known as the "Wood effect," named after the infrared photography pioneer Robert W. Wood. The chlorophyll in the leaves is transparent at infrared wavelengths, which lets light be reflected within the plant cells. Normally, the effect is masked by the amount of green visible light reflected by the foliage.
 Forbidden Drive. | Photo: Dale McCarthy
 McCarthy grew up near Pittsburgh. After earning a degree in English in college he arrived in Philadelphia and taught in public schools for several years. He now works as a color darkroom instructor at Fleisher Art Memorial. McCarthy is a member of the Kensington-based Halide Project , a group dedicated to supporting the practice and appreciation of film and historic process photography methods. He also produces portraiture for press materials and album artwork for artists, writers, and musicians.
 Forbidden Light is on display at the Space Art Gallery, 749 S. 8th Street, through April 18. Gallery hours are Wednesday through Friday 5 – 8 p.m. and Saturday 10 a.m. – 4 p.m. For more information see their website here: www.thespacephiladelphia.com 
 Tags: art exhibition Fairmount Park photography Wissahickon Valley Park 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Historic Nurses' Strike In NYC Echoes Exploitative Labor Practices at Hahnemann Hospital
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
As up to 15,000 nurses across New York City go on strike over the lack of pay increases, minimum staffing levels, possible discontinuation of health care benefits, and lack of workplace protections, we are reminded that the role of nurses is often overlooked within the medical field when compared to the more front facing role of doctors. Over the past few decades in Philadelphia and the surrounding counties, there have been a number of threatened strikes, Yet, only one, the Filipino Nurses’ Strike of 1973, became an international incident. 
 By Friday, August 3, 1973, Hahnemann Hospital had cancelled its involvement in an education exchange program that had attracted Filipino nurses since 1960 to the Philadelphia region. The program supplemented shortfalls in local staffing, trained recent nursing school graduates on American medical procedures, and provided them with enough experience to be an asset to the medical field upon their return to the Philippines. The rapid end of the program was the result of a nurses’ dispute, mainly over fair wages. Hahnemann Hospital president Edward Wharton Sober Jr. brought to light the issues of discrimination and nationalism that caused many people, including Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., to question and reexamine the roles of Filipino nurses within the United States.
 The initial Exchange Visitor Program (EVP) was developed in 1948 with the creation of the U.S. Information and Education Act that same year. According to the book Empire of Care: Nursing and Migration in Filipino American History by Catherine Ceniza Choy, “During the mid-twentieth century, exchange programs acted as vehicles for transforming nursing into an international profession.” Along with this trend came increases in both personal and family wealth via remittances and socioeconomic status.
 11 nurses from the Philippines arrive at Philadelphia International Airport for a one-year training program at Presbyterian Hospital. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 By the 1960s, travel agencies increasingly began to assist with the paperwork, promotion, and logistics of settling nurses in various foreign cities. Philadelphia, New York, Los Angeles had already established enclaves of Filipino nurses who had migrated years prior. People were advised by friends and families to go through training to become registered nurses (RN) in the Philippines and participate in the EVP.
 Almost immediately, issues arose in U.S. hospitals as nurses felt abused. “Some supervisors exploited exchange nurses by assigning them to work the least desirable work shifts, knowing that the exchange nurse’s visa status depended on her sponsorship from the hospital,” wrote Choy. Other abuses ranged from last-minute shift changes to double shifts over extended periods, while white nurses received the optimal shifts, leaving Filipino nurses to believe that they would always receive “the dirty jobs.”
 The almost two-month-long standoff with Hahnemann Hospital began with issues regarding housing for Filipino nurses. A formal statement by the hospital’s administration on May 14, 1973 ordered resident nurses to move from the 14th floor to the 16th floor of the Philadelphia Athletic Club at 306–320 N. Broad Street (demolished in 1991) in favor of plans to open a health services center at that location. Two options were given to resident nurses: either move to the 5th floor of the Nurses’ Residence at 15th and Vine Streets, which staff stated did not have cooking facilities and separated Filipino nurses from each other, or seek shelter elsewhere. Those not interested in moving were given until June 29 to move out.
 Shocked by the wording of the letter, the nurses decided to unite to get justice. According to Marcela Muneses, president of the Filipino Exchange Nurses Association (FENA), “At first, we were tongue-tied, but now we had chosen to fight back.” Muneses, along with 74 other nurses, including Corazon C. Cabeguin, Asuncion E. Cuesta, and Emerita A. Zalavarria, delivered their own demands to hospital administrators Asher Barmish and Elspeth Anderson on Monday, June 4, 1973. Their demands included an increase in yearly starting salary from $7,195 to $8,190 to be more in line with wages of white nurses, allow FENA members continue to live at the Philadelphia Athletic Club, tighter security at the club, family insurance coverage under Blue Cross and Blue Shield, hospital coverage against legal liabilities, two-thirds sick pay during sick, disability, and maternity leave, coverage under worker’s compensation laws, health benefits extended to incoming exchange nurses, and fairness in how shifts and duties are distributed.
 This photograph from 1968 shows Philippine nurses standing around a seated Consuelo C. Aguilar while she blows candles out on a cake. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 In a June 9, 1973 Philadelphia Daily News article, FENA nurses reportedly began to hold solidarity rallies outside of the hospital. The article stated, “It was unfair that American-born registered nurses made what they felt was a considerably higher salary.” According to a Hahnemann Hospital spokesperson at the time, an American nursing graduate started at $8,568 per year, but Filipino nurses, categorized as in training with an education curriculum, were paid $6,880. After three months they received $7,195. If they stay at least a year, Filipino nurses had the option of a second year at $7,810. The nurses stated that they were never given an education curriculum.
 A FENA newsletter dated June 12, 1973, stated that negotiations with administrator Barmish faltered as most requests that nurses move were rejected. In response, the counteroffer was that the nurses’ residences would be upgraded with kitchens, and movers would assist in some of the nurses’ transition to an alternative location. The issue of worker’s compensation did not receive a response. Administrator Anderson’s response to shift assignments noted that nurses who did not accept their assignments “will be disciplined.” The 75 Filipino nurses were advised not to speak with the press as it was “an internal hospital matter” and not to distribute flyers. Some of the nurses stated that they were threatened with deportation.
 By June 15, as the topics of exploitation and discrimination became prominent, Foreign Affairs Secretary Carlos P. Rómulo contacted the U.S. Ambassador of the Philippines, Eduardo Z. Romualdez, to learn if the nurses’ claims were accurate. A request was made to let Jose Naldo, labor attaché of the Philippine Embassy in Washington, step in and speak to both sides directly. After the initial meeting, he determined that the matter could be resolved soon. As protests and rallies continued, Local 1199C Union, AFL-CIO, the Philadelphia Committee for Concerned Filipinos, and other organizations began to show their support for FENA.
 By late June, the Filipino nurses won their housing demand. They were allowed to stay on the upper floors of the Athletic Club with the bottom floor still planned for a conversion to a health services center. Yet, in regard to other demands, hospital administrators did not budge, leading to a deadlock. At a June 23 meeting, Hahnemann Hospital did not allow its nurses to let representatives speak on their behalf, stating that FENA is not a union.
 A Filipino nurse protesting Hahnemann Hospital's unfair labor policies by handing out flyers. | Photo: Joseph J. Conley, Philadelphia Inquirer , June 13, 1973
 As negotiations stalled, the number of striking nurses decreased to 72. Approached by the press regarding the lack of momentum, Roger S. Hunt, director of Hahnemann Hospital, was quoted as saying that meetings were being boycotted by the nurses. In response, the nurses’ spokesperson stated, “Hunt insisted on a general meeting in the administration office, while the nurses wanted a meeting in a neutral spot.” Consequently, a formal statement by the hospital was made regarding the nurses’ futures. “We will excuse any [nurse] from her contractual obligations to Hahnemann if she wishes to transfer to another approved program or return to her home.” In response, Muneses said, “We had been threatened before with the termination of the [EVP] program.”
 Conditions remained the same into August when the decision was made to officially cancel the Filipino nurse exchange program in November 1973, leaving 49 of the 72 remaining nurses with only one year of employment. The remaining staff were allowed to finish their two years of training. Muneses called this decision a “cop out” and attempted to reverse the decision.
