In the aftermath, nurses who tried to transition to other hospitals later learned they would not be accepted elsewhere, fueling claims that they were blacklisted. Others returned to the Philippines.
 The fallout of the strike and the termination of the nurses’ exchange program resulted in criticism about how the program was used to shore up gaps in work schedules and undesirable shifts. Although the State Department did not supervise the program, it did allow the Board of Nursing Examiners in each state to supervise it and verify that nurses were receiving training. However, Cora Cabeguin, a Filipino nurse at Hahnemann Hospital was billed $738 for a one-way flight from the travel agency that assisted her after Cabeguin's arrival to the United States. President Marcos eventually cancelled the Philippine government’s involvement in the program and did not allow students or nurses to fly to the U.S. for the purpose of education under the H-Visa.
 Tags: Asian American history Hospitals Immigrants medical history 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Places Saved: Spring 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 DeBenneville Burial Ground 
 Location : 6460 N. Broad Street
 Built : 1758
 Tucked away in West Oak Lane, the deBenneville Family Burial Ground is one of Philadelphia’s oldest and least-known historic cemeteries. In 1758, Dr. George deBenneville Sr., a London-born preacher of the Universalist Church, purchased 20 acres north of the city and set aside a small cemetery plot. Raised in the English Royal Court, deBenneville came to the American colonies in 1741 seeking religious freedom and introduced Universalism to America.
 Following the Battle of Germantown, deBenneville offered space in the family plot for two deceased British officers. Although the original property has been reduced by surrounding road construction, the burial ground survives today, enclosed by its historic stone wall. Over generations, family wills dedicated resources for the cemetery’s care, underscoring its importance as a long-term family memorial.
 Placed on the Philadelphia Register of historic Places in 1987, the site was protected from development, but suffered from decades of minimal upkeep under a trust administered by successive banks. In 2024-25, that trajectory began to change. George deBenneville Bell Jr., a direct descendant, emerged as a leading advocate for the site , working to restore proper stewardship and secure the funds his ancestors intended for its maintenance. By gaining control of the trust, Bell led cleanup, documentation, and planning efforts to ensure sustainable, long-term oversight.
 The deBenneville Burial Ground is finally moving from neglect toward care. Preserving this rare and intimate link to Philadelphia’s Colonial and Revolutionary-era history demonstrates the lasting impact of family advocacy and responsible stewardship.
 Photo: J. Fusco
 Wanamaker Light Show and Dickens Village 
 Location : 100 East Penn Square
 Built : 1956
 For generations of Philadelphians, the Wanamaker Light Show and Dickens Village define the holiday season. Since 1956, the Light Show has transformed the Wanamaker Building ’s Grand Court into a spectacle of more than 100,000 lights, projecting snowflakes, ballerinas, and reindeer, set to festive music performed on the world-renowned Wanamaker Grand Organ. Upstairs, Dickens Village invites visitors into a 6,000-square-foot recreation of 1840s London, with 26 scenes from A Christmas Carol that bring a holiday classic to life.
 Behind the scenes, sustaining these traditions is an enormous undertaking. The installations rely on decades of institutional knowledge, specialized technicians, and extensive seasonal staffing to safely manage crowds that number in the tens of thousands each day. Together, the Light Show and Dickens Village generate an estimated $30 million in direct and indirect economic impact for Philadelphia each holiday season.
 That complexity became a vulnerability in early 2025 when Macy’s closed its Center City store, ending nearly 70 years of retailer stewardship and placing the future of both attractions in doubt. In response, the Philadelphia Visitor Center, working with building owner TF Cornerstone, the Friends of the Wanamaker Organ, long-serving technicians, and hundreds of individual donors, stepped in to ensure the traditions continued. A $350,000 fundraising campaign successfully brought both attractions back for the 2025 holiday season.
 Although the Light Show and Dickens Village will pause during building renovations in 2026 and 2027, their return in 2025 reaffirmed their enduring cultural and civic value to the Philadelphia region.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Maguire Hall, Woodmere Art Museum 
 Location : 9001 Germantown Avenue
 Built : 1853
 The opening of the Frances M. Maguire Hall for Art and Educatio n marks the most significant moment in Woodmere Art Museum’s history since Woodmere first opened to the public in 1910 and is a major preservation success for Chestnut Hill. The Gothic Revival stone mansion at the corner of Germantown and Sunset Avenues was built in 1853 for industrialist William Henry Trotter and later expanded with Italianate wings by Cope & Stewardson. In 1927, the property was purchased by the Sisters of Saint Joseph, who used it for nearly a century as a school and residence, most recently known as St. Michael’s Hall.
 Although listed as a contributing property within the Chestnut Hill National Register Historic District , the building lacked local historic designation and faced an uncertain future when the Sisters put it up for sale. That changed in 2021, when Woodmere, located down the block, acquired the mansion and its 4-acre grounds.
 Woodmere committed to a preservation-driven expansion rooted in adaptive reuse. Former parlors and bedrooms have been sensitively transformed into 14 new galleries featuring contemporary Philadelphia artists, illustration arts, and a new Jewelry Vault. The acquisition also expanded Woodmere’s outdoor grounds to 10 acres, adding sculptures, gardens, and public green spaces that reinforce the museum’s mission.
 Renamed in honor of artist and benefactor Frances M. Maguire, the building now serves as a vibrant cultural anchor, giving the historic architecture a renewed purpose while safeguarding it for future generations.
 Tags: Chestnut Hill North Broad Street Places Saved Wanamaker's 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: From Grape Cultivation to Gentrification: Three Centuries of Change in Francisville
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
To walk the streets of Francisville for the first time is to invite disorientation. Tilted at a diagonal from Philadelphia’s otherwise neat and tidy north-south grid, it’s easy to get lost among its small side streets and alleyways. The wanderer emerges, with seemingly even odds, among the pristine red brick facades of Fairmount or faded urban grandeur at Ridge and Girard Avenues.
 This all made sense in the 18th century when Francisville first emerged as a vineyard-turned-community a few miles outside of Philadelphia, oriented toward the only major thoroughfare passing by–Wissahickon Road, now Ridge Avenue. Yet, it’s now undergoing another major transformation: gentrification that has transformed the neighborhood over the past 15 years, driven largely by its location at the border of Center City and North Philadelphia.
 New construction encroaching upon existing homes is a running theme in Francisville. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 A Wednesday night last August saw the writing of another chapter in Francisville’s twisty-turny history. Packed into a recreation building at the Francisville Community Playground–a central hub–a few dozen neighbors new and old utilized their latest opportunity to voice their dissatisfaction to a developer who had come to seek their blessing on a zoning exemption. Like the scores of new condos and apartments built nearby in recent years, this one wanted to go big: eight apartment units over four floors–50-plus feet tall with the roof deck pilot house–on a plot that last held a single-story Baptist church. “It’s out of character,” the captain of an adjacent block briskly concluded. “I’ve talked to the surrounding neighbors. I haven’t had anybody voice support for this.”
 As the name of their RCO suggests, members of the United Francisville Civic Association indeed banded together, ultimately voting 2 to 22 against the variance request. But make no mistake. It’s not all kumbaya in a neighborhood where Black families who came north and established new lives during the Great Migration have found themselves increasingly uprooted. Seated on a bench at the same Francisville park a week earlier, two members of the Morocco’s, a 20th-century street gang turned benevolent organization, struggled to juggle a desire to accept change and welcome newer residents, with the loss of the community they came up in. “The plan is, how can we work together? We want good for the neighborhood, just like they of course want good,” Salam Glass, a long-time Morocco member, said. “They may have more invested in the banks, but we also feel like we put our lives in here, you know? So we also have a vested interest.”
 Penn’s Playground 
 Today, the adjacent neighborhoods of Fairmount and Francisville are densely packed with visual landmarks and well-known roadways–the Philadelphia Museum of Art, Eastern State Penitentiary, Girard College, Fairmount Avenue. However, only one predates European colonization: Ridge Avenue. Originally a Native American footpath by the name “Manatawney,” according to a history of the area assembled by the University of Pennsylvania’s Historic Preservation graduate program in 1996, European immigrants would later give it the names Plymouth Road (or Great Road to Plymouth), Wissahickon Road, Ridge Road, and finally Ridge Avenue.
 "Ridge does not even follow a straight line,” the report noted. “It meanders a bit, deviating [with] a sequence of dips and jogs reflecting elements of terrain that are invisible to us today, but were certainly evident to those who traversed its course through empty countryside on foot.” Perhaps none more famous than William Penn, who eyed the rural expanse between the Schuylkill River and Ridge Avenue as an ideal location for a countryside estate–Springettsbury. Among numerous pursuits at the estate, Penn sought to cultivate grapes and commercially produce wine, going so far as to hire French Huguenot refugee Andre Doz to layout vineyards on 200 acres, about a fifth of the property’s land, according to a history compiled by the National Gallery of Art. “Wine production proved unsuccessful and, just prior to his death in 1718, Penn gave a large tract of Springettsbury land that included Vineyard Hill to Jonathan Dickinson,” the history notes, adding that further subdivisions resulted in the creation of several families’ countryside manors.
 Plan of the city of Philadelphia and its environs , 1796, by surveyor John Hills. | Image courtesy of Boston Public Library
 Where exactly the modern day Francisville–about 130-acres bounded by Broad Street and Corinthian, Girard, and Fairmount Avenues–fits in is unclear. Records reflect that Vineyard Hill was located along the Schuylkill River and became modern day Lemon Hill. Dickinson later appears to have passed the land of modern day Francisville to his grandchildren, who had the last name Jones.
 According to a family history compiled by “Joshua Francis Fisher” in 1864, the Francises took over from there. A letter from July 9, 1768 written by “Tench Francis” details the final purchase of a “vineyard” from the Jones family, on which he established an estate. Tench Francis (1730-1800) had been an “agent for the Penn family” and cashier at the Bank of North America, whose father had served as Attorney General of the colony of Pennsylvania.
 After Tench Francis’ death, the estate was “divided into the sites of ‘Francisville,’” the family’s history maintains. Indeed, an 1800 newspaper ad describes the sale of two subdivided lots on a “tract commonly called the Vineyard,” along Ridge Avenue. Another 1805 newspaper ad by “T.W. Francis” also lists for sale 68 acres of a “vineyard estate” at the location of present day Francisville, while an 1808 map depicts much of the modern day, diagonally-aligned street grid coming into form beside an area marked “vineyard.” By the 1820s, records formally began to refer to the area as “Francisville,” and several of the listed street names, including Francis and Vineyard, remain today.
 Entangled Into Philadelphia 
 By the mid-1800s, Philadelphia’s urban core was expanding northwest toward Francisville. The report complied by Penn's historic preservation department notes the initial arrival of institutions such as Eastern State Penitentiary (1829), Girard College (1838) and a House of Refuge near present day and 15th Street and Fairmount Avenue.
 Yet, one curiosity remained: an 1834 map showed that some 30 years after Francisville’s streets were laid out, there was still no artistic shading that would typically represent the presence of buildings. That “may provide a shred of evidence,” the Penn history report notes, to support a belief among some that Francisville began as a Black neighborhood in a pre-Civil War America.
 “If so, it is conceivable that a mapmaker might not have considered it worthy of full documentation,” it concludes, adding that citywide population figures and abolition meetings held in the area might lend additional credence to the idea.
 Francisville is full of 19th century architectural gems, including a block of Queen Anne rowhouses (1886) at 1631, 1633, and 1635 Francis Street and the American Trust, Loan, and Guaranteed Investment Company (1890) at 684-86 N. Broad Street. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 However, the somewhat enigmatic early decades of Francisville would soon end. By the mid-1850s, maps depict the neighborhood as heavily developed. After the city-county consolidation act of 1854 arrived modern amenities such as a water reservoir, hospital, and streetcars, including along Ridge Avenue, promoting even greater density. By the 1870s, maps depict Francisville as mostly built out and surrounded by the encroaching grid of the city.
 The turn of the 20th century brought further advancements: numerous churches of the Episcopalian, Moravian, Presbyterian, and Lutheran faiths, as well as the Metropolitan Opera House (now The Met) in 1908. Later arrived architect Irwin T. Catharine’s Lydia Darrah School (1927) and the clearing of land for the present day Francisville playground by the early 1920s.
 Another period of change was just around the corner.
 Black Arrival, White Flight 
 In a 2018 documentary, Out of the Way – The Gentrification of Francisville , an 83-year-old Black woman named Ruby Sanders told the story of moving to the Philadelphia neighborhood in the 1960s after her husband fell into sharecropping debt in their native South Carolina. The couple bounced around in small apartments with their eight children before her husband was able to establish himself in the trades and purchase a house on Parrish Street.
 “That was my happy day. My children were so happy. They came, they ran all upstairs, downstairs: what room they gone sleep in, who’s gone sleep in this room,” Sanders said. “The people was nice, the neighbors was nice, it was beautiful. I didn’t want to leave my house after I’ve been there for 50-some years.”
 Today, gentrification has become a fact of life in Francisville, where generations of Black families find themselves pushed out of the neighborhood by swiftly-escalating development trends in the past 15 years. Notwithstanding the possible existence of 19th-century Black communities in the area, J.M. Brewer’s infamous “red line” map of Philadelphia from 1934 shows that certainly by then, Black residents had populated the western, southern, and eastern edges of Francisville along streets such as Uber, Oliver, and 15th Streets. By then a divide between Black residents in Francisville and white residents in Fairmount had already developed, with Corinthian Street marking its threshold, as remains the case today.
 Yet, for a time coinciding with Sanders’ arrival, Francisville proved a thriving Black community. The 1996 Penn report notes that Ridge Avenue became a “vital main drag” by the 1950s, with “commercial needs well attended,” leaving little reason for residents to leave the neighborhood. “There was stores all up Ridge Avenue. We didn’t have to go into town for nothing,” Sanders said in the 2018 documentary. “Clothes stores, food stores, farmer’s market. We had all that on the avenue.”
 Girard Avenue and Ginnodo Street. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 What happened next is open to interpretation. The Penn report traces the neighborhood’s decline to 1960 era riots (presumably the 1964 Columbia Avenue race riot ), which paired with looting along Ridge Avenue, “frightened many of the businesses away.” Combined with factors such as a loss of manufacturing jobs, banks’ persistent refusal to lend money for mortgages and improvements, and the deaths of long-term homeowners, the report notes Francisville lost half its population from the 1950s to the 1990s.
 Yet, residents interviewed for the recent documentary offer a different take and one that begins with white residents fleeing the neighborhood upon the arrival of Black families from the south. Even still, some recall Francisville as a “close knit community” of families into the 1980s that was a “great place to grow up.” Then came the arrival of the crack cocaine epidemic and the federal war on drugs, which destroyed families through the downward spiral of addiction and mass incarceration. “Once the crack era came it just seemed like overnight it swept this whole neighborhood up,” one of Sanders’ grandsons recalled in the documentary.
 Salam Glass and Bo Morocco, two members of the Morocco’s, recall a similar history . They said their organization was created as a gang in the 1940s by a man named Bunky Henshaw. For the most part, they explained, the Morocco’s were there to provide neighborhood protection, especially against encroachment from neighboring gangs. For its members, the gang provided a certain measure of organization, accountability, and even mentorship. “Being a gang member wasn’t just being… you know, when you say ganging, you get this negative effect,” Morocco said. “But being a gang member from down here, you learn some things about being a man. You learn some things about the world. Being a part of something that was, before we knew about God, the biggest thing we knew.”
 Cambridge Street and Ridge Avenue. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 To be sure, benevolence came later. Glass and Morocco said the gang life in Francisville grew increasingly violent over time, with disputes escalating from fist fights, to knives, to guns, especially during the “drug era.” They said Francisville’s diagonal orientation gave the Morocco’s a distinct home turf advantage: “The neighborhood’s got a lot of little twists and turns. You almost get trapped,” Glass explained. Added Morocco with a smile: “Once you come in, you can’t get out.”
 Eventually, the violence of gang life gave way to something else. Many of the Morocco’s found religion–some Islam like Glass and others Christianity like Morocco. “When I go to mosque, I see the brothers that I used to fight,” said Glass.
 The Morocco’s also became a Registered Community Organization with the city, replete with a board of directors and women’s group, holding social events and providing community and educational services like field trips to the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, D.C. “It’s kind of like, that era we came to terms with,” Glass said. “But this new era is something we don’t have any control over.”
 Harvesting the Fruit 
 Exactly how and why new development arrived in Francisville shifts with individual perspective, but there’s no doubt the neighborhood has rapidly transformed. Between 2010 and 2020, Census data show, three Census tracts that include areas of Francisville saw population increases of 32, 42, and 81 percent. To walk down a given street is to see it happening in real time: the neighborhood continues to see a proliferation of new construction, including apartments, condos, and other multi-unit properties, along with large new townhomes.
 Long-time residents say the increase in property taxes and other living costs have led many to leave, while policing tactics like “no loitering” enforcement have also changed the community character of the past. Many take offense that long-term residents who suffered the ups and downs of the neighborhood, but ultimately cared for it now feel they’re being pushed out. “Gentrification is coming hard, and we can see it right before our eyes,” another of Sanders’ grandsons remarked in the 2018 Francisville documentary. “It’s just bad that people you came up with, for years and years and years, you just see somebody take they house, for small amounts of money. And these people sell it for triple the price.”
 Francisville also holds a place in the hearts of members of other communities that often find a home in struggling neighborhoods. Ask Nicely, a 61-year-old trans person with they/them pronouns, points in particular to Gilbert’s Shoes, an aging two-story storefront with signage from Ridge Avenue’s heyday, now sandwiched between two large multi-unit buildings on the avenue near Poplar Street. Nicely chooses their words carefully about all that went on in the space, but describes it as a sort of DIY, “anarchist, lefty, something.” People lived in the building, including Nicely, for short stints of time in between other chapters of life, they said. Traveling musicians would crash there, a dance troupe practiced downstairs, there was hip hop presence–and Nicely heard it all through thin plywood construction when living there. “The upstairs was like a stock area. It’s a big huge space up above. And below was a shoe store, or what was a shoe store, and that front space became like an activist center for community members,” they said. “Intense work went in there, not just to resurrect the building, but also dealing with the functions and dynamics of a changing Francisville.”
 Still, some are trying to find a way to make it work. Amanda Garlen, a Penn grad and professional social worker, moved to the neighborhood years ago and is now president of the United Francisville RCO, which was founded in 2018. She believes media coverage from the same year that portrayed the group as feuding with an existing organization, the Francisville Neighborhood Development Corporation, went too far in depicting the level of strife over the neighborhood’s direction.
 The 1600 block of Ridge Avenue is a canyon of new condominiums with the exception of little holdouts like Gilbert's Shoes. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Glass and Morocco refer to United Francisville as the “new people’s” organization and say it indeed seems to be “dominating” the dynamics at present. However, they also said there is only “minor tension” in the neighborhood and reiterated they see it as a goal to work together.
 At the recent meeting of United Francisville, Garlen pointed out the organization’s members and board are also composed of a diverse mix of newer and older residents. They largely banded together to oppose the latest large multi-unit proposal. Yet, a fundamental difference of perspectives did emerge when a developer presented his plans to build affordable housing units on multiple lots in Francisville as part of Mayor Cherelle Parker’s H.O.M.E. housing plan.
 The developer, Darren Coleman of the Prime Corporation, checked a lot of the boxes for the program: a Black business owner who would build modest rowhouses matching the height of existing residences. The City would also provide large downpayment assistance for the homes, which Coleman’s firm says will cost below $300,000. City workers are to get first dibs, and purchasers can’t make more than 100 percent of area median income ($120,000 for a family of four) and also can’t rent out the property for 15 years.
 Many of the RCO members welcomed the developer’s focus on affordability, as well as its blueprints depicting homes akin to what presently exists. But Kendall Reese, a long-term resident of Francisville now in his 50s and vice president of United Francisville, lamented what he called a new definition of affordable housing: one that has moved from serving the most vulnerable of community members to those with means and incomes that historically have been defined as middle class. That still leaves the question of who’s there to help what’s left of the neighborhood’s long-term, most vulnerable residents. “It started at one space, and now they moved the goal,” Reese said, while adding that he felt the City was shutting out less-established building trade professionals from participating in development. “I don’t want people to be misled and think this is great for everybody. It’s not great for everybody.”
 Tags: Development Francisville gentrification North Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Court OKs Demolition of Boxwood, but Preservationists Vow to Fight On
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
In the fight to save Boxwood, a large, late-19th century home at 156 W. Schoolhouse Lane, preservation advocates are down to Plan C. Or is it Plan D? Maybe E? Whichever it is, there are still plenty of letters left in the alphabet, said Irwin Trauss, a longtime near-neighbor of the home and member of the Penn Knox Neighborhood Association, a local RCO that supports the building’s preservation. 
 That might be reassuring words to some, as it sure looks like the advocates are losing the fight. As previously reported by Hidden City , Boxwood has been under immediate threat of demolition since December 2023, when the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved a request from property owner Pennsylvania School for the Deaf (PSD) to raze the structure, citing financial hardship, despite the building’s listing on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. 
 Since then, advocates have struck out on appeal. First, the City’s Board of License and Inspection Review (BLIR) ruled against an appeal filed by a neighbor after a July 2024 hearing. Penn Knox then appealed the BLIR decision to the Court of Common Pleas, a state court. But in September 2025, Judge Christopher R. Hall ruled against Penn Knox, leading the Historical Commission to spike the proverbial football in its meeting minutes the following month: “In its opinion, the Court offered a stunning rebuke of the appellant’s case,” the report concluded. 
 The Pennsylvania School for the Deaf was granted approval to demolish Boxwood, a 129-year-old home listed for legal protections on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. Near neighbors and members of the Penn Knox Neighborhood Association remain vigilant in their fight to save the building. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Indeed, Judge Hall was rather unequivocal in his 16-page ruling, calling Boxwood a “low-value historic building,” dismissing Penn Knox’s legal arguments and ultimately opining that “the demolition permit would allow PSD to proceed with a plan to make its campus safer and more effective for the hearing-impaired community.” 
 Yet, Trauss said his group has since appealed the decision to Pennsylvania Commonwealth Court, the next rung up the legal ladder and one below the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania. As of March 2026, not much has happened, with the appeal still in a pre-trial stage at Commonwealth Court, and the demolition of Boxwood legally stayed all the while. Lose there, and who knows what comes next, Trauss said, while revealing what he believes is an ace in the hole for those who want to see the building preserved. “To their credit, the order that the Philadelphia Historical Commission entered did not simply permit [PSD] to demo Boxwood,” Trauss says. “It permitted them to demo it conditioned on their getting the necessary zoning, which they probably won’t be able to get without the cooperation of the neighborhood and residents.” 
 Trauss said his group also remains open to a detente with the school and is willing to return to what he says used to be an amicable relationship. Preservationists would help the school come up with an alternative plan that works for both parties, he added. Whether the PSD shares that instinct in any way appears doubtful. Matthew McClure, an attorney with law firm Ballard Spahr that is representing the PSD, wrote in an email that the Court of Common Pleas ruling “speaks for itself.” “We don’t comment on pending litigation,” he added and did not respond to a followup email asking to confirm the PSD personnel were indeed not willing to comment. 
 Thinking Outside the Box 
 A photograph from 1890 taken during the wedding of Mary West Huston and Robert Bowne Haines, Jr. | Image courtesy of Penn Knox Neighborhood Association via Wyck Papers, American Philosophical Society
 Built 1898 as the residence for a well-to-do family, Boxwood is a “handsome” example of Colonial Revival architecture popular during that latter part of the Gilded Age, according to a 2019 historical nomination authored by Germantown-based architectural historian Oscar Beisert. 
 Beisert believes the building historically significant for its distinguished architectural style and design by notable architect Mantle Fielding, Jr.. In 2021, the Historical Commission agreed, adding Boxwood to the Philadelphia Register, while also concluding the residence is “associated with an event of importance to the history of the City, Commonwealth or Nation,” could yield important information or artifacts yet discovered, and “exemplifies the cultural, political, economic, social or historical heritage of the community,” all official criteria for a building being listed on the registry and obtaining protection from demolition. 
 Boxwood was built for a wealthy couple married in 1890: Mary West Huston, a Coatesville native and heiress of the Lukens Steel Company, and Robert Bowne Haines, Jr., a Cheltenham native and industrialist with at least one patent to his name. By 1897, the couple had contracted Fielding to build their new residence. The architect quickly came up with a design that “would ultimately pay homage to the past,” while also including new modern amenities, “such as a low pressure steam heating plant,” Beisert’s nomination states. 
 Constructed largely from local Wissahickon schist, the two-and-a-half-story Boxwood features doric columns supporting a pair of porches, decorative windows including still-working wooden shutters, and a gambrel roof whose uncommon design features add an “almost oriental touch,” Beisert observed in the nomination. He added the style matches those of the existing tastes of other wealthy Germantowners of the time. 
 A letter dated December 1897 from architect Mantle Fielding to Robert and Mary Haines confirming that construction plans for the home were underway. | Image courtesy of Penn Knox Neighborhood Association via Wyck Papers, American Philosophical Society
 “Unlike the Moorish, Queen Ann, and other revivalist styles of the mid-to-late 19th century, the Colonial Revival represented a ‘return’ to chaste and tasteful, softening of more flamboyant motifs and styles associated with the 19th century,” Beisert wrote. “While the 20th century would see a hardened and more respectful interpretation of the style, important architects like Mantle Fielding bridged the gap between the old and the new in the ‘Colonial’ style.” 
 Fielding was the architect of several other notable properties in Northwest Philadelphia, including a gymnasium built on the adjacent campus of Germantown Academy, also in the Colonial Revival style. Time, of course, would alter the local dynamics. Thomas Haines died in 1932 and Mary in 1946, at which point Boxwood passed to their heirs, and ultimately out of the family altogether in 1968. Germantown Academy, founded at the site in the 1760s, had decamped for its current location in Fort Washington three years earlier. 
 Trauss said the campus then passed through several other educational tenants until they all left, leaving the property vacant and in hands of the Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority. Penn Knox then played an active role in recruiting the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf to the campus in the 1980s after they announced sale of their former location in Mt. Airy. Trauss said neighbors and the school then maintained a good relationship for several decades, as PSD did a “wonderful job” restoring old buildings, designing new ones, and preserving open space and community access. 
 Meanwhile, by the 1990s, Boxwood was being used by an organization called the Men’s Induction Center, which a Philadelphia Inquirer article from the era identified as a nonprofit housing 24 men at the location, where they received drug counseling, education, and spiritual guidance. In the 2000s, a related organization called the Teen Challenge Training Center owned and operated the building. Property records show that organization then sold Boxwood to PSD in July 2019 for $515,000. Trauss noted that sale occurred after the initial historical nomination of the building in January of that year. 
 Boxwood in 1963. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 The nomination was approved by the Historical Commission in March 2021. Less than two years later, PSD went before the Commission to successfully argue for a hardship exemption to demolish the building. School leadership at the time said they had created a new master plan for the campus and needed to destroy the building to reconfigure vehicular and pedestrian traffic, using the Boxwood footprint for parking in order to clear up space elsewhere on campus. Leadership also told the Commission that the school was running a deficit and estimated it would require $3.5 million to restore Boxwood to a productive use. 
 The Historical Commission appeared to agree, with staff alleging that its own leadership had inspected the building and concluded it was in poor condition and would need a full rehab, including all new mechanicals. PSD also insisted that the building was not ADA compliant and was ill-suited for use by deaf students. 
 All of these arguments have and continue to be dismissed by Trauss and allies as reasons to tear the building down. He believes PSD is simply taking the easiest way out, when neighbors continue to believe viable alternatives exist and are prepared to help financially “invest” in other outcomes, including converting the building back to a financially-sustainable residential use. 
 As the court case progresses, he argued, it’s not just the future of Boxwood at stake, but the City’s increasingly-imperiled historic preservation ordinance. That’s because, according to Trauss, the school was not required to try and sell the property before seeking a demolition permit. “One of the main issues of the case is a reading of the ordinance and regulation about, what is the obligation of a nonprofit to show, if they want a hardship demolition permit?” Trauss explained. “What the Commission held is that a nonprofit only needs to show that they can’t use the property. If that ruling is left to stand, it would completely undermine the preservation ordinance when a property is owned by a nonprofit.” 
 Tags: demolition Germantown Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Historic Church In Chestnut Hill Struggles for Elbow Room
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
The First Baptist Church of Chestnut Hill sits at the "top of the hill," where Germantown Avenue intersects Bethlehem Pike, both former Lenape trails. When the church was built in 1835, worshipers were baptized in Wissahickon Creek and attended services barefoot. Livestock was driven down the avenue. For the last five years, this landmark church has been under attack from by-right development on both sides, in spite of strong community advocacy.
 In 2021, when Frankle Enterprises first proposed replacing the vacant Sunoco gas station lot at 10 Bethlehem Pike next to the church with a five-story, 33-unit, mixed-use apartment complex, residents of Philly's highest income zip code took notice. This was not the first by-right construction site to rattle Limoges tea cups in Chestnut Hill. Back in 2011, Bowman Properties bulldozed a one-story Ford showroom at 8208 Germantown Avenue and replaced it with a six-story luxury condo featuring a Fresh Market on the ground floor. Before the foundation was laid, a group known as the Adjacent Neighbors Association entered into a prolonged battle with Bowman challenging zoning legislation, which was ultimately denied by the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas.
 New construction encroaches upon First Baptist Church of Chestnut Hill. | Photo: Stacia Friedman
 That was just a vacant auto showroom. This is an historic church with a graveyard containing the remains of a soldier who died at the Battle of Gettysburg. The Chestnut Hill Community Association met with Frankle to express their concerns: increased traffic, nearby properties would be deprived of sunlight, adverse impacts on water, sewage, and storm water runoff, and new construction that is out of character for a historic neighborhood. While the developer was unmoved, the Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas found that the City had “violated multiple Philadelphia Zoning Code provisions” and ruled in favor of the community association. Or so they thought. Frankle appealed, and in 2024, the Pennsylvania Supreme Court turned that ruling over in the developer's favor.
 Meanwhile, in 2022, Young Capital announced plans to demolished the one-story Santander Bank and Palladio Custom Frame Shop on the other side of the church and replace it with a four-story, 44,000 square foot mixed-use apartment building at 8623 Germantown Avenue. The $5.9 million development opened in February 2026 with its first commercial tenant, Citizens Bank, on the ground floor. The architectural rendering created the illusion of more space between the church and the new building than actually exists. If you live in 8623 Germantown Avenue, you can basically sing in the church choir from your balcony. However, the developer left enough space on the side adjacent to a boutique to create an attractive covered walkway leading to the residents' entrance. Bottom line? This massive brick, modern industrial design building that would be welcomed in Manayunk or Kensington is getting the cold shoulder in Chestnut Hill.
 "It hurts to see character and scale trounced by profit with no regard for history, context, or human scale," said retired interior designer Katherine Converse. "I first moved to Chestnut Hill in 1968. What is happening now, on either side of First Baptist Church, breaks my heart." Converse places the blame on by right zoning.
 First Baptist Church of Chestnut Hill in 1997. | Photo courtesy of Chestnut Hill Conservancy
 Retired architect James Rice, a 33-year resident of Chestnut Hill and current board member of the Chestnut Hill Conservancy, is also concerned. "I know it would be very difficult to create a zoning code that takes every urban wrinkle into account in a city of this size and age, but there must be some way to account for proximity to genuinely historic structures like the Baptist church."
 "I am not anti-development," stated Rice. "I think that thoughtful engagement with developers to guide project designs to an outcome that is mutually beneficial is a critical service the Chestnut Hill Conservancy and other community association committees can provide. I hope I am not being naive to believe that this process can engage by-right developers as well as those that require a variance." Rice, who was involved in the Community Association’s Land Use Planning and Zoning Committee from the early 1990s to 2004, fully supports the creation of historic districts. "I believe that any limitations that it may impose are well worth the controls that keep Chestnut Hill looking like Chestnut Hill. Isn’t that what attracted us all here to begin with?"
 New construction viewed from Germantown Avenue. | Photo: Stacia Friedman
 At a time when by-right development is turning into a game of whack-a-mole, creating historic districts has taken on new urgency. Lori Salganicoff, the former executive director of the Chestnut Hill Conservancy, noted in 2017 that more than 1,000 new buildings could be built in Chestnut Hill without community review. David Guest, the current executive director of the Conservancy, agrees. "As part of our 2025-2030 Strategic Plan, in 2026, we will explore options for protecting historic resources in Chestnut Hill through a community engagement process," said Guest. "Historic districts, administered by the Philadelphia Historical Commission, are one potential tool to achieve this goal. Other options include Neighborhood Conservation Overlays administered by the Philadelphia City Planning Commission, Preservation and Conservation Easements administered by the Chestnut Hill Conservancy, and alternate forms of historic districts, including tiered or flexible, as well as other zoning-related interventions."
 Given its history and architectural credentials, including Louis Khan, Oskar Stonorov, and Robert Venturi, along with Gilded Age mansions, a French Village , and Queen Anne Victorians, there is much to protect in Chestnut Hill.
 Tags: Chestnut Hill historic churches new construction 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: How World Fairs Changed the Face of Philadelphia: the 1876 Centennial
author: Thomas H. Keels
bodyText:
International expositions, at least the traditional ones fondly remembered by American baby boomers, and still staged in locales like Osaka and Dubai, are conundrums. They are supposed to be magnificent and visionary, yet by their very nature must be ephemeral and temporary.
 Composed of the flimsiest materials, world’s fair architecture must convey the public image of an industry, city, state, or country to tens of millions of visitors. Then, after six months, it all gets demolished, except for a few survivors designed to enhance the local environment permanently. Today, such diverse structures as the Eiffel Tower in Paris, the San Francisco Palace of Fine Arts, and the Seattle Space Needle owe their existence to a world’s fair.
 International expositions often left their most durable impressions beyond the fairground gates. Just as they do today for the Olympic Games, host cities lavished millions of dollars to upgrade their infrastructures to accommodate millions of visitors. Broad swaths of fallow land or swamp on their outskirts were developed and woven into the urban grid. The current-day layout and transportation networks of cities like Paris, London, Vienna, New York, and Chicago were shaped by the fairs they once hosted.
 A lithograph advertising the Centennial International Exhibition of 1876. | Image courtesy of Huntington Digital Library
 The planning and creation of international expositions seem to fall into four distinct stages:
 1. The Grand Vision: This Will Be the Greatest Fair Ever!
 2. Okay, Let’s Get Real: We Double-Checked the Budget.
 3. The Legacy: What Remains after Closing Day.
 4. Outside the Fairgrounds: Changes to the Surrounding City.
 Philadelphia’s three world’s fairs–the wildly successful 1876 Centennial, the wildly unsuccessful 1926 Sesquicentennial, and the abortive 1976 Bicentennial–all followed this pattern. Regardless of their divergent outcomes, all left indelible marks upon the City of Brotherly Love. This is the first installment of a three-part series.
 PART I: 1876 and the Centennial 
 The original design for Memorial Hall at the 1876 Centennial, drafted by Collins & Autenrieth in 1874. The grandeur of this structure was exceeded only by its price tag. | Image: Collection of Thomas Keels
 In 1876, Philadelphia created an exposition that set the standard for modern world’s fairs. The Centennial, or the “International Exhibition of Arts, Manufactures, and Products of the Soil and Mine,” to use its full title, was a celebration of the 100 anniversary of the adoption of the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. While New York had hosted an Exhibition of the Industry of All Nations in 1853, the Centennial was the first official world’s fair in the United States, sanctioned by Congress through the creation of the United States Centennial Commission on March 3, 1871.
 Despite its stellar reputation, the Centennial got off to a shaky start. In 1873, the U.S. Centennial Commission announced an architectural competition for the main building in West Fairmount Park. Originally, the commissioners intended to house most of the exposition in one vast edifice. This not only followed the example of the Crystal Palace at the 1851 London Great Exhibition, but also the interconnected complex that housed the Great Sanitary Fair, held on Logan Square in 1864. Most of this primary structure was to be temporary, while the core would remain as an art gallery called Memorial Hall.
 Over 40 architectural designs were submitted. The winner was the Philadelphia firm of Collins & Autenrieth, who crafted an elaborate Venetian Renaissance cathedral framed by vast temporary wings. The permanent core boasted a central dome 390 feet tall (100 feet higher than the U.S. Capitol), topped by a statue of Liberty. Unfortunately, the Centennial Commission realized after it had awarded the $20,000 first prize that this design would cost $8 to $10 million, more than the budget for the entire Centennial. When asked to revise their design to cost $2 million, Collins & Autenrieth withdrew.
 Forced to economize, the Centennial Commission abandoned the single structure concept. They opted to build several large, utilitarian halls, interspersed with dozens of smaller pavilions. An ornate Gallery of Art would remain as a permanent memento of the fair. This was similar to the layout pioneered at the 1873 Vienna Weltausstellung, which the Centennial directors studied closely.
 The Main Building (also called the Main Exhibition Hall) at the 1876 Centennial, designed by Joseph Wilson and Henry Pettit. | Image courtesy of Prints and Photographs, Library of Congress
 In 1874, the Commission approved the design of Exposition engineers Joseph Wilson and Henry Pettit for the Main Building. Both men had started their careers with the Pennsylvania Railroad, and their design resembled the vast rail terminals springing up across America. The 20-acre pavilion was constructed of cast-iron columns with brick and topped by a glass-and-iron frame. A great square lantern soared upward from the building’s midsection, creating a cavernous central court where concerts were held. The rectangular structure measured 464 feet wide and 1,880 feet long.
 The simple design cost only $73,000 per acre, coming in below budget at $1.4 million. Yet, it provided ample space for 13,720 exhibitors from nearly 40 countries to display their manufactures. Utilitarian and economical, the Main Building was elegant enough to inspire poet Walt Whitman to admire “the grand high roof with its graceful and multitudinous work of iron rods, angles, gray colors, plays of light and shade, receding into dim outlines."
 Wilson and Pettit also designed Machinery Hall, which held the fruits of the Industrial Revolution, from the 700-ton Corliss Duplex Engine that powered all the machines in the 13-acre hall to a seemingly insignificant gadget called a telephone. Similar in design to the Main Building, the 14-acre structure also came in below budget at $542,306.
 Hermann J. Schwarzmann’s Memorial Hall (Art Gallery), the first American art museum in the Beaux-Arts, would later serve as the model for numerous European structures including the Reichstag in Berlin. The building survives today as the Please Touch Museum. | Images courtesy of Prints and Photographs, Library of Congress
 Memorial Hall, the permanent art gallery, was designed by Hermann J. Schwarzmann, chief engineer of the Exposition. Schwarzmann’s elaborate structure has been called the first American art museum in the Beaux-Arts or “modern Renaissance” style. At $1.6 million, the roughly 100,000-square-foot building cost more than the 20-acre Main Building. The heart of Memorial Hall was its soaring Great Hall, surmounted by a glass-and-iron double dome topped by a statue of Columbia. A separate Art Annex and Photographic Hall were constructed to handle more than 5,000 works of art submitted by exhibitors.
 James H. Windrim’s 10-acre Agricultural Hall looked like a gigantic barn crossed with a Gothic cathedral. Its presence was a strong reminder of the importance of agriculture in a country where half of all Americans lived on farms. Costing a mere $260,045, the wood-frame hall was the cheapest of the Centennial’s five main structures. An additional 22 acres was allotted for livestock exhibitions. These were located 500 yards from Agricultural Hall for “sanitary considerations.”
 Horticultural Hall was the smallest of the five main structures (383 feet long by 170 feet wide). Designed by Schwartzmann in the Moorish style, the world’s largest conservatory was also destined to be a permanent adornment to Fairmount Park. The structure’s brightly colored exterior was studded with minarets, cast-iron crests, and flagpoles. The central conservatory on the ground floor was topped by a rectangular glass lantern with multi-colored panes which cast a rainbow on the vegetation below. Outside, visitors could explore 35 acres of landscaped gardens. Costing $264,000, Horticultural Hall was $65,000 over budget, but its cost overrun was covered by the savings from Machinery Hall.
 A simplified aerial view of the Centennial fairgrounds, showing only such primary structures as (from top center, clockwise): Agricultural Hall, Horticultural Hall, Memorial Hall (the Art Gallery), Main Building, Judges’ Hall, Machinery Hall, the U.S. Government Building, and the Ladies Pavilion. | Images courtesy of Prints and Photographs, Library of Congress
 These five main pavilions were complemented by roughly 250 smaller structures spread out across nearly three hundred acres. These included a federal pavilion, a woman’s pavilion, 24 state houses, 15 foreign pavilions, fire, police, and medical stations, and seven public comfort stations.
 Inadequate transportation was a contributing factor to the failure of the 1873 Vienna fair. In Philadelphia, a coordinated system of trains, trolleys, and steamboats conveyed visitors. The Pennsylvania Railroad ran excursion trains every half hour from Baltimore, New York, and Pittsburgh and built a loop train to deposit visitors at the fairground entrance. Philadelphia’s network of horse-drawn trolleys, already extensive, was expanded so that by 1876 the city possessed the largest street railway system in America. Once inside the grounds, visitors could pay five cents to ride the West-End Narrow Gauge Railway which traversed the fairgrounds. The more adventurous could board the Saddleback Railroad, a primitive monorail between Agricultural Hall and Horticultural Hall.
 Many fairgoers traveled to the Centennial via the second Girard Avenue Bridge, completed in 1874 by Clark, Reeves & Company at a cost of over $1 million. The five-span, iron-truss structure was believed to be the largest high bridge in America and symbolized Philadelphia’s industrial and technological leadership. Mayor William S. Stokley ensured the new span was open in time to accommodate thousands of Centennial visitors. Stokley also sought to beautify the exhibition district by ordering the demolition of dozens of “shanties” abutting the fairgrounds, summarily evicting their residents.
 Horticultural Hall, designed by Hermann J. Schwarzmann in the Moorish style, was the largest conservatory in the world at the time of the Centennial. | Image courtesy of Prints and Photographs, Library of Congress
 Philadelphia had begun to transform itself far in advance of the Centennial, starting with the new Public Buildings or City Hall, designed to be the world’s tallest building and most magnificent municipal edifice. Ground had been broken for City Hall in August 1871, and its cornerstone laid on July 4, 1874. Yet, little progress had been made on its construction by the opening of the Centennial on May 10, 1876.
 Across from City Hall a one-story structure sprawled across an entire city block, its Moorish decorations reminiscent of Horticultural Hall. This was the Grand Depot, an emporium opened by merchant John Wanamaker (himself a member of the Centennial Board of Finance) shortly before the Centennial opened. Inside, hundreds of concentric counters offered a dazzling variety of merchandise in a prototype of the modern department store. The Grand Depot attracted so many world’s fair visitors that it was called the Centennial Annex. Its success established Wanamaker as one of America’s great retail magnates.
 A trade card showing John Wanamaker’s Grand Depot at Juniper and 13th Streets, known as the “Centennial Annex.” | Image: Collection of Thomas Keels
 Philadelphia was filled with other new structures that benefitted from the flood of visitors. Many of them were designed by 37-year-old Philadelphia native and Civil War hero Frank Furness. His dazzling new building for the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts opened on April 22 and was thronged with both Philadelphians and tourists throughout the year. The rapturous reception accorded the Academy’s new home came close upon the architect’s recent triumphs with the Guarantee Trust and Safe Deposit Company and First City Troop Armory .
 Furness was well represented at the Centennial. His flamboyant pavilion for the Brazilian exhibit (in the inescapable Moorish style) was one of the visual highlights of the Main Building. He also contributed an ornately carved arch to promote Connecticut brownstone, later moved to East Fairmount Park. Finally, his building for the Centennial National Bank, fiscal agent for the exposition, opened at 32nd and Market Streets. Furness’s exuberant, eclectic architecture embodied the self-confidence and optimism that enveloped Philadelphia during the Centennial.
 The Brazilian pavilion in the Main Building, designed by Philadelphia architect Frank Furness in the popular “Mauresque” or Moorish style. | Photo courtesy of the Free Library of Philadelphia
 Visitors flocked to historic shrines as well as new landmarks. The Committee on the Restoration of Independence Hall had spent three years refurbishing the venerable, but neglected building. The Assembly Room, where the Declaration of Independence had been signed, became a “National Museum,” featuring the Rising Sun Chair used by George Washington during the Constitutional Convention. A new Centennial Bell pealed from the cupola. In a major coup, the committee persuaded Washington to lend Philadelphia the original Declaration of Independence to display at Independence Hall.
 The Centennial bolstered the fortunes of the two-year-old Philadelphia Zoological Gardens, the first of its kind in America, which had opened two miles away in 1874. Zoo attendance soared to 680,000 in 1876, a 36 percent increase. One of its visitors was President Ulysses S. Grant. In 1876, the zoo unveiled its new gatehouses, elephant house, and restaurant, all designed by the ubiquitous Frank Furness.
 By the time the Centennial closed on November 10, it had attracted nearly 10 million visitors at a time when the United States had roughly 45 million inhabitants. They marveled at such novelties as the banana, Hires Root Beer, Japanese art, and a metal arm clutching a torch, part of a statue of the Goddess of Liberty the French hoped to erect in New York harbor. It even looked like the Centennial would turn a profit until its managers were forced to repay a $1.5 million loan to the federal government that they had considered an appropriation.
 The entrance to the Philadelphia Zoological Gardens c. 1876, showing the gatehouses designed by Frank Furness. | Image: Collection of Thomas Keels
 After a failed attempt to repurpose it as a Permanent International Exhibition, the Main Building was demolished in 1881. Agricultural Hall and Machinery Hall were also dismantled during this period, as were most of the other exhibition structures. A few smaller buildings, including the Ohio State House, remained intact in situ. Many other state houses and foreign pavilions were moved elsewhere and repurposed.
 Memorial Hall became home to the Pennsylvania Museum and School of Industrial Art, precursor to the Philadelphia Museum of Art. Horticultural Hall, the second permanent structure, remained as the centerpiece of Fairmount Park. Sadly, the long-neglected conservatory was demolished by the Fairmount Park Commission in 1955 after suffering damage deemed irreparable from Hurricane Hazel the previous year.
 Memorial Hall almost suffered the same fate. After being used as a museum until 1954, the building stood empty while the City debated whether to demolish or preserve it. Luckily, funds were found to maintain the gallery until it was repurposed as a recreation center and offices for the Fairmount Park Commission. Since 2008, a refurbished Memorial Hall has housed the Please Touch Museum, which offers a wonderful Centennial Exploration exhibit in its basement.
 Machinery Hall, the second major exhibition hall at the 1876 Centennial, was designed by Wilson and Pettit. It was demolished in 1881. | Image: Collection of Thomas Keels
 The Centennial spurred the cultivation of West Fairmount Park as one of Philadelphia’s great recreational spaces. After the fair, the Fairmount Park Art Commission (itself a Centennial outgrowth) adorned the park with numerous statues to complement the fair’s Catholic Total Abstinence Fountain. This culminated in the Smith Memorial Arch , the grandiose memorial to Pennsylvania Civil War heroes, erected between 1897 and 1912 on the former site of the Main Building.
 Over time, the great fair (and the transportation network built to support it) promoted the residential development of West Philadelphia beyond the older communities of Spruce Hill and Powelton Village. Once the ramshackle hotels on Elm Avenue across from the Centennial grounds were demolished, they were replaced by more permanent structures. By 1890, Elm Avenue had been renamed Parkside Avenue and was lined with elaborate houses and apartment buildings.
 While not a financial success, the Centennial had a lasting impact on both the United States and Philadelphia. The fair vaulted the United States into the rank of world powers, stunning Europeans with its vision of a country bursting with dynamism and ingenuity. After viewing such wonders as the Edison Quadruplex Telegraph and the Westinghouse air brake, the London Times conceded that “the American invents as the Greek sculpted and the Italian painted; it is genius.”
 A concert in the Music Pavilion of the Main Building, showing displays for Tiffany, Gorham, and other manufacturers of fine goods. | Image: Collection of Thomas Keels
 The Centennial helped restore the confidence of an America traumatized by civil war, the assassination of one president and the impeachment of another, scandal, graft, and economic panic. Inspired by the Centennial, Congress appropriated $200,000 to complete the Washington Monument, which had stood half-built since 1854.
 Finally, the Centennial was a windfall for its host city. Many visitors, expecting to find a sleepy, provincial burg, discovered instead a modern industrial city of the first order. The financial boost provided to local industries by the fair established Philadelphia as the “workshop of the world” for the next half-century. Going forward, the Quaker City would be known as the American epicenter of manufacturing might, organizational capability, and entrepreneurial efficiency. As the Philadelphia Press announced proudly, “The Centennial is to ring the death knell of that non-enterprising, fearing-to-dare spirit which has so long ruled us.”
 Tags: Centennial Exposition Fairmount Park Frank Furness How World's Fairs Changed the Face of Philadelphia Memorial Hall Semiquincentennial 
 About the Author
 Thomas H. Keels is a historian, lecturer, and commentator specializing in the history and architecture of the Philadelphia region. He has written or co-authored seven books, including "Forgotten Philadelphia: Lost Architecture of the Quaker City" and "Sesqui! Greed, Graft, and the Forgotten World's Fair of 1926" both published by Temple University Press. His next book, "Sinners and Scandals of Laurel Hill Cemetery," will be released by The History Press in Autumn 2026.

title: Historic Preservation Advocates Continue to Rally Against Bombshell "Squilla Bill"
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
As visitors descend on Philadelphia this summer to celebrate the nation’s semiquincentennial in a quintessentially American city, preservationists remain on edge over a City Council bill they fear could put historic buildings here at increased risk of demolition.
 The so-called “Squilla Bill,” brought by City Councilmember Mark Squilla, first popped up last fall after a year of adversarial lobbying between historic preservation advocates and a collection of pro-development interests. At stake are potentially some of the most significant changes to the city’s historic preservation ordinance in decades. That includes what advocates continue to fear is a 30-day demolition loophole that would give a property owner a heads up if their building is nominated for historic preservation, thus potentially affording them an opportunity to apply for demolition or alteration permits before protections can go into place.
 Southwestern National Bank (aka Arts Bank) at 601 S. Broad Street was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in May 2025. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Development groups such as the Building Industry Association have called those fears overblown, and Councilmember Squilla also said the bill strikes an appropriate balance and has been modified to address concerns. Still, the bill remains a proverbial football: a Philadelphia Planning Commission hearing originally scheduled for last December was punted until this spring and then never occurred. Instead, a modified version of the bill was placed on the agenda of a City Council Rules committee hearing on June 3. Yet, at the last moment, that too was delayed until the fall.
 All parties say there continues to be dialogue via virtual meetings facilitated by Squilla’s office. However, historic preservation groups say the fundamentals remain the same and that they oppose the bill. As such, their vigil continues. “There have been a few revisions to the bill,” said Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia. “But none of them really resolve the underlying issue, which, if it went into effect, would erode the protections that nominated properties enjoy while they're being considered for designation.”
 Moving Target 
 The latest drama around the Squilla bill took place June 3, when Council’s Rules Committee, chaired by Councilmember Cindy Bass, was to consider the latest draft of the bill, officially registered as Bill No. 251030 . After word of the hearing got out in May, various preservation and civic groups formed social media campaigns to rally opposition. Arielle Harris, an architectural historian and board member of the historic preservation advocacy nonprofit RePoint Philadelphia , said her group started an online petition while also reaching out to RCOs and other sympathetic community organizations. RePoint also began lobbying the offices of the seven City council members who sit on the Rules committee. “All of our meetings were generally very successful,” Harris said. “The staff were all very receptive to our concerns with the bill.”
 The networks of the Preservation Alliance and other historic preservationist groups were also activated. Their efforts may have had the desired effect. On May 28, Councilmember Curtis Jones, a member of the committee, issued a letter announcing his opposition to the bill, stating it “Will open the dangerous door of demolition… [of] swaths of homes, religious institutions, and old factories that make Philadelphia beautiful.”
 At the hearing on June 3, preservation advocates filed into City Hall’s cavernous Room 400, with advocates ready to make their case through public comment and preservation leaders such as Steinke and Harris slated as official panelists. Yet, when the meeting began, they said, Bass announced the bill would be tabled and Squilla delivered brief remarks explaining his decision.
 The banking hall of the former Fidelity-Philadelphia Trust Company Building at 123 S. Broad Street was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in March 2026. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 In an email to Hidden City, Squilla further elaborated. “Members of the committee were receiving last minute questions on the legislation and believed they needed more time to fully understand the changes,” Squilla wrote. “They asked me if I could hold to a future date. I agreed.”
 In addition to Bass, Squilla, and Jones, the other members of the committee are Councilmembers Katherine Gilmore Richardson, Brian J. O’Neill, Isaiah Thomas, and Jamie Gauthier.
 Squilla said the next earliest consideration could have come in July, but that he instead opted to wait until the fall. Advocates believe consideration of the bill will be rescheduled for the committee’s September meeting. Steinke viewed the delay as mostly good news since it kept the bill from advancing. Harris agreed to an extent, but found it frustrating that opponents of the bill had made the time and effort to be there, some taking off work to do so, only to be denied an opportunity to register their discontent at the 11th hour.
 What’s in the Bill? 
 Language for the bill that was to be considered on June 3 is not yet available to the public, but those privy to it say it’s been modified from the version first presented last fall. Most significantly, Steinke said a provision that would remove landscape architecture as a qualifying attribute for historic preservation was jettisoned, a win for advocates. Squilla had previously expressly stated he wasn’t confident of the merits of the measure, which, like the rest of the bill’s text, was generated through workshopping from several City agencies.
 However, the warm and fuzzies stop there. Consternation continues to stem from the 30-day provision, which involved parties said was modified to a degree, but not to an extent that it eliminated opposition. Squilla frames the provision as fair to property owners, as it would for the first time give them knowledge of a pending nomination before Philadelphia Historic Commission staff make an evaluation of its merits. Currently, if staff determine an application warrants nomination and send a recommendation to the Historical Commission, restrictions on demolition and alteration permits immediately go into place and the property owner is then notified.
 Squilla said under his bill, the City’s Department of Licenses and Inspections still cannot issue such permits during the advanced notice period, a moratorium he added after preservationists expressed concern with the earlier version of the bill. “The main purpose of the bill is to provide a more robust notification process for property owners whose properties are being considered for designation and placement on the register of historic properties,” Squilla wrote. “With the proposed changes, there will be a preliminary phase where the property owner is notified and given an opportunity to explain to the Historical Commission why it should not be considered for designation owing to hardship, mistake, or established development plans already in place (e.g., via existing permits) etc.” If the Commission decides hardship does not exist, it can still move forward and place permit restrictions in place, Squilla added.
 The Alfred Edward Burk Mansion at Broad and Jefferson Streets was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in May 2026. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Yet, advocates remain concerned that the bill will give developers new leverage and ultimately result in increased danger of demolition to historic properties. Steinke said unchanged in the bill is language around the consideration of existing “material commitments” at a property, such as engineering workups or permits for alteration. That leaves Steinke worried it could present an opportunity for developers to produce such materials within the notification window, nipping a nomination in the bud before its merits are ever considered and protections put in place. He also worries about holes in the moratorium. “The language is murky and subject to interpretation,” explained Steinke.
 For example, according to Steinke, the City currently defines demolition as removal of at least two-thirds of a structure. Facades are also protected against demolition under current municipal guidelines. However, some buildings have multiple facades, leading Steinke to worry that developers could work to skirt the proposed permit restrictions. He added that the Historic Commission already has the ability to consider hardships when making its final decision on a nomination. “So we don’t even think it’s necessary,” to change the City’s ordinance, Steinke said.
 Harris said RePoint holds similar concerns. Analysis produced by the nonprofit states the Squilla bill will introduce a “new balancing test” that awards historic designation only if the benefits aren’t “outweighed by other policy factors.” They also believe the bill would make it easier for an existing historic property owner to remove designations due to a newly proposed clause prohibiting the Historic Commission from adopting rules that “limit or restrict” rescission.
 What Comes Next? 
 Despite their opposition to the bill, advocates credit Squilla for maintaining open lines of communication: he has held monthly Zoom calls with preservationists, the development community, and other stakeholders all in attendance. Harris was invited to one such meeting held the day before the hearing, and she said Squilla was the only committee member who agreed to a face-to-face meeting with RePoint.
 In April, the City of Philadelphia approved permits to demolish 1523, 1525, and 1527 Cherry Street, a rare block of well-maintained Federal-style rowhouses in the heart of Center City. While the construction dates of 1525 and 1527 are debatable, 1523 Cherry Street, at right, was built in the early 1800s. Given the home's proximity toRace Street Meeting House next door, it is plausible that those fleeing enslavement sought refuge there as part of the Underground Railroad. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Squilla also said he has worked to receive and utilize input from multiple parties. “We met for six months with the Law Department, Historical Commission, Preservation Alliance, BIA, lawyers Matt McClure and Michael Phillips, Planning, and added other preservationists along the way,” Squilla said. “There were many changes to the legislation from recommendations from the meetings.”
 Squilla said his office will “set up additional stakeholder meetings over the summer.”
 Preservation advocates also intend to remain active. “We’re going to continue to engage with Rules committee members,” along with Chris Rabb, the presumptive next congressman for Philadelphia’s 3rd Congressional District, Harris said.
 Tags: demolition Development Mark Squilla Philadelphia City Council Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Graterford Archives Seeks to Unlock Stories of the Incarcerated
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
Graterford State Correctional Institution during construction in 1931. | Photo courtesy of The Library Company of Philadelphia
 Graterford State Correctional Institution's 1981 escape attempt and hostage incident was unremarkable compared to the Attica Prison Revolt and San Quentin Riot in 1971, the Huntsville Prison Hostage Siege of 1974, and the New Mexico State Penitentiary Riot in 1980. As detailed by the report released in 1982 by then Pennsylvania Governor Thormburgh’s seven-member panel, “No lives were lost. No blood was shed. Damage to the institution was minor.”
 The escape attempt and five-day standoff followed two decades of predominantly race-driven frustrations, violence, and overcrowding that flowed from the 1960s into the early 1980s. In each case, the main cause of each standoff highlighted several instances of ignorance of inmates’ requests and comments leading to violence. For its part, SCI-Graterford’s riot laid the pathway to improvements and extensive prison reforms effectively end-capping the era.
 The failed escape attempt, along with interpersonal stories spanning decades, serve as one of many that the Graterford Archive and Graterford Index hope to preserve as not only a time capsule but to give a authentic image of the lives of incarcerated individuals.
 Graterford was built in 1929 and served as the largest maximum security prison in Pennsylvania. Established as Eastern State Penitentiary ’s “Farm Branch,” prison officials had a unique vision and layout designed in line with the Auburn System of Incarceration. The prison was designed with plenty of space, light, and air between cells. Inmates participated in recreational and educational activities and a mix of duties that included working the farm, workshops, and other tasks to make the prison self sufficient and labor-intensive.
 Inmates at Graterford during a jazz jam session. Date unknown. | Photo courtesy of RG 15, Department of Justice State Correctional Institute, Graterford Records, 1933 – 2015. Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg
 The auditorium and unique layout facilitated a “third space” that enabled personal interactions among the prisoners. After the prison reforms of the 1980s, programs such as the Long Incarcerated Fraternity Engaging Release Studies (LIFERS) worked on legislation for the parole of individuals serving life sentences. In its Restorative Justice Program, Mural Arts used art education to develop bonds among inmates.
 Donnell Saadiq Palmer, previously incarcerated at SCI-Graterford until his transfer to SCI-Phoenix, is currently the chairperson of Right 2 Redemption (R2R) and a member of the Coalition to Abolish Death by Incarceration (CADBI). This coalition is working toward ending life-long sentences without parole, which is Palmer’s status at SCI-Phoenix. His is one of the many stories that Palmer and former inmates, staff, and family members connected to Graterford shared with the Graterford Archive and the Graterford Index to ensure that were not lost after the prison closed its gates on July 15, 2018.
 Other stories and connections that will be preserved include the Latin American Cultural Exchange Organization (LACEO) that focuses on Latin Americans’ cultural awareness, pre-release preparation, and employment opportunities, Villanova University’s Graterford campus that traces its origin to the earlier Villanova University Alumni Association Graterford Chapter (VUAAG), the well-known NAACP and Urban League, and a variety of religious, personal development, and programs that foster personal and drug rehabilitation and decrease recidivism upon release.
 Organizations like the Youth Art & Self-Empowerment Project, Right to Redemption, Human Rights Coalition, CADBI, and others founded between 2000s and 2010 can trace their roots to one of the many programs once available at Graterford. For visitors, both the Archive and Index will bring to light the stories of activism and achievement that would normally be ignored due to the stigma of the incarcerated.
 A Philadelphia Inquirer article from 1991 features Graterford boxer and inmate Jeff Gant. | Image: Newspapers.com
 The creation of the online resource began after Akeil Robertson-Jowers, co-founder and creative director of the Graterford Archive, recounted his experiences while incarcerated at the prison to Professor Gustavus Stadler of Haverford College. Robertson-Jowers, who was involved with Haverford’s Imagining Abolitionist Future (2022), which forms as the basis of the archive, found it imperative to share these stories and connections to help humanize and dispel misconceptions about the former and current inmates.
 Robertson-Jowers, said stories about Robert Johnson, the first Black superintendent of Graterford, Civil Rights activists that were imprisoned there, and Black guards working with Black prisoners and pushing back against white guards are the origin of the reforms that came later.
 In 2022, a $2.5 million Mellon Foundation afforded the archive to be expanded to include staff and the creation of a curriculum available to students at Haverford, Bryn Mawr, and Swarthmore colleges. Formed in collaboration with R2R and various educators, the curriculum includes Prison Memory and Carceral Narratives (Visual Studies), Against Death: Art, Abolition, and the Struggle to End Capital Punishment and Death by Incarceration, and Technical Citizenship: Incarceration, Redemption, and Abolition.
 Community archivist Wynn Eakins’ time attending Drexel's Masters in Library Science program in 2020 resulted in the creation of a LibGuide for academics, scholars, and parties who are interested in supporting “deeper research and historical analysis of SCI-Graterford.” Eakins said the archive was created as a hub for all information floating around, but not yet organized. The Graterford Index is convenient for anyone who wants to continue to work on it at a later date. Unfortunately, a large number of files related to Graterford were abandoned instead of being archived during the transition to SCI-Phoenix. Eakin hopes that this dormant information becomes accessible soon.
