 Bernard Hopkins , a mural by artist Eric Okdeh, was painted inside the gymnasium at Graterford in 2005. A reproduction is featured in the new exhibition Rising Up: Rocky and the Making of Monuments at Philadelphia Museum of Art. | Photo courtesy of Mural Arts
 The database's project manager, Kali Silverman, said empowering the Graterford diaspora by supporting their storytelling will hopefully turn into “a teaching tool for students and others to learn the history of community organizing.” Pursuing this goal will be hindered by the loss of living resources as the elderly inmates who were politically active during the 1960s and 1970s are in their twilight years.
 Palmer believes that SCI-Phoenix’s smaller and more restrictive layout, compared to SCI-Graterford, is pushback against the success of the programs. On reflection, he recalled how unique and open Graterford was and how it had a community that may only continue to exist in the history and stories of the former prisoners’ interconnected lives. He hopes that individuals and groups that contribute to both the archive and index will rehumanize them in the eyes of the general public.
 Staff and volunteers of the archive are currently producing a short film about the Graterford Boxing Program which was part of the Pennsylvania State Prison Boxing Program. It will be featured in the current Rising Up: Rocky and the Making of Monuments exhibition at the Philadelphia Museum of Art by way of a screening and panel discussion on Sunday July 26. “Our film will unearth the history of boxing in the Pennsylvania state prison system, tell the story of its fighters, and feature the muralists that celebrate this legacy,” said Robertson. Some of the highlights of the film will include champion boxer Bernard Hopkins who was also incarcerated at Graterford. A mural of Hopkins was painted by inmates at the prison, which has been reproduced by muralists currently incarcerated at SCI-Phoenix and included in the Rising Up exhibition.
 Tags: Archives boxing history Graterford historic prisons 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: In Historic Parkside, Neighborhood Frustrations with Developer German Yakubov Boil Over
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
In early April, Philadelphia real estate developer German Yakubov began posting in social media groups dedicated to historic preservation in Philadelphia with what sounded like a straightforward proposition: “Save Parkside.” In accompanying photos and on a linked website, Yakubov urged the public to sign a petition supporting his redevelopment of a historic, once-handsome duplex in the West Philadelphia neighborhood that has fallen into disrepair. 
 However, the backstory is anything but simple. 
 Yakoubov’s online campaign to redevelop the three-story residences at 4204-06 Parkside Avenue, built circa 1895, has been met with jeers from near neighbors who say it’s the latest tactic the developer is using to squeeze as much density in, and profit out of, their neighborhood as possible. Working with his brother Lev under the corporate banner of Haverford Square Properties, the Yakubovs have accumulated significant holdings in West Philadelphia over the past 15 years, starting in Mantua and Belmont before pushing north into East Parkside. 
 Along the way the firm took a number of historic properties into its portfolio, at times to good effect, a product of what German Yakubov previously told Hidden City was his appreciation for the build quality and architectural details of older buildings. Yet, things appear to have gone sideways as the firm began developing in Parkside, which contains a designated historic district recognized by both the local and national registers. Walk the block of 4200 Parkside Avenue–directly across the grassy park fronting the Please Touch Museum–and at least half a dozen Haverford Square properties in various stages of development can be found, along with frustrated neighbors. “He’s building all this density with no clear plan,” said Joyce Smith, president of the nonprofit Community Development Board of East Parkside. “He’s not taking into consideration how that will impact the community.” 
 4204-06 Parkside Avenue is at the center of a fiery dispute between real estate developer German Yakubov and the Parkside community. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The twin at 4204-06 Parkside Avenue is perhaps the highest profile project. The three-story, brick-built, bay-windowed homes were originally constructed in 1895 and designed by architect Henry E. Flower . They are listed as “significant” buildings within the National Register of Historic Places District , established in 1983, as well as within a Philadelphia Register of Historic Places district created in 2009, which affords the residences legal protection against demolition and exterior modification. 
 However, residents and German Yakubov both agree the properties have deteriorated in recent history. They blame one another. City records show the Yakubovs purchased the twins in 2015 and that they have since racked up dozens of L&I violations, including “vacant and open property” and exterior weed and sanitation notices last fall. Google Street View images from the past 10 years also show an increasing number of open windows and deteriorating architectural elements. 
 Meanwhile, Haverford Square has sought to redevelop the residences into multi-unit residential . In 2021, the firm received a permit to fit the properties with 12 units, matching the historic capacity of the 6-bedroom duplexes. But the Yakubovs are now seeking a zoning variance for 16 total units, a request denied by the Zoning Board of Adjustments in February following opposition from community members. 
 In an interview this May, Yakubov said the four extra units are simply needed to make the project “pencil out" and blamed opposing neighbors for what he views is an unreasonable stubborness to accept the economic realities of redevelopment. “The most somebody is willing to pay for a unit there is $1,500 for a one-bedroom,” Yakubov said. “And what it costs to rehab that building, 11,000-square-feet, is significantly more.” 
 4204-06 Parkside Avenue, at right, in 1950. | Photo courtesy of PhillyHistory.org
 Neighbors instead believe Yakubov is trying to maximize a profit and say he is letting the building fall further into disrepair as a strong arm tactic to get them to relent. “For five or six years he has let the building sit as a public eyesore,” said Paulette Fields, a longtime resident of the 4200 block of Parkside Avenue, likening the inaction to extortion. “He’s coming back… ‘If you give me eight units in each apartment,’ then, you know, he’ll fix it up again.” 
 Yakubov didn’t dispute that he’s held back on investing money into upkeep, but framed that as logical given the situation. “Everything on that building is expensive. So, we’re doing the best we can in maintaining it, without, you know, effectively rehabbing it,” Yakubov claimed. “If we go ahead and put a brand new roof on it, brand new windows on it, we’re talking pretty much the value of the entire building as it is today.” 
 Meanwhile, things are even more contentious at another parcel, on the backside of the block, at 4283-87 Viola Street. There, Haverford Square is seeking to build, at minimum, a 16-unit apartment building on land that used to contain three rowhouses. Once again, the matter went before the Zoning Board, and, once again, the Yakubovs were denied a variance this March after residents launched a GoFundMe campaign to pay for a lawyer to fight the proposal. 
 Yet, the contest continues. Haverford Square has appealed the decision to the Pennsylvania Court of Common Pleas. The firm has also submitted additional applications to the City for an 18-unit apartment building and a group home for up to 50 residents at the site. Hearings for those proposals are presently scheduled for July and September. In an email sent to residents and provided to Hidden City, an attorney representing Haverford Square proposed to conceptually agree to limit the Viola Street property to 12 units, as part of a wider framework spanning unit counts at 13 properties in East Parkside, including 16 units at 4204-06 Parkside Avenue. Smith sees this all as further evidence of strong-arm tactics by the Yakubovs to bleed energy and money from residents while pressuring them to make a deal and accepting even more density. 
 German Yakubov, co-owner of Haverford Square, hung a sign on 4204-06 Parkside Avenue early this spring to promote his “Save Parkside” petition much to the ire of neighbors. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose 
 Yakubov pushed back against the idea that his company is acting as a bully in the neighborhood. He said he has never personally attacked any resident, despite personally being the unsavory subject of social media posts that he says have gotten “literally got millions of views.” He also asserts a “Save Parkside” petition he established has gained the support of other neighborhood residents who don’t oppose the density and want to see the properties redeveloped. 
 “I’d be the most unsuccessful bully that ever existed,” Yakubov said of the accusation he is running roughshod over neighbors, adding he remains open to meeting with residents who oppose his plans. “On a dozen or so occasions, I asked for a meeting to blend my vision with theirs. We’re in litigation with two of the neighbors, and even in spite of that, I’m still more than happy to sit down and have a conversation.” 
 Yakubov is also on the wrong side of the ledger with the most important political player in East Parkside: Philadelphia City Council member Jamie Gauthier, who in an interview, made it clear she agreed with residents opposing his development plans. “I don’t believe that German and Haverford Square are good community partners,” Gauthier said. “The disrespect that he has shown the community, and the fact that he’s always trying to trap the community in these false choices that only really benefit him, has made him undesirable as a development partner throughout East Parkside.” 
 Welcome to die Nachbarschaft 
 At stake in the neighborhood is the fabric of a historic built environment. In the decades following the 1876 Centennial International Exhibition in West Fairmount Park, it was originally German-Americans who established East Parkside on land left unoccupied in the wake of the celebration, according to the neighborhood’s historic district nomination. “The expanse of available land allowed for more suburban scale and large three-story houses and apartment buildings,” the nomination relays. 
 Also spurred by the development of new public transit systems in the area, well-to-do beer brewers and merchants with names like Poth , Trautwine, Steinmetz, Wengell, and Baltz began to construct homes there in the 1890s. They did so with a distinctly European taste, eschewing red-brick Colonial styles common elsewhere in the city for “more florid” varieties of the old continent: from “mid-Victorian to tan brick, turn-of-the-century eclectic fashion with its references to Flemish” revival styles, the nomination notes “[East Parkside] is thus of considerable interest, particularly in a city with an historically important German community,” the nomination concluded. 
 Landsdowne Apartments at 41st Street and Parkside Avenue was built in 1893 and designed by architect John C. Worthington. | Image courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 The German-American presence in the neighborhood in the 1890s quickly gave way to Russian Jewish immigrants, according to the West Philadelphia Collaborative History , a University of Pennsylvania project. Then came the Great Depression, when many of the large homes were converted into efficiency apartments and rooming houses. That was followed by white flight and transition into a predominantly African American neighborhood in the mid-20th century. Both public and private disinvestment followed: Landlords stopped caring for many of the historic homes, and some public transportation services were suspended. 
 However, the most recent arrivals to the neighborhood fought for its historic beauty in the 1980s when community leader James L. Brown IV and wife Charlotte Brown founded the Parkside Historic Preservation Corporation. The organization successfully completed the National Register nomination in 1983, allowing property owners to apply for historic preservation tax credits and enabling the rehabilitation of some 20 historic buildings. 
 Shells of former mansions line Parkside Avenue between 41st and 42nd Street in 1980. | Photo courtesy of Special Collection sResearch Center, Temple University Libraries
 Even still, other properties continued to fall into disrepair and even demolition. As of the mid-aughts, the district–bounded by Parkside Avenue, Belmont Avenue, Viola Street, and 41st Street–included 40 historically significant properties, each added to the Philadelphia Register. 57 buildings were listed as “contributing” to its history, along with 29 "non-contributing" buildings that did not receive historical protections. 
 Today the district continues to be marked by some pockets of blight, including vacant lots where contributing structures once stood, but the neighborhood also hosts handsome and well-preserved residences dating to its earliest days. 
 Competing Visions 
 What should come next for East Parkside? This question is perhaps the most crucial one underlying the feud between Haverford Square and the long-time residents who oppose the firm’s developments. Yakubov doesn’t think there is a density problem. He noted that many homes constructed around the turn of the 20th century eventually deteriorated and were demolished. The plots now existing as empty lots. With amenities including grocery stores, parks, museums, and concert venues within walking distance, along with access to public transit, he sees that as a disconnect begging for redevelopment. 
 Data from the U.S. Census show the tract containing East Parkside had a population of about 3,400 residents in 2011, 2,700 in 2022, and 3,300 in 2024. Yakubov said all of his firm’s projects, including 74-unit and 49-unit buildings on Parkside Avenue, amount to a few hundred new residents and characterized that as not out of line with historic norms. “I would challenge anybody to produce a report, data, outside of a feeling that would say that neighborhood is oversaturated,” Yakubov said. 
 Residents say all one needs to do is walk the streets. On the western half of the historic district, Haverford Square is constructing its 49-unit apartment building at 4274 Parkside Avenue on a parcel where four homes recently stood. Immediately behind it is the Viola Street parcel where Haverford Square is ostensibly seeking to house up to 50 people in a group home. 
 Work to build a 49-unit apartment building is currently underway at 4274 Parkside Avenue. | Photo: Kyle Bagenstose
 At the end of the block, a few hundred feet away, Yakubov is planning to build a 14-unit apartment building that previously drew opposition from residents for requiring the demolition of a mural celebrating the Philadelphia Stars, a Black baseball team that played in Parkside during the 1930s . Yet, after Yakubov purchased an adjoining property, he said he can now proceed with the project by-right and has donated $30,000 to the Mural Arts program to reconstruct the mural across the street. The nonprofit did not respond to a request to detail the status of that project and its funding. 
 Perhaps the project drawing the greatest ire of residents is Yakubov’s plan to construct a four-story, 22-unit apartment buildin g in a 0.15-acre triangle-shaped alleyway sandwiched between Parkside Avenue and Viola Street, right in the middle of the other three projects. The project would not have any frontage along the neighborhood’s streets. Instead, access would be through a thin strip of the alleyway. Many of the building’s windows would inevitably offer views of little, but the back of existing homes. 
 All totaled, the four projects would amount to well over 100 new residents on parcels that had until recently contained a combined nine single-family homes. The projects also do not include parking, and residents say they will lose access to the alleyway where many previously parked their cars. A dispute over property lines in the alleyway and a physical fence Haverford Square installed to partially block access already boiled over earlier this year before construction even began. 
 The Philadelphia Stars Negro League mural was created in 2005 by Mural Arts. Neighbors opposed the redevelopment of the vacant lot at Belmont and Parkside Avenues because plans for a new 14-unit apartment building called for the demolition the home the painting is featured on. The mural is now gone. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Asked for her perspective on the right path forward for East Parkside, Councilmember Gauthier said there is a desire for thoughtful redevelopment, citing collaboration with community groups like Centennial Parkside CDC and developers such as Gary Jonas, who she explained is working on a Turn the Key affordable housing development project in the neighborhood. “I think folks do want multifamily. I think folks do want home ownership. I think people in East Parkside care very much about the historical character of the neighborhood… historic assets that may not be designated as historically significant by an outside institution, but matter to the people who live there,” she explained. “Everyone wants a good quality of life. They want to live in a thriving neighborhood. But we’re not begging Haverford Square to get that.” 
 Residents who oppose Haverford Square also say they don’t have a problem with adding new development or density to the neighborhood. Yet, they stand by their view that the Yakubovs are seeking too much and are employing hardball tactics instead of organically seeking community input. “He paints us as anti-development,” said Smith. “That is not true. We do want development, but we are also asking developers to please consider how it’s going to impact the quality of our lives. We feel like we can’t negotiate with [German Yakubov] because it’s either his way or no way.” 
 Tags: German Yakubov historic district Historic Preservation Parkside Philadelphia Register of Historic Places West Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Art Deco Bank in Olney Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on June 12, the Philadelphia Historical Commission added a bank building, a church, and two industrial buildings to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, but denied designation of a midcentury modern union hall.
 The Galilee Baptist Church at 459 Roxborough Avenue was added to the local register owing to its role as a community institution for the Black population of Roxborough and Manayunk for 125 years. Designed by the firm Kennedy & Kelsey, it retains its original character despite the removal of its cupola.
 National Bank of Olney at 5th Street and Olney Avenue. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The former home of the National Bank of Olney at 5604 N. 5th Street was also recognized for its architectural and historical significance. After being chartered in 1925, the bank quickly outgrew its original storefront home and commissioned a new building from the firm of Simons, Brittain & English, who were known for designing banks, especially in small or medium-sized municipalities. The two-story, cast-stone structure, completed in 1928, was constructed in the Art Deco style, which was emblematic of a shift in bank architecture from classical to contemporary styles. The building is also considered an important example of the growth of commercial corridors outside of Center City at that time, along with 52nd and Chestnut Streets, Broad Street and Olney Avenue, and Germantown and Chelten Avenues. After serving the neighborhood for nearly three decades, the National Bank of Olney was consumed in a series of mergers and acquisitions that saw the building still serving as a bank branch until the early 1990s.
 In Chinatown, the former Tetlow Manufacturing Company at 132 N. 10th Street was added to the Philadelphia Register. Constructed around 1885, the five-story brick building was designed with Italianate and Romanesque features. It housed Henry Tetlow’s cosmetics firm, whose innovations yielded new forms of face powders that were both inexpensive and non-toxic.
 Tetlow Manufacturing Company at 10th and Cherry Streets. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Another industrial property at 4889 Umbria Street was listed for legal protections on the local register. Two buildings of the Manayunk Plush Manufacturing Company–a large one-story manufacturing building and a smaller power plant–were constructed in 1926 and 1927. They were designed by architect and engineer William Elmer Seibert Dyer, a specialist in industrial buildings who influenced the area’s development in textile and other manufacturing in the early 20th century. The factory was operating into the 1970s. Several near neighbors expressed appreciation for the building as an emblem of Manayunk’s past as a center of textile manufacturing.
 The owner of the entire 4 1/2 acre site has redevelopment plans underway, including the construction of a new building with 363 residential units and a similar amount of parking spaces, despite being directly across Umbria Street from the Ivy Ridge Regional Rail station. While the plans call for the preservation of the nominated buildings, the owner requested and received modification approval to remove any open land surrounding the historic buildings from the designation.
 The National Marine Engineers Beneficial Association building at 4th and Willow Streets. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The final nomination reviewed at the meeting was for the National Marine Engineers Beneficial Association Office at 428-34 N. 4th Street . The two-story Modernist office building was completed in 1967 to serve as a union hall for the association, which owned the property until 1990. The nomination, complied and submitted by Misha Wyllie, a student of the University of Pennsylvania's Master of Science in Historic Preservation program, describes the building's connections to Philadelphia history, including its construction that occurred during urban renewal and the Callowhill East Redevelopment Project, which saw widespread demolition in the neighborhood. Wyllie's research also suggests the building is representative of the importance of Philadelphia's history of organized labor.
 The building’s owner, Mark Rubin, president of Willow Management Corp., objected to the nomination, citing a confidential agreement of sale to the neighboring organization Gift of Life Donor Program. He claimed that reuse of the building and/or development of its front parking lot and rear addition were not possible. Real estate attorney Michael V. Phillips and Gift of Life's CEO Richard D. Hasz submitted an exhaustive 103-page letter to Historical Commission staff voicing opposition to the historic nomination. The potential new owners plan to demolish the building and develop the site with new construction. The Historical Commission unanimously declined the nomination.
 Tags: demolition Historic Banks Historical Commission Meeting Report Midcentury Modern Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Restoration Role Model: Hiester House
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Built in 1757, the Hiester House has Flemish bond glazed header bricks on all four sides. | Photo: Michael E. Myers, Steadfast Imaging
 Lisa Minardi and her husband, Philip Bradley, purchased the Hiester House in 2017 and began a five-year journey to restore the house as authentically as possible to its original appearance in 1757, when it was one of the first brick buildings in Montgomery County. Philip passed away in 2021, and Lisa carried on the faithful restoration as general contractor, enlisting experts in historic timber framing, carpentry, windows, roofing, and masonry. Extant spoke with Minardi about the outstanding restoration of the house, which she has furnished with compatible antiques mostly dating from 1750 to 1800 and made in southeastern Pennsylvania.
 Extant Magazine (EM) : What attracted you to this building?
 Lisa Minardi (LM) : I grew up nearby and was familiar with the Hiester House since I was a child, although no one was allowed into the house by the former owners. That only piqued my interest more, especially as I became a historian who focuses on Pennsylvania German architecture and material culture. Thus, the Hiester House, with its over-the-top Germanic details–such as elaborate ironwork, staircase with flat vasiform balusters, and robust moldings–was love at first sight for me. I also love the fact that it is one of the earliest brick structures in what is now Montgomery County, and that it is Flemish bond, glazed header brick on all four sides. Talk about showing off!
 The plainer of two kitchens retains the original 12-foot wide fireplace. | Photo: Michael E. Myers, Steadfast Imaging
 EM: What was the building’s original use?
 LM: The house was built in 1757 by Daniel and Catharina Hiester as their family home. Hiester emigrated from Germany in 1737 and settled in Upper Salford Township, now part of Montgomery County. The house is situated near the confluence of the Unami and Ridge Valley creeks, where Hiester had a tannery operation.
 EM: What was most important to preserve?
 LM: With a house this architecturally significant and well preserved, our mission was to restore as much as possible back to its original appearance. We documented and removed what few later changes had been made, mostly to the first floor. The second floor was virtually untouched since the house was built, retaining all of its original woodwork, plaster, flooring, three fireplaces and more. We hired experts to do paint analysis, dendrochronology, archaeology–everything we could think of to help us document and understand the house and its historical context.
 For example, we took up the Victorian floorboards and carefully mapped out the nailing pattern of the original floorboards, then used that to develop a cut list for the local sawmill. This attention to detail revealed that the grander front rooms of the house had fairly narrow, regular-width floorboards, whereas the two rear kitchens had wide, random-width flooring. We used white oak and hand-forged nails just like the original flooring.
 Paint analysis revealed that verdigris was the original color in one of the upstairs bedchambers. | Photo: Michael E. Myers, Steadfast Imaging
 EM: What was the biggest preservation challenge?
 LM: There were the usual challenges of incorporating heat, plumbing, and other modern systems into the building. We opted not to install central air conditioning as the attic of the house is so extraordinary that I couldn’t bear the thought of cluttering it with ductwork. One of the biggest challenges was that the house had six inches of sag in the middle due to badly cracked and failing structural beams in the cellar. We worked with a structural engineer who advised us on how to save and shore up the beams while jacking up much of the sag to reduce the significant sloping.
 Other challenges were how to recreate some of the rare Germanic details of the house, such as the five-plate stoves, paled insulation in the ceiling of the cellar, and built-in stone sinks to drain wastewater to the outside from the two rear kitchens. We studied the architectural evidence carefully, looked at other houses for comparison, and made our best effort to accurately restore all of these distinctive features. I’m especially proud of having restored all three of the missing five-plate stoves. We have even used one several times and are likely the first people to do so in over 200 years.
 The original built-in schrank, or wardrobe, retains a peg rack inside for clothing. | Photo: Michael E. Myers, Steadfast Imaging
 EM: Did you look to any role model for inspiration or example?
 LM: In 2007, I attended the Poplar Forest Restoration Field School and was deeply impressed with the painstaking methodology employed there as well as at Montpelier. I came away determined to apply these lessons in my own restoration efforts, first at the Speaker’s House, home of Frederick Muhlenberg, in Trappe, Pennsylvania, as part of my professional career and then at the Hiester House when I became the owner. For my graduate work at the University of Delaware, I also studied with amazing professors such as Bernie Herman and Ritchie Garrison, who furthered my love of vernacular architecture and helped me realize how truly special the Hiester House is.
 This five-plate stove retains the original masonry collar. Its decorative side and front plates were cast at Durham Furnace in 1756. | Photo: Michael E. Myers, Steadfast Imaging
 EM: What was the project’s biggest surprise (good or bad)?
 LM: There were so many surprises along the way. One that stands out to me is that the paint analysis revealed that all the woodwork in one of the upstairs bedrooms was originally painted with verdigris and would have been a vivid green color. I was stunned, as the woodwork was bright pink when we bought the house. I couldn’t imagine it being green instead. I also was surprised as verdigris was a very expensive pigment and its use is nearly unheard of in other extant 18th century Pennsylvania houses. The only examples I could think of were in Virginia at Mount Vernon and Gunston Hall. I worried about what the room would look like once it was painted bright green, but stayed the course in my commitment to authenticity. Now that it is green, I absolutely love it and how the color looks even when dimly lit at night. Another surprise was the discovery of blue polka dots painted beneath the chair rail in the best parlor, a rare feature found in a few other nearby Pennsylvania German houses.
 Tags: historic renovation Montgomery County Restoration Role Model suburbs 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: The First Bank of the United States Reopens with a Regal Restoration
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The former First Bank of the United States at 120 S. 3rd Street reopens to the public after decades of closure. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 On Wednesday, July 1 the National Park Service will unveil the restoration of the first building ever constructed for the United States government. The grand reopening invites visitors to step inside the building for the first time in many decades. The First Bank of the United States, located at 120 S. 3rd Street, was built in 1795 and embodies the history of the country’s financial system.
 No banks were permitted in the American colonies. The currency in use varied greatly from colony to colony, including coinage from foreign countries and paper notes issued by the government of the colony. Loans were secured by the value of land. Land banks were associations of landlords that would print notes and give the associated value to a person based on the value of their land like a mortgage. Britain eventually banned the practice.
 In 1789, when the Constitution was ratified, there were three banks in the United States: the Bank of North America (Chartered 1781 and its original location was at 307 Chestnut Street), the Bank of New York (1784), and the Massachusetts Bank (1784).
 Alexander Hamilton, first Secretary of the Treasury, advocated for a national bank, writing in the Federalist papers that it was needed to have “enough of the confidence of all parts of the Union.”
 The Constitution does not include the creation of a bank or issuing paper money. Thomas Jefferson felt a national bank would be a monopoly. However, Hamilton convinced Congress and President George Washington. When it was chartered in 1797, the First Bank of the United States was set up as a corporation capitalized at $10 million, with 20 percent of its shares owned by the federal government.
 In contrast to the three earlier banks which operated locally, the First Bank of the United States was given the authority to open branches in other cities. A year after opening in Philadelphia, branches were established in New York, Boston, Charleston, and Baltimore. Between 1800 and 1805, branches were added in Norfolk, Savannah, Washington DC, and New Orleans.
 A hand-colored engraving from 1799 shows the First Bank of the United States and 18th century street life. | Image courtesy of the Library Company of Philadelphia
 The success of the First Bank of the United States encouraged state legislatures to charter their own banks. However, many state bankers chafed at the control and competition the federal bank represented, which was a factor in Congress’ denial of the bank’s charter renewal in 1811.
 Prior to the First Bank of the United States, bank buildings were residential style properties in size, with staff living on the upper floors. This arrangement copied the British model, where, before the establishment of the Bank of England, banks there had to be privately owned.
 The First Bank of the United States was originally located in Carpenters’ Hall at 320 Chestnut Street during its first six years of operation. After a fire on Third Street in 1793 brought about the sale of several newly vacant lots, the bank purchased the parcel at 116 S. 3rd Street for a new home.
 The new building was designed by Samuel Blodgett, Jr., a businessman and gentleman architect. He collaborated on the design with James Hoban, best known as the architect of the White House. Blodgett may have borrowed from the Royal Exchange in Dublin for the design. Hoban had worked on the Royal Exchange and knew Blodgett through a Washington, D.C. hotel he designed for him in 1793.
 The Greek Revival building’s marble facade features two-story Corinthian columns, topped by a pediment with a 34-foot sculpted panel depicting an American eagle grasping 13 arrows, echoing the Great Seal of the United States. Although the front facade was marble, the rear and sides were brick, resembling a Georgian mansion. Later banks would be built of marble on all sides.
 It was the first building constructed for the nascent federal government. Its size and imposing style were intended to represent the strength and growth of the new country. Additionally, a carved marble allegory above the door depicts the United States as a baby in a winged helmet, surrounded by symbols of global commerce.
 116 S. 3rd Street was sold to Stephen Girard in 1812. Pictured is Girard Bank in 1920. | Photo courtesy of the Library Company of Philadelphia
 The building was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1956 and re-designated a year later. A National Register of Historic Places designation followed in 1966. It was included in the Historic American Buildings Survey, and in 1987 it was declared a National Historic Landmark.
 After Congress declined to renew the bank’s charter, the building was sold in 1812 to Stephen Girard, who opened his own Girard Bank there. Girard died in 1832, but the bank continued to operate there until 1929.
 In 1902, the bank hired architect James Windrim, who had designed the Academy of Natural Sciences and the Masonic Temple, to remodel the interior. He replaced the original barrel vaulted ceiling with a large skylight over a glass-paned dome to furnish more light in the first floor.
 After Girard Bank vacated it in 1929, followed by brief occupancies by the American Legion and Philadelphia's Board of Directors of City Trusts, the building was largely unused until the National Park Service (NPS) purchased it in 1955 as part of Independence National Historical Park. Until this restoration, it was used variously as park offices and storage and has been closed to the public.
 NPS restored the exterior in the mid-1970s. In 2020, the carved mahogany sculpture set within the building’s tympanum was preserved by the Philadelphia-based Materials Conservation Company, winning a Grand Jury Award from the Preservation Alliance of Greater Philadelphia the following year.
 John Milner Architects was selected for this most recent exterior and interior preservation. The planned work included restoring or replacing some of the exterior’s Pennsylvania blue marble, restoring the interior, and for both, accommodating mechanical systems, an accessible entry, and other contemporary necessities. The copper roof was replaced, including a portion over the portico which appeared to be the original roofing.
 The main hall the First Bank of the United States following an extensive restoration. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 “The challenge is always the balance between the historical fabric versus what we need to put in for the building to function today,” noted architect Christina Carter, senior associate with John Milner Architects. “We had to deal with the limitations of the space, especially for the mechanicals.”
 The exterior restorations went fairly smoothly. “We only replaced around three square feet of Pennsylvania blue marble around the water table and the window heads outside the portico on the east facade,” said Carter. “We used King of Prussia marble, which is a good substitute.” The reliefs on the facade, being under the portico, were in good shape and didn’t require much restoration.
 As with many historic structures, renovations can unearth surprises and challenges. “Asbestos had a greater impact than we anticipated. It was a challenge to find a balance between how much to take out without disrupting the renovation,” Carter recalled. “And then when we removed the asbestos in the ceiling of the main hall, it facilitated stringing new wiring.”
 Another consideration was the respective ages of the outside and inside of the building. “The interior is essentially 1901, while the exterior is 18th century,” Carter pointed out. “Part of our approach was to make these two periods work together.”
 While much of the project’s focus was on the building itself, consideration of the surrounding grounds became an issue. “The construction of the new addition disrupted the landscaping,” explained Rong Chen, project manager for NPS. “To meet current Philadelphia Water Department requirements, we added a stormwater management system surrounding the building.”
 The building's spectacular columned dome. | Photos Michael Bixler
 When it was decided to build an addition, chiefly for the modern upgrades, Carter said they approached it “with a light touch.” She explained that only two beams of the addition actually touch the historic building, so if in the future the wing is removed, the original facade would only bear two small, easily remedied scars.
 With the renovations completed and the building ready to open to the public, attention has turned to what it will contain. “The main exhibit on the first floor is about the building. This building is an artifact, the oldest federal building in the country. Treating as an artifact allows us to tell the story.” said Rosalind Remer, Drexel University’s senior vice provost for Libraries, Collections & Archives. “We’re going to be able to tell the story of Alexander Hamilton and the creation of our financial system.” The second floor will house a gallery for temporary exhibits.
 Items from the Atwater Kent Collection at Drexel are currently on display on the first floor. To commemorate this year’s semiquincentennial, they include artifacts from earlier anniversaries: the 1876 Centennial, the 1926 Sesquicentennial, and 1976 Bicentennial, noted Stacey Swigart, director of the Atwater Kent Collection with Drexel University’s Lenfest Center for Cultural Partnerships. “They couldn’t have the permanent exhibit done in time for the building’s opening, so the State Department brought in their traveling exhibit and we supplied items from the earlier anniversaries, which all had connections to other countries.” In the race to finish the restoration in time for the 250 celebrations centered around Independence Day, Rosalind Remer stressed, “We’ll begin planning the permanent exhibit after July 4.”
 Tags: historic renovation National Park Service Old City restoration Semiquincentennial 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Black Opals: Philadelphia’s Legendary Contribution to the Harlem Renaissance
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Despite having “Harlem” in its name, the Harlem Renaissance extended far beyond New York City. It was originally referred to as the New Negro Movement by Alain Locke , a Philadelphia native and one of its main exponents. Similar groups of writers and artists in other cities also sprang up, including the Ink Slingers in Los Angeles, The Scribblers in Baltimore, The Saturday Nighters in Washington D.C., and even smaller cities like Topeka, Kansas, which had the Book and Bench. A group in Philadelphia centered around the literary journal Black Opals .
 In Vincent Jubilee's 1980 dissertation at the University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia’s Afro-American Literary Circle and the Harlem Renaissance , he noted a particular impetus for creating Black Opals , writing “Although many of the budding Philadelphia authors had published independently by 1927, a publicly visible proof of their authenticity as serious literary professionals would be to present their own journal.”
 Two of those authors, Nellie Rathbone Bright (1898-1977) and Arthur Huff Fauset (1899-1983) were the creators of Black Opals . Bright grew up in West Philadelphia, where her father, Reverend Richard Bright, was the vicar of St. Monica’s Episcopal Church in Powelton Village. After graduating from the University of Pennsylvania in 1923, she spent a year at the Sorbonne, followed by a year at Oxford University. Upon returning to Philadelphia, Bright embarked on a long career in public education.
 A portrait of Arthur Huff Fauset. Date unknown. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Fauset studied and practiced anthropology, having earned a B.A., M.A., and Ph.D. from the University of Pennsylvania. He was the author of folklore studies, including in Nova Scotia and Black urban religious cults. Later, he married Crystal Bird Fauset, a civil rights activist and social worker who became the first Black female state legislator elected in the United States.
 Each volume of Black Opals contained 16 to 20 pages of poetry, essays, and illustrations. The print runs varied between 200 and 250. The debut issue in 1927 contained a greeting and endorsement by Locke, as well as three poems by Langston Hughes. Bright’s poem “Longings” opened that issue. Its lines “I want to look deep in a pool at night, and see the / stars / flash flame like fire in black opals,” providing the title for the journal.
 In particular, Bright and Fauset were dedicated to promoting the work of younger writers. Poet and visual artist Mae Virginia Cowdery (1909-1953), who hailed from an affluent Germantown family, had three of her poems published in the Spring 1927 edition of Black Opals , while she was still a student at Philadelphia High School for Girls.
 Fauset’s sister, poet and novelist Jessie Redmon Fauset, who was well-known in Harlem Renaissance circles, was also a contributor. Visual artist Allan Randall Freelon was the artistic director. The poet Gwendolyn B. Bennett was the guest editor of the second issue, while she was also holding a fellowship at the Barnes Foundation.
 The Rare Books Department of the Free Library of Philadelphia holds all four issues of Black Opals in its collection. | Photo courtesy of Philadelphia Area Consortium of Special Collections Libraries
 In 1927, Albert Barnes created a fellowship program for artists to come to the Barnes Foundation and take classes, providing a stipend and other financial support, with Bennett one of the first recipients. “The Barnes was a local hub for the New Negro Movement, later called the Harlem Renaissance,” explained Alison Boyd, director of research and interpretation at the Barnes Foundation. She noted that Fauset worked there in 1924 as the associate director of education, teaching both night classes in Philadelphia neighborhoods and classes in Barnes’ factory for the largely Black workers there. In correspondence, Fauset and Barnes discussed how to teach without stifling the students’ own thoughts and opinions, which Boyd sees as “a spark of an idea that fostered the mission of Black Opals .”
 Beyond Philadelphia, Black Opals had a relationship with the publication Crisis: A Record of the Darker Races . Although officially a publication of the NAACP and founded to promote political and educational topics by editor W. E. B. du Bois, Crisis went on to influence the Harlem Renaissance, especially in the years when Jessie Redmon Fauset served as the literary editor. DuBois introduced Crisis readers to Black Opals in 1927, promoting it in the column “The Far Horizon.”
 Black Opals was similar to Fire!! A Quarterly Devoted to the Younger Negro Artists, which was founded in 1926 in New York by Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston, and other luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance. According to Sandra West and Aberjhani in their Encyclopedia of the Harlem Renaissance , both featured artistic covers, a small size, erratic distribution, and a short life span, although Black Opals , emerging from Philadelphia’s Black middle-class elite, was not as avant-garde or sexually explicit as Fire!! 
 A portrait of Gwendolyn Bennett taken some time between 1920 and 1929. | Photo courtesy of Digital Collection, The New York Public Library
 The Harlem Renaissance and the Philadelphia circles were different in their sociocultural environments. Harlem’s participants hailed from diverse social levels and places like the West Indies, California, and the South. Those in Philadelphia, by contrast, were almost all from one class and geography; that of the city’s privileged, professional class descended from long-established family lines. In Harlem, many were regarded as “bohemians,” while Philadelphia’s circle included many teachers.
 Bright and Fauset ended Black Opals after just four issues due to the pressure from increasing publishing costs and a small audience. Both went on to focus on their careers in education. They would reunite in 1969 to publish America: red, white, black, yellow , a textbook of American history for elementary students with an emphasis on racial inclusion.
 June and December 1928 issues of Black Opals . | Photo courtesy of Swann Auction Galleries
 Fauset was the principal of the Joseph Singerly School at 22nd and Berks Streets for 20 years. After teaching for many years at the Alexander Wilson School at 46th Street and Woodland Avenue, Bright went on to also serve as a principal. In 1935, she was named principal of the Joseph E. Hill School at Rittenhouse and McCallum Streets in Germantown, and 10 years later assumed the same position at the Harrison Public School at 11th and Thompson Streets. Many Black intellectuals in Philadelphia taught in the city’s segregated elementary schools because they were barred from working in the junior and senior high schools and at the Board of Education.
 Despite its short run, Black Opals has had an outsized influence. In March 2021, Swann Auction Galleries in New York City sold a complete set of the four issues of Black Opals. The gallery noted “We trace 13 American institutions which hold scattered issues of Black Opals , but only two (the Schomburg Library of the New York Public Library and the Free Library of Philadelphia) which hold a complete run of all four issues.” The catalog estimated the sale price to be $5,000-7,500. The final sale was actually $45,000.
 Poet, musician, and former Philadelphia Poet Laureate Yolanda Wisher has had a long running fascination with Black Opals . “Around 1999 or 2000, I had an idea to do an anthology of living local poets and then started thinking, who came before us,” she recalled. “It spurred a lot of detective work for me as I kept going back further and further.”
 Wisher presented an event at the Rosenbach Library in 2017 called “Blues for Black Opals ,” where she invited poets to select a work to read from the journal. For her part, Wisher set some of the poems, including Bright’s “Longings,” to music. Wisher’s involvement with Black Opals continues, as she’s working on a piece called “Finding Nellie Bright.”
 On March 5, 2026, the Barnes Foundation will open Education & Empowerment: Scholarship Recipients at the Barnes Foundation, 1927–1952 , an in-person and online exhibition that will feature Gwendolyn Bennett’s fellowship there. The museum is also currently offering an online course, “The Harlem Renaissance in Philadelphia,” as a lead-up to its semiquincentennial exhibition Freedom Dreams .
 Tags: African-American history literature Philadelphia writers 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Restoration Role Model: Fairelawn
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Winter 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 The view of Fairelawn from Pelham Street looking north. | Photos: Peter Woodall
 Fairelawn was built in 1903 by the renowned firm of G.W. and W.D. Hewitt for industrialist Henry B. Curran as a wedding gift for his daughter. The Tudor Revival-style structure at 30 Pelham Road in Mount Airy later served as a convent and a bed and breakfast. A $2.8 million rehabilitation project transformed the building into law offices. Extant spoke to attorneys Pete and Katie Commons, of Commons & Commons LLP, and Marc Pinard, of Pinard Architecture and Interiors, about the superb rehab project, which received a 2025 Grand Jury Award from the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Extant Magazine (EM) : What attracted you to this particular building/site?
 Marc Pinard (MP) : Its intact character just waiting to be brought back to relevance.
 Pete and Katie Commons (PKC): The building was the right size and location for what our firm needed, and it was beautiful, well built, and structurally sound (thanks to Philly Office Retail having replaced the roof at a critical moment when it owned the property). The interior spaces are lovely, and the front porch is one of our favorite places anywhere.
 EM: What was most important to preserve?
 MP : The integrity of the floor plan. The original grand residential plan was intact and lent itself well to a program for a law firm with needs for conference space (living/dining rooms), lawyers’ offices (studies and bedrooms), paralegals and aides (anterooms and old baths), and kitchen and restrooms (kitchen and house staff areas). Carol Pinard saw that the program aligned nicely with the existing intact original floor plan and would lead to each space retaining its charm and character.
 PKC : The integrity of the space, which had survived, definitely needed to be saved. So, too, did the beautiful stonework, the porches, which were so well thought through, and the leaded glass windows. We wanted to change as little as possible while restoring the character of the place and putting it to practical use for our firm and our clients.
 Nearly all of the room, now used for meetings by the firm, needed significant restoration or replacement, including the floor, coffered ceiling, fireplace and mantle, the window shutters, and the leaded glass of the windows. | Photos: Peter Woodall
 EM: What was the client’s original vision?
 MP : To keep as much original detail and character as possible and to reconstruct any detail that was missing. Pete and Katie committed to this by hiring an in-house general contractor and craftspeople, carpenters, and subcontractors equally committed to the details.
 PKC : The best part of this project was the people. Marc and Carol understood our goals as well or better than we did ourselves. As the project came together, we just became more and more excited. We work in the building now and spend most of our waking hours here. Knowing that we were creating this place where we would spend so much time was very motivating.
 EM: What was the biggest preservation challenge?
 MP : The HVAC. Integrating modern systems within so much intact historic fabric called for constant attention to keeping plumbing, ductwork, registers and air handlers well integrated.
 PKC : Many of the windows had to be rebuilt and all of them needed to be re-leaded and then refit into their old openings. Cooper O’Neil, who repaired the leaded glass, and our carpenters did a great job of making the process happen in an organized way that preserved as much original wood and glass as possible.
 The solarium is home to plants once again, its leaded glass windows returned to their original glory. | Photos: Peter Woodall
 EM: Did you look to any role model for inspiration or as an example?
 MP : We mostly looked to the great team of craftspeople and subcontractors who were eager to offer their best effort in detailing new but historically appropriate solutions.
 PKC : We agree. It was our team of craftspeople, led by Carl Keilblock, who saw every problem as an opportunity and had a can-do attitude through each phase and with each new challenge that made the project both a success and enjoyable.
 EM: What was the project’s biggest surprise (good or bad)?
 MP : Good: The City of Philadelphia’s foresight in having zoning regulations that allow for some nonconforming uses in buildings that would otherwise fall victim to a lack of preservation resources.
 PKC : One bad surprise was learning that a squirrel trapped in a house will try to chew through the lead in dozens and dozens of windows to try to escape. The best surprise was that the building process was fun, interesting, and brought together a great group of people.
 Tags: adaptive resuse historic renovation Mount Airy Restoration Role Model 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: David Lynch, You, and Me
author: Julien Suaudeau
bodyText:
Julien Suaudeau and Anne Duchene (selfie) in front of "There is Trouble ‘Till The Robins Come" mural by Dennis McNett behind Love Brewing | Photo: Julien Suaudeau
 Author’s Note : Episodes 1 and 2 of Song of Lynchadelphia (Season 3 of Hidden City’s Song of Philadelphia Podcast ) focused on the creative big bang that took place during David Lynch’s time in Philadelphia, between 1965 and 1970. Episode 3 examined the wild ways in which the city—Lynch’s impression of the city—manifests itself in Eraserhead, Mulholland Drive, and the Twin Peaks universe. Episode 4 explored the Lynchian happenings in Philly. In episode 5 and 6, Philly’s own and Lynch’s first wife Peggy Reavey recalled how he projected his own fears on the city, while reflecting on her contributions to her husband’s art. Available today on Spotify and Apple Podcasts, episode 7 is the season’s finale. As the season’s guests and a few others share a personal David Lynch memory and reflect on how he and his work affected their life, Song of Philadelphia host Julien Suaudeau and his wife Anne Duchene join the chorus and provide conflicting accounts of the role one Lynch film played in pulling them closer to each other back in the 1990s You can listen to all 19 episodes of Song of Philadelphia, including this entire season of Lynchadelphia, on Apple Podcasts or Spotify , or directly on Libsyn . 
 I learned and unlearned a thing or two while producing Song of Lynchadelphia.
 I also remembered a lot. Revisiting David Lynch’s filmography threw me back to my teenage years, as a high school student and aspiring shoegazer with broken English in Paris.
 As Nick Cave, definitely not a shoegazer, sings: I wanna tell you about a girl.
 At the end of 11th grade, I bumped into her during lunch period at a record store close to my school. We talked about the bands we loved. On the way back to her school, I realized I had seen her the previous year in the pit at a Pixies concert, disoriented and taken to a less crowded place by a friend. I remembered the surge of sadness I had felt in that moment, thinking that I would probably never see her again.
 In front of her school, we exchanged land line phone numbers. I invited her to the studio where my band practiced. A couple of weeks later, Twin Peaks: Fire Walk with Me came out. We went together, with different expectations. I was in love with her. She wanted to see the film.
 As spring and summer went by, we became close friends. We recorded silly home videos in which we acted out, in the dubbed French version, our favorite Twin Peaks scenes. We traded cassettes of shoegaze bands and tried to figure out the lyrics. She loved Ride, the heartthrob Oxford band. She had hung out with their drummer. The odds didn’t look too good. Every time I wrote or sang in English, it felt like a reminder that there was no way I could be the real deal for her.
 She flew to the US in late summer, to DC. Later, she told me she was bored out of her mind and spent her time at a record store in Georgetown. The family that hosted her set her up on a date with a local boy. Then, they took her on a trip to Billings, Wyoming. She sent me a postcard from there. Her writing on that card gave me hope. I have no idea where the postcard is, but I remember she wrote that she missed me. My memory could be playing tricks on me.
 A couple of months later, in October, she stayed in my room later than usual—into the night. She didn’t feel like going home. I don’t think she used those words, but this is what came through. The next day, I turned 17. She came to my school, and we hung out in the courtyard. We kissed.
 14 years later, 20 years ago, she got a job at Drexel. We moved to Philly as a married couple in August 2006. The high school sweetheart had become my woman.
 The locals quickly learned not to mess with her temper. When my woman flies off the handle, Eagles anger feels like pisse de chat—cat piss. She doesn’t take shit from anyone. Being her man is a lot of work, and it’s also me at my best.
 Not a week goes by without one of us quoting a line from a David Lynch film or walking into a Lynchian situation. His dreamworld has become part of our everyday language. It’s in the fabric of our lives. Sometimes, when I think about my woman, I think about Mulholland Drive .
 This. Is. The. Girl. Even if I’m in Philly, I’m transported back to that record store in Paris. Two cities and two timelines leak into each other.
 Our children were born at Pennsylvania Hospital in 2008 and 2011. Time flew by. Last year, the four of us watched the three Twin Peaks seasons together in our Philly basement. The children understood stuff that we had missed. Passing that onto them, seeing them make it their own, felt good. It felt like going home.
Our son played the Twin Peaks theme at his middle school concert. Our daughter sends me Twin Peaks -related Instagram and TikTok videos.
 Who and where would we be without David Lynch?
 In this final episode, everyone ponders the question: from Jack Fisk to Peggy Reavey; from my neighbor Patty to Monica Hanh, the current owner of 2416 Poplar Street, where Lynch shot The Grandmother ; from The Return actor George Griffith to PhilaMOCA’s Eric Bresler and former Inquirer film critic Carrie Rickey; from street artist Dennis McNett to Josh Hitchens and Mathias Fueling.
 It was a thrilling experience to listen to all of them and to figure out how Lynch and Philadelphia intersect for them. As they examined their personal relationship to Lynch’s work, I saw myself in a new light, and I felt closer than ever to Philadelphia.
 Tags: David Lynch Eraserhood Lynchadelphia 
 About the Author
 Julien Suaudeau Julien Suaudeau is a French-American writer, documentary filmmaker, and podcaster. He was born in Evreux, Normandy, grew up in Paris, France, and moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 2006. He teaches French and Film at Bryn Mawr College. In 2024, he launched Song of Philadelphia, Hidden City's podcast.

title: Honoring the "Exalted Ruler" of Christian Street
author: Amy Cohen
bodyText:
In June 2022, the Christian Street/Black Doctors Row Historic District became Philadelphia’s first historic district based on Black history. The designated area spans from Broad Street to 20th Street. It grants protection to the structures remaining from 1910 to 1945, the era when Christian Street boasted the city’s highest concentration of African American professionals and was the locale of many important Black institutions. Among these was the Quaker City Lodge, a thriving chapter of the Improved Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks of the World (IBPOEW) or the Black Elks. Exalted Ruler John Miller Marquess was the chapter’s leader from 1930 until his sudden death in 1936. Marquess’ life story is fascinating in itself, but also because of what it reveals about 1930s African American life on and beyond what the Philadelphia Tribune called “Black Main Street.”
 Beginnings 
 Marquess was born in rural Arkansas in 1882. John was an excellent student, but lacked the skills required for life in the countryside. According to an obituary, Marquess “had an interest in hunting—but couldn’t shoot with the accuracy of a palsied octogenarian seated atop a bucking bronco.” The description continues, “Efforts, frantic at times, to teach him the technique of milking a cow were futile.”
 Thus, at 12-years-old Marquess left home to enter a preparatory program at Fisk University from which he graduated with a bachelor’s degree in 1902. Marquess was captain of the football team, a singer in the Glee Club, and had the opportunity to travel the country as a member of the Fisk Quartet. He earned an additional degree after two years at Dartmouth where he ran track and sang in the Glee Club.
 A photograph of John Miller Marquess taken circa 1904 during his studies at Dartmouth College. | Image courtesy of Black Alumni of Dartmouth Association
 Marquess became an instructor of math and languages at two small Black colleges: Shorter College in Arkansas and then Kitrell College in North Carolina. In 1916, after eight years as a high school principal in Kansas City, Kansas, he was appointed president of the State University for Colored People in Langston, Oklahoma. Marquess married Anna Dickson of Ohio, and they had three children.
 When Marquess came to Philadelphia in the mid-1920s, he was an established, educated, and worldly family man, known to have significant real estate investments and contacts in Black communities across the nation. Unsurprisingly, Marquess chose a house at 909 South 18th Street, just steps from Christian Street, for his relocating family. He also opened a pharmacy at 18th and Christian Streets. By 1920, Christian Street was 57 percent Black. By 1930 it was 92 percent Black. The Black population there would peak at 97 percent in 1940.
 Exalted Leader of the Elks 
 The period of Marquess’ residence on Christian Street coincided with a time that most Americans, especially most African Americans, were affiliated with numerous civic and social organizations. The Black Elks, founded in 1898 and continuing to this day, appealed to Black men from a range of social strata and offered a wide array of activities including athletics, musical performances, fellowship, and civil rights advocacy. They were also well known for their pageantry, from wearing purple fezzes to staging extravagant parades.
 An undated photo of an O.V. Catto Lodge gathering. Pictured at left is Exalted Leader Edward W. Henry, Marquess' frequent nemesis. | Photo: John Mosley, courtesy of the Charles L. Blockson Afro-American Collection
 The Quaker City Elks Lodge 720 was founded in 1926, and Marquess quickly emerged as a leader. Although the O.V. Catto Lodge was already established and had moved from the Seventh Ward to 15th and Fitzwater Streets, this new chapter grew quickly. Under Marquess’ supervision, the Quaker City Elks opened the Keystone Temple in 1930 at 1943 Christian Street. The official launch of the Quaker City Lodge’s new clubhouse was attended by nine thousand people that represented Elks lodges from New York to Baltimore. Marquess was especially proud that nearly all the work on the new facility had been done by Black workers. “This home is a demonstration of what the black man can do when you give him a chance,” he proclaimed.
 Marquess was reelected again and again as Exalted Leader, but that does not mean his reign was without controversy. He had numerous conflicts with Magistrate Edward W. Henry, the leader of the O.V. Catto Lodge. In August 1932, Henry accused Marquess of robbing him of his reputation because Marquess had written an editorial critical of Henry in the Philadelphia Tribune . Marquess faulted Henry for stating at the first meeting of the National Negro Association Opposed to Atheism and Communism that “Communists are employing white girls at $10 a day to entice Negro youth to the Communist’s cause.” According to Marquess, “While sensible Negroes are fighting against segregated schools and working for jobs and political advancement, Magistrate Henry gives the ‘white women and Negro men’ argument new force and direction.”
 Loyalty to the GOP 
 Despite this very public spat, less than two months later the Tribune reported that “for the one hundredth time the Honorables…John Miller Marquess and Edward W. Henry have buried the hatchet.” The newspaper attributed this reconciliation to the two leaders’ joint desire to see Herbert Hoover reelected president of the United States on the Republican ticket. Marquess had become a leading figure in the state and national Republican party. Indeed, he was tapped to make a nomination speech for Hoover at the Republican Party convention in Chicago during the summer of 1932.
 As the “Party of Lincoln,” Republicans had a solid hold on the Black vote in the early 1930s, and Hoover vowed, at least when speaking in front of Black audiences, to promote civil rights should he be reelected. Throughout the decade, however, the African American vote shifted to favor the Democrats, in large part because of the New Deal.
 The exterior of the Keystone Temple at 1943 Christian Street during a 1942 Black Elks convention. Marquess oversaw the construction of the building and died while working there in 1936. | Photo: John Mosley, courtesy of the Charles L. Blockson Afro-American Collection
 This dynamic played out nationally, but also along Christian Street. The 1700 block of Christian Street was home to four Black State Representatives. John C. Asbury (1921-1924, 1710 Christian Street), William H. Fuller (1925-1932, 1705 Christian Street), Walker Jackson (1935-1936, 1724 Christian Street), and William A. Allmond (1937-1940, 1700 Christian Street). Allmond, previously a Republican, ran successfully as a Democrat in 1936 presaging an era of Black support for that party.
 However, in 1932, ambitious Black men like Marquess were still Republicans. One reason for this was the Republican outreach to Black communities. According to the Philadelphia Tribune , Hoover told a group of 300 Black supporters that “The platform of the Republican party speaks with justifiable pride of the friendship of our party for the American negro that has endured unchanged for 70 years. It pledges itself to the continued insistence upon rights.” In contrast, the article continues, “The Democratic platform is exceedingly quiet on the Negro question. It is absolutely silent.”
 The Tribune reported another factor discouraging Black voters from supporting the Democrats in 1932: the headquarters for Black Democrats in New York was set up apart from their white counterparts. In contrast, the Republican National Committee resisted “any physical Jim Crow set up.”
 Fighting Jim Crow 
 Marquess’ period of local leadership illustrates that racial segregation was a perennial threat, even in cosmopolitan cities in the North. In February 1931, Marquess was named the general secretary of the Grand Lodge Convention Committee, responsible for organizing a national gathering of Elks in Philadelphia during the following summer. Marquess used the leverage of tens of thousands of expected visitors to address two grievances regarding segregation with the Pennsylvania Railroad.
 In a letter to the company’s leadership, Marquess indicated that he had learned of the existence of separate washrooms for Black and white employees at 30th Street Station, a terminal that was then under construction. “If the company is allowed to get away with this,” wrote Marquess, “if we sit supinely by and make no effort to stamp out such a hideous thing, the next step will be to have Jim Crow waiting rooms for the passengers.”
 In his letter, Marquess also complained that Black passengers traveling to New York were only sold tickets for seats over the wheels on Greyhound buses, a company owned by the Pennsylvania Railroad at that time. Claiming to be expecting more than 100,000 visitors from across the country, Marquess warned that if the company did not change its policies, “I shall advise all of these delegates to WALK TO PHILADELPHIA rather than come over any of your lines.”
 A Quaker City Elks parade on Christian Street in 1942. | Photo: John Mosley, courtesy of the Charles L. Blockson Afro-American Collection
 Marquess seems to have succeeded in this pressure campaign, and he was soon threatening Nevin Bus Lines with a boycott and a lawsuit after 15 students returning to Lincoln University from Washington, D.C. and Baltimore were told to board a separate bus.
 Despite Marquess’ wealth and social status, the indignity of segregation remained a perpetual peril. In November 1932, Marquess went to the Penn Athletic Club at 18th and Locust Streets to attend a meeting of the Amateur Athletic Union. When told that he would need to ride the freight elevator, Marquess walked out.
 Another battle in which Marquess was engaged was to have a Black person appointed to the Board of Education. At the time, judges on the Court of Common Pleas appointed school board members and also distributed a large number of patronage jobs, none of which had been given to Black people. In his 1934 plea to the judges to appoint a respected Black doctor, John B. Turner, to the school board, Marquess lamented, “The Negro pupil in your school system, particularly in the secondary schools meets discrimination and embarrassments in a degree which saps his courage out of him. Both he and his parents are helpless because they have no one to whom they can really make an appeal and get a sympathetic hearing. Those who do finish our High Schools should be awarded special medals for having developed a super grit, which the negro surely must have in order to put up with conditions long enough to graduate.” In 1935, Dr. Turner became the first Black person to serve on Philadelphia’s Board of Education.
 A Tribute to the Tribune 
 It is not surprising that the Philadelphia Tribune , the nation’s oldest continuing Black newspaper, printed in-full Marquess’ letter in support of Dr. Turner. As a prominent Black leader living on a prominent Black corridor, Marquess’ name and activities appeared frequently in the Tribune’s pages. Other African American newspapers, from the Chicago Defender to the California Eagle, also reported on Marquess’ leadership in the Elks, the Republican party, and in the fight for equality. His name scantly appeared, however, in the Philadelphia Bulletin or the Philadelphia Inquirer .
 Marquess was aware of the importance of the Black press. At a 1932 event celebrating the 48th anniversary of the Tribune , Marquess stated, “Negroes should not only make it a rule to patronize those firms which advertise in Negro newspapers, but they should feel it a duty to ask firms with which they trade to advertise in the Negro press.” Just months before his death, Marquess spoke in Washington, D.C. before the Executive Committee of the Eastern Federation of Negro Republicans, an organization of which he was president. He described Black newspapers as “the best medium for the dissemination of political information among Negro groups.”
 A Quaker City Elks parade on either Broad Street or Washington Avenue in 1942. | Photo: John Mosley, courtesy of the Charles L. Blockson Afro-American Collection
 Alas, Marquess, only 54-years-old, suffered a fatal heart attack while working alone in his office at the Quaker City Elks Lodge Christian Street home on Sunday, May 3, 1936. This, too, was given extensive coverage in the Tribune . The newspaper included a heartbreaking description of the great man’s final moments. “Alone, according to police records and officials of the lodge, the smooth-faced, copper-colored Elks leader staggered to the chasm that leads to Eternity with none to lend him courage, none to soften the blow of the realization that his end had come.”
 Marquess’ body lay in state at the Quaker City Elks Lodge clubhouse. His casket was carried in a procession down Christian Street to Tindley Temple where thousands attended his funeral. Marquess’ erstwhile adversary Edward W. Henry was master of ceremonies. Like so many of the city’s Black leaders, John M. Marquess was buried at Eden Cemetery, an institution founded, in part, by Marquess’ former Republican Party ally and Christian Street neighbor, John Asbury.
 Author's Note: I learned about John M. Marquess’ fight against segregation of employee washrooms at 30th Street Station from the nomination submission for Christian Street/Black Doctors Row Historic District . This impressive document was written by Kevin Block and Adrian Trevisan for the Preservation Alliance of Greater Philadelphia. In an effort to learn more about that story, I fell down a Marquess rabbit hole. This article is a much-abridged summary of what I found.
 Christian Street circa 1910 to 1945 contains so much more rich history. In addition to politicians and doctors, the street was home to performers, pastors, architects, hairdressers, shoemakers, and strivers of every stripe. Although the Quaker City Lodge home was demolished, other institutional structures including the First African Baptist Church and the E.M. Stanton School remain standing.
 Now that Christian Street is an official historic district, I hope that more researchers take a closer look. I would love to see someone develop for Christian Street a project similar to the brilliant 1838 Black Metropolis which has recreated an earlier Philadelphia Black community in vivid detail. For more inspiration on the fascinating stories waiting be told, see my talk for the Preservation Alliance given earlier this year: https://vimeo.com/1054537588/dacb65f3ab 
 Tags: African-American history historic district John W. Mosley South Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Amy Cohen is an educator, historian, and writer. Her book "Black History in the Philadelphia Landscape: Deep Roots, Continuing Legacy" was published by Temple University Press in 2024.

title: Boom Goes the Dynamite: a 250-Year History of Philly's Love Affair With Fireworks
author: Kyle Bagenstose
bodyText:
The night was warm, but precipitation threatened, as 100,000 people crammed onto Lemon Hill and other Fairmount Park points to watch Fourth of July fireworks. “People of every garb, grade, and hue” thronged together, occupying all available spots in order to witness “what promised to be the greatest spectacle of pyrotechnics that this continent has ever beheld.” Ultimately the crowds were not to be disappointed, as the rain held off and the sky filled instead with rockets, sparkles, and imagery steeped in Americana: portraits of Washington and Lincoln, the Liberty Bell, and a great temple honoring each of the United States of America.
 150 years from now, perhaps an account of Philadelphia’s celebration of the nation’s semiquincentennial this year, will read something familiar. If it does, it will be an echo of an echo. The above description of Independence Day festivities hails from July 5, 1876 when the Philadelphia Inquirer reported on centennial celebrations of the night before.
 In so many ways the account sounds similar to the Benjamin Franklin Parkway celebrations of modern times. Poetically, the night of 1876 also spoke to fireworks’ ability to help bring together a fractured nation, at least for one evening. Among the symbols ignited in the sky that night, the newspaper reported, was a “conjunction of the North Star and the Southern Cross, emblematic of the reconstructed Union. A lesson of fraternal love that was beautiful and impressive.”
 But, wait. 150 years ago could fireworks really produce iconography as complex as Lincoln’s complicated face and the Liberty Bell? Was it really true that, in 1876, a “Professor Jackson,” the organizer of the show according to the Inquirer , was able to conjure up, which the newspaper described as the “greatest spectacle of fireworks” ever seen? “It was a great temple, allegorical of the rise and progress of our great country, presented in one extended view of fifty-four by one hundred and twelve feet,” the article retold. “The central figure was a cluster of thirteen columns, emblematic of the thirteen original states of the union, the name of each state appearing on the base of the columns.”
 This engraving from 1851 shows crowds gathered at Broad & Market Streets for a Fourth of July fireworks display. | Image courtesy of Print and Picture Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 Something doesn’t add up. Fortunately, Jesse Smith was able to square things. A curator and museum director at Science History Institute, Smith and co-curator Nadia Berenstein this spring launched the exhibition Flash, Bang, Boom!, which traces the science of fireworks from their black powder origins in ancient China to the cutting edge drone displays of today.
