 The answer to the riddle of 1876, Smith said, is something called a “set piece,” essentially an old-timey pyrotechnic display that involved igniting flammable materials attached to a grounded structure. The variety of set pieces was as wide as their creators’ imaginations, from something as basic to a pinwheel propelled by sparklers to elaborate, towering images of a person’s fiery portrait or an ornate building.
 Prior to the mid-20th century, such set pieces were popular and often deployed alongside airborne fireworks. The institute’s exhibit includes a large image of one made in the likeness of President Lyndon Baines Johnson that was displayed at the 1964 Democratic National Convention in Atlantic City. However, set pieces ultimately fell out of favor.
 All of this begs the question: How have Philadelphians celebrated the Fourth of July throughout the nation’s history? Here is an abridged history.
 1777: A Thirteen Cannon Salute and Hessians Made to Beat the Band 
 Infamously, Founding Father John Adams wrote in a letter to his wife Abigail that July 2–the day that the Continental Congress voted for independence in 1776–would go down as the one worth celebrating with “with Pomp and Parade…Games, Sports, Guns, Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this continent to the other from this Time forward forever more.”
 The prediction lasted only a year. In the July 5, 1777 edition of the Pennsylvania Evening Post , the day prior was already referred to as the “Anniversary of the Independence” of the United States, having marked one year since Congress approved the actual written copy of the Declaration of Independence. On that first Fourth of July anniversary, Philadelphians indeed did celebrate. Hostilities with Great Britain were already in full swing. The battles of Lexington and Concord were fought more than two years prior in April 1775. By the nation’s first official birthday, General George Washington had already made his daring crossing of the Delaware River to attack a Hessian garrison at Trenton and wage “10 crucial days” of battle. On the following Fourth of July in Philadelphia, the spoils were on display. “The Hessian band of music, taken in Trenton the 26th of December last, attended and heightened the festivity with some fine performances suited to the joyous occasion,” the Evening Post reported.
 Philadelphia was a much smaller city at that time, with a population of little more than 30,000 oriented along the Delaware River. It was in the river that at 1 p.m., 13 armed American ships lined up, decorated with the colors of the new nation, and discharged their cannons in celebration. Later, high-level political and military leaders gathered for a feast, entertained by the Hessian band and also a corps of British army defectors, who lined up to fire their muskets in a “feu de joie .”
 The Art of Making Fireworks, Detonating Balls, &c by Christopher Grotz, 1820. | Image courtesy of Brown University
 “After dinner, a number of toasts were drank, all breathing independence, and a generous love of liberty, and commemorating the memories of those brave and worthy patriots who gallantly exposed their lives, and fell gloriously in defense of freedom and the righteous cause of their country,” the newspaper reported, adding that each toast was followed by further discharges of weapons and music from the Hessians.
 In the streets, Philadelphians also engaged in celebratory gunfire and “huzzas.” A collection of soldiers gathered for a review on Second Street. At nightfall, bells rang throughout the city, followed, of course, by the first ever edition of Independence Day fireworks, a “grand exhibition” that concluded with thirteen rockets that “beautifully illuminated the city,” the newspaper retold.
 “Thus, may the Fourth of July, that glorious and ever memorable day, be celebrated through America, by the sons of freedom, from age to age till time shall be no more. Amen, and amen,” the Evening Post concluded.
 Revolution to Evolution 
 Fireworks at Ikenohata by Kobayashi Kiyochika, 1881. | Image courtesy of Metropolitan Museum of Art
 According to Berenstein, a science historian, modern fireworks are remarkably similar to those fired even centuries ago. Much of the underlying chemistry remains the same, and the construction of airborne fireworks requires customization, as well as the dexterity of human hands, largely resisting mechanical automation that now produces so many other modern consumer products.
 Typically, a firework shell contains a central explosive propellant connected to an external fuse, which is encased in additional layers of incendiary material carefully arranged to fire and explode in a manner that creates the desired aerial design. In other words, bisect a firework shell, and you’ll find an arrangement of small black powder balls (called “stars”) in the exact same shape as the explored firework later seen in the sky.
 Of course, there has been some evolution over time. Berenstein said the story begins in China in the 9th century AD, when monks discovered the explosive nature of black powder (saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal) during a quest to create a health elixir. The discovery quickly made its way into military and celebratory applications as rudimentary rockets and fireworks.
 An advertisement from 1902 for George Miller & Son, Co., importers of Mandarin Fire Crackers, Fire Works, Etc. that was unearthed in 2001 during the Cassatt House renovation at 1320 Locust Street. | Image courtesy of the Library Company of Philadelphia
 “Putting it in a confined space, think bamboo, that then generates a loud bang,” explained Berenstein. “Or putting pyrotechnic fountains and devices on a suit of armor. Just imagine a guy coming at you at night, with, like, flames shooting out of his shield.”
 As the technology spread west, Europeans then took things to another level, primarily by applying metallurgic knowledge to create the first firearms. The Catholic Church also took up the use of fireworks as a part of religious celebrations, and it was the Italians who became continental leaders in firework productions.
 When immigrants from Italy began to arrive en masse in the United States at the turn of the 20th century, including to Pennsylvania, they brought with them bigger and better rockets than were previously available on the continent, essentially the progenitors of what are seen in firework shows today. Their immigration coincidentally aligned with an increased interest in celebrating the Fourth of July after the Civil War, kicking off a rapid expansion of the domestic commercial firework industry. However, the introduction of beautiful, Italian-designed aerial rockets also led to a reduced interest in the earthbound-set pieces like the kind that wowed The Inquirer during 1876 celebrations. “There was a desire for bigger and bigger shows. It’s almost a kind of fireworks race,” said Smith. “At the same time, you’re really limited in the number of people who can see [a set piece]. You can sit on Belmont plateau and see fireworks, but you can’t really see ground effects.”
 Exploding Casualties 
 By the early 20th century, the American fireworks craze began to get a bit out of hand. The industry had shifted from supplying products primarily to professionals, and, instead, toward everyday consumers. America was about to gain an understanding of why booze, bombs, and rambunctious boys typically don’t mix.
 A July 6, 1909 edition of The Inquirer included an article titled “Fireworks Claim Annual Tribute from Patriots” and counted casualties by the hundreds: 257 Philadelphians harmed by gunpowder, 139 by fireworks, 29 by toy pistols, 12 by cannon, 12 by firearm, 5 by bombs, and 1 by “torpedo.”
 Whole Sale Price List, Spring 1886, pg. 56, Dynamite Fiend. Published by Selchow & Righter, New York, New York. | Image courtesy of Smithsonian Libraries and Archives
 A torpedo? Rather than the cigar-shaped projectile launched via submarine, Smith said it was likely one of the many varieties of consumer-grade fireworks used at the time. Indeed, an old wooden crate within the Flash, Bang, Boom! exhibit contains the word “torpedos” on the side along with labeling identifying the “New Jersey Fireworks Manufacturing Co.” of Vineland, New Jersey.
 Smith said his research found Vineland was historically a hotbed of firework production, quite likely due to its history of Italian immigration. Online auctions of antique toys appear to indicate that torpedoes were a form of hand-thrown firecracker produced in Vineland in the early 20th century.
 Eventually, Independence Day casualty counts became too much for public officials to abide. Littered throughout the first 50 years of the 20th century are newspaper reports detailing horrible injuries and deaths. In 1909 alone, three boys were hospitalized in serious condition after they placed their faces over a large cannon, whose black powder charge prematurely misfired. Elsewhere, a 14-year-old boy had his arm amputated by cannon fire, and a six-year-old girl whose dress caught fire would “probably die” from subsequent burns across her body, the newspaper reported. And the list went on. “Many lose fingers, several are shot,” read a sub-headline from the edition, which added the vast casualty count was extreme "despite the fact that the city’s celebration was one of the quietest in years.”
 Left: William Liemer, 13, is treated at Temple University's Northeastern Hospital in 1938 after playing with fireworks on the Fourth of July. Right: two boys from New York City, bandaged up at Bellevue Hospital after accidents with fireworks, pose in front of a Works Progress Administration poster in 1938. | Photos courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries and Museum of the City of New York
 By 1938, news reports detailed how state lawmakers were being “urged to ban [the] sale of fireworks.” Indeed, an article in the July 6 edition of The Inquirer said an editorial in the paper calling for regulation was the first of its kind and would be “Exhibit A” before a Pennsylvania General Assembly hearing the following year. Already, the sale of fireworks was banned in Philadelphia, but copious amounts of bootlegged materials were entering from suburban communities such as Media, Clifton Heights, Marple, and Newtown Square. Berenstein said the regulatory action fit with a larger national trend taking place at the time. “Around the turn of the 20th century, there is a kind of alliance between the American Medical Association and progressive women’s groups. It’s in the name of child safety. They’re trying to ban the sales of commercial fireworks,” she explained.
 Interestingly, the development of tetanus inoculation during the same time period also helped reduce deaths and injuries, as shrapnel from hand-held fireworks would carry dirt from the ground and act as a vector for bacteria to enter the human body.
 "Illegal Fourth of July fireworks, seized by the Philadelphia Police Department, are dumped by Fire Marshal William A. Haas (left) and Deputy Fire Commissioner Paul B. Hartenstein on the north parking lot at Municipal stadium," 1953. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Smith noted that in modern times many states have moved to deregulate fireworks, such as a 2022 Pennsylvania law that allows consumers to now purchase “Class C” varieties such as roman candles, firecrackers, bottle rockets, and artillery shells.
 “When I was a kid growing up in the 1980s, you’d have to go to a far-flung state to get fireworks,” said Smith. “Now, with the exception of Massachusetts, every state allows some kind of fireworks. That’s been the success of the industry: self-regulating and creating new safety standards.” This all appears to set the stage for perhaps what will indeed be Philadelphia’s largest ever pyrotechnics celebrations on this Fourth of July, with a combination of modern aerials, old-time set pieces, and recently unbridled consumer-grade fireworks all on display.
 Happy 250 and party safely, Philadelphians.
 Tags: Fourth of July holiday Semiquincentennial 
 About the Author
 Kyle Bagenstose is an independent journalist based in East Mt. Airy. Previously with USA Today, he writes primarily about environmental and urban topics.

title: Places to Save: Spring 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Spring 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Minority Arts Resource Council Building 
 Location : 1421 W. Girard Avenue
 Built : Circa 1883-85
 Threat : Unsafe L&I violation
 The former Minority Arts Resource Council (MARC) Building at 1421 W. Girard Avenue faces an immediate and precarious threat, as an “unsafe” determination could trigger City-led demolition. Built circa 1883-85, the richly ornamented rowhouse is a rare American example of exterior design influenced by the British Aesthetic Movement. Its exuberant facade combines graphic rosettes, naturalistic floral carving, richly modeled stonework, and an elaborate stone-and-copper cornice, setting it apart from the surrounding brick rowhouses. It is listed on both the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places and the National Register as part of the Girard Avenue Historic District , underscoring its recognized importance.
 The building was long owned by Curtis Brown, founder of the MARC, a nonprofit organization that provided opportunities for minority artists and craftspeople. Following Brown’s passing in early 2025, the property was listed for sale by his estate. During this transitional period, deterioration and structural instability, particularly of a non-historical rear addition, prompted the Department of Licenses & Inspections to issue an unsafe determination. While legitimate safety concerns exist, we believe the building’s historic core is not beyond repair and that targeted stabilization or partial demolition could resolve hazards without total loss.
 The fate of the MARC Building now hinges on overcoming the unsafe violation long enough to allow a preservation-minded buyer to step forward. With appropriate investment and care, the MARC Building can be stabilized and restored, honoring Curtis Brown’s legacy and reaffirming Philadelphia’s commitment to protecting its irreplaceable historic resources.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Green Hill Farm House 
 Location : 6953 Greenhill Road
 Built : 1916-19
 Threat : Lack of historic designation
 The house at 6953 Greenhill Road is an example of early 20th-century suburban residential design in West Philadelphia. Yet, it is currently unprotected from demolition or inappropriate alteration. (A nomination for the property has been submitted to the Historical Commission.) Built between 1916 and 1919 as a part of the Morris Estate’s first residential development of Green Hill Farm, the house was designed by the prominent architectural firm Mellor, Meigs & Howe and later altered by noted Philadelphia architect Louis Magaziner . Together with its companion property at 7001-09 Greenhill Road, it forms an unusual and carefully composed paired estate, with a shared garden wall, pergola, and central garage pavilion that read as a unified architectural ensemble.
 Despite its architectural pedigree, the property is not listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, leaving it vulnerable at a moment of transition. The house, long used as a single-family residence, was recently purchased by a religious organization to serve as its new headquarters. No specific plans for the property have been publicly disclosed, raising concerns about potential redevelopment that could compromise its historic character.
 This uncertainty underscores the need for proactive protection. Listing the property alongside its companion house on the Philadelphia Register would ensure that any reuse plans are subject to public review and preservation standards. The loss of this property would erode a key chapter in the planned suburban development of Green Hill Farm and diminish the architectural legacy of one of Philadelphia’s most influential design firms. Local designation offers a path forward that balances growth and respect for place.
 Photos: Peter Woodall
 Fairmount Park Houses 
 Location : 19 scattered sites in East and West Fairmount Park
 Built : Primarily 18th and 19th century
 Threat : Underfunding and lack of engagement
 Philadelphia’s Fairmount Park houses are among the city’s most extraordinary and vulnerable public historic resources. These architecturally significant estates were originally built as private villas by prominent Philadelphians seeking a rural retreat along the Schuylkill River. When the City used eminent domain to create Fairmount Park beginning in the mid-19th century, it inherited these houses, embedding layers of architectural, social, and civic history into the park’s landscape. Today, 19 historic houses remain, including three relocated from elsewhere in the city, while others have been lost to fire, vandalism, and insufficient funds.
 Despite their significance, many Fairmount Park houses suffer from deferred maintenance and chronic underfunding. Underutilized sites such as The Lilacs and Rockland Mansion, along with smaller, lesser-known resources like Boelson Cottage and Ormiston Mansion, face the biggest challenges, as limited public awareness makes it harder to justify investment or consistent stewardship. Even houses with long traditions as museums, such as Woodford, Laurel Hill, and Strawberry Mansion, rely heavily on volunteer organizations and nonprofit partners, stretching already thin resources.
 Since the 2010 consolidation of park oversight under Philadelphia Parks and Recreation, responsibility for these complex historic assets has grown, but dedicated funding has not kept pace. Organizational supporters like the Fairmount Park Conservancy and Park Charms demonstrate how creative partnerships and long-term leasing can stabilize and reactivate properties, yet broader investment and visibility are essential.
 To ensure these houses remain vital, accessible, and protected, the City must pair preventive conservation and regular maintenance with stronger public engagement and sustained funding.
 Tags: Fairmount Park Francisville Louis Magaziner Places to Save West Philadelphia 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: When Soup Societies Created Safety Nets for Philadelphians in Need
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
Spring Garden Soup House at 1329-31 Buttonwood Street was built in the mid-1800s and designed by architect Samuel Sloan. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 While income inequalities may have always existed in human societies, efforts to alleviate economic suffering have changed over time. The social service safety nets of today are relatively new inventions. In the 19th century, support generally came from the private sector and individuals. A familiar denizen of that time was the soup house, or soup society. Philadelphia, with an abundance of poor residents, was home to a number of these charities.
 Soup societies were generally founded to serve a particular neighborhood and ethnic group. The first was the Southwark Soup Society, founded in 1805 by James Ronaldson, who immigrated from Scotland in 1794, co-founded the first type foundry in the United States, and would go on to become the first president of the Franklin Institute. Located at 833 S. Hancock Street, at the time known as Sutherland Street, Southwark served a growing immigrant population who settled there after arriving at the Washington Avenue docks.
 In 1814, Southern Soup Society was founded in Green’s Court, between 4th and 5th Streets and Spruce and Pine Streets. At various times it was known as Green’s Court Soup House, the Philadelphia Soup House, and the Philadelphia Society for Supplying the Poor with Soup. In 1879, the address was referred to as 338 Griscom Street (now Lawrence Court).
 Beyond supplying soup and bread to the area poor, the Northern Soup Society, founded in 1817, also offered bathing facilities. Located on the second and third floors of their building on the northeast corner of 4th and Peters (now Reno) Streets, near Brown Street, Northern Soup Society's 18 showers provided 30,000 free baths per year by 1926. In the 1890s, it operated a branch at various locations further west and north, including 28th and Cumberland Streets, 24th and Huntingdon Streets, and 27th and York Streets.
 The Western Soup Society at 1613-15 South Street also operated a bath house after its founding in 1837. The need was great, as administrators noted “not more than one in ten of the 200 families we visited have bathing facilities in their homes.” Western Soup Society charged five cents per bath, which included soap and towels, noting that “all the Public Bath Associations of the city show a deficit.”
 In 1844 the Kensington Methodist Episcopal Church founded the East Kensington Soup Society to serve the mostly Protestant portion of Kensington east of Frankford Avenue, between Norris Street, Front Street, Laurel Street, and the Delaware River. At its first location on Allen Street, East Kensington Soup Society operated as a shelter as well, but when it moved to 1036 Crease Street, it was only a soup kitchen, changing its name to the Kensington Soup Society. For the first half of the 20th century, they also distributed coal to needy residents.
 An especially industrious group founded the Spring Garden Soup Society in 1853 and raised enough funds to purchase a lot and erect a building at 1329-31 Buttonwood Street. According to their records, the architect Samuel Sloan , known for his numerous Italianate villas and asylum buildings, donated his services for the project. The Cresson & Co. iron works donated a 90-gallon black iron soup pot. Spring Garden Soup Society also benefitted from their president’s position as head of the Atmore Mince Meat Company, which supplied meat for soup.
 At times the various soup societies argued over territory. They arrived at an agreement in 1862 that defined boundaries. A map drawn up at the time shows Spring Garden as serving an area between Market and Spring Garden Streets and from 8th Street to the Schuylkill River.
 A map showing the boundaries of the various Philadelphia soup societies operating between 1862 and 1880. | Image courtesy of the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
 Nearby, the Central Soup Society’s office, soup house, and bath rooms were located at 709-711 Cherry Street, where they also distributed coal, groceries, and clothing to poor residents from Walnut to Callowhill Streets and Broad Street to the Delaware River. Central Soup Society’s annual reports note Quaker philanthropist Anna T. Jeanes as a principal contributor, whose estate gave the soup society $3,000 for its endowment. Her brothers Samuel and Joshua were among the organizers of the society.
 In South Philadelphia, the Moyamensing Soup Society was founded in 1858 on the northwest corner of S. 8th and Marriott (now Montrose) Streets, below Christian Street, where it offered its printed notices in both English and Italian.
 After the Civil War, the 1870s saw more groups being founded, including the Richmond Soup Society in Port Richmond, the Northwestern Soup Society at 19th and Thompson Streets, the North Eastern Soup Society and Relief Association of the 19th Ward at 1930 N. Front Street, and the Twentieth Ward Soup Society at 11th and Jefferson Streets.
 The soup societies operated independently from any government support or input. Volunteer managers would solicit donations of either cash or supplies. Cash contributions from individuals were generally $5 or $10, though wealthier donors would give more, like Anthony Drexel ($50) or Anna Jeanes ($100). Many prominent companies from the era appear in the donor lists, such as the H. Disston & Sons Co., the Baldwin Locomotive Works, Strawbridge & Clothier , and Bailey, Banks & Biddle.
 Most operated between December through March, offering soup and bread, and sometimes more, such as coal, tea, sugar, or other food six days a week.
 Although soup society managers were generous with money and their volunteer time, they sometimes harbored a dim view of their clientele. Tickets were issued to families deemed “worthy” poor, which entitled them to a pint of soup and a half loaf of bread per person in the household. In its annual report in 1879, the Twentieth Ward Soup Society expressed concern about “how best to distribute charitable relief by discriminating between the deserving and unworthy poor and suppressing mendicancy.” The Northern Soup Society had similar views. “Care has been taken that none but deserving cases should partake of the benefits of this charity.” Moyamensing Soup Society's 1883 annual report noted, “We are happy to say that there was a decided improvement in the appearance of the applicants above those of former years in regard to cleanliness.”
 Administrators of soup societies would usually evaluate applicants by visiting their homes or relying on referrals. However, most were nevertheless willing to help homeless residents. In 1875, the Kensington Soup Society reported serving about 40 “transients” daily, in addition to an average of 370 families.
 The Northern Soup Society building at 4th and Reno Streets in 1951. | Image courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 In the early 20th century, many of the societies expanded their efforts to include other services. These were usually overseen by an "improvement committee" and carried out by a staff person known as a "visitor." Like the concerns of serving food only to the “deserving” poor, these additional offerings also had a moralistic tone, intending to “exert such an influence on the lives of the people asking aid, as to make them self-respecting and self-reliant,” as the Northern Soup Society noted in a report.
 The services often included help in securing employment, doctor and hospital referrals, sponsoring children for summer camp outside of the city, Thanksgiving and Christmas baskets, and small loans for groceries or to help a move to better quarters.
 In addition, the Western Soup Society offered cooking and sewing classes, a branch of the Penny Saving Fund, and a temporary home for women with children. In 1916, the Richmond Soup Society offered violin and singing lessons, a children's annual outing to Smith Memorial Playground, a shoe mending service, a sewing class for women, and a class in domestic science for “women who have spent much of their lives in the mills of Kensington.”
 The activities of the soup societies reflected major events of the 19th and early 20th centuries. The impetus for the founding of the oldest of the soup societies was the War of 1812 and the Panic of 1819.
 Philadelphia experienced a smallpox epidemic in 1872, which was acknowledged in the report of the North Western Soup Society, noting that “fear of infection from contact with a crowd prevented many from availing themselves of the benefits of the Society,” reducing the amount of soup distributed. They also observed that all the city’s soup houses seemed to have experienced this.
 In 1918, the Northern Soup Society provided 100 gallons of soup each day to 11 emergency hospitals, nine health centers, six public schools and Settlement Houses during the Spanish flu epidemic . In the 7th Ward, the Western Soup Society also supplied soup to the nearby Durham Public School and to Mercy-Douglass Hospital and University Settlement House.
 Western Soup Society noticed there was less demand for their relief work in 1923, “due to better economic conditions and the advent of Prohibition.” A few years later, they would see a reversal, noting in 1931 during the Great Depression that “to meet the demands of the unemployment situation, much more relief has been given.”
 In the 1940s during World War II, Kensington Soup Society aided injured servicemen and their families.
 The Kensington Soup House at 1036-38 Crease Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 After expanding their range of services, some of the soup societies felt challenged to continue as small volunteer operations and eventually merged with other charitable organizations. Southwark Soup Society merged with the Union Benevolent Association in 1949. The Western Soup Society underwent mergers with settlement houses, ultimately becoming the community agency Diversified Community Services, now known as Greater Philadelphia Community Alliance.
 Others changed their approach to their charitable work by reorganizing as private foundations and giving grants to other organizations fighting food insecurity. Spring Garden Soup Society, with assets of about $1 million, reorganized as a private foundation. In 2023, they gave $74,000 in grants for food supplies to 11 shelters, church food programs, and soup kitchens in Philadelphia. North Eastern Soup Society & Relief Association 19th Ward Philadelphia still retains the name, but is based in Las Vegas, Nevada, giving grants to Philadelphia organizations. Central Soup Society, with current members largely in Virginia and Florida, gives grants that average about $1,500 to charities in various locations, with some focused on food, including Philadelphia’s Philabundance. Kensington Soup Society, the last of its kind operating in Philadelphia, closed its doors in 2007.
 While Philadelphia's soup society era has passed, a few of the buildings that formerly housed them remain. The successor to the Western Soup Society, Greater Philadelphia Community Alliance, still operates some of their programs from the organization's original building at 1613-15 South Street.
 The Spring Garden Soup Society building at 1329-31 Buttonwood Street was added to Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1969, and the Kensington Soup Society building at 1036-38 Crease Street was designated in 2012. Now a private residence with a state historic marker in front, the Southwark Soup Society building at 833 S. Hancock Street was designated in both 1958 and 1966. In 2022, the building for the North Eastern Soup Society & Relief Assn of the 19th Ward Philadelphia at 1930 N. Front Street was demolished to make way for a five-story apartment block.
 Tags: Fishtown food history 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Communism and the Quaker City
author: Keshler Thibert
bodyText:
The threat of communism is the newest rhetorical weapon of the Trump Administration. The president has been responding to the recent campaign wins of Democratic socialists in Philadelphia, Colorado, and New York as a communist-led “mortal threat to American liberty” that needs to be removed “like a cancer.” Inflamed propaganda used by Trump and others to miscategorize progressive politicians and groups with belligerent references to McCarthyism and the Second Red Scare of the 1950s ignores the facts of communism's core ideology and the history and legacy of its place in America.
 The Communist Party of the United States (CPUSA) reached its zenith from 1936 to 1939, kicking off the era by helping to re-elect President Franklin D. Roosevelt with his expanded New Deal. Earl Browder served as general secretary of the party under a platform of “For Jobs, Security, Democracy, and Peace,” and is still remembered for his powerful presence and February 1930 speech for the unemployed at Philadelphia City Hall. World War II loomed, and local anti-war activists like decorated U.S. Marine Corps officer Smedley Butler grew concerned the Democratic Party might lead the United States into a foreign war.
 Children demonstrate during a communist rally at Philadelphia City Hall on January 14, 1933. | Image courtesy of ExplorePAHistory.org
 Philadelphia was suffering from the Great Depression and reeling from the infamous Battle of Reyburn Plaza, where radical organizers of different races armed with makeshift weapons clashed with police over the abysmal economics of the city, leading to the arrests of hundreds and changing the dynamics of “interracial militancy.” The Spanish Civil War had just begun, attracting individuals into both the CPUSA and the Popular front. Many of those same people went on to volunteer to fight against fascism under the banner of the “Lincoln Brigade.”
 The second general convention of The National Negro Congress in May 1937 brought to Philadelphia speakers such as Walter White of the N.A.A.C.P and T.J. Kennedy of the CPUSA. Up for discussion was the end of fascism, the CPUSA, and the first Garbage Riot of March 1937, which left a stench around the city as trash pilled up on street corners. Unbeknownst to them the second Garbage Riot in July 1938 was a little over a year away. At this time, a younger generation, disillusioned by the Great Depression, lack of jobs, abysmal women’s rights, racism, and politics, joined the Communist Party.
 Come One, Come All 
 Philadelphia has always been a consequential city for the CPUSA. In 1857, Marxists marched with the unemployed for relief during the Panic of 1857. They also marched in New York and Chicago. In December 1869, the Noble and Holy Order of the Knights of Labor initially organized Philadelphia garment workers and later included other trades. The Knights of Labor expanded to Reading, Pennsylvania for its first assembly in 1878. It then went nationwide with a clear objective “to establish co-operative institutions such as will tend to supersede the wage system by the introduction of co-operative industrial system.” A few years later, the International Workingmen’s Association came to an end only days before the reorganization of the socialist Workingmen’s Party of America, rechristened the Socialist Labor Party in July 1876.
 This print from 1886 shows the leaders of the Noble and Holy Order of the Knights of Labor. Founder Uriah S. Stephens is enshrined within a shield and wreath at top-center. | Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 The Manifesto of the Communist Party, published in February 1848 by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, appealed to the labor class from European nations. It dissimilated mantras of “every class struggle is a political struggle” and “the emancipation of the working class must be the act of the working class itself” spread through publications such as Die Revolution , a German-American communist newspaper.
 The turn of the century introduced the arrival of Marxist immigrants to the United States following the Russian Revolution in 1905. However, by the 1930s they were old. A younger Jewish generation of CPUSA were recruited at gatherings in Strawberry Mansion or at party headquarters at 5th and Spring Garden Streets. They liked what was transpiring in the Soviet Union and saw potential to do more within an American framework.
 Communism on Campus 
 Oral histories of the 1930s, captured in the 1960s, reveal reasons behind joining the American communist party. Ethel Paine, a Black Communist, was inspired by activist Eslanda Goode Robeson, a supporter of communism. Tim Palen was brought in by a member who showed him what was happening in the Soviet Union and predicted the Wall Street crash of 1929. Milt Goldberg was approached at a Society of Friends Center by a couple of Swarthmore College students who commented he was “too advanced” for Quaker activities.
 “Dust Off Your Dreams, The Story of American Youth for Democracy" a 24-page booklet published by the American Youth for Democracy in 1945. | Image courtesy of the American Library Association
 Jack Ryan was influenced by an older socialist factory worker who explained the ideology in simple terms. Individuals were recruited through campus events that explained the causes behind the economic crisis and inequality, often resulting in students returning to campus to argue with professors over the causes of the Great Depression. In Philadelphia Communists, 1936-1956 , published in 1982 by Temple University Press, Arthur Liebman is quoted as saying this about campus communists: “Those who were attracted and became involved with the left, especially those who rose to leadership positions as student leftists, were not campus oddballs. They were generally the brightest, most dedicated students.”
 Racial Composition 
 Within the Philadelphia branch of the CPUSA, there were tensions within the party. Membership mainly consisted of Jews followed by Blacks. However, Fred Garst described the branch as “a Jewish organization with a goyishe cup (gentile head) and a token Negro" with a smattering of Eastern European Catholics and white Protestants.
 There were meetings, lectures, classes, and concerts. Discussions and get-togethers took place in homes, often multiple times in one day, to share food and resources with members in need. Gatherings at popular locations, such as the Horn & Hardhart Automat (aka “The Heel”) 219 S. Broad Street, provided political discussions during lunch. Over time, many proclaimed that communism felt more like a family that extended throughout the nation.
 A Communist Party campaign poster from 1932 featuring William Z. Foster and James W. Ford as candidates for president and vice president. | Image: Public Domain
 Yet, racial disparities, especially recruitment and obligations in majority Black neighborhoods, began to show. Some members thought Blacks were being used and patronized, while others thought they were not politically developed enough to be in the party. A few felt uncomfortable saying anything, believing they would be labeled as racial chauvinists.
 African American members felt discomfort around members who had Black maids or the means to travel to Atlantic City and Miami Beach for vacation. This was compounded by each group’s struggles in the workplace, which was later mitigated by Edward Strong, an African American activist that was respected among Black communists. However, many whites in the party thought he was too color-conscious and nationalistic.
 International Workers’ Day 
 Within the party, protests against the Second Italo-Ethiopian War and Spanish Civil War became cause célèbres, but the International Workers’ Day on May 1 (aka May Day) protests of 1938 attracted larger crowds. Its origin traced back to the 1820s and 1830s when demands for shorter workdays grew. The Mechanics Union of Philadelphia, often referred to as the first trade union in the world, successfully petitioned for a 10-hour workday in 1827. New York City followed a few years later during the Bakers’ Strike of 1834, eventually becoming part of a bigger movement that President Van Buren made into law.
 Slowly, new demands began for an 8-hour day under the slogan, “8 hours work, 8 hours recreation, and 8 hours rest.” This movement used the American Civil War to further its cause. Marx wrote in 1867, “The first fruit of the Civil War was an agitation for the 8-hour day–a movement which ran with express speed from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from New England to California.” The selection of May 1 for the protests was made in Paris in 1889.
 The Philadelphia branch of the Communist Party of the United States held a rally on May Day, 1935 across the street from City Hall and Broad Street Station. | Photo: Public Domain
 Over the decades the event evolved becoming a yearly rallying point for various causes. In 1938, May Day attracted crowds of up to 30,000 people to City Hall and consisted of labor unions, activists, and CPUSA members under the banner of reform. Protesters called out big businesses, such as ESSO’s unfair treatment of American seamen, autocratic City management, and characters such as Hitler, Hirohito, and Neville Chamberlain. In 16 months Germany would invade Poland and officially start World War II.
 The Molotov–Ribbentrop (Nazi–Soviet Non-Aggression Pact) of August 1939, congressional cuts to New Deal programs, and Franco’s victory in the Spanish Civil War all caused many members of CPUSA to question their membership. The slow decline lasted into the 1950s with the Second Red Scare, McCarthyism, and revelations of what was truly happening in the Soviet Union under Stalin.
 In reality, many members were too busy to meet the demands of party life. The war kept them engaged, while the intellectual class pontificated on their causes. The working class began to look at the more intellectual party members as wasting time. Others became more nationalistic by selling war bonds or taking on new positions at work that developed into distrust and divisions. By the end of 1939, the political landscape had changed dramatically and the party suffered for it.
 Tags: civil rights Donald J. Trump labor unions political history 
 About the Author
 Keshler Thibert is a voracious reader, book collector, tour guide, and current member of the Association of Philadelphia Tour Guides. He was born and raised in Philadelphia, but has also lived in Atlanta, GA, Santiago de Chile, Madrid, Patras, Greece, and Adelaide, South Australia. Thibert has an interest in social sciences, language, and local history. Read more of his work on Substack .

title: Neglected Burk Mansion on North Broad Street Gets Ready For a Revival
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on May 8, the Philadelphia Historical Commission approved the rehabilitation of two historically designated properties and offered comments on a nomination to the National Register of Historic Places.
 The Alfred Edward Burk Mansion at Broad and Jefferson Streets has sat vacant for 31 years. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Temple University received permission for alterations and new construction for the property at 1500-10 North Broad Street , which it has owned for over half a century. The Alfred Edward Burk Mansion and a rear conservatory building were built in 1909 in the Italian Renaissance style by architects Simon and Bassett, whose other credits include the Lit Brothers Store on Market Street and the Manufacturers Club at 150 S. Broad Street. A rear addition was designed in 1954 by architect Louis Manfredi. It was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1971. The following year it was included in the Historic American Buildings Survey . The building has been vacant since 1995 due to a fire.
 The repair work includes restoring a stone balustrade along the site’s perimeter, replacing windows and doors, and rehabilitating the landscaping and walkways. Many of the alterations are to improve accessibility. The proposed new construction would be an addition at the rear.
 The owners of 40 Spring Garden Street received permission from the Historical Commission to construct a three-story addition to the industrial complex's former Ice Machine House. Pictured is the in-concept proposal that was submitted to the Historical Commission. | Rendering: Lo Design
 New construction was also approved for a portion of the Philadelphia Warehousing and Cold Storage Company complex at 40 Spring Garden Street . The two-story building, known as Building D, faces North Beach Street and is clad in red brick with stone details. It was constructed between 1891 and 1900 as the Ice Machine House, later serving as a Machine Shop. The owners proposed constructing a three-story addition and other renovations to convert it to a residential mixed-use building, for which they received in-concept approval from the Historical Commission.
 De Long Hook and Eye Company Factory at 21st and Clearfield Streets. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Commission reviewed a nomination to the National Register for the De Long Hook and Eye Company Factory at 3031-49 N. 21st Street . Nominations of Philadelphia properties to the National Register are overseen by the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission and must solicit comments from the appropriate local government, which in turn must offer an opportunity for public comment. The Historical Commission speaks on behalf of the City of Philadelphia on historic preservation matters.
 The De Long Hook & Eye Company was one of the largest and best-known manufacturers of sewing accessories in the United States during the first half of the 20th century. In 1889, Frank Emerson De Long patented a new type of hook and eye fastener, which became immensely popular nationwide.
 De Long Hook & Eye advertisement, Ladies Home Journal, October 1923. | Image courtesy of National Park Service, United States Department of the Interior
 The four-story, reinforced concrete building, designed by the William Steele & Sons Company in 1917, features large, multi-light steel factory windows. The parcel also includes a one-story brick boiler house with a gabled roof. The Steele Company also built the nearby Steel Heddle Manufacturing Company, which was added to the National Register in 2010 and the Philadelphia register in 2022 . The De Long Hook & Eye Company Factory is not currently listed on the local register.
 Historical Commission members commented favorably on the nomination as a prime example of early 20th century factory buildings. They noted that National Register nominations often are submitted with the intent to subsequently apply for federal tax credits. The building's current owner, Deliverance Evangelistic Church, plans to convert it into 56 apartments designated for seniors over the age of 62 whose income is below 50 percent of the area median.
 The National Marine Engineers Beneficial Association building at 4th and Willow Streets. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The Historical Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation did not meet in April, so there were no new nominations for the full Commission to consider at this meeting. The nomination for the National Marine Engineers Beneficial Association building at 428-34 N. 4th Street , which had been reviewed by the Historic Designation Committee in May 2025, was scheduled for review at this meeting, but has been continued to the Commission’s June meeting.
 The nominations of the Morris Estate House at 6953 Greenhill Road and a house at 5000 McKean Avenue have been continued to the July meeting. The two long-standing nominations of Piers 38 and 40 South at 775 S. Christopher Columbus Boulevard , originally nominated in October 2021, and Jewelers Row Historic District , nominated in December 2018, have yet to be added to a Historical Commission meeting agenda.
 Tags: Historical Commission Meeting Report National Register of Historic Places Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Anger and Advocacy Fuel Demands for Securing University Avenue Bridge
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
University Avenue Bridge opened to traffic on May 10, 1933. Today the Beaux Arts landmark is a symbol of blight and negligence along the Schuylkill River Trail. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Paul Philippe Cret was one of Philadelphia’s greatest architects of the early 20th century and left his mark on a long list of buildings and structures that are still revered today. The Benjamin Franklin Bridge, the Rodin Museum, the old Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, the original Barnes Foundation in Merion, the Ellen Phillips Samuel Memorial in Fairmount Park, and the gates of Woodlands Cemetery are all Cret’s work and are respected and carefully maintained. So it is all the more perplexing that another surviving example of Cret’s artistry, the University Avenue Bridge, has been neglected and left to the mercy of vandals and graffiti. A petition was launched earlier this month to spotlight the vulnerable and blighted state of the bridge in hopes of turning awareness into action.
 Cret designed the bridge in 1925, working with Stephen H. Noyes, an engineer for the City of Philadelphia. The limestone-faced, concrete on steel bridge spans the Schuylkill River, connecting South 34th Street in Grays Ferry with University Avenue in University City. It is a double-leaf bascule bridge, a type of draw bridge that uses counterbalance weights and machinery to aid the raising of the decks.
 A pair of the bridge's bronze lanterns remain safe from theft for now. Much of the historic span's ornamentation and architectural details has been stolen, vandalized, or destroyed. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Cret combined modern classicism with Beaux-Arts styling, with features such as carved friezes and finials, bronze lanterns decorated with stylized leaves, scallop designs and sea horse motifs, and two octagonal bridge operator's houses with large windows on each side.
 Although most of Philadelphia’s major waterfront industry was along the Delaware River when the bridge opened in 1930, parts of the Schuylkill River’s banks were home to many industries such as coal, ice yards, and fuel oil companies that relied partly on water transport to move cargo. They employed barges pulled by tall tug boats, which meant the new bridge needed to be a drawbridge.
 Windows have been smashed and the door of the bridge's east-facing operator's house has been stolen. Used hypodermic needles and other dangerous debris currently cover the floor. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 While Cret and Noyes developed the structural design, City Chief Engineer John A. Vogelson planned the mechanical elements. Their initial design extended the west approach further into West Philadelphia with a viaduct over the Pennsylvania Railroad’s tracks. After receiving objections from Woodlands Cemetery and the University of Pennsylvania, the approach was shortened, ending at a tunnel under the tracks.
 The bridge was originally owned by the City of Philadelphia, which transferred ownership to the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT) in 1961 when the road became part of a state highway.
 Inside University Avenue Bridge. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The University Avenue Bridge was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1993 and to the National Register of Historic Places in 1994 . It was included in the National Park Service's Historic American Engineering Record in 1999.
 The National Register nomination states that the bridge received new bascule lifting machinery, including a new bascule lifting span, in 1983, although, according to PennDOT, the last opening of the bridge was two years later in 1985.
 Inside University Avenue Bridge. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Despite its storied lineage and documented significance, the bridge today is in shockingly bad condition. Thieves have stolen its bronze doors and electrical elements, vandals have smashed its many windows, and the exterior and operator’s houses are marred by graffiti.
 Cret designed his first bridge, the Delaware River Bridge (now the Benjamin Franklin Bridge), in 1922. Its planning began after the Delaware River Bridge Joint Commission, now the Delaware River Port Authority (DRPA), was created to supplement the ferries on the river.
 Inside University Avenue Bridge. The historic draw bridge's machine room sits in ruin. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Vehicular traffic on the Benjamin Franklin Bridge is double the volume of the University Avenue span. However, the University Avenue Bridge, connecting two populous neighborhoods and only a fraction of the length of the Benjamin Franklin Bridge, is also an important thoroughfare for pedestrians, runners, and cyclists. As the Benjamin Franklin Bridge receives accolades this year for its 100-year anniversary and receives regular maintenance by its owner, DRPA, the University Avenue Bridge continues to decay, seemingly ignored by PennDOT.
 Industrial traffic along the Schuylkill River waned in the 20th century, but the bridge plays an important role for entering and exiting vehicular traffic on the Schuylkill Expressway. Two recent developments have elevated the bridge’s visibility in the public eye. The University of Pennsylvania's eastward expansion includes Pennovation Works , a 23-acre site that houses around 100 entrepreneurs in its labs, offices, and co-working spaces and is literally at the foot of the University Avenue Bridge. The Schuylkill River Trail also continues grow its southward and westward segments. The trail now winds its way right under the bridge, which gives it a convenient access point for cyclists and pedestrians into and from West Philadelphia.
 The Grays Ferry's gateway to University City is covered in graffiti. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 This increased visibility has recently raised alarms. The Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia included the University Avenue Bridge on its list of "Places to Save" in the Winter 2026 edition of its publication Extant. In June, The Philadelphia Inquirer published an op-ed by classical music critic and culture writer Peter Dobrin that advocates for an immediate intervention.
 Last week local preservationist Heather Calvert launched a Change.org petition to secure and restore the bridge , urging signees to contact both PennDOT and Philadelphia City Council “to demand immediate security measures for the bridge.” 
 “I am hoping the City could secure the site–clean it, board up the windows,” she explained. “Given how close it is to the Schuylkill River Trail, and a major entry point for the city, I would think that leadership would be embarrassed and want it to be secured. If not the City than Penn or CHOP. The big employers with real estate and clout, and lobbyists, in this town.” 
 Launched on July 10 , the petition surpassed its original goal of 250 signatures within days and is now seeking 500 supporters. “I launched it the night before the Benjamin Franklin Bridge was open to pedestrians thinking there would be a lot of bridge and Paul Cret fans,” Calvert said. “I then handed out 500 flyers on the bridge [Benjamin Franklin Bridge]. Everyone who knew the bridge [University Avenue Bridge] said the same thing. They could not believe that it was being left open the way it is.” 
 Tags: abandoned National Register of Historic Places Paul Cret Philadelphia Register of Historic Places University Avenue Bridge urban blight 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: In Pursuit of Greatness: the Challenges of Creating a Groundbreaking Docuseries
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
A film still of Philadelphia looking north from 17th Street and Snyder Avenue. From Episode 1: "Freedom," In Pursuit: Philadelphia and the Making of America. | Courtesy of History Making Productions
 At this precarious moment in American history it seems prudent, even necessary, to reexamine how we got here. Fortunately, we have In Pursuit: Philadelphia and the Making of America , a richly textured and thoughtfully crafted 10-part docuseries from History Making Productions.
 In Pursuit was written by novelist and Hidden City co-founder Nathaniel Popkin, directed by multiple Mid-Atlantic Emmy Award winner Andrew Ferrett, and produced by Sam Katz, award-winning producer, director, and founder of History Making Productions. The docuseries turns the clock back to the 17th century and takes us on a journey through time and place while holding a mirror to the United States, Philadelphia, and, ultimately, ourselves. The collection is infused with lively recreations, dynamic cinematography, and imaginative visualizations of historic documents.
 David Owen Bell caught up with director Andrew Ferrett to discuss production, process, and the pursuit of a life in film.
 David Bell : What does the phrase “in pursuit” mean to you as it relates to the concept of the series?
 Andrew Ferrett : As the historian Sophia Rosenfeld says in Episode Three, the “pursuit of happiness,” named in the Declaration of Independence, offers “something like a scripture for what American life is going to be. You’ve been told in this very abstract way: Go for it.” When we recorded that interview, we did not yet have the title In Pursuit . Yet, the more we thought about the concept of the series, it became clear that each era could be defined by a different American pursuit. I think it is generally true that Americans are interested in pursuing happiness, but that usually means pursuing something else that you think will give you happiness–freedom, land, equality, wealth, escape, etc. So we worked a number of these concepts into the titles of the episodes. Sometimes the pursuits are collective or societal.
 Each of our 10 episodes matches a period of time with a corresponding American pursuit, which is named in the episode title (“Freedom,” “Wealth,” etc.). The pursuits layer on and reverberate in the story over time, and the early ones start to pop up in later episodes. The pursuits arose out of similarities we observed across stories, and we were able to use the “pursuit” frame as a guiding star for each episode. We also looked at whether a story felt relevant to the American experiment as a whole. If a story seemed primarily of local relevance, we did not include it.
 DB : Setting out to explore five centuries of history and presenting it to a wide audience over roughly 10 hours strikes me as a huge undertaking. What were the initial challenges in getting this project off the ground?
 AF : When embarking on a project at this level of ambition the first major challenge is to get people to buy into your vision at all. In 2019, after we completed a docuseries on Philadelphia history for the local ABC affiliate, my collaborators and I realized that we were sitting on a much deeper and bigger story. 
 Across hundreds of interviews we observed that Philadelphia’s history offers a strikingly true mirror on the history of the United States itself that goes well beyond the Declaration of Independence. With In Pursuit , we wanted to show how Philadelphians have lived and often defined the American experience–from the struggles for religious freedom, land, the abolition of slavery, and the creation and control of industry, to the dispossession of native peoples, the long fight for equal rights and lived equality, the transformations of urban renewal, immigration, and suburbanization. All of these are quintessentially Philadelphian and American pursuits. 
 And yet, regardless of what we thought, the history of Philadelphia has rarely been presented to the nation as a mirror of U.S. history. In fact, no documentary had posited the "mirror" idea about another American city. Even Ric Burns’ wonderful 1999 series about New York makes it clear that New York’s unique history stands apart from much of the nation. That signaled to us that an opportunity existed, but there wasn’t a clear path for making this leap. We had to grapple with how to make Philadelphia’s story feel relevant to a wider audience of Americans, all without appearing boosterish or provincial. 
 Director Andrew Ferrett and the In Pursuit crew filming at the Elkins Estate in Montgomery County. Actor Jasmine Leilani Kyle plays the role of American contralto and civil rights pioneer Marian Anderson. | Photo: Charles Bouril courtesy of History Making Productions
 DB : What were the key production and post-production challenges you and your team faced? How were they overcome?
 AF : The filmmaking challenge was sprawling: how to envision a unified, accurate, and cinematic arc that can carry a general audience across 10 hours and five centuries of history. In the first episode, for example, we knew people would connect with the deeply-felt beliefs of the original Lenape people and the English Quakers and their parallel and conflicting struggles to live their ideals of personal freedom and liberty amidst persecution. However, the available archival visuals don’t always yield perfect images for the stories we hope to tell, especially in the 1600s and 1700s, so we had to devise a combination of re-creations, scenic cinematography, and creative use of archival materials to bring life to passions from hundreds of years ago. 
 History Making Productions’ remarkable interview archive, dating back almost two decades, posed unique challenges. We didn't want In Pursuit to be visually limited by hundreds of studio interviews that we had already recorded. While they were beautifully photographed and contained essential storytelling, all were shot on the same neutral backdrop for economy of scale. I felt that the repetitive backdrop could make In Pursuit feel rather drab over 10+ hours. So, we produced Deepener segments that take the action out of doors at strategic points in each episode to re-set the visual palette as we watch some brilliant, deep thinkers reflect on Philadelphia history while at large in the city itself. We position these Deepeners at turning points in the story, which gives the added benefit of letting some information sink in before we push to the next chapter.
 DB : Were the re-enactments the most time-consuming and labor-intensive aspects of production?
 AF : It is true that we invested the largest portion of our production budget in dramatic re-creations spanning from the 1600s to the 1930s, aiming for credibility and authenticity in costumes, styling, locations, props, grit, and human density. I’m drawn to re-creations, partially because they can dramatically elevate the documentary as a whole and especially because they empower us to tell stories that exist without any visual documentation. The story of the enslaved man, Sampson, in our second episode, is a good example. From a story contained on only a few pieces of paper, re-creations allowed us to create a dramatic, vividly true picture of his experience.
 We deliberately do not record dialogue for our scenes, but rather let our on-camera experts tell the story while our terrific audio post team creates sound design of the events we have dramatized. I favor the “silent movie” re-enactment approach with its resulting emphasis on action and expression.
 Animations and b-roll are more budget-friendly routes for storytelling, but we ultimately felt our stories were so human and dramatic that they demanded the most dynamic cinematic approach that we could afford. Fortunately for us, Sam Katz convinced a broad array of donors and foundations to share our vision. That allowed us to work with a top-notch professional crew to realize the re-creations on the screen.
 DB : In Pursuit features stunning aerial footage of Philadelphia. I assume this was accomplished with drones.
 AF : Drones have changed the game for small documentary film companies. Not so long ago, getting aerial shots could mean hiring a helicopter with a specialized camera mount, all of which could run into tens of thousands of dollars. It has been fun to experiment with the agility and flexibility of drones, which can fly places a helicopter never could go and at a much lower cost.
 DB : What other relatively new technology was used and how?
 AF : Closer to the ground, our approach had some throwback qualities. Since much of Philadelphia’s fame arises from the documents created here, I wanted to bring our camera into archives to capture the way the handwriting and type press into the page on those documents. These tabletop shoots are time consuming and intricate, and are not often done any more with high-res digital scans usually available. Yet, I have always loved the tactile appearance of objects on camera in documentaries made years ago. It turns out the camera lens has a special ability to reveal the physical dimension of the page, which a scan doesn’t approach. When I see these pages through the camera, I think about how these words were written by real people like any of us.
 Cinematographer Paul Van Haute and Michael Pace of the Delaware Tribe of Indians in 2019. | Photo: Nathaniel Popkin courtesy of History Making Productions
 DB : Was there new technology that was rejected?
 AF : In Pursuit does not use any A.I.-generated imagery or video. Between our re-creation shoots, interviews, and office work, this project has employed over 100 film workers and artists in the Philadelphia area.
 DB : You and your team worked with more than 30 collaborators and partners and more than 35 funders. With their privacy in mind, were there conflicting interests, agendas, points of view, or attempts to influence subject matter that needed to be resolved?
 AF : As a director I cannot recall a project where I have felt less interference from funders or more freedom to construct the film as I intended. It was my goal to make an accurate, honest, fair, and engaging history that could connect with a broad array of people across differing points-of-view. Of course, we had internal debates that are natural in any creative project, but these stemmed from the perspectives of the filmmakers, not from any funder or partner attempting to sway our work. Over the years our team has delivered an impressive roster of civically-minded, entertaining films. It has been my experience that our funders come in with an understanding of our fair-minded and rigorous approach.
 DB : Was there anything you wanted to do but couldn’t because of time or money?
 AF : If we had more money and time (much easier said than done) I would have loved to produce dramatizations for the final third of the series. In Pursuit only includes dramatic re-creations through the seventh episode. The final three episodes–spanning the late 20th and early 21st century–draw upon archival footage and photos from newspapers, TV stations, and individuals to bring events to life. The storytelling doesn’t miss a beat, and in some ways feels even more immediate and authentic, but I can’t help but imagine how we could have applied our re-creation approach to this period. As a director, I feel invigorated when I’m creating scenes expressly to serve the film’s needs, and trying to design action as close to historical reality as possible, but time and budget did not allow us to take that on for the later episodes.
 DB : How did your personal life change over the several years of this project? Did that impact your work?
 AF : I first began working with Sam Katz on the predecessor to this project in 2008, so my personal life has changed quite a bit in those decades! I’ve since gotten married, moved several times, and later this summer we are expecting our first child. Given the total commitment required to realize a project like this, In Pursuit has probably shaped my life more than my life has shaped the project. 
 The experience of living in Philadelphia while making a documentary about Philadelphia offers endless potential inputs, whether you’re looking for them or not. Practically every block you walk–or every person you talk to–can jog the memory about a story of some historical significance. I lived for many years in South Philadelphia where our writer Nathaniel Popkin also lives, so perhaps a little South Philly bias leaked into our story selection, but since it is the oldest settled part of the city, I’d argue that focus is deserved.
 DB : What was it about this topic that attracted your interest?
 AF : I have wanted to make historical documentaries since I watched Ken Burns’ The Civil War with my dad when I was seven years old. I think I was captivated by the unique pacing and evocative visuals that seemed to create the space for the past to live again. That series yielded many conceptual offshoots, all of which I imbibed enthusiastically, including the epic series The West directed by Stephen Ives, with whom I landed my first job after college. At Ives’ company, Insignia Films in New York, I received a major education about this style of filmmaking, and I wanted to make my own attempt at one of these ambitious and inclusive grand narratives. At that time I wanted to live in Philadelphia. It was a magical coincidence that I met Sam Katz here, who had the same ambition to make such a film about Philadelphia. That opened the door.
 A film still from Episode 5: "America." Actor Quinton Alexander in the role of Octavius V. Catto. | Courtesy of History Making Productions
 DB : How did the project evolve over its lifetime? Were there any significant course changes?
 AF : It changed everything when we decided to re-conceptualize a five-hour series produced for local television into what ultimately became an 11-hour series for a wide audience. In 2019, when I made what turned out to be In Pursuit ’s first pitch document, I used the working title Great Experiment 2020 , because that’s the year I expected that we could have the former series recut and expanded along the same existing structural lines. However, as we started working it became evident that we needed to do a full overhaul to make this series work for a wide audience as we intended. Our ambitions, possibilities, technical needs, and obstacles started to multiply. We were able to continue working through the COVID-19 pandemic by transitioning to a remote editing and directing workflow over Zoom, but by the summer of 2021 our funding was exhausted. We had to take a years-long break before a new wave of fundraising made it possible for us to resume production in 2024.
 DB : In Pursuit has received much-deserved critical praise. How will you personally gauge the success of this project?
 AF : I consider the project a success in part because it now exists. Inertia would have led us to simply walk away from this work after the conclusion of the original series in 2019. The mammoth effort and sacrifices entailed just to get this engine running again, shared by my collaborators Nathaniel Popkin and Sam Katz, makes it very satisfying to see the episodes completed and posted for the world to see. Whatever happens from here, at least we have created a history program hopefully at the scale and scope that Philadelphia deserves.
 DB : Much of this country’s history has been marked by violent conflicts between two diametrically opposed groups of people over land, independence, equality, slavery, or religion, to name a few. What are the parallels today and what can we learn from the past? 
 AF : In this contentious semiquincentennial summer, the first parallel I observe is that the historical conflicts, fractiousness, and unease are not uncommon at any point in American history. So, if people think we’re falling apart now, then we’ve probably always been falling apart, and, yet, we are still together 250 years later.
 It’s interesting that the template for the landmark national birthday was set by the Centennial in 1876, which was so spectacular and celebratory in part because the nation had barely survived a civil war just a decade prior. Many people were relieved, even amazed, that the country had actually made it to 100 years. I would say that the longevity of the experiment until now has a lot to do with the repetitive cycle of battling, dissenting, adapting, and amending what was exceptional in the world and gave the U.S. unique advantages for a couple of centuries. Unfortunately, that has faded in our oversorted, siloed, and algorithmically enthralled era. I think we can learn from the past by seeking more common ground.
 DB : What ongoing role is there for Philadelphia in the making of America–today and in the future?
 AF : I think Philadelphia remains the perfect place to study America because cities this old are always influenced by the past. They are also always changing and in motion, which makes them great cinematic subjects and compelling narrative puzzles. You can find something definitively American in every corner of Philadelphia, and the lively sidewalks, eclectic architecture, and busy streets are only more beautiful seen through the camera lens. 
 Whether it remains such a mirror in the future is a difficult question to answer, because for so long Philadelphia’s major relevance rested on its size and economic significance in the nation at large. It was clear enough for a long time that what happened in Philadelphia–never less than the 5th largest city, 4th largest metro in the nation–mattered because it was one of the few places in the country that contained diverse millions. Yet, ever since 2010 that has started to change with somewhat surprising speed as other U.S. and global cities have boomed. Philadelphia now has many American peers in size, with Dallas, Miami, Washington D.C., Atlanta, Phoenix, and San Antonio all at least as big or bigger by one metropolitan definition or another. 
 If this change had happened 100 years ago it would have been challenging to make In Pursuit because the argument for continuing national pace-setting would have been much harder to make. I could go on a side tangent about how Philadelphia’s urban form inspired imitations and extrapolations across the country, which would include places like St. Louis, Buffalo, Savannah, Detroit, Washington, and even New York. Yet, it seems like sprawling new cities are more likely to imitate Houston or Phoenix and that includes a less connected, less intimate way of life than what can be experienced in Philadelphia. 
 Andrew Ferrett directs an interview with spoken word artist Ursula Rucker at The Painted Bride in 2020. | Still image: Paul Van Haute courtesy of History Making Productions
 DB : What impacts would you like to see In Pursuit have on historians, documentary film makers, or everyday Philadelphians?
 AF : My approach to this project was inspired by the PBS historical docuseries boom of the 1990s when millions of viewers could be taken in by long-form documentaries. A classic feature of that era was eloquent, insightful narration. Many history documentaries today no longer use a narrator, preferring to intercut the perspectives of different commentators and let the viewer sort it out. Of course, the filmmaker is imprinting their perspective no matter what, so I find that narration actually allows for a pretty honest approach to filmmaking. 
 It isn’t easy to write narration for five centuries of history, and the fact-checking has to be on-point. Across 10 episodes I find it essential to relate context and to give the viewer, who has invested all of this time with us, a guiding compass toward what we the filmmakers wish to express. We’ve also been lucky enough to work with actor Michael Boatman as a narrator for our films for over 15 years. When you have an interpreter as skilled and brilliant as Michael, the narration adds an even more transformative dimension.
 DB : Can you give us an idea of what to look forward to in upcoming episodes?
 AF : In Episode Five, spanning the Civil War and Reconstruction, we see the pursuit of “America” and what and for whom that nation is going to be. In the latter part of 2026, we are releasing five episodes that span the 20th century in detail, featuring interviews with eyewitnesses to the history described (Cecil B. Moore and civil rights, the Rizzo era, MOVE, the Rendell era). Many of these interviewees have since passed away, but we were fortunate enough to sit with them in lively interviews at the origins of the project years ago. 
 I am particularly excited about the seventh episode “Renewal,” which features a close and rarely-seen exploration of the eye-popping physical transformations of Philadelphia neighborhoods from the 1920s to the 1960s, from the Parkway to Society Hill. Urban renewal was, of course, a national pursuit after World War II, but we found some fascinating pre-war origins for the concept among Philadelphians like Albert M. Greenfield and Edmund Bacon. Urban history enthusiasts and city planning buffs should keep an eye out for “Renewal” in September.
 Episode 5: "America 1838-1876" will premier on Thursday, July 16 at 6:45 p.m. at the Philadelphia Film Society Film Center, 1412 Chestnut Street. Register for free tickets HERE .
 The first four episodes of In Pursuit are streaming on YouTube . For full information about the series see InPursuit.TV .
 Tags: documentary History Making Productions interview 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: Unlisted Philadelphia: Engine 6
author: Alan Jaffe and Bryan Mckinney
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Summer 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Engine 6 
 Location : 2601 Belgrade Street
 Architect : Unknown
 Built : Circa 1913
 In 2025, the Philadelphia Fire Department announced the return of its historic Engine 6 to a noble and historic firehouse in Port Richmond. The two-story brick building, crowned with stone lion heads and adorned with wood-framed windows, scrollwork, and Mural Arts tributes to the company’s heroic spirit, should be honored with designation on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places .
 Engine 6 was formed in 1871 when the fire company was located at 134 Allen Street and operated a horse-drawn steamer engine and a hand-drawn hose carriage. The company moved in 1875 to a station on Montgomery Avenue, then moved in with Ladder 16 at the Belgrade Street firehouse in 1952. From the 1950s through the 1970s, Engine 6 was chosen for pilot programs that improved firefighting equipment and water supply strategy.
 Engine 6 was one of seven companies deactivated in 2009 during the Great Recession, but the Belgrade Street station remained open as home to Ladder 16. A FEMA grant funded a major refurbishment of the building that allowed for the proud return of Engine 6 in early 2025.
 Tags: firehouses Philadelphia Register of Historic Places Unlisted Philadelphia

title: Building Modification Requests Consume Historical Commission Meeting
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
At its meeting on July 10, the Philadelphia Historical Commission did not consider any new nominations to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places. However, it did review several requests by owners to modify historic buildings to adapt to their present-day uses.
 Demolition and new addition proposal for 27 Druim Moir Lane. | Rendering: Designblendz
 The Shingle Style mansion known as Brinkwood at 27 Druim Moir Lane in Chestnut Hill was designed in 1887 by George W. and William D. Hewitt and built for industrialist Henry H. Houston’s son, Samuel Frederic Houston. It was added to the local register in 1980 and is a contributing property to both the Druim Moir Historic District and the Chestnut Hill Historic District of the National Register of Historic Places. The Historical Commission denied owner and real estate developer Ori Fiebush's request to demolish a portion of the roof and a small dormer and construct a new dormer addition on the third floor to expand the interior living space. They found it did not adhere to the Secretary of the Interior’s guidelines for historic rehabilitation, which state that alterations must not destroy character-defining historic materials. Although the proposed addition was to the building’s rear, it was noted that the Hewitts designed the house with multiple primary facades.
 Elevator tower proposal for 4619-25 Longshore Avenue. | Rendering: Toner Architects
