 The owner of the former Tacony Club at 4619-25 Longshore Avenue proposed the addition of an elevator tower to repurpose the building for a Veterans Administration housing project. The plan would expand existing windows adjacent to the tower into doorways and widen a third-floor dormer to meet the tower. The Historical Commission felt the tower as planned would disrupt the building’s exterior, but noted they would approve a concept of an interior elevator, and would consider exterior shafts with alternative designs.
 Signage proposal for 1319-25 Market Street. | Renderings: Philly Signarama
 The Marriott Residence Inn across from City Hall at 1319-25 Market Street , the former Market Street National Bank, received both an approval and a denial for a request for new signage. The 24-story Art Deco building was designed in 1930 by the firm of Ritter & Shay, which had previously built the Packard Building at 15th and Chestnut Streets and the Drake Apartment Hotel at 1512 Spruce Street. The Historical Commission approved a sign with channel letters and LED lighting on a black metal curved band incorporated into the existing awning above the hotel’s main entrance on Juniper Street. The proposal also included three fabric banner signs at three locations on the building, two at the corner of Market and Juniper Streets, and one at the corner of Commerce and Juniper Streets. The signage would be 20 feet tall by three feet wide and connected to hardware installed into mortar joints. The Historical Commission denied them based on the large portion of the building’s facade that would be covered and potential damage to its terra cotta features.
 ADA ramp, paved pedestrian paths, and storage pavilion proposals for the American Swedish Historical Museum. | Renderings: Studio Sustena
 The American Swedish Historical Museum, which occupies the City-owned building at 3500 S. Broad Street , proposed constructing an outbuilding, ADA ramp, and paved pedestrian paths to improve accessibility. The 1926 building, constructed for that year’s Sesquicentennial celebration, was named a significant asset to the FDR Park Historic District in 2000. The plans were approved, with the caveat that the roof of the outbuilding, which will be used for storage of outdoor equipment, would have a hipped roof on all sides, rather than the proposed gable roof.
 Continuances lightened the agenda for this meeting. Several nominations awaiting review by the Historical Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation have been continued to future meetings.
 Proposal to remove the former Boyd Theater's marquee and vestibule walls and install a storefront. | Renderings: Ambit Architecture
 At Friday's meeting, a one-month continuance was granted for the former Boyd Theater at 1910 Chestnut Street . The current owner seeks to remove the building’s marquee and vestibule walls and install a storefront. The 1928 Art Deco theater, designed by architects Hoffman & Henon, was the subject of three historic nominations, two hardship cases, and a Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruling before its auditorium section was demolished and replaced by a tower in 2015.
 The Wolstenholme Twin at 580 Pelham Road and 333 West Upsal Street and a stable on the property that was built in 1900. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 The nomination of the twin properties at 580 Pelham Road and 333 West Upsal Street has been continued to the August Historical Commission meeting. Built in 1894 in the Flemish Renaissance Revival Style, they are known as the Wolstenholme Twin.
 Two other continuances lack an assigned meeting date. Piers 38 and 40 South at 775 S. Christopher Columbus Boulevard were originally nominated in October 2021, and Jewelers' Row Historic District was nominated eight years ago in December 2018.
 Tags: Boyd Theater Chestnut Hill FDR Park Historical Commission Meeting Report Jeweler's Row Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Places to Save: Summer 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Summer 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Family Court Building 
 Location : 1701 Vine Street
 Built : 1938-41
 Threat : Vacancy
 The former Family Court Building is a prominent landmark on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway. Designed by John T. Windrim and William Richard Morton Keast, the building is a monumental product of the New Deal-era Public Works Administration. Conceived as a “Palace of Justice,” its neoclassical design mirrors the adjacent Free Library of Philadelphia, together forming a rare and carefully composed ensemble modeled after Paris’ Place de la Concorde.
 Since the Family Court relocated to 1501 Arch Street in 2014, the building has remained vacant despite multiple redevelopment efforts. In 2014, an out-of-town developer was awarded a contract to transform the site into a luxury hotel, but that plan was abandoned in 2020. A subsequent 2023 plan by a new development partnership, which paired hotel reuse with development of nearby parcels for a new home for the African American Museum in Philadelphia and residential towers, has also stalled. Today, no active development proposals or requests for proposals are in place, leaving the building in prolonged limbo.
 This uncertainty threatens not only the structure’s physical condition, but also its architectural integrity. The Preservation Alliance for Great Philadelphia successfully secured interior protections in 2010 and designation of its WPA murals in 2011, underscoring the importance of preserving both the exterior and its richly detailed public spaces.
 After more than a decade of false starts, the Family Court Building deserves a clear, public path forward. Rather than piecemeal or speculative redevelopment, the site calls for a transparent planning process that prioritizes preservation and meaningful use.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 William Way LGBT Community Center 
 Location : 1315 Spruce Street
 Built : Circa 1890s. Facade altered in 1929
 Threat : Demolition
 A century of architectural and social history in Washington Square West is at risk. Originally constructed as two 19th-century rowhouses, 1315 Spruce Street was unified in 1929 by the Engineers Club of Philadelphia, which introduced a Colonial Revival facade that continues to define its appearance today. This adaptation transformed earlier residential structures into a cohesive institutional building, contributing to the character of what is now listed in the National Register of Historic Places as the Washington Square West Historic District .
 For decades, the building has housed the William Way LGBT Community Center , serving as a vital gathering place, archive and cultural hub for Philadelphia’s LGBTQIA+ community . Within its walls, generations have found support, connection and visibility, while its archives have preserved stories that might otherwise be lost. The building’s significance is therefore both architectural and deeply personal, embodying the intersection of place and community identity.
 In February, the center proposed demolishing the existing structure as part of a broader redevelopment plan, raising concerns about the loss of this historic site. While the organization’s need to grow and expand is clear, the building itself represents an irreplaceable link to both neighborhood evolution and the history of LGBTQIA+ life in Philadelphia.
 As pressures for redevelopment intensify, this site presents an opportunity to demonstrate how preservation and progress can align. Retaining and adapting at least the front section of the existing structure would honor its architectural character and cultural legacy while allowing the center to better serve the community.
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 President’s House Exhibit 
 Location : Southeast corner of 6th and Market Streets
 Built : 2010
 Threat : Removal and censorship
 The President’s House site is one of the most vulnerable historic places in the United States. It once was the site of the nation’s executive mansion, housing presidents George Washington and John Adams during Philadelphia’s decade as the temporary capital. Within its walls, foundational acts of governance took place, even as the Washingtons enslaved nine Black people whose labor sustained the household. The site is a powerful testament to the contradiction between liberty and slavery during the nation’s founding.
 Top: Interpretive panel at the President’s House in 2020. Bottom: The same location after the interpretive panel was removed in January 2026. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Decades of advocacy and archaeological excavation culminated in a 2010 open-air memorial and exhibit that interpreted both the presidency and the lives of the enslaved. In January, however, the site’s core interpretive elements, panels, video monitors, and educational displays were abruptly removed by the National Park Service under the direction of a 2025 Presidential Executive Order . Today, the archaeological remains of the house are still visible, but largely devoid of explanatory content, leaving visitors without the context necessary to understand what occurred there.
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 This loss of interpretation effectively erases the site’s meaning, transforming it into an empty shell. Recognizing the urgency of this threat, the National Trust for Historic Preservation placed the site on its annual 11 Most Endangered Historic Places list in May. A coalition of advocates, including the City of Philadelphia and the President’s House Site Slavery Memorial Alliance, is pursuing legal action and public advocacy to restore the exhibits. Reinstallation is essential to ensure that the full story of the nation’s founding remains accessible to the millions who pass through this site each year.
 Tags: African-American history Family Court building LGBTQIA+ History Places to Save The President’s House William Way Center 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: From Arctic Stone to Aluminum Skies: Cryolite, Philadelphia, and the Geometry of Industrial Power
author: Christopher R. Dougherty
bodyText:
The recent fixation on Greenland’s mineral wealth presents itself as novel: a 21st century convergence of rare earths, Arctic security, climate anxiety, and geopolitical rivalry. Yet, this attention revisits an older extractive arrangement. Long before critical minerals entered strategic stockpiles and policy architectures, Greenland was already bound into American industrial power through a single, improbable material: cryolite. That connection ran decisively through Philadelphia, where industrial necessity, rather than geopolitics, first drew Greenland into an American supply chain.
 The Return of an Old Obsession 
 Founded in 1850, Philadelphia’s Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company set out to produce alkalies from salt using a patented process, ample capital, and a plant sited on western Pennsylvania salt deposits. The effort failed. After five years of losses, the firm survived only by abandoning salt itself and pivoting to the manufacture of household lyes, using cryolite as a catalytic input in caustic soda production. Sold in small domestic quantities for soap making, lye proved immediately profitable, stabilizing the company and reshaping its industrial orientation. What began as a mundane consumer product quietly anchored a transatlantic mineral dependence whose significance was not yet fully apparent.
 Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company's Greenwich Chemical Works seen here in the Philadelphia edition of Hexamer General Surveys of 1892. | Image courtesy of the Atheneum of Philadelphia via Map Collection, Free Library of Philadelphia
 Cryolite soon moved from expedient input to strategic asset. In 1865, Philadelphia’s Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company secured a royal concession from the Danish crown granting access to the cryolite deposit at Ivigtut, Greenland, the only known source in the world. Entering American industry through lye, glass, ceramics, and sanitation, cryolite appeared prosaic. Yet, this modest chemistry concealed a far larger potential, one tied to scale, energy, and a coming transformation in how modern materials would be made. By World War II, the mineral that had once kept a failing Philadelphia salt company alive had become one of the most critical supply lines of the Allied war economy. From the present, the pattern is clear. Industrial reliance precedes strategic anxiety. The rhetoric now surrounding Greenland follows paths laid down long ago when critical minerals moved through Philadelphia’s wharves a century and a half before contemporary stockpiling schemes and when a riverfront chemical city briefly sat at the axis of a global trade whose implications would only later announce themselves in the crisis conditions of modern war.
 Ice That Would Not Melt 
 Cryolite looks like a geological mistake. Friable, opaque, and white, it resembles compressed snow more than stone–a mineral that seems to have arrived unfinished. In southwest Greenland, where it cropped out improbably at the edge of a fjord, Inuit residents called it the ice that will not melt, a phrase that captured both its appearance and its refusal to behave like anything else in the landscape. Chemists, less poetic, but no less literal, rendered the same idea in Greek: cryolithos i.e ice-stone. For more than a century the world’s commercial supply of this substance came from a single place: a narrow seam breaking the surface just above the tide line at Ivigtut, Greenland. The settlement lay at 61°20′ north latitude and 18°20′ west longitude at the head of the Arksuk Fiord, where dark water cut sharply into Greenland’s granite spine. An 1879 hydrographic guide warned mariners that the coast was dismal and winding, a shoreline of bare rock, poor anchorages, and constant navigational hazard.
 The challenging mechanics of cryolite extraction and shipment. From “The Ivigtut Cryolite Mine,” Journal of Analytical and Applied Chemistry, 1892. | Image: Public Domain
 The seam’s position made extraction deceptively simple and everything else punishingly difficult. The ore emerged directly from the cliff at the water’s edge, eliminating shafts or tunnels, but exposing the mine to snow, ice, and sea. Each winter the pit was deliberately flooded to prevent drifting snow from filling the workings. Each spring it was pumped dry again. Cryolite was blasted from the rock face, tipped into small rail cars, and pushed along short tramways to a wharf built largely from the mine’s own tailings. There it was stacked into precise rectangular piles, measured and tallied before shipment, an Arctic geometry imposed on a raw and unstable landscape.
 Early shipments relied on aging whaling vessels, chosen less for efficiency than for survival. These ships could endure ice pressure and collision, but they were slow, limited in capacity, and increasingly unsuited to a trade that demanded regularity and volume. As demand for cryolite grew and schedules hardened, the limits of the whalers became impossible to ignore. Missed seasons, damaged hulls, and lost cargo exposed the fragility of relying on vessels designed for pursuit rather than transport.
 The Argenta was a part of Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company's chemical fleet. From A Two Month Voyage to Southwest Greenland by John Randolph Spears, 1890 | Image: Public Domain
 In response, the cryolite trade produced its own fleet. Purpose-built cargo ships were constructed with massively reinforced frames, thick planking, and hulls shaped to force ice downward rather than resist it. Speed and elegance were sacrificed for strength and predictability. These vessels ran on fixed seasonal schedules, carried standardized loads, and treated the Greenland passage not as an expedition, but as a repeatable industrial route. By the late 19th century, cryolite no longer moved by chance or daring, but through a disciplined maritime system engineered to extract and deliver a single, improbable mineral from a single exposed seam at the edge of the Arctic.
 From Copenhagen to the Delaware: Danish Chemical Technology and Penn Salt 
 Before cryolite ever entered American industrial systems, its value was already legible within Danish scientific and technical circles. By the middle of the 19th century, chemists in Copenhagen understood that cryolite’s unusual composition—sodium aluminum fluoride—made it a promising raw material for alkali production at precisely the moment when soda, alum, and related compounds were becoming indispensable to industrial life. This was not speculation, but laboratory knowledge, grounded in a small, but influential network of Danish chemists working at the boundary between academic science and manufacturable process.
 Among the most important of these early investigations was the work of Julius Thomsen, trained at the Polytechnic College in Copenhagen and active in its chemical laboratory in the early 1850s. Thomsen demonstrated that cryolite could be decomposed using calcium hydroxide, producing calcium fluoride as a solid residue and sodium aluminate in solution. When treated with carbon dioxide, this solution yielded aluminum hydroxide and sodium carbonate, establishing a repeatable industrial pathway for soda manufacture. Danish manufacturers quickly recognized the implications. Commercial production began in Copenhagen in 1859. Within five years additional cryolite-based plants appeared in Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland, all dependent on Danish cryolite and Danish-developed methods.
 Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company aggressively marketed lye to homemakers interested in making soap, often touted as less expensive than purchased soap. From a pamphlet published in 1904promoting the use of Lewis Lye. | Image courtesy of Hagley Museum and Library
 It was this demonstrated capacity—not abstract theory—that drew American attention. Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company, struggling to stabilize itself after early failures in brine-based soda production, did not stumble into cryolite by chance. The firm sent observers to Denmark to study the process firsthand, assess yields, and evaluate whether the mineral’s strange chemistry could be reliably disciplined at industrial scale. What Penn Salt saw was not merely a novel reagent, but a system: a mineral with singular geographic origin, a proven chemical pathway, and a manageable logistics chain. On that basis, the company moved decisively. In 1865, Penn Salt constructed a cryolite-processing facility in the United States, assisted by Gustav E. Hagermann, a Danish-trained chemist who would later establish his own cryolite operations in America. Shortly thereafter, Penn Salt secured exclusive American access to Greenland cryolite, binding Danish science, Arctic extraction, and Philadelphia production into a single industrial circuit.
 The gamble proved quietly transformative. Founded in 1850 to manufacture soda ash from brine wells, Penn Salt had nearly failed in its first decade and survived only through opportunistic petroleum exports that bought time rather than solved strategy. Cryolite changed that. By the late 19th century the company had become one of a small cohort of American industrial firms noted for longevity, steady dividends, and managerial adaptability. Business historians later pointed to Penn Salt’s control of raw material supply, vertical integration of processing and distribution, and ability to diversify without abandoning its chemical core. Cryolite refined in Philadelphia became a keystone input across a widening portfolio, long after its role in soda manufacture alone might have justified abandonment.
 In Philadelphia, the mineral entered the city at Greenwich Point, the low, marsh-edged southern reach of the Delaware River where chemical plants, rail spurs, and bulk wharves formed a continuous industrial frontage. At facilities south of Oregon Avenue, cryolite moved off ships and onto conveyors, passed across scales, and disappeared into vats. Contemporary accounts describe the docks as a site of quiet fascination. Amateur geologists lingered near the Pennsylvania Salt wharves hoping to glimpse fragments of the rare stone. Guidebooks even suggested timing a visit to coincide with the unloading of cryolite barks. It was here, in this uncelebrated stretch of riverfront, that Arctic geology became American infrastructure and where a Danish scientific insight, patiently observed and methodically adopted, paid off beyond its original chemical promise.
 From Franchise to Target 
 By the early 20th century cryolite’s role in American industry had shifted decisively. What began as a useful alkali input had become chemically indispensable to the electrolytic reduction of aluminum. In the Hall–Héroult process, alumina alone could not be reduced at practical temperatures. It required a molten bath, and that bath depended on cryolite. Without cryolite, aluminum could not be produced at scale. Without aluminum, modern electrification, aviation, and mechanized war would simply stall. The mineral’s strategic importance was not rhetorical. It was thermodynamic.
 This was where Penn Salt’s earlier investments in chemical knowledge proved decisive. Long before aluminum dominated public imagination, the company had developed expertise in handling, refining, and circulating cryolite through industrial systems. Its Philadelphia facilities had been designed to move bulk mineral inputs efficiently from ship to plant, to meter them accurately, and to integrate them into continuous chemical processes. When aluminum production surged in the early 1900s, Penn Salt was not learning cryolite from scratch. It was adapting an existing technical regime to a new, far more consequential end.
 That adaptation mattered enormously once war loomed. By 1940, American planners understood that aluminum production represented a single point of failure in Allied industrial capacity, and cryolite represented a single point of failure within aluminum itself. The U.S. Coast Guard’s Greenland Patrol history makes clear that fears of a cryolite shortage were explicit, immediate, and widely shared within the American military establishment. Greenland, although formally Danish, was viewed as an exposed and vulnerable node in the Western Hemisphere’s industrial defense system. Officials worried not only about German seizure of the Ivigtut mine, but about disruption of shipping, ice conditions, and the sheer fragility of relying on one Arctic deposit for a material essential to aircraft production.
 This sketch by Coast Guard combat artist Norman Millet Thomas depicts American and Greenlandic personnel in Greenland on December 24, 1942. | Image courtesy of the National Archives
 These anxieties translated quickly into action. Even before formal American entry into the war, the United States assumed responsibility for the defense of southern Greenland. Coastal artillery was emplaced. Patrols were established. Naval and Coast Guard bases were constructed across the fjord from Ivigtut. The mine itself, still operated by Danish personnel, became encircled by American military infrastructure. The logic was brutally simple: if cryolite stopped flowing, aluminum stopped flowing. If aluminum stopped flowing, air power collapsed.
 What is striking in retrospect is how seamlessly this military logic aligned with an older commercial geography. For decades, cryolite had traveled from Ivigtut to Philadelphia along established maritime routes, arriving at facilities purpose-built to receive it. During the war, that same corridor took on heightened significance. Cryolite shipments continued to move to Pennsylvania, where both modern works and industrial plants designed in the 19th century for alkali chemistry now functioned as critical wartime infrastructure supporting aluminum production downstream. The conveyors, scales, and storage systems in South Philadelphia were no longer merely commercial assets. They were components in a global war machine.
 German intelligence understood this structure with unnerving clarity. The mission to insert saboteurs into America by submarine, the American-coded Operation Pastorius, identified cryolite-related facilities associated with the Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company as priority targets. The sabotage mission failed when its leader surrendered to the FBI, but the selection of targets was revealing. A supply chain assembled through chemical foresight and commercial franchise had, by the early 1940s, hardened into a strategic dependency visible even to enemy planners.
 Afterlives, Denial, and the Present Tense 
 After the war, the extractive relationship receded from view without disappearing. American military installations reshaped Greenlandic life. Consumer culture followed. Greenland became embedded in the Western defense system, often without meaningful participation by Greenlanders themselves. Cryolite mining continued under Danish control until 1987, leaving behind a flooded pit at Ivittuut and an uneven legacy that was easier to abandon physically than to account for politically.
 In Philadelphia, the company’s most visible afterlife took architectural form at Three Parkway, the 20-story headquarters erected after Pennsylvania Salt had become Pennsalt Chemicals Corporation and, following its merger with Wallace & Tiernan, Pennwalt. The tower overlooked the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, orienting its offices and boardrooms toward the city’s aesthetic artery. Glass and steel replaced vats, conveyors, and scales, marking a shift not only in materials, but in managerial distance. What had once been a waterfront operation organized around bulk minerals and chemical throughput was abstracted upward into administrative space, its industrial origins increasingly obscured even as the capital derived from them was consolidated and managed at height.
 A Pennsylvania Salt Manufacturing Company advertisement in 1947 touting the benefits of DDT. | Image courtesy of Science History Institute
 By the late 1980s, the firm that had once anchored part of Philadelphia’s industrial identity had itself become a contested artifact of capital. Pennwalt, now a diversified chemical and specialty-products company, was prized less for its production lines than for its bust-up value—the worth of its constituent businesses when separated rather than held together. Pennwalt’s sprawling product portfolio spanned everything from agricultural chemicals like DDT to consumer antifungals like Desenex, testifying to the moral and chemical breadth of mid-century American industry. In early 1989, an unsolicited takeover bid by Centaur Partners exposed the company to the logic of financial arbitrage, prompting a rapid defensive reshaping of governance and strategy. That spring, Société Nationale Elf Aquitaine emerged as a white-knight suitor with a friendly tender offer of roughly $1 billion, an acquisition completed by summer under U.S. regulatory review. The arc from Arctic stone to Wall Street asset traced an irony of American industrial history: a firm that once helped shape material infrastructure found itself ceded to global capital markets, its legacy distilled not in warehouses and wharves, but in balance sheets and buyout bids.
 What has changed most sharply is the tone of the present. In 2025, the Danish public broadcaster DR withdrew a documentary detailing the colonial extraction of cryolite amid mounting political tension surrounding Greenlandic independence and resource sovereignty. The suppression was telling. Cryolite, long exhausted as a mineral, remains active as a narrative fault line. Contemporary rhetoric about Greenland’s strategic value–about minerals, leverage, and security–echoes an older logic almost exactly. The language has modernized. The geometry has not. Distant extraction continues to be translated into metropolitan power through asymmetrical control, with acknowledgment lagging far behind benefit.
 Left: A topping out ceremony for the Pennwalt Building was held on August 15, 1969. Right: A graphic from 1980 published in the Philadelphia Bulletin details Pennwalt products. | Photos courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Greenland’s minerals continue to matter, with renewed global attention in the early 2020s focused on the island’s broader suite of critical and rare earth elements exemplified by the 2021 acquisition of the historic Ivittuut cryolite mine by Eclipse Metals Ltd, which cited quartz and related mineral potential as part of its development strategy and by the February 2026 announcement of the United States’ Project Vault initiative, a multi-billion-dollar effort to build strategic stockpiles of critical and rare earth minerals. These episodes reveal how familiar narratives about strategic geology, national security, and distant extraction continue to shape policy and commercial ambition decades after cryolite’s industrial life had faded.
 Cryolite did not merely move through space. It moved through time, carrying with it the assumptions of those who controlled it. To trace its path–from a seam above a Greenland fiord, through Philadelphia wharves and wartime anxieties, into contemporary acts of erasure and appropriation–is to see how quietly empire can operate and how insistently it returns. 
 Tags: industrial history World War II 
 About the Author
 Christopher R. Dougherty , AICP, is an urban planner, researcher in economic geography, and project administrator whose work focuses on how infrastructure, public investment, and development shape cities and their landscapes. He currently works at Pennoni Associates on municipal planning and infrastructure projects in the Philadelphia region. 
Dougherty lives in South Philadelphia and serves as secretary of the Board of Directors of Fort Mifflin on the Delaware and president of the Oliver Evans Chapter of the Society for Industrial Archeology.

title: Restoration Role Model: 1518-36 Brandywine Street
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Summer 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 The Spring Garden Community Development Corporation (SGCDC) worked with architect and urban planner John Gibbons to transform the deteriorated facades of a block of historic carriage houses at 1518-36 Brandywine Street and repurpose the buildings as a community civic engagement center and SGCDC’s operations hub. Extant spoke with Gibbons about the $409,000 rehabilitation project, which engaged two rural Lancaster County Amish construction firms. The work was nominated for a 2026 Grand Jury Award from the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 1518-36 Brandywine Street before restoration. | Photos: Extant Magazine
 Extant Magazine (EM) : What attracted you to these particular buildings?
 John Gibbons (JB) : The deteriorated facades of the buildings at 1518-36 occupied a significant part of the otherwise well-maintained south side of the 1500 block of Brandywine Street. A large building immediately to the east had been adaptively reused as apartments. On the north side, a large complex of carriage house buildings had previously been historically rehabilitated for the Performance Garage. A new infill apartment building had also been constructed on the block. Acquisition of the property by SGCDC provided the opportunity for rehabilitation of the historic facade to complete the streetscape. The 16,000 square feet of available interior space and large first-floor spaces provide the opportunity for a variety of community and program spaces.
 EM : What was the original use of the buildings?
 JB : The buildings were originally three separate two-and three-story row structures, built in the mid-1880s as carriage houses and stables serving the grand post-Civil War residences on Green and Spring Garden Streets. In the early 20th century, the buildings were converted to commercial uses. 1526-36 Brandywine was owned by the nearby Baldwin Locomotive Works and used as an auto warehouse. Later in the 20th century, the party walls between the buildings were breached, some garage door openings enlarged, and the three buildings joined internally and used for warehousing and storage. In the early 21st century, the buildings housed an electronics repair shop and later a nonprofit computer refurbishment operation. The properties are currently used as SGCDC’s operations center for certain of its charitable activities and storage for local businesses.
 EM : What was most important to preserve?
 JB : The defining features of the buildings are the large carriage house door openings, particularly the handsome arched head openings. The new double-hinged doors reflect the style of paneling, glazing, and detailing of the original vehicular doors. The configuration of the infill doors and paneling at one of the original openings were modified to provide double doors for pedestrians, while maintaining the original character.
 Facade rehabilitation included masonry repair, complete cleaning and repointing of the facades, reopening of blocked original openings, removal of modern metal garage doors, and installation of historically appropriate wood carriage house doors and windows.
 EM : What was the client’s original vision? Did it change over time?
 JB : SGCDC’s first priority was the elimination of blight and the completion of the historic rehabilitation of the facades so that the buildings would make a positive visual contribution to the neighborhood and the Spring Garden Historic District . The project has set the stage for complete rehab of the interior of the properties. The transformation of blighted and deteriorated building facades has created a streetscape asset that has supported new grant applications for adaptive reuse of the buildings for community use. With the completion of the historic facade work, SGCDC is moving on to the rehabilitation and transformation of the interiors for community facilities, including meeting and activity space, classrooms, and offices to support the organization’s programs.
 The configuration of the infill doors and paneling at one of the original openings were modified to provide double doors for pedestrians, while maintaining the original character. | Photos: Extant Magazine
 EM : What was the biggest preservation challenge?
 JB : To work within its available budget, SGCDC needed to find a cost-effective, high-quality millwork shop with experience in providing and installing large, heavy custom-made doors. After extensive research and obtaining multiple bids, SGCDC identified Beechdale Woodworks, an Amish heritage custom millwork operation located in Bird in Hand, Lancaster County, that had extensive experience in fabricating heavy wood doors for oversized openings for rural barns. Beechdale and SGCDC coordinated with Triple B Exteriors, an Amish business specializing in large barn restorations, for custom installation of the windows and doors. The windows and doors are solid mahogany/sapele, stained and sealed, for longevity.
 EM : Did you look to any role model for inspiration or example?
 JB : SGCDC and I worked closely with the Philadelphia Historical Commission to develop historically appropriate designs for the door and window openings. Historic City archive photos of similar, since-demolished carriage houses on the 1600 block of Brandywine provided an excellent guide for the appropriate detailing of the replacement carriage house doors and windows.
 EM : What was the project’s biggest surprise (good or bad)?
 JB : The biggest surprise was the increase in the cost of the historic doors and windows, as a result of the pandemic and inflation, after the initial funding had been secured.
 The work was funded through a combination of Pennsylvania Department of Community and Economic Development grants, smaller grants from WSFS Foundation and Univest, and owner funds.
 Tags: adaptive resuse historic renovation industrial architecture Restoration Role Model Spring Garden 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Places Lost: Summer 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note : A version of this story was published in the Summer 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 Tulipwood 
 Location : 4024-34 Apalogen Road
 Built : 1954
 Tulipwood, a mid-century modern residence in East Falls, has been lost to time. A demolition permit issued in February cleared the way for the destruction of an architecturally and historically significant postwar residence.
 Tulipwood, designed by Elizabeth Hirsh Fleisher as her personal home to share with her husband, landscape architect Horace Teller Fleisher, reflected both professional innovation and deeply personal vision. Fleisher, the first woman to become a registered architect in Philadelphia, was best known for large-scale commissions such as Parkway House. Her residential work was rare, making Tulipwood an especially significant and intimate example of her design legacy.
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 The nearly 3,000-square-foot home was a synthesis of architecture and craft. Fleisher enlisted master woodworker Wharton Esherick to create a sculptural, floor-to-ceiling wood installation that wrapped the living room fireplace in undulating walnut, poplar, and cherry. Additional custom elements included a metal cabinet by Paul Evans and a 10-foot credenza by Phillip Lloyd Powell, embedding the house within a broader network of mid-century artistic production. 
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 Despite its significance, Tulipwood’s fate was sealed when the Philadelphia Historical Commission declined to designate the property in November 2025 , even while acknowledging it met multiple criteria for protection. The owners, local restaurateurs Valerie Safran and Marcie Turney, claiming substantial prior investment in redevelopment plans, chose to destroy the historic home and fill the parcel with new construction . Tulipwood's loss underscores the particular vulnerability of postwar architecture and works by under-recognized designers.
 Tags: demolition East Falls Elizabeth Hirsh Fleisher Midcentury Modern modernism Places Lost 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Wolstenholme Twin in Mt. Airy Added to the Philadelphia Register
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Philadelphia Historical Commission added three properties to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places and kept two "demolition by neglect" cases in check at its meeting on August 14. The session opened with a tribute to former long-serving Historical Commission member Janet Klein , who passed away on August 4 at the age of 96.
 The twin houses at 580 Pelham Road and 333 West Upsal Street were added to the local register. Known as the Wolstenholme Twin, they were designed in 1894 by the architectural firm of Boyd & Boyd as part of the Pelham development in West Mt. Airy, a project of bankers Anthony J. Drexel and Edward T. Stotesbury, contemporary to their Overbrook Farms development.
 Located on a triangular lot at the juncture of Pelham Road and West Upsal Street, the homes are distinguished by characteristics of the Flemish Renaissance Revival style, with rounded, curvilinear gable-parapets. The original owners were Thomas Wolstenholme and his son Fred, prominent manufacturers of woolen yarn at their Allegheny Worsted Mills at Frankford Avenue and Westmoreland Street in Kensington. The nomination was written by local preservation advocate Oscar Besiert and submitted by the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 The Wolstenholme Twin at 580 Pelham Road and 333 West Upsal Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Two mirror image properties at 6953 and 7001-09 Greenhill Road were nominated individually. Built between 1916 and 1919, the two stone houses with a shared twin garage were designed in the Colonial Revival style by the architectural firm Mellor, Meigs, and Howe as part of the subdivision of Green Hill Farm, which was developed from the Morris Estate in West Philadelphia.
 The owner of 6953 Greenhill Road, Chabad of Penn Wynne, Inc., received a continuance to the Historical Commission's November meeting. At today’s meeting the Commission proceeded with and approved the designation of 7001-09 Greenhill Road.
 In three separate cases, the Historical Commission also reviewed proposals that all stemmed from a situation referred to as “demolition by neglect.” Preservationists and residents alike are concerned about this seemingly growing trend, where developers covet the land under the historic properties they buy and allow Department of Licenses & Inspection (L&I) violations to accrue until demolition is required for public safety. Multiple public comments urged the Historical Commission to deny the requests, to avoid setting a precedent that would encourage this maneuver.
 4275 Viola Street is listed as contributing to the Parkside Historic District and is therefore legally protected from demolition. | Photo: Google Street View
 The first case was a request by the owner of 4275 Viola Street . Built in 1897 by architect Henry E. Flower, it was listed in 2009 as a contributing property to the Parkside Historic District. The current owner purchased the property in 2023. After numerous violations from L&I, he received and let lapse a make-safe building permit in 2025 to address them and repair the rear ell. Two days after the permit’s expiration, L&I issued another permit for complete demolition. The owner also holds title to the vacant lots at 4214, 4277 and 4283 Viola Street, the latter of which he is appealing a variance denial to construct an 18-unit apartment building.
 Philadelphia’s historic preservation ordinance allows complete demolition only if it is deemed necessary in the public interest or unless the building cannot be used for any purpose for which it is or may be reasonably adapted. In the application for the make-safe permit, the owner’s contractor stated that only the rear ell needed to be demolished, which prompted the Historical Commission to deny the full demolition request.
 Temple Beth Israel at 3135-49 West Montgomery Avenue was demolished in 2021 after the owners received and ignored numerous unsafe structure violations from the City and allowed the roof to collapse from deferred maintenance. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The second case was a recission request for the parcel at 520 Queen Street . Currently a vacant lot, it was added to the local register in 1973 when a two and a half story house stood there. In 2018, the Historical Commission approved an application for the rehabilitation of the front facade and the construction of a rear addition. When the contractor exceeded the approved scope of work by removing a front dormer and load-bearing walls and damaging the two adjacent properties, the building became unstable and was completely demolished. The owner next requested recission of the designation, stating that the historic qualities that led to its addition no longer exist. The Historical Commission denied the request.
 The third example was a recission request for 3135-49 West Montgomery Avenue , the former site of Temple Beth Israel synagogue in Strawberry Mansion. Built in 1907 and designated in 1993, the Moorish Revival synagogue was demolished in 2021 after accruing hundreds of violations and the collapse of its domed roof in 2020. The Historical Commission granted the request.
 The Robert Purvis House, a former stop on the Underground Railroad at 1601 Mt. Vernon Street, was saved from demolition by neglect and later rehabilitated after the Spring Garden Community Development Corporation successfully placed the historic home under its conservatorship in 2018. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The owner of the building at 1601 Mount Vernon Street in Spring Garden sought Historical Commission approval in the choice of facade materials. It was designated in 2000, having been a home of abolitionist Robert Purvis. After decades of neglect, the 1859 house was taken over by the Spring Garden Community Development Corporation through an Act 135 takeover, stabilized, and sold to an out-of-state developer. At August's meeting, the Commission approved the use of cast stone for new steps and window surrounds when the owner claimed marble was prohibitively expensive.
 A request to remove the marquee and vestibule walls from the former Boyd Theater at 1910 Chestnut Street was continued to next month’s Historical Commission meeting. Built in 1928 by noted Philadelphia theater architects Hoffman & Henon, it was designated in 1987 and again in 2008. Its Art Deco auditorium and the rear of the building were demolished in 2015.
 Tags: demolition Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places West Mt Airy 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Places Saved: Summer 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note: A version of this story was published in the Summer 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 FDR Park Welcome Center 
 Location : 1500 Pattison Avenue
 Built : 1919
 The reuse of the FDR Park Welcome Center stands as a compelling example of how thoughtful preservation can transform a disused historic structure into a vibrant public asset. Completed in May 2025, the project rehabilitated the park’s former guardhouse, stables, and adjacent garage into a LEED Gold-certified visitor center serving one of Philadelphia’s most heavily used parks. For this tremendous effort, the project won a 2026 Preservation Achievement Award from the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Located within FDR Park, with landscape that was designed by the Olmsted Brothers in 1914, the buildings had been closed to the public for decades and suffered from significant deterioration. Rather than pursue demolition, the Fairmount Park Conservancy embraced adaptive reuse, preserving the building’s Arts and Crafts character, including its buff brick walls, deep overhanging eaves, and red clay tile roof, while integrating modern systems and amenities.
 Historic features, including arched openings, glazed brick, and original wood elements, were carefully restored with salvaged materials repurposed throughout the interior. The transformation delivers long-desired public amenities, including restrooms, concessions, seating, and park information services, all within the historic footprint.
 Importantly, the project balances preservation with resilience. Flood mitigation strategies, durable materials, and energy-efficient systems ensure long-term sustainability. Now serving approximately four million annual visitors, the Welcome Center not only preserves a piece of Philadelphia’s park history, but also anchors a broader vision for the park’s future.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Bureau Brothers Foundry 
 Location : 2234 West Westmoreland Street
 Built : 1913
 On a quiet corner in Allegheny West, a broad brick industrial building endures as both artifact and active workshop. Constructed for heavy craft, the former Bureau Brothers Foundry has adapted over time without losing its essential purpose–a rare continuity in Philadelphia’s industrial landscape.
 Founded in the 1870s by French-born brothers Achille and Edouard Bureau, the Bureau Brothers Foundry quickly gained prominence, casting bronze and brass works for some of the nation’s leading sculptors. By 1912, demand necessitated a new, larger facility. The brothers commissioned architect W.L. Baithe to design a new plant at 23rd and Westmoreland Streets. The building’s robust construction, open spans, steel columns, and durable masonry were tailored to the physical demands of metal casting. Many of these original features remain visible today.
 After the Bureau Brothers, the John P. Kelly Foundry continued operations into the late 20th century, extending the site’s industrial legacy. Later uses were less conventional, but still tied to craft and storage, including a period storing hundreds of pianos and, more recently, occupation by Philadelphia Salvage Co. for its retail space.
 Today, the building has returned to its roots under Independent Casting, where skilled metalsmiths again produce work for artists and institutions worldwide. The foundry remains remarkably intact. Its architecture and use are still aligned more than a century later with the purpose for which it was built.
 Photo: Peter Woodall
 Quaker City National Bank 
 Location : 721 Chestnut Street
 Built : 1889
 Few buildings on Chestnut Street embody as many layers of ambition, loss, and adaptation as the Quaker City National Bank Building. It began as part of an unusually grand composition by architect Willis G. Hale, who envisioned a unified tripartite faccade spanning 713-721 Chestnut Street. Three distinct financial institutions were housed within a single architectural statement: the Union Trust Company at the center, flanked by the Chestnut Street Trust and Saving Fund Company and the Chestnut Street National Bank.
 The story quickly took a dramatic turn. Under its second president, financier William M. Singerly, the institution expanded just before the financial panic of 1897 forced its collapse, leaving 721 Chestnut Street vacant. In 1901, the Quaker City National Bank acquired the property, giving the building the name that still appears carved into its facade.
 Today, 721 Chestnut Street is the lone remnant of Hale’s original vision. The central bank was demolished in 1923 and replaced with a Classical Revival design by Paul Cret, while the eastern wing was lost by 1962. Notably, Cret’s intervention allowed the surviving structure to read as a complete and coherent building rather than a fragment. Its richly ornamented limestone facade, featuring intricate carvings and distinctive leaded glass “all-seeing eye” windows, remains a striking example of late 19th century commercial design. The former bank is listed on the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places .
 A facade restoration completed in 2025 was recognized as a Grand Jury Winner at the 2026 Preservation Achievement Awards, underscoring the building’s enduring significance.
 Tags: adaptive resuse FDR Park Historic Banks industrial architecture Olmsted Brothers Places Saved Willis G Hale 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: How World's Fairs Changed the Face of Philadelphia: The 1976 Bicentennial
author: Thomas H. Keels
bodyText:
Of Philadelphia’s anniversary bashes, the 1976 Bicentennial suffers the greatest gap between its original vision and the final reality. Dismal as it was, the 1926 Sesquicentennial produced a real world’s fair with exhibit halls, pavilions, and a new stadium. The Bicentennial started off with grandiose schemes for a transformational festival that would establish Philadelphia as a world-class city. While the final celebration spurred the completion of the city’s historic areas and the creation of several new institutions, few traces of the Bicentennial survive today.
 Originally, the Bicentennial served as a focus for the utopian visions of Edmund Bacon, Louis I. Kahn, Oscar Stonorov, and the postwar generation of Philadelphia city planners. These men dreamt of a new metropolis rising from the decaying burg that was shedding residents, jobs, and businesses at alarming speed. To communicate this dream, Bacon, Kahn, and Stonorov created the Better Philadelphia Exhibition, a vast display promoting urban redevelopment that occupied two floors of Gimbels’ Department Store in Autumn 1947.
 The City Planning Committee pitched urban renewal to the public in 1947 through the The Better Philadelphia Exhibition. Exhibits like this large-scale interactive model of the city were showcased on the 5th and 6th floors of Gimbel’s Department Store on Market Street. 385,000 visitors came to see the City's radical, reform-driven vision for the future of Philadelphia. | Photo courtesy of Haverford College
 The centerpiece was a 30-by-14-foot scale model of Center City with 45,000 buildings. As a narrator discussed future development, sections flipped over to reveal how Philadelphia might appear in 1980. The Chinese Wall, the elevated viaduct which carried trains between 30th Street Station and Center City, was replaced by an avenue of gleaming office buildings. A revitalized Society Hill and Delaware River waterfront appeared, along with a park and mall surrounding Independence Hall. In only five weeks, over 385,000 visitors viewed the Better Philadelphia Exhibition, proof of the public enthusiasm for urban renewal.
 After the exhibition closed, Stonorov asked City planners to imagine a world’s fair to “show the world Philadelphia’s and Pennsylvania’s importance.” Little came of his suggestion, but a decade later Bacon revived the dream of a transformative fair. By 1957, Bacon had been the executive director of the City Planning Commission for eight years. Under his tenure, Philadelphia had emerged as a poster child for American urban renewal. The City boasted achievements like the Schuylkill Expressway, Penn Center, Independence Mall and National Historical Park, a modern international airport, and the Pattison Avenue Food Distribution Center .
 Edmund Bacon’s concept for the Bicentennial City in December 1963, with aerial cable cars to convey passengers to Center City from the main fairgrounds on the old Centennial site. | Image courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 By 1976, the 200th anniversary of American independence, Bacon expected to have the other key components of his master plan in place. These would include a recreation area along the Delaware River (Penn’s Landing), a restored historic district in Washington Square East (Society Hill), Crosstown and Vine Street Expressways linking the Delaware Expressway (I-95) with the Schuylkill Expressway, model communities in Eastwick and the Far Northeast, a reborn Market East shopping district, and a Center City Commuter Connection. What better way to show off this reborn Philadelphia than by inviting the world to a Bicentennial Fair?
 In 1957, with the support of Mayor Richardson Dilworth and U.S. Senator Joseph Clark, Bacon began to hold meetings with the Junior Chamber of Commerce to plan a Bicentennial World’s Fair. Bacon fleshed out his concept in a 1959 article in Greater Philadelphia Magazine entitled “Tomorrow: A Fair Can Pace It” (later republished as “Philadelphia in the Year 2009”). While viewing the Bicentennial Fair primarily as a vehicle to ensure completion of his master plan, Bacon lingered over its attractions. On Independence Mall, visitors would delight to a sound-and-light recreation of 1776 called the “Lights of Freedom.” At the Delaware River Marina, they could enjoy historic ships, a maritime museum, and an aquarium. Electric trolleys would whiz them up and down a traffic-free Chestnut Street, Midway of the Fair. City Hall Courtyard would host nightly theatrical performances from around the globe, from Molière to Kabuki.
 A 1967 conceptual plan of Bicentennial Philadelphia, with new structures stretching along the West Bank of the Schuylkill River and clustering around City Hall. | Image courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 At the Schuylkill River, visitors could stroll through a park stretching along the east bank from the Art Museum to South Street, across from a stadium, amusement center, and tourist center on the west bank. Boats and aerial cable cars would convey them to the main fairgrounds at the Centennial site in West Fairmount Park, where Memorial Hall would be joined by a host of new pavilions.
 Despite Bacon’s compelling vision, few concrete steps were taken for several years. In 1964, a preliminary Bicentennial prospectus was submitted to President Lyndon B. Johnson. In 1967, Mayor James Tate and City Council formed the 50-member Philadelphia 1976 Bicentennial Corporation. This would be the primary liaison with the American Revolution Bicentennial Commission (ARBC), the federal organization charged with thematic, location, and funding decisions for a 1976 world’s fair.
 At this point, the first major fissures erupted in the unwieldy and sclerotic planning process captained by Philadelphia’s WASP (White Anglo-Saxon Protestant) oligarchy. Outside voices–people of color, community leaders, and the young–demanded a say. In response, the Bicentennial Corporation established an “Agenda for Action” headed by housing reform activist Catherine Sue Leslie to involve minorities in fair planning.
 A 1969 conceptual study of the 30th Street megastructure concept advanced by the Young Professionals as an alternative to Edmund Bacon’s design. | Image courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 A group of self-declared “Young Professionals” formed an alternative organization called the “Committee for an International Exposition in Philadelphia in 1976.” Members included lawyer Stanhope Browne, Philadelphia Magazine publisher Herbert Lipson, and architects John Andrew Gallery, Richard Saul Wurman, and David Crane. To house the exposition, the Young Professionals proposed a four-mile “megastructure” constructed over the vast Pennsylvania Railroad yards north of 30th Street Station. Extending to the Centennial site in Fairmount Park, the megastructure would include a new transportation hub, with monorails and moving sidewalks to outlying sites. After the fair, the edifice would be adapted to residential and commercial uses. It was assumed the federal government would cover most of the $800 million cost.
 Reaction from the Old Guard was swift and fierce. The Junior Chamber of Commerce mailed 10,000 postcards urging defeat of the plan. Critics stressed the difficulty of obtaining air rights for the rail yards from the Pennsylvania Railroad, facing bankruptcy and planning to merge with another railroad to form the Penn Central Transportation Company. Pushed to the periphery, Bacon withdrew from fair planning. Despite these conflicts, an anxious Mayor Tate ordered the Bicentennial Commission to absorb the Young Professionals and their ideas.
 A conceptual study of the Bicentennial World’s Fair adjacent to the 30th Street megastructure, complete with elevated moving sidewalks and monorails. | Image courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 In September 1969, the Bicentennial Commission traveled to Washington to present “Toward a Meaningful Bicentennial” to the ARBC. While maintaining the 30th Street megastructure as the heart of the international exposition, the final plan added two additional locations. Penn’s Landing and Camden would be developed as the sites of the national celebration, while decaying North Philadelphia would be reborn as a model city with innovative housing and a community college. By now, the price tag had grown to $1.2 billion, with an anticipated 50 million visitors. While the ARBC balked at the size and cost of the megastructure, it recommended Philadelphia as the “international focus point” and host of the celebration. President Richard Nixon told Congress that Philadelphia was “the natural place” for a 1976 world’s fair.
 However, by 1970, the convulsive changes in American society no longer favored a major exposition in Philadelphia. The euphoria and prosperity of the 1950s and early 1960s had yielded to a dystopic atmosphere of recession, racial conflict, environmental crisis, and anti-war protests. Nixon’s Republican administration had pledged to slash domestic spending, curtailing the generous federal funding of the Great Society. Like other American cities, Philadelphia struggled with unemployment, urban violence, and a crumbling infrastructure.
 The Bicentennial Commission’s final plan for the 1976 international exposition, showing the three sites: 1) Penn’s Landing/Camden; 2) North Philadelphia; 3) 30th Street Station. | Image from Toward a Meaningful Bicentennial, Philadelphia 1976 Bicentennial Corporation, 1969
 Even the concept of a world’s fair suffered an existential crisis. The 1964-65 New York fair and Montreal’s Expo ’67 had been popular successes, but financial failures. Writing in the New York Times , critic Ada Louise Huxtable asked, “Is a World’s Fair type Bicentennial festival appropriate in a country racked with social, racial, and environmental agonies?” Her article featured a model of the proposed megastructure with the caption, “Will they come from Boise, Idaho, to look at urban exercises?”
 Faced with multiple conflicts, the planning process disintegrated. The 1970 bankruptcy of Penn Central tied up air rights for the 30th Street rail yards interminably. The Bicentennial Corporation scrambled to find another location, considering the neighborhoods of Byberry and Port Richmond in Philadelphia, Camden, New Jersey, and even temporary islands in the Delaware River. Disgusted by the paralysis, many African American and Latino community leaders boycotted the fair. A growing number of Philadelphians viewed the Bicentennial as a boondoggle, siphoning funds desperately needed elsewhere.
 A 1972 design for the Benjamin Franklin Parkway Bicentennial celebration with fireworks and projections. | Image courtesy of Venturi, Scott Brown and Associates.
 Philadelphia architects struggled to find new concepts for the celebration. Kahn offered a surreal scheme for a Forum of the Availabilities connecting the Court of the Physical Resources and the Court of the Expressions. Robert Venturi and John Rauch proposed turning the Benjamin Franklin Parkway into a giant Gladway. During the day, the Parkway would be a “Street of the World” lined with facades of the Taj Mahal, Kremlin, and other landmarks. At night, it would be transformed with lasers, fireworks, and projections, including an enormous Benjamin Franklin floating above the Museum of Art. Sadly, lack of funding doomed this design, along with another Venturi and Rauch proposal to line the city’s dingy automobile approaches with colorful billboards promoting local attractions from William Penn to soft pretzels. 
 By 1972, the prospects for a great Bicentennial fair in Philadelphia were hopeless. The Nixon administration decided against a single international exposition and allotted smaller grants to individual cities for local celebrations. Mayor Frank Rizzo dismissed the Bicentennial Corporation and created a new corporation called Philadelphia ’76 Inc. to manage the scaled-back event. “Even though the expo is dead,” the new group assured the public, “there will be a celebration in ’76.”
 A 1975 artist’s concept of the Chestnut Street Transitway at Broad Street. | Image courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 Organizers were forced to select a few key projects, financed by $50 million in federal grants and augmented with city, state, and private funds. Foremost among them was a new home for the Liberty Bell, which had resided in Independence Hall for most of its 223-year existence. Designed by Ehrman B. Mitchell and Romaldo Giurgola, the utilitarian Liberty Bell Pavilion would handle the 20 million visitors still expected for the Bicentennial. The relic was transferred from Independence Hall to its new home during the opening minutes of 1976 and would remain there until it was moved to the current Liberty Bell Center in 2003. The Mitchell/Giurgola pavilion was dismantled and sold to an Alaskan developer in 2006.
 The Living History Center, another Mitchell/Giurgola design based on a concept by Raymond Loewy, rose at the northern end of Independence Mall. This museum featured interactive and multimedia exhibits, along with the first IMAX theater on the East Coast. At $11.5 million, the Living History Center was the most expensive Bicentennial project and perhaps its biggest flop. By May 1976, the Philadelphia Inquirer had christened it “our official Bicentennial White Elephant.” It closed in 1978. Most of the structure was demolished for the current WHYY headquarters.
 The Living History Center at 6th and Race Streets was completed in 1976 and designed by Mitchell/Giurgola. | Photo courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 Benjamin Franklin was commemorated with a complex on the site of his home and business on the 300 block of Market Street. Five federal buildings fronting Market were reconstructed, housing a post office, postal museum, and a newspaper office and press. In the courtyard behind them, the outlines of two structures in white steel tubes rose from the center of a park. Designed by Venturi & Rauch, the “ghost houses” represented Franklin’s residence and a nearby print shop, demolished in the 1800s. An underground museum dedicated to Franklin’s life and accomplishments was constructed beneath the park. After a two-year rehabilitation, it reopened in 2013.
 At 2nd and Walnut Streets, the City Tavern, where the Founding Fathers debated and drank, was reconstructed, serving as a restaurant until it closed in 2020. The Graff House, where Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, was rebuilt at 7th and Market Streets, next to the new headquarters for the Balch Institute for Ethnic Studies. The Mummers Museum opened at 2nd Street and Washington Avenue, while the Afro-American Historical and Cultural Museum (today the African American Museum in Philadelphia) opened at 7th and Arch Streets.
 Dilworth Plaza nears completion on March 30, 1976. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 As July 4 approached, Philadelphia underwent a frenzy of housecleaning. The exterior of City Hall was sand-blasted. In June, the Philadelphia Bulletin reported that “the ‘Mud Hole’ west of City Hall has blossomed into Dilworth Plaza in time for the Bicentennial,” with benches and rows of saplings in planters. In one of the few holdovers from the original Bacon plans, Chestnut Street was closed to vehicular traffic for 10 blocks, becoming a pedestrian mall and transitway. It reopened to regular traffic in 2000.
 At Independence National Historical Park, Independence Hall and Carpenters Hall were restored. The First Bank of the United States was also rehabilitated, while the Second Bank of the United States became a Portrait Gallery. The Thaddeus Kosciuszko National Memorial opened to the public. Even the 5th Street subway station received a facelift as “the Gateway to the Liberty Bell.”
 A parade on Benjamin Franklin Parkway celebrating the Bicentennial on July 1, 1976. | Photo courtesy of Special Collections Research Center, Temple University Libraries
 In Fairmount Park, 10,000 new trees were planted. The neglected Japanese House and Garden, today’s Shofuso Japanese Cultural Center , were restored with assistance from the Japanese government. A 14,000-seat performance space named Robin Hood Dell West (today the Highmark Mann Center for the Performing Arts) opened in the West Park, offering free concerts by the Philadelphia Orchestra. The Ben Franklin Parkway became an outdoor festival filled with cultural exhibits, open-air cafes, and live entertainment. The Parkway was adorned with dozens of world flags, a custom that continues to this day.
 All in all, Philadelphia’s Bicentennial was a pleasant affair, even after Mayor Frank Rizzo demanded 15,000 federal troops to combat the hordes of protestors he claimed were waiting to descend on the city. (The two major demonstrations held during the summer were both peaceful.) The celebration's highlight was Freedom Week, which began on June 26 with a Mummers Parade down the Parkway. On July 4, President Gerald Ford addressed the nation from Independence Hall. Two days later, Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip presented Philadelphia with a Bicentennial Bell made in the same foundry as the original Liberty Bell. The bell was hung in the tower of the new Visitor Center at 3rd and Chestnut Streets and remained there until shortly before the center’s demolition in 2014. Today it resides in the Benjamin Rush Garden at 3rd and Walnut Streets.
 The mammoth Bicentennial birthday cake in Memorial Hall. | Image: Sara Lee Deserts
 Despite these successes, the Bicentennial became a bitter disappointment for many Philadelphians. Its reputation was further marred by a mysterious ailment, later called Legionnaires’ disease, which sickened hundreds of American Legionnaires at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel in July, eventually killing 34. The notoriety caused dozens of other conventions to cancel their Philadelphia visits and forced the venerable hotel to close in November. Today it operates as a mixed-use facility called The Bellevue. Between seven and nine million tourists visited Philadelphia in 1976, far below the 20 million originally expected. In the words of one reporter, “the New Atlantis described in 1965 has become the Big Block Party of 1975.”
 Yet, at least it was a Block Party with a humongous Sara Lee birthday cake! The 50-foot high, 25-ton confection was displayed in the Grand Court of Memorial Hall from July 2 to July 4. The eight-tiered, octagonal cake was decorated with panels depicting great events and individuals from American history. Visitors to Memorial Hall during those three days received cupcakes. On July 5, the giant cake was sliced into more than 200,000 servings and distributed to local hospitals and charitable organizations. Sweet, yet ephemeral, those morsels of history may serve as the best metaphor for the transitory pleasure that was the 1976 Philadelphia Bicentennial.
 Tags: Bicentennial Edmund Bacon Frank Rizzo How World's Fairs Changed the Face of Philadelphia Louis Kahn Oscar Sonorov Robert Venturi 
 About the Author
 Thomas H. Keels is a historian, lecturer, and commentator specializing in the history and architecture of the Philadelphia region. He has written or co-authored seven books, including "Forgotten Philadelphia: Lost Architecture of the Quaker City" and "Sesqui! Greed, Graft, and the Forgotten World's Fair of 1926" both published by Temple University Press. His next book, "Sinners and Scandals of Laurel Hill Cemetery," will be released by The History Press in Autumn 2026.

title: Deep Green Dwelling: 1722 Pine Street
author: Stacia Friedman
bodyText:
The most interesting work in an architect's portfolio is not always the commissions they design for clients, but the homes they create for themselves. For Laura Blau and Paul Thompson, founders of BluPath Design and early adopters of the passive house movement in Philadelphia , that meant bringing their historic townhouse at 1722 Pine Street up to sustainable performance standards. Given the home's original sources of energy were candles, wood-burning fireplaces, and coal, this was a major endeavor with myriad of challenges along the way.
 The Pine Street project was completed in 2022 just short of reaching the ultimate goal of passive house certification. However, it was the first time the Philadelphia Historical Commission gave a thumbs up to retrofitting a property listed on the local historic register with passive systems.
 BluPath Design previously completed a number of deeply sustainable projects prior to the construction industry's adoption of energy-saving principles called "passive adjacent," including a gut-rehab of their former home in Bella Vista. The U.S. Green Building Counsel’s LEED for Home Program was launched in 2008. "Passive adjacent is a viable alternative for homeowners who want to improve a property's energy use, air quality, and water efficiency, but cannot meet passive house certification at the initial phase," Thompson explained. In 2025, Thompson was the lead architect of a passive house project in Mendham Township, New Jersey. Blau is currently working on a passive house under construction in Bristol, Pennsylvania. 
 1722 Pine Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The duo's townhouse at 1722 Pine Street was built in 1845 as a single-family home. In 1922, its first major renovation converted it into three apartments above a ground-floor professional office. When Blau bought it 30 years ago her first upgrade was turning the fourth floor deck into an inviting shaded space with a container garden. 
 In 2016, Blau and Thompson eagerly embarked on renovating the entire building and relocated their home and architecture office there. Their plan included converting the first-floor offices to an owners' bi-level apartment and office with upgrades and renovations in all units. Their to-do list included adding a fire sprinkler system, underpinning the basement, air sealing, and fully insulating the building, plus additional bathrooms and larger modern kitchens. They also needed to remove the gas service and convert it into an all-electric building with new mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems.
 1722 Pine Street was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1995, listed as a contributing property within the Rittenhouse-Fitler Historic District . In the beginning, the architects' requests for alterations to 1722 Pine Street presented no problem for the Philadelphia Historic Commission. "Passive house performance required that we replace the historic single-pane double-hung windows at the front and the replacement double-hung windows at the rear," said Blau. "We also wanted to add insulation with a stucco finish to the rear walls to protect the deteriorating structure and waterproof, insulate, and air-tight the porous brick face." This is where the Historical Commission dug in its heels.
 Along with sustainable system upgrades and net-zero retrofits, the Pine Street project included the addition of a roof deck and a kitchen renovation. | Photos: Sam Oberter Photography
 Attention was paid to preserving historic details throughout the process."The Pine Street facade windows are trimmed with a thermal insulation milled to the historic profiles. They were not touched, other than new windows, light brick cleaning, star bolts, and historically designed first-floor shutters," said Blau. "We preserved historic interior details such as restoring historic light fixtures and maintaining original wood floor, trim, and plaster walls wherever possible."
 While their Pine Street property was under construction, Blau and Thompson completed a passive house project in the Italian market which was the first PHIUS+ certified building in the region. "This was a totally new house, allowing for greater freedom in design than most retrofits. It was built on top of a former 7-Up soda warehouse for an Italian Market mercantile family," said Blau. Locals do a double take at this 2,200 square foot, two-story dwelling with double-high windows and sculpted metal roof that provide both light and shade, along with winter warmth and summer coolness in a zero-energy house. The 90-foot-deep warehouse now provides a rare South Philly amenity, a garage, where the homeowner keeps his cars and kit airplanes.
 After some negotiation, Blau and Thompson received permission to replace all of the windows with passive-house-simulated double hung units. However, approval to cover the rear brick took more convincing. They appealed the Historical Commission's decision, using the Environmental Bill of Rights, which guarantees current and future Pennsylvanians the right to clean air and water. That's a steep ask considering the 2025 American Lung Association report ranked Philadelphia among the worst in the nation for air pollution. "The difficulty in renovating a Philadelphia rowhouse for passive house certification is not the historical features, but the fact that it is a renovation of an old masonry building in a dense urban situation," said Thompson. The front of their house faces busy Pine Street, part of the city where finding a parking space is a white knuckle endeavor at best, let alone unloading construction materials.
 BluPath Design converted a garage with passive house design principals on Carpenter Street in the Italian Market. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 The architects' renovation went into overtime. "We thought it would be a couple of years of construction. Not four or five," said Thompson. "We went through multiple electricians, carpenters, and HVAC contractors whose work did not even meet code. The disruption was stressful." As if this wasn't enough, the City lost BluPath's structural drawings and shut work down during the basement underpinning, costing the project another nine months. Due to these and other issues, the Pine Street house is not yet certified. "At this time we are over code, but not to passive house standard," said Blau."None the less, there is not another historic district property that has come as close to certification as ours."
 BluPath Design's other projects included a Colonial-era house built in 1787 with an 1800s addition boasting the first in Society Hill to receive approval from the Philadelphia Historical Commission for a rooftop solar array. "The project was what we call a high-performance retrofit," said Thompson. "Our work included improving the house’s layout, function, and coordinating high-performance building envelope and mechanical systems, while preserving the historic character inside and out." Only from the mews along the side yard can you detect the presence of solar photovoltaic panels on the roof.
 "When wildfires impact others, we have no stink or smoke because of our HEPA-filtered energy-recovering ventilation system works so well," said Thompson. Passive houses typically lower external noise by 50 percent, while providing air quality usually found on mountain tops. "There is almost no dust so I need my cleaning service half the time than I used to, and we no longer have mice!," said Blau. For homeowners who suffer from allergies, this would be reason enough to invest in a retro-fit, if not a new passive house.
 A rendering of BluPath Design's current passive house project in Bristol, Pennsylvania. | Image: BluPath Design
 "We decided to convert our building to passive energy to be competitive in the rental market and to show that it can be done in an historic house," said Blau. "We believe that it is imperative that renovations, especially of historic properties, should be done with long-term benefits in mind, using the latest building science knowledge, while maintaining the historic features that make Philadelphia such a wonderful place to live."
