 While Blau and Thompson are aware of how the high cost of passive house conversions can affect people's decisions, they remain optimistic about its future in Philadelphia."We would love people to understand the long-term value in health, durability, and comfort passive strategies offer," said Thompson. "There are thousands and thousands of rowhouses in Philly that need work. That work should all be to passive house performance, if not certification."
 Tags: historic renovation Passive house Rittenhouse Square row houses Sustainability 
 About the Author
 Stacia Friedman is a Philadelphia freelance writer and visual artist who tried New York and Los Angeles on for size and came home to roost. Her articles have appeared in WHYY’s Newsworks, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The New York Times, Broad Street Review, and Chestnut Hill Local. She loves the city’s architecture, history, and vibrant arts scene.

title: Historical Commission Approves Proposal for 1706-10 Walnut Street
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Philadelphia Historical Commission approved a proposal for new construction at 1706-10 Walnut Street on three vacant lots at its monthly meeting on September 11. The trio of three-story buildings were contributing assets to the Rittenhouse-Fitler Historic District until they were destroyed by arson in May 2020. 
 The Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I) had subsequently deemed 1706-10 Walnut Street imminently dangerous and issued a building permit in August 2020, noting Historical Commission approval of plans that “show that the roof and third story will be demolished. The front facade will be retained. If possible, one dormer should be documented/measured and salvaged to allow for an accurate reconstruction in the future.” L&I records list this permit as “issued.” 
 1706-10 Walnut Street was destroyed by arsonists during the social unrest following the murder of George Floyd by police in Minneapolis, Minnesota. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 A permit for full demolition followed in January 2021, utilizing the same demolition company. The empty parcel was sold to the current owner, a Brooklyn-based LLC, in December 2022. 
 The proposal arrived on Friday's Historical Commission docket as a consent agenda item, having been reviewed by the Architectural Committee, which recommended approval with one modification. According to the Committee meeting minutes, there were conflicting recollections regarding the required documentation and salvage, whether they were done and, if so, where they might currently be. 
 A rendering of the final, approved proposal for 1706-10 Walnut Street. | Rendering: JKRP Architects
 The new construction will consist of two stories of retail space with a rooftop mezzanine, deck, and elevator. The front facade will feature limestone masonry cladding, a cornice, large window glazing, and bronze aluminum details. The height of the two stories will align with the three stories of the neighboring buildings. 
 The Historical Commission did not consider any new nominations to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places , the fourth such meeting in 2026 so far. The Commission’s Committee on Historic Designation, which reviews nominations prior to the full Commission, only meets six times this year, with their meetings often scheduled after the monthly Commission meeting. In addition, more than a half dozen nominations have received continuance requests, some for close to a year.
 The nomination for Piers 38 and 40 South at 775 South Christopher Columbus Boulevard , submitted in October 2021, had been scheduled for review at today’s meeting, but has been continued once again, to next month’s Historical Commission meeting.
 Pier 38 at at 775 S. Christopher Columbus Boulevard. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 At the start of the meeting, Executive Director Jon Farnham added a caution that some applicants and property owners working with the Commission have received fraudulent emails requesting payments from email addresses pretending to be the Historical Commission. He urged any recipients to delete them without replying or responding to attachments or links in them, stating that the Commission never requests payments from applicants or property owners.
 A request to remove the marquee and vestibule walls from the former Boyd Theater at 1910 Chestnut Street was continued once again to next month’s meeting. The theater was built in 1928 by noted Philadelphia theater architects Hoffman & Henon. It was designated historic in 1987 and again in 2008. Its Art Deco auditorium and the rear of the building were demolished in 2015.
 Proposal to remove the former Boyd Theater's marquee and vestibule walls and install a storefront. | Renderings: Ambit Architecture
 The owner of the former Tacony Club at 4619-25 Longshore Avenue received permission for the addition of an elevator tower to repurpose the building for a Veterans Administration housing project. A small connector will be erected between the tower and the rear wall of the building, avoiding any interference with historic window openings. A small vestibule will lead into the connector from the parking lot.
 The College of Physicians of Philadelphia received approval for alterations to two adjacent historic buildings at 2129 Chestnut Street and 15-19 S. 22nd Street. To improve accessibility, they proposed adding a new doorway to each building and connect them via a path through their garden with one doorway replacing a bay window and the other cut into a side facade. The proposal also adds a cooling tower along the rear of the College of Physicians building at 15-19 South 22nd Street, to be screened by an aluminum enclosure, replacing a bank of condensers currently along the north side of the building.
 Tags: Boyd Theater Center City demolition Historical Commission Meeting Report Philadelphia Historical Commission Philadelphia Register of Historic Places redevelopment 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Places Lost: Spring 2026
author: Extant Magazine
bodyText:
Editor’s Note : A version of this story was published in the Spring 2026 issue of Extant , a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 Robinson Building 
 Location : 1020 Market Street
 Built : 1946
 The Robinson Building at 1020 Market Street was one of Philadelphia’s most striking examples of mid-century modern commercial design and a rare surviving work by architect Victor Gruen who widely regarded as the father of the American shopping mall. Completed in 1946, the building was defined by its extraordinary wave-like facade, composed of a five-story concrete slab clad in tiny, variegated purple tiles that curved outward at the cornice and appeared to float above a glass storefront. Beneath decades of grime, the facade has remained remarkably intact.
 In 2016, recognizing its architectural significance, the Preservation Alliance nominated the Robinson Building to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places, and the Philadelphia Historical Commission voted to designate it. That protection proved short-lived. The building’s owners appealed the decision, arguing that designation would hinder redevelopment, and it was ultimately overturned. Despite years of advocacy, including efforts to retain the distinctive faccade as part of future development, the Robinson Building remained vacant and vulnerable.
 At press time, property owner Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment announced a temporary pause on their intention to clear much of the 1000 block of Market Street. These structures, many modest in scale but vital to Market Street’s historic, pedestrian-oriented fabric, are being removed without a defined redevelopment plan in place.
 Once celebrated for its glowing neon signage and sculptural presence on Market Street, the Robinson Building serves as a cautionary reminder that buildings can be lost when preservation is treated as expendable rather than integral to revitalization.
 Photo: Michael Bixler
 Grand Theater 
 Location : 2026 S. 7th Street
 Built : Circa 1870s
 For over a century, the building at 7th Street and Snyder Avenue adapted repeatedly to meet the changing needs of its South Philadelphia neighborhood. Constructed in the late 19th century as the Snyder Avenue Baptist Church, it was converted into the Grand Theater in 1911, screening silent films and adding vaudeville the following year. In 1937, architect William Harold Lee modernized the structure with a stainless-steel marquee and updated interiors, transforming it into a 949-seat neighborhood movie palace. By the 1950s, under the A.M. Ellis Theaters Co., the Grand showed films exclusively and served as a popular local gathering place.
 As entertainment habits shifted, the building changed again. In 1959, its sloped auditorium floor was leveled and the structure converted to retail use. Its ornate facade was concealed beneath aluminum siding, and the Grand Theater became John’s Bargain Stores, followed by a succession of other discount retailers that reflected evolving commercial patterns along Snyder Avenue.
 Even in decline, traces of the theater endured. The removal of siding revealed fading ghost signs: “Grand Theater,” “Talkies” and “Matinee Daily,” reminders of its former life. Today, however, rising development pressures have taken precedence to adaptation. A plan to demolish the building for a five-story, mixed-use project brings an end to the structure that spent decades reshaping itself to remain useful, embedded, and recognizable within its neighborhood. The Grand Theater’s loss reflects how easily neighborhood cultural landmarks can slip from memory once their original use fades, leaving little room for preservation when redevelopment pressures arrive.
 Tags: demolition Historic theaters Midcentury Modern Places Lost Robinson Department Store 
 About the Author
 Extant Magazine is a publication of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia.

title: Advocates Demand the Parker Administration Take Action to Repair and Reactivate Atwater Kent Building
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The City of Philadelphia closed the Philadelphia History Museum at Atwater Kent in 2018. 15-17 S. 7th Street has been sitting vacant and neglected with no plan for reuse in place for eight years. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Alarm bells are being sounded for the deteriorating condition of a historic building adjacent to Independence Mall. Shuttered since 2018, the former home of the Atwater Kent Museum, later known as the Philadelphia History Museum , has racked up multiple violations issued by the Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I) for problems with its fire protection systems, roof drainage, and exterior trash and graffiti.
 15-17 S. 7th Street is owned by the City of Philadelphia. In July, eight leaders of Philadelphia historical and cultural organizations delivered a letter to Mayor Cherelle Parker expressing concern over the state of the building. “It’s a shame that a city that supposedly values its history is letting languish a historic building they own, by an important architect, a block and a half from Independence Hall,” said Paul Steinke, executive director of the Preservation Alliance for Greater Philadelphia and a signer of the letter.
 Along with the Preservation Alliance, the letter was signed by leaders from the Greater Philadelphia Cultural Alliance, Design Advocacy Group, Mother Bethel AME Church, Arch Street Meeting House Preservation Trust, The Athenaeum of Philadelphia, Carpenters’ Company of Philadelphia, and Historic Philadelphia, Inc. 
 The Greek Revival building was the original home of the Franklin Institute. It was designed in 1824 by John Haviland , whose other buildings include Eastern State Penitentiary, the Walnut Street Theater, and the Village of Industry & Art, formerly Dorrance Hamilton Hall and originally the Pennsylvania Institution for the Deaf and Dumb. It was added to the Philadelphia Register of Historic Places in 1956 and the National Register of Historic Places in 1979.
 The former Franklin Institute at 15 S. 7th Street was completed in 1826 and designed by John Haviland. The Atwater Kent Museum took over the building in 1941. | Photo: Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress
 After occupying the building for over 100 years, the Franklin Institute moved to its current location on the Benjamin Franklin Parkway in 1934. Inventor and radio entrepreneur Atwater Kent purchased the 7th Street property and gave it to the City to create a museum dedicated to Philadelphia history.
 The gift had a caveat, however. The deed, dated July 28, 1938, stipulated that “the building shall forever hereafter be known and designated as ‘Atwater Kent Museum,’” and that if the City closed the building to the public, the trustees of the Atwater Kent Foundation may request the return of the building to them.
 Nevertheless, the City closed the museum in 2018 and received permission from the Orphans Court division of the Court of Common Pleas to transfer the collection to Drexel University in 2022 . No mention was made of the building, however.
 In a 2019 public meeting where the transfer plan was presented , Kelly Lee, then the City’s chief cultural officer, was asked about the planned fate of the building. She declared “the building is critically important to the City,” but added, “It’s not up to the City,” referencing the 1938 deed.
 Architectural drawings of 15 S. 7th Street created in 1941 for a Works Progress Administration project under the the Department of Interior's Historic American Buildings Survey office. | Images: Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress
 In 1996, a “declaration of covenants” between the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, represented by the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission, and the City of Philadelphia was signed “to ensure the preservation of the architectural and historical integrity of the Atwater Kent Museum,” defined as “those significant characteristics which qualified the building for entry on the National Register of Historic Places.” It further stipulated that “the grounds around said property will be maintained in the landscaped environment consistent with the historical and architectural character of the property.” Although it committed the City to being responsible for the cost of “maintenance, repair, and administration” of the building, it was limited to a period of 15 years, expiring in 2011.
 After the expiration of that agreement, even as the museum was still operating, L&I citations began accruing for deteriorated and unsafe walls in 2014, that were finally repaired the following year. Currently, it appears that eight violations issued in June 2025 remain unresolved, including missing downspouts and FDC locking caps, untested sprinkler and fire alarm systems, and accumulated trash, weeds, and graffiti.
 The Atwater Kent Foundation, Inc., currently based in Palm Beach, Florida, lists four Kent descendants as its board of directors and is active as a donor of small grants of a few thousand dollars, primarily to non-profit organizations in the locations where the trustees live. Last year, their Philadelphia recipients were the William Way Community Center, American Youth Hostel, and Asian Americans United.
 15 S. 7th Street's ornate gas lamps that flank the 202-year-old building's entryway clash with chain link fencing placed by the Department of Parks and Recreation. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 “I’ve spoken with [Foundation treasurer] Hewlett Kent once,” said Steinke. “He said all the right things about wanting to see the property put to good use.”
 In addition to imploring the City to correct the outstanding L&I violations and prevent further deterioration, the coalition’s letter urged the Parker Administration to establish a process and timeline for determining the building’s future. A few weeks after sending the letter, Steinke reached out to Parker and her staff to follow up on the letter. “I was told they intend to have a meeting about it soon. We expect to hear back,” he said optimistically. “Everyone would like to see it put to good use,” he continued. “From being properly maintained, cleaned up, basic maintenance, up to installing a new use.”
 A spokesperson for the Department of Parks and Recreation, which is the responsible entity for the building according to the Office of Property Assessment, replied in an email to a series of questions regarding the building, stating "PPR has plans underway to address the roof drainage and fire protection systems at the former Atwater Kent Museum. In early August, we power washed the rear garden area and continue to clean the rear area and front steps. We are continuing to assess the remaining repairs." The representative did not address questions about the building's future.
 Tags: abandoned buildings John Haviland Mayor Cherelle Parker Philadelphia History Museum at Atwater Kent 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: Revolutionary Spies: Philadelphia's Role in the Birth of American Espionage
author: David Owen Bell
bodyText:
Special agents, clandestine meetings, covert operations, spy networks, and secret committees. These were among the tools employed against the British before, during, and after their occupation of Philadelphia during the Revolutionary War. The cast of characters includes the Founding Father who planned and executed covert meetings and operations, the spymaster who created a network of informants, the Quaker midwife who risked her life to cross enemy lines, and the tavern keeper who concealed messages in balls of yarn.
 Two main factors contributed to Philly’s ascendance in espionage: the city’s role as defacto capital of the rebellion and the home of the Second Continental Congress, and the British occupation of 1777-78, which presented numerous opportunities for espionage while fostering a culture of suspicion and deception among the divided populace.
 After the first shots of the Revolutionary War were fired at Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts in April 1775, the Second Continental Congress, meeting in Philadelphia that July, noted a store of gunpowder held in the Royal Arsenal in Bermuda. Benjamin Franklin conspired with Robert Morris, then vice-president of the Pennsylvania Committee of Safety, to mount a covert operation designed to acquire the cache of gunpowder.
 "Harbor of St. George, Bermuda from Sugar-Loaf Hill." A wood engraving from 1854 by artist S.E. Brown. | Image: Wikicommons
 On August 14, two ships met off the coast of Bermuda and sent a raiding party of patriots ashore. “An American sailor was lowered into the arsenal through an opening in the roof, and the doors opened from the inside,” according to the CIA dossier, Intelligence in the War of Independence. “The barrels of gunpowder were rolled to waiting Bermudian whaleboats and transported to the American ships. 12 days later, half of the powder was delivered to Philadelphia and half to American forces at Charleston.”
 While the CIA praised Washington’s skill in managing intelligence, agency historians noted a failure that doomed one attempted covert mission. “Hearing independently of the Bermuda powder, Washington dispatched ships to purchase or seize it. Lacking a centralized intelligence authority, he was unaware of the Franklin-Morris success. When Washington’s ships arrived in Bermuda in October 1775, the gunpowder had been gone for two months and British ships patrolled Bermuda waters.”
 The Cradle of Espionage 
 By September, Congress had created the Secret Committee, with Philadelphians Benjamin Franklin, Robert Morris, John Dickinson, and Thomas Willing among its members. Tasked with furtively procuring and distributing military supplies and selling gunpowder to approved privateers, the Secret Committee obtained information about Tory ammunition depots, mounted operations to plunder British supplies, and employed oversea agents to gather intelligence.
 An east prospect of the city of Philadelphia; taken by George Heap from the Jersey shore, under the direction of Nicholas Scull surveyor general of the Province of Pennsylvania / engrav'd by T. Jefferys. 1768. | Image: Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 “It arranged the purchase of military stores through intermediaries so as to conceal the fact that the Continental Congress was the true purchaser [and] used foreign flags to protect its vessels from the British fleet,” noted the CIA. “The Committee kept its transactions secret and destroyed many of its records to assure the confidentiality of its work.”
 In November 1775, Congress created another committee to correspond with “our friends in Great Britain and other parts of the world.” Recognized by the CIA as “America's first foreign intelligence directorate,” the committee “devised codes and ciphers, funded propaganda activities, authorized the opening of private mail, acquired foreign publications for use in analysis, established a courier system, and developed a maritime capability apart from that of the Navy.”
 The Founding Father 
 As one of the committee’s original members, Franklin wasted no time in arranging clandestine meetings with Julien Alexandre Achard de Bonvouloir, a French agent traveling under cover as a Flemish merchant. The meetings, held at Carpenters’ Hall, were to lay the groundwork for French assistance in the war for independence. Similarly, Franklin was key to the “covert action plan” authorized by the Continental Congress on February 15, 1776 to induce Canadians to join the fight for independence from Britain.
 Carpenters' Hall at 320 Chestnut Street. | Photo: Michael Bixler
 Franklin also had a hand in reviewing intercepted Tory and British mail for useful intelligence and disguising leaflets that encouraged Hessian mercenaries to quit the British cause in exchange for free land. His appointment to the American mission in Paris, France in 1776 gave him the base from which to run a flotilla of Irish and French privateers. “Success in intercepting British vessels was so great that the British accused their captains of taking bribes from the Americans to surrender their ships,” according to the CIA.
 “With Franklin’s arrival in France… the vital French mission became an intelligence and propaganda center for Europe, an unofficial diplomatic representation, a coordinating facility for aid from America’s secret allies, and a recruiting station for such French officers as Lafayette and Kalb. On February 6, 1778, the French-American treaty of alliance was signed. On March 30, 1778, Franklin [was] received at the French Court as representative of the United States of America, and on July 7 of that year, Comte d’Estaing’s French fleet cast anchor in the Delaware River. France was in the war. The mission to Paris had succeeded.”
 The Spymaster 
 Months before General William Howe and the British Army took Philadelphia in September 1777, George Washington, the Continental Army Commander in Chief, ordered Major General Thomas Mifflin to establish an intelligence operation in the city. Born in Philadelphia, Mifflin would go on to become the first Governor of Pennsylvania. He recruited Colonel Elias Boudinot to manage a checkpoint and informants on the outskirts of the city and Major John Clark, a native of Lancaster County, to recruit and run a network of agents in Philadelphia to observe and report on British troop strength, movements, war plans, and plundering missions in the countryside.
 Clark set up shop in what is now Newtown Square. He built “a large network of loyal, unassuming men and women, including farmers, merchants, and others in high society who regularly mingled with British officers,” according to the U.S. Army Intelligence Center of Excellence. “Through constant observation, they gathered information on enemy troop movements and numbers, naval maneuvers, artillery emplacements, checkpoints, morale, and supply issues.”
 A portrait of Major General Thomas Mifflin by Charles Willson Peale circa 1783. | Image: Independence National Historical Park, National Park Service
 Clark’s first dispatches to Washington at White Marsh gave a more accurate account of British losses at the Battle of Germantown, which were heavier than previously thought, and plans for attacking Continental Army forts on the Delaware that the British eventually captured, although at greater cost, thanks to Clark. Posing as a disgruntled Quaker angry at the rebels for plundering his home, Clark contacted Howe with an offer to spy for the British, assuring the general that he “was determined to risque my all in procuring him intelligence.” The ploy worked, and Washington instructed Clark to feed Howe false information about troop movements and plans to retake Philadelphia.
 “Washington and Clark developed a plot to alleviate two of the General’s persistent concerns: that Sir Henry Clinton would dispatch part of his army occupying New York to Philadelphia, and that General Howe would learn the true nature of the great disparity in numbers between his army and Washington’s,” David Ritchey wrote in his master thesis for the University of North Texas. The two-prong scheme consisted of misinforming Howe about the number of troops under Washington’s command and feigning preparations for an attack against the British in New York City. “Major Clark’s success in Philadelphia owed to the boldness of his agents and the near perfect concealment of their identities,” Ritchey concluded. “Some of his agents were arrested for various minor offenses, yet the British seem to have never discovered their clandestine employment.”
 A portrait of General William Howe, Commander in Chief of the British Army, by artist Henry Bryan Hall, 1872. | Image: Public Domain
 Clark went on to serve in various Pennsylvania Regiments, retiring in 1783 and returning to York to resume his law practice. Other than a sketch imagining what he may have looked like, “No pictures are available [of] Clark, perhaps because he was such a good spy,” noted the Independence Hall Association.
 Washington communicated directly with some of his agents. After losing to the British at the Battle of Brandywine, he sent Captain Allen McLane a list of 27 questions related to enemy troop strength, movements, and equipment. As the British were preparing to leave Philadelphia in June 1778, Washington dispatched McLane and Major Alexander Clough to enter the city as soon as possible to gather whatever intelligence they could.
 The Quaker Midwife 
 Born in Ireland in 1729, Lydia Darragh and her husband emigrated to Philadelphia in 1763. By the time of the British occupation, she was a mother of five, working as a nurse and midwife, and active in the Quaker community. The Darraghs’ eldest son, Charles, was a lieutenant in the Continental Army, camped at White Marsh late in 1777.
 With his headquarters across the street, General Howe commandeered a large room in the rear of the Darragh home on South 2nd Street for staff meetings, allowing the family to occupy the rest of the house. Accounts of how Lydia spied on the British as they made plans in her parlor appeared in print throughout the 1800s, including American Quarterly Review (1827) , The Child’s History of the United States (1831 ), Godey’s Lady’s Book (1845) , Heroic Women of History (1855) , and Philadelphia Inquirer (1879). The 2025 book, Lydia’s Tale: The Mystery of Lydia Darragh, Irish Quaker, Patriot , by Robert Fanelli, is the most in-depth. 
 A photograph of the Lydia Darragh house at Little Dock Creek and 2nd Street taken between 1850-60 by photographer Frederick De Bourg. | Photo: Prints and Photographs Division, Library of Congress
 The Darraghs’ great-granddaughter, Margaret Porter Newton, gave this version in the May 24, 1891 edition of the Philadelphia Times : “For some time she sent little items of information, gathered from various sources, to General Washington’s camp. These related to the strength of the British forces, etc., and were written by her husband on scraps of paper, which she concealed under the covers of the large mould buttons then worn, covered in the same material of which the coat was made. My grandfather, then a boy of 14, would, with those, make his way to the American camp, give them to his brother, who could decipher them and carry the information to General Washington.”
 Sources differ on Lydia’s role in warning Washington about Howe’s intention to attack the Continental Army at White Marsh. On December 2, 1777, the Darraghs were informed that there would be a meeting in their house and told to go to bed early. They would be called when the meeting was over so they could extinguish the candles and fire. Lydia Darragh eavesdropped on the meeting, and the next day, under the cover story of traveling to a grain mill in Frankford, informed a Continental Army officer of Howe’s plan to attack the encampment at White Marsh.
 ‘Uncorroborated and Implausible’ 
 The CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence dismisses all of Darragh's story as “uncorroborated” and her ruse for passing through enemy lines to buy flour as “implausible,” while casting doubt on her use of a sewing needle packet to hide messages. “Some espionage historians have questioned the credibility of the best-known story of Darragh’s espionage—that she supposedly overheard British commanders planning a surprise night attack against Washington’s army at White Marsh.”
 Reluctantly, I became open to the possibility that Darragh's story was more family legend than fact—until I found a copy of the journal of Colonel Elias Boudinot, the Continental Army intelligence officer. His handwritten manuscript sold at auction for $1,050 in 1891 and soon was transcribed and published. In it, Boudinot confirms the White Marsh story, down to the details of Lydia stopping at the Rising Sun Tavern, pretending to buy flour and concealing her message in a needle kit.
 Boudinot wrote, “I dined at a small Post at the rising Sun abt three miles from the City. After Dinner a little poor looking insignificant Old Woman came in & solicited leave to go into the Country to buy some flour. While we were asking some Questions, she walked up to me and put into my hands a dirty old needle book, with various small pockets in it. On Opening the needle book, I could not find any thing till I got to the last Pocket, Where I found a piece of Paper rolled up into the form of a Pipe Shank. On unrolling it I found information that Genl Howe was coming out the next morning with 5,000 Men—13 pieces of Cannon—Baggage Waggons, and 11 Boats on Waggon Wheels. On comparing this with other information I found it true, and immediately rode Post to head Quarters.”
 An illustration from 1845 depicts Lydia Darragh passing along a warning to Captain Charles Craig of the Continental Army. | From The pioneer mothers of America; a record of the more notable women of the early days of the country, and particularly of the colonial and revolutionary periods by Harry Clinton Green and Mary Wolcott Green, 1912. | Image: Smithsonian Magazine
 Here is where accounts of the story disagree yet again. Darragh's great-granddaughter and others insist that she never met with Boudinot, but actually passed her information directly to Captain Charles Craig, who informed Washington of the impending British assault. Newton also took exception with Boudinot’s description of Lydia. “She was not an old woman, being only forty-eight and… of fair complexion, light hair, very delicate in appearance, and extremely neat.”
 Meanwhile, that same day, December 3, Clark notified Washington that a British sergeant told one on his spies that his troops “had received orders to hold themselves in readiness when called for, and to draw two days provisions.” Should the enemy move, Clark warned Washington, “it will be sudden and rapid."
 Howe launched his attack the following night. The plan was to draw the patriots out into battle, but, having been forewarned, Washington held his reinforced positions. After two days of inconclusive skirmishes, known either as The Battle of Edge Hill or The Battle of White Marsh, the British withdrew. Upon their return to Philadelphia, the Adjutant General questioned Lydia about the night of December 2.
 According to the American Quarterly Review, he concluded, “I know you were asleep, for I knocked at your chamber door three times before you heard me. I am entirely at a loss to imagine who gave General Washington information of our intended attack, unless the walls of the house could speak. When we arrived near White Marsh, we found all their cannon mounted, and the troops prepared to receive us; and we have marched back like a parcel of fools.”
 The Tavern Keeper 
 “In the original 13 colonies, women were generally considered to be domestic, innocent, and well-meaning,” wrote tour guide Dorothy Stanaitis in an essay for the Philadelphia Corporation for Aging. “Their intellect was routinely underestimated, [making] it easy for them to become experts in collecting secret information.”
 We don’t know if Molly Rinker was an expert, but she was considered “frail and incompetent,” according to Stanaitis. "Old Mom," as she was known, ran a tavern in Germantown. Serving drinks to British soldiers in the evening, she regularly overheard information that was useful to the patriots, taking “meticulous and copious notes.”
 Amrican Revolution guerilla fighters unraveling one of Molly Rinker’s hidden yarn messages cast down from Rinker's Rock. | From George Washington, Spymaster by Thomas B. Allen, 2007
 Legend has it that during the day she would sit atop an outcropping of rock in Wissahickon Valley Park, knitting socks for Continental Army troops and occasionally dropping “balls of yarn containing messages about British activities onto the ground below,” according to Barbara McCabe, former newsletter editor for Friends of the Wissahickon. “ Watching from across the creek, the Green Boys of Roxborough, an irregular band of supporters of American independence, would retrieve the messages and relay them to General Washington in Valley Forge.”
 In 1883, John Welsh, a former Fairmount Park Commissioner, had a statue in the likeness of William Penn placed atop Rinker’s Rock. Inscribed “TOLERANCE,” the statue and rock are visible from an offshoot of the Orange Trail and from a trail off Park Line Drive in Mount Airy.
 Allegiance to Laws, Not to a Monarch 
 Of course, the British had their own spies. On June 14, 1776, the Continental Congress established the Committee on Spies and directed it to revise the rules and articles of war. 10 days later, Congress resolved that all persons living in, visiting, or passing through “any of the United Colonies, and deriving protection from the laws of the same, owe allegiance to the said laws.” Therefore, anyone “who shall levy war against any of the said colonies, or be adherent to the king of Great Britain, or other… enemies of the said colonies… giving to him or them aid and comfort, are guilty of treason against such colony.” Congress went on to urge the individual colonies to pass laws to specify punishment for those acts of treason. A resolution passed on August 21 established the death penalty for anyone “who shall be found lurking as spies in or about the fortifications or encampments of the armies of the United States… by sentence of a court martial, or such other punishment as such court martial shall direct.”
 Portrait of Ann Bates. Date and artist unknown. | Image: Public Domain
 Ann Bates was one who got away. A school teacher from Philadelphia, she was married to a soldier in the army of General Sir Henry Clinton, who replaced Howe as Commander in Chief of the British forces. There, she met with John Craig, an agent in Clinton’s espionage network. When Clinton abandoned Philadelphia for New York in June 1778, Ann followed her husband.
 Posing as a peddler, she was allowed into Washington’s camp at White Plains. “As ‘Mrs. Barnes,’ she freely traveled among the American soldiers and camp followers,” wrote Christian McBurney in the Journal of the American Revolution . “She listened in on conversations, located gun emplacements, and counted artillery pieces.”
 Eventually her cover was blown, but she escaped capture. “Later, Ann was sent to escort from Philadelphia to New York City a female secret agent who had helped to turn Benedict Arnold.” Washington had appointed Arnold as Military Governor of Philadelphia, and later put him in command of West Point, but, as you know, that’s another story.
 Tags: American Revolution military Semiquincentennial 
 About the Author
 David Owen Bell writes about environment, history, and maritime subjects. He lives in the Tookany Creek Watershed.

title: National Trust Speaks Out With Its 2026 "Most Endangered Places" List
author: Kimberly Haas
bodyText:
The Presidents House at Independence National Historical Park in 2020. The National Trust for Historic Preservation has included the site on its 2026 America’s 11 Most Endangered Historic Places.| Photo: Michael Bixler
 Since 1988, the National Trust for Historic Preservation has issued an annual list of America’s 11 Most Endangered Historic Places . “All of the sites that have been listed are important because their history matters so much, and they’re having a problem,” noted Rob Nieweg, senior vice president of the National Trust. “It’s an alarm bell, but we intend it as an effort to help solve the problem. The idea is not to demonize them, but to shine a light on the situation.”
 The National Trust is a non-profit organization that supports historic preservation through education, granting, and advocacy. In addition, it owns 27 sites around the country and holds easements on several hundred others, which represent a legal interest in the sites. Although the organization was founded in 1949 by an act of Congress, it is privately funded.
 To date, their annual list has identified nearly 400 sites across the country, both urban and rural, and in every state, as well as Washington, D.C. and U.S. territories.
 To commemorate the nation’s semiquincentennial , the National Trust chose a theme for this year’s list. “We set out to list historical places that have a compelling relationship with the principle that ‘all people are created equal,’” explained Nieweg. “At each of these places you have the history of people who struggled to realize that ideal.” The list includes sites of important events in the history of American women, Blacks, Hispanics, Asians, Natives, and LGBTQ communities. The National Trust staff consulted with local historical organizations to identify the sites.
 The struggles against discrimination and for equal rights are commemorated by many of the sites, including the Ben Moore Hotel in Montgomery, Alabama, a hub of the civil rights movement, the Tule Lake Segregation Center in Modoc County, California, which interred Japanese-American citizens during World War II, and El Corazón Sagrado de la Iglesia de Jesús in Ruidosa, Texas, which served as a community support for Mexican Americans living in a segregated society.
 “We’re committed to telling the full American story. Even places that hold the most complicated stories, we need to confront them, not erase them,” National Trust CEO Carol Quillen, a historian with a Ph.D. from Princeton University, told Hidden City last year .
 Interpretive signage explaining "The Dirty Business of Slavery" in 2020 and after it was removed in 2026 under an order given by the Trump Administration. | Photos: Michael Bixler
 Many of the sites are not in the physical danger of deterioration or demolition that one often associates with the list. “Sometimes the danger is classic, like the roof is falling in, which would cause irreparable harm,” said Nieweg. “This year, these are places where the endangerment is the loss of the meaning of them, because part of the story is not accessible to the public.”
 In Philadelphia, the President’s House, located within Independence National Historical Park, appears on this year’s list. Earlier in the year, a White House executive order caused National Park Service staff to remove the panels that told the history of the nine Black Americans who were enslaved there by George Washington when the house on that site served as the President’s House. To date, only a portion of the panels have been restored following a lawsuit by the City of Philadelphia and a judge’s injunction.
 Two other National Park Service sites are also included this year, representing the struggle for women’s rights and LGBTQIA+ rights. In Seneca Falls, New York, the Women’s Rights National Historical Park was the 1848 site of the first women’s rights convention in the United States. It is one of only roughly a dozen Park Service sites that recognize women’s history , of the more than 400 total sites.
 The Stonewall National Monument in New York City also commemorates a watershed moment for LGBTQ rights–the Stonewall Rebellion in 1969. It began when the Police Public Morals Squad raided the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in Greenwich Village, which led to demonstrations against government bias and mistreatment of sexual minorities. It is widely considered a turning point in the gay rights movement.
 “We want to honor the people who fought for what we have—freedom, equality,” said Quillen. “All Americans deserve to see their history in their built environment.”
 This year, each site on the list will receive a $25,000 grant, as another part of the National Trust’s celebration of the nation’s 250th anniversary. In the case of the three Park Service sites, the grants will be given to an associated “friends” group, which is usually a nonprofit organization founded for the purpose of supporting the site’s preservation.
 Tags: Independence National Historical Park LGBTQIA+ History National Trust Semiquincentennial The President’s House 
 About the Author
 Kimberly Haas is a staff writer for Hidden City Daily. She is a long time radio journalist, both nationally and locally with WHYY and WXPN. In particular, she enjoys covering Philadelphia’s neighborhoods, culture and history, as well as urban sustainability and public policy, in both print and audio.

title: How World's Fairs Changed the Face of Philadelphia: The 1926 Sesquicentennial
author: Thomas H. Keels
bodyText:
40 years after the 1876 Centennial , one of its originators felt the time had come for his hometown to host a second international exposition. In 1876, John Wanamaker was a 39-year-old merchant whose new emporium, the Grand Depot, had prospered thanks to the millions of world’s fair visitors. Wanamaker was also a key player on the Centennial Board of Finance, ensuring the fair’s success through his drive and determination.
 In 1916, the 78-year-old Wanamaker was an iconic figure in American commerce with a net worth approaching $100 million. His emporium, housed since 1911 in an elegant Italianate palazzo designed by Daniel H. Burnham (Director of Works at the 1893 Columbian Exposition in Chicago) was one of America’s great department stores.
 The official poster by Dan Smith for the Sesqui-Centennial Exposition published as a broadside by the Philadelphia Inquirer in 1926. | Image: AbeBooks
 Wanamaker published an open letter in August 1916 to Philadelphians in local newspapers, scolding them for doing nothing to advance the city since 1876. “Are we to wait for 1976 to show our hand again in another Centennial?” he asked. “Why not celebrate the century and a half in 1926, and begin to get ready now?” In January 1917, a resolution was introduced in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives to create a Sesqui-Centennial Commission. (Sesqui is a Latinate term for “and a half,” making a sesquicentennial a “century and a half.”)
 America’s entry into the Great World War postponed Wanamaker’s world’s fair campaign. However, in 1921 the Sesqui-Centennial Exhibition Association (SCEA) was incorporated, consisting of 100 of Philadelphia’s foremost citizens. The 83-year-old Wanamaker was named honorary SCEA chairman.
 Paul Philippe Cret’s 1920 design for a Fairmount Parkway Sesquicentennial, stretching from Logan Circle to new Museum of Art and beyond. | Image courtesy of Thomas H. Keels
 Civic leaders assumed the Sesqui-Centennial would be staged on the new Fairmount Parkway (renamed the Benjamin Franklin Parkway in 1937) and adjacent areas of Fairmount Park. The great boulevard running diagonally from City Hall to the Fairmount Plateau had opened officially in October 1918. The “Sesqui” would transform the undeveloped roadway into Philadelphia’s answer to the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in Paris. In 1920, Parkway co-designer Paul Philippe Cret unveiled preliminary Sesqui plans. Cret proposed a monumental entrance to the fairgrounds at Logan Circle, which by 1926 would be framed by magnificent civic structures, including the Free Library of Philadelphia.
 Above Logan Circle, the Parkway would be lined with temporary pavilions. After the exposition, these would be replaced with permanent structures housing government offices and civic institutions. The Parkway would terminate in a magnificent museum of art atop the Fairmount Plateau. Beyond the museum, new roads through East Fairmount Park would lead to a stadium and an aviation field. An elegant bridge across the Schuylkill River would guide visitors past fountains and gardens to a string of state and foreign pavilions leading to the Zoological Gardens and the Sesquicentennial grounds.
 Cret’s visionary plan won the support of the Fairmount Park Commission, the City Art Jury, and most of the city’s newspapers. The Bulletin opined that Philadelphia would be reborn as a “City Beautiful, as a by-product of the Exposition, which will return dividends on the investment long after the great fair shall have passed into history.”
 Sadly, this vision sank in the mire of Philadelphia politics after John Wanamaker died in December 1922 at the age of 84. While the Mayor and City Council battled for control of the stalled project, disgusted civic leaders resigned from the SCEA. The Sesqui got a new lease on life when Receiver of Taxes W. Freeland Kendrick was elected mayor in November 1923. Kendrick had himself elected president of the moribund SCEA, which he packed with political allies.
 The Sesqui triumvirate: U.S. Congressman William S. Vare, Mayor W. Freeland Kendrick, and City Council President Charles Hall visit the White House in 1924 to procure Sesqui funding. | Photo courtesy of Thomas H. Keels
 Kendrick confirmed that Philadelphia would host the Sesqui-Centennial from June to December 1926. He also announced that the fair location had been moved from the Parkway to League Island Park, situated at the tip of South Philadelphia above the Navy Yard. This region had long been known as the Neck . League Island Park had been partially laid out by the Olmsted Brothers from 1912-13, but its development was abandoned during World War I.
 Many Philadelphians were stunned by the move. In 1922, a council of designers had rated the Neck 13th out of 13 possible locations for the Sesqui, while giving Fairmount Park and the Parkway top marks. The Neck was Philadelphia’s most remote, isolated, and impoverished district–a marshland dotted with farms, pigsties, and trash heaps. Only one paved road, South Broad Street, connected it to City Hall, three and a half miles north.
 However, the Neck was in the heart of Congressional District No. 1, represented by U.S. Congressman William S. Vare, Philadelphia’s undisputed political boss. As head of the Republican machine in what was then a solidly Republican city, Vare controlled nearly every elected official and civil servant in Philadelphia, including its mayor. By moving the Sesqui to the Neck, Kendrick was delivering thousands of jobs to his patron’s constituents, as well as a comprehensive infrastructure.
 Vare would profit handsomely from the Sesqui move. His construction and contracting businesses would receive lucrative contracts to prepare the fairgrounds and build its structures. Any other contractors who hoped to win contracts would have to pay Vare handsomely to play in the Sesqui game. Vare could either lease or sell his extensive real estate holdings in the Neck to the fair management at inflated prices.
 The actual Sesquicentennial layout in League Island Park, stretching from Oregon Plaza to the Philadelphia Navy Yard. | Image courtesy of Thomas H. Keels
 Plans were drawn up for a 1,000-acre fairground between Packer Avenue and the Navy Yard. Architects began to create fantastic designs for the first postwar World’s Fair in America, with an expected attendance of 50 million. At Oregon Avenue north of the main entrance, an 80-foot-tall replica of the Liberty Bell would span South Broad Street as a ceremonial gateway. At night, the 26,000 multi-colored bulbs studding its metal skin would turn it into a glimmering beacon visible as far north as City Hall.
 The second wonder of the Sesqui would be the 175-foot-tall Tower of Light, a gigantic Art Deco spire topped by the “Light of Independence,” a searchlight capable of producing a beam visible 70 miles away. Located between the two main exhibition halls, the tower would soar above the Forum of the Founders, the central court of the Sesqui.
 The event's permanent legacy would include a new stadium capable of seating 100,000, designed by Simon & Simon. A modern sports arena had been a major priority for Philadelphia since the city lost the Army-Navy football game because Franklin Field was too small for the crowds.
 Yet, before ground could be broken for a single structure, the City had to truck in nearly two million cubic yards of fill dirt to bolster the swampy soil of League Island Park. Not only did this cause further delays to a construction program already far behind schedule, but it rendered the Sesqui effectively insolvent.
 A postcard showing an architect’s concept of the 175-foot-tall Tower of Light, with the Light of Independence turning night into day for miles around. | Image courtesy of Thomas H. Keels
 By the end of 1925, the SCEA had received no funds for the Sesqui from either the federal or the state government. The City of Philadelphia had already spent over $10 million on the fair, mostly on landfill. An 11th-hour bond drive raised $3 million, enabling construction to begin on major structures. However, many attractions were scrapped, while corners were cut on the survivors. By early 1926, the only structure close to completion was the Sesqui Stadium. The Philadelphia Inquirer published an investigative report which charged that the arena was shoddily built and possibly unsafe.
 Elsewhere, civic projects meant to transform Philadelphia were also far from completion. At Logan Circle, the central branch of the Free Library would not open until 1927. The Museum of Art atop the Fairmount Plateau was even more incomplete and would not open its doors until 1928. Meanwhile, construction was accelerated on the new Delaware River Bridge at Vine Street.
 During early 1926, Philadelphia poured millions of dollars into round-the-clock construction so that something resembling a world’s fair would be ready on May 31, the Sesqui's opening day. Despite this blitz, the sparsely attended inaugural parade marched under a giant Liberty Bell at Oregon Plaza still swathed in scaffolding.
 Only two minor exhibits were open for business. The Sesqui’s vast exhibition halls were empty except for workmen installing displays. Ground hadn’t been broken for many smaller structures, including the few foreign pavilions allowing the Sesqui to call itself an international exposition. A thunderstorm on opening day turned the unpaved walkways into bogs capable of sucking shoes off the feet of visitors. Despite rushed construction on additional streetcar lines, the Broad Street trolley was the only mass transit in operation, resulting in lengthy waits to return to Center City.
 The Sesqui inaugural parade passes beneath a giant Liberty Bell still swathed in scaffolding at Oregon Plaza on Opening Day, May 31, 1926. | Photo courtesy of Thomas H. Keels
 Over 200,000 Shriners traveled to Philadelphia for the Sesqui opening, which had been moved up 24 hours to coincide with their annual convention. They were the guests of Mayor Kendrick, a former Imperial Potentate of the Mystic Shrine. After three days of searching in vain for any amusements, they returned home and spread the word that "Kendrick’s Karnival" was a bust. It was a public relations fiasco from which the Sesqui never recovered. Fewer than 300,000 people visited the fair during its first full month instead of the anticipated five to eight million.
 No single structure epitomized the unfulfilled promise of the Sesqui more than the Tower of Light. By mid-July, all that had been constructed of the Art Deco marvel was a steel skeleton resembling a fire ranger’s tower. It had cost over $365,000 to bring the tower to this rudimentary stage when the City ran out of funds to complete the project. The Light of Independence consisted of one small beacon tacked on top.
 The struggling Sesqui was further hampered by one of Philadelphia’s wettest summers, with rain on 107 of the fair’s 184 days of operation. Before long, its shoddy infrastructure began to crumble. During a torrential storm on July 4, workmen had to cut a huge hole in the flimsy wooden roof of the Palace of Agriculture and Foreign Exhibits. With its inadequate gutters and rainspouts overwhelmed, several tons of water collected on the flat surface, raising fears of a collapse. Tons of water cascaded on the exhibits below, destroying them instantly.
 By August, most of the attractions were open for business, and the Sesqui began to resemble a real international exposition. Yet, after the dazzling, rococo splendor of earlier world’s fairs, the general consensus was that the Sesqui was the dreariest exposition in memory. Only a handful of structures showed architectural merit. Among them were Ralph Bencker’s Pennsylvania State Building, a modernist masterpiece, and the Persian Building, modeled after the King’s Mosque in Isfahan by Philadelphia architect Carl Augustus Ziegler.
 A view of the High Street of 1776, one of the few successful exhibits at the Sesqui, looking southwest toward the Sesqui Stadium. | Image courtesy of Thomas H. Keels
 One of the few popular and profitable exhibits was the High Street of 1776, an imaginative recreation of a Revolutionary-era Market Street lined with reconstructions of historic, but lost buildings. This exhibit was created by the Sesqui-Centennial Women’s Committee , socially prominent women who could ignore the dictates of the Vare Organization. A team of architects headed by Richardson Brognard Okie lined the 800-foot-long byway with replicas of President Washington’s House, Franklin’s Print Shop, and the Jefferson Declaration House.
 The High Street of 1776 exhibit attracted an average of 5,000 visitors a day. Costumed docents explained the historical significance of each building, while a stream of pageants and other events entertained visitors. High Street left one of the few positive legacies of the Sesqui by jumpstarting the historical preservation movement in Philadelphia. Its impact lives on in the “Colonial Chain” of historic houses in Fairmount Park, the Philadelphia Society for the Preservation of Landmarks, and the postwar development of Society Hill.
 When the Sesqui closed on December 31, 1926, it had become infamous as “the flop heard round the world.” It attracted only 4.6 million paying visitors, versus eight to nine million paying visitors for the Centennial. This despite the fact that the U.S. population had nearly tripled, from an estimated 45 million in 1876 to 117 million in 1926.
 It was also an expensive flop. The official cost of the Sesqui was $33 million, with a loss of $10 million. Adjusted for simple inflation, that equates to a 2025 outlay of $585 million and a loss of $177 million. However, when the higher cost of labor is considered, the modern-day cost of the Sesqui mushrooms to $2.4 billion, and the loss to $714 million. Given the Sesqui’s chaotic and byzantine bookkeeping, and the Kendrick administration’s efforts to conceal expenses, its actual cost may have been three to five times the official figures.
 Top : The Pennsylvania State Building designed by Ralph Bencker, one of the few buildings of architectural merit at the Sesqui. Bottom : A view of Carl A. Ziegler’s Persian Building and the Cuban pavilion (architect unknown), along Edgewater (today Edgewood) Lake. | Images courtesy of Thomas H. Keels
 A 1927 auction of structures barely made a dent in the Sesqui debt. Buildings were sold for pennies on the hundreds of dollars. The $365,000 Tower of Light–now known as the “Light that Failed”–fetched $1,050. The giant Liberty Bell, which had cost over $100,000, was knocked down for $60. A few buildings were relocated and repurposed. Yet, most of the Sesqui was either dismantled for its raw materials or smashed into pieces. Piles of rubble from demolished Sesqui palaces would remain local landmarks for the next decade. 
 The one permanent legacy of the fair, the Sesqui Stadium, was renamed Municipal Stadium. The rarely used bowl became infamous as one of Philadelphia’s biggest white elephants. In 1936, it began to host the Army-Navy football game and became the favored site for the game until 1980, when it moved to the adjacent Veterans Stadium.
 Beyond the fairgrounds, the Sesqui accelerated the development of Philadelphia’s highway network and automotive infrastructure. One of the few Sesqui-related projects to be completed on time was the Delaware River Bridge, renamed the Benjamin Franklin Bridge in 1955. Opening on July 1, 1926, the bridge was an immediate success, carrying over 30,000 vehicles a day. Today, it handles upwards of 100,000 vehicles daily.
 Yet, the fair’s exorbitant costs did more to hinder Philadelphia’s development than to advance it. To pay off Sesqui debt, the City transferred funds allotted to upgrading its antiquated water system and developing rapid transit lines to the fast-growing northeast and northwest districts. The Sesqui is a major reason why Roosevelt Boulevard remains one of the most congested and dangerous thoroughfares in America and why the space originally designated as the Museum of Art subway station is now its Vaulted Walkway.
 Municipal Stadium in 1937. | Photo courtesy of the Athenaeum of Philadelphia
 In South Philadelphia , Sesqui-fueled infrastructural improvements led to limited growth below Pattison Avenue, but this was killed by the Great Depression. The Neck would not be fully developed until the 1950s, when construction of the Walt Whitman Bridge and the extension of the Schuylkill Expressway spurred creation of Packer Park and other residential districts. Today, the only remnant from the Sesqui is its former police headquarters, now re-purposed as the entrance to the new FDR Park Welcome Center . While the cornerstone for the American Swedish Historical Museum on Pattison Avenue was laid during the Sesqui, the building was not dedicated until 1938.
 After being renamed John F. Kennedy Stadium in 1964 , the crumbling Sesqui/Municipal Stadium hosted numerous rock concerts (including Live Aid in 1985) before being demolished in 1992. Today, its former site holds Xfinity Mobile Arena and parking lots, adjacent to the rest of the South Philadelphia Sports Complex (Citizens Bank Park and Lincoln Financial Field). So, the next time you’re stuck in traffic for hours trying to get to a Flyers game or a Dave Matthews Band concert, blame the Sesqui!

 About the Author
 Thomas H. Keels is a historian, lecturer, and commentator specializing in the history and architecture of the Philadelphia region. He has written or co-authored seven books, including "Forgotten Philadelphia: Lost Architecture of the Quaker City" and "Sesqui!
